t: Article 90 — Introduction: how this Code is set up
x: Article 90 is the front door of the Code. Before any wiring rule, it answers four questions: why the Code exists, what it covers, how the book is arranged, and who enforces it. • 90.1, purpose: practical safeguarding of people and property from the hazards of using electricity. Followed with proper maintenance, the Code gives an installation essentially free from hazard — but it is a safety floor, not a design manual, and it does not promise the most efficient or convenient system. • 90.2, scope: the Code covers premises wiring in buildings, yards, parking areas and similar locations. It does not cover most utility-owned generation and distribution, ships, railway rolling stock or mining equipment. • 90.3, arrangement: Chapters 1 through 4 apply generally. Chapters 5, 6 and 7 cover special places, equipment and conditions, and they supplement or modify the general chapters. Chapter 8 stands apart — the general chapters reach it only where a Chapter 8 rule points back. Chapter 9 holds the tables, and the annexes explain; they do not require. • 90.4, enforcement: the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) enforces the Code and approves equipment and installations, and can grant special permission where the Code allows it. • 90.5, how rules are written: 'shall' is mandatory, 'shall be permitted' allows an option, and Informational Notes only explain — a note by itself is not a requirement. Most code arguments are really Article 90 arguments: does this book even apply here, who gets to decide, and can a note fail you? Article 90 settles those questions before they turn into a fight at the inspection. Start here when the question is really about whether the Code applies at all, who enforces it, or whether a note in the book is a requirement. On a Florida job the permit date picks the edition: a permit applied for in November 2026 is inspected to NEC 2020 under the FBC 8th Edition (see the Florida note below). And when a handbook, a brochure or this app reads a rule one way and the inspector reads it another, the AHJ's reading is the one your job is judged by (90.4). Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. NEC 2023 takes effect in Florida with the FBC 9th Edition for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The trap answer quotes an Informational Note as if it were a rule. Notes explain and point to other material; they cannot create a requirement, and they cannot override a 'shall' (90.5). The other trap: calling the Code a design manual. It is a safety floor (90.1). Arguing an Informational Note as a requirement — or waving off a 'shall' rule because a note seemed to soften it (90.5). Designing the utility side of a service to the NEC — utility-owned generation and distribution sit outside the coverage in 90.2. Installing equipment the AHJ has not approved, or doing work that needs special permission without the AHJ's written grant (90.4). Applying the general chapters straight into a Chapter 8 communications job — Chapter 8 stands apart unless its own rule points back (90.3). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Purpose of the Code
x: 90.1 states the Code's one job: the practical safeguarding of persons and property from hazards arising from the use of electricity. • Compliance with the Code, together with proper maintenance, results in an installation that is essentially free from hazard. • It does not promise the most efficient or most convenient system. The Code sets the safety floor; efficiency, convenience and good design are built above it. • The Code is not a design manual, and it is not an instruction manual for untrained persons. It states the minimum an installation must meet, not the best installation that can be built. Every rule in the book traces back to this sentence. Electricity is useful precisely because it carries energy, and that energy starts fires and kills quietly when it escapes its path. The purpose clause is also the tie-breaker: when two readings of a rule are possible, the reading that protects people and property is the one the Code intends. When a plan meets the Code but works poorly, that is a design problem, not proof the Code failed. When a shortcut works but is hazardous, the Code still controls. Build to the safety floor first, then to good design above it. On a Sharma rough-in, that means the floor is not negotiable: if a builder asks to drop a required GFCI or a required circuit to save money, the answer is no — 90.1 is the reason. Upgrades above the floor, like extra receptacles or a larger service, are the customer's choice; the floor is not. The trap answer says the Code is a design manual that guarantees an efficient, convenient installation. 90.1 says the opposite: it is a safety standard. Compliance gives an installation essentially free from hazard — not necessarily efficient or convenient — and the Code is not a design manual or an instruction book for untrained persons. Work installed from a video or a handbook instead of the adopted Code, red-tagged where it conflicts with the NEC. 'It works fine' offered as the defense for a missing required protection — operation is not compliance, and the correction notice stands. A required protection value-engineered out at the customer's request; the AHJ cites the rule, not the customer's preference. A design choice enforced as if it were a Code rule — or a Code rule waived as 'just design.' The floor and the design above it are different things. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 90.1: Article 90 was reshuffled. 90.1 is now the scope of Article 90 itself, and the old purpose statement moved into 90.2, Use and Application. The purpose statement that used to be 90.1 now sits in 90.2, Use and Application, along with what the code covers and doesn't cover. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Scope — what is covered and what is not
x: This section lists the kinds of installations the Code covers and the kinds it does not. • Covered: premises wiring in buildings and structures, yards, parking areas and similar locations, and the customer side of the service point. • Not covered: most utility-owned generation and distribution installations, ships, railway rolling stock, and mining equipment. • Covered only with special permission: installations where the Code applies solely with special permission from the authority having jurisdiction. Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in a house are handled by the building code, not by this article. Every argument about whether a rule applies starts at the scope line. It keeps a crew from wiring utility plant to premises rules — and from skipping Code rules on customer wiring by calling it 'utility side.' It also keeps the NEC out of work another code owns, like house smoke alarms under the Florida Building Code. The line that matters most in the field is the utility line: work on the customer side of the service point is generally Code work; the utility's own system generally is not. If a job sits in the not-covered or special-permission area, stop and get the AHJ's position before wiring it. On a Sharma service upgrade in Ocala, the mast, the panel and every branch circuit are Code work. The utility's drop and its side of the meter are the utility's — when a homeowner asks the crew to move a utility line 'while you're here,' that is outside the scope, and outside what Sharma can sign for. House smoke alarms are FBC-Residential R314 and CO alarms are R315 / F.S. 553.885 — building code, not NEC. Existing items L-094, L-095 and L-096 carry those citations; their subsection details carry UNVERIFIED flags in v1 and are not restated here. The trap answer puts house smoke and carbon monoxide alarms under the NEC because they are electrical. In Florida they are building-code items — FBC-Residential R314 and R315. The mirror trap: assuming a utility's generation and distribution plant is Code-covered just because it carries electricity. Customer-side service wiring installed to utility practice instead of the Code, red-tagged at inspection. Work started on a special-permission installation before the AHJ's written permission was in hand. Rough-in failed for smoke alarms placed by NEC habit instead of the FBC-Residential R314 layout on the approved plans. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: How the chapters are arranged
x: The Code is built in layers, and the layer a rule sits in decides how it applies to your job. • Chapters 1 through 4 apply broadly to electrical installations: definitions, requirements for installations, wiring and protection, wiring methods and materials, and equipment for general use. • Chapters 5, 6 and 7 cover special occupancies, special equipment and special conditions. They add to or modify the general chapters — read a special rule together with the general rule it changes. • Chapter 8 covers communications systems and stands apart: the general chapters apply to it only where a Chapter 8 rule points back to them. • Chapter 9 holds the tables the rest of the book uses. • The annexes at the back are explanatory, not requirements. Electricians lose time and fail inspections by reading the wrong layer of the book. A rule in Chapter 5 or 6 exists because the general rule was not enough for that occupancy or that machine; a rule in Chapter 8 exists because communications wiring is not power wiring. Knowing which layer governs tells you which rule the inspector will cite — and which one wins when two rules speak to the same point. A Sharma rough-in on a Marion County house is Chapters 1 to 4 work: Article 100 definitions, 210 branch circuits, 334 NM cable, 406 receptacles. The same crew's next job, a small medical office build-out, pulls in Chapter 5: Article 517 adds its own grounding and receptacle rules on top of the general ones, and where 517 and the general chapters differ, 517 governs that room. The Cat 6 runs the low-voltage contractor pulls on both jobs sit in Chapter 8 and follow Article 800, not the power-wiring chapters. Two traps. First, treating an annex example as a requirement an inspector can cite — the annexes are informative only. Second, applying Chapters 1 through 4 wholesale to a communications installation: Chapter 8 stands alone, and the general chapters reach it only through a specific reference from a Chapter 8 rule. Installation built to an annex example where the annex and the Code text differ — the inspector cites the article, not the annex. Pool wiring (Article 680, Chapter 6) installed to the general Chapter 3 rules only, missing the special-equipment rules that modify them. Communications cable installed under Chapter 3 power-wiring rules where Chapter 8 carries its own rule for the work. Patient-care space in a medical office wired to plain Chapter 2 rules without the Chapter 5 (Article 517) additions. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Enforcement and the AHJ
x: The authority having jurisdiction — the AHJ — is the organization, office or individual responsible for enforcing the Code and approving equipment, materials and installations. On Florida work that is usually the local building department and its electrical inspectors. • The AHJ interprets the rules and decides how they apply to a local situation. • The AHJ approves equipment and installations, and enforces correction of work that does not comply. • Where the Code allows an alternative, the AHJ can grant special permission — its written consent. An inspector's reading on your job carries weight that a handbook, an app or a study guide does not. Somebody has to make the final call on a real building, in a real county, on a real Tuesday. The AHJ is that call. One accountable local authority keeps enforcement consistent from job to job, settles the argument between the plans and the field, and gives the public one door to knock on when an installation is unsafe. If a rule could be read two ways on a real job, ask the AHJ before rough-in, not at inspection. Write down who said what and when. The 210.8(F) protection question for outdoor HVAC outlets has been enforced differently by different Florida AHJs, so on a service change Sharma gets the local inspector's position first instead of arguing it at the final. This book is a reference aid; the AHJ and the printed NEC govern. Local amendments and AHJ positions always win over a statewide summary, especially on items where enforcement has varied, such as GFCI protection for outdoor HVAC outlets under 210.8(F). The trap is treating a study guide, a handbook commentary or this app as the authority. None of them enforces anything. The AHJ enforces the Code as adopted locally, and where the Code permits an alternative method, only the AHJ's special permission makes it legal on your job. Work covered up before a required inspection; the AHJ requires it opened up for reinspection. An alternative method installed on a verbal 'the inspector will be fine with it' — no special permission on file, cited at final. Unapproved substitute equipment swapped in after the approved submittal; the AHJ rejects gear it has not approved for the use. A handbook commentary argued against the inspector's reading — the correction notice stands until the AHJ changes it. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 90.4: The enforcement section was broken into separate subdivisions, and a new informational note sends readers to Annex H for help setting up an inspection program. The inspector's powers didn't change. 90.4 is now split into lettered subdivisions, so each power is easy to find: interpretations (90.4(B)), alternative methods (90.4(C)), products not yet available (90.4(D)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Mandatory rules, permissive rules, and explanatory material
x: The Code is written in three kinds of language, and 90.5 tells you how to read each one: • Mandatory rules — 90.5(A): the words shall or shall not. These must be followed; there is no judgment call. • Permissive rules — 90.5(B): the words shall be permitted or shall not be required. These allow an option; they never require it. • Explanatory material — 90.5(C): Informational Notes and other material that explains a rule or points to other material. A note by itself does not create a requirement you can be failed for, and you cannot use a note to override a rule. When a rule itself references another standard, that reference is part of the rule. The enforceable requirement always lives in the rule text, or in another standard the rule points to — never in the note. Reading a note as a rule, or a permission as a requirement, costs real money and can cost safety. Crews have torn out compliant work because someone treated an Informational Note like a shall, and jobs have stalled while a note was argued as if it could cancel a rule. Knowing which kind of language is speaking tells you what can be enforced, what is optional, and what is only there to help. When someone cites a note as the reason for a red tag or a change, ask for the rule section behind it. Notes are where good explanations live, but the enforceable requirement is always in the rule text or in another standard the rule points to. On a Marion County service call, a homeowner insists a note under a receptacle rule means his garage conversion does not need GFCI protection. The note explains the rule; it does not repeal it — the shall in the rule text decides, and the receptacles get protected. The flip side on the same job: where the Code says a method shall be permitted, nobody can fail you for choosing it just because they prefer another method. The trap answer starts with “the Informational Note requires…” — a note never requires anything. The second trap reads “shall be permitted” as “shall”: a permissive rule allows the method, it does not force it onto every job. Red tag written citing only an Informational Note, with no rule section behind it. Compliant work torn out and redone because a note was treated as a requirement it never made. A permitted method refused on site as “not allowed,” adding cost the Code never required. An explanatory annex table used as a mandatory design value the AHJ never adopted. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 90.5: When the code mentions another standard without giving an edition year, that reference now means the latest edition of that standard. New in 90.5(C): a reference to another standard with no date means that standard's latest edition. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Formal interpretations
x: Where there is a genuine dispute about what a Code rule means, there is a formal process for getting an official interpretation from NFPA. That process is slow and is meant for real disagreements about the text, not for settling a question on one job. One job's question goes to its AHJ. • A formal interpretation is NFPA's official reading of the text itself, reached through its committee process. It speaks to the rule, for everyone. • It does not decide your permit, your inspection or your job, and it does not arrive on a job's schedule. • A magazine article, a handbook commentary or a forum post is not a formal interpretation, however confident it sounds. For the job in front of you, the AHJ interprets how the rule applies (90.4), and that reading governs the job. One official channel keeps one meaning for the text. Without it, the same rule would read differently in every county, and a contractor could shop for the interpretation he likes. The formal process settles the words themselves, while the AHJ system keeps day-to-day calls fast and local — and it stops unofficial opinions from quietly becoming 'the Code' on a job. You will almost never use this section in the field. Know that it exists so you do not treat a magazine article or a forum post as an official interpretation. If an inspector in Marion County reads a rule differently than you do, that is not a 90.6 fight: ask the AHJ, get the reading in writing when the job turns on it, and build to it. The trap answer sends a question about one job to NFPA for a formal interpretation. Wrong road: formal interpretations settle genuine disputes about the text itself, slowly, and for everyone. The question on the job in front of you goes to its AHJ, whose interpretation governs that job (90.4). Installation built to a magazine article's reading of a rule after the AHJ read it the other way — corrected to the AHJ's interpretation. No AHJ interpretation on file for a disputed detail the whole job was built around. A forum printout offered at final inspection as the authority for a noncompliant detail — rejected; it is not an interpretation. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Examination of equipment for safety
x: This section explains how equipment gets examined for safety, normally by being tested and listed or labeled by a qualified testing laboratory. It is the background for the approval, listing and labeling language used all through Article 110. Equipment the AHJ accepts has normally been through that kind of third-party check. • Listed — the product appears in the testing organization's published list of items it has evaluated. • Labeled — the organization has attached its label after checking samples of the product. • Approved — acceptable to the AHJ (110.2). Listing and labeling are how approval is normally shown. The point of the system: somebody qualified, who does not sell the product, has tested it against a safety standard before it reaches your job. Untested gear can fail in ways nobody can see on a ladder: insulation that breaks down, parts that run hot, an enclosure that does not contain a fault. Third-party examination catches those defects before the equipment is hanging on a customer's wall, and it gives the AHJ something definite to approve instead of an opinion about a brand. Look for the listing mark and the label when gear arrives. If a piece of equipment has no mark and no paperwork, raise it before it is installed, not after it is wired. On a Sharma job, check the Siemens gear (S-02) at delivery: mark on the equipment, label readable, instructions in the box. A familiar brand is not the check — the specific piece of equipment still has to be listed and used within its listing. Sharma standard gear is Siemens (S-02). A listing problem is not solved by a familiar brand name — the specific equipment still has to be listed and used within its listing. The trap is treating a famous brand name, or a seller's assurance, as proof of safety. The 90.7 system runs on examination by a qualified testing laboratory: listed, labeled, and approved by the AHJ. No mark and no paperwork means the question goes up before the gear goes in — not after the inspection fails. Panelboard installed with no listing mark and no label — no basis for approval. Equipment on the wall before anyone checked its label; the label shows a use it is not listed for. Field-assembled gear with paperwork 'at the office' that never reaches the job file. Listed equipment installed against its instructions — the listing no longer covers it (110.3(B)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Planning for future expansion
x: Section 90.8 has two halves that work very differently: • 90.8(A) — planning for expansion. Plan an installation so later growth in load does not require tearing the system apart. Allowing room for future circuits and capacity is presented as good practice, for convenience and for the life of the installation — encouragement, not a hard sizing rule. No percentage of spare capacity is mandated here. • 90.8(B) — the number of circuits in enclosures. This half is a hard rule: an enclosure may not be filled beyond the number of circuits it was designed and listed to hold. The panel's listing, not the number of breakers that can physically be forced in, sets the limit. Read together: leave room because it is smart, and never overfill because it is prohibited. Loads only grow — the EV charger, the pool, the addition, the workshop. A panel stuffed full on day one turns every later job into a change-out, and an enclosure filled past its listed circuit count is a listing violation waiting for an inspector or a failure. Planning room at rough-in costs almost nothing; creating it later costs a service call, a permit, and a day. Spare panel spaces, an accessible junction point, and a raceway path that can be reused are cheap on rough-in day and expensive later. On a Marion Oaks new build we set a 200 A Siemens panel with 40 spaces, landed 29 circuits, and left 11 spaces open, with a spare conduit stubbed from the panel into the attic for the pool equipment the owner plans next year. When that job comes, the next electrician — often us — has a workable path instead of a change-out quote. Where the plan allows, leave that path. The trap answer turns 90.8(A) into a mandate: "The Code requires 25 percent spare panel capacity." It does not. Section 90.8(A) encourages planning for expansion; it sets no percentage and sizes nothing. The enforceable half of the section is (B): fill an enclosure beyond the number of circuits it was designed and listed to hold, and you have a violation — however neat the tandem breakers look. Panelboard filled beyond the number of circuits it was designed and listed to hold — tandem breakers stuffed past the panel's circuit limit. Circuit added to a panel already at its listed circuit count, putting the enclosure over its design limit. Breaker landed in a space the panel was not designed or listed to use as a circuit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Units of measurement
x: Every measurement in the Code is printed twice: a metric (SI) value and an inch-pound value. The pair is joined by soft conversion — each side is rounded to a clean number in its own system — so the two do not convert exactly: • The 3 ft working-space depth is printed as 900 mm. Converted exactly, 3 ft is 914 mm. • The 3 ft 6 in depth is printed as 1.0 m; the exact conversion is 1.07 m. • The 4 ft depth is printed as 1.2 m; the exact conversion is 1.22 m. • The 6½ ft headroom is printed as 2.0 m; the exact conversion is 1.98 m. Neither printed value is a misprint, and one inch is exactly 25.4 mm — the rounding is deliberate. Build to the value printed in the rule you are using, in the system your tape reads. In United States field work, that is the inch-pound value. Two crews can measure the same box in different systems and both be right only if everyone builds to the printed pair. Let each installer convert for himself and the roundings stack in both directions — one man's 900 mm becomes another man's 35 in — and the argument lands at inspection, where the printed rule was going to win anyway. Measure in inches and feet as printed in the rule you are using. On a small commercial job, a metric set of plans shows the panel working space at 900 mm; the crew tapes 3 ft, and it is the same box the inspector measures, because the Code prints the pair together. The miss to avoid is converting 900 mm back to 35.4 in and taping the shallower number. Do not convert a Code dimension yourself and then argue from your conversion at inspection. The trap is doing the math 'properly': converting 3 ft to exactly 914 mm and failing the metric drawing, or converting 900 mm to 35.4 in and building the working space shallow. 90.9 exists to kill that argument. The printed value, in the system you are measuring in, is the requirement — your calculator does not outrank the book. Working space taped at 35 in after the installer converted the printed 900 mm himself (90.9, 110.26(A)(1)). Dimension built from a home-made conversion instead of the value printed in the rule (90.9). Inspection argument made from a converted value instead of the printed pair (90.9). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 100 — Definitions: the words the Code uses
x: Article 100 defines the terms that carry a special meaning inside the Code. When a defined word appears in a rule, it means what Article 100 says it means, even if the everyday meaning is broader or narrower. • Part I: general definitions — the everyday job terms, like accessible, listed and outlet. • Part II: definitions for installations over 1000 volts. • Part III: definitions for hazardous (classified) locations. In the 2020 edition the terms sit in alphabetical order inside each part rather than as numbered sections. This chapter covers the job-critical general terms a Sharma helper meets first; it does not attempt every definition in the article. A rule is only as clear as its words. If 'outlet' meant whatever each reader guessed, the same installation could pass in one county and fail in the next. Defining the load-bearing words once, in one article, keeps every other article meaning the same thing on every job and at every inspection. When an argument turns on a single word — accessible, listed, outlet, service — come back to this article before arguing from everyday speech. A surprising number of inspection fights are really definition fights. On a Sharma takeoff the fight is usually 'outlet': a lighting point and a hardwired point are outlets too, not just receptacles, and Article 100 settles the count before it turns into a change-order argument. NEC 2023 (FL: FBC 9th Ed., permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026): the 2023 edition reorganized Article 100 into a single consolidated alphabetical list. Do not use a 2023 study book's arrangement to locate a definition under Florida's 2020 edition. The trap is answering from everyday speech — calling every plug point an outlet and every outlet a receptacle. On the exam, and in the field, the Article 100 definition in the edition on the permit controls. A second trap: hunting a definition in a 2023 study book's single alphabetical list when Florida's 2020 edition still keeps the three parts. Receptacle count short on a wall because lighting and hardwired points were not counted as outlets where the rule said 'outlet'. Work written up where a defined term — 'in sight from' — was judged by eye instead of by its Article 100 definition: visible, and not more than 50 ft away. Panel labeled with a word the Code does not use, so the inspector cannot match the installation to the rule that governs it. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 100: All definitions were moved into Article 100 (the .2 sections of each article no longer hold definitions; Article 100 is no longer split into parts). Many terms are new or revised, e.g. Counter (Countertop), Work Surface, Servicing, Short Circuit, Likely to Become Energized, Energy Management System, WSCR/WSAF. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Accessible and readily accessible
x: Article 100 uses the word two ways, and then adds a stricter version: • Accessible (equipment): a person can get close to it to operate, inspect or maintain it, without being blocked by the building's permanent structure. • Accessible (wiring method): it can be removed or reached without tearing out finished construction — nothing buried behind the finish. • Readily accessible: stricter. A person can get to it quickly, without tools other than a key, without climbing over obstacles, and without a portable ladder. The everyday test: if reaching it means demolition, it is not accessible. If reaching it means fetching a ladder and moving storage, it is not readily accessible. Equipment that cannot be reached cannot be maintained, inspected, or shut off in a hurry. A splice buried behind drywall fails silently for years — heat and arcing with no way to find it short of opening the wall. The readily accessible line is about routine work as much as emergencies: the person who needs that breaker or disconnect should not need a ladder, a toolbox and a scavenger hunt to get there. A breaker behind a locked door the occupant can open is different from a junction box buried behind drywall. Buried boxes are the classic failure: a wiring method that cannot be reached without demolition is not accessible, and splices belong in accessible boxes. On a remodel in The Villages, the previous electrician buried a junction box behind new drywall, found only because a circuit died. The box gets cut open and relocated into an accessible box with a blank cover — the splice was fine, the burial was not. The garage subpanel on the same job, behind a door the homeowner opens with a key and with clear floor in front, passes both tests. The trap is treating accessible and readily accessible as the same word. Accessible is the low bar — you can get there without demolition. Readily accessible adds speed: no tools other than a key, no climbing over or under obstacles, no portable ladder. A disconnect you can only reach by ladder may be accessible, but where the Code says readily accessible, it fails. Junction box buried behind drywall or tile — splices unreachable without demolition. Panel blocked by fixed shelving or a water heater so the cover cannot be opened. Disconnect reachable only by portable ladder where ready access is required. Access cover painted shut or screwed down over a box behind a finished ceiling. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Ampacity
x: Ampacity is the most current, in amperes, a conductor can carry continuously in its actual conditions of use without getting hotter than its temperature rating allows. It is not a single number printed on the wire; it depends on the conductor material, insulation rating, ambient temperature, and how many current-carrying conductors share a raceway or cable. • Start in Table 310.16, in the column the insulation type and the terminations allow. • Then correct for ambient heat (310.15(B)) and adjust for bundled current-carrying conductors (310.15(C)(1)). • Worked example: 12 AWG THHN copper starts at 30 A in the 90 °C column. In a 104 °F space (×0.91) with four current-carrying conductors (×0.80) it adjusts to 21.8 A — and 240.4(D) still caps the breaker at 20 A. Current makes heat, and heat is what kills insulation — slowly, inside walls, years after the inspection sign-off. Ampacity is the line between a conductor that runs warm for decades and one whose insulation cracks, faults, and starts a fire in a stud bay. Florida attics run far past the 30 °C the table assumes, so the correction step is where Florida jobs are won or lost. Start from Table 310.16, then adjust for the job's real conditions. A conductor that is fine alone in a cool space can be over its limit bundled in a hot Florida attic. One Sharma home run: two 20 A circuits of 12 AWG THHN copper in one EMT through a 104 °F mechanical space — four current-carrying conductors. The math runs 30 A × 0.91 × 0.80 = 21.8 A, which stays above the 20 A breaker, so the circuit stands. Add a third circuit to that pipe, or route it through a hotter attic, and the same wire no longer works. S-10: CCA is rated from the aluminum column of Table 310.16, which is why Sharma goes one AWG size larger when CCA is used. Florida attic temperatures make ambient correction a real design step, not a paperwork exercise. The trap is quoting the 90 °C column as the final answer: '12 AWG THHN is a 30 A wire.' The 90 °C value is only the starting point for correction and adjustment. The terminations pull the usable value into their own column, and 240.4(D) caps the breaker at 20 A no matter what the arithmetic produces. Conductors sized straight from the 90 °C column with no ambient correction in a hot attic (310.15(B)). More than three current-carrying conductors in a raceway with no adjustment applied (310.15(C)(1)). 12 AWG copper on a 25 A or 30 A breaker because 'THHN is good for 30 A' (240.4(D)). NM cable ampacity taken from the 90 °C column — 334.80 holds it to the 60 °C result. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Conductors — bare, covered, insulated, and the neutral
x: Article 100 sorts conductors by what is on the metal: • Bare conductor: no covering or insulation at all. • Covered conductor: a covering that is not recognized insulation. It may protect against weather or abrasion, but it earns the wire no insulation rating. • Insulated conductor: insulation that is recognized for the use — the normal building wire a crew handles. • Neutral conductor: the conductor connected to the system's neutral point, intended to carry current under normal conditions. • Neutral point: the common point of a wye connection, or the midpoint of a single-phase or DC system, from which the circuit conductors are referenced. The word in the definition decides which rules apply. Treat a covered conductor as insulated and you have put wire with no insulation rating where the Code counted on insulation — service-drop covering is the classic case. Treat the neutral as a spare ground and you have put normal load current on a path that was never meant to carry it. On an overhead service to a Florida house, the covering on the drop is weather protection, not insulation: do not treat a covered conductor as insulated when a rule calls for insulation. Inside the building, the neutral is a current-carrying working conductor, not a spare ground — it lands on the neutral bar and is bonded to ground only where the Code allows the bond, at the service and not in every subpanel downstream. The trap answer is “covered means insulated — something is over the metal.” A covering that is not recognized insulation earns no insulation rating, whatever it looks like. The mirror-image trap: “the neutral is basically a ground.” The neutral carries normal return current; the grounding path is a different conductor with a different job. Covered service conductor treated as insulated where the rule requires an insulated conductor. Neutral landed on the grounding bar in a subpanel, putting normal load current on the grounding path. Bare conductor run where an insulated conductor is required. Neutral used as the equipment grounding conductor on a branch circuit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Voltage — nominal voltage, voltage to ground, and circuit voltage
x: Three voltage terms run through the whole Code, and they are not interchangeable. • Voltage of a circuit: the greatest difference of potential between any two conductors of the circuit — leg to leg on a house panel, 240 V. • Nominal voltage: the value the system is named by — 120, 240, 480 — used to classify circuits and equipment, even though the actual voltage wanders a little above and below it. • Voltage to ground: the voltage between a conductor and the earth, or the grounded point of the system. On a 120/240 V house service it is 120 V; on a 208Y/120 V system it is 120 V; on a 480Y/277 V system it is 277 V. Working-space, clearance and equipment rules key on voltage to ground far more often than on the phase-to-phase number, so picking the right term is half the answer. Grabbing the wrong voltage number puts the gear in the wrong table row. A worker who reads 480 on the nameplate and uses it where a table asks for voltage to ground can undersize working space and clearances on the next system. The three terms exist so the number used matches the shock exposure a person actually faces: leg to ground. When a table asks for voltage to ground, answer with the leg-to-ground number, not the nameplate of the service. A 120/240 V panel sits in the 0–150 V-to-ground row of Table 110.26(A)(1) — 3 ft of working depth in every condition — even though 240 V appears across its bus. The same habit matters on 480Y/277 V gear at a small commercial job: the working-space row is set by 277 V to ground, not 480. The trap answer uses the biggest number on the nameplate. Asked for the voltage to ground of a 120/240 V service, the trap says 240 V. It is 120 V — the voltage from either leg to the grounded conductor. The same trap on a 480Y/277 V system says 480 V; the answer is 277 V. Working space laid out from the phase-to-phase voltage instead of voltage to ground, putting 480Y/277 V gear in the wrong row of Table 110.26(A)(1). A 120 V load landed on the high leg of a 240/120 V delta service — 208 V to ground — because all three legs were assumed to be 120 V to ground. Equipment selected by nominal voltage alone, without checking the actual system voltage it will be connected to. High leg left unidentified because the crew treated every leg of the delta service as 120 V to ground. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Appliance
x: An appliance is utilization equipment, usually built as a unit, that does a household or similar job — cooking, washing, drying, comfort heating or cooling, and the like — other than a basic luminaire or motor by itself. The word matters because several branch-circuit and disconnect rules turn on whether the load is an appliance. • Appliances: dishwashers, disposals, ranges, cooktops, dryers, built-in microwaves, storage water heaters. • Not appliances standing alone: a luminaire, a motor by itself, or a receptacle outlet. Each of those has its own article. • When the load is an appliance, Article 422 switches on: sizing from the marked rating, an individual branch circuit as the default for the big fixed appliances (422.10), the marked maximum overcurrent device (422.11), and GFCI protection that travels with the appliance for the 422.5(A) list. The definition is a sorting gate, and sorting wrong cuts both ways. Treat a dishwasher like an ordinary receptacle load and you can miss the GFCI protection 422.5 requires wherever that appliance is installed. Treat a plain luminaire like an appliance and you apply rules that were never written for it. The name of the load decides which rulebook opens, so the name has to be right first. Marion Oaks kitchen, rough-in day: the dishwasher and the disposal are both appliances, so they are planned as appliance loads, not as spare receptacle outlets. The built-in microwave gets its own 20 A circuit (Sharma S-06), and the dishwasher gets GFCI protection under 422.5 — that duty travels with the appliance and sits on top of the kitchen receptacle rules in 210.8. Before trim, walk the kitchen and name every appliance out loud. The ones nobody names are the ones that get wired like outlets. S-06 is PENDING. The microwave gets its own 20A circuit. The wire is not settled — 12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA — until Mike Holt rules. If the plan or the nameplate states a size, that statement governs. The exam loves the swap: a dishwasher hard-wired under the sink is 'just another load on the kitchen circuit.' Wrong — it is an appliance, Article 422 applies, and 422.5 puts GFCI protection on it wherever it is installed. The mirror-image trap calls a bare motor or a luminaire an appliance. The definition leaves both out when they stand alone. Dishwasher installed with no GFCI protection — 422.5(A) requires it wherever the appliance is installed. Fixed appliance sharing a general receptacle circuit where an individual branch circuit was required (422.10). Appliance protected above its marked maximum overcurrent device (422.11). Storage water heater circuit sized at nameplate instead of 125 percent (422.13). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Approved, identified, labeled, and listed
x: These four words form one family, and they are not interchangeable: • Approved means acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction. The AHJ has the final say on the installation. • Identified means recognizable as suitable for the specific purpose, function, use, environment, or application in question — fit for this use, not just some use. • Labeled means a testing organization has attached its label or other identifying mark to the product, after checking samples of it. • Listed means the product appears in that organization's published list of items it has evaluated. A product can be well made and still not be listed, and an unlisted product used where listing is required is a Code problem. The chain also runs one way: the lab lists and labels, but only the AHJ approves. These words are how the Code trusts equipment it has never seen. Listing and labeling mean an independent lab actually evaluated the product; identified ties it to the exact job in front of you; approval puts the local AHJ's judgment on top. Skip a link — an unlisted import, a breaker from the wrong panel family — and nobody has verified the gear will fail safely instead of burning. Read the box and the device. On a panel change in Ocala, the supply house substituted a breaker of another brand that physically snapped into the new Siemens panel. It fit — and it was not identified for that panel, so it came back out. Breakers must be listed and identified for the panel they go in; a breaker that physically fits a foreign panel is not thereby identified for it. That is exactly what S-02 and S-03 are for: Siemens in Siemens, Square D in Square D. S-02: all new gear is Siemens. S-03: in an existing Square D panel, use Square D breakers listed for that panel — never mix brands to fill a space. The trap swaps the family members. "Approved" does not mean the lab tested it — it means acceptable to the AHJ. "Listed" is not the sticker on the product — the sticker is the label; listed means the product stands in the lab's published list. And "it fits and it works" never makes a device identified for a use it was not evaluated for. Breaker of a different brand installed in a panel it is not listed or identified for — it fit, and that was all. Unlisted equipment installed where listing is required: no label on the product, and it stands in no lab's published list. Equipment used outside its identification — a device evaluated for dry locations installed where it gets wet. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Equipment, utilization equipment, enclosures, and fittings
x: Equipment is the Code's umbrella word for the apparatus of an installation. The family, piece by piece: • Equipment: a general term for fittings, devices, appliances, luminaires, machines and the like, used as part of or in connection with an installation — whether they carry current or just support the parts that do. • Utilization equipment: the narrower slice that actually uses electric energy to do work — heating, lighting, cooling, data processing and similar jobs. • Enclosure: the case or housing around apparatus. It keeps people away from live parts and protects the contents. Enclosed describes apparatus that has such a case. • Fitting: an accessory — a locknut, bushing or similar part — that does a mechanical job rather than an electrical one. • Handhole enclosure: a small below-grade access enclosure, set flush or buried, whose cover a worker removes by hand to reach the conductors inside. The umbrella word is what drags the safety rules along with it. The moment a thing is equipment, Article 110 wants it approved, guarded, and given working space — and the enclosure is what stands between a helper's hand and a live bus. Fittings look too small to matter, but the missing bushing is exactly how conductor insulation gets cut through. Calling something 'equipment' is what brings the Article 110 rules with it — approval, working space, guarding. Handholes are the buried splice points on site work: they are enclosures, so the splices inside still have to be made with listed methods and the cover kept accessible, not paved over. On a Marion Oaks site package, the handholes at the monument sign and the lot corners get wet-location listed splices, and their covers stay at grade where the paving crew can see them. The trap is treating 'equipment' as only the big gear — panels and air handlers. Under the definition a locknut is equipment too, as a fitting, and the exam turns on the narrower slice: utilization equipment is the part that uses the energy to do work, not everything connected to it. Handhole enclosure paved over or buried under sod — the cover has to stay accessible. Dry-location wire connectors on splices inside a below-grade handhole — a wet location needs listed methods. Damaged enclosure with live parts reachable — the apparatus is no longer enclosed. Conduit entering a box with no bushing, insulation worn through on the sharp edge. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bonding — bonded, bonding conductor, bonding jumper
x: Bonded means connected to establish electrical continuity and conductivity. Bonding is the act of joining metal parts together so they hold the same electrical potential and share a reliable, low-impedance path that can carry fault current back to the source. • Bonding jumper: the conductor or fitting that makes a bonding connection • Main bonding jumper: the connection at the service between the grounded conductor (the neutral) and the equipment grounding side • Equipment bonding jumper: the jumper that ties equipment enclosures and raceways into that path Bonding is not grounding. The grounding electrode — the rod, the Ufer, the water pipe — connects the system to the earth, and earth is a poor conductor that will not clear a fault. Bonding's job is metal-to-metal: give fault current a hard, fast path home so the breaker trips. Without a bonding path, a hot wire faulted to a metal box leaves that box sitting at line voltage, silent, waiting for a hand. The breaker never trips because the fault current has nowhere strong to flow. Bonding turns that silent, energized box into a heavy fault the breaker clears at once. Metal boxes, raceways, enclosures and equipment frames that can become energized need a bonding path back to the source. A loose locknut or paint under a fitting can quietly break that path. Picture a 20 A kitchen circuit: the hot conductor chafes through on the edge of a metal box. With the box bonded, the fault current rushes back to the panel and the breaker opens. With paint under the locknut and the locknut finger-tight, the same box sits live at 120 V — and the first person to learn about it is the one who touches it and a grounded sink at the same time. The trap answer bonds equipment by driving a ground rod next to it. A rod connects to the earth; it does not give fault current the low-impedance metal path back to the source that trips the breaker. Bonding and grounding are two different jobs that happen to meet at the service. Bonding fitting landed over paint or drywall compound — nonconductive coatings left in place where they break the fault path. Locknuts finger-tight on a service raceway — the bonding path depends on a wrench-tight, listed connection. Metal raceway run interrupted by a plastic box or fitting with no bonding jumper around it. No bonding jumper across a water meter or a dielectric union — the piping path is broken at the joint. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding conductors and electrodes — EGC, GEC, and bonding jumpers
x: The grounding family splits by job: • Equipment grounding conductor (EGC): connects the metal frames of equipment back to the source, so a ground fault becomes a big fault current that trips the breaker. It is usually the green or bare wire, but 250.118 also lets certain raceways and cable armor serve as the EGC. • Grounding electrode conductor (GEC): connects the system to the grounding electrode — the rod, plate, concrete-encased electrode or other recognized earth connection itself. • Main bonding jumper: the connection at the service between the grounded conductor and the EGC side. • System bonding jumper: the same connection made at a separately derived system instead of at a service. The Bonding page and the Grounded/Grounding page cover the base words; this page is the conductor-by-conductor map. Each conductor in this family does a different protective job, and they are not interchangeable. The EGC is the fault's road home: without it, a short to a metal frame leaves the frame energized and waiting for someone's hand. The GEC ties the system to earth for lightning and surges; it was never meant to clear faults. Swap the jobs, or bond neutral to ground in the wrong place, and fault current rides neutrals and piping instead of tripping the breaker. On a 200 A house service in Ocala, the EGCs run with the branch circuits back to the service panel, the GEC runs from the neutral bar to the ground rods, and the main bonding jumper ties the neutral bar to the enclosure. That is the only neutral-to-ground bond in the house: the subpanel in the detached garage keeps neutral and ground on separate bars, with no bond. If the house later adds a generator switched as a separately derived system, that system gets its own system bonding jumper. And before any wire is pulled, the sizing check: EGCs come from Table 250.122, the GEC from Table 250.66 — different tables, different jobs. The classic trap, on exams and on inspections: "The EGC and the GEC are both ground wires, so size them from the same table." Wrong. The EGC is sized from Table 250.122, by the overcurrent device ahead of it; the GEC is sized from Table 250.66, by the service conductors. The companion trap is bonding neutral to ground again at a subpanel — the bond lives at the service, or at a separately derived system, and nowhere downstream. Equipment grounding conductor sized from Table 250.66 — the GEC's table — instead of Table 250.122. Neutral bonded to ground at a subpanel; the bond belongs at the service only. Separately derived system with no system bonding jumper installed. No EGC path back to the source — the ground rod and GEC left to clear a ground fault. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounded and grounding — telling the conductors apart
x: Two words that sound almost the same do two completely different jobs, and Article 100 defines them separately on purpose: • Grounded: connected to the earth, or to a conductive body that extends the earth connection. • Grounded conductor: a system or circuit conductor that is intentionally grounded. In a house that is the neutral — white or gray — and it carries normal load current every day. • Grounding conductor: a conductor used to connect equipment or the grounded circuit conductor to a grounding electrode or to a point on the grounding electrode system. • Equipment grounding conductor (EGC): the conductive path that ties equipment enclosures, raceways and other non-current-carrying metal parts to the system grounded conductor and the electrode, so fault current can get back to the source and trip the breaker. • Grounding electrode conductor (GEC): the conductor that connects the system grounded conductor, or the equipment, to the grounding electrode. The one-sentence test: the grounded conductor works every day carrying load current; the grounding conductors sit idle until something goes wrong. Mix the two up and people get hurt. A neutral landed on the ground bar downstream of the service puts load current on metal enclosures and raceways, so pipes and panel covers sit energized all day. A missing grounding path does the opposite harm: a fault has no low-impedance road back to the source, the breaker never trips, and the enclosure stays live, waiting for a hand. On a 200 A house service in Marion Oaks, the white grounded conductor lands on the neutral bar, and the bare GEC runs from that same bar out to the ground rods — the service is the one place the two systems are bonded together, through the main bonding jumper. Every subpanel Sharma sets downstream keeps them apart: neutrals on an insulated bar, green and bare equipment grounding conductors on the ground bar, no bonding screw. On the branch circuits the white wire carries the load current home; the green or bare wire carries nothing until a fault, then it carries the fault back so the breaker opens. The exam loves the near-identical names. The trap answer treats “grounded conductor” and “grounding conductor” as interchangeable, or calls the white wire the grounding conductor. Remember it by the job, not the sound: grounded = the neutral that works daily; grounding = the safety path that works only on a fault. Neutral and ground landed on the same bar in a subpanel — load current riding the grounding path. Bonding screw or strap left in a downstream panel, tying the neutral to the enclosure. Green or bare conductor used as the neutral on a branch circuit. White wire pulled in conduit and landed as a hot leg. Equipment grounding conductor missing on a remodel — metal boxes and devices left ungrounded. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Ground fault, GFCI, and ground-fault protection of equipment
x: A ground fault is an unintended connection between an ungrounded (hot) conductor and normally non-current-carrying metal parts, or the earth. It is the fault the equipment grounding conductor exists to turn into a breaker trip. Two protective terms build on that definition, and they are not interchangeable: • Ground fault: the fault itself — current reaching metal or earth it was never supposed to touch. • GFCI (ground-fault circuit interrupter): protects people. It watches for current leaking outside the intended path and opens the circuit at a few milliamperes — the personnel-protection level. A Class A GFCI must trip when ground-fault current reaches 6 mA, and must not trip below 4 mA (Article 100 GFCI Informational Note, from UL 943). • GFPE (ground-fault protection of equipment): protects equipment and conductors from damaging fault currents at much higher levels — hundreds of amperes on large services. It is not intended to protect a person from shock. A ground fault through a person's body can kill at currents far below any breaker rating, so the GFCI watches in milliamperes and opens fast. GFPE exists for the opposite problem: a fault on a large service can sit at hundreds of amperes — too much current to ignore, not enough to trip an ordinary breaker — and burn until something fails. Two hazards, two devices; mixing the names mixes up the protection. A GFPE breaker on a big service will not save a helper who contacts a live part, and a receptacle GFCI is not equipment protection for a service. When a spec or an inspector says 'ground-fault protection,' ask which of the two is meant before ordering gear. On a 480Y/277 V retail service in Ocala, the gear arrives with GFPE as specified — and the crew still roughs GFCI protection at the wet-location receptacles, because the two devices answer two different hazards. The trap answer says the service 'has ground-fault protection,' so the worker is protected. Wrong device: that protection is GFPE, set in the hundreds of amperes to protect equipment. Personnel protection is the GFCI's 4–6 mA window, and nothing else on this page substitutes for it. GFPE service breaker offered as personnel protection for a wet-location task — wrong device; no GFCI protection present. Receptacle GFCI removed after nuisance trips instead of finding the load that is leaking. Spec said 'ground-fault protection' and a receptacle GFCI was installed where the service needed GFPE — the names were never sorted out. Class A GFCI still holding at 8 mA on the tester — outside its 4–6 mA window; replace it. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Branch circuit
x: A branch circuit is the part of the wiring system between the final overcurrent device protecting it — the breaker in the panel — and the outlets it feeds. Everything upstream of that breaker is a feeder or service conductor; everything downstream to the receptacles, lights and equipment is the branch circuit. Article 210 builds its rules on this definition. • It starts at that circuit's final overcurrent device — not at the meter, and not at the panel as a whole. • It ends at the outlets: receptacle outlets, lighting outlets, and hard-wired equipment. • Feeders feed panels; branch circuits feed loads. The same wire can be either one, depending on where the final breaker sits. The boundary decides which rules size the wire and which device protects the load. Feeder rules and branch-circuit rules are different articles with different math. Call a run by the wrong name and you can protect a load with a device that was only ever meant to feed a panel — or hunt a dead receptacle at the meter when the whole problem is one tripped breaker. When you size, protect or troubleshoot a circuit, find its breaker first. The conductor size, the breaker rating and the outlets all have to agree as one branch circuit. On a Sharma commercial job that agreement has a floor: every branch circuit is 20 A minimum on 12 AWG copper minimum (S-01), even where the Code would allow a 15 A circuit. On a house call, a dead bedroom receptacle is a branch-circuit problem — start at its breaker in the panel, not at the service. S-01: on commercial work every branch circuit is 20A minimum on 12 AWG copper minimum — no 15A branch circuits on commercial jobs. That is Sharma practice, stricter than the Code floor. The trap answer starts the branch circuit at the service disconnect, or at the panel itself. It starts at the final overcurrent device for that circuit. A breaker in the main panel that feeds a garage subpanel is a feeder breaker, not the final device — the garage branch circuits begin at the breakers in the subpanel. Load landed ahead of the final overcurrent device — fed from a feeder instead of a branch circuit. Panel directory that does not identify which breaker serves which outlets (408.4(A)). Multiwire branch circuit with no means to disconnect all ungrounded conductors at once (210.4(B)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Branch-circuit types — appliance, general purpose, individual, multiwire
x: Article 100 names four branch-circuit types. The base branch-circuit page covers where a branch circuit starts and ends; this page is the family tree. • Appliance: supplies energy-utilizing equipment other than luminaires. • General purpose: supplies two or more receptacles or outlets for lighting and appliances. • Individual: supplies only one piece of utilization equipment. • Multiwire: two or more ungrounded conductors that have a voltage between them, sharing one grounded (neutral) conductor that carries only the unbalanced difference between them — the shared-neutral circuit a crew meets on kitchen and home-run work. The names are not trivia. The type decides which rules follow the circuit — what may be tapped, what must disconnect together, and how the neutral behaves. The multiwire definition carries its hazard inside it: that shared neutral only carries the difference while both legs are landed on opposite sides of the system. The shared neutral is what makes a multiwire circuit efficient and dangerous at the same time: open that neutral under load and the two legs go in series across 240 V, over-volting one side. Both legs must disconnect together, and the conductors must land on opposite legs — same-leg "sharing" overloads the neutral instead of cancelling. On a kitchen rough-in, the two small-appliance circuits run home as one multiwire circuit: land them on opposite legs, on a breaker arrangement that disconnects both legs together, every time. The trap is calling any circuit with a shared neutral "two circuits sharing a spare wire." A multiwire branch circuit is a single circuit type with a definition: ungrounded conductors with a voltage between them, and one neutral carrying only the unbalanced current. Land both hots on the same leg and it stops behaving like the definition — the neutral adds the two loads instead of cancelling them. Both multiwire hots landed on the same leg — the neutral carries the sum, not the difference, and overheats. Multiwire legs on two single-pole breakers with no means to disconnect both legs together. Appliance branch circuit tapped to feed luminaires — the definition excludes lighting. Individual branch circuit found feeding a second piece of equipment — it is no longer an individual circuit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Circuit breaker, panelboard, cabinet, and the fault ratings
x: • Circuit breaker: a device that opens and closes a circuit by nonautomatic means and opens it automatically at a preset overcurrent. An adjustable-trip breaker lets that trip setting be changed without swapping internal parts. • Panelboard: a single panel, or a group of panel units, of switches or breakers designed to mount in or against a wall, inside an enclosure. The enclosure is a cabinet or a cutout box — two separately defined terms. A cabinet has a frame or trim for a swinging door; a cutout box has its door or cover hinged directly to the box walls. Either may be surface or flush, with doors or trim as designed. • Interrupting rating: the highest fault current a device itself can safely open at its rated voltage. • Short-circuit current rating (SCCR): the fault current a piece of equipment as a whole can withstand, or be protected at. The two fault ratings are constantly confused — and they answer different questions. The 110.9 and 110.10 pages carry the rules behind both. A fault is the worst second of an installation's life. If the breaker cannot interrupt what the service can deliver, it can fail violently instead of clearing. If the assembly's SCCR is below the fault current, the panel itself becomes the damage. Both numbers are printed on labels — but they only help if somebody reads them before the gear is set. Small commercial service in Ocala: the fault-current calculation comes back at 22 kA. The new Siemens panelboard gets checked at delivery, not at inspection: every breaker's interrupting rating must meet or beat 22 kA — a panel full of 10 kAIC breakers is under-rated gear — and the panelboard's own SCCR on its label must cover the installation the same way. A breaker that fits the bus is not a breaker that belongs; check both labels while the gear is still on the pallet. The trap is swapping the two ratings: 'The panel's SCCR is 22 kA, so the breakers interrupt 22 kA.' No. SCCR belongs to the equipment as a whole; interrupting rating belongs to the device itself. A panel can carry a high SCCR and still be filled with breakers whose own interrupting ratings fall short. Breakers installed with interrupting ratings below the available fault current at their terminals (110.9). Panelboard SCCR below the available fault current — the assembly rating never checked against the fault calculation (110.10). Replacement breaker that physically fits the bus but is not the type identified for that panelboard. Adjustable-trip breaker setting changed in the field with no record — the setting no longer matches the job's fault paperwork. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Feeder
x: A feeder is the set of circuit conductors between the service equipment — or another power supply source, such as a separately derived system — and the final branch-circuit overcurrent devices. It is the middle layer of the system: • Service conductors end at the service equipment. • Feeders carry power onward from the service equipment to the panels, ending at the final branch-circuit overcurrent devices. • Branch circuits run from those panels' breakers to the outlets. Rules for sizing, protection and grounding change depending on which layer a conductor belongs to, so name the layer before you apply a rule. The same copper does different work in each layer. A feeder carries the combined load of many branch circuits and is protected once, at its supply end; a branch circuit is protected at the panel and sized to its outlets. Call a feeder a branch circuit and you reach for the wrong sizing rule, the wrong protection rule and the wrong grounding rule — the detached-garage run is the everyday example of all three mistakes at once. A Marion Oaks house gets a detached garage with a 60 A subpanel. The run from the house panel to the garage panel is a feeder: it starts at the 60 A breaker in the house panel and ends at the garage panel's breakers, which is where the branch circuits start. Because it is a feeder to a separate building, the garage also gets its own disconnect and grounding electrode under 225.31 and 250.32. None of that would apply if the same run were a single branch circuit to one outlet. The trap is the panel in the middle: 'the run to a subpanel is a branch circuit because it comes off a breaker.' No. A branch circuit ends at the outlet. Any run that ends at more overcurrent devices is a feeder, and feeder rules — Article 215 — size and protect it. Detached-garage panel fed with no disconnect or grounding electrode at the garage — the run was treated as a branch circuit, not a feeder to a separate building. Feeder conductors protected above their ampacity because the run was sized with branch-circuit thinking. Neutral and ground bonded again at the subpanel — past the service equipment, a feeder's neutral stays isolated from ground. Feeder extended with smaller conductors and no overcurrent protection where the size changes. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Continuous load
x: A continuous load is a load where the maximum current is expected to keep flowing for 3 hours or more at a stretch. The three-hour line is the whole definition. • Expected to continue — the test is the load's normal pattern, not one unusual long day. • At maximum current — a load that cycles is judged by what it actually holds; cycling equipment may not be continuous at all. • The definition sets no size by itself. The sizing rules that use the term do: a continuous load is counted at 125 percent for conductor and overcurrent sizing (210.19(A)(1), 210.20(A)), unless the assembly is listed for operation at 100 percent of its rating. So a 40 A load that runs 3 hours or more is counted as 40 × 1.25 = 50 A before the wire or the breaker is picked. Heat is the reason. A conductor and a breaker carrying full current for hours reach their full working temperature and stay there — there is no cool-down between cycles. Counting the load at 125 percent buys the thermal margin that keeps terminations and insulation at the temperature they were rated for, all day, every day. Lighting in a store that stays on all day, an EV charger, and long-running HVAC loads are the usual suspects. Ask how long the load actually runs before deciding whether the continuous-load treatment applies. Worked case: a home EV charger pulling 40 A through the night is continuous — 40 × 1.25 = 50 A, so it is built as a 50 A circuit, not a 40 A one. A storage water heater gets the same treatment from its own article, at 125 percent of nameplate (422.13). The trap misses the line in both directions. Maximum current for 2 hours is not continuous — the line is 3 hours. And a load that runs all day at half its maximum is not 'continuous at maximum' either: the definition needs maximum current, expected, for 3 hours or more. Get the definition right first; the 125 percent sizing follows from it. EV charger on a circuit sized at nameplate amps only — no 125 percent for the continuous load. Store lighting circuit loaded to the breaker's full rating; the breaker runs hot and nuisance-trips by mid-afternoon. Water heater circuit figured at nameplate with no 125 percent (422.13). Conductor sized to the load while the breaker was sized at 125 percent — the two halves of the calc disagree. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Demand factor, nonlinear load, and overcurrent
x: Three Article 100 words that run load calculations and troubleshooting: • Demand factor: the ratio of a system's maximum demand to its total connected load. It is always 1.0 or less. It is what lets a feeder be smaller than the sum of everything connected to it, because not everything runs at once. • Nonlinear load: a load whose current waveform does not follow the voltage waveform — LED drivers, electronic ballasts, variable-speed drives and most plug-in electronics. It pushes harmonic current onto the system, especially the shared neutral of a multiwire circuit. • Overcurrent: any current above a conductor's or equipment's rating. Crews must tell its two causes apart: an overload is too much legitimate load on an otherwise sound circuit, while a short circuit or ground fault is a failure. The protection and the troubleshooting are different for each. Each word guards against a different expensive mistake. Size everything as if it all ran at once and you bury copper nobody needed. Ignore harmonics and a shared neutral quietly overheats while both breakers stay happy. Treat a fault like an overload and 'fix' it with a bigger breaker, and the failure stays in the wall with more energy behind it. Marion Oaks house, standard-method check: the general load adds up to 18,000 VA connected. Table 220.42 takes the first 3,000 VA at 100 percent and the rest at 35 percent, so the maximum demand is 8,250 VA — a demand factor of 8,250 ÷ 18,000, about 0.46. The feeder is sized from the demand, not the connected total. Same house, different word: the LED lighting home runs share a neutral, and because those drivers are nonlinear loads, the harmonics add on that neutral instead of cancelling — treat it as a current-carrying conductor. The trap is answering a demand-factor question with a number over 1.0 — usually 1.25, stolen from the continuous-load rule. Demand factor is a ratio of demand to connected load, so it can never exceed 1.0. The 125 percent sizing rule belongs to continuous loads, a different definition on a different page. Feeder calculation rejected at plan review: connected load used with no demand factors applied (220.42). Shared neutral on a multiwire circuit feeding LED lighting not counted as a current-carrying conductor, with the load mostly nonlinear. Breaker upsized to stop tripping; the 'overload' was a short circuit left in place in the wall. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Dwelling unit
x: A dwelling unit is one unit that gives one or more people complete, independent living facilities. The definition has four functions, and all four must be there, with permanent provisions: • Living — a real living space • Sleeping — permanent sleeping quarters • Cooking — permanent cooking provisions, not a plug-in hot plate • Sanitation — a bathroom Miss one and the space is not a dwelling unit. The label matters because a long list of house rules in the Code switches on or off with it: receptacle spacing (210.52), GFCI protection (210.8(A)), the required branch circuits (210.11(C)), AFCI protection (210.12) and the dwelling load calculation in Article 220 all key off this one definition. Dwelling rules are written for the hardest case: people asleep, children, and hours of unattended use around electricity. The definition draws the line between that kind of space and a room people only pass through, so the extra protection lands where people actually live. A one-family house in Marion Oaks is a dwelling unit, and so is every apartment in a multifamily building. So is a Kissimmee house rented out nightly as a vacation rental — rented or owned, it still provides complete living facilities, so the dwelling rules apply in full, including the 210.52 wall-space rule (no point along the floor line more than 6 ft from a receptacle). A pool house with day beds and a wet bar is not a dwelling unit: no permanent cooking and no bathroom. Add a real kitchenette and a full bath to that pool house and it becomes one — and the GFCI, AFCI and spacing rules switch on with it. The trap answer treats any room where somebody sleeps as a dwelling unit — a hotel room, a hospital room, a pool house with a fold-out bed. Sleeping alone is not enough. All four functions must be present with permanent provisions, and cooking is the one most often missing. AFCI protection skipped in a short-term rental house because 'nobody lives there' — rented nightly, it is still a dwelling unit (210.12). Dwelling living room roughed in to commercial spacing — no point along the floor line may sit more than 6 ft from a receptacle (210.52(A)). Pool house finished with a permanent kitchenette and full bath — now a dwelling unit — with no GFCI or AFCI protection. Dwelling rules applied to a hotel guest room with no permanent cooking, while the actual dwelling units on the same job were missed. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bathroom and clothes closet
x: Two definitions on this page switch whole rule sets on and off. • Bathroom: an area that includes a basin, plus one or more of a toilet, a urinal, a tub, a shower, a bidet, or a similar plumbing fixture. Both halves must be there.
