The joint heats, the heat loosens it further, and the end of that road is a glowing connection, arcing, and a fire inside a box or a panel — usually years after the installer has left. Read the lug and device markings before landing wire. CU-only means copper only. A connector for aluminum, copper and CCA together must carry the AL-CU or CU-AL marking, or the intermixed marking where the metals actually touch, and breaker and equipment lugs get the same check. On a Marion Oaks rough-in with a new 200 A Siemens panel, the check runs at every landing point: 15 A and 20 A device screw terminals take copper and CCA unless marked otherwise, but devices 30 A and up are copper-only unless marked AL/CU (S-10). S-10 CCA practice: 15A and 20A device screw terminals take copper and CCA unless marked otherwise; devices 30A and up are copper-only unless marked AL/CU. Copper and CCA are not dissimilar metals; aluminum with copper, or aluminum with CCA, is. Backstab (push-in) terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only — never backstab CCA, stranded wire, or 12 AWG. UNVERIFIED FLAG (v1 README item 9): the UL guide wording behind the CCA terminal markings (RTRT / WJQR / ZMVV / AALZ) was taken from NEMA and UL/IAEI quotations, not read first-hand in UL Product iQ, and no CC or CC/CU marking was found in the ZMVV table. Do not invent a marking. A NEMA citation to 404.15(C) for switch terminals was not checked against the code text and is not relied on here. The trap answer says copper and CCA are dissimilar metals that may never touch. They are not a dissimilar pair, and they may be intermixed where the device allows it. The pairs that need a device identified for the combination are aluminum with copper and aluminum with CCA. Aluminum feeder landed under a lug marked CU only. Copper and aluminum conductors intermixed in a connector not identified for the combination. CCA pushed into a backstab (push-in) device terminal — push-in terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only (S-10). Soldered splice carrying the mechanical load of the joint, with no mechanical connection made first. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 110.14: Terminals now have to make a mechanically secure electrical connection, replacing the old thoroughly good wording, and the example metal pairs were cut from the dissimilar-metals rule. 110.14(A): landing a conductor on a terminal has to produce a mechanically secure electrical connection, with no damage to the wire. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Temperature limits at terminations
x: A termination is the lug or terminal where a conductor lands. The conductor's insulation may be rated 90 °C, but the ampacity you may use is capped by the temperature rating of the terminations at both ends of the run. • Circuits of 100 A or less, or conductors 14 through 1 AWG: use the 60 °C column of Table 310.16, unless the equipment is listed and marked for a higher temperature. • Circuits over 100 A, or conductors larger than 1 AWG: use the 75 °C column, unless the equipment is listed and marked otherwise. • The temperature rating of a conductor cannot be used above the lowest temperature rating of any termination it lands on. One 60 °C lug holds the whole run to 60 °C. • The 90 °C column still earns its keep: it is the starting point for temperature correction and conductor-count adjustment under 310.15. The final ampacity still cannot beat the termination column. The lug is the weak point of the run. Insulation along the conductor sheds heat into the air, but at the terminal the heat is trapped in a small mass of metal bolted to a breaker or switch that was tested at 60 °C or 75 °C. Land a conductor at its 90 °C ampacity on a 60 °C lug and the terminal overheats first: nuisance trips, insulation cooked back from the lug, and a connection that loosens into a high-resistance fault. A 200 A feeder on a small commercial job in Marion Oaks — Siemens panelboard, tenant space — run in 3/0 AWG THHN copper. The 90 °C column rates 3/0 at 225 A, but both ends land on 75 °C lugs, so the feeder sizes from the 75 °C column: 200 A, exactly the feeder rating. The first pick, 2/0, reads 195 A at 90 °C — tempting, but only 175 A at 75 °C, short of 200 A. Commercial on purpose: 310.12 sizes dwelling services and feeders on its own table, where 2/0 copper is a legal 200 A dwelling service. Same rule at the small end: 12 AWG THHN on a 20 A breaker starts at 30 A in the 90 °C column for correction math, but at the breaker the circuit is a 60 °C, 20 A circuit. The classic trap: 'THHN is rated 90 °C, so 12 AWG THHN can be protected at 30 A.' Wrong twice. 110.14(C) holds a circuit of 100 A or less to the 60 °C column — 20 A for 12 AWG copper — unless the equipment is marked for 75 °C, and 240.4(D) caps 12 AWG copper at 20 A anyway. The 90 °C column is for correction and adjustment math, not for picking the breaker. Conductor ampacity taken from the 90 °C column at terminations not marked for it — re-size from the 60 °C or 75 °C column. 2/0 AWG copper landed on a 200 A commercial feeder: 195 A at 90 °C, but only 175 A at the 75 °C terminations — and 310.12's dwelling sizes do not rescue a commercial feeder. Replacement breaker with 60 °C-only terminals installed where the conductors were sized at 75 °C values. Existing equipment with no legible temperature marking, wired as if 75 °C applied to a circuit of 100 A or less. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Torque — tighten to the specified value
x: Where a manufacturer gives a torque value for a terminal, the connection has to be tightened to that value using an approved means, unless the equipment has been tested and marked so another method is known to give the same result. • The approved means is a calibrated torque tool — a torque wrench or torque screwdriver — or a device such as a shear bolt or breakaway fastener that shows the proper torque was reached. • The specified torque is normally printed on the equipment label or in its instructions. Those instructions carry Code force under 110.3(B). • Hand-tight by feel is not a value. Two installers' 'tight' can differ by half. • If no value is indicated, contact the manufacturer. In the absence of a manufacturer's value, Annex I of UL 486A-486B — reprinted as NEC Informative Annex I — gives torque values by screw and conductor size. A loose terminal is a resistor. Current through a high-resistance joint makes heat, the heat cycles loosen the joint further, and the end of that road is arcing, a burned lug, or a fire inside the panel. Too tight is its own failure: crushed strands, a cracked lug, or a screw that snaps later. The specified value is the one the equipment was tested at — that is why the Code makes it a rule instead of a suggestion. New 200 A Siemens panel on a slab home in Ocala: the torque table is printed on the label inside the door — main lugs, neutral bar and breaker terminals each carry their own value. The torque screwdriver handles the small breaker and device terminals; the main lugs take a torque wrench. Keep both on the truck, use the label value for every lug at trim and service work, and re-check after landing all conductors — a lug torqued before the last conductor went in is not finished. Existing checklist item SP-15 covers the field routine. The trap answer is 'gudentight' — snug plus a quarter turn. 110.14(D) wants the indicated value, reached with an approved means. The second trap is reaching for the Annex I fallback values when the equipment label prints a value: the manufacturer's number governs, and the fallback exists only for when no value is given. Breaker and lug terminations snugged by feel — no torque tool on the truck and no value recorded. Main lugs run down with an impact driver until the tool 'sounded right.' Label torque table ignored; generic values used even though the manufacturer printed its own. Conductor strands crushed and splayed from over-torque, lug cracked at the barrel. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: High-leg marking on 4-wire delta systems
x: On a 4-wire, 3-phase delta system where the midpoint of one phase winding is used as a circuit conductor — the common 240/120 V delta — the voltages to ground are not equal: • Two legs sit at 120 V to ground. • The third leg — the high leg — sits at 208 V to ground. 110.15 requires that high-leg conductor to be durably and permanently marked by an orange finish, or identified by other effective means, at each point on the system where a connection is made if the grounded conductor is also present. The marking is what keeps a 120 V load from being landed on the leg that sits at 208 V to ground. A 120 V load landed on the high leg sees 208 V to ground and burns up — controls, ballasts and electronics die, and equipment can be energized in ways nobody expects. A delta panel looks like any other panel from the front; the only thing standing between a tired apprentice and a fried control board is the orange identification on the odd leg. That is why the marking has to be durable and permanent, not a scrap of tape that falls off by trim-out. Sharma meets high legs on older light-commercial services. Before landing any 120 V circuit in a delta panel, identify which leg is the high leg, confirm it is orange-marked, and keep 120 V loads off it. On a panel change at a small warehouse, the crew meters every leg to ground before landing anything: A reads 120 V, B reads 208 V, C reads 120 V — B is the high leg. It gets its orange identification at the panel and at the disconnect, the 120 V lighting and receptacle circuits land on A and C only, and the panel schedule is marked so the next electrician sees it before he meters. The trap answer marks the high leg with whatever tape is in the truck, or assumes a 120 V load can share the high leg because “it is still just one phase.” 110.15 requires an orange finish or other effective means, and the 208 V-to-ground leg feeds only loads rated for it. High leg with no orange identification where connections are made — the next crew lands 120 V circuits on it. 120 V receptacle or lighting circuit connected to the high leg; equipment burned up at 208 V to ground. Orange identification at the service but missing at a downstream panel where connections are made. High leg identified in a color other than orange, with no other effective means of identification. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Arc-flash hazard warning marking
x: Equipment that is likely to be examined, adjusted, serviced or maintained while energized — such as switchboards, panelboards and motor control centers in other than dwelling settings — must carry a durable, field-applied warning marking about the arc-flash hazard: • 110.16(A) is the warning marking itself. It warns the person approaching the gear; it does not replace safe work practice, and it belongs where that person will see it before anything is opened. • 110.16(B): in other than dwelling units, service equipment rated 1200A or more also needs a permanent label meeting 110.21(B). The label shows the nominal system voltage, the available fault current at the service overcurrent devices, the clearing time of those devices based on that fault current, and the date the label was applied. It is not required where an arc-flash label is applied per acceptable industry practice. Arc flash is the hazard you cannot see coming: opening a dead-front over a faulted or miswired bus can release an arc blast before a hand can pull back. The warning makes the next person stop, suit up and plan before the cover comes off — and the (B) label puts the numbers that drive the safety decisions on the gear itself, where they are still needed ten years later. On a small commercial job — a 1600A, 480Y/277 V service for an Ocala retail plaza — the (B) label is filled in from the fault-current figures before final: nominal voltage, the available fault current at the service devices, their clearing time at that current, and the date it went on. Confirm the general arc-flash warning is present and legible before you call final. Houses are not the target of this section, but the hazard it names is real on any energized panel. Two traps. First: “Once the label is on, the gear is protected.” The marking only warns — PPE and safe work practice still do the protecting. Second, the 2023 answer on a 2020 exam: 1000A and feeder-supplied equipment. Under NEC 2020, (B) covers service equipment rated 1200A or more; the wider 2023 net is labeled in the edition box and does not apply yet. No arc-flash warning marking on a commercial panelboard or switchboard likely to be worked energized. Service equipment rated 1200A or more with no permanent 110.16(B) label — and no industry-practice arc-flash label in its place. Label missing one of the four items: no clearing time, or no date applied. Handwritten paper label, faded and peeling — neither durable nor permanent. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 110.16(B): 110.16(B) now covers service equipment AND feeder-supplied equipment rated 1000A or more (was service equipment 1200A or more), and the permanent label must be an arc-flash label per applicable industry practice, with the date applied. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Servicing and maintenance of equipment
x: Start with the edition: this section does not exist in NEC 2020, the edition Florida enforces today. 110.17 is new in NEC 2023, and it sets the rules for servicing and maintaining electrical equipment: • Servicing and maintenance are done by qualified persons. Experience alone is not the standard — the person doing the work needs the training and knowledge the task and its hazards require. • The work is done per the manufacturer's instructions or listing information, industry standards, or as approved by the AHJ. • Replacement parts and components must be suitable for the equipment: identified for it, from the original manufacturer, designed by an engineer experienced in replacement parts for that equipment, or approved by the AHJ. Equipment gets serviced for decades after the install crew leaves. A will-fit part that almost matches, or a helper set loose on gear he was never trained on, turns a repair into the next failure — a lug that overheats, a breaker that will not trip, a fault nobody can clear. The rule ties the work to trained people and identified parts so a repair restores the equipment instead of quietly changing it. On service calls, Sharma already works this way: replace a failed component with the part identified for that equipment — the breaker type the Siemens panel is listed for, not one that happens to fit the stab. Treat unfamiliar gear, especially commercial switchgear, as a qualified-persons-only job until the right person is on it. On Florida permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026, this section is not yet the enforced text; it becomes the rule with the FBC 9th Ed. for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. Not in force on Florida jobs under NEC 2020 (permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026); know it for the NEC 2023 exam. FBC 9th Ed. (NEC 2023) applies to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. Two trap answers. First: “He has twenty years in the trade, so he is qualified to service anything.” The section measures training and knowledge for the task and its hazards, not years. Second: “A replacement part that physically fits is suitable.” It is not — unless it is identified for the equipment or comes through the original manufacturer, an experienced engineer, or the AHJ. Equipment serviced by a person with no training on that equipment or its hazards. Replacement breaker or component installed that is not identified for the equipment it went into. Will-fit replacement part with no manufacturer, engineer or AHJ basis behind it. Servicing done against the manufacturer's instructions or listing information. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 110.17: New section: only qualified, trained persons can service and maintain electrical equipment, and replacement parts have to be identified and verified to product standards. Only qualified persons, trained in servicing and maintaining equipment, can do that work. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Arcing parts
x: Some parts of electrical equipment arc in normal operation. Switch and breaker contacts open under load, contactors pull in and drop out, motor brushes ride a commutator — arcs, sparks, and sometimes molten metal are part of how the equipment works. 110.18 does not try to ban the arc. It controls where the arc may happen: • Parts that in ordinary operation produce arcs, sparks, flames, or molten metal must be enclosed, or separated and isolated from all combustible material. • An arc inside properly enclosed equipment is expected, and contained. • The same arcing part sitting open near material that can ignite is a fire waiting for its fuel. There is no distance in inches in this section. The test is a condition: enclosed, or separated and isolated. Every switching operation throws a small, very hot plasma event. Inside an enclosure it dies against metal. In the open — next to cardboard, paint, solvents, or stored household goods — it is an ignition source that fires on a schedule, every time the equipment cycles. Florida garages and storage rooms put the fuel and the arcing parts within the same few feet, which is exactly the pairing this rule breaks up. On a service call in a Marion Oaks garage, the pattern is familiar: a contactor or an old open switch with its cover long gone, cycling a load, with paint cans and cardboard stacked against the same wall. Keep enclosures intact around switching equipment. Put the cover back or replace the device, move the storage off the gear, and flag arcing or sparking equipment found open or mounted tight against combustible storage for correction before you leave. The trap is hunting for a number: 'how many inches from combustibles does 110.18 require?' It gives none — the rule is a condition, not a dimension. The second trap is calling arcing parts defects by themselves. They are normal in switching equipment; the violation is leaving them open to fuel, not the arc itself. Contactor or switch cover missing, arcing parts exposed beside stored paint and cardboard (110.18). Open arcing equipment mounted tight against combustible storage, with no separation or isolation (110.18). Brush-type motor run open next to hay, straw, or feed storage in a barn (110.18). Damaged enclosure left in service so the arcing parts inside are no longer enclosed (110.18). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Light and power from railway conductors (orientation)
x: 110.19 draws one hard line: circuits for lighting and power shall not be connected to any system that contains trolley wires with a ground return. • The ban is on the connection itself, not on the voltage. A ground-return trolley system carries its return current through the rails and the earth, and a building's lighting and power circuits must never be tied into that. • One exception: the connection is permitted in car houses, power houses, and passenger and freight stations operated in connection with electric railways — the railway's own buildings, run by the railway. • Nothing else in premises wiring uses this section. Railway power installations themselves sit largely outside the Code's scope (90.2). The page is in the book so the numbering of Article 110 reads complete, not as a working rule. A ground return puts traction current in the earth and in every buried metal path it can find. Tie a building system into that and you import stray current, shock exposure, and electrolytic corrosion of piping and conductors. The rule keeps two incompatible systems apart, and the exception stays inside buildings the railway itself operates, where the railway's own engineering controls both sides. Sharma does not design or install railway power, so the field case is a request, not an installation: on a commercial job near a rail corridor, someone proposes feeding site lighting or a temporary circuit from 'railway power' because it is close. The answer is the one this page exists for — stop and escalate. Temporary power comes from the premises service under the ordinary rules, engineered work stays engineered, and no Sharma circuit connects to a trolley ground-return system. The trap answer is that the connection is fine if the voltages match. 110.19 is not a voltage rule. It bans the connection to a ground-return trolley system outright, and the only exception is inside the railway's own car houses, power houses, and stations — not in any building that happens to stand near tracks. Lighting circuit found connected to a system that contains trolley wires with a ground return (110.19). Connection to a railway ground-return system made in an ordinary commercial building — not a car house, power house, or station (110.19). Premises wiring served from railway conductors as if they were a service, with no exception applying (110.19). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Reconditioned equipment
x: There is no 110.20 in NEC 2020 — this section is new in the 2023 NEC. Under the 2020 book, the only general reconditioned-equipment rule is the marking rule in 110.21(A)(2), plus scattered article rules such as 240.62 and 240.88. What the 2023 section adds, for permits under the FBC 9th Ed.: • It governs equipment that has been reconditioned — rebuilt or restored — as distinct from equipment that has merely been serviced or had a failed part replaced with an approved equal. • Reconditioned equipment has to be evaluated and accepted under the section's terms, and the party that reconditioned it has to be identifiable. • Some categories of equipment are restricted, or not permitted to be reconditioned at all. • A previous listing does not automatically survive an extensive rebuild. A rebuilt breaker or switchboard looks like the original from the outside, but its trip curve, bus plating and insulation carry a second, unknown history. Fires and failures traced to badly reconditioned gear are why the Code wants a name, a date and an evaluation behind every rebuild — so the person standing in front of the gear can tell a documented rebuild from a cleaned-up unknown. On commercial renovations, treat refurbished switchboards, panelboards and breakers as a question, not a bargain: who reconditioned it, under what evaluation, and is that category of equipment permitted to be reconditioned? Get the answer before it is set, not at inspection. On a tenant build-out, a 400 A refurbished switchboard is not set until the reconditioner's name and date are read off the gear and the evaluation paperwork is in the job file; on today's 2020 permits, the 110.21(A)(2) marking is the first thing to check and the AHJ has the final say. Not in force on Florida jobs under NEC 2020 (permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026). FBC 9th Ed. (NEC 2023) applies to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The trap is treating "reconditioned" and "serviced" as the same word. Swapping a failed breaker for an approved equal is service; a breaker that has been opened, rebuilt and restored is reconditioned, and it carries marking and acceptance duties. The second trap: assuming the original listing survives any rebuild. It does not. Reconditioned panelboard installed with no reconditioner's name or date marked on it — 110.21(A)(2). Original listing mark still displayed on rebuilt gear, passing the equipment off as new. Rebuilt breaker or switchboard set with no evaluation paperwork the AHJ can review. Equipment installed that its own article does not permit to be reconditioned. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 110.20: New section: reconditioned equipment is allowed unless another rule bans it, and it gets accepted through a listing, a field label, the original maker's instructions, or approval by the authority having jurisdiction. Reconditioned equipment is allowed unless a rule elsewhere in the code prohibits reconditioning that item. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Marking — manufacturer marks and field-applied hazard marks
x: Equipment carries the manufacturer's name and its ratings so the user can tell what it is and what it is rated for. • Where the Code requires a field-applied hazard marking, it has to be durable enough for its environment, use signal wording everyone recognizes, and not be handwritten where the Code requires a proper marking. • A faded or missing rating plate makes equipment hard to approve and harder to service safely. • Reconditioned equipment has its own marking rule at 110.21(A)(2): it must be marked with the name or trademark of the business that reconditioned it and the date of reconditioning, identified as reconditioned, and the original listing mark must be removed or voided — reconditioned gear is never passed off as new. Markings are the equipment's memory. The ratings tell the next electrician what the gear can take, and hazard marks warn the person about to open it. When a plate fades, or a rebuilt unit still wears its original listing mark, the next worker makes decisions from information that is no longer true. Do not paint over, cover or discard rating labels. When you add a required field marking, use a proper printed label suited to the location, not a marker scrawl. On a coastal service change, the exterior disconnect's rating plate was sun-bleached blank: the inspector could not verify the rating, and the service had to be re-documented from the manufacturer's records before it passed. Five minutes protecting a plate at rough-in beats that phone call. Exterior Florida labels fade fast. Use UV- and moisture-durable labels outside so required markings survive to the next inspection. The trap answer is that any legible mark will do — "DANGER" handwritten in marker on the disconnect. Where the Code requires a field-applied hazard marking, it must be a proper, durable marking with recognized signal wording, not handwriting. Second trap: leaving the original listing mark on reconditioned gear so it reads as new. That mark comes off or is voided. Field-applied hazard marking handwritten in marker where a proper marking is required. Rating plate painted over, covered or missing — the equipment cannot be identified or approved. Reconditioned breaker installed with no reconditioner name or date, and the original listing mark still showing. Exterior label faded illegible in the Florida sun — the required marking was not durable for its environment. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 110.21: Reconditioned gear has to show who rebuilt it, when, and that it's reconditioned. The original listing mark comes off or is made unreadable, but the nameplate can stay. Required: strip off the original listing mark or deface it so nobody can read it. The rest of the nameplate, ratings included, can stay. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Identification of disconnecting means
x: Every disconnecting means has to be legibly marked to show what it shuts off, unless the purpose is already obvious from where it sits and what it feeds. • The exception is narrow: no separate marking is needed only where the purpose is evident from the disconnect's location and arrangement. • The marking must be durable for its environment. A pencil scrawl that fades in a Florida garage is not durable. • On a multi-unit or multi-tenant job, each service disconnect and fault-protection device also has to show where its supply side comes from, so no one opens the wrong gear. The person opening a disconnect is often in a hurry — a technician chasing a fault, a firefighter killing power, a tenant after a flood. A missing or wrong label means the live circuit stays live while everyone believes it is dead, or the wrong equipment gets killed mid-process. Legible, durable, source-identified marking is what lets a stranger shut the right thing off the first time. Label every breaker and disconnect with its actual load — 'condenser', 'air handler 2', 'water heater' — not 'spare' labels on live circuits or a directory copied from another house. Update the directory whenever a circuit changes. On a four-plex trim-out in Kissimmee, that means a typed or permanent-marker card at punch, each unit's service disconnect marked with the source that feeds it, and the card re-done the same day any circuit moves — not at the next visit. The trap answer: 'everyone on this crew knows which disconnect is which.' The Code does not accept local knowledge. Unless the purpose is evident from the disconnect's location and arrangement, it gets a legible mark that is durable for its environment. The second trap: a directory that says 'lights / receptacles' on every line is marked — but it identifies nothing. Panel directory copied from another house — half the labels describe circuits that are not there. 'Spare' labels on live breakers that actually feed loads. Pencil directory faded to illegible in a damp Florida garage. Multi-tenant service disconnects with no marking showing where the supply side comes from. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 110.22: Outside one- and two-family dwellings, a disconnect's label now has to say where its supply source is located, not just which source feeds it. In commercial, industrial and multifamily buildings, each disconnect's label has to identify the panel or source feeding it and where that source sits. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Current transformers
x: This section covers current transformers used with electrical equipment, including how unused current transformers mounted in place are to be treated so their secondary circuits are not left in a hazardous state. • A CT steps a large primary current down to a small secondary current in exact ratio: a CT marked 400:5 delivers 5 A to the meter while the bus carries 400 A. • The secondary is not an ordinary circuit. It is built to work into a near-short — the meter burden, or a shorting device at a test block. • Current-transformer secondaries behave unlike ordinary branch-circuit conductors: an open-circuited secondary under load can produce dangerous voltage, which is why the section and the equipment instructions govern their handling. • An unused CT that stays mounted gets its secondary shorted and made safe — never left open. A current transformer stays tame only while its secondary current has somewhere to go. The primary and secondary ampere-turns balance each other; open the secondary and that balance disappears, the core saturates, and the transformer answers by driving the voltage at the open terminals up until something gives — insulation, an arc, or the person holding the leads. It is a metering device that turns into a voltage hazard the moment its loop is broken. Metered 800 A commercial service in Winter Garden: the CTs sit on the bus ahead of the meter. Swapping the meter, the tech shorts every CT secondary at the shorting block before lifting a single lead, and the spare CT mounted for a future tenant gets its secondary shorted and tagged — not left open. On metered commercial services, never open a CT secondary casually and never leave a mounted spare CT with its secondary open: follow the equipment instructions and this section, or hand it to the person who does this work regularly. The trap: 'the meter is off, so the CT secondary is dead.' Wrong. The primary bus is still carrying load, and the open secondary is exactly when a CT produces its dangerous voltage. A CT secondary is quiet only while it is shorted or connected to its burden — never because the meter stopped reading. Spare CT mounted on the bus with its secondary leads coiled up and left open. Meter pulled while CT secondary leads were lifted and left dangling, still live from the primary. Shorting link at the CT test block removed during testing and never replaced. Secondary leads cut during demolition while the service stayed energized. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Available fault current — field marking and documentation
x: 110.24 has two parts, and both are about one number — the maximum available fault current at the service: • 110.24(A) — marking: service equipment in other than dwelling units must be legibly marked in the field with the maximum available fault current and the date the fault-current calculation was performed. The marking must be durable enough for the environment, and the calculation must be documented and made available to those authorized to design, install, inspect, maintain or operate the system. • 110.24(B) — keep it current: when a modification to the installation changes the available fault current, the calculation is redone, the marking is updated, and the equipment ratings are rechecked. Dwelling unit service equipment is the exception — it does not have to carry this marking. Fault current is invisible, and it only ever goes up. Gear rated below the available fault current can fail violently instead of opening when a hard fault hits — that is the 110.9 problem, and 110.24 is how the next person finds out about it. The dated marking tells an inspector, a maintenance tech, or Sharma on a service upgrade whether the equipment in front of them still matches what the utility can deliver. On service changes, ask for the fault-current figure, mark it with its date, and check it against the interrupting ratings of the gear you are setting under 110.9. Keep the calculation with the job documents. On a small commercial service upgrade in Ocala, the utility's figures put the available fault current at 22 kA — the same worked example the 110.9 page uses. The crew field-marks the new Siemens service equipment “Available fault current: 22 kA” with the date of the calculation, files the calculation in the job folder, and confirms the breakers are 22 kAIC, not 10 kAIC. The old gear being replaced carried no marking at all — nobody could say what it was rated to interrupt. Utility transformer upgrades in growing Florida subdivisions are a common reason available fault current rises. Recheck on service upgrades in developed neighborhoods. Two traps. First: the marking is required on dwelling unit services — it is not; 110.24 applies to service equipment in other than dwelling units. Second: the number is marked once and forgotten — 110.24(B) requires the calculation, the marking and the equipment ratings to be revisited when a change alters the available fault current. No fault-current marking on a non-dwelling service at final inspection. Marking with no calculation date, or a date from the original build after a service change. Calculation performed but not documented, or not available to the inspector on request. Utility transformer upgrade raised the fault current and the gear was never rechecked — 10 kAIC breakers on a 22 kA service. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Lockable disconnecting means
x: Some rules in this Code do not ask for a disconnect in sight of the equipment. They ask for one that can be locked open instead. Section 110.25 sets what "lockable" has to mean wherever another rule uses that option: • The disconnect must be capable of being locked in the open position. • The provision for locking is part of the installation. It is installed with the disconnect and stays in place whether or not a padlock is on it today. • The person doing the work applies their own lock and keeps control of it while the work goes on. A breaker fitted with a listed lock-off device that lives on the breaker can meet this. A wrap of wire, a strip of tape, or a zip tie around a handle cannot: none of them is installed as part of the disconnect, and none of them stays in place when the lock comes off. And 110.25 does not create the option by itself — where the governing rule never offered a lockable route, the disconnect still has to be where that rule puts it. Lockout is how a servicer makes sure the equipment in front of them stays dead while their hands are in it. An improvised lock can fall off, be cut, or be ignored, and the circuit comes back with somebody still working on it. A permanent provision that is always there — lock or no lock — makes the safe move the easy move, every visit, for every tech who follows. On a Kissimmee service call, the air-handler blower's only disconnect was the breaker in the garage panel, about 70 ft away and out of sight. Article 430 allows that arrangement only where the breaker is capable of being locked open, so we fitted the breaker with a listed lock-off provision that stays mounted on it. The tech now hangs his own padlock before he climbs into the attic, and the provision is still there for the next visit. Wherever you rely on the lockable route instead of an in-sight disconnect, confirm the provision is real, permanent hardware before you trust it. The trap answer: "Any disconnect becomes lockable if you carry a padlock and hasp in the truck, so 110.25 is satisfied." No. The provision for locking must be installed and remain in place with or without the lock. The second trap is using 110.25 where the governing rule never offered a lockable option — it defines the word for the rules that do, like 430.102(B) and 440.14; it is not a stand-alone permission to move a disconnect out of sight. Motor disconnect out of sight and not lockable — the "lock" was a loop of wire wrapped around the breaker handle. Breaker lock-off device removed and never replaced, so the disconnect relied on as lockable could not be locked open. Locking provision does not hold the disconnect in the open position — the handle can still be closed with the device fitted. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Spaces about electrical equipment — the section as a whole
x: Sufficient access and working space must be provided and kept clear around electrical equipment so people can work on it safely and maintain it. The section is five parts that work together: • (A) Working space — the clear box in front of the equipment: depth from Table 110.26(A)(1); width 30 in or the equipment width; height 6½ ft or the equipment height; doors open at least 90°. • (B) Clear space — the working space is not storage space. It stays empty for the life of the installation, not just on inspection day. • (C) Entrance and egress — at least one way in and out. Equipment rated 1200 A or more and over 6 ft wide needs an entrance at each end; personnel doors near it open in the direction of egress with listed panic hardware. • (D) Illumination — light for the working space, and it may not be controlled by automatic means only. • (E) Dedicated equipment space — the equipment's own footprint, from the floor to 6 ft above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, indoors and outdoors. Foreign pipes and ducts stay out of it. Space that exists on rough-in day and is filled by the plumber's water heater later is not working space. Each part has its own page; this page is the map. Every part of 110.26 protects the same moment: a person working on live equipment who needs room to stand, light to see by, and a way out. Gear gets serviced for decades after we leave. If the space is gone, the next worker crowds the panel, works in the dark, or has no escape when something flashes. Defend the space from rough-in to final. On a Marion Oaks garage panel we tape the box on the slab at rough-in: 30 in wide, 3 ft out from the cover, floor to 6½ ft, plus the dedicated space above it running 6 ft over the panel. The builder's shelving and the plumber's water heater get drawn outside those lines before either trade sets anything. Coordinate early — once a water heater or shelving unit is set inside the panel's space, somebody is moving something, and it is cheaper if it is not us at final. S-09 back-to-back meter and panel is Sharma's preferred layout, and it still owes this section its full working space in front of the panel. The trap is treating 110.26 as one number — "3 ft in front of the panel." The depth is only part (A). A job can have its 3 ft and still fail: shelves in the clear space, a motion-sensor-only light, a duct through the dedicated space. Run backwards: at 0–150 V to ground the depth is 3 ft in all three conditions; the 3½ ft and 4 ft depths start at 151 V to ground. Water heater set inside the panel's working space after rough-in — the space existed on rough-in day only. Shelving and stored boxes sitting in the clear space in front of the switchboard. Duct run through the dedicated space above the panelboard. Electrical room light controlled by a motion sensor only — no manual way to keep it on. Panel door blocked from opening a full 90° by a door casing. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 110.26: Open doors on any equipment can't shrink the exit path below 24 inches by 6½ feet, working-space floors have to be flat as practical, and dedicated space now includes service equipment. Doors on any equipment, opened at once, can't leave less than 24 inches of width or 6½ feet of height to get in or out. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Working space about equipment
x: Electrical equipment that may need examination, adjustment, servicing or maintenance while energized must have a clear working space in front of it. Picture an invisible box standing on the floor in front of the panel: • Depth: from Table 110.26(A)(1), measured from the exposed live parts, or from the enclosure front when the parts are enclosed. At 0–150 V to ground (every 120/240 V house panel) it is 3 ft in all three conditions. • Width: 30 in or the width of the equipment, whichever is greater. The panel does not have to be centered in it. • Height: floor to 6½ ft, or the height of the equipment, whichever is greater. Doors and hinged panels must be able to open at least 90° inside that box. Above and below the panel, 110.26(E) adds the dedicated space: the panel's own width and depth, from the floor to 6 ft above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower. Pipes, ducts and other equipment foreign to the electrical installation stay out of it. Panels get worked hot: a breaker reset, a voltage check, a meter pull. A worker who cannot stand square, step back, or swing the door has no escape from an arc flash and nothing to stop a slip onto live bus. The box also guarantees the next electrician, years from now, can still reach the gear. Garage panel on a new slab home in Marion Oaks: the plumber wants the water heater beside the panel and the builder wants shelves on that wall. Tape it out at rough-in: 30 in wide wherever the panel sits, 3 ft out from the panel cover, floor to 6½ ft. The water heater goes outside that box and not under the panel, because the dedicated space runs from the floor up. On a small commercial job, a 480Y/277 V panelboard facing a concrete block wall is 277 V to ground and Condition 2, so the depth is 3½ ft, not 3 ft. S-09 prefers the meter outside and the panel inside, back to back, where the house allows. That layout still has to leave the 110.26 working space in front of the panel. A 120/240 V panel faces a concrete wall. Is that Condition 2, so 3½ ft? No. At 0–150 V to ground every condition is 3 ft; the 3½ ft and 4 ft depths start at 151 V to ground. Also watch for the width: 30 in is a minimum, not a zone centered on the panel. Water heater, shelving, or a washer and dryer parked inside the 30 in × 3 ft box. Panel cover that cannot swing a full 90° because of a door casing, a wall return, or a cabinet. Duct, soffit or plumbing run through the dedicated space above the panel. Panel in a bathroom or a clothes closet: separate rules (240.24(E) and (D)) that get written up on the same visit. Low soffit or stair over a panel in new construction. The reduced-height allowance in 110.26(A)(3) is only for existing dwelling units, 200 A or less. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 110.26(A)(6): Added a new list item (6) at 110.26(A) to address the working space conditions of the floor at electrical equipment locations, emphasizing a need to be clear of objects and level and flat as practical. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Depth of working space and the three conditions
x: Depth is read from Table 110.26(A)(1). The table sets the distance by two things: the voltage to ground, and what faces the worker across the space. • Condition 1: exposed live parts on one side of the space, with no live or grounded parts on the other side. • Condition 2: a grounded surface on the far side — concrete, brick, tile and masonry walls count as grounded. • Condition 3: exposed live parts on both sides of the space. At 0–150 V to ground the table gives 3 ft for all three conditions, so at house voltage the condition never changes the depth. The conditions only start to matter above 150 V: at 151–600 V to ground the depths are 3 ft, 3½ ft and 4 ft, and at 601–1000 V they are 3 ft, 4 ft and 5 ft. The worse the exposure across the aisle, the deeper the space must be once voltage makes the conditions diverge. Depth is the worker's reaction room. What stands across the aisle is what the worker falls against or reaches toward when something goes wrong: nothing at all (Condition 1), a grounded wall that completes the shock path (Condition 2), or more live parts (Condition 3). The higher the voltage to ground, the more distance the Code buys back — which is why the table's rows split only above 150 V. For a house panel on a wood-framed wall with nothing live across the aisle, Condition 1 and its 3 ft depth — at up to 150 V to ground — is the everyday case. A second panel facing the first makes it Condition 3, and it is still 3 ft at house voltage, because at 150 V or less to ground all three conditions read 3 ft. Where crews get caught is the small commercial panel: a 480Y/277 V panelboard facing a block wall is 277 V to ground in Condition 2, so the depth is 3½ ft — and the tape comes out at rough-in, not at inspection. Recheck the table whenever the voltage to ground goes above 150 V. The trap: "Two panels face each other, so the depth must be 4 ft — that is Condition 3." Not at house voltage. At 0–150 V to ground, Conditions 1, 2 and 3 are all 3 ft; the 4 ft Condition 3 depth starts in the 151–600 V row. Read the row first, then the condition. Working space 3 ft deep in front of a 480Y/277 V panelboard facing a concrete block wall — Condition 2 at 277 V to ground requires 3½ ft. Depth measured from the wall face instead of from the enclosure front or the exposed live parts. Condition 3 aisle, live parts on both sides, taped out at the Condition 1 depth on a 480 V job. Material staged inside the taped working-space depth before the inspection. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Width of working space
x: The width of the working space in front of electrical equipment is the width of the equipment or 30 in, whichever is greater. • A house panel is narrower than 30 in, so the 30 in minimum governs. • Wide switchgear sets its own width — a 48 in switchboard needs a full 48 in of clear width in front of it. • The equipment does not have to be centered in the space; it may sit offset within it, as long as the full required width is clear in front of the gear. • In all cases, the space must permit equipment doors and hinged panels to open at least 90°. • Like all working space, the width must be kept clear — it is not storage. Width is what lets a worker stand square to the gear instead of reaching across it sideways. Working at an angle, half behind a door casing or a water heater, is how a hand slips onto live parts. The full width also leaves room to swing the door wide and step back fast if something goes wrong. Marion Oaks house panel, 200 A Siemens, 16 in wide: the working width is 30 in, not 16. Tape the 30 in strip on the garage floor at rough-in and keep the water heater and the builder's shelving out of it — the panel can sit off-center in the strip, but the strip itself has to stay whole. On a small commercial job, a 48 in wide switchboard flips the rule: the clear width is the full 48 in of the gear. The trap is centering. The exam wants you to say the 30 in must be centered on the panel, or that a 16 in panel only needs 16 in of width. Neither is true: the width is 30 in or the equipment width, whichever is greater, and the equipment may be offset inside it. Water heater, shelving or storage inside the 30 in width in front of the panel. Only 30 in of clear width provided in front of switchgear that is wider than 30 in. Panel door or hinged cover that cannot open a full 90° because of a wall return or door casing. Working width narrowed after the panel was set, by a framed closet or soffit cutting into the strip. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Height of working space
x: The working space in front of equipment must run from the floor or platform up to a height of 6½ ft, or to the height of the equipment itself, whichever is greater: • Height: 6½ ft minimum, or the height of the equipment if the equipment is taller. • One everyday exception tempers the number: in existing buildings, smaller service equipment or panelboards — 200A or less, in dwelling-related installations — that do not meet the height may be permitted where the AHJ allows. • Meters and meter sockets may project into the space within limits. Equipment above the space — a sprinkler pipe or a duct that is not electrical — is a dedicated-space question under 110.26(E), not a reason to shrink the height. The height is work room and escape room at head level. A worker standing on a step in front of live parts, ducking under a soffit, is one startle away from falling into the bus. Framing and ductwork get built once; if they close over the panel location, every service call for the life of the building happens in a crouch. Six and a half feet is taller than most helpers pace it off — a standard door header sits right at the line. On a new Marion Oaks house, tape the height at the garage panel location before anything is framed: if a soffit or a duct is planned over that wall, it gets caught on paper, not at final. And the reduced-height exception is narrow — it applies only to existing dwelling units, never to new construction. The trap answer is that the height is always exactly 6½ ft. It is 6½ ft or the height of the equipment, whichever is greater — tall switchgear needs its full height cleared. The second trap is using the existing-building allowance on a new build: that allowance is for existing dwelling-related equipment of 200A or less, and only where the AHJ permits it. Soffit framed at 6 ft over a new panel location, closing down the working-space height. Duct dropped through the space above a panel in new construction. Existing-dwelling reduced-height allowance claimed on a new build. Tall switchboard installed with the working space stopped at 6½ ft, short of the equipment's own height. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Limited access — working space above ceilings and in crawl spaces
x: Where equipment of 1000V or less that is likely to need examination, adjustment, servicing or maintenance while energized has to sit in a limited-access space — above a lay-in ceiling, or in a crawl space — 110.26(A)(4) adjusts the usual working-space rules to the space that exists: • The access opening has a minimum size, with one minimum above a lay-in ceiling and a larger one for a crawl space. • The working-space width is the width of the equipment or a stated minimum, whichever is greater. • Enclosure doors and hinged panels must open to a stated minimum angle. • The depth in front of the equipment must meet Table 110.26(A)(1). • The height is capped at what is needed to install the equipment, and a horizontal ceiling structural member or an access panel is permitted in the space. The specific sizes behind those minimums are held off this page until they are checked against the printed book — see the Check in print box. Gear above ceilings and in crawl spaces still gets serviced, often energized — an air handler disconnect does not stop failing because it is hard to reach. Without access rules, the opening is whatever the ceiling grid happened to leave, the door cannot swing, and the tech works the gear lying across a grid wire with no room to pull back from a fault. Air handler disconnects and rooftop-unit equipment above T-bar ceilings are the everyday Florida case: plan the ceiling access and the door swing before rough-in, while the grid and the equipment layout can still move. A disconnect that lands where its door cannot open, or where nobody can get squarely in front of it, becomes a service call nobody can work safely — and a write-up nobody can fix cheaply once the ceiling is in. The trap answer is that the full standard working-space height applies unchanged above a ceiling. It does not: (A)(4) caps the height at what is needed to install the equipment and lets a horizontal ceiling structural member sit in the space. The second trap is quoting the opening and width numbers from memory — on this page, those numbers wait for the printed book. Disconnect above a lay-in ceiling behind an access opening too small to reach and service it — below the 110.26(A)(4) minimum. Enclosure door that cannot open to the required angle because the ceiling grid or a structural member blocks the swing. Equipment set in a crawl space with no real working width in front of it. Limited-access equipment placed where the depth in front falls short of Table 110.26(A)(1). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Clear space, entrance and egress, and illumination
x: Three parts of 110.26 ride along with the working-space box of (A): • (B) Clear space: the working space may not be used for storage. Space that is not kept clear is not working space. • (C) Entrance and egress: at least one entrance lets a worker get in and out without squeezing past the equipment. On large equipment — rated 1,200 A or more and over 6 ft wide — 110.26(C)(2) requires an entrance at each end of the working space, each at least 24 in. wide and 6½ ft high. • (C)(3) Personnel doors: a personnel door within 25 ft of the working space must open in the direction of egress and carry listed panic hardware or fire-exit hardware. • (D) Illumination: working spaces must be lit so the work is not done by flashlight, and the lighting may not be controlled by automatic means only. Automatic control may supplement a switch, but it cannot be the only control. These three parts protect the worker after the box is drawn. Storage creeps back into clear space a box at a time. In an arc event, a worker needs a way out that does not pass the gear that just failed. And a light that times out mid-task leaves both hands in the dark, inches from live parts. If the panel room doubles as storage, clear it before calling inspection. Check the light over the panel works, and flag any plumbing run directly above electrical gear — that conversation is much easier at rough-in than after a leak. On a small commercial fit-out with a 1,600 A switchboard, lay out both entrances to the electrical room at framing: once the walls are up, the second door is structural work, not an afterthought. The trap is the motion-sensor-only light: "the space is illuminated, so (D) is satisfied." It is not — control by automatic means only is exactly what (D) forbids. Second trap: one door for a 1,200 A lineup because the room has another door somewhere else. (C)(2) wants an entrance at each end of the working space. Working space used for storage — boxes, ladders and spare material parked in front of the panel (110.26(B)). Electrical room light on a motion sensor only, with no wall switch (110.26(D)). Personnel door within 25 ft of the gear swinging against egress, or without panic hardware (110.26(C)(3)). Lineup rated 1,200 A or more and over 6 ft wide with an entrance at only one end (110.26(C)(2)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Entrance to and exit from working space
x: There must be at least one entrance to and exit from the working space, sized and arranged so a worker can get in, work, and get out without squeezing past the equipment. • Large equipment — rated 1200A or more and over 6 ft wide, containing overcurrent, switching or control devices — needs one entrance to and egress from the working space at each end of the space. • Each of those entrances is at least 24 in. wide and 6½ ft high. • A single entrance is permitted where the egress is unobstructed, or where the working space depth is doubled per Table 110.26(A)(1). • Personnel doors: where equipment rated 800A or more containing overcurrent, switching or control devices is installed, a personnel door intended for entrance to and egress from the working space that is less than 25 ft from the nearest edge of the working space must open in the direction of egress and have listed panic hardware — so a worker reacting to an arc event pushes out instead of pulling a door against the blast. Working-space rules are escape rules. When gear faults, the worker in front of it has a fraction of a second and one direction to move: away. A single pinched entrance, or a door that must be pulled toward the blast, turns an arc event into a trap. The each-end rule exists because a lineup over 6 ft wide can block the near exit with the fault itself. Houses rarely trip the 1200A rule, but the one-entrance principle applies everywhere: never let a panel room get framed so the only way out is past the gear. On a Winter Park commercial job, the 1600A switchboard lineup is over 6 ft wide, so it gets a personnel door at each end of the working space — each at least 24 in. wide and 6½ ft high — and the doors swing out with listed panic hardware. Count the entrances at layout, and check the door swing and panic hardware before the doors are hung. The trap: "The switchboard room has a door, so entrance and egress are covered." For equipment rated 1200A or more and over 6 ft wide, one door is not enough — there must be an entrance at each end of the working space, unless the egress is unobstructed or the depth is doubled. The companion trap is the personnel door near big gear that swings in and carries a knob: within 25 ft of the working space of equipment rated 800A or more, the door must open in the direction of egress and have listed panic hardware. Switchboard rated 1200A or more and over 6 ft wide with an entrance at only one end of the working space. Personnel door within 25 ft of equipment rated 800A or more that swings into the room and has no listed panic hardware. Entrance to the working space at large equipment less than 24 in. wide or less than 6½ ft high. Working-space entrance blocked by stored material — no unobstructed way in or out. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Illumination
x: Illumination must be provided for the working spaces about service equipment, switchboards, switchgear, panelboards and motor control centers installed indoors — a worker reading a directory, a torque spec or a fault label cannot be expected to do it in the dark. • The light may not be controlled by automatic means only, so a motion-sensor-only setup that can strand a worker in darkness mid-task does not satisfy the rule; there has to be a manual way to keep the light on. • No additional lighting outlet is required where the working space is lit by an adjacent light source, or as permitted by 210.70(A)(1) Exception No. 1 for switched receptacles. Every other part of 110.26 assumes the worker can see: breaker labels, torque specs, fault stickers, the color of the conductor in hand. A light that dies on a timer or a sensor while both hands are in the gear turns a routine task into a guess — and guesses around live bus end in arc events. An indoor panel (garage, closet, utility room) needs its light; 110.26(D) does not require a light at an outdoor disconnect. If the only light on the plan is a motion sensor, flag it at rough-in — adding the manual control after trim is a return trip. On a garage rough-in, the plan showed one sensor-controlled fixture over the panel: caught early, a wall switch went in beside the door while the walls were still open. The trap answer: "There is a light, and it comes on automatically — that is better than a switch." (D) forbids control by automatic means only; a sensor may help, but a manual control has to exist. Second trap: adding a new lighting outlet where an adjacent light source already lights the space — (D) does not require one there. Electrical closet light controlled by a motion sensor only — no manual switch (110.26(D)). No illumination at all for the working space of an indoor panelboard. Sensor timeout leaves the space dark mid-task, with no way to hold the light on. Working space lit so poorly the directory cannot be read without a flashlight. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Dedicated equipment space
x: Indoor electrical equipment owns more than the floor it stands on — it owns the column of space above it. • The dedicated space is the width and depth of the equipment, from the floor up to 6 ft above the equipment, or up to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower. • No piping, ducts or other equipment foreign to the electrical installation may be located in that zone, except where the section itself allows it. • A suspended ceiling with removable panels does not count as the structural ceiling — the zone runs to the real structure above it. • Foreign systems are allowed above the dedicated zone, but 110.26(E)(1)(b) requires protection so leaks and condensation cannot drip onto the electrical equipment below. • Outdoor equipment has a matching dedicated zone of its own, measured from the equipment footprint with its own clearances. The space above a panel is exactly where the next trade wants to run — and where a leaking pipe does the most damage. Water dripping into live gear means corrosion, ground faults and eventually a fault inside the enclosure. Keeping the column clear also means the next electrician can open the gear and work it years later without another system's pipe in the way. New 200 A Siemens panel in a Marion Oaks garage: the panel is 16 in wide and its top sits at 5 ft 6 in. The dedicated zone is that width and the panel's depth, running from the floor to the 8 ft structural ceiling — lower than 6 ft above the equipment, so the ceiling caps the zone. The plumber's water line and the HVAC line set both route outside that column, and the condensate line that crosses above the zone still gets leak protection under 110.26(E)(1)(b), because a drip over a panel is a callback nobody wants. The trap answer is that the dedicated space ends at the top of the equipment, or at the drop ceiling. It runs 6 ft above the equipment or to the structural ceiling, whichever is lower — and a suspended ceiling with removable panels is not the structural ceiling. Water line, refrigerant line set or duct run through the dedicated space above the panel. Foreign piping above the dedicated zone with no protection against leaks or condensation dripping onto the equipment below — 110.26(E)(1)(b). Dedicated space measured only to a suspended lay-in ceiling, with foreign systems run between the ceiling panels and the structural ceiling. Another trade's equipment or stored material parked in the dedicated space above the gear. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Locked electrical equipment rooms or enclosures
x: 110.26(F) is one sentence at the head of the working-space rules: electrical equipment rooms or enclosures housing electrical apparatus that are controlled by a lock are considered accessible to qualified persons. • 'Accessible' is the Article 100 idea — the equipment can be approached and reached. The lock does not make the gear 'not accessible' to the people the Code counts. • It is accessible to qualified persons — the people trained for that equipment — not to everyone. The lock is what keeps it that way. • The sentence settles access only. It changes nothing else in 110.26: the working space in front of the gear, the clear space, and the dedicated space all still apply inside the locked room, exactly as they would in an open one. Live gear has to be reachable by the people qualified to work it, and unreachable by everyone else. Without this sentence, a locked door could be argued both ways — an owner claiming the gear is 'not accessible,' so working space does not apply, or an inspector treating a locked room itself as an access violation. The rule closes both arguments: lock the room, control the keys, and the qualified crew is deemed to have access. A small strip plaza on Silver Springs Boulevard in Ocala: the service room holds a 400 A switchboard and two panelboards, and the landlord keeps the door locked, with keys held by the property manager and by Sharma's foreman. That lock is fine — the room counts as accessible to qualified persons. What failed the walk-through was inside the room: paint cans and a ladder stored in front of the switchboard. The lock never waived the working space; the room has to be kept clear like any other gear location, and the key has to actually reach a qualified person when a breaker trips at night. The room is locked, so the equipment is not accessible and no working space is required? Wrong on both ends. 110.26(F) deems the locked room accessible to qualified persons, and the working-space rules apply in full inside it — the lock controls who gets in, it does not shrink the space. Locked electrical room used for storage — paint, ladders and spare material stacked in the working space in front of the gear. The only key held off-site by the owner, so no qualified person on the job can actually get in — access that exists only on paper. Key handed to unqualified staff to 'go reset the breaker' — accessible to qualified persons is not accessible to everyone. Gear roughed in with no working space because 'the room will be locked anyway.' No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Guarding of live parts
x: Live parts of electrical equipment operating at 50 volts or more must be guarded against accidental contact. The usual way is an approved enclosure — covers and deadfronts in place. Where that is not the method, 110.27(A) allows guarding by one of these means instead: • Location in a room, vault or similar enclosure that only qualified persons can enter • Permanent, substantial partitions or screens, arranged so only qualified persons can get within reach of the live parts • Location on a balcony, gallery or platform raised and arranged to shut out unqualified persons • Elevation above the floor or working surface: at least 8 ft for 50 to 300 volts, at least 8½ ft for 301 to 600 volts Entrances to rooms and guarded locations holding exposed live parts get conspicuous warning signs. Separately, 110.27(B): where equipment is likely to be exposed to physical damage, its enclosures and guards must be arranged and strong enough to prevent that damage. The person who eventually touches an exposed bus is rarely an electrician — it is a homeowner resetting a breaker in the dark, a cleaner, a kid, a tenant's handyman. Guarding assumes an unqualified person will end up in front of the gear sooner or later, and makes sure there is nothing for them to touch. Replace every cover you remove, the same day. An open panel with live bus exposed in an occupied building is a guarding failure even if it was only meant to be open for an hour. On a Sharma commercial job, a 120/240 V panelboard in a locked electrical room is guarded two ways at once — enclosure plus a room only qualified people enter. What fails in the field is the in-between case: cover off 'for troubleshooting,' door propped open, storage creeping into the room. Guarding by location only works while the location stays controlled. The trap is the threshold: many pick 480 V, or 'only where the public can reach it.' The rule starts at 50 volts — 120 V branch circuits and 277 V lighting parts are live parts too, and a locked room full of stored paint is not guarding by location anymore. Panel cover or deadfront removed and left off in an occupied space — live bus exposed to anyone who walks up. Electrical room door propped open and the room used for storage — guarding by location fails the moment anyone can wander in. No warning sign at the entrance to a room where live parts are guarded by location. Open live parts at reach height 'because only electricians go back there' — no enclosure, no lock, no partitions, no elevation. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Enclosure types
x: Enclosures are selected by type for the environment they will live in. Table 110.28 matches each type to the exposures it is built to withstand — indoor dust and dripping liquid, outdoor rain and sleet, hose-directed water, corrosion, and the like. The common field types run from a general indoor enclosure, through the rain-tight type crews see on house disconnects, to the corrosion-resistant types used in washdown and coastal work. The type marked on the enclosure — not its appearance — is what it is rated for. A higher-duty type may substitute for a lower one in many cases, but the marked type is the rating: never the paint, never the shape. An enclosure is the only thing between live parts and the weather the building actually gets. Put an indoor type on a Florida exterior wall and rain and salt air do the rest: rusted cans, water in the disconnect, failed gear. The type system exists so the match between box and exposure is a marking you can check, not a guess. Match the type to the real exposure. On a coastal Brevard County service, the meter enclosure and disconnect on the exterior wall are Type 3R at minimum — rainproof and sleet-resistant — and corrosion-resistant Type 4X earns its cost where salt spray reaches the gear. On a service call, a corroded or wrong-type enclosure is a replacement item, not a paint job: the rating was the marked type, and the marking is gone with the metal. Salt air makes enclosure type a live issue on Florida coastal work; corrosion-resistant types earn their cost outdoors near the coast. The trap: 'Type 4 is watertight, so it must handle the coastal job.' Watertight is not corrosion-resistant. Type 4 stops hose-directed water; the corrosion resistance that salt air demands is Type 4X. Reading one type's strength as another's is how the wrong can gets set. Indoor Type 1 enclosure installed on an exterior wall — not rated for rain. Disconnect enclosure corroded through in coastal service — the type was never matched to the exposure; replacement required. Unmarked enclosure accepted as rainproof on appearance — no type marking, no rating. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Equipment over 1000 volts — enclosure and access (overview)
x: 110.31 opens Part III of Article 110 — the added rules for installations over 1000 volts, nominal — with how the equipment is enclosed and how access to it is controlled. • The starting idea: an installation in a vault, room or closet, or in an area surrounded by a wall, screen or fence, with access controlled by a lock or other approved means, is considered to be accessible to qualified persons only. The enclosure is designed and constructed for the nature and degree of the hazard. • Indoors (110.31(B)): where the installation is accessible to unqualified persons, it is made with metal-enclosed equipment, and switchgear, transformers and similar equipment are marked with appropriate caution signs. • Outdoors (110.31(C)): a wall, screen or fence encloses the installation to deter access by unqualified persons. A fence is not less than 7 ft high, or a combination of 6 ft or more of fence fabric and a 1 ft or more barbed-wire extension. The distance from the fence to live parts is not less than Table 110.31 gives. • Vaults (110.31(A)) and enclosed equipment accessible to unqualified persons (110.31(D)) carry added rules of their own inside the section. Sharma rarely installs this class of work, so this page is an orientation marker rather than a working guide. Over 1000 V, a contact or an arc can kill before a protective device operates, and the people most at risk are often not electricians — they are the curious and the unqualified who wander in. Part III therefore starts with the barrier, the lock and the sign: keep everyone but qualified persons away from the gear entirely. If a commercial job crosses into over-1000V equipment, stop and escalate — design, guarding and access rules change materially, and this work is engineered and permitted differently from ordinary premises wiring. Sharma's field work on such a job is limited to what the engineered documents direct, inside the enclosures and access controls the design establishes — not field judgment. The trap is treating Part III gear like big premises wiring: ordinary access, ordinary judgment, 110.26 habits. Over 1000 V, the enclosure and access rules come first (110.31), the design is engineered, and the answer the exam wants is the Part III rule — metal-enclosed, locked, fenced and signed — not the house-panel habit. Electrical room for medium-voltage gear found unlocked, or the key kept beside the door — access is not controlled, so the qualified-persons-only basis fails. Outdoor fence below the required height, or the gate standing open: the 110.31(C) barrier must actually deter unqualified access. Caution signs missing from metal-enclosed switchgear and transformers in an indoor installation (110.31(B)). Storage and non-electrical material piled inside the fenced enclosure, against the equipment the fence is protecting. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 110.30-110.41: The over-1000V material was reorganized into new articles: 235 (branch circuits, feeders and services over 1000V ac / 1500V dc), 245 (overcurrent protection over 1000V), 305 (wiring methods over 1000V), 315 (medium-voltage conductors and cable, formerly 311), 395 (outdoor overhead conductors over 1000V, formerly 399) and 495 (equipment over 1000V, formerly 490). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Working space, entrances and guarding over 1000 volts (110.32–110.34)
x: Part III continues with the working-space rules for over-1000V equipment — the same concerns as 110.26, in a class of work where the consequences are far worse. • 110.32 sets the working space about the equipment. • 110.33 covers entrances to and exits from the working space, including entrance size and panic hardware. • 110.34 covers the depth of working space (Table 110.34(A) by reference), guarding of live parts, and illumination. The depths and dimensions live in the printed tables and the design documents — this page is the map, not the numbers. No value from these three sections is published here: until the page is checked against the printed NEC 2020, every dimension waits in print. At these voltages the working space is escape space: room to stand square, room to step back, and a door that opens under pressure when a worker is backing away from trouble. Entrances, guarding and illumination sit in the same group of sections because a perfect clearance is worthless if the worker cannot reach it, cannot leave it, or cannot see in it.
