Doorways are the opposite: they break the run and the 6 ft count starts over at the jamb. A 2 ft wall piece between two doors left with no receptacle. First receptacle more than 6 ft from a door jamb or fireplace edge. Floor receptacle set 3 ft out from the wall counted toward the wall spacing. Receptacle above 5½ ft counted as a required outlet. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Small-appliance circuits — what they may feed
x: The two (or more) 20A small-appliance branch circuits serve the receptacle outlets in the kitchen, pantry, breakfast room and dining room — and only those. A receptacle for refrigeration equipment in those rooms may ride on one of them. The only other outlets allowed are a clock receptacle and receptacles used for supplemental equipment on a gas-fired range, oven or cooktop. A receptacle in the living room, a bathroom receptacle, or the kitchen lighting may not be added to these circuits, and these circuits may not wander off to feed outlets in other rooms. Refrigeration equipment may instead be fed from an individual branch circuit rated 15A or more (210.52(B)(1) Exception No. 2). Countertop appliances are the heaviest portable loads in the house — kettles, toasters, air fryers, coffee makers — and two of them on one circuit is a normal breakfast. Keeping the small-appliance circuits exclusive to the food-prep rooms means those loads never share a circuit with lighting or with receptacles across the house, and the two circuits can be balanced along the counter. Let one of these circuits wander, and both the protection and the load spreading the rule was built on are gone. Lay out the two circuits before rough-in so the countertop receptacles alternate between them (that layout rule is on the 210.52(C) page). Sharma rule S-06 puts the microwave on its own 20A circuit. Code-wise, a countertop microwave may plug into a small-appliance circuit; a fastened-in-place over-the-range microwave may not be fed from one (210.52(B)(2)). The trap is the refrigerator: many pick 'the fridge can never be on a small-appliance circuit.' It may — or it can have its own individual branch circuit rated 15A or more. The real bars are the kitchen lighting and a fastened-in-place microwave: neither may ride on these circuits. Kitchen lighting tied into a small-appliance branch circuit. Small-appliance circuit extended to feed a receptacle outside the kitchen, pantry, breakfast or dining room. Fastened-in-place over-the-range microwave plugged into a small-appliance circuit. Only one 20A small-appliance circuit provided for the kitchen receptacles. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Kitchen countertops, islands, and peninsulas
x: Countertop receptacles are placed so no point along the wall line of a counter is more than 24 in from a receptacle, and a counter run 12 in or wider needs one. Countertop space separated by a range, cooktop, refrigerator, or sink counts as a separate countertop space — each separated run gets its own 24 in spacing check. A receptacle installed above a countertop may sit no more than 20 in above the counter surface, and a receptacle placed face-up in a work surface must be a listed assembly for that use. Islands and peninsulas are counted by countertop area in the 2020 edition: • One receptacle for the first 9 sq ft of island or peninsular countertop, or fraction of it • One more receptacle for each additional 18 sq ft, or fraction of it So a 30 sq ft island needs three: one for the first 9, one for the next 18, and one for the remaining 3. A peninsular countertop also needs at least one receptacle within 2 ft of its outer end, measured from the connecting wall (210.52(C)(2)). Countertop appliance cords are short. Stretch one across a sink or a cooktop and it becomes a burn and shock hazard; leave no outlet within reach and an extension cord moves in instead. The 24 in rule keeps every cord short and direct, and the island area count puts receptacles where people actually set appliances down, even where there is no wall to mount them on. Count island area from the actual countertop drawing, including an overhang that is part of the work surface, and confirm the count before rough-in — adding an island receptacle after cabinets are set is the expensive version. A 10 ft by 3 ft island is 30 sq ft, so it takes three receptacles under the 2020 count. Under the 2020 rules an island or peninsula receptacle may sit on or above the counter, or below it — not more than 12 in below the countertop, where the counter extends not more than 6 in beyond its supporting base (210.52(C)(3)). Reaching for the 2023 rule on a 2020 permit. Under NEC 2020, island and peninsula receptacles are required and counted by area — first 9 sq ft, then one per additional 18 sq ft. “No longer required” is a 2023 change and lives in the edition box. The second trap: counting the island by length instead of by countertop area. 30 sq ft island roughed with a single receptacle — the 2020 area count requires three. A point along the counter wall line more than 24 in from the nearest receptacle. Island receptacle mounted more than 12 in below the countertop on the cabinet side. Face-up receptacle in the work surface that is not a listed assembly. Peninsular countertop with no receptacle within 2 ft of its outer end. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 210.52(C): Island and peninsula receptacles are no longer required. If installed they must be above or in the countertop/work surface (not on the side below the counter); if none is installed, a provision for a future receptacle must be provided at the island or peninsula. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bathroom receptacles
x: Each bathroom needs a receptacle close to every basin: within 3 ft of the outside edge of the basin, on a wall or partition next to it, on the countertop itself in a listed assembly, or on the side or face of the basin cabinet — and in no case more than 12 in below the top of the basin or countertop. A double vanity has two basins and needs the requirement met for each one. One receptacle placed between two basins can serve both, but only if it is within 3 ft of the outside edge of each. This placement rule works alongside two more rules at the same sink: • Circuit: at least one 20 A bathroom circuit serves the bathroom receptacles (210.11(C)(3)). • Protection: bathroom receptacles are GFCI protected (210.8(A)(1)). All three have to be satisfied at the same time, at every basin. Hair dryers, curling irons and electric razors live at the sink, in wet hands, over a hard floor. A receptacle placed where the appliance is actually used keeps cords short and out of the water — and the GFCI protection required at the same spot is what protects the person when something goes wrong. Measure from the basin's outside edge, not from the center of the faucet and not from the cabinet edge. On a long double vanity, one receptacle in the middle may not be within 3 ft of both basins — check both. On a 72 in double vanity in a Marion Oaks primary bath, the basins sit near the ends: a receptacle at the far left end of the counter is more than 3 ft from the right-hand basin and fails it. Centered between the basins, the same receptacle is within 3 ft of each one and passes. Tape the 3 ft reach on the wall at rough-in, before the boxes are set. The tape comes out and the measurement is taken from the center of the faucet, or from the middle of the basin. Both are wrong: the 3 ft runs from the outside edge of the basin. The second trap is 'one receptacle per bathroom' — the rule runs per basin, so a double vanity may need the requirement met twice. Receptacle 3 ft from the faucet center but more than 3 ft from the basin's outside edge. One receptacle centered on a wide double vanity, beyond the 3 ft limit of the far basin. Basin receptacle on the cabinet face, more than 12 in below the top of the countertop. Bathroom receptacle landed on a lighting circuit instead of the 20 A bathroom circuit. No GFCI protection at the bathroom receptacle. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Outdoor receptacles for a dwelling
x: 210.52(E) puts receptacles outside the house, where people actually plug things in — trimmers, pressure washers, holiday lights, a radio on the lanai. • One- and two-family dwellings, 210.52(E)(1): at least one receptacle at the front and one at the back of the dwelling. Each must be readily accessible from grade and not more than 6½ ft above grade. • Balconies, decks and porches, 210.52(E)(3): a balcony, deck or porch of 20 sq ft or more in overall area that is accessible from inside the dwelling needs a receptacle too, not more than 6½ ft above its walking surface. • Multifamily dwellings, 210.52(E)(2): each dwelling unit with direct access to grade gets its own outdoor receptacle. 'Readily accessible from grade' is part of the rule — a receptacle that can only be reached by a ladder or through a locked gate does not serve the purpose. Height is measured from the grade at that wall, which matters on a sloped lot. Yard tools and holiday lights get plugged in outside whether or not a receptacle is there. Without one, the cord runs through a window or a door — pinched, weather-exposed, and often an extension cord across a walkway. The front-and-back rule puts a receptacle within a normal cord's reach on both sides of the house, and the 6½ ft cap keeps it usable by a person standing on the ground. Marion Oaks spec house on a sloped lot: the back wall drops toward the drainage swale, so the grade at the back receptacle sits almost 2 ft lower than at the front. Set the back box by measuring 6½ ft up from the soil at that wall, not by copying the front box height off the slab — copying it leaves the back receptacle out of reach from grade. The covered lanai off the living room is 10 ft × 14 ft (140 sq ft) and opens from inside, so it gets its own receptacle within its perimeter, 6½ ft or less above the lanai deck. Front and back receptacles are GFCI-protected under 210.8(A)(3), weather-resistant, with in-use covers. Florida lots often slope toward drainage swales; measure the 6.5 ft from the grade at the receptacle, and confirm any local amendment with the AHJ. The exam shows a receptacle 6 ft above the slab and asks if it passes on the downhill side of a sloped lot where grade falls 18 in below the slab. It does not: height is measured from grade at that wall, so it sits 7½ ft above grade — over the 6½ ft limit. The other trap is counting the garage receptacle as the back receptacle; the rule wants one at the front and one at the back of the dwelling, accessible from grade. Back of the house has no receptacle at all — only the front was roughed in. Receptacle mounted 7 ft above grade at the back wall of a sloped lot; not reachable by a person standing on the ground. Covered lanai of 140 sq ft, accessible from inside, with no receptacle within its perimeter. Outdoor receptacle behind a locked gate or inside a fenced pool enclosure, so it is not readily accessible from grade. Outdoor receptacle fitted with a flat cover that cannot stay closed with a cord plugged in. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Laundry receptacles
x: In a dwelling unit, at least one receptacle outlet must be installed in the area designated for laundry equipment — a laundry room, a laundry closet, or the utility corner where the machines sit. A laundry closet counts the same as a laundry room for this placement rule. • The circuit: the receptacle is served by the laundry branch circuit of 210.11(C)(2) — a 20 A circuit that supplies the laundry receptacle outlet(s) and no other outlets. • The placement: an appliance receptacle outlet installed for a specific appliance, such as the washer, must be within 6 ft of the intended location of the appliance (210.50(C)). • The exception: in a multifamily building where laundry facilities are provided on the premises for use by all occupants, the receptacle is not required inside each dwelling unit. The 240 V dryer receptacle is a separate, larger outlet on its own circuit. It is not the receptacle this subsection requires — this one is the general laundry receptacle, usually the washer's. The washer is a motor load that runs an hour at a time in a room with water lines, a floor drain and a slab floor. A dedicated 20 A circuit keeps that steady load from sharing a circuit with whatever else gets plugged in, and the 6 ft placement rule means the machine's own cord reaches the receptacle — not an extension cord run across a wet floor. Laundry areas sit on both protection lists for the same reason: GFCI in 210.8(A) and AFCI in 210.12(A). Marion Oaks spec house, laundry room between the garage and the kitchen. One duplex receptacle goes on the wall behind the washer, about 2 ft from the machine's intended spot — well inside the 6 ft limit — on the dedicated 20 A laundry circuit, protected by a dual-function breaker under S-07, which answers both the GFCI and the AFCI listing for the area. The dryer sits beside it on its own 240 V circuit. On the plan revision that swaps the machines to the opposite wall, the receptacle moves with the washer and stays on the laundry circuit. A receptacle borrowed from the adjacent hallway circuit fails both the placement rule and the circuit rule, so it never counts. The trap answer is that the 240 V dryer receptacle satisfies 210.52(F). It does not: the subsection requires the general laundry receptacle, and 210.11(C)(2) requires that receptacle on the 20 A laundry circuit. The dryer outlet is a different outlet on a different circuit. No receptacle in the laundry area at all — the hallway receptacle outside the door offered as 'close enough.' It is in the wrong area and on the wrong circuit. Laundry receptacle tapped off the bathroom or hallway circuit instead of the 20 A laundry circuit. Laundry circuit also feeding a garage or outdoor receptacle. 210.11(C)(2) allows no other outlets. Washer receptacle left more than 6 ft from the machine after a plan revision moved the washer and dryer to the opposite wall. The 240 V dryer receptacle counted as the required 210.52(F) laundry receptacle. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Garage receptacles — one per vehicle bay
x: In the 2020 edition, a dwelling garage with electric power needs at least one receptacle in each vehicle bay, placed no more than 5.5 ft above the floor. Count bays, not garages: the bay rule replaced the older single-garage-receptacle habit, so a three-bay garage is not finished with one receptacle by the door. Attached and detached garages are both covered, and a garage with no electric power is outside the requirement. Subsection (G) — Basements, Garages, and Accessory Buildings — carries the matching receptacle minimums for unfinished basements and accessory buildings in the same place. Two companion rules ride along: the required garage receptacles are served by the dedicated 20 A garage circuit of 210.11(C)(4), and garage receptacles need GFCI protection under 210.8(A)(2). Every bay is a parking space and a workplace at once: battery chargers, air compressors, freezers and the tools that come out on weekends. One receptacle by the door meant extension cords run across bays, under tires and through door tracks — cords get pinched, driven over and overloaded. A receptacle in each bay puts the outlet where the vehicle and the work are, and the 5.5 ft cap keeps it a working receptacle within reach, not the ceiling outlet installed for the door opener. Count bays from the door layout on the plan, not from how the owner says they will park. Three overhead doors in a Marion Oaks garage means three bays and three receptacles at rough-in — Sharma sets them at 4 ft above the slab, inside the 5.5 ft limit — all on the dedicated 20 A garage circuit, with GFCI protection at the breaker. Put one receptacle in each bay at rough-in; adding the third bay's receptacle at trim is a drywall patch. The trap answer is one receptacle for the whole garage — the pre-2020 habit this rule replaced. The count follows the bays: three bays, three receptacles. Close behind it is counting the door-opener receptacle on the ceiling, which sits above the 5.5 ft limit and never counts. One receptacle by the pedestrian door for a three-bay garage. The rule is one per vehicle bay. Ceiling receptacle for the door opener counted as a bay receptacle. Above 5.5 ft, it does not count. Security-system receptacle counted as the bay receptacle — the very practice the NEC 2023 clarification calls out. Garage receptacles tapped off a general lighting circuit instead of the dedicated 20 A garage circuit. Garage receptacles with no GFCI protection. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 210.52(G): Clarified that the receptacle provided for premises security systems did not meet the receptacle requirements of 210.52(G). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Hallway receptacles
x: A dwelling hallway that is 10 ft or longer needs at least one receptacle outlet. The rule is 210.52(H), and the measurement decides it: length is measured along the centerline of the hallway, following its turns, without passing through a doorway into another room. • Measure along the centerline, around bends — an L-shaped or U-shaped hall adds its legs together • Do not measure through a doorway: length inside the rooms at each end does not count • 10 ft or more: at least one receptacle. Under 10 ft: none required by this subsection • The receptacle goes in the hallway itself, not in a room off it Short halls need none under this subsection, which is why the measurement — not a guess at 'about ten feet' — decides it. One receptacle is the minimum; a long hall can take more, and a floor receptacle counts toward a required outlet only when it is within 18 in of the wall (210.52(A)(3)). Hallways are where the vacuum, the night-light and the phone charger land, and they are also the walking path. Without a receptacle, the cord comes from a bedroom or living room outlet, crosses a doorway, and becomes a trip hazard and a damaged-cord hazard in the dark. The 10 ft line keeps short halls simple while making sure a long hall is never a cord run. L-shaped hall in a Marion Oaks ranch: 7 ft from the entry to the bend, 5 ft from the bend to the last bedroom door — 12 ft along the centerline, so it needs one receptacle even though the straight-line distance is shorter. Run the tape down the centerline and around the bend of an L-shaped hall before deciding. Set the receptacle near the middle of the run so a vacuum cord reaches both ends. Vacuum and night-light use is exactly what this receptacle is for. The straight 9 ft hall in the same plan needs none. The wrong answer measures the hall straight through the bedroom doorway, or corner to corner as the crow flies, and calls a 12 ft L-shaped hall 'about 9 ft, no receptacle needed.' The tape follows the centerline and stops at doorways: legs add up, room length does not. No receptacle in an L-shaped hallway that measures 12 ft along the centerline; the crew measured corner to corner and called it 9 ft. Hallway length figured through the doorway into the bedroom to reach 10 ft, with the only receptacle inside the bedroom. The one hallway receptacle is a floor receptacle more than 18 in from the wall, counted as the required outlet. Receptacle for a 14 ft hall placed in the laundry room off the hall instead of in the hallway itself. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Foyer receptacles
x: Most entries are judged by the hallway rule or by the spacing rule of the room they open into, but a large foyer has its own rule. This subsection applies when both are true: • The foyer is not part of a hallway • The foyer is greater than 60 sq ft Then a receptacle outlet is required in each wall space 3 ft or more in width, on walls not interrupted by door openings, other openings, or similar architectural features. A wall that is mostly front door creates no wall space, and a stub of wall under 3 ft wide needs no receptacle under this subsection. A smaller foyer, or a foyer that forms part of a hallway, is judged under the hallway rule in 210.52(H) — a hallway 10 ft or longer needs at least one receptacle — or under the spacing rule for the room it opens into instead. A large foyer works like a room: console tables, lamps, a phone charger and the vacuum all land there. With no receptacle on a usable wall, the answer is a cord across the entry — the highest-traffic walking path in the house. The 60 sq ft threshold keeps this rule off the small entries that the hallway rule already handles. Marion Oaks two-story plan: the foyer is 8 ft by 9 ft — 72 sq ft — and a cased opening separates it from the hall, so 210.52(I) applies, not the hallway rule. Walk the walls at rough-in. The long wall beside the stairs is unbroken, so it takes a receptacle. The wall piece between the closet door and the corner is 3 ft wide, exactly at the minimum, so it takes one too. The wall taken up by the front door and its sidelight is interrupted and needs none, and the 2 ft stub beside the cased opening needs none. Measure the foyer as its own space while the framing is open, when the wall spaces can still be proved with a tape. The trap answer spaces the foyer like a living room under 210.52(A), measuring 6 ft from every point along the wall. A qualifying foyer is not spaced that way: each wall space 3 ft or wider gets a receptacle, full stop. The second trap runs the other way — applying this subsection to a 50 sq ft entry. At 60 sq ft or less, or where the foyer is part of a hallway, 210.52(I) never applies. Foyer over 60 sq ft with no receptacle on a wall space 3 ft or wider. Receptacle placed on a wall segment that is mostly door opening, while the qualifying wall space got none. Foyer receptacles skipped because the entry was treated as part of the hallway, without measuring either space. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: A service receptacle near heating and air-conditioning equipment
x: For equipment that needs servicing, this section puts a receptacle within reach of it. The receptacle must be: • Rated 125V, single-phase, 15A or 20A • In an accessible location • On the same level as the equipment • Within 25 ft of the equipment • Not connected to the load side of the equipment disconnecting means The last point is the one that gets missed. If the receptacle dies with the disconnect, the tech is working dark with a dead drop light exactly when the unit is open. Wired ahead of the disconnect, the receptacle stays live for a work light and tools while the equipment itself is shut off. Rooftop units and attic air handlers are the cases Sharma meets most: both are places where the nearest house receptacle is far away, on another level, or both. A technician troubleshooting an air handler needs light and power for meters, a vacuum pump and a drill. Without a receptacle nearby, the answer is an extension cord through a scuttle hole or across a roof — a trip hazard and a damaged-cord hazard — or working in the dark. The same-level, 25 ft limit keeps the cord short and on the same working surface as the unit being serviced. Marion Oaks spec house, air handler in the attic over the garage. At rough-in, set the service receptacle on a joist beside the attic access, on the same attic level as the handler and 12 ft from it along the walkway boards — inside the 25 ft limit with room to spare. Feed it from a house circuit, never from the load side of the handler disconnect. The condenser outside gets the same check: a receptacle on the house wall 8 ft from the pad, at the same grade level, tape-measured along the wall and the access path, not through the wall. Prove both distances with a tape before the inspector does. The trap answer puts the receptacle on the load side of the equipment disconnect, 'so it shuts off with the unit for safety.' That is exactly backwards: 210.63 forbids the load-side connection so the receptacle stays live while the equipment is off. Second trap: measuring 25 ft straight through a wall, or down from a roof edge to a ground outlet. The receptacle must be on the same level, so a ground-level outlet below a rooftop unit never counts. No receptacle within 25 ft of the rooftop unit or the attic air handler at final inspection. Receptacle wired to the load side of the equipment disconnect, so it dies when the unit is shut off. Receptacle on a different level: a garage outlet claimed for attic equipment. Receptacle installed but blocked behind the air handler or duct, where it is not accessible. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Lighting outlets and wall switches
x: 210.70 decides where a dwelling must have lighting outlets and the wall switches that control them. The point throughout is simple: a person should never have to cross a dark room or a dark stair to reach a switch. • Habitable rooms, kitchens and bathrooms (210.70(A)(1)): at least one wall switch-controlled lighting outlet in each room. In habitable rooms other than kitchens and bathrooms, a switch-controlled receptacle may stand in for the lighting outlet. • Additional locations (210.70(A)(2)): hallways, stairways, attached garages and detached garages with electric power each carry their own switch rules. On a stairway, the light is controlled from each floor level and landing with an entry — a switch at the bottom and one at the top, as drawn. • Storage and equipment spaces (210.70(A)(3)): attics, underfloor spaces, utility rooms and basements used for storage, or holding equipment that needs servicing, get at least one lighting outlet, with control at the usual point of entry. Read each room by its use, not by the name written on the plan. Falls on stairs and in dark garages happen in the seconds before a light comes on. A switch at the point of entry — and at both ends of a stair — means the light is on before the first step, not after a walk across a dark room hunting for a lamp with a pull chain. The same rule puts light where the air handler and water heater get serviced, so nobody works by flashlight. Walk the plan of a Marion Oaks house as a person arriving at night. Front door: a switch inside the entry for the foyer light. Hall: a switch where you enter it. Stairs to the bonus room: a switch at the bottom landing and one at the top, three-way, so the stair is lit from either end before the first step. Kitchen, each bathroom and each bedroom: a wall switch by the door, with switch boxes set at 48 in to center where the plan is silent (S-05). Attached garage: a switch by the house door for the garage light. If any leg of that walk is in the dark, a switching rule has probably been missed — find it at rough-in, not at final walk. S-05: switch boxes at 48 in to center when the plan is silent. The trap is the switched receptacle: it may stand in for the lighting outlet in a living room or a bedroom, but not in a kitchen or a bathroom — those rooms need a real lighting outlet on a wall switch. Second trap: one switch at the bottom of the stairs only. A stairway light must be controllable from each floor level and landing it serves — the top needs a switch too. Stairway light with a switch at the bottom landing only — nothing at the top. Kitchen or bathroom roughed with a switched receptacle instead of a wall switch-controlled lighting outlet. Hallway or attached garage with a light but no wall switch where you enter. Attic, basement or utility space holding equipment with no lighting outlet, or no switch at its entry. Habitable room whose only light control is a battery remote, with no wall-mounted control at the entrance. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 210.70: Dwelling laundry areas now need a wall-controlled lighting outlet, battery-only controls must fail with the lights on, outdoor doors need a real exterior light, and bulkhead doors got their own allowance. Dwelling laundry areas join habitable rooms, kitchens and bathrooms: each needs a lighting outlet on a listed wall-mounted control near an entrance (210.70(A)(1)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Feeders — power between the service and the final panels
x: A feeder carries power from service equipment, a transformer, or another source to the panelboards where branch circuits begin. The name matters, because each run in a building is judged by the article that matches its name: • Service conductors — Article 230 • Feeders — Article 215, sized on the Article 220 load, protected under Article 240, with the equipment grounding conductor from Article 250 • Branch circuits — Article 210 Article 215 itself is short: feeder conductor sizing (215.2), feeder overcurrent protection (215.3), and ground-fault protection for certain large feeders (215.10). Most feeder questions on a Sharma job are really answered together with Article 220 for the load, Article 240 for the protection, and Article 250 for the grounding conductor that runs with it. Name the run correctly on the schedule, because the sizing and grounding rules change with the name. A feeder is the single path feeding a whole panel. Undersize it or under-protect it and every branch circuit behind it is at risk, with the full service behind a feeder fault. The feeder rules make the conductor, its overcurrent device and its grounding conductor one matched set, sized from the calculated load instead of from whatever panel happened to be on the truck. Service change on a Marion Oaks house: new Siemens meter-main outside (S-02), house panel back to back with it where the house allows (S-09). The short run from the meter-main to the indoor panel is a feeder, not service conductors — the service disconnect is in the meter-main. So it is wired like a feeder: four wires, the neutral isolated in the indoor panel, and an equipment grounding conductor run with it, sized from Table 250.122 by the feeder breaker. The sizing habit is the same on a bigger job: a feeder carrying 80 A of noncontinuous load plus 40 A of continuous load needs at least 130 A of conductor ampacity under 215.2 — 80 plus 125 percent of 40 — before derating is even discussed. S-02 and S-09 frame Sharma feeder work: new gear is Siemens, and the house panel normally sits back to back with the meter where the house allows. The trap is calling the run from an outdoor meter-main to the indoor panel 'service conductors' and bonding the neutral again in the indoor panel. Past the service disconnect, the run is a feeder: neutral and ground stay separate, and the main bonding jumper lives at the service disconnect only. Second trap: sizing the feeder from the panel's bus rating. A feeder is sized from the Article 220 calculated load, with 125 percent of the continuous part added (215.2). Neutral bonded to ground again in a subpanel fed by a feeder — bonding screw or strap left in. Feeder conductors sized from the panel bus rating instead of the Article 220 calculated load. No equipment grounding conductor run with the feeder, or one sized by guess instead of Table 250.122. Feeder breaker rated above the conductor ampacity with no Article 240 allowance that fits the job. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 215.15: Panelboards, switchboards, switchgear and motor control centers supplied through feeder taps or transformer secondaries now need barriers over line-side bus and terminals that stay live with the disconnect open. • 215.18: New in 2023: a feeder that supplies a dwelling unit, dorm unit, hotel or motel guest room, or nursing home sleeping room needs a surge-protective device (SPD) at the panel it feeds. Feeders to dwelling units, dorm units, hotel or motel guest rooms and suites, and nursing home or limited-care patient sleeping rooms now need an SPD. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Feeder conductor size and the continuous-load rule
x: Feeder conductors must have ampacity at least as large as the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load, before derating and correction are worked through, unless a listed assembly rated for continuous operation is used. Feeders supplying a dwelling's whole load may also be sized under the dwelling service and feeder table covered in Chapter 3, which is why a house feeder is not always sized from the general ampacity table alone. The calculated load itself comes from Article 220. A continuous load runs for three hours or more, and heat is what ages insulation and loosens terminations. A conductor loaded to its full ampacity all day, every day, lives at its temperature limit with no margin for a hot Florida attic or a terminal that ends up a quarter-turn loose. The 125 percent step builds the margin in before derating even starts, so the finished feeder runs cool enough to last the life of the building. Do the Article 220 number first, then size the feeder — never size from the size of the panel that happens to be on the truck. Write the continuous portion down separately so the 125 percent step can be checked. Worked example: a feeder carrying 80A of noncontinuous load plus 40A of continuous load needs conductor ampacity of at least 80 + (40 × 1.25) = 130A before correction and adjustment factors are applied. If the math is not written down in that form, the 125 percent step is the part that gets lost. Two traps: applying 125 percent to the whole load instead of only the continuous part, and applying it after derating. The rule sets the minimum ampacity first — noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load — and correction and adjustment are worked from there. Feeder sized at the straight load total — the 125 percent step on the continuous portion is missing. Continuous portion of the load not shown separately on the calculation, so the 125 percent step cannot be verified. Feeder conductors sized from the rating of the panel on hand instead of the Article 220 calculation. 125 percent step applied, then adjustment factors allowed to pull the final ampacity back below the load served. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Feeder overcurrent protection
x: A feeder is protected by an overcurrent device rated not over the ampacity of its conductors, subject to the allowances in Article 240 — including the next-higher-standard-rating allowance where it applies and the tap rules where it does not. The breaker at the start of the feeder is therefore a conductor-protection question first and a load question second. Where a feeder continues to a subpanel, the equipment grounding conductor and the neutral treatment at that subpanel are Article 250 questions, covered later in this chapter. The feeder's equipment grounding conductor is part of the feeder: it is sized from Table 250.122 by the rating of this overcurrent device and run with the feeder conductors. Where the feeder supplies a separate building, the grounding arrangement at that building follows 250.32 — this device's rating still sets the equipment grounding conductor size. Where a feeder supplies continuous loads, or a mix of continuous and noncontinuous loads, the overcurrent device rating may not be less than the noncontinuous load plus 125 percent of the continuous load (unless the assembly with its OCPD is listed for 100 percent operation). The protection itself follows Part I of Article 240. A feeder breaker has one main job: open before the conductors it protects overheat. Size the breaker to the load, or to the panel bus it feeds, and the wire becomes the fuse — insulation cooks inside conduit and walls long before anyone smells it. The continuous-load rule exists because a device carrying load for three hours or more runs hot itself; the 125 percent factor keeps it from thermal damage and nuisance trips. Match three numbers before energizing: feeder conductor ampacity, breaker rating, and the Article 240 rule you are relying on. If the middle number is larger than the first, name the allowance in the job file. Worked check: a feeder carrying 20 A of noncontinuous load and 40 A of continuous load needs an overcurrent device of at least 20 + (125% of 40) = 70 A, on conductors the Article 240 rule you are relying on actually protects. The trap answer sizes the feeder breaker from the load calculation alone — or from the bus rating of the subpanel it feeds. 215.3 protects conductors: the device is rated not over the ampacity of the feeder conductors, with only the Article 240 allowances letting it go above. A 200 A panel bus does not make a 200 A feeder, and the load answer still has to pass the 125 percent continuous check. Feeder breaker larger than the conductor ampacity, with no Article 240 allowance that applies. Continuous load carried at 100 percent of a standard breaker — no 125 percent factor applied (215.3). Equipment grounding conductor sized from the conductor size instead of from the overcurrent device rating (Table 250.122). Feeder breaker matched to the subpanel bus rating instead of to the feeder conductors. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Load calculations — proving the service is big enough
x: Article 220 is the arithmetic of the trade: it turns floor area, appliance nameplates, and heating and cooling equipment into one number in volt-amperes that sizes branch circuits, feeders, and services. It offers two ways to add a dwelling up: • The standard method counts loads item by item: floor area at the Table 220.12 unit load, 1,500 VA for each small-appliance branch circuit and for the laundry circuit, appliances at nameplate, with demand factors such as Table 220.42. • The optional method (220.82) totals the whole dwelling and applies demand factors to the total: the first 10,000 VA at 100 percent, the rest at 40 percent, with the larger of heating or cooling added. Sharma's house services are normally proved with the optional dwelling method, and the app's load calculator is built on it. Either way, the output is a calculated load the service and its feeders must carry. NEC 2026 NOTE (not a 2023 change): • NEC 2026 relocates load calculations from Article 220 to new Article 120. The 2023 NEC is still Article 220 (with the renumbering noted on the 220.12, 220.14 and 220.42 pages: 220.5(C), 220.41, 220.42(A), 220.45, new 220.57 EVSE and 220.70 EMS). Every conductor and breaker in the building traces back to this arithmetic. Size from a guess and the service either overheats and trips through a Florida August, or the customer pays for capacity nobody needed. The calculation is also the paper trail: when the inspector or the utility asks why, the worksheet is the answer. Optional-method check on a 1,800 sq ft Marion Oaks house, the worked example on the 220.82 page. General loads: floor area 1,800 x 3 VA = 5,400 VA; two small-appliance circuits 3,000 VA; laundry circuit 1,500 VA; dishwasher 1,200 VA; disposal 900 VA; water heater 4,500 VA; dryer 5,000 VA; range at nameplate 12,000 VA — a connected general load of 33,500 VA. Demand brings it down: the first 10,000 VA at 100 percent and the remaining 23,500 VA at 40 percent gives 19,400 VA. Add the larger of heating or cooling, the air conditioner at 5,760 VA: total 25,160 VA / 240 V is about 105 A. The service must be at least that figure; Sharma's standard new gear is a 200 A Siemens meter-main (S-02), which covers it with room to spare. Either way, the worksheet goes in the job file. The trap answer adds every nameplate at full value and calls the total the service load — that skips the demand factors and oversizes everything. The opposite trap is reaching for the optional method where it does not belong: it is only for a feeder or service that supplies the entire dwelling load, and only at or above its 100 A floor (220.82). And on a 2020 permit, do not count the garage in the floor area — garages join the floor area only in 2023. Service changed with no load calculation in the job file — the new service just copies the old one's size. Garage square footage counted in the floor area on a NEC 2020 dwelling calculation. Optional method used on a feeder that does not supply the entire dwelling load. Range or dryer entered at a guessed value instead of the nameplate rating. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 220.1: Article 220 got a new layout built for easier use: seven parts now, with new ones for health care facilities and for marinas and docks. Two new parts: Part VI covers health care facilities, and Part VII covers marinas, boatyards, docks and floating buildings. • 220.110: New in 2023: patient care spaces get their own demand factor tables for general-purpose receptacle circuits, one for Category 1 and 2 spaces and one for Category 3 and 4. Category 1 and 2 spaces, Table 220.110(1): first 5,000 VA in full, half of the next 5,000 VA, a quarter of the rest. • 220.5: Garages came off the floor-area exclusion list. In 2023, garage square footage goes into the dwelling's general lighting load, and the rule moved from 220.11 to 220.5(C). An attached garage now counts toward dwelling floor area, so it picks up 3 VA per square foot like the rest of the house (220.41). • 220.57: New section: each EV charger goes into a feeder or service calc at its nameplate rating, but never less than 7,200 VA. Each piece of electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) counts at its nameplate rating or 7,200 VA, whichever is higher. • 220.60: Air-conditioning loads now get the same 125 percent treatment as motors when you compare noncoincident loads. You still count only the largest of loads that never run together. New: an air-conditioning load in the noncoincident group gets figured at 125 percent, the same as a motor load, when it isn't the largest load. • 220.70: New section: when an energy management system (EMS) caps the current on a feeder or service, its maximum current setpoint can stand in for the calculated load. If an EMS that meets 750.30 limits a feeder or service, you can use its maximum ampere setpoint as that feeder or service load. • 220.120: The requirements of Section 555.6 have been moved to 220.120. This will not change the requirements for load calculations or demand factors and is a simple relocation. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above. NEC 2026 NOTE (not a 2023 change): • NEC 2026 relocates load calculations from Article 220 to new Article 120. The 2023 NEC is still Article 220 (with the renumbering noted on the 220.12, 220.14 and 220.42 pages: 220.5(C), 220.41, 220.42(A), 220.45, new 220.57 EVSE and 220.70 EMS).

t: General lighting load by floor area
x: In NEC 2020, 220.12 and Table 220.12 set the minimum general lighting load for NON-DWELLING occupancies: the table's unit load (volt-amperes per square foot) times the floor area figured under 220.11 (outside dimensions). The table values already include the 125 percent continuous-load multiplier (table note), so do not apply it again. Dwellings are no longer in this table: the dwelling 3 VA per square foot is 220.14(J). The full table is below; the chart shows the same numbers. Table 220.12 unit loads (VA per sq ft): • Automotive facility — 1.5 • Convention center — 1.4 • Courthouse — 1.4 • Dormitory — 1.5 • Exercise center — 1.4 • Fire station — 1.3 • Gymnasium (armories, auditoriums) — 1.7 • Health care clinic — 1.6 • Hospital — 1.6 • Hotel/motel, incl. apartment houses without tenant cooking (lodge rooms) — 1.7 • Library — 1.5 • Manufacturing facility (industrial commercial lofts) — 2.2 • Motion picture theater — 1.6 • Museum — 1.6 • Office (banks) — 1.3 • Parking garage (commercial storage garages) — 0.3 • Penitentiary — 1.2 • Performing arts theater — 1.5 • Police station — 1.3 • Post office — 1.6 • Religious facility — 2.2 • Restaurant (clubs) — 1.5 • Retail (stores, barber shops, beauty parlors) — 1.9 • School/university — 3 • Sports arena — 3 • Town hall — 1.4 • Transportation — 1.2 • Warehouse — 1.2 • Workshop — 1.7 Office and bank receptacle load is separate: 220.14(K), the larger of 1 VA per sq ft or the 180 VA-per-outlet total after 220.44 demand. Lighting is the one load that runs for hours at full draw, in every occupancy, every day. The unit loads force the feeder and service to be sized for that real, continuous lighting load before anyone counts receptacles or equipment, so a building's lights never become the load the service cannot carry. A 6,000 sq ft retail tenant in a Winter Garden plaza: retail reads 1.9 VA per sq ft from the table, so the general lighting load is 6,000 × 1.9 = 11,400 VA — and you stop there, because the 125 percent continuous multiplier is already in the 1.9. Receptacle load is a separate line: offices and banks use 220.14(K), and the same receptacle rules get figured apart from lighting. If the same crew roughs the model home next door, none of this table applies: the house is 3 VA per sq ft under 220.14(J). The trap answer doubles the continuous load: the candidate multiplies the table value by 125 percent a second time. The Table 220.12 note already includes it. The second trap is reading the dwelling row: there is none in 2020 — dwellings moved to 220.14(J). Lighting load calculated with the 125 percent multiplier applied twice — the table value already includes it. Dwelling lighting load taken from Table 220.12 instead of 220.14(J) at 3 VA per sq ft. Floor area figured from inside dimensions; 220.11 requires outside dimensions. Office receptacle load folded into the lighting number instead of figured separately under 220.14(K). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 220.42(A): The non-dwelling unit-load rule moved from 220.12 to 220.42(A) (Table 220.42(A)); the old 220.42 demand factors became 220.45. School/university and sports arena dropped from 3 to 1.5 VA/ft²; all other occupancy values stayed the same. The informational note now assumes 80% power factor. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Other loads — receptacles and named loads at their set values
x: Before any demand factor is applied, this section sets the values for the named loads that are not floor area. The values crews reach for most: • Receptacle outlets, other than the dwelling general-use receptacles already inside the 3 VA per square foot — 180 VA for each single or multiple receptacle on one yoke or strap • Multioutlet assemblies — 180 VA for each 5 ft (1.5 m) or fraction of the assembly where the appliances are unlikely to be used at the same time; 180 VA for each 1 ft or fraction where they are likely to be used at the same time • Show windows — 200 VA for each linear foot • A sign or outline lighting circuit — 1,200 VA minimum for each circuit the sign article requires • Fixed appliances and other named equipment — at nameplate rating, unless another part of Article 220 gives the load its own value or demand table A duplex receptacle is one yoke and counts once. A single piece of equipment with four or more receptacles counts at not less than 90 VA per receptacle (220.14(I)), so a four-plex counts 360 VA. Motors are sent by this section to the motor rules in Article 430 for their values. Dwelling general-use receptacles are included in the 3 VA per sq ft of 220.14(J) in 2020, not in 220.12. A load calculation is only as good as the values fed into it. If every receptacle counted at whatever the last tenant happened to plug in, two electricians would size the same service two different ways, and the next tenant's load would land on an undersized feeder. Set values make the calc repeatable, and they carry the ordinary load a receptacle actually serves over the life of the building, not just on move-in day. On a commercial tenant build-out, the receptacle count is the load: count straps, not device faces. Worked example: 40 receptacle straps × 180 VA = 7,200 VA of receptacle load before any demand the later sections allow. Write the count on the calc — 'recepts per plan' is not a number an inspector can check. And when the plan shows a four-plex, count it at 360 VA — 90 VA a receptacle — not at the 180 VA strap value. A quad receptacle: four receptacles in one box. The trap answer is 180 VA — 'one strap, one value.' Wrong. A single piece of equipment with four or more receptacles counts at not less than 90 VA per receptacle (220.14(I)), so the quad is 360 VA. The 180 VA value belongs to the ordinary duplex on its strap. Four-plex counted at 180 VA on the load calc — 220.14(I) requires 90 VA per receptacle, 360 VA total. Show-window load left out of a retail build-out calc — 200 VA per linear foot. Sign circuit figured below the 1,200 VA minimum. Dwelling general receptacles counted twice: inside the 3 VA per sq ft and again at 180 VA each. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 220.14(J): 220.14(J) (dwelling 3 VA/ft² lighting and receptacle rule) was deleted from 220.14; the dwelling general lighting load is now 220.41. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Demand factors for the general load — Table 220.42
x: The standard method does not size a dwelling service for every volt-ampere connected. After the general load is added up (general lighting by floor area, the small-appliance and laundry allowances, and the other general loads), Table 220.42 applies this demand factor to a dwelling: • First 3,000 VA — at 100 percent • From 3,001 to 120,000 VA — at 35 percent • Over 120,000 VA — at 25 percent The appliance, dryer, and range demands in their own sections are worked separately and added to this result. No house runs every light and every general receptacle at full load at the same time. Sizing the service for the full connected total would oversize feeders and panels on every job. The steps in the table reflect how diversity grows with load: the first block is taken whole, and the bigger the general load gets, the smaller the share of it that ever shows up at once. Worked example: a house whose general load adds to 18,000 VA before demand. First 3,000 VA at 100 percent = 3,000 VA. The remaining 15,000 VA at 35 percent = 5,250 VA. Demanded general load = 8,250 VA. Write the two steps down — anyone checking your math wants to see the 3,000 VA block, not just the answer. The trap is applying 35 percent to the whole general load. On an 18,000 VA general load that gives 6,300 VA — wrong, because the first 3,000 VA always comes through at 100 percent. The right answer is 3,000 + (15,000 × 0.35) = 8,250 VA. A second trap: running the dryer and range through Table 220.42 as well. They take their own demand sections and are added after. Demand factor applied to the whole general load, skipping the first 3,000 VA at 100 percent — the calculation undersizes the service. Dryer or range load run through Table 220.42 instead of its own demand section. Load calculation submitted as a single total, with no 3,000 VA block shown, so the math cannot be checked. Optional-method demand (220.82) and standard-method Table 220.42 factors mixed in the same calculation. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 220.45: The Table 220.42 general-lighting demand factors were renumbered as 220.45 / Table 220.45 (the 220.42 number now holds the non-dwelling unit loads). • 220.42: Schools and sports arenas fell from 3 VA to 1.5 VA per square foot. The rule moved from 220.12 to 220.42, and the table note on the built-in 125 percent got clearer. Schools and universities fell from 3 VA to 1.5 VA per square foot, and sports arenas took the same cut. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Small-appliance and laundry allowances — 1,500 VA each
x: In the standard method, the kitchen and laundry circuits enter the calculation at set values instead of nameplate numbers: • Each 20A small-appliance branch circuit — 1,500 VA (a dwelling has at least two, so at least 3,000 VA) — 220.52(A) • The laundry branch circuit — 1,500 VA — 220.52(B) These allowances are added into the general load first; the Table 220.42 demand factor is then applied to the total. They are calculation allowances only — the circuits themselves are still wired and protected as full 20A circuits. No house runs every countertop appliance and the washer at full load at the same moment, and no two houses load their kitchen circuits alike. Fixed allowances put every standard-method calculation on the same footing: the service is sized from a code-set picture of these circuits, not from whichever appliances happen to be on site the day the calculation is done. The Table 220.42 demand factor then does the diversity work once, on the whole general load. Standard-method worksheet for a 1,500 sq ft Marion Oaks house. General lighting: 1,500 sq ft × 3 VA (220.14(J)) = 4,500 VA. Small-appliance: two circuits × 1,500 VA = 3,000 VA. Laundry: 1,500 VA. The general load is 9,000 VA before demand. Table 220.42 then counts the first 3,000 VA at 100 percent and the remaining 6,000 VA at 35 percent — 3,000 + 2,100 = 5,100 VA carried into the rest of the service calculation. If your worksheet shows less than 4,500 VA on the small-appliance and laundry lines together, the sheet is wrong before it starts. The tempting wrong answer counts one small-appliance circuit at 1,500 VA because the kitchen 'only has one counter circuit drawn.' A dwelling always has at least two small-appliance circuits (210.11(C)(1)), so the floor is 3,000 VA — and every small-appliance circuit actually installed enters at 1,500 VA, including a third one for an island. Worksheet counts one small-appliance circuit (1,500 VA) — a dwelling always has at least two, so the line is 3,000 VA minimum. Laundry allowance missing from the standard-method calculation. Table 220.42 demand factor applied to each line separately instead of once to the total general load. Small-appliance circuits protected at less than 20A because 'the calc only counts 1,500 VA' — the allowance is a calc number, not a circuit rating. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Four or more fixed appliances — the 75 percent demand
x: In the standard method, a dwelling's fixed appliances almost never all run at once. Where four or more fixed appliances — other than electric ranges, clothes dryers, space-heating equipment, and air-conditioning equipment — are fastened in place on the same service or feeder, this section permits a demand factor of 75 percent on their combined nameplate load: • Applies at four or more qualifying appliances — three or fewer count at full nameplate • Demand factor — 75 percent of the combined nameplate ratings • Never applies to ranges, dryers, heating, or cooling — those have their own sections Dishwashers, disposals, water heaters, and trash compactors are the usual four that unlock it in a house. Fixed appliances cycle. The water heater runs, rests, and runs again; the dishwasher and the disposal take their turns without any help. Sizing a service as if every one of them ran at full nameplate forever would buy copper and switchgear the house will never use. The 75 percent factor is the Code's measured diversity for this group — it keeps the service honest without paying for a coincidence that does not happen. On a Marion Oaks spec house the plan shows the usual four. Worked example: dishwasher 1,200 VA + disposal 900 VA + water heater 4,500 VA + trash compactor 1,000 VA = 7,600 VA of nameplate load; × 75 percent = 5,700 VA carried into the service total. Count the appliances on the plan before you decide the factor is unavailable — the fourth appliance is easy to miss. On the same house, leave the range and the dryer out of this group entirely — they are added later under their own demand rules. The trap answers are 7,600 VA — the factor forgotten — and taking 75 percent on three appliances because a fourth one is 'coming later.' The factor unlocks at four or more qualifying appliances, and ranges, dryers, heating and cooling never join the group; they are figured in their own sections. Demand factor of 75 percent taken on only three fixed appliances — the group needs four or more. Clothes dryer or range load folded into the 75 percent appliance group instead of its own section. Appliance group totaled from guessed loads — no nameplate ratings listed on the load calculation. Load calculation appliance count does not match the appliances shown on the plan. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 220.53: EV chargers joined the list of loads kept out of the 75 percent fastened-in-place appliance group. Each one gets figured separately, using 220.57. Electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) can't be lumped into the 75 percent appliance group; it's figured on its own (220.57). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Clothes dryers — 5,000 VA each and the dryer demand table
x: A household clothes dryer enters the standard-method calculation at 5,000 VA (5 kW) or its nameplate rating, whichever is larger — per dryer. Where several dryers share a service or feeder, Table 220.54 then applies a demand factor to their combined load: • 1 to 4 dryers — 100 percent • 5 dryers — 85 percent • 6 dryers — 75 percent • 7 dryers — 65 percent • 8 dryers — 60 percent • 9 dryers — 55 percent • 10 dryers — 50 percent • 11 dryers — 47 percent The table continues downward for larger counts, which is a multifamily and laundromat case. The portion of the dryer load on the neutral may be taken at 70 percent — see the 220.61 page. The 5,000 VA figure is a floor, not a guess: allowing a dryer at less would undersize the service for a load that runs an hour at a time. The demand table then recognizes reality — in a building with ten dryers, they never all run at once, so the service is not sized as if they did. The two ideas work together: never undercount one dryer, and never pretend every dryer runs together. A single house dryer is simple: read the nameplate, and if it says less than 5,000 VA, use 5,000 VA anyway; if it says 5,600 VA, use 5,600 VA. The demand table only starts to matter on the fifth dryer. On a six-unit building, six dryers at 5,000 VA = 30,000 VA connected; Table 220.54 takes 75 percent, so 22,500 VA goes into the feeder calculation — and the neutral portion of that dryer load may be taken at 70 percent under 220.61. Two traps. First: using the nameplate when it reads 4,200 VA — the rule is 5,000 VA or the nameplate, whichever is larger, so 5,000 VA stands. Second: applying the demand table to a single house — with one to four dryers the factor is 100 percent, so a lone dryer still counts at its full 5,000 VA or nameplate value. Load calculation shows the dryer at its 4,200 VA nameplate — below the 5,000 VA floor of 220.54. Table 220.54 demand factor applied to a three-dryer building; one to four dryers must be taken at 100 percent. Dryer omitted from the service calculation because the unit 'has gas' — while an electric dryer receptacle was roughed in. A 5,600 VA nameplate dryer carried at 5,000 VA — the larger value governs. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Household ranges — the Table 220.55 demand values
x: A household range is never counted at full nameplate in a dwelling load calculation — not all of its elements run together for long. Table 220.55 Column C gives the demand for ranges rated not over 12 kW: • 1 range — 8 kW • 2 ranges — 11 kW • 3 ranges — 14 kW • 4 ranges — 17 kW Columns A and B may be used instead for appliances rated 1¾ kW through 8¾ kW (Note 3). For ranges over 12 kW, Note 1 raises the Column C value 5 percent for each kW — or major fraction of a kW — over 12 kW; for a single range that works out to 400 VA per kW, so one range rated over 12 kW through 27 kW starts at 8 kW and adds 400 VA for each kW over 12. A counter-mounted cooking unit and not more than two wall-mounted ovens, all supplied from one branch circuit and located in the same room, are added together by nameplate and treated as one range (Note 4). The portion of the range load on the neutral may be taken at 70 percent — see the 220.61 page. A range nameplate assumes every burner and the oven at full heat at the same time, which almost never happens and never for long. Counting ranges at nameplate would oversize services for a peak that diversity handles safely. The table is measured demand behavior, not a guess — it keeps the service honest without gold-plating it. Worked example: a 12 kW range counts 8,000 VA in the standard method — not 12,000 VA. A 16 kW range counts 8,000 + (4 × 400) = 9,600 VA. Two 12 kW ranges, one in each unit of a duplex, count 11,000 VA together — not 16,000 VA and not 24,000 VA. Do not carry this table into the optional method: under 220.82(B) the range goes into the general block at nameplate, and the two methods are never mixed on one calculation. The trap is the 16 kW range: 16,000 VA (full nameplate) and 12,800 VA (a flat 80 percent) are both wrong. Column C gives 8 kW for one range, and Note 1 adds 5 percent for each kW over 12 — 4 kW over adds 20 percent, for 9,600 VA. Second trap: using Table 220.55 inside an optional-method calculation, where the range enters at nameplate. Range entered at full nameplate (12,000 VA) in a standard-method calculation, oversizing the service on the permit set. Note 1 increase forgotten on a 16 kW range — counted at 8,000 VA instead of 9,600 VA. Cooktop and two wall ovens on one branch circuit counted as three ranges instead of one combined range (Note 4). Optional-method worksheet that also took the Table 220.55 demand for the range — the two methods mixed on one calculation. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The neutral load — and the 70 percent rule
x: The grounded (neutral) conductor of a feeder or service only carries the unbalanced load — the largest load connected between the neutral and any one ungrounded conductor. This section then allows demand on that neutral load: • The portion of the neutral load from line-to-neutral loads — the first 200A counts at 100 percent, and any portion over 200A counts at 70 percent • The neutral portion of range and dryer loads may be taken at 70 percent (the range and dryer demand values themselves come from 220.55 and 220.54) • No reduction is permitted for the neutral of a 4-wire, 3-phase wye system feeding nonlinear loads — discharge lighting, electronic gear, and the like can load a neutral beyond the unbalance, and the 70 percent step does not apply there. • No reduction is permitted on the neutral of a 3-wire circuit made of two ungrounded conductors and the neutral of a 4-wire, 3-phase wye system (220.61(C)(1)), and none on the portion made of nonlinear loads on a 4-wire, 3-phase wye (220.61(C)(2)). The 70 percent step over 200A applies only to the portion of the unbalanced load in excess of 200 amperes (220.61(B)(2)). On a balanced system the neutral currents cancel, so the neutral only ever carries what does not cancel. Sizing it for the full phase load wastes copper; sizing it below the real unbalance overheats it. The demand steps credit the diversity that shows up on big services, and the (C) bans exist because harmonic currents from nonlinear loads add in the neutral instead of canceling. On a large house service the neutral can legitimately come out smaller than the ungrounded conductors — but only by this arithmetic, written into the calculation in the job file. If the calc does not show the 200A step and the 70 percent step, the smaller neutral is an assumption, not a design. Worked example: a large house service calculates to a 300A unbalanced neutral load. The first 200A counts in full; the remaining 100A counts at 70 percent, or 70A. The neutral is sized for 200 + 70 = 270A, as drawn above — not for 300A, and not for 70 percent of the whole 300A. The common wrong answer takes 70 percent of the entire neutral load. The 70 percent applies only to the portion over 200A — the first 200A always counts at 100 percent. The second trap is applying the reduction to the neutral of a wye system feeding LED drivers and computers: 220.61(C) forbids it. Neutral reduced by 70 percent across the whole load instead of only the portion over 200A. Neutral reduction taken on a 4-wire wye feeder serving nonlinear loads — office LED lighting and computer loads (220.61(C)(2)). Smaller neutral installed with no load calculation in the job file showing the 200A and 70 percent steps. Neutral of a 3-wire circuit taken from a 4-wire wye system reduced below the (C)(1) limit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The optional method for a dwelling service or feeder
x: Where a feeder or service supplies an entire dwelling, this optional method lets the load be totaled with demand factors instead of adding every load at full value. The method has conditions: it is for a dwelling unit, the service or feeder must carry the entire load of that dwelling, and the service-entrance conductors must have an ampacity of 100 A or more — below that floor, the standard method governs. The calculation is two parts, worked separately and then added: the general loads of 220.82(B) — floor area, small-appliance and laundry circuits, and nameplate appliances — with the first 10 kVA taken at 100 percent and the remainder at 40 percent; and the heating-and-cooling selection of 220.82(C), where only the largest of the six selections is added. The app's calc table 220.82 carries the rule rows and worked test cases for the method. The standard method adds loads as if everything in the house runs at once. Real houses diversify: the dryer, range, and water heater cycle on and off, and heating and cooling never peak together. The optional method prices that diversity in, so a service sized by it still carries the real peak — with fewer steps and fewer chances to double-count. Use the app calculator, then hand-check the two parts before you order gear: the demand-factored general load, and the larger heating-or-cooling figure. Save the printout or worksheet with the permit paperwork. Worked example — a 1,800 sq ft house. General loads: floor area 1,800 × 3 VA = 5,400 VA; two small-appliance circuits 3,000 VA; laundry circuit 1,500 VA; dishwasher 1,200 VA; disposal 900 VA; water heater 4,500 VA; dryer 5,000 VA; range at nameplate 12,000 VA — total 33,500 VA. The first 10,000 VA counts at 100 percent and the remaining 23,500 VA at 40 percent = 9,400 VA, so the general block is 19,400 VA. Heating and cooling: the air conditioner at 5,760 VA is the largest selection, so add 5,760 VA. Total 25,160 VA ÷ 240 V ≈ 105 A — the service is sized at or above that figure. S-09 affects the gear this calculation sizes: meter and panel back to back where the house allows. Two traps: mixing methods — taking the range at its Table 220.55 demand inside an optional-method worksheet, when 220.82(B) wants nameplate; and adding air conditioning and electric heat together, when 220.82(C) adds only the largest single selection. Optional method applied where the service-entrance conductors have an ampacity under 100 A. Heating and cooling selections added together instead of taking only the largest one. Range taken at its Table 220.55 demand inside the optional method instead of at nameplate. Feeder sized by the optional method that does not carry the entire load of the dwelling. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Optional method — the general loads
x: The general-loads block of the optional method is built from: • Floor area at 3 VA per square foot • 1,500 VA for each small-appliance branch circuit, and 1,500 VA for the laundry circuit • The nameplate ratings of the appliances and motors the subsection lists — dishwasher, disposal, water heater and the rest that are fastened in place or on a specific circuit Then the demand step: the first 10 kVA of that total is taken at full value, and the remainder at 40 percent. That step is the whole advantage of the optional method, and it only applies to the loads this block covers — heating and cooling are handled separately in the next part, 220.82(C). A house never runs everything at once. The standard method adds nameplates as if it did, and oversizes the service; the optional method prices in diversity — but only for the loads on its list. Skip a block, like the laundry circuit, and the service comes out too small. Add heating or cooling here and again in (C), and it comes out too big. Both errors start in this block. Count circuits, not appliances, for the 1,500 VA blocks: two small-appliance circuits are required, and a third one that is installed also counts. Use nameplate VA where a rating is given in amps and volts. Worked example, a 2,000 sq ft house: floor area 2,000 × 3 VA = 6,000 VA; small-appliance circuits 2 × 1,500 = 3,000 VA; laundry 1,500 VA; dishwasher nameplate 1,200 VA; disposal 900 VA; water heater 4,500 VA. Total 17,100 VA. First 10,000 VA at 100 percent; the remaining 7,100 VA at 40 percent is 2,840 VA. General demand: 12,840 VA — before heating and cooling are added under (C). The trap: run the whole total at 40 percent. On the worked example that gives 6,840 VA and a service far too small. The first 10 kVA is always taken at full value — the 40 percent touches only what is above it. The mirror-image trap is counting appliances instead of circuits for the 1,500 VA blocks: three installed small-appliance circuits count 4,500 VA, even if only two are loaded today. Load calculation applies 40 percent to the first 10 kVA — the demand step is backwards. Only one small-appliance circuit counted; two are required, and an installed third counts too. Laundry circuit's 1,500 VA left out of the general loads. Heating load added in the (B) block and again in (C) — counted twice. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Optional method — heating and cooling
x: 220.82(C) covers heating and cooling in the optional method for a dwelling. Heating and cooling do not run at full load together, so you do not add both. You work out six selections, in kVA, and add only the largest one to the load calculation: • (1) Air conditioning and cooling: 100 percent of nameplate rating. • (2) A heat pump with no supplemental electric heat: 100 percent. • (3) A heat pump with supplemental electric heat: 100 percent of the compressor plus 65 percent of the supplemental heat. Leave the compressor out only if it is prevented from running at the same time as that heat. • (4) Electric space heating with fewer than four separately controlled units: 65 percent. • (5) Electric space heating with four or more separately controlled units: 40 percent. • (6) Electric thermal storage and other heating expected to run continuously at full nameplate: 100 percent. A system counted under (6) is not counted again under another selection. A service sized for heating and cooling at full load together would be sized for a day that never comes — the compressor and the strip heat carry the house in different seasons. The percentages credit how the equipment really runs: supplemental heat stages in under the compressor, and separately controlled space heaters cycle instead of all running at once. The rule keeps the service honest without paying for capacity that nothing uses. In Florida the air-conditioning figure usually wins this comparison, but a house with strip heat or a heat pump with auxiliary heat still needs the comparison done and written down. Take the compressor and air-handler figures from nameplates, not from tonnage rules of thumb. Florida heat pumps with electric auxiliary heat are common in Sharma's territory; that is the (C)(3) case — compressor at 100 percent plus 65 percent of the auxiliary heat — so do not skip the comparison on a Florida house. The trap is adding the air conditioning and the heat-pump-with-strips figures together 'to be safe.' 220.82(C) adds the largest single selection only. The second trap is taking the heat pump at 100 percent of everything — compressor plus full strip heat. Selection (3) takes the strips at 65 percent, not 100. Load calculation adds the air-conditioning load and the full strip-heat load together — 220.82(C) takes the largest selection only. Supplemental heat figured at 100 percent instead of 65 percent under (C)(3), oversizing the service on paper. Compressor dropped out of the (C)(3) figure with nothing preventing it from running at the same time as the strips. Heating and cooling figures taken from tonnage rules of thumb instead of nameplate ratings. Thermal storage counted under (C)(6) and then counted again under a space-heating selection. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Existing dwellings — adding load without changing the service
x: This is the optional method for additions to an existing one-family dwelling: it answers whether the existing service can carry new load, without rebuilding the calculation from zero. The existing load is figured from the values this section lists: 3 VA per square foot for general lighting, 1,500 VA per small-appliance and laundry circuit, and nameplate ratings of appliances. (Figuring an existing load from actual loads or demand data is 220.87, not this section.) Then: • Where the added load is other than air conditioning or electric space heating — combine the existing load and the added load, take the first 8 kVA at 100 percent and the remainder at 40 percent; if that result does not exceed the existing service rating, no service increase is required • Where air conditioning or space heating is added (220.83(B)) — air-conditioning equipment at 100 percent; central electric space heating at 100 percent; fewer than four separately controlled space-heating units at 100 percent; the first 8 kVA of all other loads at 100 percent; the remainder of all other loads at 40 percent If the result exceeds the existing service rating, the service is increased and sized under the regular methods. Houses outlive their loads. A 1960s service sized for lights and a refrigerator now feeds a remodeled kitchen, a workshop and a hot tub, and nobody rechecked it. This method forces the check onto one standard worksheet, so the answer to 'can the old service carry it' is a number, not a shrug at the panel. Worked example: an existing 200A service carries a computed existing load of 26 kVA, and the owner adds a 6 kVA workshop load. Combined 32 kVA: first 8 kVA at 100 percent, remaining 24 kVA at 40 percent = 9.6 kVA — total 17.6 kVA, or about 73A at 240V, well under the 200A service. No service change. Keep this worksheet with the permit — it is the document that proves the existing service was checked, not assumed. Florida additions often add a condenser too — and then the (B) rules apply, with the AC at 100 percent. The trap is running new air conditioning through the friendly 8 kVA / 40 percent split. Under 220.83(B) the AC load enters at 100 percent and only the other loads get the split. Use (A) on an addition with a condenser and the worksheet understates the load — and the service stays undersized on paper that says it was checked. Addition permitted with no 220.83 worksheet on file — the existing service was never actually checked. New air conditioning figured at 40 percent with the other loads instead of 100 percent under 220.83(B). Existing load built from utility demand data and labeled 220.83 — that method is 220.87. Worksheet result over the service rating, and the service left unchanged anyway. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Outside branch circuits and feeders
x: Article 225 covers wiring that runs outside — between buildings, across a yard, or overhead or underground to a detached structure. Sharma meets it on detached garages, barns, pool houses and site lighting fed from a house or a main building.
