On a high-leg delta panel, read the breaker voltage marking before you land the high leg: a 120/240 slash-rated breaker is the wrong breaker there even though the amp rating matches. Check the marking on the breaker in your hand, not the one you expected to find in the box. On a small commercial service call in Winter Park, the failed 20A breaker on the high leg gets replaced with a straight 240V Siemens breaker, not the 120/240V slash breaker riding in the truck stock. S-02: new gear is Siemens. The marking check applies to whatever breaker is actually installed — a substituted breaker with the wrong voltage rating is still the wrong breaker. The trap: a 120/240V breaker 'matches' a 240V high-leg delta because 240 is the bigger number on the label. Wrong — on the high leg the voltage to ground is 208V, which beats the 120V lower number of the slash rating. The lower number is the one that decides where a slash-rated breaker may go. Slash-rated 120/240V breaker landed on the high leg of a 240V delta panel. Breaker switching a fluorescent lighting load with no SWD marking. Replacement breaker installed with a voltage rating below the system voltage. Breaker markings painted over or illegible — the rating can no longer be verified. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding and bonding — the fault-current path
x: Article 250 is the longest and most argued article in this chapter. Grounding connects a system to earth through electrodes; bonding connects metal parts together so a fault has a low-impedance path back to the source that trips the breaker fast. Earth itself is not that fault path — the breaker trips because bonding carries the fault home. Section 250.4 states the performance test the whole article is built to pass: the path must be permanent and continuous, low-impedance, and able to carry the fault current long enough for the overcurrent device to open. When a detail is argued on site, that test settles it. The pages that follow walk the service bond, the electrodes, the sizing tables, and the piping and intersystem bonds in that order. A breaker only trips when fault current is big, and fault current is only big when the loop back to the source is low-impedance metal the whole way. Dirt is not that loop: a fault dumped into a ground rod may draw only a few amps — nowhere near enough to move a 20 A breaker — while the metal case of a washer sits live at 120 V, waiting for a hand. Bonding builds the metal loop. Grounding ties the system to earth to limit lightning and surge voltage and to hold the voltage to ground steady. On every job, trace one imaginary fault with your finger: a hot wire chafes through onto the metal frame of an air handler. The fault current runs on the equipment grounding conductor to the service, crosses the main bonding jumper to the neutral, and rides back out to the source — and the breaker opens on the way. If any link in that loop is missing, painted over, or loose, you have found the defect. On a Sharma 200 A house service the hardware in that loop is sized, not guessed: the main bonding jumper is 4 AWG copper behind 2/0 copper service conductors (250.28), and the grounding electrode conductor comes off Table 250.66 (the 250.50 page). Torque and termination discipline decide whether this article works in real life. A correctly sized conductor on a loose lug is not a fault path. The trap answer: "The ground rods trip the breaker on a fault." They do not. Earth is far too high an impedance to carry fault current back to the source, and 250.4 says plainly that the earth shall not be considered an effective ground-fault current path. The breaker trips because bonding and the equipment grounding conductor carry the fault home on metal. Bootleg ground: the neutral jumpered to the ground terminal at a receptacle to fake a grounded outlet on a tester. Subpanel "grounded" to a local rod with no equipment grounding conductor run back to the service. Bonding lug landed over paint, or torqued loose, so the fault path is a resistor. Equipment grounding conductor cut or left unlanded after a device swap into a plastic box. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 250.100: The hazardous-location bonding rule was reworded for accuracy. Raceways, metal-clad cable, equipment and enclosures still need threaded, threadless or listed bonding fittings, even with a wire-type equipment grounding conductor (EGC). In classified locations, bond with a method from 250.92(B)(2) through (B)(4): wrenchtight threaded entries, tight threadless fittings, or other listed bonding devices. • 250.109: Plaster rings and extension rings now join metal covers and fittings: each must be fastened to a metal box so the fault path holds, or bonded with a jumper or equipment grounding conductor (EGC). Metal covers, plaster rings, extension rings and metal fittings must be fastened so the fault path holds, or else bonded with a jumper or EGC. • 250.114: Cord-and-plug ice makers joined the list of appliances whose exposed metal parts must connect to an equipment grounding conductor (EGC), in homes and other occupancies alike. Ice makers now sit next to refrigerators, freezers and air conditioners in the residential list, 250.114(3). • 250.130: 250.130(C) now covers swapping out a nongrounding snap switch. An equipment grounding conductor (EGC) added for the new switch can land at the same points already allowed for receptacles. Putting a switch with a grounding terminal in an old box with no EGC? Its new EGC can run to any point listed in 250.130(C). • 250.148: A jumper to a metal box now has a size rule: Table 250.122, based on the largest breaker or fuse on circuits in the box. Rules for joining the grounding conductors got clearer too. A bonding jumper to a metal box is now sized from Table 250.122, using the largest breaker or fuse on circuits in that box (250.148(C)). • 250.36: The section now says impedance grounded systems, dropping high and neutral, and renames its conductors to match their real jobs. When you can use one hasn't changed. Renamed from high-impedance grounded neutral systems to impedance grounded systems. High and neutral both came out. • 250.6: The 2023 edition spells it out: neither ground-fault current nor current on a grounding or bonding connection Article 250 requires counts as objectionable current. Current on a required grounding or bonding connection is not objectionable current (250.6(C)). Don't remove the connection to stop it. • 250.70: Mostly a cleanup: 250.70 now splits general rules from the indoor communications strap clamp, and a new note confirms a direct-burial clamp also suits concrete encasement. New note: a clamp listed for direct burial is also suitable for concrete encasement, so it can go on a concrete-encased electrode. • 250.106: References to the NFPA 780 standard were removed for Informational Note No. 1 and updated for Informational Note No. 2. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: What grounding and bonding must accomplish
x: This general section states the performance the rest of Article 250 has to deliver, and it splits the work into two jobs: • Grounding — connecting the system and equipment to earth. It limits the voltage imposed by lightning, line surges, and accidental contact with higher-voltage lines, and it stabilizes the voltage to ground during normal operation. • Bonding — connecting metal parts together and back to the source in one continuous, low-impedance path that can carry fault current long enough for the overcurrent device to open. The section states plainly that the earth is not an effective ground-fault current path and must not be used as the sole equipment grounding conductor. When a specific installation rule is unclear, this section is the test it has to pass. A hot conductor that faults to a metal enclosure puts that enclosure at line voltage. If the only way back is through the earth, the path impedance is so high that only a few amperes flow — far too little to trip a breaker — and the enclosure sits energized, waiting for a hand to complete the circuit through a body. A bonded, low-impedance path back to the source lets a heavy fault current flow for the fraction of a second the breaker needs to open. Earth grounding handles lightning and surges; bonding is what clears faults. On a Florida slab house with a meter-main outside and the panel inside, run this page as a checklist before you call the rough-in. The grounding electrode system is bonded together at the service (250.50). The main bonding jumper lands at the meter-main, where the neutral meets ground. An equipment grounding conductor runs with the feeder to the inside panel, and the neutral is not bonded to ground again downstream (250.24(A)(5)). One rod by itself must prove 25 ohms or less, or a second rod goes in (250.53(A)(2)). Then ask the question this section asks: will it trip the breaker, fast, every time? If any link in that chain is missing, the honest answer is no. The tempting answer says a ground rod at the panel 'gives fault current a path to earth so the breaker trips.' It is wrong twice. The rod's job is lightning and surges, and the earth is far too high in impedance to clear a fault. The breaker trips because of the bonded path back to the source (250.4(A)(5)). No equipment grounding conductor run with the circuit — the installer relied on the ground rod to clear faults. Neutral bonded to ground again in a subpanel downstream of the service disconnect (250.24(A)(5)). Grounding electrode conductor spliced with a split bolt instead of an irreversible compression connector or exothermic weld (250.64(C)). Metal interior water piping left unbonded (250.104). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: How grounding and bonding connections are made
x: Grounding and bonding connections are made only by the methods 250.8(A) lists: • Listed pressure connectors • Terminal bars • Pressure connectors listed as grounding and bonding equipment • Exothermic welding • Machine-screw fasteners that engage at least two threads, or are secured with a nut • Thread-forming machine screws that engage at least two threads in the enclosure • Connections that are part of a listed assembly • Other listed means Connections to an electrode itself follow 250.70 — listed lugs, pressure connectors or clamps, or exothermic welding. Solder alone is never the connection: a soldered-only joint can melt open during a fault, which is the exact moment the path is needed. One screw or terminal takes one conductor, unless the device is listed and identified for more. The grounding path has to survive the worst second of the building's life — a fault that drives hundreds or thousands of amperes through it until the breaker opens. A connection that is merely touching, soldered, or hanging on one thread can melt or tear open under that current. The listed methods are the ones tested to carry fault current and stay together. Crimp, clamp, or weld it — never solder-only. On a service call, two grounds landed under one ordinary green screw and a soldered splice in the grounding path are both rework items: correct them with listed connectors while the panel is open. On a 200 A service change in Ocala, the old grounding electrode conductor was spliced with solder and tape inside the wall. It was replaced with a listed irreversible crimp before the new meter-main went on — the splice you cannot see is the one that fails. The trap answer is solder: a neat soldered splice looks permanent and tests continuous, but solder alone is not a permitted connection method — it can melt open under fault current. Second trap: a machine screw engaging one thread. The rule is at least two threads, or a nut. Grounding electrode conductor spliced with solder only. Not a 250.8 method. Two grounding conductors under one terminal screw that is not listed for two. Sheet-metal screw used as the bonding fastener — it does not engage two threads like a machine screw. Ground clamp on the rod not listed for the purpose, loose enough to turn by hand. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Which AC systems must be grounded
x: Some AC systems are required to be grounded, and the common Florida systems are on the list: • A system that can be grounded so the maximum voltage to ground stays at or below 150 volts must be grounded • Systems whose neutral is used as a circuit conductor are grounded systems — the 120/240V house service, and the 208Y/120V and 480Y/277V commercial services Grounding the system fixes the voltage to ground, gives lightning and surge energy a reference, and makes the fault-clearing path on the 250.4 page possible. Whether a delta system is grounded, and which conductor is the grounded one (250.26), is set by this article — never by field preference. An ungrounded system is not a shortcut around bonding: the equipment grounding and bonding rules still apply to it. An ungrounded or floating system has no fixed voltage to earth, so the first ground fault raises the other conductors to full line voltage above ground and delivers no fault current to trip anything. Grounding the system pins the voltage to ground, gives lightning and surges a reference point, and lets a ground fault draw enough current to open the breaker. Identify the system before you bond anything: wye or delta, which conductor (if any) is grounded, and where the single grounding point is. On an unfamiliar commercial service, the transformer configuration answers these questions — get it from the drawings or the utility, not by testing until something looks right. On a 480Y/277V retail service in Winter Park, the drawings showed the neutral grounded at the service only; the separately derived system in the tenant space needed its own grounding arrangement under 250.30, not a second bond on the service neutral. The trap is '480Y/277 cannot be a grounded system because 277 volts to ground is over the 150-volt limit.' The 150-volt test is only one path onto the list. A wye system whose neutral is used as a circuit conductor is grounded regardless of its voltage to ground. Neutral bonded at the service and again at a subpanel. One grounding point for the system; downstream neutrals stay isolated. Corner-grounded delta treated as if it were ungrounded — the grounded phase never identified or marked. Grounding electrode conductor landed before anyone confirmed which conductor the system grounds. Identify the system first. 480Y/277V service roughed in as if it were ungrounded — the neutral never connected to the grounding electrode system. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding at the service — and nowhere downstream
x: At the service, three connections come together in the service equipment: • The grounding electrode conductor lands on the grounded conductor (the neutral). • The main bonding jumper ties the neutral to the equipment grounding conductors and to the enclosure. • From that one point on, the neutral carries load current and the grounding system carries fault current. That is the one place in a premises system where neutral and ground meet. Downstream of the service — in subpanels and feeders — the grounded conductor is kept isolated from equipment grounds and enclosures, so normal neutral current never travels on metal parts and fault current has one clear path home. Add a second bond in a subpanel and neutral current splits: part of it rides the conduit, the water pipe and every equipment ground back to the service. Metal that should sit at zero volts now carries current every minute of the day, and if that neutral ever loosens, full load current can push onto parts a person can touch. One bond at the service keeps normal current on the neutral, where it belongs, and reserves the grounding path for faults — so a fault draws the heavy current that trips the breaker fast. Sharma's standard is the S-09 back-to-back: the outdoor Siemens meter-main is the service equipment, so the main bonding jumper and the grounding electrode conductor land there. On a 200 A service with 2/0 copper service conductors, the main bonding jumper is 4 AWG copper, sized from Table 250.102(C)(1) by way of 250.28. The indoor panel is a subpanel: four-wire feeder, neutral bar isolated and floating, ground bar bonded to the can, bonding screw left out. Photograph the first subpanel on a job and check it against this page. S-09's back-to-back service is where Sharma's bond is made; every panel downstream of it is wired isolated-neutral, no exceptions for a detached building panel that is actually a subpanel — see 250.32 for the separate-building case. The trap answer: "Bond the neutral in every panel — more grounds are safer." Wrong. Every bond past the service puts load current on metal parts, all day long. The only neutral-to-ground connection in the premises system is the main bonding jumper at the service. (A separately derived system, and a separate building under 250.32, follow their own pages and their own rules.) Bonding screw or bonding strap left in a subpanel, tying the neutral bar to the can. Neutrals and equipment grounds landed on the same bar in a subpanel. Main bonding jumper missing at the service, or a green screw standing in for a sized jumper. Grounding electrode conductor landed in a downstream panel instead of the service equipment. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 250.24: Made several changes within Section 250.24 to meet the requirements of the NEC Style Manual. • 250.24(D)(2): Received substantiation to clarify the requirements concerning grounded parallel conductors for service equipment. As a result, Section 250.4(D)(2) was revised. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Main and system bonding jumpers
x: The bonding jumper is the conductor or connection that ties the grounded conductor, the equipment grounding system, and the enclosure together at the service, and the system bonding jumper does the same job for a separately derived system. This section covers their material and how they are sized — for the main bonding jumper, by reference to the same sizing table used for the grounding electrode conductor, with the limits the section states. A jumper that is present but undersized or poorly landed does not do the job. The sizing numbers: a main bonding jumper is sized from Table 250.102(C)(1) by the size of the largest ungrounded service conductor (250.28(D)(1)). Where the service conductors are larger than 1100 kcmil copper (1750 kcmil aluminum), the table stops and the jumper must be not less than 12-1/2 percent of the cross-sectional area of the largest phase conductor. On ordinary house services the table rows are the whole answer: 8 AWG copper behind a 100A service on 4 AWG copper conductors, 4 AWG copper behind a 200A service on 2/0 copper. The main bonding jumper is the link that ties the enclosure, the equipment grounding system and the grounded conductor together at one point — the service. When a hot conductor faults to the enclosure, that jumper is part of the path that carries the fault back to the source so the overcurrent device opens. A jumper that is missing or undersized is a bottleneck in that path: the enclosure can sit energized while the breaker never trips. Factory-installed straps and screws count only when they are the listed means for that equipment and actually installed. On a service change, verify the jumper exists before you call for inspection — it is a small part with a whole article riding on it. On a 200 A Siemens meter-main with 2/0 copper service conductors, the table answer is a 4 AWG copper jumper — confirm the factory strap is the listed means for that can and that it is actually landed, not still in the parts bag. The trap answer sizes the main bonding jumper from the service breaker rating — or, on a service over 1100 kcmil copper, grabs the largest row in the table. The table is keyed to the largest ungrounded service conductor, not the breaker. And past 1100 kcmil copper (1750 kcmil aluminum) the table stops: the jumper must be not less than 12-1/2 percent of the largest phase conductor's cross-sectional area. No main bonding jumper installed at the service — the factory strap or bonding screw was never landed. Bonding jumper undersized for the service conductors (Table 250.102(C)(1)). Panel swapped on a service change and the bonding strap left off the new enclosure. Bonding jumper present but landed loose, so the connection is not doing the job. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Separately derived systems — generators and transformers
x: A separately derived system (SDS) is a source — a transformer, or a generator whose neutral is switched — that has no direct electrical connection to the supply system's circuit conductors; the two systems touch only through grounding and bonding. Because it is its own system, it needs its own grounding arrangement: • A system bonding jumper connecting the derived neutral to the equipment grounds and enclosure, made at the source or at the first disconnecting means — at one point only; both locations are permitted only where doing so does not create a parallel path for neutral current (250.30(A)(1) Exception No. 2) • A grounding electrode conductor run to the building or structure grounding electrode system, as near as practicable to the point where the system bonding jumper connects (250.30(A)(4)), sized from the derived conductors by the same table used at a service (250.66) A new rod is only needed where the building has no electrode system. A ground rod driven beside a generator, without the bonding jumper and electrode conductor, is decoration, not grounding. A derived system has no metallic path back to the utility source, so a ground fault inside it has no way to trip anything until the system gets its own bond and electrode connection. That bond is also a hazard when doubled: two neutral-to-ground bonds split neutral current onto equipment grounds and enclosures, where it heats connections and shocks anyone who touches metal. The transfer switch decides the design. If the switch does not switch the neutral, the generator is usually NOT separately derived, and the neutral stays bonded only at the service. If it does switch the neutral, the generator is an SDS and gets its bonding jumper at the generator end. Confirm which design the job has before anyone bonds a generator neutral — two bonding points put neutral current on the grounding path. The trap is “every generator is separately derived.” A generator fed through a transfer switch that does not switch the neutral is usually NOT separately derived, and bonding its neutral creates the second bond the rule forbids. The switch gear decides, not the generator. Generator neutral bonded at the generator and again at the service — parallel neutral current on the grounding path. Separately derived transformer with no system bonding jumper, or the jumper made at both the source and the first disconnect with a parallel path. Ground rod driven at the generator with no grounding electrode conductor to the building electrode system. GEC for the derived system sized by guess instead of Table 250.66 from the derived conductors. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 250.30(C): Removed the word "neutral'' from 250.30(C) to be consistent with other locations within the NEC and with language found at 250.36 and 250.187. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: A separate building fed by a feeder
x: When a feeder or branch circuit supplies a second building or structure, that building is treated almost like a service — but it is not one. The building needs: • A disconnecting means for the supply (225.31) • Its own grounding electrode system (250.32(A)). Exception: a building fed by a single branch circuit, individual or multiwire, that includes an equipment grounding conductor needs no electrode system • An equipment grounding conductor run with the feeder (250.32(B)(1)), sized from 250.122. The disconnect and the electrodes connect to that EGC • The grounded conductor (neutral) is NOT bonded at the separate building. A neutral run with the feeder stays isolated from the EGC and the electrodes — the one neutral-to-ground bond stays at the service One narrow exception, for existing installations only: the grounded conductor may be connected at the separate building if all three are true — no EGC was run with the supply, there are no continuous metallic paths bonded to the grounding system in both buildings (a metal water line between them kills it), and ground-fault protection of equipment is not installed on the supply side. That grounded conductor cannot be smaller than the larger of 220.61 and 250.122. The Article 250 companion to the Article 225 pages. Bond the neutral a second time and normal neutral current splits onto every parallel metal path — the EGC, the water piping, the earth itself. That objectionable current raises touch voltage on equipment, corrodes buried metal, and can leave bonded parts live if the neutral ever opens. One bond at the service, plus a separate EGC, gives fault current a solid metal path home so the breaker trips instead of the equipment case going hot. Detached garage behind an Ocala house, fed from the house panel: run a four-wire feeder — two hots, an isolated neutral, and an EGC. At the garage, set the disconnect, land the EGC on the ground bar, and drive two 8 ft rods 6 ft apart, bonded to that bar; a single rod is enough only with a 25-ohm test on file. Leave the panel's bonding screw out. If you open an older garage panel and find a three-wire feed with the neutral bonded, do not just copy it: check the three exception conditions first, and write down what you found. The trap answer: 'A separate building gets its own service, so bond the neutral there like a main.' Wrong — a feeder is not a service. The bond stays at the service; the separate building gets electrodes and an EGC, with the neutral isolated. The only re-bond allowed is the existing-installation exception, and it dies the moment an EGC is run or a metal water line links the buildings. Neutral bonded in the detached garage panel — bonding screw in or strap landed — putting neutral current on the EGC and the water piping. No grounding electrode system at the separate building fed by a feeder. New feeder run as three wires with no EGC, claiming the existing-installation exception on new work. Ground rods driven at the garage but never bonded to the panel ground bar. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Portable generators — frame grounding and the neutral bond
x: A portable generator is not automatically a separately derived system. Where the generator supplies only equipment mounted on it and cord-and-plug equipment plugged into its own receptacles, the generator frame itself serves as the grounding reference and the Code does not require a ground rod to be driven for it; the frame is bonded to the equipment grounding terminals of its receptacles. Whether the neutral is bonded to the frame depends on the generator's design — bonded-neutral and floating-neutral portables both exist, and they behave differently with GFCI receptacles and transfer equipment. The picture changes when the generator feeds premises wiring: then the transfer equipment and the rules on the 250.30 page decide whether the neutral is switched, where the single bonding point is, and what electrode connection is required. A generator connected the wrong way can kill somebody who never touched it. Back-feeding a panel energizes the service and the utility lines outside, where a line worker expects a dead circuit. A second neutral bond puts neutral current on grounding paths and metal frames. The frame bond and the single neutral bond are what decide where fault current and neutral current actually go. Read the generator's label before connecting it to a house: 'neutral bonded to frame' versus a floating neutral changes the transfer-switch design. The field failure is a bonded-neutral portable plugged into a system that also bonds at the service — neutral current on the grounding path and nuisance GFCI trips. That is why Sharma's hurricane-season answer is always the same: a listed inlet and an interlock or transfer switch, with the generator's neutral arrangement checked against the transfer design before the first storm, not during it. Hurricane season makes portable generators a standing Florida case — and homeowners back-feeding a panel through a dryer receptacle is a lethal, illegal arrangement. Sharma's answer is a listed inlet with an interlock or transfer switch, sized and bonded per the design, every time. The trap is 'every portable generator needs a ground rod' — or its twin, 'no portable ever does.' Feeding only cord-and-plug loads from its own receptacles, the frame is the grounding reference and no rod is required. The electrode question starts only when the generator feeds premises wiring, and then 250.30 and the transfer equipment decide it. Portable generator back-fed through a dryer receptacle, main breaker on, no interlock or transfer switch. Bonded-neutral portable on a non-switched-neutral inlet: neutral current riding the equipment grounding path and GFCI receptacles tripping. Receptacle ground terminals on the generator not bonded to the frame. Transfer switch that switches the neutral paired with a floating-neutral generator, leaving the system with no bond while on generator power. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The grounding electrode system — all of it, bonded together
x: Every grounding electrode that is present at a building must be bonded together into one grounding electrode system. You cannot pick the easiest electrode and ignore the others. The electrodes 250.52(A) recognizes: • Metal underground water pipe with at least 10 ft in direct contact with the earth (it must be supplemented by another electrode) • Metal in-ground support structure in direct contact with the earth • Concrete-encased electrode: at least 20 ft of ½ in or larger rebar, or bare 4 AWG or larger copper, in at least 2 in of concrete in a footing or foundation in contact with the earth • Ground ring: at least 20 ft of bare 2 AWG or larger copper, at least 30 in deep • Rod and pipe electrodes: at least 8 ft in contact with soil; rods at least 5/8 in diameter unless listed • Plate electrodes: at least 2 sq ft exposed to soil • Other local metal underground systems or structures Where none of these is present, you install a rod, pipe, plate or ring. In an existing building, a concrete-encased electrode is not required if reaching it would disturb the concrete (250.50 Exception). One electrode can corrode, dry out or be cut by a backhoe. Bonding every electrode present gives one connection to earth that limits voltage from lightning, utility surges and accidental contact with higher-voltage lines, and keeps buried metal at the same potential. It does not clear faults: the earth is not an effective fault path (250.4(A)(5)). The equipment grounding conductor back to the source clears faults. New slab home: the footing rebar is the best electrode on the job, and the chance to use it ends when the concrete is poured. Before the pour, confirm the qualifying rebar in the footing and a stub-up or bare 4 AWG copper tail near the meter-main. Florida water services are usually PVC or PEX, so the water line is not an electrode, but interior metal water piping still gets bonded under 250.104. If rods are also driven, they are present electrodes and must be bonded in. A single rod needs a second rod unless a 25-ohm test is on file. Land the GEC at the meter-main, where the main bonding jumper is. A 400 A service on 500 kcmil copper: what size GEC to the ground rods? Table 250.66 says 1/0 copper, but a conductor that is the only connection to rods never has to be larger than 6 AWG copper (250.66(A)). The table size applies to electrodes with no cap, such as a metal water pipe or building steel. Ufer rebar in the footing but never connected: the stub was cut off or buried. One ground rod, no resistance test on file. Rod top above grade with no protection, or a clamp not listed for direct burial. GEC spliced with a split bolt. Only irreversible compression connectors or exothermic welds are allowed (250.64(C)). 8 AWG GEC run exposed without RMC, IMC, Schedule 80 PVC, EMT or armor (250.64(B)). Neutral bonded to ground again in the indoor panel fed from the meter-main (250.24(A)(5)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 250.50: The term "reinforcing steel or rods" was replaced with "rebar." This revision was done in all three sections of the Code for consistency. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Electrodes that are permitted — and the ones that are not
x: This section lists what may serve as a grounding electrode, from underground water pipe with its conditions, through building steel and concrete-encased electrodes — at least 20 ft of the stated rebar or bare copper conductor encased in the foundation — to rods, pipes, and plates. It also lists what may not be used, which includes metal underground gas piping and aluminum electrodes. A water pipe electrode has its own supplementing rule, covered with the installation section. The electrode specifications in numbers: • Metal underground water pipe — at least 10 ft of pipe in direct contact with the earth • Concrete-encased electrode — at least 20 ft of 1/2 in or larger rebar, or at least 20 ft of bare 4 AWG copper conductor, encased in at least 2 in of concrete in the footing or foundation • Ground ring — at least 20 ft of bare 2 AWG copper, buried at least 30 in below grade • Rod and pipe electrodes — at least 8 ft long in contact with the soil; pipe not smaller than 3/4 in trade size; rods not smaller than 5/8 in diameter unless listed for the use • Plate electrodes — at least 2 sq ft of surface exposed to the surrounding soil The electrode is the building's one connection to earth for lightning, utility surges and line-to-ground faults on the supply side. Each permitted type has a proven minimum size and contact with the soil; below that minimum the connection is too weak or corrodes away too fast to trust. The banned list is just as important: a gas pipe must never carry electrical fault energy, and aluminum corrodes in soil and concrete. The concrete-encased electrode is the one to coordinate with the builder: 20 ft of qualifying rebar or conductor, encased as the section requires, with an accessible connection. Confirm it with the concrete crew before the pour, in writing on the job notes. On a Florida slab home the crew's default set is the concrete-encased electrode in the footing plus the rods the AHJ expects; Florida water services are usually PVC or PEX, so do not count a water pipe that is not metal in the earth for 10 ft. Two traps: counting a metal underground gas pipe as an electrode — it is prohibited, not just discouraged — and accepting 10 ft of rebar as a concrete-encased electrode. The Ufer needs 20 ft; 10 ft is the water pipe number. Concrete-encased electrode short of 20 ft, or the stub-up cut off before the GEC lands. Metal gas piping bonded in as a grounding electrode — prohibited by 250.52(B). Ground rod driven less than 8 ft, or a rod under 5/8 in that is not listed. Water pipe electrode with no supplemental electrode (250.53(D)). Aluminum electrode, or an aluminum GEC in direct contact with concrete or earth. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Installing electrodes — rods, depth, and the second rod
x: Electrodes must be installed as this section requires: driven or buried to the depths it states, kept as close as practicable to each other and to the service, and supplemented where a single rod, pipe, or plate does not meet the stated resistance to earth — 25 ohms or less — or is not tested at all. In practice that means a second rod, spaced at least 6 ft from the first, on almost every job. Rod connections must be accessible or of the irreversible or exothermic type the article allows where they are buried. The installation numbers: • Rod, pipe, and plate electrodes — at least 8 ft of the electrode in contact with the soil, with the top end flush with or below grade level unless the connection is protected • Two rods — spaced at least 6 ft apart; the 6 ft is a floor, and wider spacing makes the pair work better • A single rod, pipe, or plate may stand alone only with a measured resistance to earth of 25 ohms or less — without that measurement on file, the second electrode is required, not optional The electrode system gives lightning and surge energy a path into the earth and holds the service near earth potential. A single rod in dry sand can measure far above 25 ohms — the connection to earth is then mostly wishful thinking. Two rods, spread apart so their resistance areas do not overlap, bring the pair down where one rod alone could not. Drive two rods at least 6 ft apart unless you have a tested 25-ohm-or-less result in the job file. Keep the grounding electrode conductor run short, straight, and protected where it is exposed. On a 200A slab house in Marion Oaks, plan on two 8 ft rods from the start: drive the first, clamp the grounding electrode conductor, then drive the second at least 6 ft away and land the same run on it — no test instrument, no argument at inspection. The trap: 'one 8 ft rod is always enough — the second rod is just belt and suspenders.' Wrong. A single rod, pipe, or plate stands alone only with a measured resistance to earth of 25 ohms or less. No measurement on file means the supplemental electrode is required. Single ground rod with no 25-ohm test result in the job file. Two rods driven 3 ft apart — under the 6 ft minimum spacing. Rod left sticking above grade with the clamp connection unprotected. Buried rod connection made with a clamp not listed for the purpose — not accessible, irreversible, or exothermic. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Installing the grounding electrode conductor
x: The grounding electrode conductor is sized on the 250.66 page; this section is how it must be run: • Continuous, in one unbroken length, without a splice or joint — except splices made with irreversible compression connectors listed as grounding and bonding equipment, or by exothermic welding • Bare or covered aluminum or copper-clad aluminum GECs without an extruded polymeric covering may not be installed where subject to corrosive conditions or in direct contact with concrete; terminations inside listed enclosures identified for the environment are allowed within 18 in. of the enclosure bottom; outside buildings or enclosures, they may not be terminated within 18 in. of the earth • Where exposed, a conductor 6 AWG or larger may follow the surface of the building construction without a raceway where it is securely fastened and not subject to physical damage; smaller conductors, and any run exposed to damage, must be protected — in rigid metal conduit, IMC, EMT, schedule 80 PVC, RTRC-XW, or cable armor, or another method this section lists • A ferrous metal raceway or armor enclosing the conductor must be electrically continuous and bonded to the conductor at both ends — an unbonded steel sleeve chokes the fault path it was meant to protect The GEC is the path that ties the electrode system to the service. A splice that corrodes, a split bolt that loosens, or a steel sleeve that chokes the conductor all break that path silently — nothing trips and nothing looks wrong until lightning or a fault finds the weak point. One unbroken, protected, properly bonded run is what keeps the connection real for the life of the building. Plan the run as one piece from the service to the electrode before anything is cut. A grounding electrode conductor that comes up short gets replaced or extended by an irreversible splice — never by a split bolt that will end up buried in a wall or a trench. The trap answers name the split bolt as an acceptable GEC splice. It is not: splices must be irreversible compression connectors listed as grounding and bonding equipment, or exothermic welds. The second trap is forgetting that a ferrous raceway around the GEC must be bonded at both ends. GEC spliced with a split bolt inside a wall or trench. Steel sleeve or ferrous raceway around the GEC with no bonds at the ends. 8 AWG GEC run exposed on the building surface with no raceway or armor (250.64(B)). Bare aluminum GEC terminated within 18 in of the earth outside the building. GEC cut short and extended with a mechanical connector instead of an irreversible splice. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 250.64: New 250.64(G): a grounding electrode conductor (GEC) can't pass through an enclosure's ventilation openings. Bring it in through a knockout, hub or other proper opening. A GEC can't pass through a ventilation opening in an enclosure (250.64(G)). Bring it in through a knockout, hub or other proper opening. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Sizing the grounding electrode conductor
x: The grounding electrode conductor is sized from Table 250.66 by the size of the largest service-entrance conductor, not by the amperage of the service disconnect alone. Read the table across: the largest service conductor picks the row, and the row gives the GEC — copper or aluminum. The section then caps what is actually required for particular electrodes: • The portion of the GEC that is the sole connection to a rod, pipe, or plate electrode never has to be larger than 6 AWG copper (250.66(A)) • The portion that is the sole connection to a concrete-encased electrode never has to be larger than 4 AWG copper (250.66(B)) • The portion that is the sole connection to a ground ring never has to be larger than the ring conductor itself (250.66(C)) The table size governs a run that serves the whole electrode system; the caps limit a run to one kind of electrode. Aluminum and copper-clad conductors used for this purpose have material and installation limits in the surrounding sections (see 250.64). The GEC carries lightning and surge energy and holds the service at earth potential, so it is sized from the service conductors — in proportion to the energy the service can deliver. The caps recognize the other end of the run: a single rod or a concrete-encased electrode cannot usefully take more than a 6 or 4 AWG conductor can carry, so the Code stops requiring copper the electrode cannot use. Read the service conductor size off the actual conductors, then open the table — a 200A service on compact conductors is not automatically the row you expect. Where one conductor serves several electrodes, size and cap it electrode by electrode as the section directs. The two house rows, worked: a 100A service on 4 AWG copper or 2 AWG aluminum service conductors reads the first row — 8 AWG copper grounding electrode conductor. A 200A service on 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum reads the third row — 4 AWG copper. Those two answers cover most Sharma services before the per-electrode caps are applied. Running the full Table 250.66 size out to a pair of ground rods on a 400 A service and calling the extra copper safer. The rod portion never has to exceed 6 AWG copper (250.66(A)). The dangerous mirror image: capping the run to a metal underground water pipe at 6 AWG. The (A) cap covers rod, pipe, and plate electrodes — a water pipe electrode takes the full table size. GEC picked from the disconnect size instead of the largest service-entrance conductor. 200 A service on 2/0 copper roughed with an 8 AWG GEC — Table 250.66 reads 4 AWG copper. 6 AWG cap applied to the run to a metal water pipe electrode — the cap is only for rod, pipe, and plate electrodes. Concrete-encased run installed at 6 AWG where the table reads above the cap — the required size is the 4 AWG cap of 250.66(B). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Connections to electrodes — accessibility and continuity
x: Grounding electrode conductor connections must be made so they stay effective: clamps and connectors listed for the electrode and the conductor, connections to a water pipe made at an accessible point within the stated distance of where the pipe enters the building, and the conductor kept continuous or spliced only by the methods this section allows. Interior metal water piping farther into the building is a bonding question, not a substitute electrode connection point. The stated distance, in numbers: interior metal water piping may be used to interconnect electrodes only within 5 ft of the point where the water pipe enters the building. Beyond that first 5 ft the piping is bonded under 250.104, but it is not part of the electrode path. A grounding connection fails silently. A clamp that corrodes, loosens, or gets buried where nobody can inspect it leaves the electrode looking connected while the path is open — and nobody finds out until lightning or a fault needs that path. The accessibility and continuity rules keep the connection inspectable and the conductor unbroken from the service to the electrode. Land the water-pipe clamp where it can be inspected, on clean metal, and do not bury a mechanical splice in the grounding electrode conductor run. If a run is cut short on a remodel, replace it or use an allowed irreversible splice — not a split bolt in a wall. On a slab home where the water service enters at the far end of the house from the panel, do not just clamp where the panel is and call the piping run the electrode path: land the connection within the first 5 ft of the entry, or run the grounding electrode conductor to where the pipe enters. The trap is treating any point on the interior metal water piping as an electrode connection because the whole run is metal. Past the first 5 ft from the entry point, that piping is a bonding path under 250.104 — it is not part of the electrode system, and the electrode connection cannot be made there. GEC clamped to the water pipe well past the first 5 ft from where the pipe enters — the piping run is not the electrode path. Split-bolt splice in the grounding electrode conductor buried inside a wall. Clamp landed on painted or corroded pipe with no clean metal contact. Electrode connection buried below grade with a mechanical clamp where it cannot be inspected. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The intersystem bonding termination
x: Other systems — telephone, cable, antenna, and similar communications systems — need a place to bond to the electrical grounding system, and this section requires an intersystem bonding termination (IBT) for them, at the service or metering equipment, accessible for connection, with room for the stated number of terminations. It is the small bar or bridge by the meter that keeps a cable installer from clamping onto a random pipe. It does not replace the bonding those systems' own articles require; it gives them the listed place to land. Where it goes: • At the service equipment or the metering equipment enclosure, external to the enclosure. • Also at the disconnecting means of any other building or structure on the property supplied by a feeder or branch circuit. What it must be (250.94(A)): • Accessible for connection and inspection. • A set of terminals with the capacity for connection of not less than three intersystem bonding conductors. • Mounted so it does not interfere with opening the enclosure. • Securely mounted and electrically connected to the service equipment, the meter enclosure, or the grounding electrode conductor. • Listed as grounding and bonding equipment. Lightning and utility surges do not respect trade boundaries. If the cable system and the power system sit at different potentials during a surge, the difference equalizes the violent way — arcing between systems, cooking electronics, and shocking whoever touches both at once. One bonded termination point keeps every system at the same potential. Install it where the other utilities actually arrive at the house, and leave it accessible after siding and landscaping. Point it out on the final walk — half its failures are being buried behind finishes. On a Sharma new home, the phone and cable drops land at the meter-main, so the IBT goes on the wall beside it with its terminals free. If the cable installer arrives before the IBT is up, he will clamp the nearest pipe — and the correction lands on us. Two wrong answers show up. First: 'the IBT is a grounding electrode' — it is not; it is a termination point that connects other systems to the grounding electrode system. Second: 'landing on the IBT replaces the bonding required by the communications articles' — it does not; those articles still require the bond. The IBT is simply the listed place it lands. No IBT at the service — the cable bond is clamped to a hose bibb or a random pipe. IBT buried behind siding, stucco or landscaping, no longer accessible. Feeder-supplied detached garage with its own cable drop, but no IBT at its disconnecting means. IBT mounted where it blocks the meter enclosure door from opening. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 250.94(A): Made minor wording changes in 250.94(A)(4) a and b, and removed Informational Note 1, which did not have much value within the code and did not comply with the NEC Style Manual. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bonding metal piping systems
x: Metal water piping in a building supplied by a grounded system must be bonded, sized and connected as this section directs, and other metal piping that is likely to become energized — gas piping is the standard example — must be bonded as well. The bonding jumper is sized by the circuit or service that could energize the piping, using the tables this section points to. Bonding a pipe is a different job from using it as an electrode, and a pipe can need both treatments in different places. Which table sizes which bond: • Metal water piping at a service — the bonding jumper is sized from Table 250.102(C)(1), by the size of the service-entrance conductors (250.104(A)(1)), the same table that sizes the grounding electrode conductor • Metal water piping in a building supplied by a feeder — sized per 250.102(D), which uses Table 250.122 based on the rating of the feeder overcurrent device (250.104(A)(3)) • Other metal piping, such as gas — the jumper is sized from Table 250.122, by the rating of the circuit that is likely to energize the piping Any metal pipe that can become energized becomes a building-wide shock path — every faucet, valve and appliance handle is connected to it. A fault, a failed neutral or a lightning event can put voltage on piping that runs to every room. Bonding ties the piping into the grounding system, so that voltage is held down and a fault gets the low-impedance path it needs to open the overcurrent device. Trace the water piping bond from the panel to clean pipe, and check any jumper over a water meter or filter so the path stays continuous when the meter is removed. For gas piping, bond per this section and the appliance and piping instructions — and see the Florida note on CSST. CSST gas piping carries manufacturer bonding instructions and FBC Fuel Gas requirements beyond this section. The v1 item L-059 is simplified to this section's rule; do not treat this page as covering CSST bonding. The trap answer treats bonding the water pipe and using the water pipe as a grounding electrode as one job — or sizes the gas-piping bond out of the service table. They are different jobs with different tables: water piping at a service bonds per Table 250.102(C)(1), while other piping, like gas, bonds per Table 250.122 by the rating of the circuit likely to energize it. Metal water piping not bonded at the service. No bonding jumper across the water meter or filter, so the bond opens when the meter is pulled. Gas piping with no bonding jumper sized for the circuit that could energize it. Bond clamp landed on painted or corroded pipe with no clean metal contact. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Equipment grounding conductors — what counts as one
x: The fault path back to the source may be a wire, or it may be one of the wiring methods this section recognizes as an equipment grounding conductor: • A wire-type conductor — copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum, bare, covered, or insulated, run with the circuit conductors • Rigid metal conduit, intermediate metal conduit, and electrical metallic tubing — the raceway itself is the ground path, which is why its fittings must be listed and made up tight • The armor of Type AC cable, with its internal bonding strip; and Type MC cable where the armor, alone or combined with its contained grounding conductor, is listed as the ground path • Flexible metal conduit and liquidtight flexible metal conduit — only within this section's limits on length (6 ft combined in the ground-return path), fitting listing, and overcurrent rating; outside those limits a wire-type ground must be pulled with the circuit A method not on this section's list is not a ground path, however solid it looks. The equipment grounding conductor is the path that carries fault current back to the source so the breaker trips in a fraction of a second. That path has to be permanent and low-impedance. A raceway only works as the path while every fitting stays listed and tight — one loose coupling or corroded joint raises the impedance, the fault current drops, the breaker never trips, and the metal case of the equipment sits energized waiting for a hand. An EMT run with tight listed fittings is its own ground; a loose set-screw coupling is a break in that ground. On a long flexible whip to a motor or rooftop unit, pull the green wire instead of asking the flex to be the path. Count the flex in the ground path, not just the piece in your hand: two 4 ft whips joined in one run put 8 ft of flex in the return path — over the 6 ft combined limit — so a wire-type EGC goes in with the circuit conductors. The trap: 'the EMT is the ground, so the green wire is optional — and a flex whip is the same thing.' Wrong twice. Flex only counts within its limits — 6 ft combined in the ground-return path, listed fittings, and the overcurrent limits of the section. Past those limits the flex is just a raceway, and a wire-type EGC must be pulled with the circuit. Loose set-screw EMT coupling left in the ground path — the raceway ground is broken at the joint. Flexible whip over 6 ft in the ground-return path with no wire-type EGC pulled in. MC armor relied on as the only ground where the cable is not listed for it. Wire-type EGC run outside the raceway instead of with the circuit conductors. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 250.118: Stainless steel flexible metal conduit (FMC), and liquidtight flex (LFMC) with a stainless core, can't serve as the equipment grounding conductor (EGC) anymore. Add a wire-type EGC or a bonding jumper. Stainless steel FMC doesn't count as the EGC. Install a wire-type EGC, or a bonding jumper that meets 250.102(E)(2) (250.118(A)(5)(f)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Identifying the equipment grounding conductor
x: An equipment grounding conductor is identified by its color: continuous green, green with one or more yellow stripes, or bare. The reservation runs in both directions: a white or gray conductor is never an equipment ground, a green conductor is never used as a current-carrying conductor, and a green conductor may not be re-marked into something else at the ends. • 6 AWG and smaller: the conductor itself must be green, green with a yellow stripe, or bare for its full length. In a multiconductor cable, an insulated conductor may be re-identified as the equipment grounding conductor at each end and at every accessible point only where maintenance and supervision ensure that only qualified persons service the installation (250.119(B)). • 4 AWG and larger (250.119(A)): an insulated conductor of another color may be identified as the equipment grounding conductor by green marking at each termination and at every point where the conductor is accessible. The equipment grounding conductor does its whole job on the worst day of the circuit's life: a fault to a metal frame. If the green was re-marked as a hot, or a white got landed as the ground, the fault path is broken or a grounded conductor is carrying load current, and the breaker never sees the fault it was supposed to clear. The color is how the next person in the box knows the path is real. In a pull, if the green is missing, the pull is wrong — stop and fix the wire order rather than planning to tape a black conductor green at both ends of a 12 AWG run. Tape-marking is the large-conductor allowance, not a small-wire shortcut. The trap is 'green tape fixes anything.' Tape marking is the allowance for conductors 4 AWG and larger (250.119(A)). On 6 AWG and smaller, the insulation itself must be green, green with a yellow stripe, or bare for the full length — a taped black 12 AWG is a violation, not a shortcut. Black 12 AWG taped green at both ends and run as the equipment grounding conductor. Green conductor re-marked with black tape and used as a hot. White conductor landed on the ground bar as the equipment grounding conductor. 4/0 equipment ground marked green at the lugs but left unmarked at an accessible splice point. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Sizing the equipment grounding conductor
x: The green or bare conductor that runs with a circuit is sized from Table 250.122 by the rating of the overcurrent device ahead of it — not by the size of the current-carrying conductors. The one adjustment: when circuit conductors are upsized, the equipment grounding conductor is upsized in the same proportion (250.122(B)). The EGC must carry fault current back to the source for as long as the breaker takes to open, which is why a long, upsized run with a standard ground is a defect even though every receptacle tests 'grounded.' The table below runs to 1200A; it continues to 6000A for large commercial work. Where one equipment ground serves several circuits in a raceway, it is sized for the largest overcurrent device among them. On a ground fault, the EGC is the path that lets the breaker see a large current and trip fast. An undersized ground chokes that path: fault current falls, tripping slows or never happens, and the metal case of the faulted equipment sits energized, waiting for a hand. Sizing the ground to the breaker ahead of it matches it to the fault current that breaker can pass. When you upsize a run for voltage drop, upsize the ground in the same proportion and write both sizes on the plan. Cable assemblies do this for you; conduit runs do not — check the pull list. Worked example: a 20A circuit is upsized from 12 AWG to 8 AWG for a long run, and the ground grows by the same proportion — 12 AWG to 8 AWG — not the 12 AWG the table alone would give a 20A circuit. On a commercial job, that upsized ground goes on the pull list next to the upsized conductors, or it does not get pulled. S-10: on a CCA branch run, the equipment grounding conductor and its connectors still have to be suitable for the installation — check AL-CU markings where CCA is involved. The trap is sizing the ground off the conductor size on the pull list. A 100A feeder pulled in oversized conductors still takes the 8 AWG copper ground Table 250.122 assigns to a 100A device. The reverse also fails: conductors upsized for voltage drop with a table-size ground left behind — 250.122(B) grows the ground in the same proportion. Conductors upsized for voltage drop, equipment ground left at table size — 250.122(B) requires the same proportion. One ground in a shared raceway sized for the smallest circuit instead of the largest breaker ahead of it. 14 AWG ground pulled on a 30A circuit — Table 250.122 requires 10 AWG copper. CCA branch run with EGC connectors not marked AL-CU (S-10). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Frames of ranges and dryers on existing circuits
x: New work is 4-wire: the frames of ranges, wall-mounted ovens, counter-mounted cooking units, clothes dryers, and the outlet or junction boxes on their circuits connect to the equipment grounding conductor. This section keeps the older 3-wire arrangement lawful only for an existing branch circuit where no equipment grounding conductor is present in the outlet or junction box, and only if all four conditions are met: • The supply is 120/240-volt, single-phase, 3-wire, or 208Y/120-volt from a 3-phase, 4-wire wye system. • The grounded conductor is not smaller than 10 AWG copper or 8 AWG aluminum. • That conductor is insulated, or uninsulated only as part of a Type SE cable on a circuit originating at the service equipment. • The grounding contacts of receptacles furnished as part of the equipment are bonded to the equipment. On a 3-wire hookup the frame is bonded to the neutral, so the metal case of the dryer sits at neutral potential. If that neutral ever opens or goes high-resistance, the frame can rise toward line voltage through the heating element — and the person touching the dryer and a faucet at the same time becomes the path. Four-wire wiring gives the frame its own grounding conductor, so a fault trips the breaker instead of energizing the case. On a service call, identify what is actually in the wall before quoting a receptacle swap. If the circuit is being replaced or extended as new work, pull 4-wire and set a 4-wire receptacle and cord; never create a new 3-wire installation, and never leave the strap in place on a 4-wire hookup. On a dryer swap in an older Kissimmee home, check the box first: a 3-wire SE run from the service panel, with a 10 AWG copper neutral and the receptacle's grounding contacts bonded to the frame, meets all four conditions, so the existing circuit may stay. The same run from a subpanel with a bare SE neutral fails the third condition — that is a rewire conversation, not a receptacle swap. The trap answer is that 3-wire range and dryer circuits are simply 'grandfathered.' They are not: 250.140 allows the arrangement only on an existing circuit, with no equipment grounding conductor in the box, and all four conditions met. The second trap is leaving the bonding strap in place when a 4-wire cord goes on — the strap ties the frame back to the neutral and defeats the new grounding conductor. Bonding strap left in place on a 4-wire dryer or range hookup — the frame is still tied to the neutral. New 3-wire receptacle and cord installed on a remodel circuit. 3-wire arrangement kept on a circuit fed from a subpanel with an uninsulated SE neutral — fails the originating-at-service condition. Grounded conductor smaller than 10 AWG copper (or 8 AWG aluminum) on a kept 3-wire circuit. Range or dryer frame not connected to the equipment grounding conductor on new 4-wire work. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 250.140: Old 3-wire range and dryer circuits fed with service-entrance (SE) cable from a panel that isn't the service can keep using the neutral for the frame, once the bare neutral is covered. New 250.140(B)(5): existing SE cable from equipment other than the service can bond the frame through its neutral, if that neutral is insulated or covered. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wiring methods — general rules
x: Article 300 is the rulebook that sits over every wiring method in this chapter. Whichever cable or raceway you pick later — NM, MC, EMT, PVC — these general rules still apply: protect the wiring from damage, give underground runs enough cover, support what you install, and leave enough free wire at every box to make a proper joint. Read this article first, then go to the article for the specific method. • Protection (300.4): cable and raceway through framing stays 1-1/4 in back from the nearest edge of the wood, or gets a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick. • Cover (300.5): underground wiring is buried to Table 300.5 — in open ground, 24 in of cover over a direct-burial cable, 18 in over PVC raceway, 6 in over rigid metal conduit. • Support (300.11): every method is secured and supported at the spacing its own article sets; wiring never hangs off other raceways, pipes or ceiling wires. • Free conductor (300.14): at least 6 in of free conductor at every outlet, junction and switch point, and 3 in out of the opening where the box opening is under 8 in. • A box at every point (300.15): conduit, tubing and cable methods get a box or conduit body at each splice, outlet, switch, junction, termination and pull point. These rules exist because most wiring damage does not happen on the day of the install. It happens later: a drywall screw finds a cable, a shovel finds a shallow run, a device gets changed on wires too short to remake the joint. Article 300 puts distance, steel, depth and slack between the wiring and the people who will dig, drill and remodel around it for the next fifty years. Before you choose a method, ask three questions: Where does it run (dry, damp, wet, underground, exposed)? What can hit it? How will it be supported? The answers pick the method and trigger the 300 rules. On a Florida house, one 20 A circuit shows all three at once: NM stapled through the stud bays inside (300.4 setback, plates where a hole lands close), a PVC run out to the pool equipment buried with 18 in of cover (300.5), and 6 in of free conductor folded into the box at the disconnect (300.14). The trap is treating Article 300 as fine print that the method article overrides. It does not. A perfectly legal NM run still fails when the bored hole sits 1/2 in from the stud edge with no plate: 300.4 applies on top of Article 334, not instead of it. Bored hole 1/2 in from the stud edge, no steel plate (300.4(A)(1)). UF cable buried at 10 in in open ground; Table 300.5 wants 24 in of cover. Conductors cut to 3 in at a device box; 300.14 wants 6 in free. Splice floating in a wall cavity with no box (300.15). Cable draped over the ceiling grid, tied to a sprinkler pipe (300.11). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 300.17: Cables pulled into a raceway now fall under the general fill limit too, not only individual conductors. Too many cables trap heat and get skinned on the pull. Cables are now named in 300.17: a raceway can only hold as many conductors or cables as heat and a clean pull allow. • 300.26: New 300.26 sorts remote-control and signaling circuits into three groups and points each to its rules: Article 724, Article 725, or the general wiring rules of Article 300. Circuits that aren't power-limited are wired like any power circuit, using the general rules of Article 300 and Chapter 3 wiring methods. • 300.6: Enclosures, other than fences and walls, are now on the corrosion lists. Any thread not cut at the factory counts as field-cut and needs conductive compound where corrosion protection is needed. Enclosures, except fences and walls around equipment, now join raceways, boxes and fittings in needing materials fit for the location. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: All conductors of a circuit run together
x: Every conductor of a circuit — the ungrounded conductors, the grounded (neutral) conductor, and the equipment grounding conductor — is installed in the same raceway, cable, trench, or cord. • Ungrounded (hot) conductors: in the same run as the rest of the circuit. • Grounded (neutral) conductor: in the same run. • Equipment grounding conductor: in the same run. The rule keeps the circuit's magnetic fields canceling each other (conductors run separately heat surrounding metal and behave unpredictably), and it guarantees the ground path travels with the circuit it protects. The exceptions are narrow — conductors in parallel sets, and a few underground and existing-installation arrangements this section names — and even they require the conductors to be grouped so each raceway or cable carries a complete, balanced set. Current that goes out by one path and returns by another makes a loop, and that loop induces voltage and heat in every piece of metal it circles. A ground borrowed from somewhere else may not be there — or may not carry this circuit's fault — on the one day it is needed. Run together, the fields cancel and the fault path is the one you can see and test. The field failure is the borrowed ground or the lone neutral: a ground pulled from a different cable, or one circuit's neutral run in another conduit. On a multiwire branch circuit the shared neutral stays in the same cable as both hots, start to finish. If the conductors did not arrive together, they do not splice together — re-pull the run. A parallel feeder can run all the phase A conductors in one conduit and all the phase B conductors in another — same total copper, easier pull. Wrong. Each raceway of a parallel set carries a complete, balanced set: one conductor of each phase, the neutral where one is used, and the equipment grounding conductor. An equipment ground for a circuit pulled from a different cable because the run's own ground was cut short. One circuit's neutral run in a separate conduit from its hot conductors. Hot conductors in one raceway and the neutral in another on a long commercial run. A parallel set grouped by phase — all of one phase in one raceway, the next phase in another — instead of a complete set in each raceway. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Protecting wiring from physical damage
x: This is the nail-and-screw section. Where cable or raceway passes through or runs alongside wood or metal framing, it has to sit far enough back from the face of the framing that drywall screws and nails miss it — or be shielded by a steel plate. • Through wood framing (300.4(A)(1)): bore the hole so the edge of the hole is at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the wood. If that cannot be kept, protect the cable with a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick. • Through metal framing (300.4(B)): a bushing or listed grommet covers all metal edges and is fastened in the opening before the cable is installed. Where nails or screws threaten NM cable or ENT, add a steel sleeve, plate or clip at least 1/16 in thick. • Parallel to framing (300.4(D)): keep the nearest surface of the cable or raceway at least 1-1/4 in from the framing edge wherever nails or screws are likely — or plate it. Rigid metal conduit, IMC, rigid nonmetallic conduit and EMT need no plate; the raceway is its own protection. • Under metal-corrugated roof decking (300.4(E)): keep cables, raceways and boxes at least 1-1/2 in below the lowest surface of the decking, and never run them concealed inside the decking itself. The fastener here is the roofing screw. Drywall screws, trim nails and roofing screws are driven blind — the installer cannot see the cable behind the surface. A screw through a conductor may not trip anything today; it leaves a nicked, arcing fault inside a closed wall. Setbacks keep copper out of the strike zone, and the 1/16 in plate is thick enough to stop or deflect the fastener when the setback cannot be had. Center your holes, keep the 1-1/4 in setback in 300.4(A)(1), and plate anything that ends up closer. Kick plates / nail plates are not extras — if the cable is in the strike zone, the plate goes on before drywall, every time. On a Marion County rough-in, walk every stud bay before insulation: any hole that ends up closer than 1-1/4 in to a face gets its plate the same day, not on the punch list. Kick plates are always in Sharma takeoffs — stock them on every rough-in truck, do not treat them as an optional add-on. The trap: measuring the 1-1/4 in to the center of the bored hole. The rule measures from the edge of the hole to the nearest edge of the wood. A hole that looks centered in a shallow stud can still be too close on one face — check both faces before you pull. Bored hole 3/4 in from the stud face, cable pulled, no nail plate (300.4(A)(1)). NM cable through a punched steel stud with no grommet — jacket sliced on the raw edge (300.4(B)(1)). Cable run tight along the stud edge in the screw zone, unplated (300.4(D)). Raceway strapped hard against metal roof decking, inside the 1-1/2 in roofing-screw zone (300.4(E)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 300.4(E): Exception No. 1 — rigid metal conduit and intermediate metal conduit, with listed steel or malleable iron fittings and boxes, shall not be required to comply with 300.4(E). Exception No. 2 — the 1-1/2 in spacing is not required where metal-corrugated sheet roof decking is covered with a minimum thickness 2 in concrete slab, measured from the top of the corrugated roofing. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bored holes in wood framing
x: A hole bored through a wood stud or joist for cable or raceway must be drilled so the edge of the hole is at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the wood. If that distance cannot be kept, the cable must be protected by a steel plate at least 1/16 in thick, of a suitable length and width, installed to protect the wiring. The measurement runs from the edge of the hole to the nearest edge of the wood — never from the center of the hole. Check both faces of the member: on a stud drilled slightly off line, one face can pass while the other fails. Where the setback cannot be held, the plate is the fix: steel, at least 1/16 in thick, long and wide enough to shield the cable where it passes the framing. The same 1/16 in plate protects cable in metal framing under 300.4(B)(2). Drywall goes up with screws, cabinets and trim go up with nails, and nobody can see the cable behind the board. The 1-1/4 in setback puts the wiring deeper than the fasteners reach; the plate is armor for the spots where the framing is too shallow to buy that depth. Drill in the middle third of the stud width where you can. Check both faces — a hole can be legal from the front and too close from the back on a shallow stud. Plate first, then pull cable, so the plate is not forgotten. Worked case on a 2×4 (3-1/2 in deep): a 7/8 in hole drilled dead center leaves 1-5/16 in from the hole edge to each face — legal, no plate. Step up to a 1-3/8 in hole for a fat cable and the same centered hole leaves only 1-1/16 in — that hole gets a steel plate before the cable is pulled. The trap is measuring from the center of the hole. A hole centered 1-1/4 in from the face, drilled with a 1 in bit, leaves only 3/4 in from the hole's edge — the rule measures edge to edge, and that run needs a plate. Bored hole with its edge 7/8 in from the stud face, no steel plate (300.4(A)(1)). Plate installed but narrower than the cable run it is supposed to shield. Hole drilled off-center: 1-3/8 in from the front face, 15/16 in from the back, no plate. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Cables through metal framing — bushings and plates
x: Metal studs change the protection hardware: • Through a hole: where a cable passes through a hole in a metal framing member, it is protected by a bushing or a listed grommet. Under 300.4(B)(1) the bushing or grommet must cover all metal edges and be securely fastened in the opening before the cable is installed. • Where nails or screws are likely to penetrate: protect NM cable or ENT in metal framing with a steel sleeve, steel plate or steel clip at least 1/16 in thick (300.4(B)(2)). A raw punched steel edge will saw through a cable jacket under vibration and thermal movement — the bushing is not optional trim. A punched steel-stud hole is a knife edge with a cable resting on it. Building vibration and thermal movement work the jacket against that edge until the insulation is cut and the conductor faults to the stud — inside a closed wall. The steel plate rule covers the second attack: the drywall screw headed for the same cable.
