Stock grommets on the truck for steel-stud work and snap them in as you lay out the holes, not after the cable is pulled — a grommet forced over a pulled cable usually ends up in a pocket instead. Walk the run before insulation: every hole, every cable, one bushing. On a steel-stud tenant job, make that walk a two-man pass: one man with the grommet pouch, one with the cable, and nobody pulls the next stud bay until the last one is bushed and checked. The trap is trusting the grommet to do both jobs: "A listed grommet is in the hole, so the cable is protected." The grommet covers the edge, but where nails or screws are likely to penetrate, 300.4(B)(2) wants steel — a sleeve, plate or clip at least 1/16 in thick. NM cable through a punched steel-stud hole with no bushing or listed grommet (300.4(B)(1)). Grommet loose in the opening, not fastened in place, cable resting on the bare steel edge (300.4(B)(1)). Cable in metal framing where drywall screws will land, with no 1/16 in steel sleeve, plate or clip (300.4(B)(2)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Cables and raceways parallel to framing members and furring strips
x: This is the along-the-framing companion to the bored-hole rule. In exposed or concealed work, where a cable or raceway runs parallel to a framing member — a joist, rafter or stud — or parallel to furring strips, it has to be installed and supported so the nearest outside surface of the cable or raceway is at least 1-1/4 in from the nearest edge of the framing member or furring strip, wherever nails or screws are likely to penetrate. Where that distance cannot be kept, the cable or raceway must be protected from nail or screw penetration by a steel plate, sleeve or equivalent at least 1/16 in thick; a listed and marked thinner steel plate that provides equal or better protection is also permitted. Steel plates are not required for rigid metal conduit, IMC, rigid nonmetallic conduit or EMT — the raceway is its own protection — and for concealed work in finished buildings, cables may be fished between access points where supporting them is impracticable. Drywall screws and trim nails are driven blind, and they go in along framing edges — exactly where a parallel cable wants to lie. A cable held 1-1/4 in off the edge sits outside the fastener path; one hugging the edge is a short circuit waiting for the finisher. The steel plate is the fallback for the stretches where the distance cannot be kept. Running down a stud bay in a wood-frame house in Ocala, the NM drops are held on cable stackers so the nearest surface of the cable stays 1-1/4 in off the stud edge the drywall screws will come through. One stretch has to pass a furring strip tight to the edge — that stretch gets a 1/16 in steel plate before the wall closes. If a stretch of the run has to hug the edge, plate that stretch; finding it after the screw does is a callback and a patch. The trap: "The 1-1/4 in rule is only for bored holes." 300.4(A)(1) covers holes; this section, 300.4(D), covers cables and raceways running parallel to framing members and furring strips — same distance, different run. The second trap is plating everything: rigid metal conduit, IMC, rigid nonmetallic conduit and EMT are their own protection and need no plate. NM stapled tight along the stud edge, right in line with the drywall screws. Parallel run 1/2 in from the edge of a furring strip, with no steel plate. Plate thinner than 1/16 in, not listed or marked, used as the protection. Cable crossing to the edge of the framing at a doorway with no plate before the wall closed. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Protecting large conductors where they enter enclosures
x: Where raceways contain insulated circuit conductors 4 AWG and larger, and those conductors enter a cabinet, a box, an enclosure or a raceway, the conductors have to be protected from abrasion at the entry (300.4(G)). The protection is one of the following: • An identified fitting providing a smoothly rounded insulating surface — the classic insulating bushing. • A listed metal fitting that has smoothly rounded edges. • Separation from the fitting or raceway using an identified insulating material that is securely fastened in place. • Threaded hubs or bosses that are an integral part of the enclosure or raceway and provide a smoothly rounded or flared entry. Two limits ride along: a bushing made wholly of insulating material may not be used to secure a fitting or raceway, and the insulating fitting or material must carry a temperature rating at least equal to the insulation rating of the conductors it protects. Big conductors are stiff, heavy and expensive; a sharp knockout edge plus one hard pull is insulation damage you cannot see after the cover goes on. The edge of a knockout, a locknut corner or a threaded raceway end is a knife under pulling tension. A 4/0 conductor dragged across it shaves its own insulation, and the damage hides inside the enclosure. The fault shows up later — under load, as a ground fault or an arc inside the gear. The smooth, rounded surface spreads the contact so the insulation survives the pull. Fit the insulating bushing before the pull, not after you see the scrape. On service and feeder entries, check every entry edge with a fingertip before conductors go in. On a 200 A Orlando service change, the 4/0 conductors entering the new Siemens meter-main through a threaded nipple got insulating bushings on every entry first — and the fingertip check found one burred knockout edge that would have skinned a conductor on the pull. The trap: 'Only 1/0 and larger needs a bushing' — or 'any metal bushing counts.' The trigger is 4 AWG and larger, and a plain metal bushing with a sharp inner edge is not on the list: the metal fitting must be listed with smoothly rounded edges, or the surface the conductor bears on must be insulating. 4/0 feeder conductors entering a panel over a bare threaded nipple — no bushing or fitting at the entry (300.4(G)). Insulation shaved bright at a knockout edge on 2 AWG conductors; tape wrapped over the damage instead of listed protection (300.4(G)). All-plastic bushing used as the means of securing the raceway to the enclosure (300.4(G)). Entry protected with an insulating fitting rated below the temperature rating of the conductors' insulation (300.4(G)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 300.4: Bushings for 4 AWG and larger now have to be on before the pull. Under metal roof decking, a concrete exception was added, and the rigid and intermediate metal conduit pass now depends on fittings. Where conductors 4 AWG or bigger enter a box or enclosure, the bushing or other protection now goes on before they're pulled (300.4(G)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Underground wiring — cover, protection and sealing
x: Underground runs have to be in a wiring method approved for burial and buried deep enough that digging, traffic and frost do not reach them. Cover is measured from the top of the cable or raceway to finished grade, and the required depth depends on the method and what is above it — a yard, a driveway and a slab are not the same row of the table. Risers coming out of the ground need protection from damage. Under 300.5(G), a raceway through which moisture could contact energized live parts has to be sealed or plugged at either or both ends, with a sealant identified for use with the cable or conductor insulation; the separate seal for a raceway that passes between different temperatures, where condensation is known to be a problem, is in 300.7(A), not in this section. Direct-buried splices and taps are permitted without a splice box only when made under 110.14(B), and wire connectors or splicing means used for direct burial must be listed for that use. Buried wiring sits out of sight for decades, and its enemies are shovels, car tires, settling soil and water. Cover puts dirt between the run and the next person digging. Sealing keeps the moisture that does get into a raceway from traveling inside and reaching live parts in the building. The rows Sharma digs to most (Table 300.5, cover over the top of the cable or raceway): in open ground — direct-burial cable 24 in, nonmetallic raceway (PVC) 18 in, rigid metal conduit 6 in. Under a one- or two-family dwelling driveway or outdoor parking area used only for the dwelling, all three methods are 18 in. Under streets, roads, alleys, driveways and parking lots (the commercial row), 24 in for every method. The 12 in figure is only the separate column for a residential branch circuit of 120 V, 20 A or less with GFCI protection — it is not the depth for PVC in general. Slabs and building interiors have their own rows: check the row for the actual location before you trench, and never carry one depth to every location. NEC 300.5(D)(3) itself requires a warning ribbon — that part is code, not local preference — but only for underground service conductors that are not encased in concrete and are buried 18 in or more below grade: their location must be identified by a warning ribbon placed in the trench at least 12 in above the underground installation. The NEC does not impose that ribbon rule on ordinary feeders and branch circuits. Local AHJs may add bedding or tape requirements beyond it — confirm at permit, and do not assume the table is the whole job. The trap is answering '18 in' for everything because that is the PVC row in open ground — or worse, '12 in,' which is only the GFCI-protected 120 V residential branch-circuit column. Under a commercial driveway every method is 24 in, and in open ground direct-burial cable is 24 in while rigid metal conduit is only 6 in. The answer is always a row and a column, never one number. PVC feeder buried at 12 in in open ground — that depth belongs only to the GFCI-protected 120 V, 20 A residential branch-circuit column (Table 300.5). Raceway entering the building unsealed where moisture can contact live parts (300.5(G)). Direct-buried splice made with connectors not listed for direct burial (110.14(B)). Underground service conductors buried 18 in or more with no warning ribbon placed 12 in above them (300.5(D)(3)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 300.5: EMT now has its own burial depths in Table 300.5(A), and the underground damage protection rules, warning ribbon included, now apply to conductors in raceways as well as direct-buried ones. EMT now has a spot in Column 3 of Table 300.5(A): 18 inches of cover in general, 24 inches under streets and roads. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Sealing raceways that pass between different temperatures
x: Where part of a raceway sits at a much lower temperature than another part — a run from a warm building into a cold-storage room is the textbook case — the warmer air inside the raceway circulates into the cold part and its moisture condenses there, wetting conductors that were installed dry. This section requires the raceway to be filled with an approved sealing material at the temperature boundary, to stop that air circulation. It is a condensation seal, not a waterproofing seal: the separate rule for sealing a raceway so moisture cannot reach live parts is 300.5(G), and explosionproof sealing fittings are a hazardous-location subject in Article 501, not this section. 300.7(A) does not say which side gets sealed; it requires the raceway or sleeve to be filled with an approved material to prevent circulation of warm air to a colder section. It also applies where a raceway passes from the interior to the exterior of a building, and sealants must be identified for use with the cable or conductor insulation, bare conductors, shields or other components. 300.7(B): expansion, expansion-deflection or deflection fittings are required where thermal expansion or contraction is expected. A raceway is a pipe for air as well as wire. Warm air holds moisture; when that air drifts into a cold section and cools, the water falls out on the conductors and terminations. The seal breaks the chimney: no circulation, no condensation cycle, no corroded lugs or nuisance faults in a cooler that was wired dry. The Florida case is any conduit that leaves a hot attic or a sun-baked exterior wall and enters an air-conditioned space or a walk-in cooler: put the duct seal in the run where the temperature changes, before the conductors are pulled or as the section's method directs. A run that drips at the panel in August is usually this rule, missed. The trap answer calls the 300.7 seal 'waterproofing' and reaches for an explosionproof sealing fitting. Both are the wrong subjects: keeping moisture from reaching live parts is 300.5(G), and explosionproof seals belong to Article 501 hazardous locations. 300.7(A) is a condensation seal — fill the raceway with an approved material at the temperature boundary to stop the air circulation. No duct seal where a conduit leaves a hot attic and enters a walk-in cooler — 300.7(A). Sealant not identified for use with the conductor insulation installed. Long sun-exposed run with no expansion or expansion-deflection fitting where movement is expected — 300.7(B). Panel dripping water in August: unsealed raceway from a sun-baked exterior wall into the air-conditioned space. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Securing and supporting — general
x: Raceways, cables and enclosures must be secured in place and supported at the intervals their own article requires — 300.11 is the general rule, and each wiring method's article carries its own numbers (see the table). • Nothing hangs off something else's support. Raceways and cables may not be used to support other raceways, cables or equipment unless the rule for that method specifically allows it. • Cable may not rest on, or be tied to, the ceiling grid or its support wires. In a fire-rated ceiling assembly the support must be independent of the ceiling, so the wiring does not come down when the ceiling does. • One narrow 2020 exception: Class 2 control cable may be supported by the raceway that carries power to the equipment that cable controls — and only that equipment. When in doubt, support it yourself: your own strap, on structure, at the spacing in the method's article. A run that is not supported sags onto sharp edges, pulls sideways on terminations and works its connections loose over years of thermal cycling. In a fire, the ceiling grid is expected to fail — anything tied to it falls into the egress path and onto firefighters. Supporting from structure keeps the electrical system where it was inspected, for the life of the building. When in doubt, support it yourself: your own strap, on structure, at the spacing in the method's article (334.30 for NM, 330.30 for MC, 358.30 for EMT, 352.30 for PVC). Never lay cable on a ceiling tile or tie it to a sprinkler pipe. On a Winter Park bakery build-out, Sharma's 3/4 in EMT home runs took straps within 3 ft of the panel and every box, then at least every 10 ft. The write-up on that job was the thermostat cable another trade zip-tied to our EMT: their cable, our raceway, one violation under 300.11. The tempting wrong answer: “The ceiling wires hold the ceiling, so they can hold the cable.” Ceiling support wires hold tiles, not wiring. Above a fire-rated ceiling, cable support must be independent of the ceiling assembly — and everywhere else, cable still may not rest on the grid or hang from its wires. MC cable draped across the ceiling grid, resting on tiles — supported by nothing (300.11, 330.30). NM stapled at 7 ft intervals in the attic — 4-1/2 ft is the maximum spacing (334.30). EMT with no strap within 3 ft of the box it enters (358.30). Low-voltage cable zip-tied to a sprinkler pipe for support. Cable tied to ceiling support wires above a fire-rated corridor ceiling — support must be independent. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 300.11: Class 3 control cable can now be supported by the power raceway for the equipment it controls. In 2020, only Class 2 cable got that allowance. A raceway carrying power to equipment can hold up Class 2 or 3 control cable that serves only that same equipment (300.11(C)(2)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Free conductor length at boxes
x: At every outlet, junction and switch point, leave at least 6 in of free conductor, measured from where the conductor comes out of its raceway or cable sheath. • At least 6 in of free conductor at the point, measured from where it emerges from the raceway or sheath. • Where the box opening is smaller than 8 in in any direction, the conductors also have to stick out of the opening by at least 3 in, so devices can be made up and folded back without fighting short wires. • Conductors that pass straight through a box without a splice or termination are not counted by this rule. The rule applies at switch points too — a switch loop made up short is the same violation as a short receptacle tail. Short conductors are a slow failure: devices get made up under tension, splices sit at the edge of the box where they chafe, and the next electrician cannot re-make a connection without re-pulling the whole run. The extra length is working room and service life, not waste — it is what lets a device be pulled out, tested and replaced years later. Strip and make up with the full 6 in in hand. If you are short, the fix is a bigger pull or a re-pull — not a wire nut buried with 2 in stubs. Leave the same working length on the spare conductors you cap off. Measure the 6 in from the back of the box, or from the connector. Wrong start point, short wires. The measurement starts where the conductor emerges from its raceway or cable sheath. And the 3 in past the opening does not replace the 6 in — on a small box you owe both. Wire nuts made up on 2 in stubs at a receptacle — no working length to fold the device back. Conductors cut flush at the cable sheath, so nothing reaches out of the box opening. A switch loop with tails too short to pull the switch out of the box for testing. Spare conductors in a junction box snipped short instead of capped at full length. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 300.14: It's settled: the 6 inches of free conductor at a box can be spliced or unspliced, so a short conductor can be pieced out with a pigtail. The 6 inches of free conductor at each outlet, junction or switch point can now be spliced or unspliced. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: A box or fitting at each splice, outlet and junction
x: Where the wiring method is conduit, tubing, Type AC cable, Type MC cable, Type MI cable, nonmetallic-sheathed cable or another cable method, a box or conduit body has to be installed at each of these points — unless one of the exceptions in 300.15(A) through (L) permits otherwise for that case: • each conductor splice point • each outlet point, switch point and junction point • each termination point and pull point A fitting identified for the use may be used in place of a box or conduit body where conductors are not spliced or terminated inside the fitting, and that fitting has to stay accessible after installation unless it is listed for concealed installation. Boxes themselves have to stay accessible under 314.29, without tearing the building apart. A joint made in open air, in a wall cavity, or inside a raceway run, with no exception behind it, is not a joint the next electrician — or an inspector — can ever find. Splices are where circuits fail first: a loose connection in open air arcs against framing and nobody can find it later. The box gives the splice a listed, contained home and keeps it reachable for the life of the building. A buried joint passes rough-in because nobody sees it, then hides a fault for thirty years of service calls. Plan box locations while the walls are open. If a splice has to exist, it gets a box with a cover that stays reachable after finishes go on. On a Sharma rough-in, a home run that comes up short of the panel does not get spliced inside the stud bay and buried — it gets a junction box where it can be reached, or the run is re-pulled. The box costs minutes; the buried splice costs a failed inspection and a callback. The trap: "an identified fitting can always stand in for a box." Only where no conductors are spliced or terminated inside it — a fitting used as a splice point is not the exception, it is the violation. And a box that gets buried behind tile still fails: accessibility under 314.29 is part of the rule. Splice buried in a wall cavity with no box — found at trim, when the circuit is dead and the wall is closed. Junction box drywalled over with no access — a box that cannot be reached fails 314.29. Conductors spliced inside a plain fitting that is neither a box nor a conduit body. Fitting used in place of a box where conductors are terminated inside it — the identified-fitting allowance ends where splices and terminations begin. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 300.15: A change from one wiring method to another, like MC cable to EMT, is now on the list of spots requiring a box, conduit body or fitting. A box, conduit body or identified fitting is now required where one wiring method changes to another, such as MC cable to EMT. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Finish the raceway before the wire goes in
x: A raceway system is installed complete — runs finished, boxes set, fittings in place — before the conductors are pulled into it (300.18(A)). • Cut ends are reamed or otherwise finished so no sharp edge waits inside to skin insulation during the pull. The reaming rule itself lives in the wiring-method articles — 344.28 for rigid metal conduit, 358.28 for EMT — not in 300.18. • Exception: short sections of raceway used only to protect conductors or cable assemblies from physical damage do not have to be installed complete before the conductors or cables are installed (300.18(A) Exception). • The everyday nipple between two enclosures still follows its own fill rules — 60 percent for a nipple 24 in or shorter (Chapter 9, Table 1). Pulling wire into a half-built run and 'finishing around it' damages insulation where nobody can see it. The pull is the roughest hour of a conductor's life. A burr, a missing coupling or a sharp box edge skins insulation under pulling tension, and the damage hides inside the finished run until it becomes a ground fault or an arc. A complete, reamed raceway is the only one that cannot hurt the wire. Walk the run with a flashlight before the pull: every coupling tight, every end reamed, bushings on. The time to find a burr is before 200 ft of THHN is sitting in the pipe. On a tenant rough-in, that walk is the foreman's last check before the pull crew starts: the run that is short one coupling gets finished empty, not threaded. The trap: "300.18 requires reaming." It does not — 300.18 requires the complete raceway before conductors. Reaming lives in the wiring-method articles, 344.28 and 358.28. The exam pairs the two ideas and credits the answer that keeps each rule in its own section. Conductors already pulled into an incomplete run, with a coupling being added around the installed wire (300.18(A)). EMT cut end left unreamed; conductor insulation skinned during the pull (358.28). Wire threaded through a gap in the run to save time, raceway finished around the conductors afterward (300.18(A)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Firestopping penetrations of rated construction
x: Where wiring passes through a fire-rated floor, wall or ceiling, the opening around it has to be firestopped with an approved system so fire and smoke do not travel through the penetration. The electrical work does not end at the conduit — the annular space around it is part of the rated assembly's performance. • The system is matched to the assembly: the construction type and fire rating, the penetrating item — conduit, cable, tray — and the size of the opening all come from the system's listing. • Ordinary expanding foam from the truck is not a firestop system unless it is listed as one for that assembly and penetration. • Every penetration counts. One unsealed conduit is a hole in the rating of the whole wall. Rated walls and floors buy time — time for people to get out and for firefighters to work. Fire and smoke hunt for the holes, and a conduit penetration is a ready-made chimney between floors and units. Firestopping restores the barrier at the one place the trades had to break it. On commercial and multi-family work, plan the firestop with the run: listed system for the assembly, the raceway type and the opening size, installed before the wall is signed off. Photograph it — the next inspector cannot see inside a closed wall either. A typical Sharma multifamily punch item: a bank of six conduits through a rated demising wall between units, each penetration sealed with the system listed for that wall — not one tube of generic red caulk spread over all six. Firestop systems are assembly-specific; Florida inspectors on rated multi-family and commercial work check them by listing, not by color. The trap: 'If it is red, it is firestop.' Color is not a listing. Generic foam or caulk fails even in red. The right answer is always a listed, approved system matched to the assembly, the penetrating item and the opening size. Conduit through a rated demising wall sealed with ordinary expanding foam — not a listed firestop system (300.21). Annular space left open around a conduit bank penetrating a rated floor (300.21). Firestop system listed for a concrete floor installed in a wood-frame wall assembly (300.21). Penetration stuffed with insulation scraps and smeared with caulk — no system at all (300.21). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wiring in ducts, plenums and other air-handling spaces
x: Spaces made for moving environmental air — ducts, plenums and the space above a ceiling used as a return-air plenum — restrict what wiring may run there and how, because anything burning or smoldering in that space feeds the whole building's air. The section splits the spaces three ways: • Ducts for dust, loose stock or vapor removal (300.22(A)): no wiring system of any type inside. • Ducts or plenums specifically fabricated to transport environmental air (300.22(B)): equipment only where it is necessary for direct action on, or sensing of, the contained air. The wiring methods are Type MI cable; Type MC cable with a smooth or corrugated impervious metal sheath and no overall nonmetallic covering; EMT; flexible metallic tubing; IMC; and RMC without a nonmetallic covering. Flexible metal conduit up to 4 ft may connect physically adjustable equipment. • Other spaces used for environmental air (300.22(C)) — the space above a suspended ceiling or below a raised floor that carries return air: metal raceways such as EMT, IMC, RMC and flexible metal conduit, Type AC cable, Type MC cable without a nonmetallic cover, and, where accessible, surface metal raceway or metal wireway with metal covers. Equipment needs a metal enclosure, or a nonmetallic enclosure listed for the use. • NM cable is on neither list. It does not go into a plenum ceiling. Return air touches every room the system serves. A fault that smolders in a plenum ceiling is blown building-wide as smoke long before flames show anywhere. Metal wiring methods and listed enclosures keep fuel out of the airstream, and the fabricated-duct list is the shortest because that wiring sits directly in the air path. The field trap is the plenum ceiling that looks like an ordinary ceiling: before you run a method through a ceiling space on commercial work, ask whether that space is a return-air plenum. If it is, the method list shrinks — when in doubt, ask the AHJ before rough-in, not at inspection. On a Sharma tenant fit-out, the lighting home runs above that ceiling go in EMT or jacket-free MC. The NM whip that passes in a house fails here. Two wrong answers mirror each other. One treats the space above a suspended ceiling like a fabricated duct and applies only the short 300.22(B) list — that space is a 300.22(C) other space, with its own wider list. The other says NM cable is fine above any ceiling — NM is on neither list, so it fails in both spaces. NM cable run above a return-air plenum ceiling — NM is not a 300.22(C) wiring method. Jacketed MC cable installed in a fabricated duct — 300.22(B) requires an impervious metal sheath with no overall nonmetallic covering. Equipment inside a fabricated duct that neither acts on nor senses the contained air. Cable in a plenum space secured with ordinary cable ties not listed for use in the space. Nonmetallic junction box, not listed for air-handling use, installed in a plenum ceiling (300.22(C)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wiring in exit enclosures
x: Exit enclosures — the protected stair towers and exit passageways people escape through — may contain only the wiring that serves the exit enclosure itself. The 2020 text: where an exit enclosure is required to be separated from the building, only electrical wiring methods serving equipment permitted by the authority having jurisdiction in the exit enclosure shall be installed within the exit enclosure. Ordinary branch circuits passing through a stair tower on their way somewhere else do not belong there — not even pulled inside a shared conduit. • What belongs: the tower's own lighting and exit signs, and equipment the AHJ permits there — fire alarm devices, security and public address systems, and fire department emergency communications are the examples the Life Safety Code annex gives. • A panelboard or junction box for other floors does not become permitted because the tower is convenient space; it takes the AHJ's documented permission. • This section was new in the 2020 NEC, which is why older study material and older habits do not mention it. Its informational note points to NFPA 101, Life Safety Code, 7.1.3.2.1(10)(b). The stair tower is the one part of the building that must stay usable while everything else is on fire. Foreign wiring brings foreign fuel, extra penetrations through the rated walls, and a chance for a fault in a through-circuit to start a fire inside the escape route itself. Keeping the tower's wiring to the tower's own equipment keeps the protected path protected for its full rating. On multi-family and commercial work, route around the stair tower by default. If a run must enter it, stop and check what it serves before it goes in. The tempting shortcut on a Florida mid-rise is the tower shaft for a water-heater or corridor circuit — that is exactly the run 300.25 removes. The tower keeps its own lighting and exit-sign circuits; everything else goes around, even when around is longer. If the design truly needs equipment in the tower, get the AHJ's permission documented before rough-in, not at final. The trap is 'the circuit is in EMT, so it may pass through.' 300.25 is not about the wiring method — it is about what the wiring serves, and a foreign branch circuit in conduit is still foreign. The second trap is age: the section was new in 2020, so a 2017-based answer that ignores it is wrong. Corridor or water-heater branch circuit piped straight through the stair tower (300.25). Panelboard for other floors mounted in the exit enclosure without AHJ permission. Foreign conductors sharing a conduit that passes through the tower. Junction box in the tower serving loads outside it. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 300.25: A new exception lets the egress light outside a stair tower's exterior door run off the wiring inside the stair. The rule itself now hinges on the building code's fire-resistance rating. New exception: the egress light over the stair's exterior exit door can be fed from the stair's own wiring. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Conductors for general wiring
x: Article 310 is about the conductors themselves: what they are made of, how they are insulated, and — most used of all — how much current they may carry. The ampacity work lives in 310.12 for dwelling services and feeders, 310.15 for correction and adjustment, and Table 310.16 for the ampacity values themselves. Termination temperature limits live back in 110.14(C) in Chapter 1; this article hands you the number, Chapter 1 tells you which column you may actually use. • The metals: copper fills the left of Table 310.16; aluminum and copper-clad aluminum share the right-hand columns. CCA reads the aluminum values, never the copper ones. • Dwelling services and feeders (310.12): a single-phase dwelling service, or a feeder carrying the whole dwelling load, rated 100 A through 400 A, may be sized at 83 percent of the rating — a 200 A service takes 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum. • Correction and adjustment (310.15): ambient heat over 30 °C, and more than three current-carrying conductors in one raceway, both cut the ampacity before the breaker is picked. • The cap (240.4(D)): whatever the table allows, copper 14, 12 and 10 AWG stop at 15, 20 and 30 A breakers; aluminum and CCA 12 and 10 AWG stop at 15 and 25 A. A conductor is a heater that happens to carry current. Push it past its ampacity and the insulation ages, cracks, and finally fails against a stud or a box wall. Article 310 matches the wire to the load and to the place it runs through, so the insulation outlives the building. Start every sizing question here in this order: load, then Table 310.16 column allowed by the terminations, then correction/adjustment in 310.15, then the small-conductor caps in 240.4(D) from Chapter 2. Worked Sharma example: a 200 A house service. The dwelling rule (310.12) sizes the service conductors at 83 percent, so 2/0 copper THHN — 175 A in the 75 °C column — carries the 200 A service. Run that same 2/0 as a partial-load feeder to a garage subpanel and the 83 percent gift disappears: full Table 310.16 value, no shortcut. The exam trap is reading the 90 °C column as the answer. THHN 12 AWG shows 30 A there, but the terminations cap the usable value at the 60 or 75 °C column, and 240.4(D) caps the breaker at 20 A. The 90 °C column is only the starting point for derating. 12 AWG copper on a 30 A breaker — 'the 90 °C column says 30 A' (the 240.4(D) cap is 20 A). CCA sized out of the copper columns of Table 310.16. The 310.12 83 percent rule used on a partial-load feeder to a subpanel. Four current-carrying conductors in one raceway with no 310.15 adjustment. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 310.10: Parallel conductor rules were rewritten for clarity, supply-side bonding jumpers joined the list of conductors that must match, and both temperature correction and adjustment now clearly apply. Supply-side bonding jumpers run in parallel now have to match each other in length, material, size, insulation and termination (310.10(G)(2)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Conductor minimums — size, material, stranding
x: This section sets the floor for building wire. The smallest conductor for branch circuits and feeders is 14 AWG copper or 12 AWG aluminum or copper-clad aluminum — which is why there is no 14 AWG CCA branch-circuit wire in 2020 work. Conductors are copper, aluminum, or copper-clad aluminum, and the material decides which ampacity column and which termination rules apply. Conductors 8 AWG and larger installed in raceways are stranded. Smaller conductors and special circuits (fixture wires, control and signaling circuits, and the other cases other articles govern) follow their own articles — this floor is for general wiring. Wire that is too small for its breaker overheats in the wall, and the wrong metal on the wrong lug loosens as it heats and cools. The floor in 310.3 keeps the smallest branch-circuit conductor big enough for its overcurrent device and its terminations — and it is written by material, because copper, aluminum and CCA do not carry current the same way at the same size. The material also decides the termination rules and the ampacity column, so a size that is legal in copper is not automatically legal in aluminum or CCA. Ordering rule that follows from this page: a '14 AWG' line on a takeoff means copper. If the job is CCA, the smallest branch-circuit reel on the truck is 12 AWG — and per S-10 it lands on a 15A breaker, not a 20A. S-10: copper by default; CCA one size up. This section is where the 'no 14 AWG CCA' rule lives. The trap answer is '14 AWG is the minimum, whatever the metal.' In 2020 work there is no 14 AWG CCA branch-circuit conductor: the minimum is 14 AWG copper or 12 AWG aluminum or CCA. The follow-up trap is landing 12 AWG CCA on a 20 A breaker because '12 is 20 A' — under S-10 and 240.4(D) it is a 15 A conductor. 14 AWG CCA pulled for a branch circuit — CCA starts at 12 AWG (310.3). 12 AWG aluminum or CCA landed on a 20 A breaker — it is capped at 15 A (240.4(D)). Solid 8 AWG installed in a raceway — 8 AWG and larger in raceways must be stranded. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 310.3: Copper-clad aluminum got its own material rule in 310.3(B): an AA-8000 series aluminum core wrapped in copper that makes up 10 percent or more of the cross-section. Copper-clad aluminum (CCA) now has its own item in 310.3(B): the aluminum core has to be AA-8000 series alloy. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The dwelling 83% rule for services and whole-load feeders
x: For a single-phase dwelling service rated 100A through 400A that carries the entire load of the house, the service conductors may be sized at 83% of the service rating instead of at full Table 310.16 ampacity. The same allowance covers a feeder that carries the entire dwelling load — the classic case is the feeder from an outside meter-main to the inside main panel. • The rule covers a one-family dwelling, or an individual dwelling unit of a two-family or multifamily dwelling. • It does not apply to a partial-load feeder — a feeder to a garage subpanel is sized at full value. • Table 310.12 may be used directly only where no adjustment or correction factors are required. Where factors are required, size from Table 310.16 with the factors applied — and the result may not be smaller than the 83% minimum. • Feeders are not required to be larger than the service conductors (310.12(B), (C)). The full Table 310.12 is in the tables below: the service or whole-load feeder rating, then the conductor it permits. A whole house never runs everything at once — cooking, cooling, laundry and water heating cycle on and off. Decades of demand data sit behind the 83%: a whole dwelling load is predictable in a way a single feeder is not. That is why the discount exists only where the conductor carries the entire load, where the diversity is real. The pair Sharma uses daily: a 200A house service is 2/0 copper or 4/0 aluminum where this rule applies; a 150A service is 1 AWG copper or 2/0 aluminum. A feeder to a garage subpanel carries only part of the load, so it is sized at full value from Table 310.16 — no 83%. The trap answer sizes the garage subpanel feeder at 83% because 'it is a dwelling feeder.' The rule follows the load, not the building: only a service or feeder carrying the entire dwelling load gets 83%. A partial-load feeder is full size from Table 310.16. 83% sizing used on a partial-load feeder to a garage subpanel. Table 310.12 used where derating factors apply, without the Table 310.16 check. 83% applied to a service under 100A or over 400A. 83% applied to a three-phase or commercial service. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Ampacity correction (temperature) and adjustment (bundling)
x: Table 310.16 assumes no more than three current-carrying conductors together and a 30°C (86°F) surrounding temperature. When reality is hotter, or more conductors share a raceway or cable, the ampacity goes down: an ambient correction factor for temperature, and an adjustment factor for the count of current-carrying conductors — 80% for 4 to 6, 70% for 7 to 9, 50% for 10 to 20, 45% for 21 to 30, 40% for 31 to 40, and 35% for 41 or more. Equipment grounding conductors do not count, and a neutral carrying only unbalanced load usually does not count either. You may start the math from the insulation rating (the 90°C column for THHN, say) as long as the final number stays under the termination column and the method's own limit. Ambient correction factors (Table 310.15(B)(1)), above the 30°C base: • At 31–35°C — 0.91 (60°C), 0.94 (75°C), 0.96 (90°C) • At 36–40°C — 0.82 / 0.88 / 0.91 • At 41–45°C — 0.71 / 0.82 / 0.87 • At 46–50°C — 0.58 / 0.75 / 0.82 • At 51–55°C — 0.41 / 0.67 / 0.76 • At 56–60°C — 60°C column: — (no longer corrects) / 0.58 / 0.71 • At 61–65°C — — / 0.47 / 0.65 • At 66–70°C — — / 0.33 / 0.58 Where both apply, the factors multiply — count and temperature together. 2020 rooftop rule: raceways or cables exposed to sunlight on or above rooftops and less than 7/8 in. above the roof add 33°C (60°F) to the outdoor ambient (310.15(B)(2)); Type XHHW-2 is exempt. A conductor heats from the current it carries. In a 50°C attic it starts halfway toward its insulation limit before any load flows, and bundled conductors heat each other. Correction and adjustment put the margin back before the insulation cooks. Count honestly on a home-run bundle: three 12/2 NM cables bundled over 24 in are six current-carrying conductors, not three circuits at full ampacity. Hot Florida attics are the ambient case Sharma hits most — see the attic tip AH-07. Worked example: 12 AWG THHN starts at 30 A in the 90°C column. In a 50°C attic the correction is 0.82, giving 24.6 A — still enough for its 20 A breaker. Run as NM cable, the same conductor is capped at its 60°C table value of 20 A before the 240.4(D) cap is even reached, so a single attic circuit rarely changes; a bundle of home runs, where the count factor stacks on the temperature factor, is where the answer moves. Florida attics routinely run far above 30°C in summer; that is a design condition here, not an edge case. The trap is applying only one factor: derating for the hot attic but forgetting the bundle, or counting the conductors but using the room-temperature factor. Where both conditions exist, the factors multiply. The second trap counts the equipment ground as current-carrying — it never counts. Home runs bundled over 24 in with no adjustment factor applied (310.15(C)(1)). Ampacity figured at a 30°C ambient for a run through a Florida attic (Table 310.15(B)(1)). Rooftop raceway in direct sun, less than 7/8 in above the roof, with no 33°C (60°F) adder (310.15(B)(2)). Derated ampacity allowed to exceed the termination column value at the breaker (110.14(C)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 310.15: Raceways and cables in direct sun now escape the 60°F rooftop adder once they sit 3/4 inch above the roof, down from 7/8 inch. The ambient correction tables were also renumbered. Raceways or cables in direct sunlight less than 3/4 inch above a roof get 60°F added to the outdoor temperature (310.15(B)(2)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Table 310.16 — how to read the ampacity table
x: Table 310.16 gives the allowable ampacity of insulated conductors rated up to 2000 V, with not more than three current-carrying conductors in a raceway, cable or earth, at an ambient of 30 °C (86 °F). Read it in four steps: • Size and metal. Copper is on the left. Aluminum and copper-clad aluminum share the right-hand columns. • Temperature column: 60, 75 or 90 °C. The insulation sets the highest column you may start from. The terminations set the column you finish in (110.14(C)): circuits of 100 A or less, or 14 through 1 AWG, use 60 °C unless the equipment is listed and marked for 75 °C; over 100 A or larger than 1 AWG, 75 °C. • Correct and adjust. Hotter than 30 °C, or more than three current-carrying conductors? Apply 310.15(B) and 310.15(C)(1), normally starting from the 90 °C value. • Check the breaker cap. 240.4(D) limits small conductors whatever the table says: copper 14, 12 and 10 AWG at 15, 20 and 30 A; aluminum or CCA 12 and 10 AWG at 15 and 25 A. Every conductor heats as current flows, and insulation that runs too hot for years cracks and fails. The table keeps current within what the insulation can take. The termination rule exists because breaker and device lugs are often tested only at 60 or 75 °C. The 240.4(D) caps build margin into the small wire that runs bundled and insulated through every wall. A Sharma home run: two 20 A circuits of 12 AWG THHN copper in one EMT through a 104 °F mechanical space, so four current-carrying conductors. 30 A (90 °C) × 0.91 × 0.80 = 21.8 A. That is above the 20 A breaker and below the 25 A 75 °C value, so the 20 A breaker stands. The same circuit in NM cable is held to the 60 °C result (20 A) by 334.80. On a commercial tenant job, a 100 A feeder on 3 AWG copper THHN works with 75 °C lugs (100 A) but not at 60 °C (85 A), so read the lug marking before you pull wire. S-10: branch circuits are copper by default — 14 AWG on 15A, 12 AWG on 20A. When CCA is used, go one AWG larger (12 on 15A, 10 on 20A) because Table 310.16 rates CCA in the aluminum column. Terminations must be marked for the conductor (110.14); wire connectors and lugs need AL-CU / CU-AL marking, CU-only connectors are not rated for CCA, and push-in terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only. Never backstab. The microwave circuit wire is PENDING under S-06 (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA). THHN is 90 °C, so 12 AWG THHN carries 30 A? On the exam, the usable ampacity is the 75 °C or 60 °C value the terminations allow, and the breaker is still capped at 20 A by 240.4(D). The 90 °C column is only the starting point for derating. And 12 AWG aluminum is 15 A at 60 °C, not 20 A. 12 AWG on a 25 A or 30 A breaker because 'THHN is good for 30 A' (240.4(D)). NM cable sized from the 90 °C column. 334.80 holds the result to the 60 °C value. More than two NM cables bundled through a fire-caulked or foamed hole without derating (334.80). CCA sized like copper. CCA reads the aluminum columns. Aluminum or CCA landed on lugs marked CU only (110.14). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 240.4(D)(3) / Table 240.6(A): 14 AWG copper-clad aluminum is protected at not more than 10 A, with continuous load not over 8 A, by a breaker or fuse listed and marked for 14 AWG CCA. 10 A is now a standard rating in Table 240.6(A). The 240.4(D) items renumber as (D)(1)–(D)(8). • Table 310.16: the 2023 change sources reviewed show no change to the values in this page's tables. Confirm in a printed 2023 book. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: CCA in every calculation — ampacity, voltage drop, fill, terminations, sizing
x: Copper-clad aluminum is a material choice inside the same calculations, not a separate code. Run each calculation the same way; pick the CCA line where the table has one: • (1) Ampacity — CCA reads the aluminum column of Table 310.16, with the 240.4(D) caps for aluminum. Cable-article minimums apply: the smallest CCA branch conductor in 2020 work is 12 AWG; there is no 14 AWG CCA NM. • (2) Voltage drop — Chapter 9 Table 8 lists copper and aluminum only; there is no CCA row, so this page gives no CCA resistance for design use. A CCA figure must come from the cable maker's data for the actual product, at operating temperature — never from a resistivity-class calculation. • (3) Terminations — follow the actual cable's identification and the marking and listing of the device, connector or lug in hand. Sources do not all state the same marking rule, so check the marking before the splice. Push-in backstab terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only: CCA is never backstabbed. • (4) Fill — box fill (314.16) and conduit fill (Chapter 9 Tables 4 and 5) go by size and insulation, never by metal: 10 AWG CCA takes the same 2.50 cu in box allowance and the same Table 5 area as 10 AWG copper. The difference shows up one step earlier, in the bigger AWG the ampacity rule chose. • (5) Loads and sizing — Article 220 load math does not change with metal; pick the conductor in the chosen material from Table 310.16. Whether Table 310.12's aluminum sizes may size a CCA dwelling service or whole-load feeder is unconfirmed in print — confirm before using it. CCA exists because copper is expensive: an aluminum core carries current, a copper skin takes the termination. The hazard is treating it as copper — it sizes and heats like aluminum — or inventing numbers no table gave it, above all a voltage-drop resistance. Crew version: aluminum column, one size up. On a Marion Oaks house wired in CCA under S-10: 15 A circuits pull 12 AWG CCA, 20 A circuits pull 10 AWG CCA — check the roll before it is pulled, not at the panel. Do not use a CCA resistance from this page in a voltage-drop calculation: the calculator will not compute one until a cited 75°C source exists. Check the connector marking before the splice: if it does not say AL/CU or CC, it does not touch CCA. S-10 in calculation form: copper default; CCA one AWG up (12 on 15A, 10 on 20A); the microwave wire is PENDING under S-06 (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA). Sharma's CCA is Copperweld NM-B; torque CCA terminations to the printed value once — do not re-torque. No 14 AWG CCA branch-circuit wiring in Florida 2020 work: 310.3(A) sets the minimum at 14 AWG copper or 12 AWG aluminum or copper-clad aluminum. Later editions debated 10-ampere branch circuits and 14 AWG CCA, and published sources disagree on what the 2023 edition actually adopted for 14 AWG CCA — do not rely on any later-edition 14 AWG CCA rule in 2020 work. The trap answer treats CCA as copper: '12 AWG is 12 AWG — 20 A.' CCA reads the aluminum column and takes the aluminum caps, so 12 AWG CCA is a 15 A conductor. The second trap invents a CCA resistance by splitting copper and aluminum — Table 8 has no CCA row to split. 12 AWG CCA landed on a 20 A breaker — sized as if it were copper (240.4(D)). CCA terminated on connectors or lugs marked CU only — the marking was never checked before the splice (110.14). CCA conductor backstabbed into a push-in terminal — those terminals are 14 AWG solid copper only. Voltage-drop figure for a CCA run taken from an unsourced resistance instead of the cable maker's data. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Medium-voltage conductors and cable
x: Article 311 covers medium-voltage conductors and cable, Type MV: a single or multiconductor solid-dielectric cable rated 2,001 volts up to and including 35,000 volts, nominal. The article carries the use, installation, construction specifications and ampacities for that cable. It was new in the 2020 NEC, built from material formerly in Articles 310 and 328, and Article 328 was deleted. Sharma does not pull medium-voltage cable on ordinary work. This page exists so the book's map is complete, and so nobody cites the wrong edition's article number. • Type MV: solid-dielectric cable, 2,001 V to 35,000 V nominal. • The 2020 home of the MV rules: Article 311, built from Articles 310 and 328. • Article 328 no longer exists in the 2020 book. Medium-voltage conductors carry fault energy that ordinary 120/240 V work never sees. A bad MV splice or termination can fail explosively, and the stress grading inside an MV termination is engineered, not field-improvised. The article keeps that work inside listed construction and engineered design. The edition warning matters for the same reason: a citation to a deleted article sends the crew and the inspector to two different books. If a job genuinely involves Type MV cable — systems rated over 2,000 volts, up to 35,000 volts — that is engineered, utility-coordinated work. Stop at this page and escalate to the office; do not extend house habits (NM, ordinary splices, ordinary terminations) into this article. On a Florida campus, hospital or industrial service, Sharma's part ends at the low-voltage side of the transformer unless an engineered MV scope is signed. The trap is the article number. On a 2020 permit or a 2020-based exam, the medium-voltage rules are in Article 311 — not 315, and not 328. Article 315 is the 2023 renumbering, and 328 was deleted in 2020. The second trap is the voltage floor: Type MV starts at 2,001 V, not at 600 V or 1,000 V. MV cable specified or cited from Article 328 on a 2020 permit set — 328 was deleted; plan review sends it back. Ordinary wire connectors or a tape splice on a medium-voltage conductor, instead of listed MV joints and terminations. MV feeder work started with no engineered design and no utility coordination — the AHJ stops the job. Type MV cable terminated with house-wiring habits: no stress control at the termination, cable bent and supported like NM. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 311: Article 311 was renumbered and expanded as Article 315, 'Medium Voltage Conductors, Cable, Cable Joints, and Cable Terminations' (new 315.6 listing, 315.17 marking of MV joints and terminations). • 305: Article 305, the general article for systems over 1,000 volts, is also new in the 2023 NEC. There is no Article 305 in the 2020 book. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Cabinets, cutout boxes and meter socket enclosures
x: Article 312 covers the enclosures the conductors in Article 310 land in: panel cabinets, cutout boxes and meter sockets. Its job is room and protection inside the enclosure: • Enough space to deflect and bend conductors entering the top or bottom — deflection and bending space are set by 312.6 and Tables 312.6(A) and (B). • No sharp edges cutting insulation, and unused openings closed (312.5(A)). • Doors and covers that close properly. • Enclosures kept out of damp and wet locations unless they are rated for them. In a damp or wet location a surface enclosure is mounted with at least 1/4 in. of air space behind it, and an enclosure in a wet location must be weatherproof (312.2). A nonmetallic enclosure on concrete, masonry or tile may go without the air space. • Working space in front of the enclosure is a Chapter 1 rule (110.26), not this article. The cabinet is where the biggest conductors in the building bend, land and get worked on for decades. Crowded bending space presses insulation against steel edges, an open knockout invites pests and fingers, and a can rusting against a damp wall fails from the back where nobody looks. The room, the closures and the air space keep the enclosure from becoming the fault. On a Sharma house this is the meter enclosure and the panel cabinet. Check conductor bending room before you land a 4/0 service conductor, not after, and keep the enclosure plumb so the deadfront and door seat correctly. In the S-09 back-to-back layout the meter can sits on an exterior wall in a wet location — it goes up weatherproof, on its 1/4 in. air space, not sealed flat to the stucco. S-09 puts the meter outside and the panel inside, back to back, where the house allows — both enclosures still have to meet this article and the 110.26 working space. FPL and other Florida utilities have their own meter-socket approval lists on top of the NEC — the socket must be on the serving utility's list. The exam swaps the articles: it credits Article 312 with the working-space rule. Working space in front of the panel is 110.26, in Chapter 1. Article 312 governs the enclosure itself — the bending space inside it (312.6), damp and wet mounting (312.2), and closed unused openings (312.5(A)). Surface-mounted cabinet on a damp or wet location wall with no 1/4 in. air space behind it (312.2). Unused knockout openings left open in the panel cabinet (312.5(A)). 4/0 service conductors forced in against a sharp enclosure edge with no bending room (312.6). Cabinet racked out of plumb so the deadfront and door will not seat and close. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 312.10: For the first time, screws that poke into a cabinet, cutout box or meter can are limited: blunt tips only, and 1/4 in. of reach unless the tip is protected. A field-added screw for a label or other gear must be a blunt machine screw reaching 1/4 in. or less, unless its tip is protected. • 312.102: New in 2023: cabinets, cutout boxes and meter cans all need a door or a cover. No open cans. Doors or covers are now mandatory on all three Article 312 enclosures: cabinets, cutout boxes and meter cans (312.102). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Cables entering a cabinet — and the conduit-stub exception
x: Ordinarily each cable entering an enclosure gets its own cable connector or clamp. The exception lets a group of cables enter the top of a surface-mounted enclosure through one short raceway instead — but only when every condition below holds: • The raceway is nonflexible, at least 18 in. and not more than 10 ft long, and enters only the top of the surface-mounted enclosure. • Each cable is fastened within 12 in. of the outer end of the raceway, measured along the sheath. • The raceway is installed directly above the enclosure and does not penetrate a structural ceiling. • A fitting provided at each end protects the cables against abrasion, and the fittings remain accessible after installation. • The outer end of the raceway is sealed or plugged. • The cable sheath extends through the raceway and continues at least 1/4 in. into the enclosure. • The raceway is secured and supported at its outer end and as required by its article. • Cable fill does not exceed Chapter 9, Table 1 — the 60% nipple rule does not apply to this raceway. Miss one condition and the exception is gone: every cable goes back to its own connector. An unsecured cable dumps every tug, snag and settling pull straight onto its terminations, and loose terminations overheat. The exception does not drop that protection — it moves it. The short, straight, sealed stub shields the cables as a group, and fastening each cable within 12 in. of the end does the strain-relief work the individual clamps would have done. Sharma panel swap, Orlando garage: the new surface-mounted 200 A Siemens panel takes the home runs through one 6 ft EMT stub out the top. Each cable is strapped within 12 in. of the stub's outer end, the end is plugged against debris and critters, and every sheath runs through and 1/4 in. into the can. The checklist gets one look before the cover goes on — miss a condition and the cables get individual connectors instead. The trap: 'the 60% nipple fill applies to the stub.' It does not — fill under this exception is Chapter 9, Table 1. Second trap: treating the exception as permission to skip connectors at any panel top. It covers only a nonflexible raceway, 18 in. to 10 ft, into the top of a surface-mounted enclosure, with every condition met. Conduit stub over 10 ft long used as the cable entry — outside the exception. Cables not fastened within 12 in. of the raceway's outer end. Outer end of the stub left open — not sealed or plugged. Stub run through a structural ceiling. Sheath cut off at the raceway end instead of running 1/4 in. into the enclosure. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Conductor bending and deflection space in enclosures
x: Large conductors cannot be bent around a thumb. This section sets the minimum space inside cabinets, cutout boxes and meter enclosures for conductors to deflect and bend where they enter and land — figured from the tables in the section by conductor size, the number of conductors per terminal, and whether the conductor turns or runs straight through. An enclosure can be big enough on the wall and still be too small for the 4/0 or 250 kcmil that has to land in it. Two tables split the work: • Table 312.6(B) — wire-bending space at terminals, where the conductor enters or leaves the enclosure through the wall opposite its terminal • Table 312.6(A) — deflection space and gutter width, where the conductor does not enter or leave through the wall opposite its terminal and turns inside the enclosure instead Two conductors landing on one terminal need more space than the one-conductor figure — the tables carry separate columns for that. This page is not yet verified: the bending-space values an earlier draft listed here were removed until they are checked row by row against the printed 2020 Tables 312.6(A) and 312.6(B). Read the values from the printed tables (see Check in print). A feeder forced around too tight a bend is damaged goods: the insulation stretches thin on the outside of the bend, the strands splay, and the lug takes a side load every time the conductor tries to spring back. Bending and deflection space is what lets a large conductor land flat on its lug and stay there for the life of the gear. Size the enclosure from the conductor, not the wall space: check the bending-space table for the largest conductor and the entry direction (top, bottom, side) before the gear is ordered. Forcing a feeder into too-tight a bend is damaged insulation and a failed inspection in one move. On a Sharma service change, that check happens at the estimate stage, while a bigger can is still a line item and not a return trip. The trap: picking whichever table gives the smaller number. The entry geometry picks the table — a conductor that enters or leaves through the wall opposite its terminal is a Table 312.6(B) bending-space case; one that turns inside the gutter is Table 312.6(A). The other trap is "the can fits the wall, so the wire fits": bending space is figured from the conductor, not from the enclosure's footprint. Large feeder forced into a bend the enclosure was too small for — insulation creased at the lug. Gear ordered by wall footprint, with bending space never checked until the wire would not land. Gutter width for a conductor turning inside the enclosure figured from Table 312.6(B) — the wrong table for that entry. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: What may live inside an enclosure for switches and overcurrent devices
x: An enclosure that houses switches or overcurrent devices is not a general-purpose junction box, but it is not sealed against all other wiring either. Under 312.8(A), conductors may feed through, splice and tap inside the wiring space, within set limits: • Feed-through conductors: the total of all conductors at any cross section of the wiring space does not exceed 40 percent of that space. • Splices and taps: all conductors, splices and taps together do not exceed 75 percent at any cross section. • A warning label on the enclosure identifies the location of the disconnecting means for the feed-through conductors. Power-monitoring and energy-management equipment may also live in the wiring space under 312.8(B): it must be identified as a field-installable accessory of listed equipment, or a listed kit evaluated for field installation in these enclosures, and everything at any cross section — conductors, splices, taps and the equipment — stays at or under 75 percent. The wiring space in a breaker enclosure is sized for that enclosure's own conductors to bend, land and be serviced. Foreign splices packed into the gutter trap heat, block breaker work, and leave live feed-through conductors inside a panel the next electrician opened expecting one disconnect to make it safe. The limits and the label keep the enclosure's own job possible and its hidden hazards announced. Do not treat a panel as free splice space on a remodel. If feed-through or splices are planned in an overcurrent enclosure, count the space and keep it in the wiring gutter area. Example: a gutter cross section of 20 sq in allows 8 sq in of feed-through conductors at the 40 percent limit, and 15 sq in total once splices and taps are added at the 75 percent limit. Be ready to show the inspector the section you relied on. Splices and taps may fill 75 percent of the wiring space, so feed-through conductors may too. Wrong swap. Feed-through conductors alone are capped at 40 percent of the cross section. The 75 percent figure is the total — conductors, splices and taps together. A panelboard used as a junction box for unrelated circuits, with no fill count done at all. Splices and taps packed into the gutter past 75 percent of the wiring space at a cross section. Feed-through conductors passing through a panel with no warning label identifying where their disconnecting means is. Monitoring equipment screwed into the gutter that is not a listed kit or an identified accessory for the enclosure. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 312.8: Switch and breaker enclosures carrying feed-through conductors, splices or taps now need enough bending space for 4 AWG and larger conductors, on top of the old 40 and 75 percent fill limits. New item (3): 4 AWG and larger conductors in the wiring space need bending room that meets 314.28(A)(2), the angle-pull rule for pull boxes. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Outlet, device, pull and junction boxes
x: Article 314 is the box article: which box, how big, how it is set, how it is supported, and what may live in it. • The sizing heart is 314.16: a box is big enough only if its marked volume holds every conductor, device, clamp and ground the counting rules charge against it. • 314.17 covers conductors entering the box — cables secured to it, and the sheath carried at least 1/4 in inside, past the clamp. • 314.23 covers support: the box must not move when devices are plugged in and pulled out for twenty years. • 314.28 takes over at 4 AWG and larger, where sizing stops being cubic inches and becomes pull geometry. • 314.29 requires every box to stay accessible without removing any part of the building. The volume math is the part you can settle at the truck. The placement rules around it are what inspectors check after the math passes. An overfilled box overheats its splices and crushes insulation when the device is forced in — and the damage hides behind the cover plate. A box nobody can reach turns one failed splice into a wall demolition. The fill count and the accessibility rule exist so the weakest point of every circuit stays cool, intact and findable for the life of the building. Run the fill math before the rough-in, not at trim. A box that fails fill in the wall fails the same way on paper — cheaper to catch it on paper. Sharma kitchen case: two 12/2 NM cables and one receptacle in a 4 in square × 2-1/8 in box. The conductors charge four allowances, the grounds one, the clamps one and the yoke two — 8 × 2.25 = 18.0 cu in against the box's 30.3. It passes with room to work. Add a third cable and the count climbs past what the shallow 1-1/2 in box (21.0 cu in) should carry — that is the call to make before the drywall, not at trim. The wrong answer: “A receptacle counts once, like one conductor.” Each device yoke counts as two allowances, figured at the largest conductor connected to that device (314.16(B)(4)). Undercounting the yoke is how a box that looked fine on the truck fails the count on paper. 4 in square × 1-1/2 in box (21.0 cu in) holding three cables and two devices — the count exceeds the marked volume (314.16). Junction box covered by fixed kitchen cabinets — not accessible (314.29). Box held up only by the NM cables entering it — a box must be supported (314.23). Finished junction box left without a cover (314.25). Straight pull through a 12 in box on a 2 in raceway — 314.28(A)(1) needs 16 in. Sheath stripped off outside the box, conductors crossing the clamp unprotected (314.17). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 314.24: New clearances where wiring enters a box: at a side entry, the device stays behind the knockout centerline or 1/2 in. off that wall. A center-back entry adds room behind 12 or 10 AWG equipment. With a side entry, the back of the device can't reach past the centerline of that knockout or entry (314.24(C)(1)). • 314.25: Conduit bodies joined boxes in the closure rule: on a finished job, every LB and other conduit body needs a cover, faceplate, luminaire canopy or lampholder. On a finished job, every conduit body needs a cover, faceplate, luminaire canopy or lampholder, the same as a box. • 314.5: New fastener limits for boxes and conduit bodies: blunt machine screws, set reach limits for cover and wall screws, and nothing poking past flush in small boxes or conduit bodies. Pointed screws are out: field-added screws in boxes and conduit bodies must be blunt-end machine screws, unless the manufacturer supplied or specified them. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Box fill — volume, allowances and counting
x: Box fill is a counting exercise with a hard ceiling: add up the volume allowances of everything in the box, and the total may not exceed the volume stamped or tabulated for that box. Table 314.16(A) gives the volume of standard metal boxes; Table 314.16(B) gives the allowance each conductor size costs. Both tables are reproduced below. • What counts is decided by 314.16(B)(1) through (5): conductors, internal clamps, support fittings, device yokes, and equipment grounding conductors. • The grounds rule is the 2020 version: up to four equipment grounding conductors or bonding jumpers together cost one allowance, and each one past four adds a quarter allowance. • A plaster ring, extension ring or cover marked with its volume adds that volume to the box; an unmarked one adds nothing you may count on. Count first, then pick the box — the worked example in On the Job shows how fast a standard box runs out of room. Conductors folded into a box are bent, pressed and heated in a tight space. The allowances guarantee free space around every splice and device, so insulation is not crushed against box edges and the device can sit flush without forcing the wires. An overfilled box fails slowly — chafed insulation and hot connections, long after the cover is on. Run the five counts in field order: (1) conductors — each conductor that enters from outside and is terminated or spliced counts once, a conductor passing through unbroken counts once, and a pigtail that starts and ends in the box counts zero; (2) clamps — all internal clamps together count once; (3) support fittings — one allowance for each type; (4) device yokes — each yoke counts twice; (5) grounds — up to four count once, each one past four adds a quarter. Worked example: a 4 in square × 1-1/2 in box holds 21.0 cu in. Three 12/2 NM cables, one receptacle and internal clamps charge: 6 conductors × 2.25 = 13.50, grounds 2.25, device yoke 4.50, clamps 2.25 — total 22.50 cu in. It fails. The 4 in square × 2-1/8 in box at 30.3 cu in passes. Box height on the wall is not a 314 rule — Sharma S-04 (receptacles 18 in to the bottom of the box, plan silent) and S-05 (switches 48 in to center) govern placement; 314 governs whether the box you placed is big enough and set right. Two traps meet here. First: 'pigtails count.' A pigtail that starts and ends in the box counts zero. Second, the 2017 habit: 'all the grounds together are one allowance, period.' In the 2020 book up to four grounds count once, but each ground past four adds a quarter allowance — in a crowded box, that quarter is the one that fails you. Three 12/2 cables and a receptacle fitted into a 4 in × 1-1/2 in square box — 22.50 cu in of charge in a 21.0 cu in box. Device yoke counted once instead of twice. Five or more grounds with no quarter allowances added past four. Unmarked plaster ring counted toward the box volume. Grounds not counted at all — up to four still cost one allowance. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The five counting rules, one by one
x: • (B)(1) Conductors: each conductor from outside the box that is spliced or terminated counts once; a conductor that runs through unbroken counts once; an unbroken loop or coil of at least twice the minimum free-conductor length required by 300.14 — so 12 in or more of loop — counts twice; pigtails that originate in the box count zero. • (B)(2) Clamps: where one or more internal cable clamps are present, all of them together count once, at the largest conductor in the box; a cable connector with its clamping mechanism outside the box counts zero. • (B)(3) Support fittings: count one allowance for each type of fitting present — all luminaire studs together count once, and all hickeys together count once, so a box with both a stud and a hickey counts two — at the largest conductor in the box. • (B)(4) Devices: each device yoke or strap counts twice, at the largest conductor connected to that device; a device wider than a single 2 in device box counts twice for each gang required to mount it. • (B)(5) Grounds — the count that changed in 2020: up to four equipment grounding conductors and equipment bonding jumpers entering the box together count once, at the largest ground in the box, and each additional one beyond four adds a quarter of that allowance. Isolated-ground conductors count in with the rest of the grounds; the old separate extra allowance for an isolated-ground set is a 2017 rule and does not apply in 2020. Boxes are where conductors get spliced, heated and crowded. The count is a heat-and-damage budget: every allowance is room for insulation and for the next electrician's hands. Undercount, and the box gets stuffed — insulation nicks on sharp edges, devices strain their terminations, and heat has nowhere to go. Say the counts out loud as you tally: wires, clamps, studs, yokes, grounds. Field example at 12 AWG (2.25 cu in): four grounds = 2.25 cu in; six grounds = 2.25 + (2 x 0.25 x 2.25) = 3.38 cu in. In a normal house box with two or three cables the ground count is four or fewer, so the old habit gives the same answer — the quarter rule only bites in crowded multi-cable boxes, which is exactly where fill was already tight. The 2020 quarter-allowance count is what this page, the calculator, the starter quiz, and lookup L-064 now teach. The printed 2020 text of 314.16(B)(5) was checked in the 2026-11-18 verification pass. The old 'all grounds count as one, however many' rule is the 2017 rule. The trap is the 2017 habit: 'all the grounds count as one, however many enter.' In 2020 the first four grounds together count once, and every ground after that adds a quarter allowance. The second trap counts a pigtail that starts inside the box — pigtails count zero — or counts a device yoke once instead of twice. Six equipment grounds counted as a single volume allowance — the 2017 rule (314.16(B)(5)). Device yoke counted once instead of twice in the fill tally (314.16(B)(4)). Long unbroken loop of conductor left in the box counted once instead of twice (314.16(B)(1)). Box filled past the cubic-inch capacity marked inside it (314.16). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 314.16: New in 2023: a terminal block inside a box takes up box fill. Count one volume for the whole block, based on the biggest wire terminated on it. Add one volume allowance for each terminal block assembly, using the largest conductor terminated on it (314.16(B)(6)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Conduit bodies — fill and splices
x: Conduit bodies follow fill rules too. • Conductors passing through: the fill may not exceed what the Chapter 9 tables allow for the raceway size the body belongs to. • Splices, taps and devices: allowed inside a conduit body only where the body is durably and legibly marked with its cubic-inch capacity by the manufacturer. Then the fill is counted the same way box fill is counted, against that marked volume, using the Table 314.16(B) allowances — 2.00 cu in for each 14 AWG, 2.25 for each 12 AWG, 2.50 for each 10 AWG. • An unmarked LB is a pulling fitting, not a junction box: no splices live in it. A conduit body is a small sealed pocket. Cram splices into one that was never sized for them and the wirenuts sit crushed against the cover, insulation chafes on the casting, and the heat of a loaded splice has nowhere to go. The marking rule makes the manufacturer state the volume up front, so the splice count is a math problem with an answer — not a guess made with the cover in your hand. Read the casting before you splice: no cubic-inch marking, no splice. The count, worked: a splice joining two 12 AWG conductors charges 2 × 2.25 = 4.50 cu in, the grounds count once at 2.25, total 6.75 cu in — so the casting has to read at least 6.75 cu in before that splice is legal in that body. If the job needs a splice at that point and the body is unmarked, the fix is a marked body or a real box — not a bigger wirenut. Plan the box at rough-in instead of discovering it at final.
