The trap is calling an LB a small junction box. An unmarked conduit body is a pulling fitting only; splices, taps and devices need a body durably and legibly marked with its cubic-inch capacity, and the fill then counts exactly like box fill. The mirror trap is using the Chapter 9 raceway fill for a body that holds splices — those tables govern conductors passing through, not splices. Splices wirenutted inside an unmarked LB — no cubic-inch marking, no splices (314.16(C)). Marked body filled past its marked volume — the splice charge outran the casting number. Capacity marking scraped off or illegible — the capacity must be durably and legibly marked. Device mounted in a conduit body that was never marked for one. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Conductors and cables entering boxes
x: Cables entering a box have to be secured to the box, or fastened close enough that the entry stays put, and the cable sheath has to continue into the box so the conductors are protected where they enter. Metal boxes with clamps secure the cable at the box itself; a box without a clamp leans on the fastening distance instead. • Sheath: at least 1/4 in inside the box, past any clamp (the v1 field rule, L-065). • Single-gang nonmetallic boxes: fasten the cable within 8 in of the box — the sheath still goes 1/4 in in. • Unused openings get closed. An open knockout is a hole in the enclosure, not a spare. The entry is where a cable gets yanked and chafed. If the cable is not secured, every tug lands on the terminations and works them loose — and loose terminations arc and overheat. The 1/4 in of sheath past the clamp means the clamp bites the jacket, not the bare conductors, so insulation is never the thing being squeezed. A closed unused opening keeps the enclosure an enclosure: fingers, dust and sparks stay on their own side of the box wall. On a Florida rough-in with single-gang nonmetallic boxes, the staple is the securing: staple the NM within 8 in of every box, every time. Strip the sheath outside the box, not inside it: 1/4 in of sheath past the clamp is protection; 2 in of sheath inside the box is fill you did not count and a make-up fight at trim. The trap answer is stripping the sheath flush at the box face 'to keep the box neat.' The rule wants the opposite: the sheath continues at least 1/4 in into the box, past the clamp. The second trap is fastening 'close enough' on a single-gang nonmetallic box — the number is 8 in, not 'within a foot or so.' Sheath stripped flush at the clamp — no jacket inside the box past the clamp (314.17). NM drifting into a single-gang plastic box with the nearest staple 2 ft away — not fastened within 8 in. Open knockout left in the back of a box — unused opening never closed. Two inches of sheath left inside the box, eating fill that was never counted. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 314.17: The section now names cables in its title alongside conductors and was reworded for accuracy. The working rules for closing openings and securing NM and UF cable carry over. NM or UF through a clamp: jacket 1/4 in. or more into the box and past the clamp, and the cable secured to the box. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: How a box sits in a wall or ceiling
x: How far a box may sit behind the finished surface depends on what that surface is made of: • Noncombustible — concrete, tile, gypsum board (drywall), plaster: the front of the box, plaster ring, extension ring, or listed extender may be set back no more than 1/4 in. • Combustible — wood or other combustible material: the box or extender has to reach the finished surface or project past it. No setback. • Gypsum board counts as noncombustible for this rule, even when it is screwed to wood studs. A box buried farther than the rule allows is both a device problem — the yoke ears cannot reach — and a code problem. The gap is the hazard. A box sunk too deep leaves an open slot between the device and the box where an arc or a loose, hot connection can reach the wall cavity and the framing behind it. It also leaves the device floating on its yoke screws, so every plug insertion works the receptacle a little looser. Set box depth off the stud face for the finish that is actually going on that wall: 1/2 in drywall is not tile on backer board. Use the adjustable-depth or extension option before the wall closes, not a stack of goof rings at trim. Tile makes the point: backer board and tile build a kitchen backsplash wall out about 7/8 in, so a box set for 1/2 in drywall alone can land 3/8 in behind the tile face — over the 1/4 in limit even though tile is noncombustible — and it needs its extension ring at rough-in, not at trim. S-04 and S-05 set the height (18 in to bottom for receptacles, 48 in to center for switches, plan silent); this section sets the depth. Both have to be right on the same box. The trap: "The studs are wood, so the wall is combustible and the box must sit flush." Wrong — the surface is what counts, and gypsum board is noncombustible for 314.20 even over wood studs, so the 1/4 in setback is allowed. Flip it onto a wood-paneled wall and that same setback fails. Box set back 3/8 in behind a tile surface with no extension ring (314.20 allows 1/4 in max in noncombustible material). Box recessed behind wood paneling instead of reaching or projecting past the finished surface (314.20). Device floating on stacked goof rings with the box opening gaping into the wall cavity (314.20). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Repairing the surface around a box
x: Where a box is set in a noncombustible wall or ceiling, the broken or chipped surface around it has to be repaired so there is no gap or open space bigger than 1/8 in around the box. The plate cannot be the patch — the surface itself has to come back to the box. • The limit is on the finished repair: no gap or open space over 1/8 in at any point at the edge of the box. • The surfaces covered are the noncombustible ones — concrete, tile, gypsum board, plaster and the like, the same family 314.20 uses for box setback. • Do not swap the two numbers: 314.20 lets the box face sit back up to 1/4 in in noncombustible material; 314.21 separately caps the gap around the box at 1/8 in. • In combustible material this repair rule is not the governing one — 314.20 requires the box to reach the finished surface or project past it. The gap around a box is a chimney. Fire and hot gas in the wall cavity use it to reach the room, and smoke takes the same path. A cover plate hides the gap but does not close it — the plate is thin, often plastic, and is not part of the wall surface. Closing the surface itself keeps the wall the barrier it was built to be, and it gives the device yoke something solid to seat against. On remodel work, check the gap before you set the device. A 1/4 in crater around a cut-in box is a fail here and a wobbly device later; use the right box or repair the opening. On a Florida bathroom remodel, that means patching the chipped tile or plaster back to the box edge before the device goes in — five minutes of patching beats a red tag at final and a callback for a receptacle that rocks every time a plug is pulled. The trap answer is that an oversized — jumbo — cover plate fixes a broken opening. It does not: 314.21 requires the surface itself repaired so no gap over 1/8 in remains, whatever plate goes on top. The second trap is swapping the numbers: 1/4 in is the 314.20 box setback in noncombustible material; 1/8 in is the 314.21 gap around the box. Gap of 1/4 in between the box edge and the broken drywall, hidden behind an oversized plate (314.21). Tile chipped away around a cut-in box and left open behind the cover plate. Cratered plaster around a box wider than 1/8 in at final inspection. Device floating on its yoke screws because the surface around the box was never repaired. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Supporting boxes
x: A box has to be supported — screwed, nailed, braced or hung by a method the article allows for that box type — rigidly enough that it does not move when devices are plugged in and pulled out for twenty years. Surface boxes, pendant boxes and boxes in walls and ceilings each have their own allowed supports in this section, and a box supported by a raceway alone is allowed only in the narrow cases the section describes. • Surface and structure (314.23(A) and (B)): fasten the box to a surface that can hold it, or to a structural member, directly or on a brace — metal braces at least 0.020 in thick, wood braces at least a nominal 1 by 2. • Finished surfaces (314.23(C)): a cut-in box is held by clamps, anchors or fittings identified for the purpose. • Suspended ceilings (314.23(D)): boxes of 100 cu in or less may fasten to the ceiling framing members, or hang from added independent support wires — never from the ceiling's own wires. • Raceway support, no devices (314.23(E)): an enclosure with no device or luminaire, 100 cu in or less, threaded entries or identified hubs, held by two or more conduits threaded wrenchtight, each conduit secured within 3 ft — 18 in where every entry is on the same side. • Raceway support, with devices (314.23(F)): the same 100 cu in cap and threaded entries, two or more conduits — and each conduit secured within 18 in of the box. Devices get pushed, pulled and leaned on for decades. A box that gives a little at every plug-in works its splices loose, cracks the plate, and finally arcs inside a wall. Rigid support keeps the mechanical stress on the bracket and the stud, where it belongs, instead of on the terminations. Wiggle test at rough-in: grab the box and push. If it moves, the device will move at trim and the plate will never sit flat. Add the brace or bracket now. On a Sharma rough-in the test catches most of it: device boxes nailed to the stud with the bracket flange flat, ceiling boxes on listed bar hangers between the joists. The fan location gets a listed fan box — marked for the weight, good to 70 lb before the fan needs independent support (314.27(C)) — not a standard octagon box on a strap. The trap: 'the conduit holds it, so it is supported.' One EMT stub under a device box fails 314.23(F) three ways — it takes two or more conduits, threaded wrenchtight or on identified hubs, each secured within 18 in, and the box can be no bigger than 100 cu in. Device box supported by a single EMT stub; 314.23(F) wants two or more threaded conduits, each secured within 18 in. Octagon box and luminaire hung from the ceiling grid wires; boxes need the framing members or their own independent wires (314.23(D)). Pendant box on a cord with the cord's weight hanging on the terminals; the fitting has to keep tension off the joints (314.23(H)(1)). Cut-in box loose in the drywall, rocking when the receptacle is plugged in (314.23(C)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 314.23: Pendant boxes hung from cord: a box with a hub now has to hang from a listed cord grip that carries a threaded-hub marking. Cord-hung box with a hub? It has to be held by a listed cord grip marked for threaded-hub use (314.23(H)(1)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Boxes at lighting outlets — the 50-pound rule
x: A box used at a lighting outlet has to be listed for the purpose, and it may support a luminaire (or lampholder) weighing up to 50 lb. A heavier luminaire may be supported by the box only where the box is listed and marked for the weight it will actually carry; otherwise the fixture is supported independently of the box. • Up to 50 lb: a listed lighting-outlet box carries the luminaire. • Over 50 lb: the box must be listed and marked for the actual weight, or the fixture gets independent support from the structure. • Ceiling fans are not luminaires under this rule — a fan needs a fan-rated box under 314.27(C), even if the fan weighs less than 50 lb. Fan boxes are listed for fan support and marked with the weight they may carry, up to 70 lb; a heavier fan is supported independently. A luminaire hangs over the people who live and work under it, held by screws and box ears that also carry its wiring connections. A box that lets go drops a live fixture into the room and tears conductors loose on the way down. The weight limit, the marking rule and the separate fan rule exist because weight plus vibration is what works a support loose over time. Big foyer and lanai fixtures are the trap: weigh the fixture or look up its weight before trim-out. A 62 lb chandelier in a two-story Kissimmee foyer is over the line for a plain box — if the box is not listed and marked for 62 lb, the fixture gets an independent support from the structure. Plan that support at rough-in, not with the fixture hanging from your lift. The fan weighs 42 lb — under the 50 lb limit, so a standard lighting box is fine. Wrong. The 50 lb limit is for luminaires. A ceiling fan is a moving, vibrating load, and 314.27(C) requires a box listed and marked for fan support no matter what the fan weighs. A 65 lb chandelier hung from a standard ceiling box with no weight marking on the box. A ceiling fan mounted on a plain lighting box because 'it only weighs 30 lb' — no fan-support listing or marking. A fixture over 50 lb supported by a box marked for less than the fixture's actual weight. An 'independent support' that is screwed to the box itself instead of to the building structure. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Boxes at ceiling-fan outlets
x: Where an outlet in the ceiling of a habitable room is in a spot that could support a ceiling fan — wired and placed the way a fan location is — the box has to be listed for fan support, and the maximum weight it may carry is marked on it. • The box must be listed for the purpose and marked by the manufacturer as suitable for fan support. • A fan over 35 lb up to 70 lb needs a box marked for that weight. • A fan heavier than 70 lb is supported independently of the box. • A lighting-outlet box does not qualify, even for a light fan: under 314.27(A) a fan is not a luminaire, so a fan outlet always needs the fan-rated box. A ceiling fan is a moving load: it vibrates, wobbles and pulls on its support every hour it runs, over the heads of the people below. A box chosen for a static light fixture works loose under that movement. The listed box, the weight marking and the 70 lb cutoff keep a spinning load on hardware that was tested to hold it. If there is a ceiling outlet in a bedroom or living room with a switch leg, rough it in with a fan-rated box whether or not the plan shows a fan today — the next owner will hang one there. That is checklist BL-09. At trim, read the marking inside the box before the fan goes up: if the fan going in weighs 48 lb, the box marking has to cover 48 lb. A box marked for a lighter fan, or with no fan marking at all, does not pass. The exam answer is that a 40 lb fan can hang on a box listed for a 50 lb luminaire, because 40 is less than 50. Wrong twice: the 50 lb figure in 314.27(A) covers luminaires only, and a fan over 35 lb needs a box listed for fan support and marked for the fan's weight under 314.27(C). Ceiling fan hung on a standard lighting-outlet box — no fan-support listing or marking (314.27(C)). Fan over 35 lb on a box whose marking does not cover the fan's weight. Fan over 70 lb carried by the box instead of supported independently of it. Fan-capable ceiling outlet in a bedroom roughed in with a plain lighting box because the plan showed a fixture. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 314.27: The rules for plug-in ceiling receptacles that hold up a fixture or fan now use the defined names WSCR and WSAF, and spell out when the pair can carry a paddle fan. A listed weight-supporting ceiling receptacle (WSCR) paired with a compatible attachment fitting (WSAF) can solely support a paddle fan, if 314.27(C) is met. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Pull and junction boxes for conductors 4 AWG and larger
x: Once conductors reach 4 AWG and larger, box sizing stops being a cubic-inch question and becomes a geometry question: the box must be big enough to pull and bend stiff conductors without damaging them. • Straight pull — in one wall, out the opposite wall: the distance from the entry to the opposite wall must be at least eight times the trade size of the largest raceway. • Angle pull, U pull or splices: that distance must be at least six times the largest raceway in the row, plus the sum of the trade sizes of the other raceways in the same row on the same wall. • Raceways that enclose the same conductor: the distance between them must be at least six times the larger raceway. • These rules are in 314.28(A)(1) and (A)(2). Conductors 4 AWG and larger are stiff, heavy and expensive. Force one around too tight a bend and the insulation scrapes, kinks or splits — damage that may not show until the feeder runs loaded and hot. The 8-times and 6-times geometry gives the wire a bend it can survive, and gives the electrician room to actually make the pull. Worked example: a straight pull with a largest raceway of 2 in needs at least 16 in from entry to opposite wall. An angle pull in a row with a 2 in and a 1 in raceway needs at least (6 x 2) + 1 = 13 in to the opposite wall. Cubic inches do not rescue a box that fails this geometry. That is the check to run at layout, tape in hand, before the box is ordered — on a Sharma commercial job the box size comes out of this math, not out of the cubic-inch table. The trap answer sizes the box by cubic inches, the way 314.16 sizes device boxes. For conductors 4 AWG and larger, 314.28 is geometry, not volume: eight times for a straight pull, six times plus the row for an angle pull. A deep, high-volume box with a short wall-to-wall distance still fails. Straight pull in an undersized box: 2 in raceway needs 16 in entry-to-opposite-wall; a 12 in box fails (314.28(A)(1)). Angle pull box sized by cubic inches instead of six times the largest raceway plus the row sum (314.28(A)(2)). Raceways enclosing the same conductor entering less than six times the larger raceway apart. Smaller box substituted at trim with splices added — the angle/U geometry now applies and fails. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Boxes must stay accessible
x: A junction or pull box has to remain accessible without removing any part of the building — no drywall, no tile, no fixed cabinetry over the cover. If reaching the splice means cutting the building open, the box was in the wrong place when the walls were open. • The rule covers boxes, conduit bodies and handhole enclosures alike: the wiring inside has to be renderable accessible without removing or damaging the building or structure (314.29). • Accessible does not mean visible from the middle of the room. A cover above a lift-out ceiling tile, behind a removable access panel, or in a closet wall is fine — the test is reaching it with the building finished and intact. • It pairs with 300.15: a box or conduit body is required at every splice, outlet, switch, junction, termination and pull point in the first place. A legal splice in a box nobody can reach still fails. • Buried junction boxes fail twice — the splice is entombed and the cover can never come off. Underground work uses handhole enclosures that stay reachable from grade. Splices are where installations fail first — a loose joint heats, arcs, and needs hands on it years later. Accessibility is what turns a hidden failure into a service call instead of a fire investigation. The rule protects the next electrician and the building owner, not the installer: the cheapest day to move a box is rough-in day. Before close-in, walk the job and photograph every junction box location. If a cover will be behind a fixed finish, move the box or move the splice now. On Sharma houses the classic trap is the kitchen: a junction box drawn on the wall where the builder's fixed pantry cabinets land. Moving the splice 2 ft at rough-in costs minutes; after the cabinets are set, the same fix is a cabinet removal, a drywall patch, and a callback nobody bills. The trap answer is 'accessible means you can get to it by cutting a small hole — drywall is easy to patch.' The rule is accessibility without removing any part of the building. The moment the saw comes out, the installation has already failed: the box had to be reachable with the building finished and intact. Junction box buried behind drywall with no cover showing — 'the splice is in there somewhere' is the write-up (314.29). Box cover blocked by fixed kitchen cabinetry or a tiled shower wall (314.29). Splice made loose in a wall cavity with no box at all (300.15) — found years later with a toner on a service call. Conduit body used as a junction point and then entombed in a slab pour. Handhole enclosure paved over or left below finished grade. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Armored cable — Type AC
x: Type AC is a factory cable with its conductors inside a flexible metal armor, with an internal bonding strip in contact with the armor so the armor can serve as the equipment ground path. Sharma meets this article most often through one cross-reference: 334.23 sends NM cable in accessible attics to the attic protection rules written here in 320.23. • Across the top of floor joists, or within 7 ft of the floor or floor joists across the face of rafters or studding, cable in an accessible attic must be protected by substantial guard strips at least as high as the cable (320.23(A)). • Where the attic is not accessible by permanent stairs or a ladder, that protection is required only within 6 ft of the nearest edge of the scuttle hole or attic entrance. • Cable run parallel to the sides of rafters, studs, or ceiling or floor joists needs neither guard strips nor running boards (320.23(B)) — and the run must still comply with 300.4(D). • The cable itself shows up on Sharma jobs mainly in older work and the occasional commercial job. Attic cable gets stepped on, knelt on and buried under stored boxes. A cable crushed flat across a joist is a fault waiting for the next footstep, so the guard strips take the traffic instead. In the cable itself, the bonding strip keeps the armor a continuous ground path, so a fault to the armor trips the breaker instead of energizing the run. Do not confuse AC with MC: AC carries its bonding strip and uses fittings listed for AC; MC (Article 330) usually carries a separate green ground conductor. The fittings are not interchangeable by habit — use the fitting listed for the cable in your hand. In a Florida attic this article is daily work even when no AC cable is on the truck: 334.23 applies the 320.23 guard-strip rule to the NM cable Sharma crews run every day. Two traps. First: AC and MC are the same cable with two names — they are not. AC's ground path is its armor with the internal bonding strip; MC usually carries a separate green conductor, and each takes its own listed fittings. Second: guard strips are an NM rule — they are written here in 320.23 for AC, and 334.23 is what applies them to NM. MC fitting used on Type AC cable, or an AC fitting on MC — the fitting must be listed for the cable type in hand. Cable across the tops of attic floor joists, within 7 ft of the floor, with no guard strips (320.23(A), applied to NM by 334.23). Guard strips shorter than the cable they are supposed to protect. Bonding strip cut off flush at the connector instead of folded back, breaking the armor's ground path. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 320.23: The attic rule now speaks of framing members instead of floor joists, and measures the 7-ft zone from the floor or an equivalent horizontal surface. The distances didn't change. Cable laid over the tops of framing members in an accessible attic needs guard strips as tall as the cable or taller. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Flat cable assemblies — Type FC
x: Type FC is a factory flat-cable assembly: parallel conductors formed integrally with an insulating web. It is made to be field-installed in a surface metal raceway identified for the use. It is a specialized listed system — cable, raceway, tap devices and fittings together — installed by this article and the manufacturer's instructions. It is not a substitute for NM run loose in a wall. • Branch circuits only, rated not over 30 A. • Loads: suitable tap devices for lighting, small appliances, or small power loads. • Exposed work only, in locations where it will not be subject to physical damage. • Installed less than 8 ft above the floor or a fixed working platform, it needs a cover identified for the use. The flat cable has no armor and no raceway of its own — the surface metal raceway and its cover are the protection. Run loose or pinched, the thin web insulation is the only thing between the conductors and a nail, a chair leg, or a cleaning cart. The 30 A cap and the listed tap devices keep the system inside what that thin construction can safely carry. Sharma does not install Type FC on ordinary work. If a spec calls for it — usually a specialty surface-raceway system on a retrofit — the listed system components come as a set: cable, raceway, tap devices and fittings from the same system. Do not mix in ordinary boxes or fittings, and do not substitute NM where the drawings show FC. The trap answer treats Type FC like flat NM: staple it in a wall and feed it from any breaker. Wrong twice. FC goes only in a surface metal raceway identified for the use, and only as a branch circuit of 30 A or less. A 40 A feeder on FC, or FC buried in a wall without its raceway, is not this article at all. Type FC run without the surface metal raceway identified for the use — stapled or loose in the wall. FC used as a feeder, or on a branch circuit over 30 A. FC installed below 8 ft with no identified cover over it. Ordinary device boxes and fittings mixed into the listed FC system. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 322.56(8): Made changes to flat cable assembly requirements by removing the term "color-coded" and replacing it with "marked" in Section 322.56(B). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Flat conductor cable — Type FCC
x: Type FCC is a flat conductor cable system designed to be installed under carpet squares: flat cable taped down on a hard, smooth floor over insulating bedding, protected above and below by metal shields, feeding floor pedestals and outlets exactly where the desks land. It is a different method from Type FC flat cable assemblies (Article 322) — the two are not interchangeable, and neither is ordinary branch wiring in a flat jacket. • Branch circuits only: general-purpose circuits at not over 20 A, individual branch circuits at not over 30 A; not over 300 V between ungrounded conductors and 150 V to ground (324.10). • The cable and its fittings are listed as a system (324.6). A 20 A power run is three flat 12 AWG copper conductors — hot, neutral and equipment grounding conductor — sandwiched between the shields. • Not permitted in residential buildings, and not in schools or hospitals outside their administrative areas (324.12). • Not more than two cable runs may cross at any one point (324.18). • Carpet squares over the system may not be larger than 1 m (39.37 in.) square, and they go down with release-type adhesive so the system stays reachable (324.41). • The metal shields are grounded, with connectors made for that connection (324.60). People walk, roll chairs and drag desks across this wiring every day. The shields spread the load and guard the flat conductors against heels, casters and dropped equipment, and the shield grounding rule exists because a damaged shield that is not bonded can sit at line voltage under someone's feet. The carpet-square size cap keeps any section of the system liftable for inspection and repair. Encountered almost only in specialized commercial fit-outs. Identify the system by its listing before touching an existing FCC installation. In an Orlando office remodel, the find is usually a floor pedestal with no conduit in the slab and no poke-through fitting: lift one carpet square — they come up, release adhesive — and the shielded flat run is underneath. Sharma does not extend FCC with field improvisation; a change means the manufacturer's transition fittings, and a check that the circuit still sits inside the 20 A and 30 A limits. The trap is calling FCC and Type FC the same thing because both are flat. Type FC (Article 322) is a factory flat-cable assembly installed in a surface metal raceway. Type FCC (Article 324) is the under-carpet floor system with shields and carpet-square rules. Reaching for the FC numbers fails the FCC question: FCC general-purpose circuits cap at 20 A, not 30 A. Carpet squares larger than 1 m (39.37 in.) square over the system, or squares glued down with permanent adhesive (324.41). Metal shields left ungrounded, or bonded with a random screw and lug instead of the connector made for the shield (324.60). Three or more cable runs crossed at one point, lumping under the carpet (324.18). FCC installed in a residence, or run through a school outside its administrative areas (324.12). Type FC parts or ordinary flat cable mixed into an FCC system — the two systems are not interchangeable. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Integrated gas spacer cable — Type IGS
x: Type IGS is a specialized underground cable: a factory assembly of one or more individually insulated conductors — solid aluminum rods laid parallel — enclosed in a loose-fit nonmetallic flexible conduit, insulated with dry kraft paper and pressurized sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) gas. • Rating: 0 through 600 V. • Use: below grade only — service conductors, feeders and branch circuits, including direct earth burial. • Never: as interior wiring, exposed in contact with a building, or above ground. It exists in the book so the map is complete — far outside house and light-commercial branch work. The gas is part of the insulation system: pressurized SF6 inside a sealed assembly keeps moisture out and gives the cable its dielectric strength underground, where a conventional jacket would sit in wet soil for decades. That is also why the prohibitions are absolute. The assembly is engineered as a buried system; brought indoors, run above ground or laid against a building, it is outside everything it was built and listed for. No Sharma field use. If IGS appears on a drawing, it is an engineered system — escalate, do not substitute a familiar cable. That means a call to the engineer of record before rough-in, not a swap to UF or SE cable from the truck: nothing Sharma stocks replaces a gas-insulated assembly, and the 600 V rating does not make it interchangeable with ordinary 600 V building wire. The trap is treating IGS like another direct-burial cable you can bring up into the building. You cannot: below grade only — never interior wiring, never exposed against a building, never above ground. The second trap is the gas: it is sulfur hexafluoride (SF6), and it is part of the insulation, not a tracer gas or a shipping fill. IGS run above grade on a site job — Article 326 is a below-grade method only. IGS brought inside and used as interior wiring — a prohibited use. IGS left exposed in contact with the building instead of staying below grade. IGS swapped for a familiar cable in the field — an engineered assembly is not field-substitutable. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Metal-clad cable — Type MC
x: Type MC is a factory assembly of insulated conductors inside a metal sheath — smooth, corrugated or interlocked armor — with its own equipment grounding arrangement. It is the commercial counterpart to NM: it can be used exposed or concealed, in dry locations and the other locations its listing allows, fished in existing walls, and run where NM cannot go, such as many commercial ceilings and walls. It may not be used where it will be subject to physical damage, in wet locations unless the specific cable is listed for it, or in the other prohibited uses its article lists. The support numbers (330.30): MC is secured at intervals not exceeding 6 ft; cables with four or fewer conductors no larger than 10 AWG are also secured within 12 in. of every box, cabinet, fitting or other termination (330.30(B)). Listed cables with 250 kcmil or larger ungrounded conductors in vertical runs may be secured at up to 10 ft. Short lengths to luminaires and fished runs in existing walls have their own exceptions in that section — the 12 in and 6 ft figures are the default rhythm. The metal armor is the point of MC: it protects the conductors where NM would be exposed to damage, and it gives commercial work a factory assembly that can run exposed. The support rhythm keeps long runs from sagging, chafing at studs and pulling on terminations — most MC failures start as a loose run vibrating against a sharp armor edge. Cut MC with the right tool and use listed MC connectors — a Romex connector is not an MC connector. Support and securing follow 330.30 (see the companion lookup), with the familiar pattern of securing close to boxes and supporting at regular intervals, plus exceptions for fished runs and short lengths to luminaires. S-01 applies on commercial work, where MC is most used: 20A minimum branch circuits, 12 AWG copper minimum. The trap answer treats MC like NM: a Romex connector at the box and supports 'every so often.' Both fail. MC takes listed MC connectors, and 330.30 sets the rhythm — supports at intervals not exceeding 6 ft, and small cables (four or fewer conductors, 10 AWG or smaller) secured within 12 in of every termination. NM (Romex) connector used on MC cable — MC requires listed MC connectors. MC supported at 8 ft intervals — 330.30 caps support intervals at 6 ft. 12 AWG MC landed in a box with nothing securing it within 12 in of the termination — 330.30(B). MC run where subject to physical damage without protection. MC installed in a wet location where the cable is not listed for wet locations. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 330.112(A): Made a few editorial changes in Section 330.112(A) to correlate with the addition of 16 AWG copper conductors for general use wiring methods used with metal-clad cable (Type MC). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Where MC may — and may not — be used
x: Type MC is the commercial workhorse because its list of permitted uses is long: • Exposed or concealed, in dry locations. • In cable tray. • Fished into existing walls and ceilings. • In wet locations — only where the specific cable assembly is listed for it. An impervious jacket or corrosion-resistant construction is what makes an MC cable wet-location legal; plain interlocked armor is not. The not-permitted list is shorter but firm: • Where subject to physical damage. • As a direct-burial cable, unless the specific cable is identified for burial. • Embedded in concrete or aggregate, unless identified for it. Read the jacket print: the ratings live on the cable, not in the article's title. The armor on ordinary MC is a spiral of interlocked metal tape. It is not sealed, it is not a shield against water, and it is not armor plate against a forklift. Water walks down the spiral into boxes, and one hard hit crushes conductors against the armor edge. The listing on the jacket — wet, burial, concrete — is the difference between the cable that survives the location and the one that fails in it. Before MC leaves the shop, match the jacket print to the location: wet location, tray, plenum — each is a marking on the actual cable. On a Sharma commercial job in Winter Park — six 20 A Siemens branch circuits for a retail tenant — standard interlocked MC above a dry ceiling is fine. The same reel is not fine for the two circuits that cross the damp mechanical yard wall: those get the jacketed, wet-listed assembly. 'MC is MC' is how a dry-location cable ends up in a damp mechanical room and fails inspection. The trap is 'MC is MC.' The exam — and the supply-house counter — want you to treat every MC reel as wet-rated, burial-rated and concrete-rated. Plain interlocked armor is none of those. The rating is on the jacket print of the specific cable, and 330.12's short list (physical damage, burial, concrete) fails the generic reel every time. Plain interlocked-armor MC run in a wet location — no wet listing on the jacket print. MC run exposed and low on a warehouse or shop wall where carts and lifts hit it — subject to physical damage. MC direct-buried in a trench without a burial identification on the cable. MC poured into a concrete slab when the cable is not identified for embedment. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Securing and supporting MC cable
x: MC cable is secured within 12 in of each box, cabinet, or fitting, and supported at intervals of not more than 6 ft. The exceptions carry the field cases: • Fished through existing walls or ceilings — no securing required where the cable cannot be reached • A length of not more than 6 ft from the last point of support to a luminaire or other equipment within an accessible ceiling — the ceiling whip • Short lengths at terminals where flexibility is needed for equipment that moves or vibrates • Flexibility after installation — not more than 3 ft from the last point of support or securing where flexibility is needed (330.30(D)(2)) Outside those cases, a long unsupported drape of MC across a ceiling is a violation even if it happens to be resting on the grid. The 12 in securing distance applies to cables with four or fewer conductors no larger than 10 AWG; the 6 ft support interval applies to all MC. Unsupported MC sags under its own weight. The armor edges work at the connectors, the terminations take mechanical stress they were never meant to carry, and a run dropped loose across a ceiling gets stepped on, buried under other trades' work, and damaged. Securing at the box and supporting the run keeps the stress off the terminations and keeps the cable where the next trade expects to find it. On a Sharma tenant build-out in Orlando — 20 A Siemens circuits in MC over a lay-in ceiling — the run leaves the panel, straps within 12 in of the connector, then supports at 6 ft or less down the corridor. The drop to each lay-in fixture is a whip of not more than 6 ft, and that 6 ft is measured from the last real support — not from wherever the cable happened to leave the bundle. Strap MC like you mean it, with straps that fit the cable: a loose strap is not a support. The trap: MC lying on the ceiling grid is "supported by the grid," and a whip can run 6 ft from wherever the cable leaves the bundle. Both are wrong. The grid is not a support, and the whip's 6 ft is measured from the last point of support. The other classic miss is giving MC the NM numbers — the 12 in securing distance is shared, but the support interval is 6 ft for MC, not 4-1/2 ft. MC draped across the ceiling grid with no supports — the grid is not a support. Ceiling whip measured from the cable bundle instead of the last support, landing at 8 ft. MC secured 18 in from the box connector instead of within 12 in. Oversized straps that let the cable slide and sag between supports. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Mineral-insulated, metal-sheathed cable — Type MI
x: Type MI is a factory assembly: solid conductors packed in highly compressed magnesium oxide — a refractory mineral insulation — inside a continuous liquidtight, gastight sheath of copper or alloy steel. There is no plastic anywhere in it. That is why it is chosen where extreme heat, fire survival or mechanical abuse rules out ordinary methods: fire-pump and critical circuits, and harsh industrial spots. Article 332 permits it almost anywhere (332.10): • Services, feeders and branch circuits — power, lighting, control and signal circuits • Dry, wet or continuously moist locations; indoors or outdoors; exposed or concealed • Embedded in plaster, concrete or masonry, above or below grade • Hazardous (classified) locations, and where exposed to oil or gasoline • Underground runs, where protected against physical damage and corrosive conditions The hard stop is 332.12: not where conditions are destructive or corrosive to the metal sheath, unless the sheath gets added protection. Bends stay gentle for a metal tube — inside radius at least 5 times the cable's outside diameter up to 3/4 in diameter, 10 times over 3/4 in up to 1 in (332.24). Supports run at intervals of not more than 6 ft (332.30). Terminations are sealing fittings, and the end seal goes on immediately after the sheath is stripped (332.40) — the mineral insulation drinks moisture from the air, so moisture control at the ends is part of the installation. Magnesium oxide does not burn, melt or smoke, and the metal sheath holds together through a fire that destroys ordinary insulation. That is the point: the fire-pump and egress circuits stay alive when everything around them is not. The sealing rule exists because the same powder that survives fire absorbs moisture from the air — a damp end quietly drops the insulation resistance until the circuit faults. Sharma meets MI mainly as existing work in older or specialized installations — a fire-pump feeder in a mid-rise, a heat-soaked run near commercial kitchen equipment. Do not cut or terminate it with NM/MC habits — the sealing fitting and its instructions govern. If an MI run has to be extended or replaced, treat it as engineered work and flag it for the office: there is no ordinary field splice for MI, and a stripped end left open over a weekend can ruin the run. The trap is treating MI like armored cable with a fancy jacket: strip it Friday, seal it Monday. The mineral insulation absorbs moisture the whole time the end sits open, and the circuit fails its insulation test — or faults in service. The seal goes on immediately (332.40). Second trap: bending it like NM. The inside bend radius is 5 times the outside diameter, 10 times on the larger sizes (332.24). Stripped MI end left unsealed over the weekend — moisture in the magnesium oxide, insulation resistance gone (332.40). Bend kinked tight at a corner — inside radius under 5 times the cable diameter (332.24). MI run through cinder fill or corrosive soil with the copper sheath unprotected (332.12). Supports spaced over 6 ft, cable sagging between straps (332.30). Termination made with a generic connector instead of the listed sealing fitting for Type MI. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Nonmetallic-sheathed cable — Types NM, NMC, NMS (Romex)
x: This is Sharma's house cable. NM is two or more insulated conductors with an equipment ground, factory-wrapped in a nonmetallic sheath. Article 334 says where it may be used (334.10), where it may never be used (334.12), how it is protected and run (334.15, 334.17, 334.23), how it is bent (334.24), how often it is secured and supported (334.30), and how its ampacity is limited (334.80). Almost every Sharma rough-in decision — staple spacing, attic runs, the 60°C ampacity limit — traces back to this one article. • Secured and supported (334.30): within 12 in of every box, cabinet and fitting, and at intervals of 4-1/2 ft or less; a run through bored holes counts as supported by the framing. Flat cable is never stapled on edge. • Bends (334.24): the inner edge of a bend keeps a radius of at least five times the cable diameter — wide, lazy turns, no kinks. • Ampacity (334.80): NM is sized from the 60 °C column. 12 AWG NM lands on a 20 A breaker, and no 90 °C math changes that. • Protection (334.15, with 300.4): where the cable passes through framing it keeps the 1-1/4 in setback, or gets the 1/16 in steel plate. NM is a soft cable in a hard world: a plastic sheath over conductors that drywall screws, picture nails and careless staples all want to cut. Article 334's spacing, bend and ampacity limits keep the sheath whole and the conductors cool for the life of the house. If you learn one article in this chapter cold, learn this one. The other methods are variations; NM is the daily work. A Sharma home run in 12/2: stapled within 12 in of the panel and of the device box, supported every 4-1/2 ft or less between, bored holes centered in the studs. The run feeds a 20 A circuit — Sharma commercial work also starts at 20 A — and 334.80 holds that 12 AWG to its 60 °C value, 20 A, whatever the conductors inside could carry in conduit. The trap is the 90 °C escape: 'the conductors inside NM are rated 90 °C, so 12 AWG can carry 30 A.' 334.80 closes that door — NM ampacity is the 60 °C result, 20 A for 12 AWG, before any derating. Staples 6 ft apart on a vertical run; 334.30 caps the interval at 4-1/2 ft. First staple 2 ft from the box; 334.30 wants it within 12 in. Flat NM stapled on edge, the sheath crushed by the staple (334.30). 12 AWG NM protected at 30 A off the 90 °C column (334.80). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 334.19: A new NM cable-entry section: wherever NM enters a box, cabinet or other enclosure, at least 1/4 in. of its jacket has to extend past the clamp or entry point. Where NM enters an enclosure, its outer jacket has to run at least 1/4 in. beyond the clamp or entry (334.19). • 334.40: Splicing NM cable with no box inside walls and ceilings is now allowed on new work too, not just repairs, as long as the splice uses a listed NM cable interconnector. Listed NM cable interconnectors can join nonmetallic-sheathed (NM) cable without a box, exposed or hidden in walls and ceilings, new or existing (334.40(B)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Where NM may be used
x: NM may be used exposed or concealed, but only in normally dry locations, and only in the buildings this section names: • One- and two-family dwellings, and their detached garages and storage buildings. • Multifamily dwellings permitted to be of Type III, IV or V construction. • Other buildings and structures permitted to be of Type III, IV or V construction — and there the cable must be concealed inside walls, floors or ceilings that provide a thermal barrier with at least a 15-minute finish rating. • In cable trays inside those permitted structures, where the cable is identified for tray use. • In Type I and II construction, only inside a raceway. • Fished into the hollow voids of masonry block or tile walls, in dry locations. Two gates decide every NM call: the location is normally dry, and the building is one the section permits. The construction type is what the building code permits the building to be for its occupancy — not just what the framing in front of you happens to be. The NM sheath is a light plastic jacket with no armor and no wet-location rating. Kept dry and protected, it lasts the life of the building. The building-type limits are fire rules: in combustible Type III, IV and V construction the cable hides behind rated finishes, and in noncombustible Type I and II buildings the wiring belongs in raceway, so a cable fault does not become a fire path through a rated building. House, garage and accessory work in dry interiors: NM is the default. Anything wet, damp, underground or in a bigger occupancy: stop and check 334.12 and pick another method. On a Sharma single-family rough-in that means 12/2 NM on the 20 A kitchen and bath circuits and 14/2 on the 15 A lighting, all inside the dry envelope — and the detached garage is on the same permission. The lanai receptacles and the pool equipment are a different story: that is UF or THWN in PVC, because the location is not normally dry. On a Type V wood-frame retail shell, NM is allowed only concealed behind the 15-minute finish — the same cable run exposed across the ceiling is a violation. The exam's favorite wrong answer: “NM is permitted exposed in any Type III, IV or V building.” In dwellings, exposed NM is fine. In other Type III, IV and V structures the cable must be concealed behind the 15-minute thermal barrier — exposed NM across a small commercial ceiling fails even though the building type is on the list. NM run exposed across the ceiling of a Type V retail shell — 334.10(3) requires it concealed behind a 15-minute finish barrier. NM feeding pool equipment and lanai receptacles — not a normally dry location. NM run exposed above the drop ceiling of a Type II tenant space — Type I and II means raceway. NM fished into a damp below-grade block wall — the masonry-void permission is for dry locations. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 334.10: NM can now wire the detached garages that serve Type III, IV and V multifamily buildings, the same as the buildings themselves. NM is allowed in Type III, IV or V multifamily dwellings, and now in their detached garages too (334.10(2)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Where NM may not be used
x: NM may not be used: • In wet or damp locations — including inside a raceway that is itself underground or outdoors, because the interior of that raceway is a wet location (300.5(B), 300.9) • As service-entrance cable • In any dwelling or structure 334.10 does not permit — Type I and II buildings, outside a raceway • Exposed within a dropped or suspended ceiling in anything other than one- and two-family and multifamily dwellings • In commercial garages that have hazardous (classified) locations (511.3) • In theaters, or in motion picture studios • In storage battery rooms • In hoistways, or on elevators or escalators • Embedded in poured concrete or aggregate • In hazardous (classified) locations, except where another article specifically permits it • Where exposed to physical damage, unless it is protected It is a dry, protected, interior method — every item on this list is one of those three words failing. Water inside the sheath wicks along the cable, corrodes the bare equipment ground and rots the filler, so a “protected” outdoor run fails from the inside years later. The occupancy bans are ignition rules: theaters, battery rooms and classified locations cannot carry a light plastic-sheathed method where fault arcs, hydrogen or solvent vapors are part of the design case. Embedded cable cannot be inspected or replaced, so concrete is out too. The classic fail: NM sleeved in PVC down an outside wall and underground to a yard light. The PVC does not make the location dry. Use UF or conductors in raceway for that run (Articles 340 and 352). The same thinking kills two more Florida habits: NM as the cable between the meter and the panel on a service upgrade — that is Type SE cable or conductors in raceway, never NM — and NM stapled across a lanai ceiling for a pool light, where wind-driven rain makes the location damp. Florida's humidity does not reclassify an interior dry location, but any exterior or underground raceway interior is wet — plan the method for the location, not the weather. The wrong answer everyone reaches for: “The NM is inside PVC conduit, so the location is dry.” The Code counts the inside of an underground or outdoor raceway as a wet location, full stop. The conduit protects against physical damage, not against the location classification — the cable inside still has to be a wet-location method. NM in PVC conduit underground to the yard light — the interior of the raceway is a wet location (334.12). NM used as service-entrance cable between the meter and the panel. NM embedded in the concrete slab for a floor outlet. NM run exposed above the suspended ceiling in a retail tenant space. NM feeding the pool pump across the lanai ceiling — damp and wet exposure. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: NM in exposed work and through framing
x: Exposed NM has to follow the surface it is run on and be protected where it can be hit. Where it passes through a floor, a wall or framing, the Article 300 protection rules ride along: bored-hole setbacks and nail plates from 300.4, and protection where the cable passes through slots or notches. In unfinished basements and crawl spaces, this section sets how larger cables may run through joists and how smaller cables are run on running boards or through bored holes. The basement and crawl-space case has its own subsection, 334.15(C): where cable runs at angles with the joists, a cable at least as large as two 6 AWG or three 8 AWG conductors may be secured directly to the lower edges of the joists; smaller cables must run through bored holes in the joists or on running boards. NM on the wall of an unfinished basement must be protected — in listed conduit or tubing, or protected the way 300.4 requires — with a bushing or adapter where the cable enters the raceway. Exposed NM has a soft jacket and no armor. In a basement or crawl space it lives where stored boxes, tools and foot traffic can hit it, and where a later finish job can bury a mistake under drywall. Following the surface and protecting the cable at floors, walls and joist edges keeps the jacket — and the insulation under it — intact until the space is finished. Florida has few basements, so here this is a crawl-space and garage rule. In a raised Kissimmee house, the 12/2 and 14/2 NM crossing the crawl space goes through bored holes in the joists or on running boards — never stapled along the joist bottoms. Treat the space like a wall someone will finish later: keep the cable tight to the framing, bore or board every small run, and plate anything in the strike zone. The one cable that may ride the lower joist edges is a feeder-sized run, at least two 6 AWG or three 8 AWG conductors. The trap: "334.15(C) lets NM run on the bottom edges of the joists in a crawl space." Only the big cables — at least two 6 AWG or three 8 AWG conductors. The 12/2 and 14/2 branch-circuit cables everyone pictures must go through bored holes in the joists or on running boards. Picking "any NM, secured to the joist bottom" is the wrong answer. 12/2 NM stapled along the bottom edges of crawl-space joists — smaller cables go through bored holes or on running boards (334.15(C)). NM passing through a floor with no 300.4 protection at the framing. NM sleeved in conduit with the jacket skinned where it enters — no bushing or adapter at the raceway entry. Exposed NM run loose across a garage wall instead of following the surface and protected where it can be hit. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 334.15: Conduit or tubing that protects exposed NM from damage now needs a bushing or adapter at both ends, where the cable goes in and where it comes out (334.15(B)). A conduit or tubing sleeve protecting exposed NM needs a bushing or adapter where the cable enters and where it exits (334.15(B)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: NM in accessible attics — the scuttle rule
x: For accessible attics, this section points NM cable at the attic rules written for AC cable in 320.23: 334.23 says the installation of cable in accessible attics or roof spaces shall also comply with 320.23. Under 320.23(A), cable run across the top of floor joists, or within 7 ft of the floor or floor joists across the face of rafters or studding, has to be protected by substantial guard strips that are at least as high as the cable; where the space is not accessible by permanent stairs or ladders, that protection is required only within 6 ft of the nearest edge of the scuttle hole or attic entrance. Under 320.23(B), cable installed parallel to the sides of rafters, studs, or ceiling or floor joists needs neither guard strips nor running boards, and the installation must also comply with 300.4(D). Sanjay's own ruling in the Sharma note is separate company practice — stricter and simpler than the code rule — and it is what Sharma crews follow on Sharma jobs. Attics get traffic: insulators, HVAC techs and homeowners hauling storage boxes all climb through the same scuttle and step on whatever crosses the joists. NM lying across joist tops in that zone gets crushed and nicked, and a damaged jacket in a hot attic is a fault waiting for a load. Guard strips and the scuttle-zone rules keep cable out from underfoot, right where everyone enters. Route attic runs the Sharma way from the start and the inspection question mostly disappears: runs hug the framing, nothing crosses the scuttle opening, and nothing invites a foot. On a Sharma house, the run is planned that way from the panel — within 6 ft of a scuttle with no permanent stairs, NM runs along the sides of the joists or trusses only, parallel to the framing, bends stay at least 1.5 ft clear of the opening, and the attic light sits about 1.5 ft beside the opening with its switch at the entry. That is the company rule in the Sharma note below: stricter than 320.23, and the one the crews are graded on. SHARMA RULE (Sanjay, definitive 2026-11-09 — company practice, not a code quote): within 6 ft of an attic scuttle with no permanent stairs, run NM along the sides of the joists/trusses only, parallel to the framing, never diagonally across it and never across the opening; no guard strips; bends stay at least 1.5 ft clear of the opening; the attic light sits about 1.5 ft beside the opening with its switch at the entry. This is how BuzzDraws and the crews run it, regardless of how the 320.23 wording settles. The trap is answering with a distance out of 334.23 itself. 334.23 sets no distances — it sends NM to the AC cable attic rules in 320.23: guard strips within 7 ft across joist tops and rafter faces, and protection within 6 ft of the scuttle edge where there are no permanent stairs or ladders. "NM is banned in attics" is also wrong; it is permitted, protected. NM across the top of floor joists, or within 7 ft across the face of rafters, with no guard strips (320.23(A) via 334.23). Cable crossing the scuttle opening, or run unprotected within 6 ft of the scuttle edge where there are no permanent stairs (320.23(A)). Guard strips lower than the cable they are supposed to protect. Diagonal run across joists inside the scuttle zone — fails the Sharma rule on every Sharma job. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bending radius of NM cable
x: NM may not be bent so sharply that the bend damages the sheath or the conductors inside it; the rule of this section is expressed as a minimum radius measured to the inner edge of the bend — five times the cable diameter. • Measure to the inner edge of the curve — not the centerline, not the outside. • The multiplier is 5: a cable 1/2 in across needs an inside radius of at least 2-1/2 in. • A kinked flat cable at a tight stud turn is exactly the damage this section is aimed at: a creased sheath and conductors pinched at the crease. • Flat cable has no true diameter to measure. The 2020 wording still holds it to the same gentle-bend standard; the 2023 wording for flat cable is in the edition box. A tight bend does its damage quietly. The sheath creases and thins on the outside of the curve while the conductors inside are pinched and work-hardened at one point — and the fault shows up years later, inside a finished wall, at exactly that bend. A wide radius spreads the strain over length so no single point takes it all. Make wide, lazy turns. If you have to force it around a corner with your thumb creasing the sheath, the bend is too tight — re-route or move the hole. Worked check on a Sharma rough-in: a flat cable whose widest dimension is 1/2 in needs an inside radius of 2-1/2 in or more — about the curve you get sweeping cable around a coffee mug, not folding it around your thumb. Staple back from the bend so the sweep survives drywall. Two traps. First, measuring the radius to the centerline or the outside of the bend — the rule measures to the inner edge, the tightest point, so both of those measurements flatter a bad bend. Second, sizing a flat cable's bend off its thin edge: under the 2023 wording flat NM is measured by its widest dimension, and even under 2020 the damage standard bans the kink. The multiplier is 5 either way. NM kinked around a stud corner, the sheath creased white at the bend (334.24). Cable folded flat back on itself to take up slack inside a wall. Bend pulled tight against the edge of a bored hole, inside radius nearly zero. Flat NM bent around its thin edge with a radius sized off the thickness, not the width. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 334.24: Flat NM no longer gets measured by a diameter it doesn't have. The minimum bend radius is now 5 times the cable's widest dimension. Every NM bend needs an inside radius of 5 times the cable's widest dimension or more. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Securing and supporting NM
x: NM must be secured and supported at intervals not exceeding 4-1/2 ft, and within 12 in of every box, cabinet and fitting. The hardware — staples, cable ties listed and identified for securement and support, straps, hangers or similar fittings — must be installed so it does not damage the cable. • Cable run horizontally through bored holes or notches in framing counts as secured and supported by that framing, where the support spacing stays within the same limits (334.30(A)). • Flat cable may not be stapled on edge, and the staple has to hold the cable snug without crushing the sheath. • Two runs may go unsupported (334.30(B)): cable fished between access points in a finished building where support is impracticable, and a tail of not more than 4-1/2 ft from the last point of support to a luminaire or other equipment connection, inside an accessible ceiling in a dwelling. • At a single-gang nonmetallic box with no cable clamp, the 12 in becomes 8 in — the cable must be secured within 8 in of that box (314.17(C) exception). An unsupported cable sags, rubs on framing edges, and levers against the terminations at the box every time something tugs the run. The 12 in rule keeps the last stretch from working the connector loose. The snug-not-crushed half matters just as much: a staple driven like a nail deforms the sheath and pinches the conductors — a support that damages the cable is a defect, not a support. Staple pattern on a stud run: within 12 in of the box, then at least every 4-1/2 ft, snug not crushed. A staple that deforms the sheath is a damage point, not a support point. On a Sharma rough-in with studs 16 in on center, the bored holes carry the horizontal runs — but the drop to each box still gets its own staple within 12 in, and within 8 in at a clampless single-gang plastic box. Save unsupported runs for fished old work and short luminaire tails in accessible ceilings. The trap is quoting MC cable numbers — MC gets 6 ft intervals; NM gets 4-1/2 ft. The second trap is the box number: 12 in is the rule, 8 in applies only at a single-gang nonmetallic box without a clamp, and neither one is the 4-1/2 ft run interval. An answer that mixes the three numbers is wrong. NM stapled at 6 ft intervals — the MC spacing used on NM (334.30). No staple within 12 in of the box; the cable hangs off the connector. Flat 14/2 stapled on edge to fit a crowded stud. Staples driven until the sheath is visibly crushed and deformed. Long unsupported tail across an attic to a luminaire, well past the 4-1/2 ft allowance of 334.30(B). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Ampacity of NM cable — the 60°C limit
x: The conductors inside NM are 90 °C rated, but the cable's ampacity is taken from the 60 °C column of Table 310.16. • Start at 90 °C. Correction and adjustment under 310.15 may begin from the 90 °C value — that is what makes a bundled or hot-attic NM run survivable on paper. • Finish at 60 °C. The final ampacity after 310.15 may not exceed the 60 °C value. • The 240.4(D) small-conductor caps still apply on top: 15 A for 14 AWG copper, 20 A for 12 AWG copper. The 60 °C cap is the limit of the finished cable, not of the conductor insulation. The conductors can take 90 °C; the cable assembly — jacket and all — is held to the 60 °C column by 334.80. Run NM at 90 °C ampacities year after year and the jacket ages early and turns brittle, and the margin the listing was built on is gone. The two-step math keeps the derating benefit of the 90 °C column without cooking the cable. Field translation: 14 AWG NM on a 15 A breaker and 12 AWG NM on a 20 A breaker, full stop. Florida attic check: two 20 A NM home runs share a foamed hole in a 104 °F attic — four current-carrying conductors. Start at 90 °C: 30 A × 0.91 × 0.80 = 21.8 A on paper. But 334.80 caps the answer at the 60 °C value, 20 A, so the 20 A breaker stands and the extra 1.8 A buys nothing. Do the math from 90 °C, then cap the answer at the 60 °C column — the same place the 240.4(D) breaker cap lands. S-10 still governs the wire choice: copper by default; CCA one size up. NM ampacity limits apply the same either way, read in the correct 310.16 column for the metal. The trap: 'The conductors in NM are 90 °C, so size it from the 90 °C column.' Wrong finish — the 90 °C column is only the starting point for correction and adjustment, and the result may never land above the 60 °C value. The mirror trap is derating from the 60 °C column, which throws away ampacity the code lets you keep on paper. 12 AWG NM on a 25 A breaker because 'the conductors are 90 °C' — the final ampacity is held to the 60 °C column (334.80). Bundled NM home runs through a foamed hole with no adjustment taken at all. 10 AWG NM protected at 40 A from the 90 °C column — the 60 °C value and the 240.4(D) cap are both 30 A. Derating started from the 60 °C column, then a circuit failed on paper that the code would have passed. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Power and control tray cable — Type TC
x: Type TC is a factory assembly of two or more insulated conductors, with or without an associated grounding conductor, under one overall jacket. It is listed for power, lighting, control and signal circuits. Where it may run (336.10): • In cable trays — including trays with mechanically discontinuous segments up to 1 ft • In raceways • In outdoor locations, supported by a messenger wire • As Class 1 circuits (Article 725) and as non-power-limited fire alarm circuits (760.49) • In wet locations, where the cable is also resistant to moisture and corrosive agents • Direct buried, only where the cable is identified for direct burial • In one- and two-family dwellings, a TC-ER cable that carries both power and control conductors and is identified for pulling through structural members (marked JP), installed under Part II of Article 334 Tray-rated is the load-bearing word: a cable in a tray must be a cable type Article 392 allows, and TC is the common one. Ratings beyond plain TC — exposed run, sunlight, burial — exist only when the jacket is marked for them. TC's jacket is a covering, not armor. Inside a tray or raceway, the system around the cable provides the protection; outside, the cable has to bring its own. The TC-ER crush-and-impact tests are what separate a cable that may step out of the tray from one that may not — which is why the whole article turns on reading the jacket print instead of the cable's shape. On a light-commercial tray job, read the jacket print before the cable leaves the shop: TC alone is not every rating — check for the marking that matches the actual installation. On an Orlando warehouse job, the tray runs themselves took plain TC. The drops down to the dock motors were the fight: 8 ft of exposed drop on plain TC is a 336.12 violation, so the drops were re-pulled in TC-ER on strut, secured at intervals not over 6 ft, with only the last short transition unsupported where nothing could hit it. The wrong answer: “TC-ER is just tray cable with a tougher jacket, so it can be run exposed anywhere, like MC.” The exposed-run permission is narrow — between a cable tray and utilization equipment, in industrial establishments where only qualified persons service the installation, continuously supported and protected, and secured at intervals not over 6 ft. A TC-ER cable sold with a mini-split does not become a general exposed wiring method for a house. Plain TC run exposed from the tray down to a motor — no TC-ER marking (336.12(2)). TC-ER drop left unsupported for 12 ft between tray and equipment — transitions cap at 6 ft (336.10(7)). TC in direct sun on a rooftop tray, jacket not marked sunlight resistant (336.12(3)). TC direct buried to a sign, cable not identified for direct burial (336.12(4)). TC strapped across a forklift route at bumper height — exposed to physical damage (336.12(1)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 336.10: Type TC tray cable can now carry service-entrance conductors, but only when the jacket shows TC-ER and the cable is also identified for service use. Type TC power and control tray cable can now be used for service-entrance conductors (336.10(12)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Type P cable
x: Type P is a rugged, flexible cable construction that comes out of marine and drilling work. In the 2020 NEC it is listed in Article 337 for the applications the article describes, including certain hazardous-location uses noted in the 2020 changes. • Origin: ships and drilling rigs — service with vibration, movement and rough handling. • Status: its own listed cable type, with its own article. • It is not a house cable, and it is not an ordinary commercial branch-circuit cable. When Type P appears, it appears because an engineer specified it for a specialized job. It is never the cable that just happens to be on the truck. Marine and drilling service punishes cable. Constant vibration, flexing, moisture and rough handling destroy ordinary constructions, and a failed cable in that service can shut down equipment or start a fire where help is far away. Type P exists because that work needs a cable built to take the abuse. The same logic runs the other way: a specialty cable dragged into ordinary work it was not listed for is a mismatch the inspector and the engineer will both catch. No Sharma field use on ordinary work. Its presence on a drawing signals a specialized, engineered specification. If a plan set for an industrial or marine job calls out Type P, the callout stays as drawn: the crew does not substitute a familiar cable type on its own, and any change goes back through the engineer who specified it. The trap is treating Type P like a familiar general-use cable — a name you can substitute freely or pull for ordinary branch circuits. In the 2020 book it is its own listed type in Article 337, born in marine and drilling work, and it belongs only in the applications its article describes. A house or an ordinary commercial job is not one of them. Type P specification changed to a general-use cable type without the engineer's approval. Type P installed outside the applications its article describes. Type P pulled as ordinary branch-circuit wiring on a house or standard commercial job. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • Article 337: Changed all references to the former Type P cable to Type IM in Article 337. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Service-entrance cable — Types SE and USE
x: Type SE cable is a single-conductor or multi-conductor assembly, primarily used for services. • Type SE: a flame-retardant, moisture-resistant covering — the above-ground form. • Type USE: identified for underground use, with a moisture-resistant covering, but not required to have a flame-retardant covering. On a house, SE is the cable that can carry the service where individual conductors in a mast or raceway are not used. Where SE is used for interior branch-circuit or feeder wiring, 338.10(B)(4) makes the Article 334 installation rules apply to that run — see the 338.10(B)(4) page. Type SE and Type USE are not interchangeable: • SE shall not be used underground, with or without a raceway. • USE shall not be used for interior wiring. A cable that is also marked and listed as another wiring type is used indoors under that other rating, not as USE. SE and USE look alike on the reel, but their coverings are tested against different enemies. SE's covering resists flame spread above ground and inside a building; USE's covering resists ground moisture but was never required to resist flame. Bury SE and the soil works on a covering not identified for it; bring USE indoors and fire can travel along a covering that never passed a flame test. The wrong swap usually passes a glance on rough-in day and fails years later. A 200 A service on a Florida block house: the utility drop lands on the mast, and 4/0 aluminum Type SE runs from the meter into a Siemens meter-main (S-02), sized from Table 310.12 (200 A — 2/0 copper / 4/0 aluminum). Where the layout allows, the panel sits back to back with the meter (S-09) and the SE run stays short. The same reel never goes in the trench to the detached garage: underground is USE territory, or conductors in raceway. Keep service work in its own lane — conductor sizing is 310.12 / 310.16 work, the disconnect and grounding live in Chapter 2 and 250 territory, and this article governs the cable itself. S-02: new meter-mains and disconnects are Siemens. S-09: meter and panel back to back where the house allows. The serving utility (FPL and the Florida co-ops/munis) controls the drop, meter and its own connection rules on top of the NEC. The trap answer: "USE is just the underground version of SE, so either cable works anywhere the other does." Wrong in both directions — 338.12 bars SE underground even inside a raceway, and bars USE for interior wiring. A dual-marked cable used indoors follows its other listing, not its USE marking. SE cable buried to a detached garage or pool panel — SE is barred underground, with or without a raceway (338.12). USE cable run inside the house as a feeder — USE is not permitted for interior wiring. Interior SE feeder with no nail plates where it passes within 1-1/4 in of a stud edge — indoors, SE follows Article 334 Part II protection. Service SE sized off the breaker handle instead of Table 310.12 / 310.16. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: SE cable used as interior wiring
x: Type SE cable is a service-entrance cable first, but 338.10(B)(4) also lets it be used as interior wiring for branch circuits and feeders inside a building. Used that way, the run is installed like NM cable — with one named exception: • Routing, protection and support: Part II of Article 334 applies to the indoor SE run. • Ampacity: 334.80 does NOT apply. The NM ampacity cap stays behind. • SE has its own narrow ampacity rule instead: for ungrounded conductor sizes 10 AWG and smaller, where installed in contact with thermal insulation, the ampacity is in accordance with the 60 °C conductor temperature rating. • Everything else about sizing comes from Article 310. Once SE cable leaves the service and runs through studs, it faces the same nails, drywall screws and bored holes as Romex, so it gets the same physical protection and support rules. Its ampacity is a different story: SE conductors are not built like NM, so instead of borrowing NM's blanket cap, the Code keeps only the one heat case that matters for this cable — small conductors in contact with insulation. An SE cable feeding a subpanel inside the house is roughed and protected like Romex once it is indoors: bored-hole and notch protection, and the Article 334 support intervals, travel with it. Staple it within 12 in of the subpanel and support it at intervals not over 4-1/2 ft (334.30). On a Kissimmee house the feeder crosses a stud wall: holes are drilled so the cable edge sits at least 1-1/4 in from the stud edge, or a 1/16 in steel plate goes on (300.4(A)(1)). The 334.80 ampacity cap does not travel — 338.10(B)(4) excludes 334.80.
