x: A wireway is a sheet-metal trough with a hinged or removable cover, used in light commercial work to carry feeders and branch circuits where conductors need to be laid in and remain accessible along a run — above panels, along shop walls, in electrical rooms. Conductors are laid in, not pulled, and the cover is what makes the system legal: no cover, no wireway. • Fill (376.22): the conductors at any cross section may not exceed 20 percent of the wireway's interior cross-sectional area. • Derating (376.22): ampacity adjustment factors do not apply while a cross section holds 30 or fewer current-carrying conductors. Past 30, they apply in full. • Splices and taps (376.56) are permitted inside a wireway that remains accessible, provided they fill no more than 75 percent of the wiring space at that cross section. • Supports (376.30): horizontal runs are supported at each end and at intervals not exceeding 5 ft, and never more than 10 ft between supports. Vertical runs are supported at intervals not exceeding 15 ft, with not more than one joint between supports. A wireway packed solid traps heat around every conductor, and bundled conductors heat each other — that is why the fill cap and the 30-conductor line exist. The cover and the access rules exist because a splice nobody can reach again fails silently. A wireway is a raceway you can open along its whole run; the rules keep it that way. On a Winter Park tenant fit-out, Sharma ran a 6 in × 6 in wireway above a row of new Siemens panels. Twenty-eight current-carrying conductors at the busiest cross section stayed under the 30-conductor line, so no adjustment factors applied. When the tenant added one more 3-phase circuit, the count passed 30 and derating entered the job — the fix was a second wireway, not bigger wire stuffed into the same trough. Do the 20 percent fill math at layout, not with the cover in your hand. The trap: treating the wireway like conduit, where derating starts at four current-carrying conductors — or like a trough you may fill to the brim. In a wireway the fill cap is 20 percent, adjustment factors wait until you pass 30 current-carrying conductors, and then they apply in full. Conductors packed past the 20 percent fill limit, cover forced on (376.22). More than 30 current-carrying conductors at one cross section with no ampacity adjustment applied (376.22). Splices and taps filling more than 75 percent of the wiring space at a cross section (376.56). Horizontal wireway supported 12 ft apart — over the 10 ft maximum span (376.30(A)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 376.60: The wireway article now has its own grounding section, 376.60: a listed metal wireway is allowed to be the equipment grounding conductor (EGC). A listed metal wireway can act as the equipment grounding conductor (EGC) for the circuits run through it (376.60). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wireway fill — 20 percent, and splices inside
x: A metal wireway is a trough with a cover, not a pipe to stuff full. Three numbers run the page: • Conductor fill: the conductors at any cross section may not exceed 20 percent of the wireway's interior cross-sectional area (376.22). • Splices and taps: splices and taps are permitted inside a wireway that remains accessible, provided they do not fill more than 75 percent of the wiring space at that cross section (376.56). • Derating relief: the ampacity adjustment factors of Table 310.15(C)(1) do not apply where the number of current-carrying conductors in the wireway is 30 or fewer. Past 30, derating enters the job (376.22). A wireway packed past its fill cooks its conductors: the heat has nowhere to go, insulation ages fast, and the next man cannot pull a wire out or land a new one. The splice cap and the access rule exist because a splice you cannot reach is a splice you cannot inspect — and splices are where wireway jobs fail first. Do the 20 percent math at layout, not with the cover in your hand: list the conductors, take their areas from Chapter 9 Table 5, and check the total against one-fifth of the wireway's inside area. If the count of current-carrying conductors passes 30, derating enters the job — that is the moment to upsize the wireway or split the run. Worked check: a 4 in by 4 in wireway over a Siemens panel has 16 sq in of interior, so the 20 percent cap is 3.2 sq in. Twenty-four 12 AWG THHN conductors at 0.0133 sq in each (Chapter 9, Table 5) total about 0.32 sq in — the area passes easily. The count is the watch item: 24 current-carrying conductors is under 30, so no derating. Two more 20 A circuits put the count at 28, still clear — but the next tenant's circuits will not be. The trap is the conduit number: "Raceways fill to 40 percent, so the wireway does too." Wrong — a wireway is 20 percent, half the conduit figure. The second trap is reading the 30-conductor relief as a 30-conductor limit: past 30 the wireway is still legal, but Table 310.15(C)(1) derating applies. Conductors packed past 20 percent of the wireway's interior area at a cross section (376.22). Splices filling more than 75 percent of the wiring space at the splice point (376.56). More than 30 current-carrying conductors in the wireway with no Table 310.15(C)(1) derating applied (376.22). Splice made in a wireway section that no longer remains accessible (376.56). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Nonmetallic wireways
x: Article 378 is the nonmetallic counterpart to Article 376's metal wireways: a flame-retardant trough with a removable cover, listed as a system, with conductors laid in after the wireway is installed. Use it where a nonmetallic system is wanted — above all where corrosion makes a metal trough a poor choice. • Exposed work only (378.10). It may pass transversely through a wall if the length in the wall is unbroken and the conductors stay accessible on both sides. • Wet locations only where listed for the purpose; corrosive environments only where identified for the use. • Not permitted where subject to physical damage, in hazardous (classified) locations, in sunlight unless listed and marked for it, or at temperatures outside its listing (378.12). • Fill: conductors at any cross section may not exceed 20 percent of the interior area (378.22). Splices and taps are permitted inside, may fill up to 75 percent at that cross section, and must stay accessible (378.56). • Derating is the trap in this article: the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors apply to the current-carrying conductors here. There is no 30-conductor free pass — that relief is written for metal wireways in 376.22(B). • Support: horizontal runs at intervals not over 3 ft, and never more than 10 ft between supports; vertical runs at intervals not over 4 ft (378.30). • The plastic trough cannot be the ground path. Run an equipment grounding conductor with the circuits. The cover and the fill limits are the heat and damage controls. Conductors laid in a trough still heat each other, and plastic gives up strength sooner than steel as temperature climbs — which is why this article makes you derate bundled conductors instead of borrowing the metal wireway's 30-conductor relief. The exposed-only and no-damage-location rules exist because a plastic trough has no impact strength to forgive a forklift or a ladder strike. Use where corrosion makes metal wireway a poor choice and the location is permitted. The cover still makes the system — no cover, no wireway. On a coastal Florida job, a beachside condo electrical room in Brevard County, a 4 in. by 4 in. nonmetallic wireway has 16 sq in. inside, so the 20 percent limit allows 3.2 sq in. of conductors. Lay in six 20 A circuits of 12 AWG THHN and the current-carrying count already forces the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment — do that math before the wire is ordered, not with the cover in your hand. The trap is borrowing the metal-wireway rule: 'wireways never derate under 30 conductors.' That is 376.22(B), metal only. In a nonmetallic wireway the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors apply to the current-carrying conductors from the start, so the same conductor count that passes in a steel trough fails in a plastic one. Wireway run where carts and lifts can hit it — nonmetallic wireway is not permitted where subject to physical damage (378.12). Thirty current-carrying conductors with no ampacity adjustment — the 30-conductor relief belongs to metal wireways (376.22(B)), not this article. Conductors stuffed past 20 percent fill, or a splice packed past 75 percent at its cross section (378.22, 378.56). No equipment grounding conductor run with the circuits — a plastic trough is not a ground path. Supports 6 ft apart on a horizontal run — 3 ft maximum for nonmetallic wireways (378.30). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Multioutlet assemblies
x: A multioutlet assembly is a surface, flush or freestanding raceway designed to hold conductors and receptacles, assembled at the factory or in the field — the hard-wired strip over a workbench or lab counter, in metal or nonmetallic form. • It is permitted in dry locations only. • It may not be installed concealed — except that a metal assembly may be surrounded on its back and sides by the building finish and a nonmetallic one may be recessed in a baseboard. • It is barred where subject to severe physical damage, in hoistways, and in the other locations its article lists (380.12). • A metal assembly may pass through a dry partition if no outlet sits inside the partition and the cover can be removed on both sides. • In a dwelling it is not a dodge around the receptacle rules, but it is not banned from counting either: for kitchen countertop spacing, each 12 in of assembly containing two or more receptacles counts as one receptacle outlet under 210.52(C). The strip packs receptacles and splices into one long raceway that people lean on, plug into and clean around every day. Keeping it in dry locations, out of hoistways and out of impact zones protects a device-dense assembly that takes daily abuse. Keeping it unconcealed means the cover can come off — a failed splice inside a buried assembly would cook inside a wall nobody can open. Use it where it belongs — benches, counters, retail and lab work — and count its load like any receptacle run; the strip does not create capacity, it only distributes outlets. On a Kissimmee kitchen remodel, a 4 ft assembly under the upper cabinets with receptacles every 12 in: for 210.52(C) spacing, each 12 in length with two or more receptacles counts as one receptacle outlet, so the strip counts as four — and it still lands on the same small-appliance branch-circuit rules as any other countertop receptacle. The trap: "It's just a raceway, so bury it in the wall like one." Wrong — 380 bars concealed installation, with only the two narrow exceptions (metal surrounded on back and sides by the finish; nonmetallic recessed in a baseboard). The second trap counts every receptacle in a kitchen strip separately for 210.52(C) spacing; the rule counts each 12 in length holding two or more receptacles as ONE receptacle outlet. Multioutlet assembly installed where it is not a dry location (380.10). Assembly concealed behind the building finish with no way to remove the cover. Metal assembly through a partition with an outlet inside the partition. Assembly installed in a hoistway or where subject to severe physical damage (380.12). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Nonmetallic extensions
x: Article 382 covers nonmetallic extensions: listed surface extension wiring systems that start from an existing outlet and serve additional outlets along a wall surface. It is a narrow, specific method with its own fittings and limits — not a license to surface-run ordinary cable. • What it is: a listed assembly — base, cover, fittings and receptacles made as one system — that extends an existing outlet along the wall. • How it starts: from an existing outlet only. It extends a circuit; it does not create one. • Where it cannot go: the article bars it from many of the places people first think of. It is a short list of permitted uses, not a general wiring method. • The Sharma answer: know it to recognize it. A proper surface raceway (386 or 388) or a new circuit is usually both legal and better. An extension run lives exposed on the wall, where furniture, feet and vacuum cleaners hit it, and it taps an existing circuit that was never sized for the added load. The listing and the use limits exist because a surface run has none of the protection of cable inside a wall — the system has to provide that protection itself, and the circuit behind it has to stay within what it was built for. Rarely the right answer on Sharma work; a proper raceway (386/388) or a new circuit is usually both legal and better. Know the article mainly to recognize the method. The call usually comes from a tenant finish-out: a desk row needs two more receptacles and someone suggests a surface extension kit off the supply-house shelf. Price the real fix instead — a short run of surface metal raceway on a new 20 A circuit with a Siemens breaker, done once. The extension kit still leaves the tenant on the old circuit, and the callback lands on Sharma. The trap answer treats a nonmetallic extension like surface raceway — a general way to add outlets anywhere. It is not: it is one listed system, fed from an existing outlet, with its own fittings and a short list of permitted uses. 'Run NM cable on the surface under a cover' is never the answer; ordinary cable has no place in it. Ordinary NM cable surface-run under a cover strip and called a nonmetallic extension — only the listed system is permitted (Article 382). Extension tapped from a junction box or a new source instead of from an existing outlet. Cover, base and fittings mixed from different systems — the extension is listed as one assembly. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Strut-type channel raceway
x: Article 384 covers strut-type channel raceway: a listed wiring system built on metal strut channel with covers and fittings made for electrical use — the channel is the raceway. • What makes it a raceway: the listed covers, fittings and conductor limits of this article. Ordinary structural strut by itself is a support, not a raceway. • What goes inside: conductors installed as a wiring method, in the sizes and counts the listing allows — not cable assemblies dropped into open channel. • What strut usually is on our jobs: a support system — trapeze racks and stands holding conduit and equipment. That strut follows the support rules of whatever it holds. • The test: if conductors run inside the channel, it is this article and it must be the listed system. If conduit runs on top of it, it is support work. Conductors inside bare structural channel sit against sharp steel edges with no listed cover, no tested fill limits and no protection from the next trade's screws and straps. The listing exists so the channel, covers and fittings are tested as one wiring system — insulation protected, fill controlled, covers secured — instead of a steel trough that only looks like a raceway. Common confusion on commercial jobs: strut holding conduits is support work; strut carrying conductors inside it is this article. Keep the two apart in the takeoff and the inspection conversation. On a retail tenant job the miss shows up as a takeoff line: 'strut channel' priced once, when the job actually needs the listed raceway system — covers, fittings and all — for the counter run, plus plain strut for the trapeze racks overhead. Price them as two different materials, because the inspector will treat them as two different things. The trap is 'strut is strut.' A length of ordinary structural channel with conductors laid in it is not a raceway, however neat it looks — without the listed covers, fittings and conductor limits of Article 384 it is a support with wire in it, and the exam answer that calls it a wiring method is wrong. Conductors laid in ordinary structural strut with no listed covers — channel is not a raceway without the listed system (Article 384). Strut raceway covers missing or unsecured at inspection. Cable assemblies run inside the channel instead of the conductors the listing permits. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Surface metal raceways
x: Surface metal raceway is the low-profile metal channel system mounted on walls and ceilings in finished spaces — the office and retail retrofit standard — carrying branch circuits to surface boxes and devices made for the system. Fill, fittings and grounding are the system's own; it is a raceway, not a decorative cover for loose cable. • Dry locations (386.10). It may pass transversely through dry walls, partitions and floors if the length passing through is unbroken, with access to the conductors on both sides. • Not permitted where subject to severe physical damage (unless approved), where subject to corrosive vapors, in hoistways, or concealed (386.12). • A voltage condition: at 300 V or more between conductors, the metal must be at least 0.040 in. (1.02 mm) thick nominal (386.12). • No conductor larger than the raceway is designed for, and never more conductors than it is designed for (386.21, 386.22). • The derating break: the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors do not apply when all three hold — raceway cross section over 4 sq in., current-carrying conductors 30 or fewer, and conductor fill not over 20 percent of the interior (386.22). • Splices and taps are permitted where the cover is removable and stays accessible, and conductors including the splice may not fill over 75 percent at that point. Without a removable cover, splices live in boxes (386.56). • Support follows the manufacturer's instructions (386.30). Finished spaces still need power where the walls cannot open, and this system answers without demolition. The limits guard its weak points: thin metal dents and opens under impact, a concealed run disappears from inspection forever, and a packed channel cooks its conductors — hence the damage, concealment, voltage and fill conditions written into the article. The retrofit answer where walls cannot open. Plan device boxes and fittings from the same system — mixing ordinary boxes defeats the listing. On a Winter Park retail refresh, Sharma runs a listed two-piece raceway down an existing block wall to feed new counter receptacles: circuits at 20 A on Siemens breakers, one manufacturer's system end to end, and every splice under a cover the next tech can pop with a screwdriver. The trap is the fill answer: 'surface raceway derates like conduit, always.' Under 386.22, when the raceway is over 4 sq in., holds 30 or fewer current-carrying conductors and stays at 20 percent fill, the 310.15(C)(1) adjustment factors do not apply. Miss any one of the three conditions and derating is back on. Raceway buried behind new drywall 'to hide it' — concealed is prohibited (386.12). 480 V run in light-gauge raceway under 0.040 in. thick — at 300 V and up, the metal must be 0.040 in. nominal (386.12). Splice buried inside a raceway section with no removable cover (386.56). Ordinary 4-square boxes and devices mixed into a listed raceway system, defeating its listing. Raceway run into a damp back room — the article permits dry locations (386.10). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Surface nonmetallic raceways
x: The nonmetallic counterpart to Article 386: surface-mounted plastic raceway systems for finished spaces, common for both power and low-voltage in offices and homes. Power and communications sharing one system is allowed only where the system is listed and arranged for it. The system — raceway and fittings — must be listed (388.6), and it is secured and supported following the manufacturer's instructions (388.30). Uses permitted (388.10) are only two: • In dry locations • As an extension passing transversely through dry walls, partitions and floors, where the length passing through is unbroken and access to the conductors is maintained on both sides Uses not permitted (388.12): where concealed, except for that through-wall case; where subject to severe physical damage; where the voltage between conductors is 300 volts or more, unless the raceway is listed for the higher voltage; in hoistways; in hazardous (classified) locations, except as other articles permit; where ambient temperatures exceed the raceway's listing; and with conductors whose insulation temperature rating exceeds the listing. Combination raceways (388.70) carry power and signaling or communications in separate, identified compartments of the same listed system. Splices and taps (388.56) are permitted where the cover stays accessible, and conductors, splices and taps together may not fill more than 75 percent of the raceway at that point. No conductor larger than the raceway is designed for (388.21). This is a light plastic channel living on a finished wall — no armor, no metal to shed heat, nothing hidden. The dry-location, damage, voltage and temperature limits keep it in the gentle indoor work it was listed for. Conceal it, cook it, or hang it where carts and lifts run, and the first anyone knows of the damage is the fault. Neat retrofit work, within its damage and location limits — it is surface wiring, so it lives where people and furniture can reach it. Protect or re-route accordingly. Orlando medical office: two new 20 A receptacle circuits in a listed combination raceway along a private-office wall — power in one compartment, data in the other — passing unbroken through one dry partition with access on both sides. At 120 volts the run sits well under the 300 volt between-conductors cap, and the run stays high on the wall, out of the chair and cart zone. The trap is assuming 388 goes everywhere its metal twin 386 goes. It does not: the nonmetallic article drops the Class I, Division 2 and raised-floor permissions, adds ambient and conductor temperature limits, and caps the system at 300 volts between conductors unless it is listed for more. Surface raceway concealed behind new drywall — only the unbroken through-wall length may pass through (388.10(2), 388.12(1)). Raceway run at cart height in a warehouse or garage — severe physical damage exposure (388.12(2)). 277/480 V circuits in a raceway not listed for 300 V or more between conductors (388.12(3)). Power and data mixed in one compartment of a raceway not listed and arranged as a combination system (388.70). Raceway installed in a damp or wet location — dry locations only (388.10(1)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Underfloor raceways
x: Underfloor raceways are distribution ducts set in or under a concrete floor — the older office-building system of floor ducts and junction boxes feeding floor outlets. New work is uncommon; existing systems are met on commercial remodels, where inserts and outlets must match the system. The installation rules (390.3): permitted beneath the surface of concrete or other flooring, and in office occupancies laid flush with the concrete floor under linoleum or equivalent covering. Not permitted where subject to corrosive vapors or in hazardous (classified) locations, and unprotected metal raceways, boxes and fittings do not go in concrete or severe corrosive areas. • Covering (390.4): raceways not over 4 in wide need at least ¾ in of concrete or wood above them; wider flat-top raceways need 1 in of concrete, or 1½ in where spaced less than 1 in apart • Conductors (390.5, 390.6): no conductor larger than the raceway is designed for, and all conductors together may fill no more than 40 percent of the raceway's interior • Splices and taps (390.7): only in junction boxes. Loop wiring — a continuous, unbroken conductor running through the outlets — is not a splice or a tap • Discontinued outlets (390.8): when an outlet is abandoned or removed, its conductors come out of the raceway; no splices or re-insulated conductors stay behind Junction boxes sit level with the floor grade, sealed against water and concrete, and runs are laid straight, box center to box center, with markers at the ends so the system can be found under the finished floor. Once the floor is poured, this system is invisible for decades. Straight runs, end markers and boxes flush at grade are what let the next electrician find it, open it and pull new conductors. The splice and abandoned-conductor rules keep hidden joints and dead copper out of a duct nobody can see into. On a remodel, find the junction boxes before promising floor outlets. An abandoned duct with no access is archaeology, not distribution. Orlando office remodel: the survey is markers first, then open every junction box on the run, check the existing fill against the 40 percent limit before adding two 20 A receptacle circuits, and pull the conductors of every outlet the new plan deletes — 390.8 does not let them stay in the duct, taped off and forgotten. The trap answer says loop wiring is a splice at every outlet it passes through, so it can't be used. 390.7 says the opposite: a continuous, unbroken conductor connecting the outlets is not considered a splice or tap. The real splice rule is the location — junction boxes only. Splice or tap made inside the duct run instead of in a junction box (390.7). Conductors of a removed outlet left in the raceway, taped or re-insulated (390.8). Junction box set below floor grade or unsealed — concrete and water inside the system. Raceway filled past 40 percent of its interior cross-section (390.6). Floor outlet insert that does not match the raceway system, or a dead-end run left open. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Cable tray systems
x: Cable tray is a support system, not a raceway: an open ladder, ventilated or solid-bottom structure that supports cables. • What may lie in it: the wiring methods listed in Table 392.10(A) — including tray-rated Type TC, metal-clad cable, raceways, and, where identified for the use, nonmetallic-sheathed cable in the structures Article 334 permits. • The restricted case: single insulated conductors. Outside the industrial-establishment rules of 392.10(B), they do not belong in tray. • The tray itself must be bonded and grounded as the article requires. • Fill is figured by the cable-area and sum-of-diameters rules of 392.22, not by the Chapter 9 conduit tables. A tray holds cables up; it does not enclose or protect them the way a raceway does, and it becomes a ground path only if it is bonded on purpose. Cables never identified for tray were not evaluated lying in an open structure where they can be abraded, stepped on or loaded past their limits. The 392.22 fill rules keep a tray from becoming a solid mat of cable that traps heat and crushes the bottom layer. If Sharma reaches for tray on a light-commercial job, the cable choice changes first (a wiring method Table 392.10(A) permits for that building), then the tray size. Do not lay loose single building conductors in tray and call it supported — apart from the narrow industrial exception in 392.10(B), they are not a tray wiring method. NM is not automatically barred either: it may sit in tray only where Article 334 permits it and the cable is identified for tray use. Two trap answers share one page: "tray is just an open raceway, so figure fill from Chapter 9," and "single conductors are fine in tray anywhere." Fill comes from 392.22, and single insulated conductors in tray are the industrial-only case of 392.10(B). Loose single THHN conductors laid in ladder tray on a retail job — single conductors are the 392.10(B) industrial-establishment case only. Tray sections bolted together with no bonding and no ground — the tray must be bonded and grounded as Article 392 requires; contact luck is not a bond. Tray loaded past the 392.22 cable-area limits because the fill was figured from the Chapter 9 conduit tables. NM cable draped in tray in a building type where Article 334 does not permit NM at all. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Low-voltage suspended ceiling power distribution systems
x: Article 393 covers listed low-voltage power distribution systems that use the suspended ceiling structure to distribute power to ceiling-supported equipment. Read the limit in that sentence: this is one specific, engineered, listed system. • The components, the connections and the loads are the system's own — they come with the listing, not from the parts shelf. • The article is not permission to treat the ceiling grid as a raceway. • It is not permission to use the grid as a support for ordinary wiring either. Ordinary ceiling work does not move into this article. It stays under the general rules: securing and supporting under 300.11, and wiring in spaces used for environmental air under 300.22. Article 393 loosens neither one. Ceiling grid is light structure, built to carry tiles and the fixtures made to sit in it — not to serve as a wiring method. Ordinary cable laid on grid or hung from it gets damaged, sags the grid, and sits in the ceiling plenum where fire and smoke rules are strict. A listed 393 system is engineered and tested for exactly this use, with defined components and loads. Field-invented 'grid power' has none of that behind it, and the failure shows up above a ceiling nobody watches. Specialized commercial systems only. Ordinary ceiling work stays under 300.11 and 300.22 — this article does not loosen either. On a Florida office tenant job, if the space has a listed ceiling power system, Sharma works to that system's components and instructions, with no field substitutions. Everything else above the ceiling — the 20 A branch circuits for the lighting layout and the rest of the ordinary work — is installed the regular way under 300.11 and 300.22. The trap answer says Article 393 lets you distribute ordinary branch power through the ceiling grid. It does not. Article 393 covers a listed low-voltage system with its own components, connections and loads. For everything else above the ceiling, 300.11 and 300.22 still apply in full — the article does not loosen either. Ordinary branch-circuit wiring laid on the ceiling grid and called a 393 system. Parts substituted into a listed ceiling power system that are not the system's components. Loads connected to a ceiling power system beyond the system's own listed connections. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Concealed knob-and-tube wiring
x: Knob-and-tube is the oldest method in the chapter: single conductors run open on porcelain knobs and through porcelain tubes, found in older Florida houses. Article 394 governs its very limited permitted extensions and uses today. New knob-and-tube installations are effectively a closed door, and insulation contact with it is a known fire concern that other codes also address. The prohibition that matters most on Florida re-insulation jobs sits in 394.12: • Knob-and-tube is not permitted in the hollow spaces of walls, ceilings and attics where loose, rolled, or foamed-in-place insulation envelops the conductors. Blowing insulation over live knob-and-tube buries a heat source the method was never designed for, and hides it. Where insulation work is planned over knob-and-tube, the wiring is replaced or the insulation plan changes — that conversation happens before the insulation truck, not after. Knob-and-tube was designed to shed heat into open air: single conductors, air space around them, porcelain between the wire and the wood. Wrap it in insulation and the heat has nowhere to go, on conductors whose own insulation is a century old. Buried, it also disappears — nobody can see the splice or the frayed covering cooking inside the blanket. Section 394.12 keeps the blanket off the wire. On remodels in older houses, Sharma practice is identification and safe handling: document it, do not bury it in new insulation or extend it casually, and put replacement options in front of the customer. On a pre-war Tampa bungalow survey, that means photographs of every knob-and-tube run in the attic, a note on the estimate before any insulation line item, and the rewire conversation at the kitchen table — not after the insulation crew has been scheduled. Older Florida housing stock — the pre-war bungalows of Tampa, Orlando, and Jacksonville — is where Sharma meets knob-and-tube, and it is exactly where blown-in attic insulation retrofits are sold hardest. Flag it on every survey. 'It is grandfathered' is the trap. Existing knob-and-tube may stay in service, but 394.12 still forbids enveloping it in loose, rolled or foamed insulation in wall, ceiling and attic spaces. Grandfathered wiring does not grandfather the insulation job — the blown-in retrofit over live knob-and-tube is the violation. Blown-in attic insulation installed over live knob-and-tube — 394.12. Foamed-in-place insulation sprayed around knob-and-tube inside a wall cavity — 394.12. Knob-and-tube extended casually, with new NM spliced open in the attic — no box, no office decision. Insulation crew scheduled before anyone surveyed the attic for knob-and-tube. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Messenger-supported wiring
x: Messenger-supported wiring carries cables or conductors on a steel messenger strand strung between structures — overhead spans to outbuildings, site lighting and similar runs, using cable assemblies listed for the method. The messenger carries the load; the electrical cable is not its own support. Article 396 recognizes four constructions (396.2): • A messenger with rings and saddles supporting the conductors • A messenger with field-installed lashing material • Factory-assembled aerial cable • Multiplex cables — duplex, triplex, quadruplex — twisted around a bare messenger Only the cable types in Table 396.10(A) may ride a messenger: medium-voltage cable, Type MC, Type MI, Type SE, Type UF, tray cable, and other factory-assembled multiconductor cables identified for the use — each under its own article's conditions. In industrial establishments only, where qualified persons service the system, single conductors of the Table 310.4 types and MV cable are also permitted; outdoors they must be listed for wet locations and sunlight resistant. The messenger is supported at dead ends and at intermediate points so the conductors carry no tension, and the conductors must not rest against the messenger supports, walls, pipes or the structure (396.30). The method is not permitted in hoistways or where subject to physical damage (396.12). A span of cable strung between buildings sags, swings in the wind and takes storm loads. If the cable carried its own weight, that tension would land on the terminations, and the insulation would chafe at every support until it failed. The steel messenger takes the mechanical load so the cable only carries current. The clearance rules then keep the whole span out of reach of trucks, ladders and pool poles. Detached garage feeder, Marion County: a 60 ft span of quadruplex aerial cable on its bare messenger, house to garage. At final sag the span must still clear the residential driveway by 12 ft and the pedestrian-only parts of the yard by 10 ft (225.18) — string it on a cool morning and it will sit lower on a hot August afternoon. Overhead spans live outdoors and age outdoors: check the strand, attachments and clearances as one system at every service call. The trap answer is that any cable can be lashed to a messenger — Type NM shows up on spans in the field. NM is not in Table 396.10(A), so the run fails no matter how neat the lashing looks. The messenger fixes the support problem; it does not widen the list of permitted cables. Messenger corroded through or broken, with the cable carrying its own weight and pulling on the terminations. Span sagging below the required clearance at final sag — 12 ft over a residential driveway, 18 ft over a road (225.18). Type NM or another unlisted cable type lashed to a messenger; Table 396.10(A) types only. Conductors resting against messenger supports or the structure, insulation chafed through. Messenger-supported wiring run where subject to physical damage (396.12). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Open wiring on insulators
x: Open wiring on insulators — individual conductors run exposed on insulators with set separations — is a legacy and specialized method (agricultural and industrial settings are its remaining home), governed by its own clearances and protection rules. It is not a shortcut version of knob-and-tube and not a method for new house work. The gate is narrow (398.10): open wiring is permitted only in industrial or agricultural establishments, on systems of 1000 volts, nominal, or less — indoors or outdoors, in wet or dry locations, where subject to corrosive vapors, and for services. It is never permitted where concealed by the building structure (398.12). The working rules are separation and protection: • Conductors within 7 ft of the floor are considered exposed to physical damage and must be protected — guard strips, running boards, boxing, or conduit (398.15(C)) • In dry locations, conductors may be enclosed in flexible nonmetallic tubing in continuous lengths of 15 ft or less, strapped at intervals of 4½ ft or less (398.15(A)) • Conductors entering damp, wet or corrosive spaces get drip loops, then pass upward and inward through noncombustible, nonabsorbent insulating tubes (398.15(B)) • Conductors stay separated from each other — 2½ in — and pass through framing on insulating tubes or bushings (398.17, 398.30) There is no raceway and no cable jacket — each conductor hangs in the open with only its own insulation on it. Separation keeps conductors from touching each other or grounded surfaces, and the guards and boxing keep people, ladders, tools and livestock from reaching the low runs. Lose either one and the insulation is the only thing left between a fault and a fire. Service call at a Marion County horse barn: an open-wiring feeder on porcelain insulators along the barn wall, installed decades ago and still legal where it stands. The check is the article in one pass — conductors below 7 ft boxed or in conduit, drip loops where the run enters the wash rack's wet area, spacers still holding the 2½ in separation on the long span, nothing concealed by the new ceiling in the tack room. Know it to recognize it. New Sharma work does not start here. The trap is treating 398 as knob-and-tube with better PR. Knob-and-tube is Article 394, a different method with different rules — and 398.12 flatly prohibits concealing open wiring, the one thing remodelers most want to do with it. The second trap is the voltage: older books said 600 volts; the 2020 limit in 398.10 is 1000 volts, nominal. Open wiring concealed by a new wall or ceiling finish — 398.12 prohibits it outright. Conductors within 7 ft of the floor with no guard strips, boxing or conduit protection (398.15(C)). Conductors touching each other or lying against the wall — separation and spacers lost on the span (398.30). Open wiring installed in a dwelling, retail or office occupancy — industrial and agricultural only (398.10). No drip loops where conductors enter a wet or corrosive location (398.15(B)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 398.15(C): Removed high-density polyethylene conduit (HDPE) as a permitted means to provide physical protection for open wiring on insulators in Section 398.15(C). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Outdoor overhead conductors over 1,000 volts
x: Article 399 is the last article in Chapter 3. It covers outdoor overhead conductors that operate at over 1,000 volts and belong to the property owner — the campus- or plant-style medium-voltage distribution on a big site — not the serving utility's lines. • What it is: a short, engineered article. It sets no prescriptive clearances of its own. • Structures: 399.30 requires the supporting structures to be designed and documented by a licensed professional engineer. • Clearances: the detailed clearance and construction rules live in the National Electrical Safety Code (NESC), not in the NEC. • What it is not: utility installations under a utility's exclusive control sit outside the NEC altogether, under 90.2(B)(5). • The number: in the 2020 NEC this article is 399, not 395 — the research draft's body text used 395 before its own index corrected it. A span carrying thousands of volts over a parking lot or a walkway can kill without anyone touching it, and the failure is usually structural — a pole, a guy or a crossarm that was never engineered. That is why this article does not hand the installer a clearance table: it sends the design to a licensed engineer and the clearances to the NESC, the code written for overhead line construction. This is not Sharma field work, and the field skill is knowing where our work stops. On a Central Florida industrial park or campus job, if the owner asks us to re-hang or extend an owner-owned overhead span over 1,000 volts, the answer is that the span belongs to the owner's engineer under 399.30 and the NESC — we document it, flag it to the owner in writing, and keep our scope on the premises wiring at 1,000 volts and under. The trap is answering from the familiar tables: 399 has no clearance table like 225.18, and its 2020 number is 399 — picking '395' imports the 2023 renumber into a 2020 permit. The other wrong answer is treating the owner's span like a utility drop; exclusive-control utility work is outside the NEC, but an owner-owned span is premises wiring with an engineered article. Owner-owned overhead span over 1,000 V with no engineered design or documentation for its supporting structures (399.30). Premises span over 1,000 V laid out from the 225.18 / 230 clearance tables instead of the NESC. Crew working on the utility's exclusive-control side of the service point as if it were premises wiring (90.2(B)(5)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 395: Article 399 was renumbered as Article 395, Outdoor Overhead Conductors over 1000 Volts. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Flexible cords and cables — article intro
x: Article 400 covers flexible cords and flexible cables — the connections between equipment and the building wiring, not wire that is installed as part of the building. It sorts cord types by construction (Table 400.4) and permitted use, and it draws a hard line against using a cord as a substitute for permanent wiring. If the wire is meant to stay in the building, it belongs in a Chapter 3 wiring method, not in a cord. Uses permitted (400.10) are the ones that need to move or be serviced: • Pendants • Portable lamps and portable appliances • Elevator and hoist cables • Parts of listed equipment, and similar flexible connections Uses not permitted (400.12) — a flexible cord may not be: • (1) Used as a substitute for the fixed wiring of a structure • (2) Run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors • (3) Run through doorways, windows, or similar openings • (4) Attached to building surfaces, except as 368.56(B) and 590.4 permit • (5) Concealed by walls, floors, or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings • (6) Installed in raceways, except as otherwise permitted in the Code • (7) Installed where subject to physical damage The 2020 numbers are 400.10 and 400.12; in the 2017 book the same lists were 400.7 and 400.8. A cord jacket is not a raceway. Building wire gets mechanical protection, support, and a box at every splice; a cord pressed into permanent service gets none of that. Stapled, buried, or pinched in a doorway, its insulation fails quietly — and nobody re-checks it, because everyone assumes the 'temporary' cord was removed years ago. When you reach for a cord, ask whether the equipment is meant to move, be serviced, or be exchanged. If the answer is no, run a permanent wiring method instead. On a service call at a small Orlando warehouse, Sharma found an air compressor 'temporarily' cord-connected through a hole bored in the wall for over a year, the cord pinched flat where it crossed a doorway. The fix was not a heavier cord: the crew ran a dedicated 20 A branch circuit in EMT to a receptacle beside the compressor — Sharma's commercial minimum — and the cord went back to being the compressor's own short connection. Check the cord jacket marking for the type letter before you trust it in a damp or hard-use location. The trap answer is 'use a heavier cord.' A 12 AWG hard-service cord through a wall hole is still a 400.12(2) violation, and an extension cord feeding a fixed appliance is still a substitute for fixed wiring under 400.12(1). Cord size and jacket type never cure a prohibited use. Flexible cord run through a hole in a wall, ceiling, or floor to reach fixed equipment (400.12(2)). Cord passing through a doorway or window opening, pinched by the door (400.12(3)). Extension cord or cord set left as the permanent supply to a fixed appliance (400.12(1)). Cord concealed above a suspended ceiling, or attached to building surfaces outside the permitted exceptions (400.12(4), (5)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Uses permitted and not permitted — flexible cords (400.10 / 400.12)
x: Sections 400.10 (uses permitted) and 400.12 (uses not permitted) draw the line for flexible cords; 400.7 and 400.8 are the 2017 numbers. Permitted uses are the ones that need to move or be serviced: pendants, portable lamps and appliances, elevator and hoist cables, parts of listed equipment, and similar flexible connections. The not-permitted list is the one that fails inspections: a cord may not substitute for the fixed wiring of a building, run through holes in walls, ceilings, or floors, pass through doorways or windows, attach to building surfaces outside the narrow exceptions, hide inside walls or conduit, or sit where it will be damaged. If a cord is doing a cable's job permanently, it is the wrong wiring method. The 400.12 list, in Code order — flexible cords may not be: • (1) As a substitute for the fixed wiring of a structure • (2) Run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors • (3) Run through doorways, windows, or similar openings • (4) Attached to building surfaces (except as 368.56(B) and 590.4 permit) • (5) Concealed by walls, floors, or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings • (6) Installed in raceways, except as otherwise permitted in the Code • (7) Installed where subject to physical damage A flexible cord has no armor and no raceway around it. Run through a wall or under a door, it gets pinched, abraded, and cooked out of sight, and nobody sees the damage until it faults or starts a fire. Fixed wiring methods are built to live inside a building for decades; a cord is built to flex, be inspected at a glance, and be replaced. The two lists keep each method doing its own job. Service call in a Winter Park home: a chest freezer in the garage is fed by a cord that passes through a hole drilled in the wall from the laundry room, and the garage door closes on it. It has been 'temporary' for two years. The fix is not a heavier cord — it is a real receptacle on its own 20 A circuit where the freezer stands, and the cord run comes out. The same answer applies to the window air conditioner found on the next call, running on a cord pinched under a bedroom door. The trap answer is that 400.12 bans cords attached to building surfaces, period. Two exceptions exist — 368.56(B) and 590.4 permit attachment in their cases. The reverse trap also shows up: a cord inside a raceway is not automatically fine; 400.12(6) allows it only where the Code otherwise permits. Cord run through a hole in the wall to feed a garage freezer — 400.12(2). Cord passing through a doorway and pinched by the door — 400.12(3). Extension cord stapled along a baseboard as permanent wiring — 400.12(1) and (4). Cord hidden above a dropped ceiling feeding a sign — 400.12(5). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: What flexible cords may be used for
x: Section 400.10 lists the jobs a flexible cord is allowed to do: hanging fixtures, connecting portable equipment, appliances that need to be moved for cleaning or service, and similar uses where flexibility is the point. The common thread is that the equipment, not the building, is what moves. A cord feeding a fixed outlet box or a permanent load is outside this list. Cord ampacity comes from Table 400.5(A)(1) for the cord type and the number of current-carrying conductors — the table below gives the sizes a crew actually holds, figured for two current-carrying conductors. A third current-carrying conductor in the same cord drops the value (the table's next column), which is why a cord's rating is read off its own table and not off the building-wire ampacity table. A cord is built to flex, not to live inside a wall for thirty years. Its insulation and strands are lighter than building wire, and nothing protects it where it passes through framing or gets pinched in a door. Kept to the listed uses, a cord stays out in the open where damage shows. Buried as permanent wiring, it becomes the hidden weak link that overheats or shorts. Before you plug or hard-wire a cord to anything, name the 400.10 use out loud. If you cannot name one, stop and run conduit or cable. Watch especially for cords run through walls, ceilings, or doorways, which this article does not allow. Workshop rough-in: pendant drops over the benches are a listed use, and the portable saw connects the same way. When the owner later asks for a cord through the wall to feed a new fixed outlet, that is the stop point — the use is gone, so the cord goes. The trap is treating a heavy cord like building wire: '12 AWG is 12 AWG.' A cord's ampacity comes from Table 400.5(A)(1), not Table 310.16, and no cord size buys a use that is not on the 400.10 list. A cord feeding a fixed outlet box fails on the use before size is even discussed. Flexible cord run through a wall, ceiling or doorway to reach a fixed load. Cord used as a substitute for fixed wiring — feeding an outlet box or a permanent appliance. Cord ampacity taken from Table 310.16 instead of Table 400.5(A)(1). Three current-carrying conductors in the cord, but the two-conductor ampacity used. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Uses not permitted — flexible cords and cables
x: Section 400.12 is the stop list for flexible cords and cables. In the 2017 edition this list was numbered 400.8; the 2020 reorganization of Article 400 moved it here. Unless 400.10 permits the use, a flexible cord, flexible cable, cord set, or power-supply cord may not be used: • (1) As a substitute for the fixed wiring of the structure. • (2) Run through holes in walls, structural ceilings, suspended or dropped ceilings, or floors. • (3) Run through doorways, windows, or similar openings. • (4) Attached to building surfaces — except that cords used for temporary wiring under 590.4 may be attached. • (5) Concealed by walls, floors, or ceilings, or located above suspended or dropped ceilings — except within an enclosure for use in other spaces used for environmental air, as permitted by 300.22(C)(3). • (6) Installed in raceways — except as 400.17 permits in industrial establishments where only qualified persons service the installation. • (7) Where it is subject to physical damage. Most failed cord installations fail here, not on ampacity: the cord is usually heavy enough — it is just doing a job the Code reserves for fixed wiring. A cord is built to flex, not to live inside a wall for thirty years. Hidden or pinched, its jacket dries, cracks, and chafes where nobody can see it, and it has no raceway or cable armor to protect it. The stop list keeps cords out in the open, where damage shows, and reserves hidden runs for wiring methods built to be buried. On a service call, trace the whole cord, not just the ends. If any part of it is stapled, hidden, or passing through a partition, the fix is a permanent wiring method, not a heavier cord. A Marion Oaks garage call: a freezer in the corner runs on a 14 AWG cord stapled along the wall and passed through a hole into the house — three items on the stop list at once. The fix was a new 20 A circuit in 12 AWG to a receptacle at the freezer, not a 12 AWG cord. And when a plan shows a cord doing a building's job, price the Chapter 3 wiring method instead. The trap answer treats the stop list as an ampacity problem: 'use a heavier cord and it passes.' It does not. A 10 AWG cord run through a wall still violates (2), and a cord stapled to the wall still violates (4), whatever its size. The only cure for a 400.12 violation is a fixed wiring method — or a use that 400.10 actually permits. Extension cord stapled along a garage wall feeding a freezer — a substitute for fixed wiring, 400.12(1) and (4). Cord run through a hole in the wall between the house and the garage, 400.12(2). Appliance cord pinched through a doorway that closes on it, 400.12(3) and (7). Cord draped above a dropped ceiling to feed a projector, 400.12(5). Cord pulled into a raceway on a commercial job outside the 400.17 industrial exception, 400.12(6). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Fixture wires — article intro
x: Article 402 covers the small conductors used inside fixtures and equipment, called fixture wires. They are for wiring within a luminaire or similar equipment and for connecting that equipment over a limited distance, not for general branch-circuit runs through a building. Sizes run smaller than branch wiring, which is exactly why they must stay inside the equipment they belong to. • Uses permitted (402.10): inside luminaires and similar equipment, enclosed or protected and not subject to bending or twisting in use, and for connecting luminaires to the branch-circuit conductors that supply them. • Uses not permitted (402.12): fixture wires are not branch-circuit conductors, except where another article permits them, such as Class 1 remote-control and signaling circuits. • The smallest size is 18 AWG (402.6), and ampacity comes from Table 402.5, not Table 310.16: 18 AWG is 6 A and 16 AWG is 8 A, whatever the insulation type. • Protection is by the tap rules (240.5(B)(2)): on a 20 A circuit, an 18 AWG tap may run 50 ft and a 16 AWG tap 100 ft. Fixture wire ratings are figured for the inside of a fixture: short runs, known loads, and the fixture's own heat. Run it through a building like branch wire and a 6 A conductor can end up sitting on a 20 A breaker with nothing to save it. The tap limits in 240.5 are the compromise: short, load-limited whips are fine; a building run is not. If you find a fixture wire run acting like a branch circuit through a wall or ceiling, flag it. Replace that run with a Chapter 3 method sized for the circuit. Keep fixture-wire splices inside the fixture or its listed outlet box. On a high-bay retrofit the pattern is: 12 AWG branch wiring to the box on the 20 A circuit, then the fixture's own 18 AWG whip down to the luminaire. A 25 ft tap is inside the 50 ft limit, and the LED driver draws about 1.5 A against the whip's 6 A ampacity. The wire between two fixtures is not a tap: it is branch wiring, and it stays Chapter 3 wire. The trap is reaching for Table 310.16, or for the small-conductor rules, to rate fixture wire. Fixture wire has its own table: 18 AWG is 6 A, not 15 A. The 20 A breaker is allowed behind it only because 240.5(B)(2) treats the whip as a tap with a length limit, not because the wire carries 20 A. Fixture wire run through a wall or ceiling as a branch circuit. 18 AWG fixture wire tap over 50 ft long on a 20 A circuit. Fixture wire spliced in the open, outside the fixture or its listed box. Fixture wire loaded past its Table 402.5 ampacity. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Fixture wire ampacity — small wire, small numbers (Table 402.5)
x: Fixture wires are the small conductors inside luminaires and equipment, and Table 402.5 gives them their own ampacities — not the branch-circuit numbers for the same gauge. The whole table is five rows: • 18 AWG fixture wire — 6 A • 16 AWG fixture wire — 8 A • 14 AWG fixture wire — 17 A • 12 AWG fixture wire — 23 A • 10 AWG fixture wire — 28 A Fixture wire is protected and tapped under the fixture-wire rules (240.5), never treated as branch-circuit wire, and it never leaves the fixture or equipment it belongs to. No fixture wire is smaller than 18 AWG (402.6). Fixture wire runs inside a hot, closed metal box, bundled against ballasts and drivers, in sizes too small to survive a hard fault on a big breaker. Its own ampacity table, and the tap limits in 240.5, keep a fault inside the fixture from turning the whip into a heating element. Extend a run with it, or load it to branch-circuit numbers, and the weak link is hidden where nobody will see it smoke. Rewiring a fixture whip or a driver lead: match the fixture wire to what the fixture came with. Never extend a circuit with fixture wire because it was handy on the truck. A 16 AWG whip is an 8 A conductor — plenty for an LED driver lead, nowhere near a circuit. Where fixture wire taps a 20 A branch circuit, 240.5(B)(2) caps the run: 18 AWG up to 50 ft, 16 AWG up to 100 ft, and 14 AWG or larger without the length cap. The trap is answering from the wrong table. '12 AWG is 20 A wire' is the branch-circuit answer (240.4(D)); as fixture wire, Table 402.5 rates 12 AWG at 23 A, and 14 AWG fixture wire is 17 A, not 15 A. The exam names the conductor — fixture wire gets the fixture table. The dangerous reverse is loading a branch circuit to the 23 A fixture number. Fixture wire run out of its fixture to feed the next light down the row. 18 AWG fixture-wire tap on a 20 A circuit run past 50 ft (240.5(B)(2)). 16 AWG fixture whip loaded past 8 A (Table 402.5). Fixture wire landed in a junction box as if it were a branch-circuit conductor. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Switches — article intro
x: Article 404 covers switches: the devices that open and close a circuit, from a simple single-pole snap switch to motor-circuit switches. It handles which conductor a switch may interrupt, where a grounded (neutral) conductor must be available at a switch box, how high and how accessible a switch must be, and how switch terminals are marked for conductor materials. The working rules: • Switching belongs in the ungrounded (hot) conductor — a switch never interrupts the neutral alone (404.2(A)). • A grounded conductor (neutral) must be present at most switch locations, so electronic controls, timers and sensors can power themselves (404.2(C)). Listed exceptions exist — raceways where the neutral can be pulled in later, certain replacements — so read the exception list for the exact job. • Switches must be readily accessible, and the center of the operating handle, in its highest position, may not be more than 6 ft 7 in. above the floor or platform (404.8(A)). That is a ceiling, not a mounting height. Start here whenever a switching question is about the device itself rather than the circuit feeding it. A switch is the one part of the circuit a person touches every day, often in the dark, sometimes with wet hands. Switching the hot conductor means the load is dead when the switch is off; switching the neutral leaves the fixture live and waiting. The neutral in the box exists because a generation of dimmers, timers and sensors was stranded in boxes with no way to power itself, and the height ceiling keeps a switch or disconnect within reach of a person standing on the floor. On rough-in, the two 404 questions to settle before the walls close are neutral availability at switch boxes and switch height. Both are cheap at rough-in and expensive after drywall. Sharma sets switches at 48 in. to the center of the box when the plan is silent (S-05) — a company preference, not a code number; the code only caps the operating handle at 6 ft 7 in. (404.8(A)). Pull the neutral through every switch box on the rough, even where today's device is a plain snap switch: the dimmer or occupancy sensor that replaces it later will need it. S-05: when the plan is silent, Sharma sets switches at 48 in. to the center of the box. That is a company preference, not an Article 404 requirement. Two traps live on this page. First: 'the Code requires switches at 48 inches.' It does not — 48 in. to center is Sharma's S-05 preference; Article 404 sets no standard house height, only the 6 ft 7 in. handle ceiling. Second: 'a switch loop needs no neutral.' Under 404.2(C) the grounded conductor belongs in the box unless a listed exception fits the job — a box roughed in without it fails the next device change. Switch interrupting the neutral — the fixture stays energized with the switch off (404.2(A)). No grounded conductor in the switch box, and no 404.2(C) exception applies. Operating handle center over 6 ft 7 in. in its highest position (404.8(A)). Snap switch loaded past its limit for the load type — motor load over 80 percent of rating (404.14). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 404.1: The switch article's scope now makes clear that wireless controls with no connection to circuit conductors aren't covered, and an informational note sends readers to 210.70. Wireless control gear that never connects to circuit conductors, like a battery-powered remote, falls outside Article 404. • 404.16: New 404.16 sorts switches into rebuild-allowed and replace-only. Snap switches, dimmers, electronic controls and molded-case switches must be new; knife, butt-contact and bolted pressure switches can be reconditioned. Lighting switches, snap switches of any type, dimmers and electronic control switches like timers can't be reconditioned. Replace them with new devices. • 404.30: New 404.30: if opening a switch enclosure's door with the switch on would expose bare live parts, the door must need a tool or another approved way to keep unqualified people out. With the switch closed (on), a door that opens onto uninsulated live parts must take a tool to open. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Three-way and four-way switching — what the switch may control
x: Section 404.2(A) is about which conductor a switch interrupts. For three-way and four-way switches the rule is stated outright: all switching must be in the ungrounded (hot) conductor. • The grounded (neutral) conductor is never switched. It runs unbroken to the load and lands on the screw shell of a lampholder, so the shell — the part fingers touch — stays on the grounded side. • In a traveler system, the hot lands on the first switch's common terminal, the two travelers carry it from switch to switch, and the switched leg leaves the last switch's common for the load. Two or more locations control one load while the rule stays intact. • The banned pattern is the old Carter system: hot and neutral both landed on the traveler terminals, so depending on the switch positions the shell could sit on the hot side — with the light off. Prohibited since the 1923 NEC, it still turns up in old Florida houses. A lamp that is 'off' should be safe to re-lamp. If the switching scheme leaves the screw shell connected to a hot conductor, the person changing the bulb — standing on a ladder, one hand on the shell — becomes the path. Switching only the hot conductor, and keeping the shell on the grounded conductor, is what makes 'off' mean off. Wire 3-way/4-way runs by function, not by color habit: common, travelers, switched leg, neutral, ground. On a Sharma house rough-in — a Winter Park two-story with switches at both ends of the hall and at the top and bottom of the stairs — the travelers on the long runs get labeled at rough-in, per the Sharma practice note below, so the trim crew is not ringing out pairs through finished walls. Test every switch position at trim and confirm the load is fully controlled from each location before you leave. Never borrow a neutral from another circuit to make a traveler scheme work. Sharma practice note (job practice, not code text): label travelers at rough-in when a run is long or passes through several boxes. It saves the trim crew from ringing out pairs. The trap is wiring by 'it works.' A Carter-wired 3-way turns the light on and off from both locations, so it passes a lazy test — but in some switch combinations the socket shell is hot with the light off. 'The light works from both switches' is not the test; 'all switching is in the ungrounded conductor' is. The same goes for landing a traveler on the common because the colors looked right. Neutral switched instead of the hot — the lampholder shell stays energized with the light off (404.2(A)). Carter-style wiring found or recreated: hot and neutral both on the traveler terminals. Traveler landed on a common terminal, so the load obeys only one switch or the positions disagree. Neutral borrowed from another circuit to make a traveler scheme work. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: A neutral must be available at most switch locations
x: Section 404.2(C) requires a grounded conductor — the neutral — to be installed at the switch locations where switches control lighting loads on a grounded general-purpose branch circuit: bathrooms, hallways, stairways, and habitable rooms. The reason is practical: modern controls, timers, occupancy sensors and smart switches need a neutral to power themselves. • The neutral must be there even if today's device is a plain snap switch that never touches it. • Where 3-way or 4-way locations control the same load and the whole floor area is visible from the switch locations, the neutral is required at only one location. • Exceptions (2020) let you omit it where the conductors enter through a raceway with room to add the neutral later, where a cable can still be added or replaced without removing finish materials, for snap switches with integral enclosures complying with 300.15(E), where the lighting is controlled by automatic means, and where the switch controls a receptacle load. Read the exception list for the exact job instead of assuming — and pull the neutral anyway when in doubt. Electronic controls need power while the light is off. Without a neutral in the box, the old workarounds leaked current through the load or borrowed the equipment ground — flickering lamps and current on grounding paths. Requiring the neutral at rough-in, while the walls are open, turns every later control swap into a device change instead of a demolition job. At rough-in, pull the neutral through every switch box even when the planned device is a plain snap switch that does not use it today. Cap it neatly in the back of the box. That one habit prevents the most common 404.2(C) correction and makes later smart-switch work possible without opening walls. On a Marion Oaks entry, the 3-gang box gets the feed, three switch legs, and the neutral spliced through and capped; the hall 3-ways need the neutral at one location only, because the whole hall is visible from both ends. Sharma note: this is why the Honeywell / ecobee-era control work and smart switches on Sharma jobs assume a neutral in the box. Do not design a switch location that strands a future electronic control without one. The trap answer is 'no neutral needed — the specified device is a plain snap switch.' The rule is about the location, not today's device: if the switch controls lighting in a habitable room, the neutral goes in the box. The related trap is powering a smart switch by borrowing the equipment grounding conductor as its return — electronic control switches are not permitted to put their operating current on the ground (404.22). Switch loop roughed with no neutral in a bedroom or hallway switch box. Smart dimmer landed on the equipment grounding conductor for its return current. Neutral present in the box, but from a different circuit than the switch leg it serves. No neutral at any 3-way location where the room is not visible from the switch locations. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 404.2: One escape hatch for skipping the neutral at lighting switches is gone: a box you can get into later without opening up the finish no longer counts. Gone in 2023: the pass for a switch box reachable later without removing finish materials. Pull the neutral anyway (404.2(C)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Switches in damp or wet locations — and out of the tub/shower wet location
x: Article 404 requires switches installed in damp or wet locations to be in enclosures suited to the location, and it separately restricts switches in a bathtub or shower space: • A switch may not be installed within the wet location of a tub or shower unless it is part of a listed tub or shower assembly made for that purpose. • The rule parallels the receptacle and luminaire zones in 406.9(C) and 410.10(D) — measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or the shower threshold — so the wettest part of the room is kept free of devices a wet person would operate. • A switch on the dry wall outside that space is an ordinary installation. Water on skin drops the body's resistance, and a person in a tub is usually wet, barefoot, and in contact with grounded plumbing — the worst possible position to touch a line-voltage device. Keeping switches out of the wet location removes the device from the reach of the person least able to survive contact with it. The weatherproof enclosure rule does the quieter job outdoors: it keeps water out of the device so the device does not fail wet. At layout, treat the tub/shower wet location as a no-switch zone the same way you treat it as a no-receptacle zone: in a Florida master bath, the switch bank goes on the dry wall outside the 3 ft / 8 ft zone, not on the wall beside the tub where the sketch first puts it. Exterior and patio switches get weatherproof enclosures suited to whether a cover must close over a plug or cord. Pool and spa switching also answers to Article 680 — check Chapter 6 before you place a switch near water. Florida note: outdoor kitchens, lanais, and pool-adjacent switching are damp or wet locations in practice; enclosure choice matters more here than the switch itself. The trap answer is that GFCI protection makes a switch legal inside the tub/shower wet location. It does not — this is a location rule, and the only way in is as part of a listed tub or shower assembly. The second trap is treating a damp-location cover as a wet-location installation. A wet location needs an enclosure suited to wet use, not just a gasketed plate over an indoor switch. Switch installed inside the tub/shower wet location, not part of a listed tub or shower assembly. Standard indoor switch and plate on a lanai wall — no enclosure suited to the damp or wet location. Switch roughed in beside the tub inside the 3 ft / 8 ft zone and never moved at trim. Pool-area switch placed without checking Article 680. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Switches must be reachable — operating handle height
x: Section 404.8(A) requires switches to be readily accessible and sets a ceiling on height: the center of the operating handle, in its highest position, may not be more than 6 ft 7 in. above the floor or working platform. The point is that a person standing on the floor must be able to operate the switch without a ladder or a reach tool. It does not set the normal mounting height for a house switch — that comes from the plan or company practice. • The measurement is to the center of the handle with the handle up — not to the top of the box or the plate. • Special cases exist for switches next to the equipment they serve and for busway-type installations, so check the exceptions before you relocate a switch that looks too high. A switch is the control a person reaches for in the dark, in smoke, or in a hurry. If it takes a ladder or a broom handle, it is not really a control — people leave the light on, or worse, cannot shut a circuit off at the device. The 6 ft 7 in. ceiling keeps every switch within a standing person's reach. Sharma roughs house switches at 48 in. to the center of the box when the plan is silent (S-05), so the ceiling in 404.8(A) rarely comes up — until it does. On an Ocala final, the garage switch for the yard lights had been set high to clear a workbench: the center of the handle in the up position measured 6 ft 8 in. One inch over the limit, and it failed. It moved down to 5 ft 6 in., still clear of the bench. S-05: Sharma's default is 48 in. to the center of the box when the plan is silent. The plan governs when it states a height. Do not present 48 in. as a code number — 404.8(A) is the code ceiling, S-05 is our working height. The trap is answering 48 in. That is Sharma's working height (S-05), not a code number. The code gives a maximum, not a mounting height: 6 ft 7 in. to the center of the operating handle in its highest position. The second trap is measuring to the top of the box — the rule measures the handle. Switch handle center at 6 ft 9 in. above the floor — over the 404.8(A) ceiling. Switch reachable only from a step stool or ladder in a garage or stairwell. Switch blocked by fixed equipment or stored material — not readily accessible. Height checked to the top of the plate at trim and a high switch passed on that measurement. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding snap switches (404.9)
x: Section 404.9 requires snap switches — including dimmers and control switches — to be connected to an equipment grounding conductor (EGC), so the metal yoke and any metal faceplate are bonded. • Metal box: the box is bonded by its EGC, and the switch's mounting screws bond the yoke to the box (250.109). The screws are the bond — use the switch's own mounting screws, tight. • Nonmetallic box: there is no box to bond through, so the EGC lands on the switch's own green grounding terminal. • Faceplates: 404.9(A) also requires the plate to completely cover the box opening and seat against the finished surface. The replacement exception matters in old houses. Where an existing switch is replaced in a box with no grounding means — no EGC in the wiring method — an ungrounded replacement is permitted for replacement only, on the exception's terms: a nonmetallic, noncombustible faceplate with nonmetallic screws, or GFCI protection for the circuit. Where the switch sits within 8 ft vertically or 5 ft horizontally of ground or exposed grounded metal objects, those terms are the whole allowance. Landing a standard switch with a metal plate on a 2-wire box and moving on is not one of the paths. The yoke and the plate screws sit right where fingers land in the dark. If a hot conductor faults to an unbonded yoke, the plate and its screws sit at line voltage with nothing to trip the breaker, and the first person to touch the switch becomes the fault path. The EGC gives that fault a low-impedance road home, so the breaker opens instead. On remodels, check for a ground before trim-out, not during the final walk. In a 1960s Orlando ranch wired with 2-wire cable, Sharma's crew found no EGC in any switch box on the lighting circuits.
