Because the panel was being replaced with new Siemens gear anyway, the fix was GFCI breakers on those lighting circuits, which puts every replacement switch on the exception's GFCI path; on the one circuit that stayed unprotected, the plates went on nonmetallic, with nonmetallic screws. No EGC in the box changes what devices you may land — flag it at discovery. The trap: 'The switch is in a metal box, so it is grounded.' A metal box is a grounding path only when the box itself is connected to an EGC. A steel box fed by old 2-wire cable bonds the yoke to a floating box — worse than plastic if the box ever faults. The second trap: GFCI protection does not create a ground. It is the exception's alternative protection for a replacement, not an equipment ground. Replacement switch landed on a 2-wire box with a metal faceplate and no GFCI protection — none of the exception's paths taken. Ground wire clipped off or left loose in a nonmetallic box instead of landed on the switch's green terminal. Metal box assumed to be a ground because it is metal, with no EGC in the cable feeding it. Faceplate that does not completely cover the box opening, or stands off the finished surface (404.9(A)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Snap switch ratings and the loads they may control
x: Section 404.14 ties a general-use snap switch to the kind of load it controls. A switch marked for AC only, or for AC/DC, has different limits for motor, inductive, and tungsten-type loads, and a switch may not be loaded past the rating that applies to that load type. In plain terms: the amp number on the yoke is not a promise for every load — the load type decides which limit applies. The working limits, by load type: • Resistive loads — up to the switch's full marked ampere rating • Inductive loads (ballasts, transformers) — full rating on an AC general-use switch; 50 percent of the rating on an AC/DC general-use switch • Motor loads — 80 percent of the rating on an AC general-use switch, or the switch's marked horsepower rating where it has one • Tungsten-filament lamp loads — full rating at 120V on an AC general-use snap switch (404.14(A)); the 'T' rating question applies to AC/DC switches (404.14(B)) Worked example: a 15A AC-only snap switch may carry a 12A motor load (15 × 0.80) and up to 15A of tungsten lighting at 120V; the 'T' marking question applies to AC/DC switches. A snap switch's contacts are small. Motor and inductive loads draw inrush current and throw an arc every time the switch opens, and cold tungsten filaments pull many times their running current at switch-on. Load a switch past the limit for that load type and the contacts pit, weld shut, or cook inside the box — you get a motor that will not turn off, or a switch that heats every time it is used. The load-type limits keep the contacts alive for the life of the switch. On a Sharma commercial service call in Orlando, a 15 A AC-only snap switch controls a small exhaust fan motor that draws 12 A. The check before touching it: motor loads are limited to 80 percent of the switch rating, and 15 × 0.80 = 12 A, so this switch is right at its limit and legal. The same switch on a 14 A motor would be over the limit — that one gets a switch with a marked horsepower rating, or the motor gets controlled through a rated contactor. Read the yoke marking before any snap switch goes on a motor, a ballast bank, or a heater, and run the percentage for that load type. The trap is treating the yoke number as universal: '15 A switch, 15 A load, done.' A 15 A AC/DC switch on an inductive load is limited to 50 percent — 7.5 A — and a 15 A AC switch on a motor load tops out at 12 A. The load type picks the limit, not the number stamped on the yoke. 15 A snap switch switching a 14 A motor load — over the 80 percent motor limit of 404.14. AC/DC-rated switch loaded to its full ampere rating on a fluorescent ballast bank. General-use snap switch with no horsepower rating used to control a motor beyond its rating. Switch controlling a heater bank loaded past its marked ampere rating. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 404.14: Switch terminals now have wire rules: copper or copper-clad aluminum unless CO/ALR, and push-in holes are for 14 AWG solid copper, only on 15-amp circuits. Dimmers now follow the same load rule as timers. Push-in (back-stab) holes take only 14 AWG solid copper on a 15-amp circuit, unless the switch is listed and marked for other wire (404.14(D)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Switch terminal markings for conductor materials (CO/ALR)
x: Section 404.15(C) carries the CO/ALR marking rule for switches — the switch-side twin of 406.3(C) for receptacles: • A switch designed for the direct connection of aluminum conductors must be marked CO/ALR. • The terminal rules that go with the marking, stated for the 2020 NEC in NEMA Engineering Bulletin No. 122 from the UL guide information for snap switches: terminals of 15A and 20A snap switches are for use with copper and copper-clad aluminum conductors only, unless marked CO/ALR, which adds aluminum. • Terminals of switches rated 30A and above are for copper only, unless marked AL/CU. • Plain aluminum never lands on an unmarked device terminal. Aluminum and copper do not age the same way under a screw. Aluminum oxidizes and creeps under pressure, so a terminal that was not designed and tested for it can work loose over years of heating and cooling until the connection runs hot. A CO/ALR device is built and tested for that behavior. The marking is how the installer knows which test the terminal passed — from the outside, the two switches look the same. On a service call in a 1970s Florida house with aluminum branch wiring, the replacement switch on the truck is not automatically the right device. Read the terminal marking on the switch you are holding and match it to the conductor you are landing: no CO/ALR marking, no plain aluminum on the terminal — get a CO/ALR device instead of landing it and leaving. With CCA the terminal itself is fine, but land it on the screw terminals only: do not backstab CCA (see S-10). S-10 applies: CCA is sized one AWG larger than copper and terminations must be listed for the conductor. Never backstab. The trap answer is that CO/ALR and AL/CU are two names for the same marking. They are not: 15A and 20A snap switches take aluminum only when marked CO/ALR, while switches rated 30A and above are copper only unless marked AL/CU. The second trap is treating CCA as plain aluminum. The bulletin puts copper-clad aluminum with copper on an unmarked 15A or 20A terminal; plain aluminum is the conductor that needs the marking. Plain aluminum branch conductor landed on a 15 A snap switch with no CO/ALR marking. Aluminum landed on a 30 A switch terminal not marked AL/CU. CCA conductor backstabbed into a switch instead of landed on the screw terminal. Standard copper-only switch installed where the existing aluminum wiring required a CO/ALR device. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Receptacles, cord connectors, and attachment plugs — article intro
x: Article 406 covers receptacle outlets and the plugs and cord connectors that go into them: how receptacles are rated and grounded, when a replacement must upgrade protection, where face-up devices may be used, what damp and wet locations demand, the tub and shower exclusion zone, and where tamper-resistant receptacles are required. It is the article behind most device-level corrections on a residential final. • Ratings, grounding and replacements (406.4): receptacles match the circuit's rating and configuration, are grounding type where the wiring method provides a ground, and a replacement follows the 406.4(D) upgrade ladder, including GFCI protection and 'No Equipment Ground' marking where no grounding means exists. • Damp and wet locations (406.9): weather-resistant receptacles and the covers the location demands. • Tub and shower zone (406.9(C)): no receptacles within a zone measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or shower stall threshold. • Tamper-resistant (406.12): TR receptacles in dwelling units and the other listed occupancies, with exceptions such as receptacles more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor. Receptacles are the part of the system people touch every day, often with wet hands, near water, or through a child with a paperclip. Article 406 is where the Code puts the device-level defenses: the right rating, a real ground, GFCI protection on replacements, weather resistance outside, shutters for kids, and a hard line keeping devices away from tubs and showers. At trim, work 406 as a checklist room by room: correct replacement type, WR where the location needs it, in-use cover where the location is wet, TR where 406.12 requires it, and nothing inside the tub/shower zone. The bathroom is where the zone bites: the basin receptacle has to sit within 3 ft of the basin (210.52(D)) and still stay out of the 3 ft by 8 ft zone measured from the tub rim, so measure from the rim, not from the basin, before the box is set. S-07: points marked GFI on a Sharma plan get a standard tamper-resistant receptacle protected by the dual-function breaker. Sharma does not install GFCI receptacles as the standard device. The trap is mixing up the two 3 ft rules in a bathroom. The basin rule (210.52(D)) wants a receptacle within 3 ft of the basin; the zone rule (406.9(C)) bans receptacles within 3 ft horizontally of the tub rim. A receptacle can satisfy the basin and still fail the zone. Receptacle installed inside the tub and shower zone (406.9(C)). Standard receptacle in a wet location: not weather-resistant, and no in-use cover. Non-TR receptacle in a dwelling unit where 406.12 requires tamper-resistant receptacles. Replacement receptacle swapped like-for-like where 406.4(D) requires GFCI protection and 'No Equipment Ground' marking. Face-up receptacle in a countertop that is not listed for face-up use. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 406.2: One section, 406.2, now holds the no-reconditioning rule for receptacles, cord connectors, plugs and flanged surface devices. The ban itself dates to 2020. None of these four can be reconditioned: receptacles, attachment plugs (caps), cord connectors and flanged surface inlets or outlets. • 406.3: 406.3(D) now spells out what wire receptacle terminals take: copper or copper-clad aluminum unless CO/ALR, and push-in holes are for 14 AWG solid copper, only on 15-amp circuits. Push-in (back-stab) holes are for 14 AWG solid copper only, on a 15-amp branch circuit, unless the receptacle is listed and marked for other wire. • 406.6: Cover plates with a night light or USB charger that draw power through spring contacts on the receptacle screws are now limited to 1 watt and brass or copper alloy screws. A plate whose only connection is spring-tensioned contacts touching the receptacle's terminal screws can't draw more than 1 watt (406.6(D)). • 406.9: The tub and shower zone now reaches inside and below the tub and gained new exceptions. Weather-resistant listing now covers 30-amp, 50-amp and other wet-location receptacles, and hinged hood covers must open 90 degrees. The zone now covers inside the tub or shower and everything below the rim; a wall, floor, door, window or fixed barrier ends it. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Receptacle installation and replacement — the general rules (406.4(A)–(C))
x: Section 406.4 sets the baseline before the replacement details in 406.4(D). Receptacles must be of the grounding type where the wiring method provides a ground, must match the circuit's rating and configuration, and replacements follow a ladder: • Grounding-type for grounding-type where an EGC exists. Where an EGC exists or is connected under 250.130(C), the replacement is a grounding-type receptacle (406.4(D)(1)). • Where no grounding means exists, the permitted paths are a nongrounding replacement, a GFCI replacement marked 'No Equipment Ground,' or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI and marked the same way. • The third replacement option is exactly this: a grounding-type receptacle supplied through a GFCI, marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground' (406.4(D)(2)(c)). The markings are part of the rule, not paperwork. A grounding-type receptacle on a circuit with no ground tells a lie to the next person who plugs in: the third slot promises a fault path that is not there. The replacement ladder keeps the protection honest. A GFCI gives real shock protection without pretending to be a ground, and the 'No Equipment Ground' marking tells the truth about what is actually in the box. Old two-wire house work — a 1960s Orlando home with no EGC in the boxes: carry GFCI receptacles and 'No Equipment Ground' stickers on the truck. Where the owner wants a three-slot receptacle, the path is a GFCI replacement marked 'No Equipment Ground,' or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI and marked 'GFCI Protected' and 'No Equipment Ground.' An unmarked GFCI swap in a no-ground box fails the detail even though the device itself works. The trap is the unmarked GFCI swap: 'the GFCI trips, so the replacement is legal.' The device working is not the rule — on a no-ground circuit the GFCI replacement must be marked 'No Equipment Ground,' and a grounding-type receptacle fed through one needs both markings. The second trap is a plain grounding-type receptacle on a two-wire circuit. Without the GFCI and the markings, the ground slot promises a ground that does not exist. GFCI receptacle swapped into a no-ground box with no 'No Equipment Ground' marking. Grounding-type receptacle on a two-wire circuit with no GFCI protection and no markings — a ground slot with no ground behind it. Receptacle fed through a GFCI but missing its 'GFCI Protected' marking. Replacement receptacle that does not match the circuit's rating or configuration. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 406.4: Food court and transit waiting-area floor receptacles now need GFCI, a CO/ALR replacement on aluminum wire can skip tamper-resistant, and a replacement must provide GFPE wherever GFPE is now required. GFCI now covers 125-volt, 15- and 20-amp floor receptacles in food courts and airport, bus and train waiting areas that allow food or drink (406.4(G)(2)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Replacing a receptacle — the replacement must meet today's rules for that location
x: Section 406.4(D) sets the rules for swapping an existing receptacle. The replacement is not grandfathered: where today's code requires GFCI, AFCI, tamper-resistant, or weather-resistant protection at that location, the replacement must provide it. • Ground in the box — 406.4(D)(1): if a grounding means exists in the enclosure, or an equipment grounding conductor is run under 250.130(C), the replacement must be a grounding-type receptacle, connected to that ground. • No ground in the box — 406.4(D)(2): exactly three paths are permitted. (a) Another non-grounding-type receptacle. (b) A GFCI-type receptacle marked "No Equipment Ground." (c) A grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI, marked "GFCI Protected" and "No Equipment Ground." • The protection family rides along: GFCI where required (D)(3), AFCI where 210.12 requires it (D)(4), tamper-resistant where 406.12 requires it (D)(5), weather-resistant where required (D)(6). An automatically controlled receptacle is replaced with an equivalently controlled one (D)(7). A plain grounding receptacle on an ungrounded circuit, left unmarked, is never one of the paths. A replacement is the one moment an old installation gets touched, so the code uses it to close the gaps that hurt people: ground-fault protection where water is present, arc protection on bedroom circuits, shutters where children push objects into slots. The marking rules exist because a three-prong face on an ungrounded circuit lies to the next person. Plug-in testers, surge strips, and metal-cased tools all assume that ground pin is real. Service call in a 1962 Orlando ranch: the bathroom receptacle by the sink is dead, the box has no equipment ground, and the panel is an older one with no GFCI or AFCI protection at the breaker. Test first — no ground. The legal swap is a GFCI-type receptacle marked "No Equipment Ground," which also gives that location the GFCI protection today's code requires there. Apply the marking before you leave and photograph it for the job record. On Sharma's own newer work the picture flips: protection lives at the dual-function breaker (S-07), so a replacement on that circuit normally stays a standard tamper-resistant device. S-07 note: on new Sharma work the GFCI/AFCI protection lives at the DFN breaker, so a replacement on a Sharma DFN circuit normally keeps a standard TR device. On older panels without that protection, 406.4(D) is what forces the upgrade at the device. The trap answer: "The old receptacle was three-prong, so a standard three-prong replacement is fine." If there is no equipment ground in the box, that device is not on the list. The permitted paths are a non-grounding replacement, a marked GFCI replacement, or a grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI and marked. And a GFCI does not create a ground — it protects people, and the device has to say so. Standard grounding-type receptacle installed on an ungrounded circuit, unmarked — not a permitted 406.4(D)(2) path. GFCI-type replacement in a no-ground box without the "No Equipment Ground" marking (406.4(D)(2)(b)). Grounding-type receptacle fed through a GFCI but missing the "GFCI Protected" and "No Equipment Ground" markings (406.4(D)(2)(c)). Replacement at a bath or kitchen location without the GFCI protection current code requires (406.4(D)(3)). Neutral jumpered to the ground terminal — a bootleg ground — to make a tester read "grounded." NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 406.4(D)(3): Substantiation was provided to that will require ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) receptacles to be listed per 406.4(D)(3). • 406.4(D)(8): Substantiation has been provided to to require ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) to be provided for replacement receptacles that require GFPE protection by current Code requirements elsewhere in the NEC FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Receptacle assemblies in countertops and work surfaces — listed for the surface
x: A receptacle assembly installed in a countertop surface has to be listed for countertop applications — an ordinary receptacle in a cut-in box does not become countertop equipment by being set into the surface. • Where the assembly is required to provide GFCI protection under 210.8, it is permitted to be a GFCI receptacle assembly listed for countertop applications. • Section 406.5(F) applies the same listing rule to receptacle assemblies in work surfaces. • Whether a receptacle may sit face-up in that surface at all is the next rule, 406.5(G): face-up is allowed only for assemblies listed for countertop or work surface use, and never in the area below a sink. The listing is the point: a countertop assembly is tested for the spills, heat and cleaning that a countertop actually sees. A countertop is a wet work surface. Liquids spill, pots overflow, and crumbs and metal utensils sit on it all day. An ordinary receptacle face set into that surface collects whatever lands on it, straight into the slots. A listed countertop assembly is built and tested for that exposure — sealed, spill-shedding, and made to be cleaned. On a Winter Park kitchen island, the plan shows one receptacle in the island top and one on the cabinet side. The one in the top goes on the material list as a listed pop-up countertop assembly — the GFCI version, because kitchen countertop receptacles need GFCI protection under 210.8. The side receptacle is an ordinary tamper-resistant duplex in the cabinet side; it is not in the surface, so 406.5(E) does not govern it. Do not let the counter fabricator cut a hole sized for a standard duplex in the stone. The trap answer is 'any receptacle can go in the countertop as long as it is GFCI protected.' GFCI protection and countertop listing are different requirements — the assembly must be listed for countertop applications. The reverse trap is 'face-up receptacles are banned everywhere': a listed countertop assembly may sit face-up, just never in the area below a sink. Standard duplex receptacle cut into a quartz island top. Desk or grommet outlet assembly used in a kitchen counter — not listed for countertop applications. Countertop assembly without GFCI protection where 210.8 requires it. Face-up receptacle installed in the counter area below the sink. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Face-up receptacles in countertops — the prohibition is 406.5(G)
x: 406.5(G) carries the face-up rule for receptacles in countertops and work surfaces. • (G)(1): a receptacle may not be installed in a face-up position in or on a countertop or work surface unless it is listed for countertop or work surface applications. • (G)(2): a receptacle may not be installed face-up in the area below a sink at all — the listed-assembly exception does not apply there. • The hazard is the position itself: a face-up device collects spills, crumbs and liquids directly into its face. • The listing rule for the receptacle assemblies made for these surfaces is at 406.5(E) and (F), covered on the previous page. A face-up receptacle is a shallow cup wired to power. Coffee, dishwater and cleaning spray fall straight into the slots, and crumbs and dropped utensils land across the contacts. Below a sink it is worse: a slow plumbing leak can drip into the device for weeks before anyone opens the cabinet and notices. The listing requirement, and the flat ban below a sink, keep liquid and debris out of live parts. On a Marion Oaks kitchen, the island is 8 ft long with the sink at one end. The plan's island receptacle cannot be a standard duplex cut face-up into the stone — it is not listed for countertop use. The fixes: a listed pop-up assembly in the counter away from the sink, a receptacle on the side of the cabinet, or one on the wall at the backsplash. Nothing goes face-up in the area below the sink, listed or not. The trap is 'listed means anywhere.' A listed pop-up assembly is legal face-up in the counter under (G)(1), but (G)(2) bans every face-up receptacle in the area below a sink — no exception, listed or not. The second trap: GFCI protection does not rescue a standard duplex cut face-up into a counter. Protection is not listing. Standard duplex cut face-up into an island countertop; the device is not listed for countertop applications — 406.5(G)(1). Listed pop-up assembly set face-up in the counter area below the sink — 406.5(G)(2) allows no exception there. Face-up countertop receptacle defended as 'GFCI protected' — protection is not listing, 406.5(G)(1). Receptacle face-up in a work surface using an assembly listed for wall use only. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Receptacles in damp locations
x: Section 406.9(A) covers receptacles in damp locations — places that are protected from direct weather but can be damp, such as a covered porch or a carport. Damp is the middle category: not dry indoors, not taking direct rain. • The receptacle must be weather-resistant (WR) type. On houses and light commercial work that means the 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V devices — the same WR devices 406.9(B) requires in wet locations. • The enclosure must keep moisture out of the wiring connections when no plug is inserted. A cover that is weatherproof when the plug is out — the flip lid — is the usual way this is met. • The cover does not have to stay weatherproof while a cord is plugged in. The in-use (bubble) cover belongs to the wet-location rule, 406.9(B). Damp air, condensation and wind-blown mist corrode contacts and creep across damp surfaces inside a box. A receptacle that is not weather-resistant loses contact pressure and insulation resistance after a few Florida summers, and an enclosure that lets moisture sit on the connections does the same damage from outside. The rule keeps the damp away from the device and its wiring connections. Covered lanai on a Florida home: the receptacles sit under the roof, but afternoon storms blow mist across them — that is damp, not dry. Fit WR receptacles and flip-lid covers that close weatherproof with nothing plugged in. Look up before you decide: if the device can get rained on with the cover open or closed — past the roof drip line, or under a leaking gutter — treat it as wet, not damp, and use the 406.9(B) arrangement: a WR receptacle plus a listed extra-duty in-use cover. When in doubt, install the wet-location setup — it satisfies the damp case too. The trap is calling a covered porch a dry location. Covered and protected from direct rain is the definition of a damp location, and the receptacle still has to be WR type with a cover that is weatherproof when the plug is out. The other wrong pick is the bubble cover: damp locations do not require an in-use cover — that requirement is 406.9(B), the wet rule. Standard (non-WR) receptacle installed on a covered porch or in a carport. No cover, or a cover that is not weatherproof with the plug removed, so moisture sits in the box. Receptacle past the roof drip line treated as damp — it takes direct rain and needs the wet-location in-use cover. Indoor cover plate on a damp-location box, or the gasket missing and the cover hanging open. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Receptacles in wet locations — in-use covers and weather-resistant devices
x: Section 406.9(B) covers receptacles in wet locations — places where water can reach the device whether or not something is plugged in. Two parts work together: • The enclosure must stay weatherproof while a plug is inserted and the cord is in use. That is the bubble, or in-use, cover: protection with the plug IN, not just with the cover closed. • 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V receptacles in wet locations must be weather-resistant (WR) type. An unattended wet-location receptacle, such as one on a house exterior, needs that in-use protection; the rule has specific treatment for receptacles that are attended while in use. Two details decide inspections here. First, the in-use cover (the outlet box hood) must be listed and identified as extra duty — the heavier hinged cover — where 406.9(B)(1) requires it; a light flip lid is a damp-location part, not a wet-location one. Second, the WR requirement in this section reaches the 15 A and 20 A, 125 V and 250 V receptacles a house and a light commercial job actually use; larger pin-and-sleeve and locking devices follow their own listing for the location. An ordinary receptacle outdoors corrodes: springs and contacts green up, resistance rises, and the device heats or fails — often with a pump or charger plugged in and nobody watching. The WR device is built with corrosion-resistant parts and UV-stable plastics, and the in-use cover keeps driven rain out of the connection while it is actually working, which is when it matters most. Stock both parts on the truck: a WR receptacle and an extra-duty in-use cover. A flat flip lid on an exterior receptacle that runs a pump, a charger, or landscape equipment is a correction waiting to happen. Seat the cover gasket fully and route the cord out the bottom notch so the cover can close. On a Florida exterior, assume wet until proven damp: afternoon storms drive rain sideways under most soffits, so the lanai receptacle by the pool equipment gets the WR device and the bubble cover even when the plan just says 'exterior.' Florida note: afternoon rain and irrigation spray make most Florida exterior receptacles wet locations in practice, whatever the plan calls them. Default to WR + in-use cover outside. The trap swaps the two covers. A flip lid is weatherproof only with the plug out — that is the damp-location rule in 406.9(A). A wet location demands weatherproof with the plug inserted, the in-use cover, and the heavy extra-duty version where 406.9(B)(1) applies. Picking 'flip lid' for a wet location is the classic wrong answer — and WR alone does not fix it: the device and the cover are separate requirements. Flat flip-lid cover on an exterior receptacle in a wet location — weatherproof only with the plug out. Standard (non-WR) receptacle installed outdoors; no WR marking on the face. In-use cover not extra duty where 406.9(B)(1) requires it, or gasket not seated so the cover cannot close. Cord routed out the side of the bubble cover so the lid stands open in the rain. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: No receptacles inside the tub or shower zone
x: Section 406.9(C) keeps receptacles out of the zone directly inside and immediately around a bathtub or shower stall. • The zone measures 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the bathtub rim or the shower stall threshold. • No receptacle may be installed within that zone. GFCI protection does not change the answer — this is a location rule. • The receptacle the basin requires still has to be provided; it just has to land outside the zone. The rule exists because a person in water is in the worst possible position to contact a device or a cord connected to it. Water, bare skin, and a grounded tub or drain make the person in the tub the best conductor in the room. A receptacle inside the zone puts a device and its cord within reach of a wet hand — the hair dryer cord draped toward the water is the classic case. No protective device buys what distance buys, so the Code keeps the receptacle out of reach of the water entirely. On layout, mark the zone on the floor plan before you place bath receptacles, not at trim. Vanity receptacles belong outside the zone even when the counter runs close to the tub. If the only wall space is inside the zone, move the discussion to the builder before rough-in, not to the inspector at final. On a tight Florida production bath — a tub-and-shower combo beside a long vanity — measure both 3 ft rules before the box is nailed up: the basin receptacle has to be within reach of the basin and still clear of the zone measured from the tub rim. The trap answer is “it is GFCI protected, so it can sit by the tub.” Section 406.9(C) is a location rule, not a protection rule: in the 2020 Code no receptacle is permitted inside the zone at all, GFCI or not. Protection never cures a prohibited location — the device has to move, not get a better breaker. Receptacle installed inside the tub/shower zone, within 3 ft horizontally of the tub rim. Zone measured from the faucet or the tub center instead of the top of the rim or threshold. Vanity receptacle landed in the zone because the counter ran long — never re-measured at rough-in. Receptacle added inside the zone at trim for a bidet seat or towel warmer without checking 406.9(C). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 406.9(C): Clarified receptacle restrictions in and around bathtubs and showers in Section 406.9(C). A new Exception #4 was added to allow single receptacles within 36" of the tub or shower with limitations. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Tamper-resistant receptacles in dwellings and other listed occupancies
x: Section 406.12 requires tamper-resistant receptacles in dwelling units and in a list of other occupancies where children are present, such as guest rooms, childcare and preschool areas, dormitories, and certain medical and office waiting areas. A TR receptacle has internal shutters that only open when both blades of a plug go in together, so a key or paperclip pushed into one slot does not reach a live contact. The requirement applies at the receptacle locations the article covers, generally those at normal reachable height rather than the listed exceptions such as receptacles high above the floor or inside a luminaire. The exceptions matter on service work. The TR requirement does not reach: • Receptacles located more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor • Receptacles that are part of a luminaire or an appliance • A single receptacle for one appliance, or a duplex for two, in the dedicated space for an appliance that is not easily moved in normal use • Nongrounding-type replacements installed under 406.4(D) where the box has no grounding means Everything else at normal device height in the occupancies this section lists is TR — when in doubt, the TR device is the answer. Small children explore with whatever is in their hand — a key, a paperclip, a hairpin. Pushed into one slot of an ordinary receptacle, that metal reaches a live contact and the child becomes the path to ground. The shutters in a TR receptacle stay closed unless both plug blades press in together, so a single object in one slot touches nothing live. The rule puts that protection everywhere children live, sleep, wait, or are cared for. On a Sharma trim-out in a new Ocala single-family home, every receptacle at normal device height gets a TR device — bedrooms, living areas, kitchen, halls. Protection comes from the dual-function breaker in the Siemens panel (S-07), so the devices are plain TR receptacles, not GFCI receptacles. Two spots on that job are not TR: the single receptacle behind the refrigerator, sitting in its dedicated appliance space, and a receptacle mounted more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor for a wall-mounted TV. On a service call, a TR receptacle with a failed shutter is replaced with another TR device (406.4(D)) — never with a standard receptacle just because it was on the truck. S-07 pairs with this page: the standard Sharma dwelling device is a TR receptacle, with GFCI/AFCI protection supplied by the DFN breaker rather than by a GFCI receptacle. The trap answer is that TR receptacles are only required in nurseries and children's bedrooms. 406.12 covers dwelling units in all the areas 210.52 specifies, plus the other listed occupancies. The second trap is reading the height exception as 5 ft — the exception starts at more than 5-1/2 ft above the floor. Standard (non-TR) receptacle installed in a dwelling bedroom — 406.12 requires tamper-resistant devices. Damaged TR receptacle replaced with a standard device on a service call. Non-TR receptacles in a childcare facility playroom. Receptacle claimed under the height exception but measured at 5 ft above the floor, not more than 5-1/2 ft. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 406.12: The tamper-resistant (TR) list grew to ten location groups, adding boathouses, fitness centers, group homes, rehab facilities, nursing homes, foster care, psychiatric hospitals and farm buildings open to the public. Item (1) now lists boathouses, mobile homes and manufactured homes by name, along with dwelling units and their garages, outbuildings and common areas. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards — article intro
x: Article 408 covers the boards themselves: switchboards, switchgear, and the panelboards Sharma installs on nearly every job. For residential and light commercial work, the live parts of this article are: • The circuit directory: every circuit identified specifically at the board, spares marked as spares (408.4(A)). • Identification of the source of supply where a board is fed from another board (408.4(B)). • A short-circuit current rating at least equal to the available fault current (408.6). • Unused openings closed with closures listed for the enclosure (408.7). • Overcurrent protection of the panelboard itself, at no more than the panelboard's rating (408.36). • One grounded (neutral) conductor per terminal (408.41). • Breakers of the type listed for the panel they sit in. The industrial switchboard sections matter on larger commercial gear; the directory and listing rules matter everywhere. The panelboard is where every circuit in the building starts, and where fault energy is highest. A board protected above its bus rating, fitted with breakers it was never listed for, or left with open spaces becomes the failure point itself. The directory rules exist because the next person — a servicer, a firefighter, a homeowner at midnight — has to kill the right circuit fast, and a wrong label sends them to the wrong breaker. Treat the panel as a document, not just a box: directory filled in, circuits identified at every disconnect, unused openings closed, and only listed breakers installed. An inspector can fail a beautiful rough-in on a blank directory. On a Sharma trim, that means a new Siemens board (S-02) with the directory written from the actual schedule and checked circuit by circuit, spares marked 'SPARE,' and every open space closed with the Siemens filler listed for that panel. In an existing Square D panel, only Square D breakers listed for that panel go in (S-03). And check the protection: a 100 A panelboard never sits behind a 200 A breaker just because the feeder is big (408.36). S-02: all new Sharma gear is Siemens. S-03: in an existing Square D panel, install Square D breakers listed for that panel — never mix brands to fill a space. The trap answer: 'Any breaker that snaps into the panel is fine.' It is not. A breaker must be listed for that panelboard — a foreign breaker that physically fits still voids the listing and draws a correction. The companion trap: protecting a 100 A panelboard with a 200 A breaker because the feeder conductors are large. Section 408.36 protects the bus, not the wire. Circuit directory blank, generic ('lights,' 'plugs'), or not updated after a circuit change (408.4(A)). Unused breaker opening left open, or closed with tape instead of a listed filler plate (408.7). Breaker of another brand installed in the panel — not listed for that panelboard. 100 A panelboard protected by a 200 A overcurrent device (408.36). Panelboard SCCR below the available fault current at a commercial service (408.6). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 408.38: The enclosure rule now ties to fault current: once available fault current passes 10,000 amps, the panelboard and its enclosure have to be evaluated as a matched combination. If available fault current tops 10,000 amps, the interior and its enclosure need to be evaluated as one combination. • 408.9: Two paths for a replacement panelboard in an existing enclosure: listed for that enclosure keeps its rating; if not, it's identified for the use up to 10,000 amps available fault current, field labeled above. Listed for that specific enclosure, by catalog number or dimensions? The replacement keeps its short-circuit current rating (408.9(A)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The circuit directory — specific, on site, and kept current
x: Section 408.4(A) requires a circuit directory at every panelboard, and identification specific enough to tell the circuits apart: • Every circuit, and every circuit modification, is legibly identified with a clear, specific description of its purpose or use — the actual load, in the actual building. • Generic words that fit any house — "plugs," "lights," "bedroom" — do not meet the rule. Neither does a directory copied from the plan or from another job. • Spare positions are identified as spares. • The directory is updated whenever circuits are added, moved, or changed. The directory lives at the board, so the next person who opens the panel can kill the right circuit without guessing. Troubleshooting and lockout both start at the directory. A wrong or vague label sends a tech to kill "Kitchen" while the water heater stays live, or leaves a crew guessing which breaker feeds the circuit they are about to touch. A specific directory is a safety device that costs nothing but ten honest minutes at trim. Fill the directory at trim, from the actual panel schedule, and have the person who wired the house verify it circuit by circuit with a tester or by switching loads on and off. A directory copied from the plan without field verification is how "Kitchen" ends up feeding the water heater. Sharma standard: neat, specific, and correct — "NE bedroom receptacles," not "BR." Sharma note: the directory is part of the finished product the builder sees. Neat, specific, and correct — 'NE bedroom receptacles,' not 'BR.' The trap: copying the directory from the plan set, or from the identical house next door. The exam — and the inspector — want the directory that describes this building's circuits as actually wired and verified. "Lights" and "plugs" are the classic wrong answers: they identify nothing, and they distinguish nothing. No circuit directory provided at the panelboard (408.4(A)). Directory entries generic — "plugs," "lights" — the circuits cannot be distinguished from one another. Spare breaker positions not identified as spares. Directory not updated after circuits were added or moved. Directory written for a different building — labels do not match the loads actually fed. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 408.4(A): Circuit directory rules became a six-part checklist that now requires explaining any abbreviations or symbols. In buildings other than one- and two-family homes, feeder-fed panels must also show where their source physically sits. Feeder-supplied panels outside one- and two-family dwellings must name the equipment feeding them and where it physically is (408.4(B)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Identification of the source of supply
x: Section 408.4(B) addresses panelboards supplied by a feeder: the board must be marked to identify where its supply comes from when that source is in a different location or is not obvious, so that a person standing at the panel can find the disconnect that kills it. • The source marking goes at the feeder-supplied panelboard itself. • The directory rules in 408.4(A) work the other direction: they identify what each circuit in the board feeds. • Disconnects and circuits are likewise marked for their purpose where it is not self-evident. The theme of the whole part is that nobody should have to guess what feeds what. The dangerous panel is the live one nobody can kill. A sub-panel fed from another building, a second service, or a generator can stay energized after the main in front of you is opened — the classic surprise during service work and firefighting. A source marking at the board turns a hunt through the building into one trip to the right disconnect. On a sub-panel, label the feeder source (for example, “Fed from Main Panel, Garage”) at the sub-panel and label the feeder breaker at the source panel. Do the same for any panel fed from a generator or a second service, and make the two labels agree with each other. On a Florida house the everyday case is the detached garage or pool-house sub-panel: five minutes at trim decides whether the next tech kills the right breaker on the first try. The trap is marking the circuit directory and calling the panel identified. The directory in 408.4(A) says what each circuit feeds; 408.4(B) answers the other direction — what feeds this panel, and where that source sits. A perfect directory on a feeder-fed board with no source marking still leaves the next person guessing which building, main, or generator keeps it live. Feeder-fed panelboard with no identification of its source of supply. Sub-panel in a detached building, with nothing naming the panel or building that feeds it. Source labels at the two ends disagree — the sub-panel names a source the main panel does not. Panel fed from a generator or second service, not marked to show the other source. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 408.4: Circuit directory rules became a six-part checklist that now requires explaining any abbreviations or symbols. In buildings other than one- and two-family homes, feeder-fed panels must also show where their source physically sits. Feeder-supplied panels outside one- and two-family dwellings must name the equipment feeding them and where it physically is (408.4(B)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The equipment's short-circuit current rating must cover the available fault current
x: Section 408.6 requires switchboards, switchgear, and panelboards to have a short-circuit current rating (SCCR) at least equal to the available fault current where they are installed. A panel that matches the job on volts and amps can still be the wrong panel if its SCCR is below the fault current the service can deliver into a short. • The SCCR is marked on the equipment. The available fault current comes from the utility or the design documents — it is not a number you estimate in the field. • At service equipment in other than dwelling units, the available fault current and the date of the calculation must be field-marked on the equipment (110.24). • The breakers inside the gear carry interrupting ratings of their own (110.9). The gear's SCCR and the devices' interrupting ratings both have to cover the same fault current. This requirement was added in the 2020 edition, which is why older change-out habits never asked the question. A bolted fault lets the service deliver thousands of amps in a fraction of a cycle. Gear whose SCCR is below that current can rupture, vent molten metal, or blow its doors instead of riding through the fault until the overcurrent device clears it. The rating is what stands between a cleared fault and an exploding enclosure. Small commercial service change in Orlando: the utility letter puts the available fault current at 22,000 A at the new 400 A service. The value panel on the truck is marked 10 kA SCCR — it cannot go in, even though its bus rating and voltage match. Per S-02 the replacement gear is Siemens, selected with an SCCR of 22 kA or higher, and both numbers — 22,000 A available and the gear's marked SCCR — go in the job file before the gear is ordered. If the fault current is unknown, that is an engineering question for Mike, not a field estimate. S-02 pairs with this page: new Sharma gear is Siemens, and the SCCR check is part of selecting it, not an afterthought at inspection. The trap answer reads the panel's ampere rating as its fault rating: 'a 200 A panel on a 200 A service handles the fault.' Bus amps and SCCR are different numbers. A 200 A panel marked 10 kA SCCR still fails on a service that can deliver 22,000 A of fault current. Panelboard installed where the available fault current exceeds its marked SCCR (408.6). Gear ordered and set before the available fault current was obtained from the utility. No fault current documented in the job file — nothing to compare the SCCR against. Available fault current not marked at the service equipment, or the marking left out of date after a utility change (110.24). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Unused openings must be closed
x: Section 408.7 requires unused openings in a panelboard, switchboard or switchgear to be closed with closures that give protection substantially equal to the wall of the enclosure. • A spare breaker space with no breaker in it is an unused opening: it takes the manufacturer's listed filler plate or blank. • An unused knockout in the enclosure wall is the same problem in a smaller hole: close it with a listed knockout closure. • Tape is not a closure. Neither are cardboard, foam, or a near-fit plate from another brand. An open space is an exposed live-part opening, a dust and vermin path, and an automatic correction on inspection. The bus behind the deadfront stays live even where no breaker is installed. An open space lets fingers, a dropped screwdriver or a curious kid reach it, and it lets dust and roaches build up on the bus until tracking and a short do the rest. A closure as strong as the enclosure wall keeps the box a box. Keep listed filler plates for the panel brand on the trim truck. Before final, open every panel, run a finger check for open spaces, blank plates, and missing knock-out closures, and close them with the manufacturer's part. On a Sharma job the panel is Siemens, so the fillers on the truck are Siemens fillers: a near-fit plate from another brand is a correction waiting to happen (S-02/S-03). S-02/S-03 apply to the closure as well: use the filler listed for that panel, not a near-fit from another brand. The trap is treating an empty breaker space as harmless because nothing is connected to it. The opening itself is the violation: the live bus stab sits right behind it. 'We will add a breaker later' does not close the hole today. Spare breaker space left open with no filler plate: live bus exposed behind the deadfront. Duct tape or cardboard over an unused opening. Neither is a closure. Unused knockout in the side of the panel never closed. Filler plate from a different panel brand forced into the space: not the listed closure for that panel. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The panelboard itself must be protected
x: Section 408.36 requires a panelboard to be protected by an overcurrent device rated no higher than the panelboard's rating, located within the panelboard or at any point ahead of it on the supply side. In plain terms, a 100 A panel may not sit behind a 200 A breaker just because the feeder wires are large. The bus has its own limit and something must enforce it. The exceptions are narrow: • Exception No. 1: service equipment with multiple disconnecting means under 230.71 (the split-bus case); with three or more mains, they may not supply a second bus structure. • Exception No. 2: two main breakers or two sets of fuses on the supply side with a combined rating not over the panelboard rating — and no more than 42 overcurrent devices in the board, counting a 2-pole as two and a 3-pole as three. • Exception No. 3: existing panelboards used as service equipment for an individual residential occupancy. A panelboard supplied from a transformer under 240.21(C) gets its protection on the secondary side — in a separate enclosure ahead of the board, or in the board itself (408.36(B)). Feeder conductors are sized for the load and the run; a panelboard bus is built for its rating and nothing more. Put a 100 A bus behind a 200 A breaker and an overload inside the board can push twice the bus rating through stabs and bus bars that were never built for it — the breaker sits happy while the panel cooks. Section 408.36 makes the board's own rating a ceiling that some device, in the board or ahead of it, must enforce. When you set a sub-panel, check three numbers together: panel bus rating, feeder conductor ampacity, and the breaker feeding it. The smallest applicable limit governs. Record all three on the panel schedule for the office file. Sharma's light-commercial habit: a 100 A Siemens sub-panel gets a 100 A feeder breaker even when the feeder conductors could carry more — the breaker is protecting the bus, not just the wire. The trap: 'the feeder is 200 A wire, so a 200 A breaker ahead of a 100 A panel is fine — the wire is protected.' The wire is; the panelboard is not. Section 408.36 protects the panelboard at its own rating. The reverse trap is calling every split-bus service a violation — the 230.71 multiple-disconnect arrangement is Exception No. 1, not a defect. 100 A main-lug panelboard fed from a 200 A breaker — board protected above its rating (408.36). Replacement main breaker rated higher than the panelboard bus it protects. Two-main exception claimed on a board holding more than 42 overcurrent devices. Transformer-fed panelboard whose only protection is on the primary side (408.36(B)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Each grounded (neutral) conductor gets its own terminal
x: Section 408.41 requires each grounded conductor in a panelboard to terminate in its own individual terminal that is not used for any other conductor, unless the terminal is specifically identified for more than one. • One grounded (neutral) conductor per terminal. Doubling two neutrals under one screw is a classic correction. • The hazard is mechanical: when one circuit is worked on, loosening the shared terminal can open the neutral of a live circuit sharing it. • Equipment grounding conductors follow their own termination rules and the panel's listing; the one-per-terminal discipline on this page is about the grounded conductors. A shared neutral terminal is a single point of failure for two circuits. Back one screw out to move a circuit and the other circuit loses its neutral while it is still hot — on a multiwire branch circuit the loads end up in series across 240 V and electronics burn. Even without that, two conductors under one screw seat unevenly, loosen over time, and heat. At trim, land neutrals one to a screw and torque them; never park a second neutral under a screw 'temporarily.' On a panel change-out — new gear is Siemens per S-02 — budget the time to separate doubled neutrals: an older Florida panel typically hides several, and finding them is part of the job. The directory update in 408.4(A) happens on the same visit. The trap is treating neutrals like grounds: 'two under one screw is fine — the bar is all one piece anyway.' Section 408.41 is written about grounded conductors, one per terminal, and a terminal specifically identified for more than one conductor is the only way out. Doubling neutrals because they land on the same bar is the write-up. Two grounded (neutral) conductors under one terminal screw in the panelboard (408.41). Grounded conductor landed with another conductor in a terminal not identified for more than one conductor (408.41). Doubled neutrals left in place through a panel change-out. Neutral terminal screws backed off or untorqued after circuits were moved during service work. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: A panelboard may not be installed face-up
x: Section 408.43 prohibits installing a panelboard in a face-up position. A load center belongs on a vertical surface with its breakers oriented as the listing intends; a face-up board collects debris and water, and its breakers do not operate or indicate as designed. The rule was added in the 2020 edition and most often matters on custom commercial millwork and unusual equipment layouts, not on a standard house panel. • Legal: the panelboard's front faces a wall — breakers in their listed, vertical orientation. • Banned since 2020: face-up, front pointing at the ceiling. • Still legal under the 2020 book, banned in 2023: face-down, front pointing at the floor — see the edition note. A panelboard is a listed assembly tested in one orientation. Lay it face-up and the gutter becomes a tray: dust, screws, water and whatever the next trade drops all land on live parts and breaker mechanisms. Breakers lying flat also do not trip, reset or read the way their listing assumes. The rule keeps the equipment in the only position it was ever evaluated in. If a plan or a cabinet detail shows a panel lying flat, stop at rough-in and raise it with the builder — the fix is a layout change, not a field workaround. Check orientation on any pre-built equipment package before it is set. On a Sharma commercial job, the millwork detail for a coffee-bar cabinet showed the load center flat under the counter: the cabinet grew a vertical section at rough-in, the panel went on it upright, and the directory (408.4(A)) stayed readable standing in front of it. The trap answer is 'face-up is fine if the cover stays on' — 408.43 bans the position outright, cover or not. The subtler trap is the calendar: face-down is banned only in the 2023 edition. On a 2020 permit a face-down board is bad practice but not a 408.43 violation; on a 2023 permit it fails. Panelboard set face-up in a counter or bench detail (408.43). Panelboard mounted face-down under a platform or ceiling on a 2023 permit (408.43 as amended). Breakers installed sideways in a vertical board so handles do not operate as listed (110.3(B)). Flat-mounted board with debris and water standing in the gutter at rough-in inspection. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 408.43: Panelboards can't be installed facing down now. Added to the 2020 face-up ban, a panelboard's front can point neither at the ceiling nor at the floor. A panelboard can't be mounted face-down, with its front pointing at the floor, such as on the underside of a ceiling or platform. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Industrial control panels — article intro
x: Article 409 covers industrial control panels: the factory- or field-assembled panels that control industrial machinery and equipment. The article sets the rules for the panel's short-circuit current rating (SCCR) marking, supply conductor sizing, and internal wiring and grounding. • The SCCR is the headline item. The panel must be marked with it (409.110), and a panel may not be installed where the available fault current at its supply exceeds the rating marked on it. • Read the label before the panel is set: supply voltage, phases, full-load current, and SCCR all come off the manufacturer's marking. • Supply conductors are sized from the panel's marked ratings, and the panel's grounding follows 409.60. Sharma meets this article on light commercial and equipment work rather than in houses — rooftop equipment, lift stations, and machine controls. A short circuit does not ask permission. If the fault current at a panel is higher than the panel was built and tested to withstand, the failure is not a tripped breaker — it is bus bars tearing loose, contacts welding, and an enclosure coming apart in front of whoever is standing there. The SCCR marking is the panel's tested ceiling, and the available fault current is the number it has to beat. Read the SCCR on the panel label and compare it with the available fault current at its supply before you set the panel. On a light-commercial equipment swap in Orlando, the utility letter put the available fault current at 22 kA. The replacement control panel's label read 10 kA SCCR — that panel does not get set, no matter that its breakers are rated 22 kA; the assembly's marked SCCR is the ceiling. A panel marked 65 kA SCCR clears the same supply with room to spare. If the panel has no SCCR marking or the fault current is unknown, stop and take it to Mike — that is an engineering check, not a field guess. The trap answer is the breaker's interrupting rating: 'The main breaker is rated 22 kA, so the panel is good for 22 kA.' The breaker's AIC is one component's rating. The panel's SCCR is the tested rating of the whole assembly — the weakest part sets it — and 409.110 makes the marked SCCR the number the installation is judged against. Industrial control panel installed where the available fault current exceeds the SCCR marked on the panel (409.110). Panel set with a missing or illegible SCCR marking — the ceiling was never checked. Field modifications inside a listed panel that void its listing and its SCCR. On a job permitted under the NEC 2023, an industrial control panel with no surge protection (409.70). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 409.60: Section 409.60 for industrial control panels was restructured, creating (A) Grounding and (B) Bonding. • 409.70: New Section 409.70 has been added requiring surge protection for industrial control panels. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Industrial control panels — marking and short-circuit current rating (409.110)
x: Section 409.110 requires every industrial control panel to be marked with its electrical ratings, the way a motor carries a nameplate: • The manufacturer's name or trademark. • Input voltage and number of phases. • Full-load current. • The short-circuit current rating — the SCCR. The SCCR is a ceiling, not a suggestion: the panel may not be installed where the available fault current at its supply exceeds the marked rating. A panel that matches the job on voltage and amps can still be the wrong panel. Read the label before the panel is set. A missing or illegible SCCR is a stop-and-ask, not a guess. Switchboards and panelboards carry the same idea under 408.6. When a fault hits, a panel has to survive the energy the service can deliver until a breaker clears it. A panel whose SCCR sits below the available fault current can come apart instead of just tripping. The marking rule puts the one number that decides "can this panel live here" on the panel itself, where the installer reads it before the panel is bolted down — not after the fault. Light-commercial equipment swap in Orlando: the utility letter puts the available fault current at the service at 22 kA. The replacement control panel's label reads the right voltage and phases — and SCCR 10 kA. That panel does not get set, even though the breakers inside it are rated 22 kA: the assembly's marked SCCR governs, not the highest-rated part inside. Photograph the label with the rest of the nameplates, and if the SCCR comes up short, that is an engineering conversation with the office before the panel is set, not after. The trap answer: "The breakers inside are rated 22 kA, so the panel is good for 22 kA of fault current." No. The panel's rating is the SCCR marked on its label under 409.110. Strong parts inside do not raise the assembly rating — the marked SCCR is the ceiling for the whole panel. Control panel installed where the available fault current exceeds its marked SCCR (409.110). Panel set with the SCCR marking missing or illegible — the rating was never verified. Panel supplied at a voltage or phase arrangement different from its 409.110 marking. Available fault current for the location never obtained or recorded before the panel was set. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Luminaires, lampholders, and lamps — article intro
x: Article 410 covers light fixtures in the broad code sense: luminaires, lampholders, and lamps — where they may be installed, how they are supported, temperature limits near combustible material, and the special zones in bathtubs, showers, and clothes closets. The parts Sharma hits constantly: • The tub and shower zone (410.10(D)): 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or the shower threshold. Inside it, a luminaire must be listed for damp locations, and for wet locations where shower spray hits it. Pendants, hanging fixtures, and ceiling-suspended fans are not permitted in the zone at all. • Clothes closets (410.16): clearances are measured from the closet storage space — 12 in for a surface-mounted enclosed incandescent or LED fixture, 6 in for surface fluorescent and for recessed fixtures. Open-lamp incandescent fixtures and pendants are not permitted at any clearance. • Recessed fixtures: insulation contact and thermal protection (410.116). Fixture listing and its instructions (110.3(B)) do half the work in this article — the box and the spec sheet are part of the code answer. Fixtures make heat inches from the things that burn — clothes on a closet rod, insulation over a recessed can — and they hang over water where people stand wet and barefoot. The zone and clearance rules keep hot lamps off combustibles and keep the wrong fixture types out of reach of a person in a tub. Read the fixture's own listing before you rough the box: weight, temperature rating, damp/wet rating, and closet or shower suitability are all on the label or the cut sheet, not in the field manual. On a Florida master bath, mark the 3 ft by 8 ft zone on the plan at rough-in: the architect's shower light inside it must be the listed wet-location model, and the vanity fixtures sit outside the zone. In the closet, default to an enclosed LED fixture, surface-mounted at 12 in clear of the storage space — never a pendant or an exposed lamp. Sharma bath practice (company practice, not 410): vanity lighting plus the architect's wet-location shower light, with no extra general ceiling light added by habit. Follow the plan; do not add or delete bath lights on your own. The trap: 'A pendant is fine in the closet if it hangs 12 in from the storage space.' Clearance never rescues a banned type — 410.16(B) bars pendant luminaires and open or partially enclosed incandescent lamps in clothes closets outright. The second trap is measuring closet clearances from the wall or the clothes instead of from the storage space the Code defines. Pendant or open-lamp fixture installed in a clothes closet (410.16(B)). Closet fixture closer than 12 in (surface) or 6 in (recessed) to the storage space (410.16(C)). Damp-only fixture installed where shower spray hits it inside the tub/shower zone (410.10(D)). Ceiling-suspended fan installed inside the tub/shower zone (410.10(D)). Fixture installed against its listing instructions — wrong location rating (110.3(B)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 410.184: Cord-connected grow lights on circuits over 150 volts to ground, like 277 volts, now need a listed special-purpose GFCI (SPGFCI). The rule also now spells out which cords trigger it. Grow lights on a circuit over 150 volts to ground, such as 277 volts from a 480Y/277 system, must be protected by a listed SPGFCI. • 410.71: LED fixtures with double-ended (tube-style) lamps and drivers serviceable in place now need the same disconnect fluorescent fixtures already needed. The rule moved from 410.130(G) to 410.71. Indoors outside dwellings, a disconnect is now required on LED luminaires that use double-ended lamps and have field-serviceable drivers (410.71(1)). • 410.2: Determined that ballasts, LED drivers, and lamps should be added into updated Section 410.2 for items not allowed to be reconditioned. • Article 410: A new Part XVII was added to Article 410 to address the increasing use of germicidal luminaires for disinfecting purposes. These products are increasingly being used due to the COVID 19 pandemic and other concerns. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Luminaires in the bathtub and shower zone
x: Section 410.10(D) controls luminaires inside the bathtub and shower zone — the space measured 3 ft horizontally and 8 ft vertically from the top of the tub rim or the shower threshold. • Inside the zone, a luminaire must be listed for damp locations, and for wet locations where it is subject to shower spray. • Some types are not permitted in the zone at all, including hanging luminaires, pendants, and ceiling-suspended fans. • A luminaire outside the zone is not governed by this subsection, even if it is in the same bathroom. A fixture over a tub or inside a shower lives in steam and direct spray, within reach of a wet person standing in water. The listing rules keep water away from the fixture's live parts, and the banned types are the ones that hang down into reach — a pendant a bather can grab, or a fan hanging over the water. Mark the zone on the plan at rough-in and check every bath fixture against it, including the shower light and any fan/light combo. Confirm the damp or wet marking on the fixture label matches where it actually sits, and keep the label information in the job file. Watch the fan/light combo centered over a tub-shower: the fan makes the fixture a ceiling-suspended fan — a type the zone prohibits — even when its light half is wet-listed. The whole fixture has to be a type the zone allows, in the listing the location requires. Sharma note: the architect's specified shower light is the fixture of record — install the listed wet-location model specified, not a damp-only substitute from stock. The trap is answering from the room instead of from the zone: “the whole bathroom needs wet-listed fixtures,” or the reverse, “the pendant is wet-listed, so it may hang over the tub.” Location decides first. Outside the zone, this subsection does not apply at all; inside it, a prohibited type stays prohibited no matter what its listing says. Pendant or hanging luminaire installed over the tub, inside the zone. Damp-location luminaire installed where shower spray reaches it — a wet-location listing is required. Ceiling-suspended fan, or fan/light combo, installed over a tub-shower inside the zone. Fixture listing label not available at inspection, so the damp or wet rating could not be verified. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Luminaires in clothes closets — permitted types and clearances
x: Section 410.16 controls what may light a clothes closet and how far it must sit from the closet storage space — the volume defined in 410.2: • Storage space: 24 inches out from the side and back walls, from the floor up to 6 feet or the highest clothes-hanging rod; then 12 inches out from the walls, or the width of the shelf if greater, from there up to the ceiling. • Permitted [410.16(A)]: surface-mounted or recessed incandescent or LED luminaires with a completely enclosed light source; surface-mounted or recessed fluorescent luminaires; and surface-mounted fluorescent or LED luminaires identified as suitable for installation within the closet storage space. • Not permitted [410.16(B)]: incandescent luminaires with open or partially enclosed lamps, and pendant luminaires or lampholders. • Minimum clearances from the nearest point of the storage space [410.16(C)]: 12 inches for a surface-mounted incandescent or LED luminaire with a completely enclosed light source, on the ceiling or the wall above the door; 6 inches for a surface-mounted fluorescent in the same positions; 6 inches for a recessed incandescent or LED with a completely enclosed light source; and 6 inches for a recessed fluorescent. • A surface-mounted fluorescent or LED luminaire identified for use within the closet storage space may be installed inside the storage space itself [410.16(C)(5)]. A closet is a box full of fuel: clothes, blankets, and boxes stacked toward the ceiling. A hot or bare lamp touching fabric, or a broken lamp dropping hot parts onto clothes, starts a fire behind a closed door where nobody sees it. The clearances keep the heat off the stored material, and the enclosed-source rule keeps lamp parts off it too. Measure the clearance from the storage space, not from the wall or the clothes — that 24-inch and 12-inch volume exists on paper even in an empty closet. The Sharma default is an enclosed LED fixture: surface-mounted on the ceiling at 12 inches clear of the storage space, or recessed at 6 inches, and never a pendant or an exposed lamp in a closet. Check the shelf before placing the fixture: a shelf wider than 12 inches pushes the top of the storage space out with it. The trap answer measures the 12 inches from the wall. Clearances run from the nearest point of the closet storage space — the paper volume in 410.2 — whether or not clothes are hanging there yet. Second trap pick: a pendant is fine if its lamp is enclosed. It is not; pendants are prohibited outright. Pendant luminaire or bare lampholder in a clothes closet (410.16(B)). Surface-mounted LED fixture 8 in. from the storage space where 12 in. is the minimum (410.16(C)). Open-lamp incandescent fixture mounted over the closet shelf. Clearance measured from the wall instead of from the 410.2 storage space. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Recessed luminaires — insulation contact and thermal protection
x: Section 410.116 covers recessed luminaires — the cans and downlights that sit inside ceilings: • Combustible clearance — 410.116(A)(1): a fixture not identified for insulation contact keeps its recessed parts at least 1/2 in from combustible material. Points of support and the trim at the ceiling opening may touch. • Insulation clearance — 410.116(A)(2): unless the fixture is Type IC, thermal insulation may not be installed above the fixture or within 3 in of its enclosure, wiring compartment, ballast, transformer, LED driver, or power supply. • Type IC fixtures are identified for direct contact with insulation, and may touch insulation and combustible material. • Thermal protection: recessed fixtures are thermally protected — a sensor shuts the fixture down if it overheats — except where the fixture is identified as inherently protected. The IC rating belongs to the specific fixture and is printed on its label. It is never a property of recessed fixtures in general. A recessed can is a heat source sealed inside a wood-framed ceiling. Insulation that belongs everywhere else in a Florida attic traps that heat against framing and wiring. The clearances keep an air path around a non-IC fixture, and thermal protection is the backstop that kills the light before the heat does damage. An IC rating moves the protection into the fixture itself, so the ceiling can be insulated tight without cooking the can. Florida attic, blown insulation going in over a finished ceiling: read every housing label at rough-in, before the ceiling closes. Type IC cans can be buried. A non-IC can needs its 3 in of clear air and 1/2 in from combustibles — in blown insulation that means a dam or cover that survives the insulation crew. Flag it at rough-in, while the fix is still cheap, not after the blower truck leaves. The trap: "All modern LED cans are IC rated, so insulation can touch any of them." The IC rating belongs to the specific fixture and is printed on its label — plenty of cans are non-IC. The reverse trap cuts the other way: a non-IC fixture is not banned from an insulated ceiling. It just has to keep its clearances. Non-IC recessed fixture buried in blown insulation — no 3 in clearance (410.116(A)(2)). Recessed parts of a non-IC fixture against combustible framing — less than 1/2 in clearance (410.116(A)(1)). Fixture with no Type IC marking installed in direct contact with insulation. Thermal protection defeated or bypassed after repeated shutoffs. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Lighting systems operating at 30 volts or less — article intro
x: Article 411 covers lighting systems operating at 30 volts AC or 60 volts DC or less — and only 15 volts AC or 30 volts DC where contact with water is likely. It covers the listed system as a package: the power supply, the fixtures, and the secondary wiring between them. • Listed system: the system is installed as a listed assembly — a complete listed system, or one assembled from listed parts (411.4). Loose parts gathered in the field do not make an Article 411 system. • Power supply: the listed power source limits the secondary circuit — the article caps secondary output at 25 amperes. • Secondary wiring: the conductors on the load side of the power supply follow Article 411's own rules, not ordinary branch-circuit wiring rules. • Locations: bare-conductor systems are not concealed and do not run through walls, floors or ceilings unless the specific listed system permits it, and the secondary wiring stays out of the pool zone — not within 10 ft of pools, spas, fountains or similar locations unless Article 680 permits it (411.5). Sharma meets this article mainly in landscape-style and specialty accent lighting inside a project. Thirty volts sounds harmless, so these systems get treated like doorbell wire. But a secondary that can deliver up to 25 amperes will heat a bad splice or an undersized conductor until something chars. The listing is the protection: the power supply, cable and fixtures were tested together, with the supply limiting what a fault can draw. Field-assembled parts have no tested limit. A Lake Nona lanai job: the owner wants 24 V DC LED accent lighting around a covered patio that sits near the pool. Spec the listed system — the manufacturer's listed driver, cable and fixtures as one family. The driver is rated 100 W at 24 V DC; the tape and puck runs total 72 W, inside the rating. Route the secondary so the nearest fixture stays 12 ft from the pool water — outside the 10 ft limit in 411.5 — and keep the driver accessible in the garage, not buried in the soffit. The trap answer is '30 volts or less means wire it like a doorbell — any parts, any method.' An Article 411 system is a listed system: a random driver and a roll of tape bought online is not one, no matter how low the voltage. The second trap is the pool: within 10 ft of the water the location rules bite, and where contact with water is likely the ceiling drops to 15 volts AC or 30 volts DC.
