Unlisted power supply and tape installed as a 'system' — no listing for the assembly (411.4). Secondary conductors concealed in the wall with no listed system permitting it (411.5). Low-voltage fixtures within 10 ft of pool water with no Article 680 basis (411.5). Secondary splices buried in mulch or underground where the listing does not allow them. Power supply inaccessible — sealed above a closed soffit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Low-voltage lighting systems — where they may and may not go (Article 411)
x: Article 411 covers lighting systems operating at not more than 30 volts AC or 60 volts DC (411.1) — the listed low-voltage systems behind a lot of LED tape, under-cabinet, and accent work. Section 411.4 itself is the listing rule: • The system must be listed as a complete system, or assembled from listed parts. A loose power supply and a roll of tape bought online is not an Article 411 system. • The power source limits the secondary circuit: the article caps secondary output at 25 amperes. • Where contact with water is likely, the limits drop to 15 volts AC or 30 volts DC (411.1). The location limits live in 411.5: • Bare-conductor systems are not concealed and do not run through walls, floors, or ceilings unless the specific listed system permits it. • Secondary wiring is not concealed or extended through a building wall, floor, or ceiling unless it is wired with a Chapter 3 method, or with Class 2 wiring where the power supply is Class 2. • The system stays at least 10 ft from pools, spas, fountains, and similar locations unless Article 680 permits it. Low voltage feels harmless, so it gets installed casually — unlisted drivers buried in walls, bare tape stapled where hands and water reach. The listing rule makes one manufacturer answer for the whole chain: supply, cable, and fixtures tested together. The location limits keep a system nobody thinks of as 'wiring' from being hidden like wiring, or from reaching the pool zone. Spec the listed system — power supply, cable, and fixtures from one listed family — and keep the driver accessible. Inspectors ask whose system it is; 'the homeowner bought it online' is not an answer. On the Lake Nona lanai job the pattern held: a listed 24 V DC driver rated 100 W feeding tape and puck runs totaling 72 W, inside the rating with room to spare, and the secondary routed so the nearest fixture stays 12 ft from the pool water — outside the 10 ft limit in 411.5. The driver went in an accessible spot, not buried behind the tile. The trap is treating 30 volts as 'not real wiring,' so any parts on hand will do. The exam answer is the listing: a complete listed system, or listed parts assembled as a system. A loose online power supply plus unlisted tape fails 411.4 before any location question is even reached — and the 25 A secondary cap and the 10 ft pool clearance still apply to the listed system. Unlisted LED tape and a loose online driver installed as an 'Article 411 system' — no listing, 411.4. Driver buried inside a closed wall or above a sealed ceiling where it cannot be reached for service. Bare-conductor system run concealed through a wall where the listed system does not permit it, 411.5. Low-voltage accent fixtures 6 ft from the pool water with no Article 680 basis, 411.5. Secondary cable extended through an exterior wall in plain cord instead of a Chapter 3 or Class 2 method, 411.5. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Appliances — article intro
x: Article 422 covers appliances: water heaters, dishwashers, disposals, ranges and cooktops, dryers as appliances, space heaters that plug or hard-wire as appliances, and similar equipment. Its working parts: • Branch-circuit sizing from the appliance's marked rating; an individual branch circuit — one appliance only — is the default for the big fixed appliances (422.10). • Overcurrent protection: where the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, the marking governs. An unmarked single non-motor appliance rated over 13.3 A may be protected at up to 150 percent of its rating (422.11(E)). • Storage water heaters of 120 gallons or less: the branch circuit is sized at 125 percent of the nameplate — a continuous load (422.13). • GFCI protection that travels with the appliance, wherever it is installed: dishwashers, sump pumps, vending machines, and the rest of the 422.5(A) list. • A disconnecting means that lets a servicer kill the appliance safely (422.31). Where an appliance is also a motor load or also HVAC equipment, Articles 430 and 440 may govern instead or in addition — check the appliance's own article first. Appliances are the loads that run unattended — a water heater recovering a tank at 3 a.m., a dishwasher cycling while the house is empty. Sized wrong, the circuit cooks slowly inside a wall; serviced without a disconnect, the appliance stays live in the tech's hands. The article ties circuit, protection, and disconnect to the one document that knows the load: the nameplate. For every appliance on a job, settle three things from the nameplate before rough-in is closed: circuit size, cord-and-plug or hard-wired, and where the disconnect will be. The nameplate, not the catalog photo, is the source. Worked example, the standard Florida water heater: 4,500 W at 240 V draws 18.75 A; at 125 percent that is 23.4 A, so it lands on a 30 A circuit with 10 AWG copper. The dishwasher gets its GFCI protection because 422.5 names the appliance — on Sharma work the dual-function breaker supplies it. The microwave gets its own 20 A circuit (S-06). S-06 is PENDING. The microwave gets its own 20A circuit and is not lumped onto a circuit shared with the hood or anything else. The wire (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA) is not settled until Mike Holt rules. The trap: size the water heater circuit at 100 percent of nameplate 'because it is just a resistance load.' Section 422.13 treats a fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less as a continuous load — 125 percent. The 4,500 W heater's 18.75 A becomes a 23.4 A minimum, so the 20 A answer fails before the breaker is even picked. Water heater wired at 100 percent of nameplate — no 125 percent continuous-load sizing (422.13). Breaker larger than the appliance's marked maximum overcurrent device (422.11). Dishwasher with no GFCI protection (422.5). Hard-wired appliance with no disconnecting means a servicer can reach (422.31). Microwave sharing a circuit with the range hood or another load (Sharma S-06). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 422.16: Dishwasher and trash compactor cords now follow matching rules, and a smoothed edge is named as acceptable protection where a cord passes through a cabinet opening. Trash compactor cords now get the same protection dishwasher cords already had where they pass through a cabinet wall. • 422.18: A new 422.18(B) keeps metal paddle fan parts out of the 3 ft by 8 ft zone around a tub or shower, and fan support now uses the new WSCR terms. New 422.18(B) bars metal paddle fan parts from the zone 3 ft out and 8 ft up from a tub's rim or a shower's threshold. • Article 422: Sections 422.3, 422.4, 422.15, 422.23, 422.46. 422.50 for appliances were deleted from the 2023 edition of the NEC. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: GFCI protection required for specific appliances
x: Section 422.5 names the appliances that must have Class A GFCI protection for personnel wherever they are installed. The duty travels with the appliance. It sits on top of the room rules in 210.8, and meeting one does not erase the other. • Scope: appliances rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amperes or less, single- or 3-phase, cord-and-plug-connected or hardwired. 210.8(D) points to this same list. • The 2020 list at 422.5(A): automotive vacuum machines; drinking water coolers and bottle fill stations; cord-and-plug-connected high-pressure spray washing machines; tire inflation machines; vending machines; sump pumps; and dishwashers. • NEC 2020 removed the 'provided for public use' condition and added sump pumps. • The protection must be readily accessible. 422.5(B) allows five places for it: the branch-circuit overcurrent device; a device or outlet within the supply circuit; an integral part of the attachment plug; within the supply cord not more than 12 in. from the attachment plug; or factory-installed within the appliance. • Edition caution: wider appliance lists circulating from NEC 2023 research are not the 2020 list. In 2020, ranges, dryers, and microwaves pick up their GFCI duties through the location rules in 210.8, not through 422.5. These appliances are used with wet hands, on wet floors, or around water: a dishwasher in a kitchen, a sump pump standing in a flooded pit, a spray washer on a wash pad. A ground fault can put the metal case at line voltage and send current through the person touching it. Class A GFCI senses that small leak and opens the circuit before the current through the person can kill. Check an appliance against both lists: 210.8 for the room and receptacle, and 422.5 for the appliance itself. The everyday Sharma case is the dishwasher in a new Marion County kitchen — 422.5(A) names dishwashers, so it needs GFCI wherever the kitchen sits. On Sharma work the dual-function breaker usually supplies this protection for a 120 V appliance circuit (S-07); confirm the breaker type actually provides GFCI, not AFCI only. A sump pump in a garage pit is the second everyday case: hardwired or cord-and-plug, it is on the list either way. S-07: every 120V breaker on new Sharma work is dual-function AFCI/GFCI, which is what makes the breaker the protection point for these appliances. The trap answer builds the list from 2023: it adds electric ranges, clothes dryers, and microwave ovens to 422.5. Under the 2020 Code those appliances pick up GFCI duties only through the location rules in 210.8 — the 422.5(A) list has seven appliances. The pick candidates forget is the sump pump, added in 2020. Dishwasher on a plain breaker, with no GFCI protection at any point in the supply circuit (422.5(A)). Sump pump plugged into an unprotected receptacle — 'it is only a pump' is not an exception. GFCI protection at a point that is not readily accessible, such as a device trapped behind the appliance (422.5(B)). Vending machine cord-and-plug connected with no GFCI in the plug, the cord, or the circuit. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 422.5 / 210.8(D): 2023 210.8(D) adds electric ranges, wall-mounted ovens, counter-mounted cooking units, clothes dryers and microwave ovens to the appliances needing GFCI, correlated with the 422.5(A) list. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Branch circuits for appliances (422.10)
x: Section 422.10 starts appliance work with the circuit: the branch circuit must be sized for the appliance it serves, using the appliance's marked rating, and an individual branch circuit — one that supplies only that appliance — is the default pattern for the big fixed appliances. Where two or more appliances share a circuit, this section's load rules and the general rules of Articles 210 and 220 both apply. The numbers that ride with it: • Where the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, the marking governs (422.11) • A single non-motor appliance rated over 13.3 A, not marked with a maximum, may be protected at up to 150 percent of its rating; at 13.3 A or less the ceiling is 20 A (422.11(E)) • A fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less is sized at 125 percent of nameplate — a continuous load (422.13) When the nameplate and the circuit disagree, the circuit gets corrected; the appliance does not get derated by hope. An appliance is a known, fixed load that runs exactly as hard as its nameplate says, sometimes for hours. A circuit sized by habit instead of by the rating either nuisance-trips under a load that was never a fault, or leaves conductors and terminations carrying more than they were built for. Starting from the marked rating is what keeps both the appliance and the circuit honest. Takeoff habit: every fixed appliance on the plans gets a line — appliance, rating, circuit, disconnect. If a plan shows the appliance but no circuit home, that is an open question for the packet, not a field surprise. Worked line: a 4,500 W storage water heater at 240 V draws 18.75 A; as a continuous load under 422.13 the circuit is sized at 125 percent — 23.4 A minimum — so the line reads: water heater, 18.75 A, 30 A circuit on 10 AWG copper, lockable disconnect. Every fixed appliance on the plan gets the same four boxes filled before the packet goes out. The trap is protecting an unmarked 16 A appliance with a 20 A breaker 'because it fits.' Section 422.11(E) works the other way: over 13.3 A with no marked maximum, the ceiling is 150 percent of the appliance rating — the breaker follows the appliance, not the other way around. The other common miss is sizing the storage water heater at 100 percent; at 120 gallons or less it is a continuous load at 125 percent (422.13). Appliance landed on a circuit sized by habit, not by the appliance's marked rating. Unmarked appliance over 13.3 A protected above 150 percent of its rating (422.11(E)). Storage water heater of 120 gallons or less wired at 100 percent instead of 125 percent (422.13). Fixed appliance on the plans with no circuit assigned — found in the field, not on the takeoff. Appliance marked with a maximum overcurrent device protected above the marking (422.11). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Overcurrent protection for appliances (422.11)
x: Section 422.11 protects the appliance at the size the appliance was built for. • Where the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, that marking governs. • For a single non-motor appliance fastened in place that is not marked with a maximum OCPD: 20 A maximum if the appliance is rated 13.3 A or less; 150 percent of the rated current maximum if rated over 13.3 A — and where 150 percent does not land on a standard rating, the next higher standard size is permitted (422.11(E)). That 150 percent is a ceiling, not a target. • Motor-operated appliances follow the motor rules for their protection. • Infrared heating appliances carry their own subdivision limits in this section. • 422.11(F): resistance-type heating elements in electric heating appliances rated over 48 A must be subdivided, each subdivided load not over 48 A and protected at not more than 60 A. An appliance's internal wiring, switches and controls are tested and listed with a specific maximum protective device ahead of them. A larger breaker lets a fault inside the appliance cook its own small conductors long before the breaker trips. The 150 percent allowance exists because some appliances draw starting surges — but it is a ceiling set by the listing, not a size to aim for. Read the appliance label before the breaker is chosen, every time. 'It matched the panel schedule from the last job' is how a 50 A device lands on an appliance marked 30 A maximum. Worked example with no marking: an unmarked fastened-in-place appliance rated 16 A gets 150 percent of 16 A = 24 A; 24 A is not a standard rating, so the next higher standard size, 25 A, is the ceiling. If that appliance were marked 'MAX 30 A,' the label — not the math — would set the breaker. The trap is treating 150 percent as the required size, or applying it to a marked appliance. When the appliance is marked with a maximum overcurrent device, the marking governs and the percentage math never starts. And where 150 percent lands between standard sizes, only the next higher standard size is permitted — not the next one after that. 50 A breaker on an appliance marked 'MAX BREAKER 30 A' — the marking governs, 422.11(E). Unmarked 16 A appliance protected at 40 A 'to stop nuisance trips' — the ceiling is 150 percent (24 A, next standard size 25 A). 90 A electric heating appliance fed as one load — elements over 48 A must be subdivided, each load not over 48 A, 422.11(F). Subdivided heating load protected at 80 A — subdivided loads are protected at not more than 60 A, 422.11(F). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Storage water heaters — treat the load as continuous for circuit sizing
x: Section 422.13 sizes the branch circuit for a fixed storage water heater of 120 gallons or less at not less than 125 percent of the heater's nameplate rating. In practice that is why a common 4500W, 240V heater (18.75A) lands on a 25A minimum calculation and is conventionally wired on a 30A circuit with 10 AWG copper — the arithmetic must be run for the actual nameplate on the actual job, not copied from the last house. The heater is treated this way because it can run for long stretches recovering a tank. A storage heater does not sip power. After showers or a full tank draw, the elements run flat-out for a long stretch to recover the tank, exactly like a continuous load. A circuit sized at exactly the nameplate amps would run its breaker and terminations at the edge for hours. The 125 percent factor is the continuous-load margin that keeps the circuit cool over those long runs. Do the division every time: nameplate watts divided by voltage, times 1.25, then choose the standard breaker and conductor that cover it. Write the result on the panel schedule so the next person does not have to reverse-engineer it. Worked example: a 5,500 W, 240 V heater draws 5,500 ÷ 240 = 22.9 A; × 1.25 = 28.6 A minimum circuit — a 30A breaker on 10 AWG copper covers it. The standard 4,500 W heater works out to 18.75 A × 1.25 = 23.4 A, which is why it also lands on the same 30A / 10 AWG circuit. The trap is sizing to the nameplate alone: 4,500 W ÷ 240 V = 18.75 A, so a 20 A breaker on 12 AWG. Wrong — 422.13 treats the heater as a continuous load, so the circuit minimum is 18.75 × 1.25 = 23.4 A, and the job lands on a 30 A breaker with 10 AWG copper. 4,500 W heater on a 20 A breaker and 12 AWG — sized at nameplate amps, no 125 percent (422.13). 5,500 W heater on a 25 A breaker: below the 28.6 A minimum the 125 percent rule sets. Circuit copied from the last house without reading the nameplate on the heater actually installed. Panel schedule shows the heater circuit with no rating recorded — the calc was never run. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Cord-and-plug connection for range hoods
x: Section 422.16(B)(4) lets a listed range hood — and an over-the-range microwave/range hood combination — be cord-and-plug connected instead of hard-wired, but only when every condition in the subsection is met: • The flexible cord is identified as suitable for use on range hoods in the manufacturer's installation instructions. • The cord is not less than 18 in. and not over 4 ft long. • The cord has an equipment grounding conductor and ends in a grounding-type attachment plug. Exception: a listed hood marked as double-insulated does not need the grounding-type plug. • The receptacle is located so the cord is protected against physical damage. • The receptacle is accessible. • The receptacle is supplied by an individual branch circuit. Cord connection is what lets the hood come down for service without unwiring it. It is a listed, conditioned permission — not a general shortcut for any fixed appliance. Hoods live over a hot cooktop in grease-laden air, and they come down for cleaning and service more than almost any other fixed appliance. The cord makes that practical. The conditions keep the cord itself from becoming the hazard: short enough to stay off the burners, grounded, protected from damage, and on its own circuit so the hood is not sharing a loaded kitchen circuit. Marion Oaks kitchen: the plan shows an over-the-range microwave/hood combination. Under S-06 it gets its own dedicated 20 A circuit — never shared. The receptacle goes in the cabinet above the unit, where the cord reaches it without crossing the cooktop: the factory cord is 24 in., inside the 18 in. to 4 ft window. Before rough-in, confirm the unit's instructions identify the cord for range hood use; a hood listed for hard-wiring only gets hard-wired, cord kit or not. Sharma note (company practice, not a 422 rule): the range hood often rides the dishwasher/disposal circuit in Sharma design practice. S-06 still stands on its own — the microwave keeps its own dedicated 20A circuit and is never lumped in with the hood. The wire size on that circuit is PENDING (12 AWG copper versus 10 AWG CCA). The trap is treating cord connection as permission to plug the hood into any handy receptacle — the countertop small-appliance circuit, or the dishwasher/disposal circuit. For a cord-and-plug hood, 422.16(B)(4) requires an individual branch circuit. The other trap is the cord length: over 4 ft fails, even if everything else is right. Cord-and-plug hood receptacle fed from the small-appliance or dishwasher circuit — not an individual branch circuit. Hood cord 5 ft long, draped behind the range to reach a receptacle. Receptacle hidden behind the hood's duct cover — not accessible. Cord kit added to a hood whose instructions list it for hard-wiring only. Receptacle located where a cabinet door or the duct pinches the cord. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Disconnecting means for permanently connected appliances
x: Section 422.31 covers how a permanently connected appliance is disconnected for service. Every appliance needs a disconnecting means that opens all ungrounded conductors at once (422.30), and the person servicing the appliance must be able to cut its power and keep it cut. Which device may serve depends on the appliance's rating: • Not over 300 VA or 1/8 hp — 422.31(A): the branch-circuit switch or circuit breaker may serve as the disconnecting means, where it is within sight from the appliance or is capable of being locked in the open position in compliance with 110.25. • Over 300 VA or 1/8 hp — 422.31(B): a switch or circuit breaker within sight from the appliance, or capable of being locked in the open position per 110.25, may serve. If the breaker is out of sight and not lockable, provide a disconnect within sight of the appliance. • Motor-operated appliances over 1/8 hp — 422.31(C): the disconnecting means must be within sight from the appliance, unless a unit switch complying with 422.34 serves as the disconnect. Within sight means visible and not more than 50 ft away (Article 100). The branch-circuit breaker can serve this role only where the conditions for doing so are met. Appliances get serviced by someone with the cover off and hands inside — a water heater element swap, an air handler blower. If the only disconnect is a breaker in another room, anyone in the building can turn the unit back on mid-repair. A disconnect within sight of the appliance, or one the servicer can lock open, keeps the person who opened it in control of it. At rough-in, decide where each hard-wired appliance's disconnect lives and confirm a servicer can reach it. Florida example: a 4,500 W water heater in the garage on a 30 A circuit. The panel is in the same garage, visible from the water heater and well within 50 ft, so the breaker serves as the disconnect. Put that same water heater on a panel inside the house, out of sight, and the job changes: make the breaker lockable per 110.25 or set a disconnect at the unit. A water heater, an air handler, or a cooktop whose only disconnect is an unlabelled breaker two rooms away is a conversation to have before final, not after. The trap answer: 'the branch-circuit breaker is always the appliance disconnect.' For an appliance over 300 VA whose breaker is out of sight and cannot be locked open, the breaker alone does not comply — 422.31(B) wants a disconnect within sight, or a breaker capable of being locked in the open position per 110.25. Water heater over 300 VA with no disconnect within sight, and the breaker is not capable of being locked open (422.31(B)). Breaker lockout is a loose clip-on device that does not remain in place with the lock removed (110.25). Disconnect provided, but it does not open all ungrounded conductors at once (422.30). Motor-operated appliance over 1/8 hp with no disconnect within sight and no unit switch complying with 422.34 (422.31(C)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Fixed electric space-heating equipment — article intro
x: Article 424 covers heating that is built into the building: baseboard heaters, wall heaters, radiant panels and cables, duct heaters, and boilers used for space heat. Three ideas run the article: • Heating is a continuous load. Branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent protection are sized at 125 percent of the total heating load on the circuit (424.4(B)) — a heater runs for hours at full draw; it is not a convenience load that happens to get warm. • The equipment must be listed and installed to its instructions (110.3(B)). • Disconnects and controls must let the heater be serviced and shut off safely. The 424.19 disconnect kills the heater, its controller and any supplementary overcurrent devices in one operation, is lockable in the open position, and is rated at least 125 percent of the load it switches. Circuits supplying two or more heater outlets are rated 15, 20, 25 or 30 A; fixed infrared heating in other than dwelling units may go to 50 A (424.4(A)). In Florida houses Sharma meets this article most often at duct heat strips in an air handler and at the occasional wall or bath heater. A heater does not cycle like a receptacle load — on a cold morning it pulls full nameplate current for hours. Sizing at 100 percent runs conductors and breakers at their limit until something fails, so the article builds the 125 percent margin in. The one-operation disconnect exists because a strip heater with a live blower, or a second live element, is exactly how a service tech gets burned or shocked inside an air handler. A Sharma new-construction home in Ocala gets a 3-ton air handler with a 10 kW strip kit. The strip nameplate reads 10 kW at 240 V, which is 41.7 A. Treat it as continuous: 41.7 × 1.25 = 52.1 A, so the circuit lands on a 60 A breaker with 6 AWG copper. Confirm the disconnect and control arrangement before the air handler is set: the switch at the unit must kill the strips, the blower and the supplementary fuses together, and lock open. Heat strips are also a load-calc input — tell the office the strip size you actually installed, not the one the plan first showed. The trap is sizing the heater circuit at 100 percent because 'resistance heat is a simple load.' Fixed electric space heat is a continuous load: conductors and overcurrent protection go at 125 percent of the nameplate. A 41.7 A strip on a 50 A breaker is the wrong answer — it needs 52.1 A of capacity before you pick the device. Heater circuit sized at 100 percent of nameplate — no 125 percent continuous factor (424.4(B)). Air-handler disconnect kills the heat strips but leaves the blower and controller live (424.19). Disconnect cannot be locked in the open position while the heater is serviced (424.19, 110.25). Heater installed against its listing instructions — clearances to combustibles not kept (110.3(B)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 424.48: New 424.48 allows heating cable in, on or behind walls if the cable is identified for walls, has GFCI, AFCI and a grounding means, and stays at or below 4 ft. Effective January 1, 2026. Heating cable can now go in, on or behind a wall when the cable or cable set is identified for wall use. • 424.10: Section 424.10, Special Permission, was deleted, and 424.9, General, was relocated to 424.10 at the beginning of Article 424 Part II. • 424.93(C): This new first-level subdivision created will allow heating panels and heating panel sets to be installed in walls with specific protection and limitations. The provision includes a January 1, 2026, effective date. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Branch circuits for fixed electric space heating (424.4(A), 424.4(B))
x: Fixed electric space heating — baseboard, wall heaters, ceiling heat, and the electric heat built into equipment — is served by individual branch circuits under 424.4(A), with the central systems the article names as the exception pattern. • 424.4(B): the heating load is treated as continuous. Branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent protection are sized at 125 percent of the total heating load on the circuit, before any other load is considered. • Circuits supplying two or more heater outlets are rated 15, 20, 25 or 30 A. • In other than dwelling units, fixed infrared heating may be on circuits up to 50 A (424.4(A)). • (424.3(A)/(B) are the 2017 numbers for these rules.) A heater is not a convenience load that happens to get warm; it runs for hours at full draw. On a cold night a space heater does not cycle — it sits at full current for hours. Conductors and a breaker sized at exactly the load would run at their thermal limit the whole time, aging terminations and inviting nuisance trips. The 125 percent continuous factor keeps every part of the circuit below its rating during the longest run the heater can make. Worked example: a 4,800 W, 240 V wall heater draws 20 A (4,800 ÷ 240). Continuous sizing makes the circuit 20 × 1.25 = 25 A — so the circuit is built at 25 A or above, never the 20 A circuit the raw math suggests. Same math in a Florida bonus room: two 1,500 W baseboards on one circuit draw 3,000 W ÷ 240 V = 12.5 A, and 12.5 × 1.25 = 15.6 A, so that circuit is 20 A, not 15 A. The trap is sizing the heater circuit at nameplate amps: 20 A heater, 20 A breaker, done. 424.4(B) treats the load as continuous, so the exam answer is 25 A. The second trap is the section number — in a 2017 book these rules sit at 424.3; in the 2020 book they are at 424.4. 4,800 W wall heater on a 20 A circuit — heating load not sized at 125 percent, 424.4(B). Two baseboard heaters sharing a general lighting circuit instead of an individual branch circuit, 424.4(A). 40 A circuit feeding three heater outlets — circuits for two or more heater outlets stop at 30 A, 424.4(A). Fixed infrared heaters in a shop on a 60 A circuit — outside dwelling units the cap is 50 A, 424.4(A). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Branch-circuit sizing for fixed space heat — 125 percent
x: Section 424.4(B) is where this rule lives in the 2020 edition — it was 424.3(B) in 2017, before the Article 424 reorganization. The 2020 text states the sizing directly instead of using the old 'shall be considered continuous load' sentence: the branch-circuit conductors for fixed electric space-heating equipment and any associated motors shall be sized not smaller than 125 percent of the load. Overcurrent protection is sized at the same 125 percent through the continuous-load rules of 210.19(A)(1) and 210.20(A), so in practice both the conductors and the breaker come out at 125 percent of the total load connected to the circuit, heater plus any blower or fan motor in the same equipment. Electric space heat is the classic continuous load: on the coldest night the strips run for hours without cycling off. Conductors and a breaker sized at exactly the load amps would sit at their thermal edge all night, heating terminations and inviting nuisance trips that leave the house cold. The 125 percent factor is the margin that keeps a long, full-load run safe. Run the math at 125 percent: total nameplate amps, heater plus motor, times 1.25 — then select the conductor and the breaker. Worked example: a 10 kW duct heater at 240 V draws 41.7 A; × 1.25 = 52.1 A — conductors rated at least 52.1 A (6 AWG copper at the 75°C column gives 65 A) on a 60A breaker, and the blower motor amps in the same equipment are added to the heater amps before the 125 percent is applied. Same math with the air handler's blower in the calc: heater 41.7 A plus a 6 A blower motor is 47.7 A connected; × 1.25 = 59.6 A — still a 60A breaker, and the 6 AWG copper still covers it. Leave the motor out and the paperwork says 52.1 A for a circuit that really carries more. Two traps live here. First, hunting for the rule under its 2017 address, 424.3(B) — in the 2020 book it is 424.4(B). Second, applying 125 percent to the heater nameplate and forgetting the blower motor in the same equipment: the motor amps are added first, then the whole total is multiplied. Heat circuit sized at 100 percent of the heater nameplate — no 125 percent (424.4(B)). Blower motor amps left out of the calc; conductors and breaker sized on the strips alone. 8 AWG copper (50 A at 75°C) on a heat load that calculates to a 52.1 A minimum. Breaker bumped up for the 125 percent but the conductors left at the old size. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Disconnecting means for fixed space-heating equipment
x: Section 424.19 requires a disconnecting means for fixed electric space-heating equipment — baseboard and wall heaters, duct heaters, and heat strips in an air handler. One operation has to kill the whole machine: • The disconnect must simultaneously disconnect the heater, the motor controller(s) and any supplementary overcurrent protective device(s) from all ungrounded conductors. • It must be lockable in the open position under 110.25 — the locking provision is part of the switch or breaker and stays in place with or without the lock. • The disconnect must have an ampere rating not less than 125 percent of the total load of the motors and the heaters. • Equipment with supplementary overcurrent protection: the disconnect is within sight from those devices — visible and not more than 50 ft away. • Equipment without supplementary overcurrent protection: the branch-circuit switch or breaker may serve as the disconnect, if it is within sight from the heater or lockable under 110.25 [424.19(B)]. • A unit switch that is part of the equipment, with a marked "off" position, may serve as the disconnect where it disconnects all ungrounded conductors [424.19(C)]. A duct heater in an air handler is normally disconnected at the air handler's disconnect — the 440/424 boundary matters on a change-out, because the strips and the blower are one piece of equipment at service time. Heat strips and a blower share one cabinet, and the tech services them with the cabinet open and both hands inside. If the switch he opened kills the strips but leaves the blower or the controls live — or someone resets a breaker down the hall mid-repair — the "dead" unit starts or bites. One disconnect that opens everything and locks open is what makes the equipment safe to open up. Air-handler change-out in a Florida garage: the new unit carries 10 kW of strip heat and a blower, fed as one piece of equipment. The disconnect at the air handler must kill the strips, the blower and the controller together — test all three dead before your hands go in. The strip circuit is sized at 125 percent under 424.4(B): 10 kW at 240 V is 41.7 A — 52.1 A minimum, 60 A breaker. If you move the disconnect on the change-out, re-verify at the new location that it still opens the whole unit, and check the heat-strip circuit before start-up. Keep the disconnect within reach of the person servicing the unit. The trap answer is "the panel breaker is the disconnect, full stop." That only works for equipment without supplementary overcurrent protection, and only when the breaker is within sight of the heater or lockable under 110.25. If the unit carries its own supplementary fuses or breakers, the disconnect must be within sight from those devices. Disconnect opens the heat strips but the blower and controls stay live — it must open the heater, the controller and the supplementary protection together. Out-of-sight disconnect with no lockable provision, or a portable hasp clipped on — 110.25 requires the provision to stay in place with or without the lock. Unit has supplementary fuses inside, and the disconnect is around the corner, out of sight from those devices. Unit switch used as the disconnect with no marked "off" position, or it opens only one ungrounded conductor. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Fixed resistance and electrode industrial process heating equipment — article intro
x: Article 425 covers electric heating used for an industrial process rather than for comfort: process tanks, ovens, and similar equipment. • The article follows the use, not the hardware: the same heating element is 424 work when it warms people and 425 work when it heats a product. • Sharma's residential and light commercial work rarely installs it, so this page is the article's scope page. • Where a commercial job includes process heat, work the article with the equipment listing, and ask Mike before treating it like space heat under 424. Process heaters run unattended for long cycles, often around water, chemicals and product that cannot tolerate a fault. The article exists because a tank or an oven is not a baseboard heater: its controls, disconnects and protection follow the process and the listing, not comfort-heating habits carried over from 424. Do not borrow 424 rules for a 425 load by habit. Identify the article from the equipment's use, then apply that article plus the listing. Example: a small commercial job adds an electric process tank heater. Before quoting, get the nameplate and the listing instructions, confirm which article the job falls under, and let Mike review the plan: the wire and protection follow 425 and the listing, not the duct-heater job from last week. The trap is answering a 425 question with 424. The exam, or the inspector, describes a heater built into a process tank, and the space-heating rules come out by habit: wrong article. If the heat serves the product or the process, it is 425, and the listing leads. Fixed industrial process heating equipment installed without regard to its listing and Article 425. Process heater treated as space-heating equipment: the wrong article applied at rough-in. Nameplate data for the process equipment not on file: ratings unverified at inspection. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 425.10: Section 425.10 was deleted by CMP-17 for special permission requirements and 425.8 General was relocated to 425.10 as the beginning of Article 425 Part II. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Fixed outdoor electric deicing and snow-melting equipment — article intro
x: Article 426 covers fixed electric equipment installed outdoors to melt snow and ice: heating cable and panels in pavements, walks, driveways, roofs and gutters. It is a later-pass article for a Florida book — Sharma does not install snow-melting in its territory — and it is included here so Chapter 4 walks the NEC in complete official order. The rules that do the work when this equipment appears: • Continuous load (426.4): branch-circuit conductors and the overcurrent device are sized at not less than 125 percent of the total heater load. • Ground-fault protection of equipment (426.28): GFPE must be provided for the equipment, except for mineral-insulated, metal-sheathed cable embedded in a noncombustible medium. GFPE protects equipment — it is not a personnel GFCI. • Disconnecting means (426.50): a means that disconnects all ungrounded conductors at the same time, capable of being locked open. • Identification (426.13): the presence of a deicing or snow-melting installation must be indicated, so nobody cores or cuts into a heated slab blind. Heating cable lives buried in concrete and asphalt, where a nicked cable or failed splice leaks current into wet, grounded pavement. That leakage is far too small to trip a breaker, but it can sputter and arc inside the slab until something catches — which is why 426.28 puts ground-fault protection of equipment on the circuit. The 125 percent sizing exists because the load runs for hours in the coldest weather: conductors and breakers sized at exactly 100 percent would cook at their terminals. If a Florida job somehow specifies deicing equipment — a northern builder's standard detail copied onto a Florida plan is the usual way — flag it to the office rather than installing or deleting it silently. If the office ever approves one, the math looks like this: a 2,400 W heated walk on 240 V draws 10 A; treated as the continuous load it is, the circuit sizes at 125 percent, 12.5 A, so a 15 A breaker is the smallest standard pick — and it must be a GFPE breaker, not a standard one (426.28). Florida note: no snow load in Sharma's territory; treat any 426 equipment on a Florida plan as a probable copy-over from another climate and confirm with the builder. The trap is treating GFPE and GFCI as the same device. A personnel GFCI trips at 4–6 mA and can nuisance-trip on a long heating-cable run; the ground-fault protection of equipment that 426.28 requires typically trips around 30 mA (manufacturers vary) and exists to keep a damaged cable from arcing inside the slab. The reverse trap is skipping ground-fault protection entirely because 'nobody touches a slab' — the protection is for the equipment, not for people. Snow-melting circuit on a standard breaker — no ground-fault protection of equipment (426.28). Heater circuit sized at 100 percent of load; deicing is a continuous load, 125 percent (426.4). Disconnect opens only one ungrounded conductor, or cannot be locked open (426.50). Heated slab not identified at the panel or on the plans (426.13). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 426.14: Section 426.14 pertaining to special permission for fixed outdoor electric deicing and snow-melting equipment was deleted • 426.28: Recognizes that manufacturers of fixed outdoor electric deicing and snow-melting equipment have an option to require ground-fault protection with reduced current and time threshold values providing a higher degree of protection than previously required. Therefore, Section 426.28 was revised, allowing the manufacturer to specify the ground fault trip level. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Fixed electric heating equipment for pipelines and vessels — article intro
x: Article 427 covers fixed electric heating equipment for pipelines and vessels: heat-tracing cable and heating panels that keep a pipe from freezing or hold a process fluid at temperature. • Scope: the heating cable or panel, its controls and its branch circuit (427.1). • The load is continuous: branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent protection are sized at 125 percent of the total heating load (427.4). • Ground-fault protection of equipment is required on the branch circuits that supply heat tracing and heating panels (427.22). It is equipment protection, commonly a 30 mA trip — not a 4–6 mA personnel GFCI. A narrow exception covers industrial plants with alarm indication and qualified maintenance. • Heating cables carry a grounded conductive covering: the metal braid or jacket is the fault path that lets the protection see a failure (427.23). • Caution signs or markings go on the pipe or vessel at intervals of not more than 20 ft, and next to equipment that gets serviced (427.13). • Each installation has a disconnecting means that opens all ungrounded conductors (427.55(A)). Sharma meets this article as pipe heat trace on exposed commercial plumbing and in freeze protection details, not in ordinary house work. A heat-trace cable lives outdoors, under insulation, wrapped on a pipe full of water. When its insulation fails, the fault can arc and sputter without ever drawing enough current to trip a plain breaker — heating the pipe covering instead. GFPE watches for that small leak to ground and opens the circuit, and the grounded braid gives the fault a path the protection can see. The caution signs warn the next trade off a live cable hidden under insulation. A small commercial building in Ocala has 40 ft of exposed domestic water pipe and a backflow preventer in an unconditioned meter room. Sharma installs self-regulating heat trace under the pipe insulation, fed from a 20 A GFPE breaker — Sharma's commercial minimum branch circuit is 20 A. The cable load is 8 A; figured as a continuous load at 125 percent, that is 10 A, well inside the circuit. Caution markings go on the pipe at 20 ft intervals and at the valve that gets serviced. Install the heat trace exactly to its listing: correct cable for the pipe, correct controller and sensor location, GFPE in place and tested. Photograph the controller setting at turnover. The trap is reaching for a Class A GFCI. Section 427.22 asks for ground-fault protection of equipment, which trips around 30 mA to catch a failing cable; a 4–6 mA personnel GFCI is a different device that nuisance-trips on long runs. Second trap: sizing the branch circuit at 100 percent of the cable load — heating is a continuous load and takes 125 percent (427.4). Heat-trace branch circuit with no ground-fault protection of equipment (427.22). No caution signs or markings along the heated pipe, so the next crew buries a live cable under insulation with no warning (427.13). Cable installed without its grounded conductive covering, or the braid left ungrounded at the termination (427.23). Branch circuit sized at 100 percent of the heating load — a continuous load takes 125 percent (427.4). Controller sensor hanging in the air instead of strapped to the pipe, so the cable cooks the covering or the pipe freezes. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 427.35: Section 427.35, which covered the installation of line frequency induction heating equipment and accessories for pipelines and vessels, was deleted. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Motors, motor circuits, and controllers — article intro
x: Article 430 is the longest working article in Chapter 4 and the one most often misapplied, because it is a system, not a single rule. Five jobs, five sizing bases: • Conductors — from table full-load current, at 125 percent for a continuous-duty motor (430.22). • Overload protection — separate from the breaker, sized from the nameplate current of the motor actually installed: 125 percent for a motor with a marked service factor of 1.15 or greater, or a marked temperature rise of 40 °C or less; 115 percent for all other motors (430.32). • Short-circuit and ground-fault protection — from the Table 430.52 percentages of table FLC: an inverse-time breaker may go to 250 percent, which is why a motor breaker can look oversized for its wire. • A controller rated for the motor. • A disconnect within sight (430.102), rated at least 115 percent of table FLC or by its horsepower rating (430.110). 430.6 is the traffic rule behind all of it: everything except the overloads starts from the Article 430 tables, because the next replacement motor may differ from this nameplate. Using one number for all five jobs is the classic 430 error. Air-conditioning equipment is pulled out of parts of 430 by Article 440, which has its own nameplate-driven rules — always check which article governs the equipment in front of you. A motor draws several times its running current at start-up, and it can sit stalled and cooking without ever tripping protection sized for ordinary loads. Article 430 splits the protection into separate jobs so starting current can pass, a stalled motor still gets cleared, and the overload device — not the big breaker — watches the motor and its conductors against a slow overload. Work a motor in this order, every time: (1) table FLC for conductors and short-circuit protection, (2) nameplate FLA for overloads, (3) disconnect within sight, (4) controller rating. Write all four down before you order material. Example: a 10 hp, 208 V three-phase motor has a table FLC of 30.8 A. Its conductors need 125 percent — 38.5 A of ampacity. The inverse-time breaker may go to 250 percent — 77 A — which is why it looks oversized next to the wire; the overloads, set from the nameplate, are the protection that actually watches the load. The trap is one number for the whole job — usually the nameplate FLA, used for the conductors, the breaker, the overloads and the disconnect. Only the overloads come off the nameplate. Conductors, short-circuit protection and the disconnect all start from table full-load current under 430.6, because a replacement motor may not match this one's nameplate. Conductors sized from nameplate FLA instead of table full-load current (430.6). Overload heaters set from the table value — the motor nuisance-trips or cooks (430.32). Breaker replaced with one that 'matches the wire,' and the motor will no longer start (430.52). No disconnect within sight of the motor (430.102). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 430.2: Rebuilt motors now have a home in 430.2: they're allowed when the work follows the manufacturer's instructions, or a nationally recognized standard if the maker offers none. A reconditioned motor can go back into service when the rebuild followed the manufacturer's instructions. • 430.1: The previous figure at Section 430.1 has been deleted, and an expanded figure has been added to include all relevant parts of the motor circuit and what parts of Article 430 apply. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Which current do you size from — table values vs. nameplate
x: Section 430.6 is the traffic rule for the whole article. For sizing conductors, disconnects, controllers, and short-circuit/ground-fault protection, you use the full-load current values from the Article 430 tables for the motor's horsepower and voltage — not the amps printed on that particular motor's nameplate, because the next replacement motor may differ. Overload protection is the exception: it is sized from the actual nameplate current of the motor installed, because it protects that specific machine. Mixing those two bases up is the single most common motor calculation error. The fuller table is on the 430.250 page. If the horsepower and voltage in front of you are not listed here, pull the value from the printed table for that combination — do not scale from a nearby row. Motors of the same horsepower are not identical — one maker's 5 hp motor draws more than another's. If conductors were sized from one motor's nameplate, the replacement motor installed ten years later could overload them. The tables give one standard current for each horsepower and voltage, so the wiring outlasts any single machine. Overload protection is the opposite case: it guards the motor actually bolted down, so it follows that motor's nameplate. A Sharma crew replaces a 5 hp, 230 V single-phase air compressor motor in a Lakeland shop. Table 430.248 gives 28 A for that motor, so the conductors, disconnect, and short-circuit protection are all figured from 28 A — the conductors at 125 percent of it under 430.22. The new motor's nameplate reads 26 A, and that number goes only on the overload line of the worksheet. If the nameplate had read 30 A, the overloads would follow 30 A — but the conductors would still be sized from the 28 A table value. The trap is using the nameplate for everything because it is the motor in front of you. Nameplate current sizes only the overload protection. Conductors, disconnects, controllers, and short-circuit and ground-fault protection all come from the Article 430 tables — Table 430.248 for single-phase, Table 430.250 for three-phase. Motor branch-circuit conductors sized from the nameplate current, below the table value — 430.6(A). Overload protection sized from the table value instead of the installed motor's nameplate current. Replacement motor installed on conductors that were sized to the old motor's lower nameplate amps. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Conductors for a single motor — 125 percent of table full-load current
x: Section 430.22 sizes the branch-circuit conductors feeding one continuous-duty motor at not less than 125 percent of the motor's full-load current as taken from the Article 430 tables. • Start from the table FLC for the horsepower and voltage — Table 430.248 for single-phase motors — not from the nameplate amps. • Multiply by 1.25, then select the conductor from the ampacity table using the temperature column the terminations allow. • Intermittent and short-time duty motors are treated under their own parts of this section, so the duty rating on the nameplate decides which rule you are in before you do any arithmetic. The extra quarter covers the heating of a motor that runs for long periods at full load. A continuous-duty motor can sit at full load for hours — a well pump on a dry day, a shop compressor on a busy one. Conductors sized at exactly full-load current would run at their ampacity limit the whole time, with no margin for a hot attic or a tight bundle. The 125 percent factor is thermal headroom, so the wire never becomes the weak point in the circuit. Take the table FLC for the horsepower and voltage, multiply by 1.25, then select the conductor from the ampacity table using the correct temperature column for the terminations. Do not size the wire from the nameplate amps and do not round the 125 percent away. Worked example, a shop compressor in Marion County: a 5 hp, 230 V single-phase motor has a table FLC of 28 A (Table 430.248). Conductors: 28 × 1.25 = 35 A minimum — 10 AWG copper at the 75 °C column (35 A) is the smallest conductor that covers it, before any voltage-drop or adjustment checks. The trap is reading the amps off the motor nameplate and sizing the conductors to that number. 430.22 wants the table full-load current times 125 percent. The nameplate current is what the overload protection is set from — it is not the conductor number. Motor conductors sized from nameplate amps instead of the Article 430 table FLC, 430.22. 5 hp, 230 V motor wired with 12 AWG copper (25 A at 75 °C) — 125 percent of the 28 A table FLC is 35 A. 125 percent factor dropped because 'the motor never runs that long' — continuous-duty sizing is not optional, 430.22. Conductor picked from the 90 °C column where the equipment terminations are rated 75 °C. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Conductors feeding several motors
x: Section 430.24 sizes conductors that feed two or more motors (or motors with other loads): • Take 125 percent of the full-load current of the largest motor. • Add the full-load currents of the other motors at 100 percent. • Add any other loads under their own rules. All full-load currents come from the Article 430 tables — Table 430.248 for single-phase, Table 430.250 for three-phase — not from nameplates (430.6). The largest motor gets the continuous-duty margin; the rest are added at face value, on the reasonable basis that the feeder sees the sum. It is the feeder-level companion to the single-motor rule in 430.22. The feeder carries every motor at once, in one raceway, where heat has nowhere to go. The largest motor is the one most likely to run loaded for hours at a stretch, so it carries the continuous-duty margin. Size the feeder at a flat 100 percent of the sum and it runs hot on exactly those long runs — insulation ages in the conduit where nobody sees it. Small Orlando shop, one feeder for three 230 V single-phase motors: a 5 hp compressor at 28 A table FLC, a 3 hp at 17 A, and a 2 hp at 12 A. Largest first at 125 percent: 28 × 1.25 = 35 A. Add the rest at face value: 35 + 17 + 12 = 64 A minimum conductor ampacity. A 6 AWG copper conductor in the 75°C column is rated 65 A (Table 310.16), so it covers the feeder before any adjustment or correction factors. Build the sum in a labelled column — largest motor first at 125 percent, then each additional motor at 100 percent — so the next person can audit it. Do not apply 125 percent to every motor on the feeder, and do not size a multi-motor feeder from one nameplate. Two trap answers: applying 125 percent to every motor on the feeder — only the largest gets the margin — and sizing from the largest motor's nameplate amps. Section 430.24 runs on table full-load currents under 430.6, with the 125 percent factor on the largest motor only. Feeder conductors sized at 100 percent of the sum of motor FLCs — no 125 percent factor on the largest motor (430.24). Motor feeder sized from a nameplate current instead of the Article 430 table values (430.6). Non-motor load on the same feeder left out of the conductor calculation. Feeder calculation missing from the job paperwork — the conductor size cannot be audited. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Overload protection — protects the motor from running too hot
x: Section 430.32 requires overload protection for continuous-duty motors over the small sizes the article sets. Size it from the motor's nameplate full-load current — the actual machine in front of you — with the percentage set by the motor's service factor and temperature-rise markings. The overload device watches running current over time and trips before the windings cook; it is not there to clear a short circuit, which is the branch protective device's job. A motor with built-in thermal protection meets this requirement through its own device where the article allows it. The percentages in 430.32(A)(1), applied to the nameplate full-load current: • Motor with a marked service factor of 1.15 or greater — 125 percent • Motor with a marked temperature rise of 40 °C or less — 125 percent • All other motors — 115 percent If an overload selected at those percentages will not let the motor start or carry its load, 430.32(C) permits stepping up — to not more than 140 percent for the first two cases, 130 percent for all others. The step-up is a documented exception for a motor that will not run, not the starting point for selection. A motor rarely fails at a dead short; it fails cooking slowly at 120 or 130 percent of rating, hour after hour, until the insulation gives up. The breaker cannot see that — it is sized to ride through starting current. The overload is the one device watching the motor's own heat, which is why it is set from that motor's nameplate and not from a table. Read service factor and rise off the nameplate before you select or set an overload. Worked example: a 3 hp, 230 V pool pump on a Marion Oaks job — the tables give 17 A for that horsepower, but the overload comes off the plate: nameplate FLA 15.2 A, service factor marked 1.15, so 15.2 × 125% = 19.0 A, and the overload is set at 19 A. If the overload trips repeatedly, measure the running amps and find the mechanical cause — a failing bearing, a clogged pump basket, low voltage — do not solve a tripping overload by setting it higher than 430.32 permits. The trap is sizing the overload from the Article 430 tables, the way conductors and disconnects are sized. Tables are for everything except the overload: 430.32 works off the nameplate FLA of the installed motor, because the overload protects that specific machine. The second trap is starting at the 430.32(C) step-up percentages — 140 and 130 percent are the ceiling for a motor that will not run at the first selection, not the selection. Overload set from the Table 430.250 value instead of the installed motor's nameplate FLA. Overload cranked past the 430.32(C) ceiling to stop nuisance trips, with no mechanical cause found. No overload protection at all on a continuous-duty motor — a breaker alone does not do this job. Overload sized at 125% on a motor with no service factor or rise marking that qualifies for it — 115% is the pick. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for motors
x: Section 430.52 sizes the device that clears a fault on a motor branch circuit, using the percentages in Table 430.52 applied to the table full-load current. The device type decides which percentage applies. These percentages are deliberately far above running current, because the device must ride through motor starting inrush without opening, while still clearing a fault. That is why a motor circuit can legally have a breaker that looks oversized for its wire — the overload device, not the breaker, protects the motor and, through its sizing rules, the circuit against overload. • Worked example: the 5 hp, 230 V motor at 28 A table FLC takes an inverse-time breaker of at most 28 × 2.50 = 70 A. • If that device will not hold through starting, 430.52(C)(1) Exception No. 2(c) permits an inverse-time breaker up to 400 percent where the FLC is 100 A or less — an exception to document, not a habit. • Exception No. 1 is the next-higher-standard-size permission, for where the table percentage does not land on a standard rating. • Instantaneous-trip breakers: 430.52(C)(3) Exception No. 1 permits up to 1300 percent where the 800 percent setting won't let the motor start; Design B energy-efficient premium motors may go up to 1700 percent. A motor draws several times its running current for the first seconds of every start. A device sized like a house-circuit breaker would trip on every start, so the fault device is set high and has one job: clear short circuits and ground faults fast. Running protection is a separate job, given to the overload device. Never judge a motor circuit by house-circuit instincts. Check all three together: conductor at 125 percent of table FLC (430.22), overload from the nameplate (430.32), fault protection from Table 430.52. If one of the three is missing from the job paperwork, the calculation is not finished. On a Sharma pump or air-handler swap, that three-line check goes on the work order before the old disconnect is reused. The trap answer downsizes the breaker to match the wire — 'a 70 A breaker on wire sized for 35 A is a violation.' On a motor branch circuit it is not: Table 430.52 allows an inverse-time breaker up to 250 percent of table FLC, and the overload device provides the running protection. The violation is the reverse — a fault device above the table percentage with no exception behind it. Inverse-time breaker above 250% of table FLC with no documented exception (Table 430.52). Breaker swapped larger after nuisance trips, with no check of the Table 430.52 ceiling. Overload protection missing, or set from the table FLC instead of the motor nameplate (430.32). Conductors under 125% of table FLC feeding the motor (430.22). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Feeder protection where several motors share a feeder (430.62)
x: When one feeder supplies several motor branch circuits, 430.62(A) caps the feeder's protective device: • No larger than the largest branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault device on the feeder, • plus the full-load currents of the other motors on that feeder. The feeder conductors themselves are sized under 430.24 — 125 percent of the largest motor plus 100 percent of the rest. The two rules work as a pair: the wire math keeps the feeder from running hot, and the device math keeps a fault on one motor from being invisible to a feeder breaker sized for everything at once. The 430.62 result is a ceiling, not a target — a smaller standard device is always permitted. If the feeder breaker is sized like a service — big enough for every motor's starting surge added together — a fault on the smallest motor may never draw enough current to open it, and the fault burns until something else gives. Capping the feeder device at the largest branch device plus the other motors' running currents keeps it close enough to see a branch fault, while the branch devices and the motors' overloads do their own jobs. Worked example: three motors at 14 A, 10 A, and 10 A table FLC, largest branch device 40 A. Feeder device ceiling: 40 + 10 + 10 = 60 A — a 60 A feeder breaker is the largest permitted, and anything bigger is a violation even if the conductors could carry it. Feeder conductors, by the other formula: 14 × 1.25 + 10 + 10 = 37.5 A minimum ampacity before other adjustments. Write both numbers on the panel schedule; they come from different sections and answer different questions. The trap answers swap the pair: sizing the feeder device with the 430.24 conductor formula, or sizing the conductors with the 430.62 device formula. The device ceiling is the largest branch device plus the other motors' full-load currents — there is no 125 percent factor anywhere in it. Feeder breaker larger than the 430.62(A) ceiling — largest branch device plus the other motors' FLC. Feeder protective device sized with the 430.24 conductor formula (125 percent of the largest motor). Feeder conductors sized with the device formula — no 125 percent factor on the largest motor (430.24). Largest branch-circuit device upsized without rechecking the feeder device ceiling. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The motor disconnect must be within sight
x: Section 430.102 places the disconnecting means for a motor and its controller within sight from the equipment it disconnects. 'In sight' is the Article 100 meaning: visible, and not more than 50 ft away. • Stand at the motor: you must be able to see its disconnect. • Where the disconnect cannot be within sight, it must be capable of being locked in the open position under the conditions the article allows. A breaker in a panel across the building, with no lockable arrangement, does not give a servicer control of the machine in front of them. The person servicing a motor has to know the machine cannot be re-energized behind their back. A disconnect you can see is a disconnect you control: nobody restarts the equipment without walking into your line of sight. Where sight is impossible, a lock in the open position is the substitute — your lock, your key, your machine. Stand at the motor and point at its disconnect before you call the job done. If you cannot see it, either move it, add the local disconnect, or confirm the lockable arrangement the article permits and document it. On a Sharma service call at a Kissimmee house, the air-handler blower's only disconnect was the breaker in the garage panel — about 70 ft away and around two corners. That fails the within-sight test, so a local disconnect went in 8 ft from the air handler, in plain view of anyone working on it. The same within-sight habit is what 440.14 demands for HVAC equipment. The trap answer is 'in the same room' or 'on the same floor.' Within sight is a defined term with two parts: the disconnect must be visible AND not more than 50 ft away. A labeled breaker in a panel 80 ft down the hall fails both the exam question and the rule, unless it can be locked open as the article allows. Motor disconnect in a remote panel — not within sight and not lockable (430.102). Disconnect visible from the motor but more than 50 ft away. Sight line blocked — stored material between the motor and its disconnect. No disconnect within sight of the condenser unit (440.14). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: What may serve as the motor disconnect
x: Section 430.109 lists the types of switches and devices permitted to serve as a motor disconnect. The general list at 430.109(A): • A listed motor-circuit switch rated in horsepower • A listed molded case circuit breaker • A listed molded case switch • An instantaneous-trip breaker that is part of a listed combination controller, or a listed self-protected combination controller • A listed manual motor controller additionally marked 'Suitable as Motor Disconnect,' installed between the final branch-circuit protective device and the motor Small motors get their own paths. For stationary motors of 1/8 horsepower or less, the branch-circuit overcurrent device may serve as the disconnect (430.109(B)), and cord-and-plug arrangements for small motors sit with 430.111. For stationary motors of 2 horsepower or less and 300 volts or less, a general-use switch rated at not less than twice the motor full-load current is permitted, as is an AC general-use snap switch where the motor current is not more than 80 percent of the switch rating (430.109(C)). A general-use switch that is fine for a lighting load is not automatically a motor disconnect; the device must be rated for interrupting a motor circuit of that horsepower. A motor is not a light bulb. Starting current runs several times the running current, and opening a loaded motor circuit draws an arc the device has to survive thousands of times. A switch chosen by amps alone can weld its contacts or fail closed, leaving a servicer working on a machine that is still alive. The horsepower rating is the proof the device was tested to make and break motor current. Read the horsepower rating on the switch, not just the amp rating, before you land a motor on it. When the disconnect is a breaker in a panelboard, confirm it is a permitted type for that motor and that the within-sight rule in 430.102 is separately satisfied. Small-motor case: a 1/2 hp, 115 V exhaust fan motor has a table full-load current of 9.8 A (Table 430.248). On the 430.109(C) path, a general-use switch rated at least twice that — 19.6 A — serves as the disconnect, so a 20 A switch is the pick; a 15 A lighting toggle is not, whatever is on the truck. The trap answer is 'a 20 A switch for a 20 A motor circuit.' Section 430.109 is a type list, not an amp list: outside the small-motor paths, the disconnect must be a horsepower-rated device or another listed type the section names. The companion trap is forgetting that type is only half the check — 430.110 still sizes the disconnect at not less than 115 percent of the table full-load current, and 430.102 still wants it within sight. General-use lighting switch installed as the disconnect for a motor over the small-motor limits, with no horsepower rating. Manual motor controller used as the disconnect without the 'Suitable as Motor Disconnect' marking (430.109(A)(6)). Disconnect sized under 115 percent of the motor's table full-load current (430.110). Permitted device type, but the disconnect is not within sight of the motor (430.102). General-use switch under twice the full-load current on a 2 hp or less stationary motor (430.109(C)(1)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Rating of the motor disconnect — at least 115 percent
x: Section 430.110 sizes the disconnecting means for a motor circuit: • A general-use switch used as a motor disconnect must have an ampere rating of at least 115 percent of the motor's full-load current, taken from the Article 430 tables — not the nameplate (430.6). • Horsepower-rated devices are selected by their horsepower rating for the motor served. The disconnect is a switching device that must safely make and break motor current, which is why its sizing basis is its own rule and not simply 'match the breaker.' Worked check: a 5 hp, 230 V single-phase motor has a table full-load current of 28 A. 115 percent of 28 A is 32.2 A — so a 30 A general-use switch is too small, even though 30 A sits above the running current. Combined with 430.102 (within sight) and 430.109 (permitted types), this completes the disconnect picture. A motor disconnect does not just carry current — it has to close onto a starting motor and open a running one without welding its contacts or failing in the switchman's hand. The 115 percent margin puts the switch's rating above the motor's full-load draw, so the device is never working at its limit every time the machine cycles. Check two markings on a motor disconnect: the amp rating against 115 percent of table FLC, or the horsepower rating against the motor. If either fails, the disconnect is the wrong device even if it has worked for years on the old motor. On a Sharma commercial service call, a replacement 5 hp exhaust motor went in where the existing disconnect was a 30 A general-use switch. Table FLC is 28 A, so 430.110 wants at least 32.2 A — the 30 A switch came out and a 60 A switch went in, even though the old switch had 'always worked.' The trap is matching the disconnect to the breaker, or running the 115 percent off the nameplate amps. The breaker is sized from Table 430.52 percentages — a different rule. The disconnect starts from table full-load current under 430.6 and takes 115 percent, or it is picked by its horsepower rating. A 30 A switch 'because the motor draws 28' is the wrong answer. 30 A general-use switch disconnecting a motor that needs 32.2 A at 115 percent (430.110). Disconnect picked to match the breaker, with no 115 percent or horsepower check. Horsepower-rated switch smaller than the motor it disconnects. Disconnect rating figured from nameplate FLA instead of table FLC (430.6, 430.110). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Conductors to drives and power conversion equipment (430.122)
x: Section 430.122 sizes the conductors feeding adjustable-speed drives and other power conversion equipment from the equipment's own ratings — not from the motor's horsepower table: • Supply (input) conductors: ampacity not less than 125 percent of the drive's rated input current [430.122(A)]. The drive nameplate — input amps — is the document that sizes this wire. • Output conductors, drive to motor: ampacity not less than 125 percent of the motor's full-load current as determined by 430.6 [430.122(B)]. Where the drive is listed and marked "Suitable for Output Motor Conductor Protection," the output conductors must be at least the larger of that 125 percent value or the minimum conductor size marked on the drive. • Where the equipment has a bypass, the section follows the larger demand — the conductors must suit the bypass arrangement as well as the drive [430.122(C)]. A drive can draw more at its input than the motor table suggests, so both sides of the drive get sized: input from the drive plate, output from the motor. A drive is not a starter. Its input current includes the losses and the harmonic-rich draw of the conversion electronics, and it is set by the drive's rating, not by the motor behind it. Wire sized from the motor table can run hot feeding a drive whose motor is loafing — and a later swap to a larger drive frame on the same motor silently overloads wire that nobody re-checked. Swapping a starter for a VFD on a pump or air handler: photograph the drive's input rating before ordering wire. Example: the plate reads INPUT 460 V, 21 A — the supply conductors need an ampacity of at least 21 × 1.25 = 26.25 A, whatever the motor table says. Reusing the old starter's wire size without the input-current check is the standard failure. Check the output side too: drive-to-motor conductors are sized at 125 percent of the motor's full-load current from 430.6. The trap answer sizes the drive's supply conductors from the motor's table full-load current (430.6, 430.22) because "it is a motor circuit." Part X changes the input side: supply conductors come from the drive's rated input current at 125 percent [430.122(A)]. The motor table still governs the output side — not the input. Drive supply conductors sized from the motor horsepower table instead of the drive's rated input current. Old starter wire reused on a VFD retrofit with no input-current check. Output conductors to the motor undersized — not 125 percent of the motor full-load current. Bypass installed and the conductors never checked for the across-the-line demand. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Motor full-load current tables — the working values (430.248 / 430.250)
x: Tables 430.248 (single-phase) and 430.250 (three-phase) give the table full-load current used for conductor, disconnect, controller, and short-circuit and ground-fault sizing under 430.6.
