The combinations in the tables on this page are the ones Sharma's crews meet most; the printed tables govern for anything not listed here. • Read the value for the horsepower and for the voltage actually supplied — the same motor draws roughly half the current at the higher voltage. • Use the table FLC even when the installed motor's nameplate amps differ. A replacement motor of the same horsepower uses the same table FLC. • The nameplate is not ignored: it sets the overload protection (430.32). Table for sizing, nameplate for overloads — that split is 430.6. Motors of the same horsepower do not all draw the same current, and nameplates get swapped, painted over, and misread. The tables give every installer and inspector one standard current for a given horsepower and voltage, so the wire, disconnect, and fault protection come out the same on every job. Keep the two bases separate (430.6): these table numbers size the wire, the disconnect, and the fault protection; the overloads still come off the nameplate of the motor actually installed. A replacement motor of the same horsepower uses the same table FLC even when its nameplate amps differ from the old motor's. Field example: a 5 hp, 230 V single-phase well pump on a Marion County job — the table says 28 A, so the conductors size at 125 percent, 35 A, before anyone looks at the pump's nameplate; the overload setting still comes off that nameplate. The trap is sizing the conductors from the nameplate amps because 'that is the real motor.' Under 430.6, conductors, disconnects, controllers, and fault protection are sized from the table FLC; the nameplate current is used for the overloads only. A motor with a low nameplate reading does not shrink the wire. Conductors sized from the nameplate amps instead of the Table 430.248/430.250 FLC (430.6). Overload device set from the table value instead of the installed motor's nameplate (430.32). 230 V column used for a motor reconnected and running at 115 V — wrong FLC, wrong protection. Replacement motor wired to the old motor's table value after a horsepower change. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment — article intro
x: Article 440 takes hermetic refrigerant motor-compressors and air-conditioning equipment out of the general motor rules and gives them a nameplate-driven system. • The equipment nameplate states the minimum circuit ampacity (MCA) and the maximum overcurrent protection (MOCP, sometimes marked MOP or 'max fuse/breaker'), and those two printed numbers — not a horsepower table — size the circuit. • Article 440 also sets the disconnect rule Sharma's crews use daily: within sight, readily accessible, at the equipment. • Where 430 and 440 disagree for a compressor, 440 governs. Florida settles the common condenser question for houses: FBC-Residential §E3408.1 amends 210.8(F) with Exception No. 2 — GFCI protection is not required for listed and labeled HVAC equipment on one- and two-family dwellings. A hermetic compressor is sealed in a can with its overload protection inside it, and its starting current dwarfs its running current. General motor rules built on horsepower tables would mis-size both the wire and the breaker. The nameplate system puts the manufacturer's tested numbers in charge — MCA for the conductors, MOCP for the breaker — so the circuit matches the machine that actually shows up on the pad. Read the nameplate before you run the wire, every unit, every change-out. A replacement condenser with a higher MCA than the old one is a new circuit calculation, not a like-for-like swap. The arithmetic behind a typical plate: a compressor with a 20 A rated-load current gives an MCA of 25 A (125 percent, per 440.32) and an MOCP of 35 A (175 percent, per 440.22(A)) — conductors at least the MCA, breaker never above the MOCP. Photograph the nameplate for the job file at rough-in and again at start-up. Sharma practice (tip, not an S-rule): the condenser is wired to the nameplate MOCP with a standard 2-pole breaker. The 210.8(F) GFCI question for outdoor outlets/equipment has varied by TIA and local amendment — confirm the AHJ position on the job rather than assuming; see the Chapter 2 cross-link on the 440.4(B) page. The trap is sizing a condenser circuit from the tonnage or a horsepower table, or choosing the breaker to match the wire's ampacity. Article 440 is nameplate-driven: the MCA sizes the conductors and the MOCP caps the breaker, and the breaker is allowed to be larger than the conductor ampacity because the equipment's own overload protection does the running protection. Borrowing that allowance for a general circuit outside Article 440 is the second trap — it exists only inside this system. Breaker larger than the nameplate MOCP — rounded up past the printed maximum. Conductors sized from the unit's tonnage or a horsepower table instead of the MCA. Change-out condenser with a higher MCA landed on the old circuit with no recalculation. Disconnect not within sight of the equipment, or mounted where it covers the nameplate. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 440.11: If unqualified people can readily reach an A/C or refrigeration disconnect, any door or hinged cover that exposes energized parts must take a tool to open or accept a lock. Disconnect readily accessible to unqualified people? A door or hinged cover that opens onto energized parts must need a tool or be lockable. • 440.8: Section 440.8 now also controls location: A/C and refrigeration equipment can't sit in the zone 3 ft out and 8 ft up, measured from a bathtub's rim or a shower's threshold. Air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment stays out of the zone 3 ft out and 8 ft up, measured from a bathtub's rim or a shower's threshold. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Reading the HVAC nameplate — MCA and MOCP do the sizing
x: Section 440.4(B) covers the nameplate marking for equipment with a hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor. The plate carries the rated-load current and the branch-circuit selection current, and the manufacturer's marked minimum circuit ampacity (MCA) and maximum overcurrent device rating (MOCP) are built from them. In field language: • MCA tells you the smallest conductor ampacity the circuit may have. • MOCP tells you the largest fuse or breaker you may protect it with. A breaker smaller than MOCP is allowed; a conductor smaller than MCA is not. The plate, not a tonnage rule of thumb, is the calculation. A hermetic compressor hides its motor inside the refrigerant circuit, so nobody can read a motor nameplate or apply the general motor tables to it. The manufacturer tests the whole unit and prints the answer: MCA already carries the 125 percent conductor sizing of 440.32, and MOCP already carries the starting-current allowance of 440.22. Reading the plate replaces a calculation the field cannot do — and removes the excuse for guessing from tonnage. On every condenser and air handler: record MCA, MOCP, voltage, and phase from the plate. Wire to at least MCA, protect at no more than MOCP, and if the installed breaker or wire disagrees with a change-out unit's new plate, stop and tell the office before start-up — that is a change order conversation, not a field improvisation. Worked example: a condenser plate reads MCA 24.5 A, MOCP 40 A. The conductor ampacity must be at least 24.5 A — 10 AWG copper (35 A at the 75°C column) covers it — and the breaker may be anything up to 40 A; Sharma's standard install protects it at the MOCP with a standard 2-pole breaker. A same-tonnage change-out plate reading MCA 17.5 / MOCP 30 is a different circuit — the plate, not the tons, decides. Cross-link (Chapter 2): the question of GFCI protection for outdoor HVAC equipment under 210.8(F) is handled on the Chapter 2 pages and is deliberately not resolved here; local AHJ position governs on the job. The trap treats MCA and MOCP like a general-purpose circuit: 'MCA 24.5 A, so a 25 A breaker and wire sized to the breaker.' Two errors stack up. The conductor is sized to MCA, not to the breaker — and the breaker may be anything up to MOCP, here 40 A, larger than the conductor's plain ampacity, because the unit's own overload protection does the running protection. The mirror-image error — a breaker above MOCP 'because it trips' — is just as wrong. Breaker larger than the nameplate MOCP left in place on a change-out — the old 50 A breaker kept for a unit marked MOCP 40. Conductors below the plate MCA because 'it is only a 3-ton' — tonnage is not an ampacity. New unit wired and started without anyone recording MCA and MOCP from the new plate. Breaker swapped to a larger size to stop start-up trips instead of diagnosing the unit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Short-circuit current rating of air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment
x: Section 440.10 requires the motor controllers, the disconnecting means, and the combination load controllers used with air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment to have a short-circuit current rating (SCCR) at least equal to the available fault current where the equipment is installed. The rating is marked on the equipment. It is the Article 440 companion to 408.6 for panelboards and 409.110 for industrial control panels. • MCA and MOCP can both be perfect and the installation can still be wrong: a unit whose SCCR sits below the available fault current is a mismatch. • The SCCR is read off the unit nameplate or control panel label, with the MCA and MOCP, before the unit is set. • The available fault current comes from the utility or the design documents. It is never estimated in the field. The problem arises on commercial rooftops and larger services, where fault current runs high. It rarely decides anything on a house condenser. Fault current is what the service can push into a dead short. Gear built for less than that does not clear the fault — it becomes the fault: contacts weld, enclosures rupture, and the failure happens in front of whoever is standing at the unit. The SCCR marking exists so the comparison is made on paper, from the nameplate and the design, before the equipment is set. On commercial HVAC work, add SCCR to the nameplate photograph set: MCA, MOCP, and SCCR, plus the available fault current when the design provides it. A mismatch goes to Mike before the unit is set, not to the inspector at final. Worked case, a rooftop package unit on a small retail job: the design shows 22 kA of available fault current. The first unit submitted is marked SCCR 10 kA — it cannot be installed, even though its MCA and MOCP fit the circuit. The approved unit is marked 65 kA, which covers the 22 kA. Record both numbers, the marked SCCR and the available fault current, in the job file. The trap is treating SCCR as one more number the nameplate sizes for you, like MCA or MOCP. Those two size the circuit to the unit. SCCR runs the other way: the building's available fault current is fixed by the service, and the unit's marked rating has to cover it. A 10 kA unit on a 22 kA service fails even with perfect wire and the perfect breaker. Packaged unit installed where the available fault current exceeds its marked SCCR. No SCCR comparison on record — the submittal shows MCA and MOCP only. Control panel label missing or illegible, so the SCCR cannot be verified. Change-out unit set with a lower SCCR than the equipment it replaced, never re-checked against the service. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Rating the air-conditioning disconnect (440.12)
x: The disconnecting means for hermetic refrigerant motor-compressor equipment is rated under 440.12, separately from the branch-circuit protection in 440.22. The disconnect's ampere rating must be at least 115 percent of the nameplate rated-load current or the branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater — or the disconnect may be chosen by the horsepower-equivalent method the section allows. A disconnect that matches the breaker size by habit can still be undersized by this section, because the two devices answer different questions. • Rating: this page — 115 percent of the greater nameplate current (440.12). • Location: within sight of the equipment (440.14). • Protection: the breaker or fuses answer to 440.22 and the nameplate MOCP. The disconnect is the switch the service tech throws and then trusts with his hands inside the unit. It carries the compressor's current through every start, all day, for years — so it is rated above the running current, not at it. An undersized disconnect overheats at its contacts, welds, or burns open, and the 'off' the tech trusted is not off at all. Worked example: nameplate rated-load current 28 A. Disconnect minimum: 28 × 1.15 = 32.2 A — so the common 60 A disconnect is the shelf pick, and a 30 A disconnect fails this section even though it exceeds the running amps. Sharma practice at trim: the condenser gets a standard disconnect and whip, set within sight of the unit (440.14) — and the rating still comes from this section, while the breaker follows the nameplate MOCP under 440.22. When a change-out unit's plate shows a higher rated-load current than the old one, re-run the 115 percent before reusing the old disconnect. Sharma practice (not code): the condenser gets a standard disconnect and whip at trim — the rating still comes from this section, and the breaker follows the nameplate under S-03. The trap: 'The disconnect matches the 30 A breaker, so it must be right.' With a 28 A rated-load current, the disconnect minimum is 32.2 A — the matched pair is a violation. The breaker answers to 440.22 and the nameplate MOCP; the disconnect answers to 440.12 at 115 percent. Different questions, different numbers. 30 A disconnect on a unit with 28 A rated-load current — under the 115 percent minimum (440.12). Disconnect rating copied from the breaker size instead of the nameplate current (440.12). Fused disconnect fitted with fuses above the nameplate MOCP (440.22). Disconnect mounted out of sight of the condenser (440.14). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The HVAC disconnect — within sight and readily accessible
x: Section 440.14 requires the disconnecting means for air-conditioning and refrigerating equipment to be within sight from the equipment and readily accessible to it, with an exception for certain industrial/process installations where conditions are met. • 'Within sight' carries the Article 100 meaning: visible and within 50 ft. • The disconnect may be on the equipment or separate from it, but a person servicing the unit must be able to reach it and see the unit from it. • A breaker inside the house panel does not satisfy this by itself. • The disconnect also may not be mounted on a panel that is designed to allow access to the equipment itself, and it may not be placed where it obscures the equipment nameplate. A tech working on a condenser has the cabinet open and his hands inside. If the only way to kill power is a breaker inside the house, someone can flip it back on without knowing he is there, and he cannot lock it out from where he stands. A disconnect he can see and reach means the unit stays dead while he works, and he can prove it is dead before he touches anything. Set the disconnect where the service tech stands: at the condenser pad, in sight, with working space in front of it, not behind a fence line or above reach. On a Marion Oaks change-out, the old disconnect sat in the old unit's shadow, so we relocated it onto the wall 8 ft from the new condenser as part of the job and noted it on the invoice record. Measure the sight line, not just the distance: at 8 ft the tech sees the unit and the disconnect in one look. If the old disconnect was never installed, add it — the change-out is not finished without it. Florida note: exterior disconnects live in weather — use listed outdoor equipment and keep the working space clear of the condensate line and landscaping at final. The trap answer is that the breaker in the house panel is the disconnect. It is not: 440.14 wants a disconnect within sight of the equipment — visible and not over 50 ft away — and readily accessible to it. A second trap is reading 'within sight' as 'on the same lot'; a disconnect 80 ft away around the corner fails both parts of the test. No disconnect at the condenser at all — only the breaker inside the house panel. Disconnect mounted on the unit's own access panel, so it comes off with the panel. Disconnect set where it covers the equipment nameplate. Disconnect behind a fence or above reach — not readily accessible from the unit. Disconnect out of view of the unit, even though it is under 50 ft away. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 440.14: The A/C and refrigeration disconnect now has to have 110.26(A) working space, on top of the long-standing in-sight and readily accessible rules. The disconnect for A/C or refrigeration equipment must now have working space that meets 110.26(A). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a compressor circuit
x: Section 440.22 sizes the branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault protection for a hermetic motor-compressor circuit. It ties the device to the equipment's rated-load current or branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater; on a listed unit, the marked MOCP on the nameplate is the number the installer works to. As with motors generally, this device is allowed to be larger than the conductor's plain ampacity, because the equipment's own overload protection does the running protection and the breaker must ride through compressor starting current. That allowance only exists inside Article 440's system — never borrow it for a general circuit. • The arithmetic behind the nameplate MOCP, from 440.22(A): not more than 175 percent of the rated-load or branch-circuit selection current. • If a device at 175 percent will not carry the starting current, the rating may be increased, but not above 225 percent. • 440.22(A) also sets a floor: the device may not be less than 125 percent of the rated-load current. • Worked example: a compressor with a 20 A rated-load current takes protection at 20 × 1.75 = 35 A; if 35 A will not start it, the ceiling is 20 × 2.25 = 45 A. On listed equipment the manufacturer's printed MOCP already reflects this math, so the plate still governs — this arithmetic is for the compressor-only case and for checking a plate that looks wrong. • 440.22(B) covers equipment with more than one motor or other loads. A hermetic compressor starts hard, and its motor is sealed inside the shell under the equipment's own overload protection. The branch device has one job: clear a short circuit or ground fault without tripping on every start. Sizing it by house-circuit rules would nuisance-trip a healthy unit; oversizing it past the MOCP leaves fault energy unchecked. If a condenser trips a breaker sized at or below its MOCP, the fault is in the equipment or the circuit, not in the arithmetic: measure starting and running current and inspect the contactor and conductors before anyone proposes a larger breaker. A breaker above the nameplate MOCP is never the fix. On a Sharma change-out, the new unit's plate is photographed at set time, and the existing breaker is checked against the new MOCP before the disconnect is closed. The trap is reaching for a bigger breaker when a condenser trips — 'go up one size and see.' If the breaker is already at the nameplate MOCP, a larger one violates 440.22 and hides the real fault. The other trap pick: sizing the device at 175% of the MCA. The percentages run off rated-load or branch-circuit selection current, not MCA. Breaker larger than the nameplate MOCP on a listed condenser (440.22). Device below 125% of rated-load current, tripping on every compressor start (440.22(A)). Protection raised past 225% of rated-load current because the unit 'would not start.' Article 440 percentages borrowed for a general-purpose circuit outside Article 440. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Conductor sizing for a single motor-compressor
x: Section 440.32 sizes conductors for a single hermetic motor-compressor: • The conductor ampacity must be not less than 125 percent of the compressor's rated-load current, or of the branch-circuit selection current, whichever is greater. • On listed equipment the manufacturer has already done this work and printed it as the MCA (minimum circuit ampacity) on the nameplate. The field rule and the nameplate rule agree: the conductor ampacity must be at least the MCA. • Where you are sizing from a compressor's own data rather than a unit plate — a compressor-only replacement — this section is the arithmetic behind the plate. Worked example: a compressor with a 20 A rated-load current needs conductors with an ampacity of at least 20 × 1.25 = 25 A, before any other checks. A compressor runs for hours at a stretch through a Florida summer, and its current does not politely stop at the nameplate value on a hot roof or a low-voltage afternoon. The 125 percent margin keeps the conductors from living at their temperature limit for the whole cooling season — which is what cooks insulation, loosens terminations and starts nuisance trips that turn into callbacks. When the plate is present, wire to the MCA and do not re-derive it — on a condenser change-out, the MCA and MOCP printed on the new unit's plate are the whole sizing job. When the plate is missing or illegible on existing equipment, stop and get the data from the manufacturer rather than estimating from tonnage: a "3-ton" guess is not a current rating, and two units of the same tonnage can carry different compressors. Photograph the plate at the survey so the wire gets ordered right the first time. The trap answer sizes the wire from the MOCP — or from tonnage. The MOCP is short-circuit and ground-fault protection (440.22), and it is allowed to be far larger than the conductor ampacity; it does not size the wire. Conductors come from the MCA, which is 440.32's 125 percent already worked out by the manufacturer. Conductors sized to the MOCP, or to a tonnage guess, instead of the nameplate MCA. Old conductors reused on a change-out without checking them against the new unit's MCA. Compressor-only replacement wired from the old unit's plate instead of the new compressor's rated-load or selection current. MCA guessed from a faded, sun-bleached plate — the data was never pulled from the manufacturer. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Room air conditioners (440.60–440.65)
x: Part VII of Article 440 covers the cord-and-plug room air conditioner — the window and through-wall units a tenant or homeowner plugs in. Part VII covers room units rated not over 40 A, 250 V, single-phase (440.62(A)). • A single room unit on a branch circuit of its own may not exceed 80 percent of that circuit's rating. • Where the same circuit also feeds lighting or other receptacles, the unit may not exceed 50 percent of the circuit rating. • 440.65 adds the plug protection: single-phase room units must have leakage-current detection (LCDI) or arc-fault protection in the attachment plug or cord. • 440.65 also allows a factory-installed heat-detecting circuit interrupter (HDCI) besides LCDI or AFCI on single-phase cord-and-plug room air conditioners. The fat plug with the test buttons is a requirement, not an accessory. A room unit is a motor load that runs for hours, plugged into whatever circuit is nearby. On a shared circuit it can hold half the capacity all afternoon, heating wiring that was roughed for lights and chargers. The plug protection exists because these cords get pinched in windows, aged and wet; LCDI, AFCI or HDCI in the plug catches cord damage before it starts a fire. A window unit tripping a shared bedroom circuit is usually the 50 percent rule announcing itself. The numbers: a 12 A unit in a Winter Garden rental bedroom sits on a 20 A circuit that also feeds the lights and receptacles, so the cap is 50 percent — 10 A — and the unit is already over it. The fix is a dedicated circuit under the 80 percent rule, where the cap is 16 A and the 12 A unit fits — not a bigger breaker on the shared circuit. The trap: 'The unit draws 12 A and the breaker is 20 A, so it complies.' On a circuit shared with lighting or other receptacles the cap is 50 percent of the rating — 10 A on a 20 A circuit — so the 12 A unit fails. The 80 percent figure only applies when the unit is alone on its own branch circuit. 12 A window unit on a 20 A bedroom circuit shared with lighting — over the 50 percent cap of 10 A, 440.62. Room unit's LCDI plug cut off and replaced with a plain plug after nuisance trips, 440.65. 'Dedicated circuit' fixed by swapping in a larger breaker on the shared circuit instead of running a new circuit. Room unit rated 45 A treated under Part VII — Part VII stops at 40 A, 250 V, single-phase, 440.62(A). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Generators — article intro
x: Article 445 covers generators themselves: their marking, conductor ampacity, overcurrent protection, and shutdown controls. The working rules Sharma uses most: • Listing: stationary generators at 600 volts or less must be listed (445.6) • Overcurrent protection for the machine itself (445.12) • Conductors from the generator sized at not less than 115 percent of the nameplate current rating (445.13) • Shutdown controls, including the outdoor shutdown for a generator at a one- or two-family dwelling (445.18(D)) The transfer equipment and the optional-standby-system rules that decide what a generator may feed live mainly in Chapter 7 (Article 702), and required standby systems in 700/701 — this article is about the machine. Sharma meets 445 on whole-house generator work in dwellings, where the 2020 outdoor shutdown rule is the item inspectors ask about. A generator is a second power source that starts by itself, often at 2 a.m. in a storm, with nobody watching. If its conductors are sized like a normal feeder, a long outage at full load overheats them. If it cannot be shut down from outside the house, first responders stand next to a running machine they cannot stop. Article 445 keeps the machine itself from becoming the emergency. Separate the two questions on a generator job: is the machine itself installed to 445, and is the system it feeds wired and sized to Chapter 7? Passing one does not pass the other. On a typical whole-house job the unit is a 22 kW standby generator at 240 V single-phase, nameplate current about 92 A. The feeder conductors are sized from that nameplate: 92 × 115 percent = 105.8 A, so conductors rated at least 106 A — 2 AWG copper at the 75°C column is 115 A (445.13). The shutdown device goes outside the dwelling, where occupants and first responders can reach it (445.18(D)). Cross-link to Chapter 7 for transfer-switch sizing; do not size a transfer switch from this chapter. The exam trap is sizing generator conductors at 100 percent of nameplate, like an ordinary feeder. 445.13 wants not less than 115 percent of the generator's nameplate current rating, because the machine can be asked to carry its full rating for an entire outage. A second trap: answering a transfer-switch or load question from Article 445 — what the generator may feed is decided in Chapter 7, not here. Generator not listed, or the listing label missing on a stationary unit at 600 V or less (445.6). Feeder conductors sized at 100 percent of nameplate instead of 115 percent (445.13). No readily accessible shutdown device outside the dwelling on an outdoor generator at a one- or two-family dwelling (445.18(D)). Generator with no overload protection — no inherent design, breaker, or fuses (445.12). Transfer switch sized from Article 445 instead of the Chapter 7 system rules. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 445.18: A generator's disconnect can now sit inside the unit behind a hinged cover, provided a sign points to its location. The emergency shutdown rules moved out to 445.19. The disconnect can be inside the generator, behind a hinged door, cover or panel, as long as a sign meeting 110.21(B) shows where it is. • 445.19: Generator shutdown rules moved to their own section, 445.19. Remote and dwelling shutdown switches can now mount on the generator enclosure, labeled "Generator Emergency Shutdown." The remote shutdown switch and the dwelling shutdown device can now mount on the outside of the generator enclosure. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Stationary generators must be listed (2020 addition)
x: Section 445.6, added in the 2020 edition, requires stationary generators operating at 600 volts or less to be listed. Before this edition a generator could arrive on a job with no listing requirement stated in Article 445 itself; now the machine's listing is a code item, checked the same way as any other equipment's. The listing carries the installation instructions that 110.3(B) makes enforceable, including clearances, exhaust, and the shutdown arrangement in 445.18. A standby generator is an engine, a fuel system and a power source in one box, installed a few feet from a house. The listing is the proof that the whole machine — not just its alternator — was evaluated as a system: fuel shutoffs, exhaust temperatures, enclosure clearances, controls. Without it, every one of those judgments lands on the installer and the inspector, one job at a time. At quote stage for a standby generator, confirm the exact model is listed and get its installation manual into the job file before the pad is poured. An unlisted or grey-market unit is a stop, not a discount. On a Sharma house job that means the quote names the exact listed model, the manual's clearance and exhaust pages go in the job file, and the outdoor shutdown arrangement (445.18) is planned from the manual — not improvised at trim-out. Florida note: hurricane-season generator work is where unlisted units most often appear in Sharma's territory; the listing check happens at quote, not at inspection. The trap is the voltage line. Under the 2020 book, 445.6 reaches stationary generators at 600 volts or less — a bigger unlisted machine is outside this section's text (other rules still apply). The 2023 edition removes the limit: every stationary generator must be listed. Answering 'any voltage' on a 2020 question — or '600 volts or less' on a 2023 question — is the classic miss. Generator with no listing label, or a label for a different model than the one quoted (445.6). Grey-market or imported unit delivered with no recognized listing mark. Installation manual not on site, so clearances and exhaust are guessed instead of per 110.3(B). Listing label painted over or weathered off before the final inspection. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 445.6: Stationary generators of any voltage now need a listing. The 2020 rule only reached units rated 600 volts or less. All stationary generators must be listed, whatever their voltage rating. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Overcurrent protection for generators (445.12)
x: Section 445.12 requires generators to be protected from overload: • The protection may be inherent in the machine's design, circuit breakers, fuses, or another identified means — but one of them must be there, and it is chosen from the nameplate. • It works with 445.13, which sizes the conductors from the generator at 115 percent of nameplate current. The generator's own protection and the wire leaving it are both chosen from the nameplate. • A transfer scheme must never leave the generator feeding a fault or an overload with nothing able to open. Together they mean a fault or an overload cannot cook the machine that is supposed to be the backup. During an outage the generator is the only source the building has, and it will try to feed whatever is connected — including a fault — until something opens or something burns. A generator's windings are not sized to carry fault or overload current while it waits for help. Overload protection at the machine is what lets the backup survive the emergency it was bought for. Read the generator nameplate for both numbers at the site survey: rated amps for the 445.13 conductor math, and the machine's built-in protection for the 445.12 check. Both go on the job record. Example: a 22 kW standby unit at 240 V single-phase has a nameplate current of about 92 A, so the conductors leaving it need an ampacity of at least 92 × 1.15 = 105.8 A — call it 106 A minimum. On that same visit, confirm the unit's own breaker or inherent protection is in place before the transfer scheme is built around the machine. The trap answer is "the feeder breaker in the panel protects the generator, so the machine needs nothing of its own." 445.12 puts the overload protection on the generator itself — inherent design, its own breakers or fuses, or another identified means. A downstream panel breaker is distribution protection; it is not the machine's overload protection. Generator installed with no inherent overload protection and no breaker or fuses at the machine. Conductors from the generator sized at 100 percent of nameplate instead of the 115 percent 445.13 requires. Nameplate rated amps never recorded at the survey, so the conductor math and the protection check were both guessed. Transfer arrangement leaves the generator able to feed a fault with no device able to open. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Generator conductors — 115 percent of nameplate current
x: Section 445.13 sizes the conductors from a generator to its first distribution device or devices at not less than 115 percent of the generator's nameplate current rating, with the article's own provisions for cases where design prevents overloading. The margin exists because a generator can be asked to carry its full rating for the whole duration of an outage. Neutral conductor treatment has its own paragraphs in this section, so do not assume the neutral is automatically the same size as the ungrounded conductors on every system type. Worked example: a 22 kW standby unit at 240 V single-phase has a nameplate current of about 92 A; 92 × 1.15 = 105.8 A minimum conductor ampacity — the feeder lands on conductors rated at least 106 A (2 AWG copper at the 75°C column is 115 A), with the overcurrent arrangement set by the generator and transfer equipment design. A standby generator earns its keep in the worst hours: a Florida outage after a storm can run for days, with the machine carrying its full rating the whole time. Conductors sized at exactly the nameplate current would run at their limit for that entire run. The 115 percent factor is the standing margin, so the feeder from the machine never becomes the weak point in the middle of an outage. Size from the nameplate on the actual machine, and confirm whether the installation is a separately derived system before you settle the neutral and grounding arrangement — that decision belongs with the Chapter 2/Chapter 7 pages and the transfer equipment, and it changes this section's wiring. On a whole-house standby job in Marion County, read the plate before ordering wire: on the 22 kW unit in the example, the 92 A nameplate set the feeder — not the rounded numbers on the sales sheet. The trap is sizing the generator feeder like an ordinary feeder at 100 percent of the load, or working from kilowatts alone. 445.13 starts from the nameplate current rating and takes 115 percent of it: a 92 A plate means conductors of at least 105.8 A ampacity before any other adjustment is even considered. Generator conductors sized at 100 percent of nameplate current — no 115 percent (445.13). Feeder sized from the kW rating on the sales sheet; the nameplate current on the machine was never read. Neutral assumed the same size as the ungrounded conductors without checking the system type and transfer arrangement. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Outdoor shutdown for a generator at a one-family dwelling
x: Section 445.18(D) covers the emergency shutdown of a generator installed outdoors at a one- or two-family dwelling. In addition to the shutdown provisions that apply to generators generally, a dwelling-unit generator located outside must have a readily accessible disconnecting/shutdown device located outside the dwelling. The location is the point: the machine can be shut down by occupants or first responders without entering the building, and without standing at the machine itself. Read it together with the rest of 445.18, which governs shutdown of the prime mover generally — this shutdown stops the engine, not just the electrical output. When a generator faults, catches fire, or keeps feeding a damaged service at 2 a.m., the people who arrive first are family and firefighters — not electricians. Neither should have to enter the house, hunt for a panel, or stand next to a running machine to stop it. An outside shutdown puts the kill switch where a responder would look for it. On a dwelling generator job, locate the outdoor shutdown where a responder would look for it — at the normal entry side of the house, plainly identified — and test it at start-up. On a Sharma standby job in Winter Park, the shutdown went on the exterior wall beside the front entry, labeled as the generator emergency shutdown, where the homeowner and a fire crew would both find it. Confirm the device you installed is the one the generator's listing and the AHJ expect; note its location on the job record and the panel directory. The trap answer is that the generator's own disconnect, or the breaker in the house panel, satisfies the dwelling rule. 445.18(D) wants a separate shutdown device, located outside the dwelling and readily accessible, so the prime mover can be stopped without entering the building or standing at the machine. Outdoor dwelling generator with no shutdown device outside the house (445.18(D)). Shutdown device behind a locked gate or inside the garage — not readily accessible. Shutdown device unlabeled; a responder cannot tell what it kills. Shutdown location missing from the panel directory and the job record. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 445.19: The emergency-shutdown rules moved from 445.18 to new 445.19; for one- and two-family dwellings the remote emergency shutdown must be outside the dwelling (445.19(C)). 445.18 now lets the generator disconnect sit inside the unit behind a cover if a 110.21(B) sign shows where it is. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Transformers and transformer vaults — article intro
x: Article 450 covers transformers: overcurrent protection of the transformer and its conductors, location, guarding, ventilation, and the vault construction rules for indoor installations. Sharma's day-to-day contact is the small dry-type transformer in light commercial work — a 480-to-208/120 step-down or a control transformer — where the protection table and the primary/secondary conductor rules are the working content. Vault and liquid-filled rules are later-pass material for this book. • Protection comes from the 450.3 tables — Table 450.3(B) for transformers at 1000 V and below. The answer depends on the transformer's rated currents and on whether protection is primary-only or on both sides; never carry one remembered percentage to a different case. • Location has teeth: an indoor dry-type of 112½ kVA or less sits at least 12 in. from combustible material, unless a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier separates them (450.21). Larger indoor dry-types go in a transformer room of fire-resistant construction. • Ventilation is an installation requirement, not housekeeping (450.9): air must circulate and carry the heat away, and the vents stay clear. A transformer is a heater that also changes voltage — its losses come out as heat, and its failure mode is insulation cooking slowly until a winding shorts. The protection table balances two jobs: small enough to clear a faulted winding, large enough to ride through magnetizing inrush every time the primary is energized. The clearance and ventilation rules keep the transformer's steady heat away from things that burn. For a dry-type install: confirm primary and secondary protection against the 450.3 table for the actual voltages, confirm the secondary conductors are protected as Chapter 2 requires, and keep ventilation clearances the listing demands. Photograph the transformer nameplate into the job file. Worked example from the 450.3 page: a 45 kVA, 480-to-208/120 V dry-type draws about 54 A on the primary, so primary-only protection at 125 percent is 67.5 A and a 70 A device is the standard pick. Set the unit with its 12 in. of air off the combustible wall, vents open top and bottom. The trap is memorizing '125 percent' as the transformer rule. That is one row of Table 450.3(B): primary-only protection where the rated currents are 9 A or more. The same table allows primary protection up to 250 percent when the secondary is protected at not over 125 percent, up to 167 percent for primary currents under 9 A, and up to 300 percent under 2 A. The exam hands you a case; the table hands back the percentage. Primary protection picked from a remembered percentage instead of the 450.3(B) row for the actual case. Dry-type transformer set tight to a combustible wall — 12 in. or a fire-resistant barrier (450.21). Vent openings blocked by stored material, transformer top used as a shelf (450.9). Secondary conductors landed with no protection as 240.21(C) requires. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 450.2: 450.2 is no longer a definition. It's now a rule: each transformer must meet Article 450 on its own, unless a specific rule allows units to be tied together and run as one. Each transformer has to meet Article 450 by itself. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Overcurrent protection for transformers
x: Section 450.3 sets transformer overcurrent protection through its tables, one for transformers over 1000V and one for 1000V and below, with the required protection depending on voltage, whether protection is primary-only or primary-and-secondary, and the transformer's impedance where the table calls for it. Primary-only protection is permitted only within the table's limits; beyond them, both sides must be protected. The percentages are table lookups for the specific case — do not carry one remembered percentage to a different voltage or impedance. The Table 450.3(B) rows (1000 V and below) that cover the dry-type work Sharma actually sets: • Primary and secondary currents of 9 A or more, primary protection only — 125 percent of rated primary current • Same size range, protection on both sides — primary up to 250 percent, secondary not over 125 percent • Primary current under 9 A, primary protection only — up to 167 percent • Primary current under 2 A, primary protection only — up to 300 percent Where the calculated percentage falls between standard device ratings, the table's notes permit the next higher standard rating in the cases they cover. Worked example: a 45 kVA, 480-to-208/120 V transformer draws about 54 A on the primary; primary-only protection is 54 × 1.25 = 67.5 A, so a 70 A device is the standard pick. A transformer must survive its own magnetizing inrush every time it is energized, so its protection cannot be sized like an ordinary load. But leave a faulted transformer under-protected and it cooks its windings and can damage everything fed from it. The table balances the two: percentages high enough to ride through inrush, low enough to open on a real fault — with the case in front of you, not a remembered number, deciding which percentage applies. Sharma sets a 45 kVA Siemens dry-type transformer in a small Orlando retail build-out, 480 V in and 208/120 V out. The primary draws about 54 A. The design protects the primary only, and the primary and secondary currents are both 9 A or more, so Table 450.3(B) gives 125 percent: 54 × 1.25 = 67.5 A, and the standard device picked is 70 A. The worksheet states the case in writing — 1000 V and below, primary-only, currents 9 A or more — so the next person does not have to guess which table row produced the 70 A device. The trap is remembering one number — usually 250 percent — and using it everywhere. 250 percent is the primary ceiling only when the secondary is also protected at not over 125 percent. A primary-only installation with currents of 9 A or more is limited to 125 percent. Transformer protected primary-only at 250 percent with no secondary protection — that percentage requires protection on both sides (Table 450.3(B)). Primary device set at 167 percent on a 54 A primary — the 167 percent row covers primary currents under 9 A only. Protection picked from a remembered percentage without working the table for the case — voltage class, impedance, one side or both. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Transformer ventilation — and no storage on top
x: Section 450.9 requires a transformer to be installed so air can circulate and carry its heat away. Ventilation is an installation requirement, not a housekeeping preference. • Keep every vent opening clear — no stored material against the vented faces, and no wall, cover, or other equipment set so close that it chokes the airflow the manufacturer designed for. • The horizontal top surface of a covered dry-type transformer is marked against use for storage. Treat the top as equipment space, never as a shelf. • A transformer is a heater by design losses. Even idling it warms up; under load the heat has to leave, or the winding temperature climbs and the insulation ages fast. Heat leaving the unit is only half the location check. Section 450.21 covers keeping that heat away from combustible material: 12 in of separation for dry-types rated 112½ kVA or less, unless a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier separates them. Insulation life is a temperature story. A dry-type transformer that cannot shed heat runs its windings hotter every loaded hour, and the insulation breaks down years early — brittle leads and heat damage first, and in the worst case a fault inside a sealed case in an occupied building. Blocked vents and storage on top trip nothing and alarm nothing; they just cook the unit quietly until it fails. On a service call at a Winter Park strip center, Sharma found a 45 kVA, 480-to-208/120 V dry-type — the size the shop sets most — with paint cans and spare ceiling tiles stacked on its top and boxes of lamps tight against both vented sides. The case was hot to the touch and the unit was humming hard. The crew cleared the top and the vents, confirmed the 12 in to the wood-framed closet wall (450.21), and photographed the storage for the job report rather than just moving it quietly — storage moved without a word is back within a month. The trap is treating the flat top of a dry-type transformer as dead space: 'It is only storage — the transformer still runs.' The top of a covered dry-type is marked against storage, and blocking the unit's heat path is an installation failure whether or not anything has failed yet. The second trap is calling ventilation the manufacturer's problem. Section 450.9 puts it on the installer. Boxes, paint cans and spare parts stacked on top of a dry-type transformer, over the factory no-storage marking. Vent openings blocked by stored material, or a wall or cover set inside the manufacturer's clearance so the unit cannot breathe. Dry-type transformer rated 112½ kVA or less set closer than 12 in to combustible material with no fire-resistant barrier (450.21). Indoor dry-type over 112½ kVA installed in an ordinary closet instead of a fire-resistant transformer room (450.21). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: A transformer needs a disconnecting means
x: Section 450.14 requires a disconnecting means for every transformer except Class 2 and Class 3 units. The disconnect opens all ungrounded primary conductors, and it has exactly two legal places to live: • In sight of the transformer — visible from the transformer and not more than 50 ft away (Article 100). • In a remote location — allowed only when the disconnect is lockable in the open position under 110.25, with the locking provision in place whether or not the lock is installed, and the disconnect's location is field-marked on the transformer. The primary breaker or a safety switch can serve as the disconnecting means. What the section will not accept is a remote disconnect that nobody can lock or find. A transformer stays energized from its primary side even with every secondary breaker off, and a switch closed somewhere upstream can re-energize it without warning. The rule guarantees the person servicing the unit a way to open its source and keep it open — and, when that switch is in another room, a way to find it. Lockable means the off state survives other people: the locking provision stays in place with or without the lock. A 45 kVA dry-type transformer, 480 V to 208Y/120 V, in an Orlando tenant build-out. It draws about 54 A on the primary, protected at 70 A under Table 450.3(B) — the worked example on the sibling page. The panel feeding it sits in an electrical room 60 ft away, out of view: that is a remote disconnect, not an in-sight one. So the primary breaker gets its lockable arrangement in place, and the transformer gets a field-applied label — "Primary disconnect: Panel MDP, electrical room." Decide both with the transformer location, not after, and record them in the job file. The trap: "The transformer is fed from a breaker in the panel, so it already has a disconnect — nothing else is required." Only half true. The breaker can serve as the disconnecting means, but when it is not in sight of the transformer, 450.14 adds two conditions: lockable under 110.25, and its location field-marked on the transformer. Miss either one and the installation fails. Transformer installed with no disconnecting means (450.14). Remote disconnect not capable of being locked in the open position (450.14, 110.25). Remote disconnect location not field-marked on the transformer (450.14). Disconnect treated as "in sight" when it is not visible from the transformer, or is over 50 ft away. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Where dry-type transformers may sit (450.21)
x: Section 450.21 governs indoor dry-type transformer locations. • Transformers rated 112½ kVA or less must sit at least 12 inches from combustible material, unless separated from it by a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier. • That rule does not apply to transformers rated 1000V or less that are completely enclosed, except for ventilating openings (450.21(A) Exception). • Larger indoor dry-types — over 112½ kVA — go in a transformer room of fire-resistant construction with a minimum 1-hour fire rating. • Exception No. 1 to the room rule covers Class 155 or higher insulation systems separated by a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier, or by at least 6 ft horizontally and 12 ft vertically from combustible material. Ventilation under 450.9 keeps the heat moving; this section keeps the heat away from things that burn. A dry-type transformer is a box of heat by design, and a fault inside one can throw sparks and flame. Combustible material close by turns an equipment failure into a building fire. The 12-inch gap, the barrier, and the rated room all do the same job at different sizes: keep the transformer's worst day from reaching anything that burns. Setting a 75 kVA dry-type in a wood-framed electrical closet on a small commercial build-out: at 75 kVA the unit is under the 112½ kVA line, so the rule is 12 inches from combustible material, or a fire-resistant, heat-insulating barrier between the unit and the wall. Measure the 12 inches before the transformer is hung, not after. The closet's wall finish decides which rule you are under — confirm what the wall is made of before the unit goes up. The trap is applying the 12-inch rule to every dry-type. A unit over 112½ kVA does not get in with 12 inches and good intentions — it needs the 1-hour fire-resistant transformer room unless an exception applies. The reverse trap also fails: a completely enclosed unit rated 1000V or less is excepted from the 12-inch rule, ventilating openings and all, so demanding 12 inches there is not the code either. Dry-type rated 112½ kVA or less set a few inches from a wood-framed wall with no barrier. Transformer over 112½ kVA installed in an ordinary electrical closet — no 1-hour fire-resistant room, and no exception met. Clearance checked to the studs while the combustible wall finish was ignored — the finish is combustible material. Separation provided by a barrier that is not fire-resistant, heat-insulating material. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Phase converters — article intro
x: Article 455 covers phase converters, the equipment that lets three-phase motors run from a single-phase supply. • Two kinds (455.2): rotary converters, which make the third phase with a rotating idler, and static converters, which do it with capacitors and electronics. • Marking (455.4): the nameplate states the maker, input and output voltages, frequency, rated single-phase input full-load amperes, and the minimum, maximum single, and total load the converter may serve. • Supply conductors (455.6(A)(1)): for variable loads, ampacity at least 125 percent of the nameplate single-phase input full-load amperes. • Overcurrent protection (455.7): not over 125 percent of the rated input current. • Disconnect (455.8): in sight of the converter, rated at least 115 percent of the nameplate input amperes. • The manufactured phase (455.6(B), 455.9): the leg the converter creates gets a distinctive marking everywhere it is accessible, and no single-phase load is connected to it. Sizing throughout the article is tied to the converter and the largest motor or load it serves. Sharma meets converters rarely, on small commercial and agricultural-type jobs at the edge of its territory; this page gives the article its place and scope. A converter is a motor load with heavy starting current, and its nameplate input is the only honest measure of what the supply will see. Undersize the input and the three-phase motors start hard, run hot and trip. The manufactured leg is its own hazard: it is not a utility phase, and a 120 V load landed on it can be damaged, or damage the balance of the system. A converter is sized to its load, not to the building service. Get the motor data for everything the converter will ever run at once, and give that list to the office before quoting the install. Worked example: a small shop's rotary converter is nameplated 40 A single-phase input. The supply conductors need at least 125 percent of 40 A, so 50 A ampacity (8 AWG copper). The breaker may not exceed 125 percent, so 50 A. The disconnect must be at least 115 percent, which is 46 A, so a 60 A switch goes in, in sight of the converter. The trap is sizing the supply from the three-phase motor's full-load amps, the way a normal motor feeder is figured. Article 455 keys everything to the converter's nameplate single-phase input: conductors at 125 percent of that number, not of the motor's. Supply conductors sized to the motor load instead of 125 percent of the converter nameplate input. Manufactured phase not identified: no distinctive marking where the conductors are accessible. Single-phase load connected to the manufactured phase. No disconnect in sight of the converter, or one rated under 115 percent of the nameplate input. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Capacitors — article intro
x: Article 460 covers capacitors installed on electrical systems, most often for power-factor correction on commercial services and large motor loads. • Conductors are sized above the capacitor's rated current: ampacity not less than 135 percent of rated current (460.8(A)). Conductors tying a capacitor into a motor circuit are also at least one-third the ampacity of the motor circuit conductors. • Overcurrent protection and a disconnecting means are part of every capacitor installation, and the disconnect is rated not less than 135 percent of rated current (460.8). • A capacitor holds its charge after it is switched off. A discharge means must bring the residual voltage down to 50 volts or less within 1 minute after disconnection; equipment over 1000 volts gets 5 minutes (460.6). • Capacitor cases are grounded (460.10), and every capacitor carries a nameplate giving the manufacturer, rated voltage, frequency, kvar or amperes, number of phases, and whether it has an internal discharge device (460.12). That stored charge is the safety point of the article: a disconnected capacitor is not automatically a dead capacitor. A capacitor is a battery that charges in a fraction of a second. Open the disconnect and the bank can sit at full voltage, waiting for the next pair of hands. The discharge rule exists so the stored energy bleeds off on a timer instead of through a person. The 135 percent conductor rule exists because a capacitor circuit runs hotter than its nameplate suggests once harmonics and tolerance stack up in service. On a power-factor correction job at a small commercial service, the bank's nameplate reads 60 A rated current. The conductors are sized at 135 percent — 81 A ampacity minimum — before the run is pulled. Treat capacitor terminals as live until discharged and verified with a meter. Allow the discharge device its time, then test — never assume. Include the capacitor's kvar and voltage from its nameplate in the job record. The trap answer is 'the capacitor is dead once the disconnect is open.' It is not: it holds its charge until the discharge means bleeds it down, and 460.6 allows a full minute to get to 50 volts. Test before touch, every time. Second trap: sizing the conductors at 100 percent of rated current — capacitor circuits take 135 percent (460.8(A)). Capacitor conductors sized at 100 percent of rated current instead of 135 percent (460.8(A)). No discharge means connected, or a discharge resistor removed during service and never reconnected (460.6). Capacitor case not connected to the equipment grounding conductor (460.10). Nameplate data — kvar and voltage — missing from the job record, so the replacement bank is a guess (460.12). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Resistors and reactors — article intro
x: Article 470 covers separate resistors and reactors installed on electrical circuits — starting and braking resistors for motors, current-limiting and neutral-grounding reactors, and similar equipment bought as a device, not built into another machine (470.1). • These devices make heat by design. Space separation is the headline rule: if a resistor or reactor sits less than 12 in from combustible material, a thermal barrier is required (470.3). • They are not placed where they are exposed to physical damage (470.2). • Enclosure and guarding keep hands off live, hot parts, cases are grounded, and clearances to grounded surfaces suit the voltage. • Conductors are sized for the duty: a starting resistor sees short, heavy bursts, while a reactor carries load current continuously. Sharma encounters this equipment mainly inside larger commercial gear rather than as field-installed material, so this page is the scope and the heat rules. A resistor turns electricity into heat on purpose. Set it against wood, dust or stored cardboard and the device does its normal job while it starts a fire. The 12 in space-separation rule and the thermal barrier exist because the failure is not a malfunction — it is the equipment working exactly as designed, in the wrong place. Heat is the installation: keep the clearances and ventilation the listing requires, and do not enclose a resistor bank in a way its manufacturer did not intend. On a commercial service call, Sharma finds a motor starting-resistor bank mounted over a wood platform with stored boxes pushed against it: the boxes come out, the 12 in separation is restored, and the heat discoloration on the frame is reported in writing. If a reactor or resistor shows heat discoloration on a service call, report it rather than just resetting the equipment. The trap is treating a resistor bank like a junction box — mount it anywhere and close it in. Article 470's first question is heat: less than 12 in from combustible material without a thermal barrier fails (470.3), no matter how neat the conduit work looks. Resistor bank mounted against a wood wall or stored combustibles with no thermal barrier (470.3). Resistor or reactor installed where carts, forklifts or stored material can hit it (470.2). Bank enclosed or covered so its heat cannot escape — against its listing and instructions (110.3(B)). Heat-discolored resistor found on a service call and simply reset, with nothing reported. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 470.2: Made new Section 470.2 the placeholder for reconditioned equipment, indicating that reconditioning of a resistor is not permitted and that reactors shall follow manufacturers' guidelines. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Storage batteries — article intro
x: Article 480 covers stationary storage battery installations: the battery systems that back up services, feed UPS equipment, and increasingly pair with solar and generator work. Its working rules: • Disconnecting means for the battery circuits (480.7) • Overcurrent protection for battery conductors • Wiring and interconnections between cells and batteries (480.12) • Ventilation and spill concerns that depend on battery chemistry Chemistry drives the details. Under 480.3, storage batteries and battery management equipment must be listed; the requirement does not apply to lead-acid batteries. The listing carries the room and protection details for that system. The article works alongside the energy-storage rules in Chapter 7 (Article 706), which govern the system as a whole — 480 is about the battery installation itself. A battery bank is stored energy that never turns off. Opening a breaker does not discharge it, and a bank can deliver enormous fault current at very low impedance. Heat, vented gas and corrosive electrolyte depend on the chemistry in the rack. Article 480 exists so the bank can be disconnected, protected and serviced without the room or the wiring becoming the hazard. Identify the chemistry and the system listing before you wire anything: vented, sealed, and lithium systems have different room and protection needs. On a small commercial UPS job, a 120 V DC string — ten 12 V batteries in series — is over the 60 V line in 480.7(A), so it gets a DC-rated disconnect, readily accessible and within sight of the bank, labeled with the nominal voltage and the available short-circuit current. Put the battery disconnect where it is identified for the system and label it at the service as the system rules require (see Chapter 7 cross-links). Florida note: battery rooms and garages in Florida heat age batteries faster; record the install date and chemistry in the job file so replacement is planned, not discovered during an outage. The trap is treating Article 480 and Article 706 as the same article. 706 governs the energy storage system as a whole; 480 governs the battery installation itself. A second trap: assuming every battery needs a listing. In the 2020 rules the 480.3 listing requirement does not apply to lead-acid batteries — it is the other chemistries and the battery management equipment that must be listed. Battery disconnect is an AC-only switch with no DC rating on a string over 60 V DC (480.7). No disconnecting means for the ungrounded battery conductors, or the disconnect is out of sight of the bank. Non-lead-acid batteries installed with no listing (480.3). Interconnection lugs loose or torqued by feel on a bank that can deliver thousands of amps of fault current (480.12). Battery disconnect unlabeled: no nominal voltage or available short-circuit current marking (480.7(D)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 480.1: Article 480 is now Stationary Standby Batteries and covers only standby battery systems over 1 kWh. Smaller ones, like a fire alarm panel battery, fall outside it. Article 480 now applies only to stationary standby batteries with more than 1 kWh (3.6 MJ) of capacity. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Battery disconnects — DC is its own problem
x: Section 480.7 sets the disconnecting methods for battery circuits, reorganized and expanded in the 2020 edition as battery requirements were gathered back into Article 480 from Article 706. What it requires: • A disconnecting means for all ungrounded conductors derived from a stationary battery system with a voltage over 60 volts DC (480.7(A)) • The disconnect must be readily accessible and located within sight of the battery system (480.7(A)) • Where remote controls operate the disconnect from out of sight, it must be capable of being locked in the open position, with a label showing where the controls are (480.7(B)) • A marking at the disconnect giving the nominal voltage and the maximum available short-circuit current, with the date it was calculated (480.7(D)) The field point that matters most: interrupting DC is harder than interrupting AC, because DC has no natural current zero to help an arc die. A switching device must be rated for the DC voltage and current it will actually break; an AC-only device is not assumed suitable, whatever its amp rating says. A battery bank does not stop being a source when you open a switch somewhere else. Its fault current is enormous and its arc does not self-extinguish the way AC does at each zero crossing. The wrong device can weld shut or keep arcing while a servicer believes the circuit is dead. The DC rating, the sight line, and the fault-current label are what make the disconnect a real disconnect. Read the DC rating on any battery disconnect, fuse holder, or breaker before it goes in, and confirm polarity markings on polarized DC devices. If the rating plate does not mention DC, the device does not go on a battery circuit. Worked case: a small commercial UPS string of ten 12 V batteries is 120 V DC nominal — well over the 60 V line — so the string gets its own DC-rated disconnect within sight of the bank, and the label at the disconnect states 120 V nominal and the available short-circuit current from the battery calculation, dated. The trap answer is that a 200 A AC-rated switch can disconnect a 120 V DC battery string because 'amps are amps.' Interrupting DC is a different job: there is no current zero, so the device must carry a DC rating for the voltage and current it will break. The second trap is the threshold: 480.7(A) is triggered over 60 volts DC, not at 250 or 600. AC-only switch or breaker installed as the battery disconnect; no DC rating on the device. No disconnecting means for the ungrounded conductors of a battery system over 60 V DC. Disconnect out of sight of the battery system, or not readily accessible. Remote-controlled disconnect that cannot be locked open, with no label showing where the controls are (480.7(B)). No marking of nominal voltage and available short-circuit current at the disconnect (480.7(D)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Battery interconnections (moved into 480 in 2020)
x: Section 480.12 carries the battery interconnection requirements that the 2020 edition moved into Article 480 from Article 706: the conductors and connections that join cells and batteries into a bank. • Interconnections are sized for the maximum current the bank can deliver. • Terminals and connection methods must be suited to the battery system installed. • The manufacturer instructions for the specific battery system govern the details the article leaves to the listing. Battery banks can deliver enormous fault current at very low impedance, so connection quality — correct lugs, correct torque, protected runs — is a safety item, not a neatness item. A battery bank does not sag the way a utility feed does. Its impedance is so low that a loose or undersized interconnection becomes the weak point of a circuit that can deliver enormous current: the bad joint heats under ordinary load, corrodes faster in battery-room air, and can arc or melt under fault current. Sound, listed, protected connections keep the bank's energy in the cables where it belongs. Torque interconnection hardware to the battery manufacturer's specification and record it; a loose intercell connection announces itself as heat under load. Keep interconnection runs protected from physical damage and from the electrolyte environment of the battery type installed. Worked case: the battery string behind a small commercial UPS is ten 12 V batteries in series — 120 V DC. Its intercell connectors are the battery maker's own parts, each one torqued to the maker's specification with the values written into the job file. At 120 V DC the string is over the 60 V line in 480.7(A), so its disconnect is the DC-rated, within-sight disconnect covered on the 480.7 page. The trap is treating intercell links like ordinary jumpers: any lug that fits, tightened by feel. Section 480.12 sizes the link for the maximum current the bank can deliver, and the connection method and torque come from the battery system's listing and the manufacturer's instructions, not from habit. “Snug” is not a torque value, and an unrecorded torque cannot be verified later. Intercell connection loose or corroded, with heat damage showing at the terminal. Lugs or connectors that are not the battery manufacturer's parts for the system. Interconnection hardware not torqued to the manufacturer's specification, or no torque record in the job file. Interconnection runs left unprotected where they cross the rack or are subject to physical damage. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Equipment over 1000 volts, nominal — article intro
x: Article 490 covers equipment operating over 1000 volts nominal: medium-voltage switchgear, conductors' termination practices, and clearances for the gear Sharma's crews do not normally install but may work around on commercial and utility-adjacent sites. It closes Chapter 4 in official order. • Scope: equipment over 1000 V nominal — switchgear, terminations, and the clearances around them. • Sharma's line: nothing in Sharma's residential work is installed under this article, and no Sharma field employee works on over-1000 V equipment under this book. • Work on the medium-voltage side is referred to qualified medium-voltage contractors. The article's working message for a Sharma crew is recognition: know what the gear is, know whose it is, and know that it is not ours to touch. Above 1000 volts, fault energy and arc flash stop being forgiving. Clearances, insulation, and gear ratings are what stand between a worker and an arc that gives no second chance — and the first protection the article builds in is keeping unqualified hands off the equipment entirely. Your job with 490 equipment is recognition and respect: identify it, keep clear of it, and never open, rack, or test it. On a commercial walk-through, pick out the utility transformer and any medium-voltage switchgear first, and keep stored material out of the clear space in front of it. Sharma's scope stays on the 1000 V-and-under side of the service. If a job appears to require work on the medium-voltage side, stop and take it to Sanjay and Mike the same day. The trap is an edition trap: answering 'Article 495' to a 2020-code question. In the NEC 2023 edition this material was renumbered as Article 495 — but permits under the FBC 8th Ed. run on the 2020 book, where it is Article 490. Name the edition before you name the article. Working clearances in front of medium-voltage gear blocked by stored material. Unqualified personnel opening or racking medium-voltage switchgear. Damaged or missing guards and covers on over-1000 V equipment left unreported. Crew treating the utility / medium-voltage side as part of a service change-out scope. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 490: Article 490 was renumbered as Article 495, 'Equipment Over 1000 Volts ac, 1500 Volts dc, Nominal'; 490.21 equipment-specific provisions were deleted/relocated. • Article 495: All the requirements previously found in Article 490, Equipment Over 1000 Volts, Nominal, have been moved to Article 495. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Hazardous (classified) locations — the starting point
x: Some areas hold enough flammable gas or vapor, combustible dust, or ignitible fibers in the air that a normal spark or hot surface could start a fire or explosion. Article 500 is the foundation for those areas: it explains how a location gets classified, how materials are grouped, which protection methods exist, and what equipment markings mean. Articles 501 through 516 then give the working rules for each kind of location. Before anyone picks a fitting, three questions have to be answered for the exact area: • What is in the air? That sets the class — Class I gases and vapors, Class II combustible dusts, Class III ignitible fibers and flyings • How often is it there in an ignitible amount? That sets the division — Division 1 for normal operation, Division 2 for abnormal conditions • What is the material, exactly? That sets the group — Class I Groups A through D, Class II Groups E through G Article 500 also covers the protection techniques in 500.7 — explosionproof and dust-ignitionproof enclosures, purging and pressurizing, intrinsic safety, and others — and the equipment marking rules in 500.8, including the temperature code that must stay below the ignition temperature of the material present. Ordinary electrical gear makes sparks and hot surfaces in normal use — contacts open, motors run, lamps get hot. In a classified area the air itself is fuel, so one ordinary device can be the ignition source for the whole room. Article 500 exists to force the classification question first: once class, division and group are fixed, every later choice — wiring method, seals, enclosures, temperature marking — has a right answer instead of a guess. Before any work in a suspect area, find the classification drawing or ask the engineer and the AHJ what the classification is. If nobody can tell you the class, division or zone, and group, stop — that answer decides every wiring method and every fitting that follows. On Sharma jobs this comes up at fueling and paint work: a dispenser island (Article 514), a spray application area (Article 516), a bulk storage plant (Article 515). The classification drawing is part of the bid documents — if it is missing, that is an open question for the packet, not a field decision. Sharma does not design hazardous-location classifications. When a job touches a classified area, the classification comes from the plans or the AHJ, and Mike Holt reviews the method before anyone roughs it in. The trap is jumping straight to a wiring article — 'just use explosionproof boxes' — without a classification. Explosionproof is one protection technique for one kind of location; dust locations, fiber locations and Zone-system locations each have their own rules, and Division 2 is not Division 1. No class, division and group means no right answer. Work roughed in inside a classified area with no classification drawing on file. Ordinary-location fittings installed inside a classified boundary. Equipment identified for the class but not for the group of the material actually present. Equipment temperature marking hotter than the ignition temperature of the gas or dust present (500.8). A classified boundary moved in the field without the engineer or AHJ revising the documents.
