NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 500.4: Hazardous (classified) areas, and areas judged unclassified, now go on an area classification drawing, and the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) gets access to the documentation. Areas classified as hazardous, and areas determined to be unclassified, now get documented on an area classification drawing backed by related documents. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: How locations are classified — class and division
x: Classification starts with what the hazardous material is and how likely it is to be present in an ignitible amount. Class I covers gases and vapors from flammable or combustible liquids, Class II covers combustible dusts, and Class III covers easily ignitible fibers and flyings. Division 1 means the hazard can be present during normal operation, while Division 2 means it is normally contained and shows up only when something fails or operates abnormally. • Class I — flammable gases and vapors, and vapors from flammable or combustible liquids; gasoline and propane vapors are the everyday examples • Class II — combustible dusts, such as grain dust, coal dust and metal dusts • Class III — easily ignitible fibers and flyings, such as textile lint, that are handled, made or stored in the area Class and division are read together: Class I Division 1 and Class II Division 1 are different locations with different wiring articles (501 and 502), and the group in 500.6 then narrows the classification to the exact material. The class tells you what can burn; the division tells you how much of the time the fuel is actually in the air. That pairing keeps the rules proportionate: gear where vapor is present every day (Division 1) is built to contain an explosion, while gear where the same vapor appears only when a seal fails (Division 2) gets a lighter — but still deliberate — set of methods. Classify wrong in either direction and you either leave an ignition source sitting in fuel or gold-plate a room that never needed it. Read the class and division off the classification documents for the exact room or area, not the whole building — one bay can be classified while the next is not. Treat a Division 1 boundary line on the drawing as a hard wall for wiring methods and seals. Worked example from the group page: gasoline vapor is Class I, Group D. Around an open transfer point it is Division 1; in the sealed-tank room next door, the same vapor is Division 2. Same building, same material, two different wiring jobs. The trap is classifying the whole building by its worst room — or the reverse, calling a Division 1 pocket 'Division 2 because the door is usually shut.' Classification is by the exact area and by how the material behaves in normal operation, not by convenience. A second trap: fibers and flyings are Class III, not Class II. Dust is Class II; fibers that settle and burn as a layer are Class III. Whole building classified from its worst room instead of the exact area on the documents. Division 1 boundary on the drawing ignored — ordinary-location fittings inside it. Fibers and flyings area wired as a Class II dust location instead of Class III. Classification copied from the last job instead of this job's classification documents. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 500.5: Class III now splits fibers and flyings into combustible ones that can explode as a cloud and ignitible ones that mainly burn as a layer. Metal combustible fibers are Class II, Division 1, Group E. Class III now sorts fibers/flyings two ways: combustible ones that can form an explosive cloud, and ignitible ones that mainly burn as a settled layer. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Material groups
x: Within each class, materials are sorted into groups by how easily they ignite and how much pressure an explosion can build. Class I groups run A through D and Class II groups run E through G, with the earlier letters generally the more severe materials. Equipment has to be identified for the specific group in the location, not just for the class. Examples that fix the letters in memory. Class I: Group A is acetylene; Group B is hydrogen and gases or vapors of equivalent hazard; Group C covers ethylene-type vapors; Group D covers the everyday fuels — gasoline, propane, natural gas, and alcohol vapors. Class II: Group E is metal dusts; Group F is carbonaceous dusts such as coal and coke; Group G is grain, flour, and other agricultural and plastic dusts. The classification documents name the group for the material actually present — these examples are orientation, not a substitute for them. Class alone does not describe the material. Acetylene and hydrogen ignite more easily and build more explosion pressure than gasoline vapor, and metal dust behaves nothing like grain dust. Equipment is tested and identified against a specific group's ignition and pressure behavior. Put Group D gear in a Group B location and the enclosure may not contain the explosion it was supposed to survive. On a Florida job — a fueling area, a propane yard, a feed mill — read the classification documents first; they name the group for the material actually present. Check the group letter on the plans against the group letters on every luminaire, motor, and enclosure nameplate before installation. A fitting approved for Group D does not automatically cover Groups A, B, or C, and a submittal that names the class but not the group goes back. The trap answer is 'Class I, Division 1 approved is enough.' It is not: the equipment must be identified for the specific group in the location. The letters also run with severity — in Class I, Group A (acetylene) is more severe than Group D (gasoline) — so a Group D listing never stretches upward to cover A, B, or C. Equipment nameplate lists the class and division but no group — or the wrong group for the material present. Group D fittings installed where the classification documents name Group B (hydrogen). Submittal approved on class alone; the group letters were never checked against the classification documents. Dust-area equipment matched to Class II but not to its dust group — grain dust (G) area fitted with gear identified for a different group. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Protection techniques
x: 500.7 lists the accepted ways to keep electrical equipment from igniting the surrounding atmosphere. Each technique only counts where the section and the equipment marking allow it: • Explosionproof enclosures, 500.7(A): built to contain an internal explosion and cool the escaping gases. Permitted in the Class I locations the equipment is identified for. • Dust-ignitionproof enclosures, 500.7(B): keep dust out, and keep arcs, sparks, and heat inside from igniting dust outside. A Class II technique. • Dusttight enclosures, 500.7(C): keep dust out. Permitted in Class II, Division 2 and in Class III locations. • Purged and pressurized systems, 500.7(D): clean air or inert gas held inside the enclosure keeps the hazardous atmosphere out. Permitted in any classified location the system is identified for. • Intrinsic safety, 500.7(E): the circuit's energy is limited below ignition level, even under fault conditions. Permitted across Class I, II, and III, Division 1 and 2 — the standard technique for instrumentation. • Nonincendive circuits, equipment, and components, 500.7(F)–(H): cannot ignite the atmosphere under normal operation. Division 2 techniques. • Oil immersion, 500.7(I): current-interrupting contacts under oil. Class I, Division 2. • Hermetically sealed equipment, 500.7(J): sealed against the surrounding atmosphere. Permitted in Class I, Division 2; Class II, Division 2; and Class III. • Combustible gas detection systems, 500.7(K): a protection method only in industrial establishments with restricted public access, where qualified persons service the installation. Classified air is fuel waiting for a spark. Every technique on this list breaks the same triangle a different way: contain the explosion, keep the atmosphere away from the arc, or keep the energy too low to ignite anything. Pick the wrong one and the enclosure itself becomes the ignition source it was hired to prevent. Match the technique on the equipment to the technique the design calls for — do not substitute a dust-ignitionproof box for an explosionproof one because it looks similar. Keep enclosure bolts, covers, and flame paths complete and undamaged, or the technique is defeated. On a fleet fueling area with a Class I, Division 1 location at the dispenser, the starter and disconnect must carry a technique permitted for that exact class and division — a similar-looking dust box off the shelf is a failed inspection and a real hazard. The trap is the look-alike swap. Dust-ignitionproof sounds like explosionproof, but it is a Class II dust technique — it does not belong in a Class I, Division 1 vapor area. In Division 1 vapor, the short list is explosionproof, intrinsic safety, or a purged and pressurized system identified for the location. Dust-ignitionproof enclosure installed in a Class I, Division 1 vapor area. Explosionproof enclosure with bolts missing and the cover not fully engaged — the flame path is defeated and the technique with it. Nonincendive equipment installed in a Division 1 location. General-purpose enclosure substituted where the design calls for a 500.7 protection technique. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 500.7: Five protection techniques, (P) through (T), joined 500.7 in 2023: two heating methods, enclosed-break and nonsparking devices, and sealed equipment. A new Chapter 9 table matches protection types to each area. Five techniques were added at 500.7(P) through (T). A new table in Chapter 9 (Table 13) shows which protection types suit each area classification. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Equipment suitability, marking, and temperature
x: Equipment for a classified location has to suit the exact class, division, and group where it sits, and gear approved for Division 1 may also serve in Division 2 of the same class and group. Nameplates carry the class, division or zone, group, and a temperature marking that shows the hottest surface the equipment can reach. That temperature marking has to stay below the ignition temperature of the gas, vapor, or dust involved. Temperature codes (the T-marking) run from the hottest permitted surface down: • T1 — 450°C (842°F) • T2 — 300°C (572°F) • T3 — 200°C (392°F) • T4 — 135°C (275°F) • T5 — 100°C (212°F) • T6 — 85°C (185°F) The equipment's marked maximum surface temperature must stay at or below the ignition temperature of the material in the location — a T3 device, allowed a 200°C surface, has no place where the gas present ignites at 180°C. Table 500.8(C) also has intermediate codes (T2A–T2D, T3A–T3C, T4A) — read the exact code off the nameplate. A classified area is a place where the air itself can burn. Any hot surface in that air is a possible match. The T-marking is the maker's tested promise of how hot the gear can get, and the ignition temperature is the point where the material lights without a spark. Keeping the first number under the second is what stops the equipment itself from becoming the ignition source. On a small commercial job — a spray booth at an Orlando body shop — the classification drawing shows a gas that ignites at 180°C. The replacement exhaust motor on the truck is marked Class I, Division 1, Group D, but its T-code is T3: a 200°C surface in a 180°C gas. Right class, right group, wrong temperature — it stays on the truck, and the T4 motor (135°C) goes in. Photograph every nameplate on classified work for the job record; the photo is the proof the check happened. The trap is reading the T-number backwards: T6 sounds like the heavy-duty rating, so it gets picked for the hottest job. It is the opposite — T1 allows the hottest surface (450°C) and T6 the coolest (85°C). A bigger T-number means a cooler, safer surface, never a stronger one. Temperature code too hot for the material present — T3 equipment (200°C) installed where the gas ignites at 180°C. Equipment marked for the class and division but not for the group of the gas or dust in the area. Nameplate painted over, damaged, or missing, so class, group, and T-code can't be verified. Division 2 equipment installed in a Division 1 location. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 500.8: Class III equipment now has a temperature rule in 500.8: its marking can't exceed the fibers' ignition temperature, with a 165°C (329°F) cap, or 120°C (248°F) for overloadable gear around ignitible fibers. In a Class III area, the equipment's temperature marking can't go above the ignition temperature of the fibers/flyings that make it hazardous (500.8(D)(3)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Class I locations — gases and vapors
x: Article 501 gives the wiring, sealing, and equipment rules for Class I locations, where the hazard is flammable gas or liquid vapor. It is the article behind fuel-handling rooms, some process areas, and the classified pockets inside garages and hangars covered later in this chapter. • Wiring methods, Division 1 (501.10(A)): threaded rigid metal conduit or threaded steel IMC is the everyday method. Type MI cable, and Type MC-HL cable where its conditions are met, are also permitted. Ordinary-location methods — NM cable, EMT with set-screw fittings, unsealed conduit — stop at the boundary. • Wiring methods, Division 2 (501.10(B)): the list relaxes — more cable types and threadless fittings on rigid conduit are permitted — but the boundary and sealing rules still apply. • Seals (501.15): a seal fitting goes within 18 in of an explosionproof enclosure that holds arcing or hot parts, and every run leaving the classified area gets a boundary seal within 10 ft of the boundary, on either side. Seal compound is poured at least as thick as the conduit's trade size, and never less than 5/8 in. • Grounding and bonding follow 501.30: the metal raceway system and the equipment in the area are bonded into the grounding system — a conduit system is only as good as its continuity. Flammable vapor does not stay politely in the room where it leaked. It migrates through the inside of a conduit system and can carry an ignition from an arcing device to equipment in a safe room. Seals break the raceway into short, closed segments so an explosion inside the pipe stays a pipe event, and threaded joints plus explosionproof enclosures keep an internal blast from lighting the room. On a Winter Park garage job, the classified pocket around the fuel-handling bench is wired from the classified drawing Mike Holt reviewed: threaded RMC throughout, the seal for the explosionproof disconnect poured 12 in from the enclosure — inside the 18 in limit — and the boundary seal set 6 ft inside the line, well within 10 ft. Nothing from the ordinary side of the shop — no NM, no ordinary boxes, no unsealed conduit — crosses that line. The classic trap swaps the two seal distances: 18 in is the enclosure seal, 10 ft is the boundary seal. An answer that puts the boundary seal “within 18 in of the boundary” or the enclosure seal “within 10 ft of the enclosure” is wrong both ways. Seal fitting installed 3 ft from the explosionproof enclosure it serves. No boundary seal where the conduit run leaves the Division 1 area. EMT with set-screw fittings run inside a Class I, Division 1 area. Seal fitting poured with compound thinner than the conduit trade size. NM cable carried across the boundary into a classified pocket. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 501.10: Threaded rigid and intermediate metal conduit wearing an extra anti-corrosion coat, PVC-coated rigid being the common one, is now named as an acceptable Class I, Division 1 wiring method. The first item in 501.10(A)(1) now covers threaded RMC (rigid metal conduit) and IMC (intermediate metal conduit) that carry a supplemental corrosion-protection coating. • 501.30: 501.30 now splits grounding from bonding, adds cable trays and tray-cable strut to what gets bonded, and narrows the Division 2 short-flex jumper exception to meter, instrument and relay circuits. New: bond any metal strut, channel or angle used to hold up or shield ITC, TC or power-limited tray cable in a Class I area. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Class II locations — combustible dusts
x: Article 502 covers Class II locations, where combustible dust is the hazard — grain, feed, wood and other manufacturing dusts. The goals are keeping dust out of enclosures, keeping surfaces cool enough not to ignite a dust layer, and wiring methods that do not let dust accumulate on live parts. Dust thickness on equipment is part of the hazard picture, not just dust in the air. • Groups (500.6): Group E is metal dusts, Group F is carbonaceous dusts such as coal and coke, and Group G is grain, flour and similar dusts. Equipment must be identified for the group actually present. • Wiring methods (502.10): Division 1 runs on threaded RMC or threaded steel IMC, Type MI cable, and dusttight boxes and fittings with threaded entries. Division 2 relaxes the list — EMT, dusttight wireways and listed cable types join it — but boxes and fittings stay dusttight. • Sealing (502.15): Class II seals are dust seals, not explosionproof seals. Where a raceway connects a dust-ignitionproof enclosure to an enclosure that is not, dust is kept out by a permanent and effective seal, a horizontal raceway at least 10 ft long, or a vertical raceway at least 5 ft long extending downward from the dust-ignitionproof enclosure. Where the other enclosure is in an unclassified location, no seal is required. • Temperature still rules: the equipment's marked surface temperature must stay below the ignition temperature of the dust (500.8) — and a dust blanket raises the risk, so housekeeping is part of the installation. Dust burns two ways. A layer settled on a hot motor is fuel resting on an ignition source, and the layer insulates the motor so it runs hotter still. And a small first event can loft settled dust into a cloud that explodes through the whole room. The article's answer is housekeeping built into the hardware: dust kept out of enclosures, surfaces kept cool, and no easy path for dust to travel into the box. In a Marion County feed store, the back room is Class II, Division 2, Group G. The dust-ignitionproof starter for the auger motor connects to a general-purpose enclosure with a horizontal raceway run of 12 ft — over the 10 ft option in 502.15, so no sealing fitting is needed on that run. Receptacle circuits are 20-ampere (S-01), boxes are dusttight, and the crew blows the dust off the motor and starter before either enclosure is opened. The trap is importing the Class I seal rules: “Class II seals must be explosionproof and within 18 in.” Neither is true. 502.15 seals only have to stop dust, they need not be explosionproof, and the raceway-length options — 10 ft horizontal or 5 ft vertical down — often replace the seal entirely. Raceway into a dust-ignitionproof enclosure with a 6 ft horizontal run and no seal — none of the 502.15 options met. Thick dust layer caked on the motor and starter, undisturbed at inspection. Ordinary open-type enclosure installed where a dust-ignitionproof enclosure is required in Division 1. Set-screw EMT fittings and non-dusttight boxes in a Division 1 dust area. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Class III locations — fibers and flyings
x: Article 503 covers Class III locations: places where easily ignitible fibers or flyings are handled, made, or stored, but do not normally float in the air in ignitible amounts. Textile mills, clothing plants, and woodworking shops that make sawdust and flyings are the classic cases. • Division 1: the fibers or flyings are manufactured, handled, or used — the saw room and the mill floor. • Division 2: the fibers are stored, or handled outside the process itself — the bale warehouse. • Heat is the main enemy. Equipment must run cool enough not to dry out and carbonize fibers piled against it: no more than 165°C (329°F) for equipment not subject to overloading, and 120°C (248°F) for equipment that can be overloaded, like motors and power transformers (503.5). Carbonized fiber can ignite by itself. • Wiring methods (503.10) are the same in both divisions: rigid metal conduit, rigid nonmetallic conduit, RTRC, IMC, EMT, dusttight wireways, or Type MC or MI cable with listed fittings. Every box and fitting is dusttight. One Division 2 exception: a storage-only area with no machinery may use open wiring on insulators (Article 398). • No sealing fittings are required in Class III — the seals of Articles 501 and 502 do not carry over. • Luminaires (503.130) keep fibers and flyings out and sparks and hot metal in, under the same 165°C (329°F) surface cap. Fibers do not need a cloud to burn. Lint settles on a hot motor or luminaire, the heat dries it and chars it, and charred fiber can smolder and ignite with no spark at all. The blanket also insulates the motor, so it runs hotter and chars the layer faster. The answer is cool surfaces, dusttight enclosures that keep fibers off live parts, and luminaires that cannot drop sparks or hot metal. Cabinet shop outside Ocala: the saw and sanding room is Class III, Division 1, and the lumber racks next door are Division 2. The takeoff runs EMT with dusttight boxes inside the boundary, enclosed and gasketed luminaires over the line, and a totally enclosed motor on the dust collector. Receptacle circuits are 20-ampere — Sharma's commercial minimum. Before any cover comes off, the crew blows the lint off the motor and fixtures — that layer is part of the hazard, not dirt. The trap is wiring Class III like Class I: sealing fittings within 18 in of every enclosure. Class III has no seal requirement at all — the enclosures are dusttight, not explosionproof, and 503.10 is the whole wiring rule. The second trap is the reverse: treating Class III as ordinary space because 'it is only lint.' The classification is real, and the 503.5 temperature caps are the write-up when a hot standard luminaire goes in. Open luminaire over the saw line, its lens packed with lint. Standard (not dusttight) box and fittings inside the classified boundary. Type NM cable run through the Class III area. Open drip-proof motor installed where a totally enclosed motor is required. Luminaire surface temperature over the 165°C (329°F) limit for the fibers present. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Intrinsically safe systems
x: Article 504 covers intrinsically safe (IS) systems. The protection is in the circuit itself: the energy is limited so low that the circuit cannot ignite the classified atmosphere, even under fault conditions. These systems live mostly in instrumentation and control wiring for classified areas. • Listed gear only. Intrinsically safe apparatus and the associated apparatus — the barrier or isolator — must be listed. • The control drawing runs the job. Section 504.10 requires installation in accordance with the manufacturer's control drawing: allowed interconnections, cable limits, and grounding all come off that drawing. • Ordinary wiring methods can serve. Section 504.20 permits the wiring methods allowed for unclassified locations, because the circuit energy is already limited. • Separation is the heart of the article. Keep IS conductors away from non-IS conductors: at least 50 mm (2 in.) of space, or a grounded metal partition, or an insulating partition (504.30). • Identification. Where a color code identifies IS wiring, the color is light blue, and raceways and wiring methods carry labels reading "Intrinsic Safety Wiring" at intervals of not more than 7.5 m (25 ft) (504.80). • Grounding and seals. Barriers and shields are grounded as the control drawing and 504.50 direct, and conduits are sealed where the article for the class requires a seal (504.70). An ordinary control circuit can spark with more than enough energy to ignite a gas or dust atmosphere. Intrinsic safety removes the ignition source instead of containing the explosion: even under fault conditions, the circuit cannot release enough energy to ignite. The separation and identification rules protect that design for the life of the plant — one later power conductor landed in the wrong duct can feed in energy the barrier never allowed. On a Sharma controls job at a chemical blending plant outside Lakeland, the engineer specifies IS loops for tank level transmitters in a Class I, Division 1 room. The crew pulls the IS pairs in their own raceway, keeps the light-blue identified cable, and lands the barriers in the safe-area panel exactly as the control drawing in the submittal shows. In the one shared junction box, the IS terminals sit across a grounded metal partition from the 120 V control power — no shared raceway, no shared duct. Mike Holt checks the control drawing against the field wiring before the loops are energized. The trap answer: "IS wiring needs explosionproof enclosures and Division 1 raceways like everything else in the room." It does not — the energy limit is the protection, so 504.20 allows ordinary wiring methods. The opposite trap also fails: "the barrier makes it ordinary wiring, so separation doesn't matter." Separation per 504.30 and the control drawing are what keep the energy limit real. IS and non-IS conductors in the same raceway or duct with no partition and less than 2 in. of separation (504.30). No control drawing on site, or field wiring that does not match the drawing (504.10). IS raceways not labeled "Intrinsic Safety Wiring," or labels spaced more than 25 ft apart (504.80). Barrier landed without the grounding the control drawing shows (504.50). IS wiring not identified — no light blue where the color code is the identification method (504.80). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Zone 0, 1, and 2 locations — the zone system for gases and vapors
x: Article 505 is the zone system for Class I gas and vapor hazards — the alternative to the class-and-division system of Article 501, used more in industrial and international-style designs. • Zone 0: an ignitible atmosphere is present continuously, or for long periods — inside a tank, above a liquid surface. • Zone 1: the atmosphere is likely to be present in normal operation — around vents and open handling points. • Zone 2: the atmosphere is not likely in normal operation, and if it shows up it lasts only a short time. • Material groups (505.6) replace the division groups: IIA covers propane, gasoline, and methane; IIB covers ethylene; IIC covers hydrogen and acetylene and is the most severe. Equipment marked IIC also suits IIB and IIA areas. • Protection techniques live at 505.8 — flameproof, pressurized, intrinsic safety, oil immersion, increased safety, encapsulation, powder filling, type 'n', and gas detection. Zone 0 takes only the most restrictive: intrinsic safety and oil immersion are the techniques that reach it. • Wiring follows the zone (505.15). Zone 0 permits only intrinsically safe wiring installed under Article 504. Zone 1 adds the heavy methods — threaded rigid and intermediate conduit, Type MI, and listed cable systems — and Zone 2 relaxes the list one step further. • Equipment is marked for the system: zone, material group, and a temperature class, T1 through T6, running from a 450°C maximum surface down to 85°C (505.9). The zone system grades the hazard by how often the ignitible cloud is actually there, then matches the protection to the exposure. Zone 0 gear lives in the cloud, so only techniques that cannot release ignition energy at all are allowed in. The marking system is the safety system: a fixture certified under the division rules was tested to a different standard, and its nameplate says nothing about zones, II groups, or T classes. Industrial job with an engineer-sealed classification drawing: the area around a process vent is Class I, Zone 1, Group IIB, and the takeoff prices threaded rigid conduit and checks every fixture submittal for a nameplate that reads Zone 1, IIB, with a temperature class at or under the gas ignition temperature — T3, a 200°C maximum surface, on this design. A Division 1 fixture with the right look does not get substituted, and Mike Holt reviews the method before anything is ordered. The trap: 'Zone 1 is just Division 1 with a new name, so Division 1 equipment is fine.' It is not. The two systems run side by side, but the markings are not interchangeable — 505 equipment is marked with the zone, the II material group, and a T class. Ordering off the division nameplate is the classic fail on a zone-classified job. Division-rated fixture installed in a Zone 1 area; its nameplate carries no zone marking. Threaded entries not made up wrenchtight, or fewer than five threads engaged into flameproof equipment. Group IIA equipment installed where the gas is Group IIC. Temperature class hotter than the ignition temperature of the gas present. Ordinary wiring methods run into a Zone 0 space that allows only intrinsically safe wiring. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 505.9(C): Created a new Table 13 in Chapter 9 entitled Equipment Suitable for Hazardous (Classified) Locations. The text was deleted at 505.9(C)(2)(4) referencing Table 505.9(C)(2)(4) with new text added to reference Chapter 9 Table 13. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Zone 20, 21, and 22 locations — zones for dusts and fibers
x: Article 506 extends the zone system to combustible dusts and ignitible fibers or flyings. It pairs with Article 505 the way Articles 502 and 503 pair with 501. • Zone 20 is the most severe: ignitible dust, fibers, or flyings present continuously, often, or for long periods. • Zone 21: the ignitible cloud is likely to be present in normal operation. • Zone 22: not likely in normal operation, and present only briefly if it happens at all. • Material groups replace classes (506.6). Group IIIA is ignitible fibers and flyings, Group IIIB is combustible dust other than metal dust, and Group IIIC is combustible metal dust and metal fibers — the group that drives the strictest gear. Metal dust is only ever Zone 20 or Zone 21, never Zone 22. • Equipment must be identified for the zone and marked with the zone, the material group, and a temperature limit (506.9). Protection techniques are listed at 506.8. • Wiring methods step down by zone (506.15). Zone 20 takes the Division 1 style methods — threaded rigid or intermediate metal conduit, or Type MI cable — and what is permitted in Zone 20 is permitted in 21 and 22, never the reverse. Dust ignites two ways: as a suspended cloud, and as a layer that builds up on a hot surface and smolders. The zone grades how often the cloud is there; the material group grades how bad the dust is when it comes — a conductive metal dust can also bridge live parts. Matching zone, group, and temperature marking to the actual dust keeps both ignition paths closed. As with 505, follow the zone marking on the equipment and the classification drawing. On a Sharma bid at a feed mill outside Winter Haven, the engineer's drawing zones the dust collector room Zone 21, Group IIIB, and the inside of the collector Zone 20. The takeoff prices threaded rigid for the Zone 20 drops and dusttight fittings where 506.15 allows them in Zone 21. If a dust area is classified by zone instead of division, work from this article with Mike Holt reviewing the method — every fixture submittal gets checked for a Zone 21, IIIB marking before anything is ordered. The trap: reading Zone 21 as "Division 1" and Zone 22 as "Division 2" and ordering Division-rated gear. The two systems run side by side, but the markings are not interchangeable — Article 506 equipment is marked with the zone, the III material group, and a temperature limit. A fixture marked only "Class II, Division 1" is not automatically a Zone 21 fixture. Equipment marked for Class II, Division 1 only, with no zone marking, installed in a Zone 21 area (506.9). Material group mismatch — Group IIIB equipment installed where the dust is Group IIIC metal dust (506.6, 506.9). Zone 22 wiring methods run inside a Zone 20 boundary (506.15). Ordinary-location luminaire installed inside the Zone 21 boundary (506.9, 506.15). Equipment temperature marking hotter than the dust layer on it can stand (506.9). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Hazardous locations — specific occupancies gateway
x: Article 510 is the short gateway article that points from the general classified-location rules to the specific occupancies that follow it in this chapter. Commercial garages, aircraft hangars, fuel dispensing, bulk storage, and spray operations each get their own article because each one pre-decides common classifications for that occupancy. When one of those articles applies, it works together with Articles 500 through 503: • Article 511 — commercial garages, repair and storage. • Article 513 — aircraft hangars. • Article 514 — motor fuel dispensing facilities. • Article 515 — bulk storage plants. • Article 516 — spray application, dipping, coating and printing processes. The general articles still do the heavy lifting inside the classified parts — 500 for the classification framework, 501 for Class I, 502 for Class II, 503 for Class III. The occupancy article tells you where the classified areas are; 500 through 503 tell you how to wire inside them. Every one of these occupancies has the same argument waiting to happen: how much of the building is really classified? Article 510 ends the argument before it starts, by sending each occupancy to an article where the common answers — the pit, the floor band, the dispenser island — are already decided. That keeps five estimators and five inspectors from drawing five different maps of the same garage. When a job is one of the named occupancies, start with its own article to see what classification has already been decided for you. Then use 500 through 503 for the wiring and equipment rules inside the classified parts. On a repair-garage bid in Belleview, the takeoff opened at 511, not 501: the 511 pages had already settled the floor band, the pits, and the GFCI scope, and 501 only came out for the seal and raceway rules inside those pockets. Starting at 500 would have meant re-deciding classifications the book had already decided. The trap is treating Article 510 as if it held rules of its own to memorize, or skipping it and wiring a hangar straight out of Article 501. 510 is a signpost: the occupancy article first, because it pre-decides the classification, then 500 through 503 for the methods inside. An answer that classifies a garage pit from the general rules alone has taken the long way to the wrong map. Hangar floor-band receptacles wired with ordinary commercial methods — the takeoff never opened Article 513. Garage classified pockets priced from Article 501 alone, missing the classifications 511 had already decided. Spray booth wired as ordinary industrial space; Article 516 never applied. Fuel dispensing disconnects laid out without Article 514’s placement rules. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 512: New Article 512, Cannabis Oil Equipment and Cannabis Oil Systems Using Flammable Materials: covers preparatory, extraction and post-processing equipment and booths using flammable solvents; equipment and systems must be listed for the location (512.20); fixed wiring above classified areas in metal raceway, PVC, RTRC, ENT or MI/TC/MC cable (512.13). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Commercial garages — repair and storage
x: Article 511 covers places that service or repair self-propelled vehicles that run on flammable liquids or gases — auto repair shops, dealership service bays, and similar light-commercial work Sharma bids. • Scope, 511.1: covers service and repair operations for self-propelled vehicles using volatile flammable liquids or flammable gases as fuel. • Major or minor, 511.2: a major repair garage is where engine overhauls, painting, body and fender work, and repairs that require draining the fuel tank are performed. A minor repair garage handles lubrication, inspection, tune-ups, and routine fluid changes. • Parking is not repair, 511.3(A): parking or storage garages are not required to be classified. • Where the class lands, 511.3(C): gasoline vapor is heavier than air and pools at the floor. In a major repair garage without the required ventilation, the entire floor area is Class I, Division 2 up to 18 in above the floor, and a pit with no ventilation is Class I, Division 1 up to the floor level. Mechanical ventilation at a minimum of four air changes per hour leaves the floor area unclassified. Lighter-than-air fuels (natural gas, hydrogen) flip the problem to the ceiling: the band within 18 in of the ceiling is classified the same way without that ventilation. • Fuel dispensing, 511.3(B): if fuel is dispensed on site, the dispensing functions are classified from Table 514.3(B)(1), and Article 514 joins in. Inside classified areas, wiring and equipment follow the Class I rules of Article 501 (511.4); above the band, 511.7 allows a defined list of fixed wiring methods. Gasoline vapor sinks and spreads across the floor, and a pit collects it like a bowl. One spark from an ordinary switch, motor, or drop light inside that layer can light the whole floor. The classification draws the boundary where the fuel actually gathers, so the equipment inside it is built not to be that spark. First question on any garage bid: is it repair or parking only, major or minor repair, and is there a pit or fuel dispensing? Those answers set the classification before anyone prices conduit and fittings. On a six-bay dealership service department in Orlando — major repair, no pit, ventilation not yet on the drawings — price the floor band as Class I, Division 2 to 18 in: keep receptacles and drops above the band, and run 20 A minimum branch circuits on 12 AWG copper per S-01, with Siemens gear per S-02. S-01: commercial branch circuits are 20 ampere minimum on 12 AWG copper. S-02 and S-03: new gear is Siemens, and breakers in an existing panel match that panel's listing. The trap is treating every garage the same. A parking-only garage is unclassified, and an oil-change shop is minor repair — neither prices like a major repair garage. The other direction fails too: the floor band in a major repair garage is 18 in, not the 12 in or 24 in the exam offers. Receptacles and a drop light installed inside the 18 in floor band of a major repair garage, wired and equipped as an ordinary location. Pit lighting and receptacles wired with general-purpose devices — the unventilated pit is Class I, Division 1 up to the floor. The floor band classified only around the workbenches — without the required ventilation, the entire floor area is Division 2 up to 18 in. A fuel dispensing area inside the shop classified under Article 511 alone — dispensing functions classify from Table 514.3(B)(1). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Classification of garage areas
x: This section classifies the spaces inside a commercial garage. Three questions decide every answer: major repair or minor repair (511.2), which part of the space — floor, pit, or ceiling — and whether the ventilation the section specifies is provided. • Parking and storage, 511.3(A): a garage with no repair work is not required to be classified. • Major repair floor, 511.3(C)(1): with mechanical ventilation at a minimum of four air changes per hour, the floor area is unclassified. Without it, the entire floor area is Class I, Division 2 up to 18 in. above the floor. • Pits, 511.3(C)(3): a pit in a lubrication or service room is Class I, Division 2 with ventilation at a minimum of six air changes per hour, and Class I, Division 1 up to the floor level without it. • Ceiling, 511.3(C)(2): for lighter-than-air fuels such as natural gas or hydrogen, the band within 18 in. of the ceiling is Class I, Division 2 without ventilation, and unclassified with ceiling exhaust ventilation of at least 1 cfm per square foot, taken within 18 in. of the highest point. • Minor repair, 511.3(D): floor areas are unclassified, except pit areas, which follow the pit rule above. • Fuel dispensing, 511.3(B): the dispensing functions classify from Table 514.3(B)(1) instead. The ventilation is part of the classification, not a mechanical extra: a pit drawn Division 2 'with ventilation' is Division 1 work the day that ventilation leaves the mechanical scope. Gasoline vapor is heavier than air: it sinks, spreads across the floor, and collects in a pit like water in a bowl. Lighter-than-air gases do the opposite and gather at the ceiling. The classification draws the boundary where the fuel actually collects, and ventilation earns its place in the answer because moving air keeps the mixture too lean to ignite. On a four-bay repair shop in Winter Haven — major repair, one lube pit, no fuel dispensing — work the three questions space by space and write the answers on the takeoff. The mechanical set provides four air changes per hour, so the floor prices as unclassified and the bays rough in with ordinary commercial methods on 20 A minimum branch circuits (S-01). The pit is the swing item: its Division 2 answer needs six air changes per hour of pit ventilation in the mechanical scope. If that line is not there, price the pit as Division 1 and say so on the bid. The trap answer is 'the floor of a major repair garage is always Class I, Division 2 up to 18 in.' That is only the no-ventilation answer. With the ventilation 511.3(C)(1) specifies, the floor area is unclassified — the trap prices classified-location methods the job does not need. Ordinary-location receptacles and a drop light installed inside the 18 in. floor band of an unventilated major repair garage — that band is Class I, Division 2. Pit wired as Division 2 with no pit ventilation on the mechanical drawings or in the building — an unventilated pit is Class I, Division 1 to the floor level. Equipment within 18 in. of the ceiling over natural-gas vehicles treated as an ordinary location in a garage with no ceiling exhaust ventilation. Fuel dispensing equipment classified by the garage floor rules instead of Table 514.3(B)(1). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wiring and equipment inside the classified areas
x: Inside the parts of a garage that 511.3 classifies, wiring and equipment follow the Class I rules of Article 501: • Division 1 pockets, 501.10(A): threaded rigid metal conduit or threaded steel IMC is the everyday method; Type MI cable, and Type MC-HL cable where its conditions are met, are also permitted. Ordinary-location methods — NM cable, EMT with set-screw fittings, unsealed conduit — stop at the boundary. • Seals, 501.15: a seal fitting goes within 18 in of an explosionproof enclosure that holds arcing or hot parts, and seals are also required where conduit leaves the classified area. • Portable lighting: portable lighting used in those areas has to be identified for the location or arranged so it cannot be used inside the classified space. The practical message is that the classified pocket is wired like any other Class I, Division location, even though the rest of the shop is ordinary. The pocket exists because fuel vapor collects there. Vapor also travels — it creeps along conduit runs and pools inside enclosures. Threaded metal raceway contains it, and seals stop the raceway from becoming a pipe that carries vapor, or a flame front, into the clean part of the building. One set-screw fitting is all it takes to break that chain. Price and rough classified pockets with Article 501 methods — threaded metal raceway, seals, and listed fittings — not with shop-standard materials. Keep portable trouble lights for classified areas in the identified type only. On a repair garage in Ocala, the pit and floor-band work ran in threaded rigid with a seal within 18 in of every explosionproof box, while the bays above the band roughed in the shop's normal methods. The material split is the whole bid: price the pocket like a gas station, not like a garage, or the job loses money at the first fitting order. The trap is 'the garage is a commercial building, so commercial methods apply throughout.' Inside the classified pocket they do not. The boundary is the whole game: the same conduit run is ordinary on one side of it and threaded, sealed Class I work on the other — and an answer that carries EMT and set-screw fittings through the pocket is wrong. EMT with set-screw fittings run through the classified floor pocket. Explosionproof enclosure in the pit with no seal fitting within 18 in. Ordinary shop trouble light used inside the classified area; not identified for the location. Conduit leaving the classified area unsealed at the boundary. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wiring and equipment above the classified areas
x: Above the classified area at the floor of a commercial garage, 511.7 relaxes the wiring rules to a defined list — but it does not turn the space into an ordinary location. • Fixed wiring above the classified area: metal raceways, Type AC or MC cable, manufactured wiring systems, and certain listed cables. • Equipment that can arc or spark and sits within 12 ft of the floor above a classified area has to be enclosed or guarded so hot particles cannot fall into the classified zone. • Fixed luminaires over classified areas, traffic lanes, or anywhere a vehicle could strike them carry their own height and protection conditions — 12 ft is the key dimension in the common cases. Measure the heights from the floor the vehicles sit on — not from a curb, a pit edge, or the top of a lift. Gasoline vapor hugs the floor of a repair garage, and the classified area sits in that vapor layer. A spark, or a hot particle dropping from a motor, a switch, or a broken lamp above, can fall straight into the vapor and ignite it. Enclosing the arcing parts and pushing luminaires up to the 12 ft line keeps ignition sources and falling debris out of the fuel-air mix. On a shop fit-out in Orlando, the high-bay luminaires over the bays hang at 14 ft, clear of the 12 ft line — but the lift raises a truck bed up toward a wall pack mounted at 9 ft over the traffic lane. Measure heights from the floor, not from the slab finish you wish you had, and confirm the 12-foot line before hanging luminaires over bays. Where a lift raises vehicles into the luminaire zone, flag it to Mike Holt before trim-out. S-01 applies above the classified area too: 20 ampere minimum branch circuits on commercial work. The trap answer is 'above the classified area, anything goes — it is an ordinary location up there.' 511.7 gives a list, not a free pass: the fixed wiring methods are named, arcing equipment within 12 ft still has to be enclosed or guarded, and a luminaire a vehicle can hit fails no matter how high the ceiling is. Luminaire over a bay hung below the 12 ft line with no guard or physical protection. Open motor or other arcing device within 12 ft of the floor over the classified area, not enclosed or guarded. NM cable, or another method not on the 511.7 list, run as fixed wiring above the classified area. Wall pack over a traffic lane set where a vehicle raised on the lift can strike it. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Underground wiring in garages
x: 511.8 does not write its own underground rules — it sends you to Article 514: underground wiring in a commercial garage is installed in accordance with 514.8, the motor fuel dispensing underground section. • Base method: threaded rigid metal conduit or threaded steel intermediate metal conduit. • Type MI cable is also permitted. • Nonmetallic conduit — Type PVC, Type RTRC or Type HDPE — is permitted only where it is buried under not less than 2 ft of cover. Where nonmetallic conduit is used, the last 2 ft of the underground run, up to where it emerges or connects to the aboveground raceway, must be threaded RMC or IMC, and an equipment grounding conductor runs inside the raceway. • Underground conduit below a classified location is sealed within 10 ft of the point where it emerges above grade. • Ordinary site habits do not carry over: the cover depths and methods of Table 300.5 are not the rule under a repair floor — 514.8 is. Fuel spilled on a repair floor soaks into the soil below it, and gasoline vapor is heavier than air — it sinks, then travels through any open path, including the inside of a conduit, into panels and equipment in unclassified rooms. Threaded metal raceway, real depth, and seals at the emergence point keep that vapor path shut and give the run mechanical protection under a floor that carries vehicles. On a Lakeland garage addition, two under-slab runs feed a lift and a compressor: both go in as threaded RMC before the pour. A third run, the feeder to a future bay, is Type PVC buried with 30 in of cover — more than the 2 ft minimum — and it changes to threaded RMC for the last 2 ft before it stubs up at the panel, with a copper EGC pulled in the whole way. Each emergence gets its seal within 10 ft. The method was confirmed with Mike Holt at takeoff, before the slab was scheduled — not after. The trap is pricing the under-slab work from Table 300.5, the general burial table — “PVC at 18 inches is fine everywhere else.” Under a commercial garage, 511.8 sends you to 514.8: nonmetallic conduit needs a full 2 ft of cover and a threaded metal finish for the last 2 ft, whatever the general table allows elsewhere. PVC conduit stubbed straight up through the slab at the panel — no threaded metal for the last 2 ft. EMT run underground below the repair floor. Nonmetallic run buried at 18 in of cover under the slab. No equipment grounding conductor inside the nonmetallic raceway. Underground conduit emerging above grade with no seal within 10 ft of the emergence point. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Special equipment in garages
x: This section collects requirements for particular garage equipment — the two kinds of charging equipment that show up in a repair garage. • Battery charging equipment (511.10(A)). Battery chargers, their control equipment, and the batteries being charged shall not be located within the locations classified in 511.3. Charging adds its own gas and ignition concerns on top of the garage's general classification, so the charging spot lives outside the classified pockets. • Electric vehicle charging equipment (511.10(B)). Inside a repair garage, EV charging is installed in accordance with Article 625, with garage-specific rules added: no connector shall be located within a Class I location as defined in 511.3, and flexible cords shall be of a type identified for extra-hard usage. • The overhead cord rule. Where an EV charging cord is suspended from overhead, it shall be arranged so that the lowest point of sag is at least 6 in. above the floor (511.10(B)(3)). • The classification map it points to. In a major repair garage without the ventilation 511.3(C)(1)(a) describes, the entire floor area is Class I, Division 2 up to 18 in. above the floor, and an unventilated pit is Division 1 up to floor level — so "outside the classified area" is a line you can measure, not a guess. Charging concentrates two ignition stories in one corner of the shop: batteries that vent gas while they charge, and connectors that make and break contact where people handle them daily. Gasoline vapor settles low, into the classified floor layer and the pit. Keeping chargers and connectors out of that layer separates the spark from the fuel. If the bid includes vehicle charging inside a repair garage, note it separately on the takeoff instead of folding it into general receptacles. On a Sharma bid for a dealership service department adding two EV chargers, the layout keeps both connectors out of the 18 in. classified floor layer, the cords are extra-hard usage, and the overhead drop is set so the cord's lowest sag stays at least 6 in. above the floor. Ask for the charger nameplate and the ventilation design before pricing — the ventilation answer decides whether the floor layer is classified at all. The trap: "EV charging in a garage is just Article 625." In a repair garage, 511.10(B) sends you to 625 and then adds the garage rules — the connector still cannot sit in a Class I location, and the cord must be extra-hard usage. The companion trap: parking the battery charger wherever it fits. Section 511.10(A) keeps chargers and batteries being charged out of the 511.3 classified areas, full stop. Battery charger, or batteries on charge, sitting inside the classified floor area (511.10(A)). EV charging connector located within the Class I floor layer (511.10(B)(2)). Overhead charging cord sagging to less than 6 in. above the floor (511.10(B)(3)). Ordinary-duty flexible cord on garage charging equipment — extra-hard usage is required (511.10(B)(1)). Charging receptacles installed without the GFCI protection the garage rules require (511.12). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: GFCI protection in commercial garages
x: 511.12 is one sentence long: ground-fault circuit-interrupter protection for personnel in a commercial garage is provided as required in 210.8(B), the non-dwelling GFCI list. On that list, item (8) is garages, accessory buildings, service bays and similar areas — vehicle exhibition halls and showrooms are the only garage spaces carved out. • Scope: 125-volt through 250-volt receptacles, on single-phase branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground and 50 amperes or less, or three-phase branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground and 100 amperes or less. • The 2020 wording is broader than the old rule. Earlier editions tied garage GFCI to receptacles serving diagnostic equipment, hand tools or portable lighting; the 2020 list drops that limit, so plan on protecting essentially every receptacle in the work areas. • The rule applies whether or not the receptacle sits inside a classified area. Classification changes the wiring method; it does not switch off 511.12. • A 240-volt receptacle for shop equipment is covered just like a 120-volt one — the range runs to 250 volts. A mechanic works on a conductive slab, often wet from wash-downs, holding a grounded vehicle with one hand and a corded tool with the other. A fault that leaks current through that path can stop a heart at a level no breaker will ever notice. GFCI protection watches for current leaking outside the circuit and opens in a fraction of a cycle, before the shock becomes lethal. Price a four-bay repair shop in Kissimmee: three 20-ampere receptacle circuits (S-01) serve the lifts, benches and wash bay — 14 receptacles in all — and every one lands on GFCI protection from the Siemens panel, breakers per the plans. The 240-volt receptacle for the tire machine is on a 2-pole GFCI breaker, not a standard one, because the rule runs to 250 volts. The two showroom receptacles stay standard: the showroom is carved out of item (8). Test every device at trim and write it on the punch list. S-07 is Sharma's residential pattern — a dual-function breaker feeding a standard tamper-resistant receptacle, with no GFCI receptacles. Article 511 requires personnel GFCI protection but does not dictate breaker versus receptacle; on a commercial garage, use the device the plans specify and confirm a breaker-based method satisfies the spec before relying on the S-07 pattern. The trap answer is “only the receptacles used for diagnostic equipment and hand tools need GFCI.” That was the pre-2020 wording of the garage item. NEC 2020 deleted the limit, so on a 2020 permit the whole service bay is protected, not just the bench where the scanner plugs in. Service-bay receptacles on standard breakers — no GFCI protection anywhere in the bays. 240-volt shop-equipment receptacle protected by a plain 2-pole breaker. Receptacle inside the classified floor area left unprotected because “classified rules take over.” GFCI device installed where it cannot be reached for testing — not readily accessible. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Aircraft hangars
x: Article 513 classifies and wires aircraft hangars, where fuel vapors gather near the floor and in pits much as they do in garages, but around aircraft instead of cars. The classification is decided by height above the floor and by distance from the aircraft: • Pits, 513.3(B): any pit or depression below the hangar floor is Class I, Division 1, up to the level of the floor. • Floor band, 513.3(A): the entire floor area up to 18 in above the floor is Class I, Division 2. Adjacent areas that are not suitably cut off from the hangar share that classification. • Around the aircraft, 513.3(C): within 5 ft horizontally of aircraft power plants or fuel tanks, the Division 2 area runs from the floor up to 5 ft above the upper surface of the wings and engine enclosures. • Adjacent areas, 513.3(D): an area next to the hangar can stay unclassified where it is suitably cut off, or ventilated at not less than four air changes per hour. Inside the classified parts, wiring and equipment follow Article 501, and the rest of the article adds hangar-specific equipment and grounding rules. Sharma sees this rarely, but a hangar bid is never priced with ordinary commercial methods. Aircraft fuel vapor is heavier than air. It sinks, spreads across the floor, and pools in pits — exactly where a dropped tool, a receptacle, or a motor can spark. The floor band and the pit rules put the strictest wiring where the vapor actually sits, instead of treating the whole tall hangar like a bomb. Recognize the occupancy on the bid walk and route the takeoff to Mike Holt. The classification tables in this article decide the methods before any labor number makes sense. On a hangar service call in Ocala, price the floor-level work as classified work: a receptacle added at 12 in above the floor sits inside the Division 2 band, so it is threaded rigid conduit, seals, and listed fittings — not the EMT and set-screw fittings a normal commercial job would take. The same receptacle at 24 in, above the band and away from the aircraft, is ordinary work. Height is money on this article. The trap is calling the whole hangar Division 1, or the whole hangar ordinary. Both are wrong. Division 1 is the pit. The floor band up to 18 in is Division 2, the zone around the aircraft reaches 5 ft above the wing, and above those zones the space is generally unclassified. Receptacle roughed in EMT with set-screw fittings at 12 in above the hangar floor, inside the Division 2 band. Pit lighting and devices wired with ordinary-location methods in a Class I, Division 1 pit. Equipment not identified for the location used down in the floor band instead of above the 18 in line. Conduit run through the floor slab left unsealed where it leaves the classified floor area. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Motor fuel dispensing facilities
x: Article 514 covers gas stations and any place motor fuel is dispensed into vehicles, including dispensing inside a repair garage. It classifies the area around dispensers and tanks, requires seals and specific underground wiring, and requires emergency disconnect controls that kill power to the dispensing equipment. • Classification comes from Table 514.3(B)(1). The inside of a dispenser enclosure is a Class I, Division 1 location. Around an outdoor dispenser, Division 2 runs up to 18 in above grade and out to 20 ft horizontally from the dispenser. • A tank vent discharging upward is Division 1 within 3 ft of its open end in all directions, and Division 2 from 3 ft to 5 ft. • Wiring and equipment inside the classified areas follow Article 501 (514.4), underground wiring is threaded rigid metal conduit or threaded intermediate metal conduit (514.8), and seals go where 501.15 requires them (514.9). • Emergency disconnects (514.11) sit not less than 20 ft and not more than 100 ft from the dispensers they serve, and they disconnect all conductors, including the grounded conductor — equipment grounding conductors stay connected. Underground rules from this article are also borrowed by garages in 511.8 and by marinas for fueling docks. Gasoline vapor is heavier than air and pools at grade around the dispensers, exactly where ordinary wiring devices can spark. The classified zones, the sealed conduits, and one clearly identified emergency disconnect exist so that a leak, a drive-off, or a fire at one island does not find an ignition source — and so the first person on scene can kill every dispenser circuit from a safe distance. Fuel dispensing is specialty work: emergency shutoff location, dispenser seals, and underground method all come from the plans and this article. Flag any dispensing scope on a bid the day it is seen, not at rough-in. On a convenience-store island replacement, the classified zone drives the takeoff: threaded rigid conduit underground to each dispenser, seals at the dispenser entries, and the emergency disconnect verified between 20 ft and 100 ft from the dispensers it serves — measure it on the site plan before the bid goes out, because moving it later is a change order. The trap is placing the emergency disconnect close to the pumps for convenience. Inside 20 ft it can sit in the classified area and inside the very fire it is meant to control; 514.11 sets a band, not just a minimum — not less than 20 ft and not more than 100 ft from the dispensing devices. The second trap is switching only the ungrounded conductors: the emergency disconnect must open the grounded conductor too, while the equipment grounding conductors remain connected. Emergency disconnect mounted 12 ft from the dispensers — inside the 20 ft minimum of 514.11. PVC conduit run underground to a dispenser where threaded rigid metal conduit or IMC is required (514.8). Missing conduit seals where runs enter the dispenser enclosure (514.9, 501.15). Ordinary-location junction box installed inside the Division 2 zone — within 20 ft of a dispenser and below 18 in above grade. Emergency disconnect that leaves the grounded conductor connected (514.11). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Fuel dispensing areas — where the classified space actually is (514.3)
x: Section 514.3 and Table 514.3(B)(1) draw the classified map around motor fuel dispensing equipment: • Inside the dispenser enclosure is the harshest space — Class I, Division 1. • Around an outdoor dispenser, Division 2 runs up to 18 in above grade and extends 20 ft horizontally from the dispenser. • A tank vent discharging upward is Division 1 within 3 ft of its open end in all directions, and Division 2 from 3 ft to 5 ft. • Any pit below grade inside the area is Division 1. Wiring methods, seals, and equipment all follow the classification of the exact spot they occupy — one conduit run can cross two classifications on a single wall. Fuel vapor is heavier than air and pools low — inside the dispenser, in pits, and in a shallow layer over the pavement around the pumps. The table's steps put Division 1 where vapor is present in normal operation and Division 2 where it shows up only when something leaks or fails. Wire a Division 1 pocket with ordinary-location parts and the first spark has fuel waiting for it. On a fuel-station service call, treat the classification drawing as part of the plans: if the set has no classified-area plan, stop and get one before choosing fittings or breaking a seal. Ordinary-location parts do not go inside the table's lines. On a convenience-store pump swap, that means checking where the seal-offs sit against the 20 ft line before the dispenser is lifted, not after. Florida convenience-store work is usually a design-build handoff from the tank contractor — confirm whose permit carries the classified wiring before pricing it. The trap answer flips the two zones: 'Division 2 inside the dispenser, Division 1 around it.' It is the opposite — inside the enclosure is Division 1, the harshest space on the site. The second trap is measuring the 20 ft from the island edge or the canopy column; the table measures from the dispenser. Ordinary-location fitting or device installed inside the dispenser enclosure — that space is Division 1. Seal-off missing where the conduit leaves the classified envelope. Work started with no classified-area plan in the set — fittings chosen by habit instead of by the table. Junction box set in a below-grade pit inside the area and treated as an ordinary location. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Emergency disconnect at fuel dispensing
x: Fuel dispensing areas need clearly identified emergency electrical disconnects — the control a station attendant or firefighter reaches for when fuel is flowing where it should not. Operated, the disconnect must simultaneously open all conductors of the circuits involved, including the grounded (neutral) conductor. One operation cuts power to: • The dispensing devices • The remote pumps serving them • The associated power, control, and signal circuits • The other electrical equipment in the classified area around the dispensers 514.11(A) also fixes where the disconnect sits: an approved location not less than 20 ft and not more than 100 ft from the fuel dispensing devices it serves, and where more than one disconnect is provided, all of them are interconnected. Resetting after an emergency shutoff takes manual intervention, in the manner the AHJ approves. Its location, identification, and the circuits it actually kills are inspection items, not details to assume. Fuel flows by the gallon a few feet from ignition sources and moving cars. When a hose fails or a driver pulls away with the nozzle still in the tank, somebody has seconds to kill every circuit that can spark or keep pumping. Opening the grounded conductor matters too: leave it connected and current can still find a path and arc. A disconnect that stops only the dispenser leaves the remote pump pushing fuel to the leak. On a Central Florida convenience-store repump, Sharma's crew lands the emergency disconnect on the store wall 40 ft from the nearest dispenser — inside the 20 ft to 100 ft window — and interconnects it with the second disconnect at the canopy. During a dispensing walkdown, operate the emergency disconnect and prove every dispenser circuit it serves is dead, then reset per the equipment instructions. Put its location on the job record the crew and the owner both get. Adopted after reconciliation with the ChatGPT research Sanjay supplied 2026-11-11; verified 2026-11-18 against NEC 2020 sources (514.11(A) is extracted from NFPA 30A 6.7): the 20 ft to 100 ft location and the simultaneous opening of all circuit conductors, grounded conductor included, are as this page states. The trap is the disconnect that drops the dispenser power but leaves the grounded (neutral) conductor connected — or one mounted right at the island 'so it is easy to reach.' 514.11(A) wants every circuit conductor open at once, neutral included, from an approved location 20 ft to 100 ft away, with a manual reset. Close and partial both fail. Emergency disconnect opens the ungrounded conductors only — the grounded (neutral) conductor stays connected. Disconnect located less than 20 ft, or more than 100 ft, from the dispensing devices it serves. Two disconnects provided but not interconnected. Disconnect kills the dispensers but leaves the remote pumps or the control circuits live. Disconnect not clearly identified, or it resets automatically after an emergency shutoff. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bulk storage plants
x: Article 515 covers bulk storage plants and terminals — property where flammable liquids arrive by tank vessel, pipeline, tank car or tank vehicle, are stored or blended in bulk, and go back out the same way (515.1). • The classified map comes from Table 515.3. It classifies the areas around tanks, pumps, vents, fills, loading racks and pits, and gives the extent of each classified area. • Inside a classified area, wiring and equipment follow the Class I rules of Article 501 (515.4). • Above a classified area, fixed wiring runs in metal raceways, Schedule 80 PVC, or the other methods 515.7(A) lists, and arcing fixed equipment is totally enclosed or built so sparks cannot escape (515.7(B)). • Underground wiring is threaded rigid metal conduit or threaded IMC; where it is buried under at least 2 ft of cover, Type PVC conduit, Type RTRC conduit or a listed cable is permitted instead (515.8). • Conduit seals follow 515.9, and all metal parts are bonded so no two sit at a different potential (515.16). • Fuel dispensers at a bulk plant are not wired under 515 — they follow Article 514 (515.10), including its emergency disconnect 20 ft to 100 ft from the dispensers. It is industrial work. Sharma touches it only with an engineered classification package in hand. A bulk plant moves flammable liquid through pumps, meters and open connections all day, so vapor is not an accident there — it is a normal byproduct of the work. One arcing contact inside the vapor's reach can ignite it. The classification table, the sealed raceways and the bonding exist to keep ignition sources out of that reach and every metal object at the same potential. A fuel distributor outside Ocala asks Sharma to rewire a pump pad and loading rack. If a bulk plant appears in an invitation, the first deliverable is the classification drawing, not a price. No drawing, no takeoff. When the engineered package lands, the takeoff reads off it: threaded RMC for the underground run to the rack, seals where conduits leave the classified envelope, bonding across the tank and rack steel, and the dispenser island priced under Article 514 with its emergency disconnect 20 ft to 100 ft out. If the package shows ordinary-location wiring inside the Table 515.3 envelope, that is a question for the engineer, not a field fix. The trap is treating a bulk plant like a gas station. Article 514 covers dispensing fuel into vehicles; a plant that receives, stores and transfers flammable liquids in bulk is Article 515, and its classified areas come from Table 515.3 — not from the 514.3 dispenser table. The twist: dispensers installed at the plant still follow Article 514 (515.10). Underground run to the loading rack in PVC at 12 in of cover — the 515.8 exception needs at least 2 ft of cover, or the run belongs in threaded RMC or IMC. Conduit leaving the classified area with no seal where 515.9 requires one. Tank, rack steel and piping not bonded together — a difference of potential between metal objects is exactly what 515.16 is written against. Ordinary-location junction box installed inside the Table 515.3 classified envelope. Dispenser island wired as 515 equipment, with no Article 514 emergency disconnect. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 515.10: Changed the title of Section 515.10 from "Gasoline Dispensers" to "Motor Fuel Dispensers." FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Spray application, dipping, coating, and printing processes
x: Article 516 covers spray booths and rooms, dip tanks, and similar processes using flammable or combustible materials. Body shops and finishing operations are the light-commercial face of this article, and the classification comes from 516.5 — it follows the process, not the building. • Division 1 pockets. The interior of a spray booth or room, the interior of exhaust ducts, and any area in the direct path of spray operations are Class I, Division 1 (Class II, Division 1 where the hazard is combustible powder). • Tight bubbles. All space within 3 ft of open containers, spray gun cleaners, and solvent recovery units is Division 1, and sumps, pits, and below-grade channels within 25 ft of a vapor source are Division 1. • Around the booth. Wiring and equipment within 3 ft of any opening of an open-face or open-front booth are Division 2. • Open spraying is the big footprint. With no booth, Division 2 reaches 20 ft horizontally and 10 ft vertically from the spray area. • Inside the classified pockets, wiring and equipment follow the division rules for the class. Luminaires over or beside a booth sit behind sealed panels or carry the approval for the area they are in, and the spray equipment is interlocked with the ventilation so spraying stops when the air stops. Spraying atomizes paint and solvent into exactly the cloud a classified location worries about, and overspray deposits add a layer hazard on every nearby surface. The booth and its exhaust contain the cloud; the classified distances around openings and around open spraying mark how far the vapor can travel and still reach ignitible strength. A paint booth on a commercial bid pulls this article in even when the rest of the building is ordinary. On a Sharma bid for an auto body shop in Orlando — one listed spray booth, prep area outside it — the takeoff prices the booth interior and the 3 ft band at its door with the methods the classification demands, keeps the prep-area receptacles ordinary beyond the 3 ft line, and asks for the booth listing and ventilation details before pricing the booth circuits. The interlock between the spray equipment and the exhaust fan is a priced item, not a note. The trap answer: "the whole paint shop is Division 1." The classification is a set of pockets with hard edges — booth interior Division 1, 3 ft at the openings Division 2, ordinary beyond. The reverse trap fails too: treating the booth interior as ordinary because "the fan runs all day." Ventilation is part of the system, but 516.5 classifies the interior Division 1 regardless. Ordinary receptacle or switch inside the booth, or within 3 ft of the booth opening (516.5). Spray equipment that still operates with the exhaust ventilation off — interlock missing or bypassed. Luminaire over the booth not approved for the Division 2 area it sits in, and not behind a sealed panel. Open solvent container or dip tank wired as ordinary space inside its 3 ft Division 1 bubble (516.5). Pit or sump within 25 ft of the vapor source wired as unclassified (516.5). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Health care facilities — the light-commercial slice
x: Article 517 covers electrical work in facilities that examine or treat patients — hospitals at the deep end, and clinics, medical and dental offices at the end Sharma is likely to bid. Four themes run through it: • Redundant grounding in patient care spaces (517.13): every branch circuit gets two independent ground paths — a wiring method that itself qualifies as an equipment grounding conductor, plus an insulated copper equipment grounding conductor inside it. • Hospital-grade receptacles at patient bed locations (517.18): listed hospital-grade devices, identified by the green dot on the face, where patients are treated. • An essential electrical system for hospitals (517.30): a second source feeding separated life safety, critical, and equipment branches. • Scope that follows the spaces (517.10): the article turns on room by room, where patients are examined or treated — not building by building. This first pass covers only the small-clinic slice; hospital design belongs to engineers and later passes of this book. Patients under treatment are connected to equipment, often wet, often unable to let go or pull away. A ground fault that would tingle in an office can kill in an operatory. The article answers with two ground paths where one would do elsewhere, tougher receptacles at the bed, and backup power that treats an outage as a life-safety event, not a nuisance. On a clinic or dental bid, the first question is which rooms are patient care spaces — that answer, from the plans or the facility, turns this article on.
