Service equipment 38 ft from the exterior wall — over the 30 ft limit, however visible it is. Enclosure bottom less than 2 ft above finished grade. Disconnect handle above 6 ft 7 in. above the ground or platform. Service equipment mounted on the home itself, with no permanent-foundation exception in play. Equipment rated under 100 A, or the feeder landed with a cord instead of a permanent wiring method. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 550.32: Mobile home service equipment now has to be within sight from the home, meaning visible and up to 50 ft away, instead of within 30 ft. Its disconnect can double as the emergency disconnect. Service equipment for a mobile home must be within sight from the home: visible and no more than 50 ft away (see 110.29). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The feeder — four insulated conductors, 100-ampere capacity
x: The feeder from the service equipment to the home is four continuous, insulated, color-coded conductors: • Two ungrounded conductors • One grounded (neutral) conductor • One insulated equipment grounding conductor A bare grounding conductor inside a cable assembly does not count — the ground must be insulated like the rest. Under 550.33(B) the feeder conductors must have a capacity and ampacity of not less than 100 amperes, even when the home's calculated load comes out smaller. Where the conductors are spliced, the splice goes in a suitable junction box — never inside the raceway. A mobile home feeder lives underground, where a bare ground corrodes and disappears years before anyone opens the run. The insulated equipment grounding conductor survives the burial, so the fault path back to the service equipment is still there on the day a fault happens. The 100-ampere floor keeps a small calculated load from shrinking the feeder below what the home's service equipment is built for. Setting a manufactured home on a lot in Polk County: the park pedestal sits within sight and 30 ft of the wall (550.32), and the feeder trench is open. Pull four insulated conductors every time; standard SER with a bare ground does not make a mobile home feeder. Size for the 100-ampere minimum capacity, and land the insulated ground on the grounding bus at both ends, keeping neutral and ground separate inside the home. The trap is the SER cable on the truck: 'SER has all four conductors, so it works as the feeder.' It does not — the grounding conductor in standard SER is bare, and 550.33 requires the equipment grounding conductor to be insulated. The second trap is sizing the feeder to a small calculated load; the 100-ampere minimum capacity applies even when the math comes out smaller. Feeder pulled in SER cable with a bare grounding conductor. Feeder sized to a small calculated load — under the 100-ampere minimum capacity (550.33(B)). Splice buried inside the raceway instead of in a suitable junction box. Neutral and ground bonded together in the home's panelboard — the home is fed by a feeder, not a service. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Recreational vehicles and recreational vehicle parks
x: Article 551 covers recreational vehicles themselves and, more importantly for site work, RV parks — the site supply equipment, receptacle configurations, and grounding for each RV lot. Part VI covers the parks. • Every site with electrical supply gets site supply equipment with the receptacles travelers carry: 20-ampere, 125-volt; 30-ampere, 125-volt in the TT-30 configuration; and 50-ampere, 125/250-volt. • The mix is code, not preference: at least 70 percent of sites get a 30-ampere receptacle, at least 40 percent of new sites (20 percent of existing) get a 50-ampere — and every 50-ampere site also carries a 30 (551.71). • Each site's equipment includes its own disconnect and overcurrent protection, and the receptacles carry the ground-fault protection the article requires. • Park services and feeders are calculated from the sites: 9,600 VA per 50-ampere site, 3,600 VA per site with 20- and 30-ampere supply, 2,400 VA per 20-ampere-only site, and 600 VA per tent site — then reduced by the demand factors of Table 551.73(A) (551.73). Park work is a feeder and pedestal job repeated many times, with GFCI and polarity details at every site. It pairs with Article 552, which covers park trailers separately. An RV is a dwelling that plugs in outdoors, often on wet ground, plugged and unplugged by the traveling public, not an electrician. The pedestal rules standardize what every traveler finds, put a disconnect and breaker in reach at the site, and put ground-fault protection where hands, water and cord caps meet. The demand table exists because a park never draws full rating at every pedestal at once — sizing without it prices the job out. A 40-site RV park expansion off US-27: count sites and pedestal types carefully and confirm the supply equipment listing. Do not price park pedestals as ordinary receptacle posts. The code mix drives the count: at least 28 of the 40 sites (70 percent) get 30-ampere receptacles, and at least 16 new sites (40 percent) get 50-ampere supply, each also carrying a 30. Load basis before demand factors: 16 × 9,600 VA + 24 × 3,600 VA = 240,000 VA. Table 551.73(A) then steps that down as sites are added — the difference between a service that prices the job and one that prices Sharma out of it. The trap is calculating an RV park service at the straight sum of the pedestal ratings. Section 551.73 counts each site at its supply rating — 9,600 VA for a 50-ampere site — and then applies the demand factors of Table 551.73(A), which step down as sites are added. Skipping the table oversizes the service badly. The reverse trap is forgetting the mix itself: at least 40 percent of new sites must be 50-ampere sites (551.71). Pedestal with no disconnecting means or no overcurrent protection at the site. 50-ampere site with no 30-ampere receptacle beside it — every 50-ampere site also carries a 30 (551.71). Park service sized on raw pedestal totals with no Table 551.73(A) demand factors applied. Wrong receptacle configuration for the rating — a 30-ampere RV site takes the TT-30 travel-trailer configuration, not a dryer receptacle. Site receptacles missing the ground-fault protection the article requires. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 551.3: Substantiation was submitted to for the need to address recreational vehicle sites located next to natural bodies of water. As a result, a new Section 551.3, Electrical Datum Plane Distances, was added. • 551.40(D): Section 551.40(D) was changed to eliminate the need for a Reverse Polarity Device in a recreational vehicle. Substantiation was submitted to for the addition of language for a loss of a ground device. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: RV site supply equipment — what each pedestal must offer (551.71)
x: Section 551.71 is the pedestal page for RV parks. Each RV site with an electrical supply gets site supply equipment — receptacles, a disconnecting means, and overcurrent protection, all at the site. The receptacle mix is set by the section, not by preference: • Every site: at least one 20-ampere, 125-volt receptacle. • At least 70 percent of sites: a 30-ampere, 125-volt receptacle in the TT-30 travel-trailer configuration. • At least 40 percent of new sites — and 20 percent of existing sites: a 50-ampere, 125/250-volt receptacle. Every 50-ampere site also carries a 30-ampere receptacle. • Ground-fault protection (551.71(F)): the 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles get listed GFCI protection for personnel. The 30- and 50-ampere supply receptacles do not — they are the RV's feeder connection, not general-purpose outlets, and GFCI protection is not required for them. A pedestal is a small service repeated down a row: rating, configuration, and protection repeat with it. A traveler plugs a 40 ft RV into a pedestal in the rain, at night, with wet hands and a cord dragged through wet grass. The GFCI protects the person at the small receptacle used for outdoor equipment, the disconnect and breaker at the site keep a fault local to one site, and the standard configurations mean the plug in the traveler's hand fits a pedestal at any park in the country. New 50-site park outside Ocala: the mix is code math before it is a purchase order. All 50 sites get the 20-ampere receptacle. At least 35 sites — 70 percent — get the TT-30. At least 20 sites — 40 percent of new — get the 50-ampere, 125/250-volt receptacle, and each of those 20 also carries a 30. The owner wants 50-ampere supply at every site for the winter season; that is permitted, and it feeds the 551.73 load math at 9,600 VA a site. On the existing park across the road, added 50-ampere sites only have to reach the 20 percent floor for existing sites. Confirm who furnishes the pedestals before the number is final. Florida RV parks run full through the winter season — size and stage the work for occupied parks; pedestal swaps are usually one row at a time with live sites on either side. The trap answer is “every pedestal receptacle needs GFCI, including the 50-ampere.” 551.71(F) limits GFCI protection to the 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles. The 30- and 50-ampere receptacles are the RV's feeder connection — the Code deliberately leaves them off the GFCI list, because RV appliance leakage can exceed what a personnel GFCI allows. Pedestal with a 50-ampere receptacle and no 30-ampere receptacle beside it. New park laid out with 50-ampere supply at 25 percent of sites — under the 40 percent floor for new sites. No GFCI protection on the pedestal's 20-ampere, 125-volt receptacle (551.71(F)). Site supply equipment with no disconnecting means or no overcurrent protection at the site. GFCI breaker fitted on the 50-ampere supply circuit — not required by 551.71(F), and RV leakage current nuisance-trips it. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Sizing RV park services and feeders (551.73)
x: Section 551.73 calculates an RV park's service and feeders from the sites themselves. • The load basis (551.73(A)): 9,600 volt-amperes per site with 50-ampere, 208Y/120V or 120/240V supply; 3,600 volt-amperes per site with both 20- and 30-ampere supply; 2,400 volt-amperes per site with only 20-ampere supply; and 600 volt-amperes per site with only 20-ampere supply dedicated to tent sites. A site with several receptacles counts once, at its highest-rated supply. • The total is then reduced by the demand factors of Table 551.73(A), which step down as the number of sites grows — 100 percent for one site, 50 percent at 10 to 12 sites, and 41 percent at 36 sites and above — because a whole park never draws full load at every pedestal at once. • The demand factors apply to the sites only. Bathhouses, recreation buildings, pools, and similar park loads are calculated separately and added at full value. The demand table is not optional color: on a forty-site park it is the difference between a service that prices the job and one that prices Sharma out of it. Pedestals are sized for the biggest rig that might plug in, but a park's rigs cycle air conditioners, water heaters, and chargers at different times. Sizing the service on the straight sum buys copper for a peak that never happens. The demand table is the Code's measured diversity for parks: enough headroom for a full winter weekend, without a service sized for a fantasy. Worked example: ten sites, all 50-ampere — 10 × 9,600 = 96,000 VA connected. Table 551.73(A) gives 50 percent for 10 to 12 sites, so the demand load is 48,000 VA — at 240 volts, a 200-ampere service. Price the same park without the table and you are quoting a 400-ampere service nobody needs. Scale it up: forty 50-ampere sites are 384,000 VA connected; the 41 percent factor gives 157,440 VA, about 656 amperes at 240 volts — before the bathhouse and laundry are added separately, at full load. Pull the factor for the actual site count from the printed table on the worksheet; do not carry a remembered percentage between jobs. The trap is skipping the table in either direction. Sizing at 100 percent “to be safe” prices Sharma out of the job — and applying the 41 percent floor to a 10-site park undersizes it, because 10 to 12 sites take 50 percent. The factor follows the site count on the printed table, every time. Service sized on the straight sum of site volt-amperes — the demand factors of Table 551.73(A) never applied. Every receptacle on a multi-receptacle pedestal counted as its own site load, instead of the site counting once at its highest rating. Bathhouse, laundry, and pool loads run through the site demand factor instead of added separately at full value. A remembered demand percentage carried from the last job instead of the printed factor for the actual site count. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Park trailers
x: Article 552 covers park trailers — the trailer-type units built for park placement rather than highway travel, defined around a size threshold that separates them from recreational vehicles. Its rules parallel the mobile home and RV articles for supply and connection. Confusing a park trailer with an RV or a mobile home sends the job to the wrong article, so identification comes first. Identification turns on the definition: • Built on a single chassis mounted on wheels • 400 sq ft or less of gross area in its set-up mode • Bigger units, or units sited permanently, fall to other articles Supply follows the unit's listing: park trailers are typically served by a cord connection or a permanent feeder sized to the unit's load under this article, with the disconnect and protection at the site. When the paperwork and the unit disagree, the nameplate and listing govern. Three different articles cover units that all arrive on wheels, and they do not ask for the same supply, disconnect, or protection. Wire a park trailer under the RV rules or the mobile home rules and the job is wrong before the first box is mounted — wrong feeder, wrong disconnect, a failed inspection. Identification is cheap; rework is not. A park-model unit is delivered to a lot in a Central Florida park. Before choosing between 550, 551, and 552, read the unit's label and paperwork: single chassis on wheels, at or under 400 sq ft set up — a park trailer, Article 552. Sharma's work is the site side: the cord connection or permanent feeder the unit's listing calls for, sized to the unit's load, with the disconnect and protection at the site. When the unit type is unclear, ask the AHJ rather than guessing the article. The trap is calling every wheeled unit an RV and working under 551 — or a mobile home under 550. The article turns on the definition, not the sales name: a single chassis on wheels and 400 sq ft or less of gross area in set-up mode is a park trailer under 552. Over that size, the unit belongs to another article. Unit wired under the wrong article — a park trailer treated as an RV (551) or a mobile home (550). Supply sized from the sales paperwork instead of the unit nameplate and listing. No disconnect and protection at the site for the park trailer supply. Unit over 400 sq ft in set-up mode permitted and wired as a park trailer. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 553 — deleted in 2020 (floating buildings now live in Article 555, Part III)
x: Article 553 no longer exists as its own article. • In the 2020 NEC it was deleted, and its subject — floating buildings, structures supported by water rather than by a foundation, other than boats — was folded into Article 555 as its Part III (555.50 and following). • The substance carried over: the shore-to-building supply, service equipment and disconnecting means located on land rather than on the floating structure, and ground-fault protection for the supply. • A floating building is a structure, not a vessel — it is worked like a building that happens to float. Work a floating building from Article 555, Part III — not from an old 553 printout. A floating building moves with the water, so anything mounted on it flexes, chafes and corrodes faster than the same gear on land. Keeping the service equipment and the disconnect on solid ground gives firefighters and maintenance crews a disconnect they can reach without boarding a moving structure. Ground-fault protection on the supply matters because a fault on a floating structure leaks straight into the water where people swim. Floating restaurant on a lakefront lot in Tavares. The service equipment and the disconnect go on adjacent land, not on the floating structure, and the feeder crosses from the shore disconnect to the building. Coordinate early with the marina scope in Article 555 so the two articles do not get priced twice or missed entirely — the shore work, the disconnect and the ground-fault protection each belong in one takeoff line, not both. Coastal and lakefront AHJs in Florida look hard at floating structures; confirm the local position on shore disconnect placement before the takeoff is final. The trap is working from an old Article 553 printout or a pre-2020 code book. 553 was deleted in 2020, so an answer — or a takeoff — built on 553 misses that the rules now sit in Article 555, Part III, alongside the marina rules the same crew is already working from. Service equipment mounted on the floating structure instead of on adjacent land. No disconnecting means on shore, reachable without boarding the structure. Feeder to the floating building with no ground-fault protection. Takeoff priced from a deleted Article 553 printout, missing the 555 Part III rules. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Marinas, boatyards, floating buildings, and docking facilities
x: Article 555 covers wiring and equipment at fixed and floating piers, marinas, boatyards, boathouses, and residential and commercial docking facilities, plus floating buildings in their own part of the article. 555.1 expressly includes docking facilities associated with one-family dwellings, so a private residential dock is inside this article — not an AHJ judgment call. • The driving hazard is electric shock drowning: stray current in the water around an energized boat or dock can paralyze a swimmer without any visible warning. • The electrical datum plane (555.3) sets the heights: on a floating pier, 30 in above the water level and at least 12 in above the deck; on land, 2 ft above the highest tide or water level. • Receptacles sit at least 12 in above the deck and never below the datum plane (555.33); shore power receptacles are rated not less than 30 A. • Ground-fault protection comes in layers (555.35): shore power receptacles get equipment protection set at not more than 30 mA, feeders and branch circuits to a dock or slip get equipment protection at not more than 100 mA, and ordinary 15- and 20-ampere receptacles get Class A GFCI protection for people. • The service equipment stays on land, adjacent to the structure it serves — never on or in the floating structure (555.4). Electric shock drowning kills swimmers who never touch a wire. A fault on a boat or a dock leaks current into the water, the voltage gradient through the swimmer's body paralyzes muscles, and the swimmer slips under silently. That is why this article layers ground-fault protection, bonding, and strict height rules over ordinary outdoor wiring: the protection has to trip before the water becomes the conductor. A homeowner on a Lake County canal calls: the pedestal trips every time the boat lift runs. Treat every marina circuit as life-safety work. Test the ground-fault devices, verify the bonding, and never defeat a tripping device to keep a boat powered. The shore power receptacle's equipment protection is set at not more than 30 mA and the feeder protection at not more than 100 mA, so find which layer is tripping and fix the fault it found. If a pedestal keeps tripping, the trip is the protection working. Florida is Sharma's marina state — salt water corrosion, storm surge, and coastal AHJs all bear on this work; use marine-listed equipment and confirm the local datum and inspection practice before bidding coastal docks. The trap is treating a residential dock like a backyard outlet: 'It is only a one-family dwelling, so Article 555 does not apply.' It does — 555.1 includes docking facilities at one-family dwellings by name. The second trap is swapping the two numbers: 30 mA protects shore power receptacles, 100 mA is the feeder ceiling — and a feeder device set at 30 mA is not 'safer,' it is a nuisance trip that tempts defeat. Shore power receptacle replaced with a hardware-store receptacle — not part of a listed marine power outlet, or rated under 30 A (555.33). Receptacle mounted below the electrical datum plane, or less than 12 in above the deck (555.33). Feeder to the dock with no ground-fault protection of equipment, or set above 100 mA (555.35). Service equipment mounted on the floating dock instead of on land (555.4). Tripping ground-fault device jumpered out or swapped for a plain breaker to stop nuisance calls. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 555.14: New in 2023: outdoor marina service equipment and disconnects for in-water equipment need an equipotential plane when the system tops 250 volts to ground and the gear sits within 10 ft of the water. Both triggers have to be present: a system over 250 volts to ground, and equipment sitting within 10 ft of the body of water. • 555.15: New in 2023: replacing or modifying dock enclosures, devices or wiring means the new work meets the current code and the whole circuit gets inspected. Damaged gear found gets documented and repaired. Swap or modify a dock's enclosure, device or wiring method, and that new work has to meet the edition in force now. • 555.38: New in 2023: marina luminaires must be listed for their location and fastened against boat damage and sea-life tangles, and fixtures that can end up underwater have extra rules. A light mounted below the highest high tide or the electrical datum plane, where it can end up underwater, must be identified as submersible. • 555.6: The marina shore power demand factors moved out of Article 555 and into Article 220 at 220.120, with the table renumbered Table 220.120. The factors themselves didn't change. Shore power demand factors for marina, boatyard, floating building and docking facility services and feeders now live at 220.120 and Table 220.120. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Electrical datum plane — heights above the water
x: The electrical datum plane is the reference height above the water below which certain equipment, connections, and receptacles may not be installed. 555.3 sets the plane by the kind of structure: • Floating piers and floating facilities, 555.3(A): the plane is 30 in above the water level, and at least 12 in above the deck level. • Land areas subject to tidal fluctuation, 555.3(B): the plane is 2 ft above the highest tide level for the area, under normal circumstances. • Land areas not subject to tidal fluctuation, 555.3(C): the plane is 2 ft above the highest water level for the area, under normal circumstances. Normal circumstances is the key phrase. The plane is figured from ordinary high water — not from the water level on the day of the install, and not from storm surge. Water rises. Equipment set by eye on a calm day sits under water at the next ordinary high tide, and energized equipment in the water is a shock hazard for everyone in it. The datum plane turns 'high enough' into a number the whole job can measure against. Establish the datum line on site with the marina operator and mark it on the pier before rough-in — then set nothing the article restricts below it. Re-check after any deck or float work that changes deck height. On a floating dock on a Central Florida lake, work both numbers — 30 in above the water and at least 12 in above the deck — and hold the higher line. The same line controls the shore power receptacles: 555.33 keeps them at least 12 in above the deck and never below the datum plane. The trap is using the floating-pier numbers everywhere. Thirty inches above the water is the floating case, 555.3(A). A fixed installation on tidal land uses 2 ft above the highest tide level, and the measurement starts from the highest normal level — not from the water you see at low tide on rough-in day. Shore power receptacle mounted below the electrical datum plane. Datum plane figured from the water level on the day of rough-in instead of the highest level under normal circumstances. Junction box left below the datum plane after new floats raised the deck — the line was never re-checked. Floating-pier datum (30 in above the water) applied to a fixed installation in a tidal area. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Location of service equipment — on land, not on the structure
x: The service equipment for a floating building, dock, or marina is installed on land, adjacent to the structure it serves — never on or in the floating structure itself. A floating structure rides up and down with the water, so the service stays on solid ground, where it can be reached and worked on like any other service. Everything downstream of it — the feeders out along the pier — is supplied from that shore-side point. • The service equipment sits on land, adjacent to the structure it serves • It is never installed on or in a floating building or a floating dock • Feeders run from that shore-side service out along the pier to the shore-power pedestals and dock loads • Heights near the water still have to respect the electrical datum plane in 555.3 — for floating piers, 30 in above the water level and at least 12 in above the deck level A floating dock is a moving platform. It rises and falls with tide and wake, flexes every conductor attached to it, and can swamp, break loose or sink in a storm. Service equipment belongs where it stays put: on land, where the utility connection is stable, the disconnect is reachable in an emergency, and nobody has to work on live service equipment while standing on a wet, moving platform. Set the service on land next to the dock or marina it serves and run the feeder out to the pier from there. If a plan or an existing installation shows the service mounted on a floating dock, flag it before rough-in — that location fails this section. At a Lake County marina re-power, the pattern is the meter and main disconnect on land by the seawall, with feeders in conduit along the fixed pier to the floating slips. If the existing service is found on the floating dock, price the relocation to land in the bid — leaving it there is not something an inspector can pass. The trap answer puts the service on the floating building because 'that is what it serves.' 555.4 is blunt: on land, adjacent to the structure — never on or in the floating structure itself. The feeder goes out to the dock; the service does not. Service equipment mounted on a floating dock or floating building. Service disconnect not reachable from land in an emergency. A panel on the floating section used as the service equipment for the dock. Receptacles or equipment set below the electrical datum plane (555.3). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 555.4: Service equipment for a marina, dock or floating building must now sit on land at least 5 ft horizontally from the structure it serves and at least 12 in. above the electrical datum plane. Set service equipment for a floating building, docking facility or marina on land, at least 5 ft back from the structure it serves, measured horizontally. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Pier power distribution — the 250-volt limit
x: Pier power distribution systems are limited to 250 volts phase to phase. • The cap is on the distribution system serving the pier — the feeders and branch circuits that run the docking facility. • The single exception is an engineered installation: where qualified personnel service the equipment under engineering supervision, the system may run above 250 volts, but never above 600 volts phase to phase. • Ordinary marina and dock work is designed well under the cap, at the standard voltages — the higher band is not a field upgrade. • The cap is measured phase to phase, so a three-phase pier system is judged on its phase-to-phase voltage, not phase to ground. A pier is a wet, public place. Boaters, kids, and dock hands — not electricians — plug in, unplug, and handle equipment standing in or beside the water. Capping the distribution voltage keeps the shock and fault energy on the pier at the level ordinary marine equipment and ordinary users are built around. Read the distribution voltage on the plans before ordering gear. If a pier design shows more than 250 volts phase to phase, stop and confirm the qualified-personnel and engineering-supervision conditions are actually part of the job — that call belongs to the engineer, not the crew. A residential dock or a small marina panel at the standard single-phase voltages never comes near the cap; the flag goes up when a plan set shows a three-phase feeder above 250 volts headed down the pier. The trap is reading the exception as a permission slip. 'Our shop has qualified electricians' is not enough — the exception needs qualified personnel servicing the equipment under engineering supervision as part of the installation, and 600 volts is the absolute ceiling, not a design target. For ordinary pier work the answer stays 250 volts phase to phase. Pier distribution run above 250 volts phase to phase with no engineered installation behind it. A higher-voltage feeder extended down the pier as a field change, with no engineering supervision on the job. Distribution voltage on the pier exceeding the 555.5 limit, with no qualified-personnel or engineering-supervision conditions documented. A marina distribution system designed at 600 volts as the standard voltage, treating the exception ceiling as the target. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Boat hoists — GFCI protection at dwelling docks
x: A boat hoist rated not more than 240 volts at a dwelling unit docking facility must have GFCI protection. The 2020 edition moved this rule out of 210.8(C) and into Article 555, with the rest of the marina and dock rules. It is the lift on a house dock that raises the boat out of the water — a motor, a control pendant, and people standing on a wet dock, often barefoot, which is exactly the combination the GFCI is there for. The rule covers the hoist itself; shore-power receptacles and the rest of the dock carry their own Article 555 rules on their own pages. Water changes the shock math. A hoist motor fault can energize the hoist frame, the dock hardware, and the water around the ladder at the same time, and a person climbing out of the water is a near-perfect ground path. The GFCI watches for current leaking out of the circuit and trips in a fraction of a cycle — before the fault current through a swimmer becomes fatal. On a residential dock job on the Winter Park chain of lakes or a Lake County lakefront, feed the hoist from the dock panel through GFCI protection and test it at trim with the hoist under load. If an existing hoist outlet has no GFCI protection, call it out to the owner in writing — a hoist motor fault over water is the shock path this rule exists to break, and 'it worked when we got here' is not a defense anybody wants to make later. The trap is answering 210.8(C). That was the rule's home before 2020; the 2020 edition moved boat hoists into 555.9, with the other dock rules. The second trap is scope: 555.9 covers hoists at dwelling docking facilities — a commercial marina hoist is a different conversation, and a hoist rated over 240 volts is outside this section entirely. Boat hoist circuit at a dwelling dock with no GFCI protection anywhere in the circuit. GFCI device found tripped or failed at final inspection and left in service without replacement. Hoist receptacle swapped for a standard receptacle on a service call, dropping the protection the circuit was built with. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Warning signs — the shock hazard notice
x: A permanent safety sign is required at docking facilities, boatyards and marinas, warning of the electrical shock hazard in the water. • The sign must warn with effective words, colors or symbols meeting 110.21(B)(1). • It must be durable enough to withstand the environment. • It must be clearly visible from all approaches to the facility. • At a minimum it must state: WARNING — POTENTIAL SHOCK HAZARD — ELECTRICAL CURRENTS MAY BE PRESENT IN THE WATER. • A sign that can only be seen from inside the facility does not comply — visibility is judged from the approaches. This is the electric shock drowning warning, and the sign is part of the installation, not an extra. Electric shock drowning kills quietly: a swimmer near a leaking boat or a faulted dock is paralyzed by current in the water and slips under without a mark on them. Nobody can see electricity in water, so the warning has to do the seeing. A sign at every approach is the last chance to keep swimmers out of water that a fault could energize at any moment. Final walk at a small marina in Sanford. Put the sign in the job scope and photograph it at final — the job can fail inspection for a missing sign even when every circuit is right. Mount it at the dock entrance, facing the approach, where someone heading for the water will actually see it, not on the back of the service equipment where only the electrician ever looks. The trap is treating the sign as the owner's problem or a closeout extra. 555.10 makes it part of the installation, with required wording. A paraphrased warning — 'Danger: electricity in water' — is wrong; the minimum wording is set by the section, and the sign has to be visible from all approaches, not just from the office door. No shock-hazard sign at the final inspection. Sign wording paraphrased instead of the required minimum text. Sign mounted where approaching visitors cannot see it — back of the service equipment. Light-duty sign already fading and peeling in the marine environment. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bonding at marinas and docking facilities
x: 555.13 is the bonding rule for marinas, boatyards, and docking facilities — including the private dock at a one-family dwelling. • What gets bonded: metal parts in contact with the water, metal piping, and non-current-carrying metal parts that are likely to become energized — ladders, lifts, hoists, and metal framing all read as one list. • Where it lands: every one of those parts bonds back to the grounding bus in the panelboard that serves the dock. Not to a rod driven at the pier, and not to the nearest green screw — to the panelboard grounding bus. • The conductor: solid copper, insulated, covered, or bare, and not smaller than 8 AWG. • The point is equipotential: dock metal, boat metal, and the water around them are held at the same voltage, so a fault raises everything together and the ground-fault protection trips, instead of leaving one ladder hot against the water. • Bonding is one layer of the marina system. Shore power receptacles get ground-fault protection of equipment at not more than 30 milliamperes, and feeders to the dock at not more than 100 milliamperes (555.35), and equipment heights are set off the electrical datum plane (555.3). The killer at a dock is electric shock drowning. A fault on a boat or lift puts current into the water, and the voltage gradient around the hull can paralyze a swimmer who never touches anything metal. Bonding every metal part back to the panelboard bus holds the dock, the boat, and the water at one potential and gives fault current a solid path back to trip the protection. An unbonded ladder next to an energized hull is the accident this section exists to prevent. Residential dock on a Marion County lake: the takeoff bonds the aluminum ladder, the boat lift frame, and the metal water piping back to the panelboard grounding bus with a continuous run of 8 AWG solid copper, protected where the run crosses the pier framing. At trim, the crew tests continuity from the farthest lift bolt back to the bus — a bonding jumper cut by later dock work is a silent failure, and continuity is the last thing checked before the job is called done. The trap is driving a ground rod at the end of the pier and calling the dock 'bonded.' A rod connects the metal to the earth; 555.13 bonds it to the grounding bus in the panelboard, which is what makes the dock one equipotential system and gives a fault a path that trips the breaker. Second trap: grabbing stranded 8 AWG because it is on the truck. The 2020 text calls for solid copper. Boat lift or ladder never bonded — no conductor back to the panelboard bus. Bonding conductor cut during later dock work and never repaired. Stranded or undersized conductor substituted for the 8 AWG solid copper. Bond landed on a driven rod at the pier instead of the panelboard grounding bus. Bonding run left unprotected where dock traffic and framing damage it. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 555.13: Metal parts already grounded through a branch-circuit or feeder equipment grounding conductor no longer need their own 8 AWG bonding conductor. Everything else still bonds to the panelboard grounding bus. Metal parts already connected to a branch-circuit or feeder equipment grounding conductor (EGC) no longer need a separate bonding conductor. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Disconnecting means for shore power connections (2020 section 555.36)
x: Each boat's shore power connection needs its own disconnecting means that isolates that boat from its supply. • The disconnect is a circuit breaker, a switch, or both. • It is identified to show which receptacle it controls. • It is readily accessible, and it sits ahead of the receptacle in the circuit. • It is located not more than 30 in from the receptacle it controls. Breakers or switches inside a marine power outlet can serve as this disconnect when they meet those conditions. The disconnect belongs to the connection, not to the dock — that is the whole shape of the rule. When a boat has an electrical fire, a failed shore cord, or a fault near someone in the water, the power to that one boat has to die fast — by whoever is standing there, in the dark, without hunting through a dock full of pedestals. One identified disconnect within reach of the receptacle makes that a single motion. Label every pedestal disconnect with the slip and receptacle it controls, and measure the 30-inch limit before the pedestal is set. A boater in the dark needs to kill one connection, not the whole dock. On a two-pedestal replacement, that means each pedestal carries its own breaker for its own receptacle — a shared disconnect at the head of the dock does not satisfy this section, even if it is labeled. This is the 2020 section number, 555.36. The older number 555.17 is not the 2020 section, and 555.36 is not a 2023-only number. The trap answer is one main disconnect at the head of the dock for every boat. 555.36 wants a disconnect per connection, identified, within 30 in of its receptacle. The second trap runs the other way: breakers inside the marine power outlet are allowed to serve as the disconnect when they meet the conditions — 'the breaker doesn't count' is the 2023 emergency-shutoff rule, not the 2020 disconnect rule. Disconnecting means located more than 30 in from the receptacle it controls. Pedestal disconnect with no identification — nothing shows which receptacle or slip it controls. One disconnect at the head of the dock killing every shore power connection on the run. Receptacle wired ahead of its disconnect, so the receptacle stays live with the disconnect off. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 555.36: New in 2023: each marina power outlet or enclosure feeding shore power needs a listed emergency shutoff marked for that use, within sight of it. A breaker handle doesn't count. Each marina power outlet or enclosure that feeds boats needs its own listed emergency shutoff within sight, marked with the words "Emergency Shutoff" (555.36(C)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Receptacles at marinas and docking facilities (2020 section 555.33)
x: 555.33 is where the 2020 NEC keeps the receptacle rules for marinas and docking facilities. • Every receptacle mounts at least 12 in above the deck surface, and never below the electrical datum plane. • Shore power receptacles are part of a listed marine power outlet, installed in a listed enclosure protected from the weather, and rated not less than 30 A. • Shore power receptacles rated 60 A or more are the pin-and-sleeve type. • Receptacles other than shore power get GFCI protection under 210.8. • A replacement receptacle has to meet this section too. Height, listing and location work together — a correct receptacle set too low still fails. A marina deck is wet, salty and walked on barefoot, and the water level moves. A receptacle down at deck level sits in wash water and splash, corrodes fast, and puts line voltage within reach of wet hands and wet feet. The datum plane rule ties the mounting height to the water level the AHJ designs for, not just to the boards under your boots today. Pedestal replacement at a marina in Cape Canaveral, one dock with 18 slips. Set receptacle heights from the finished deck — 12 in minimum — and re-check them if the decking is replaced after rough-in, because new deck boards over old stringers can eat the clearance. Use only marine power outlets listed for shore power service where boats connect; a standard weatherproof receptacle in a bell box is not a shore power outlet and will not pass. This is the 2020 section number, 555.33. The older number 555.19 is not the 2020 section, and 555.33 is not a 2023-only number. The trap is the old section number: answers keyed to 555.19 come from a pre-2020 book. In 2020 the receptacle rules are at 555.33. The second trap is height alone — a receptacle 12 in above the deck that still sits below the electrical datum plane fails. Shore power receptacle mounted less than 12 in above the finished deck. Receptacle installed below the electrical datum plane. Standard receptacle used for shore power instead of a listed marine power outlet. Shore power receptacle rated under 30 A, or a 60 A device that is not pin-and-sleeve. Non-shore-power receptacle on the dock with no GFCI protection. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Ground-fault protection — GFPE and GFCI at marinas
x: The 2020 edition organizes this section into three clear layers of ground-fault protection. • Shore power receptacles get individual ground-fault protection of equipment (GFPE) set to open at not more than 30 mA. • 15- and 20-ampere receptacles other than shore power get Class A GFCI protection for people. • Feeder and branch circuit conductors supplying a dock or slip get GFPE set at not more than 100 mA. GFPE protects equipment and wiring at milliampere levels far above the 4 to 6 mA Class A GFCI trip that protects people, so the two are not interchangeable labels. Stray current in marina water paralyzes a swimmer without ever tripping an ordinary breaker — that is electric shock drowning. Leakage from one boat or one damaged cord can energize the water around a whole dock. Layered protection catches leakage at the receptacle and again at the feeder, at levels high enough that normal boat leakage does not black out the dock, and low enough to clear a real fault. Pedestal replacement at a boatyard in Fort Pierce, 24 slips on two feeders. Build the protection in layers exactly as the design shows — 30 mA GFPE at each shore power receptacle, Class A GFCI on the 15 and 20 A convenience receptacles, 100 mA GFPE on the feeders — and record the trip settings at startup. Never swap a GFPE device for an ordinary breaker because a boat keeps tripping it; find the leaking boat instead. S-07 caution: Sharma's residential DFN breaker is a personnel GFCI and AFCI device. It is not, by itself, the GFPE protection this section requires at 30 and 100 milliamperes — do not carry the house device pattern onto a dock without Mike Holt confirming the specified marina equipment. Florida coastal AHJs test marina ground-fault protection seriously after electric shock drowning incidents nationally; expect the settings and signage to be checked at final. The trap is treating GFPE and GFCI as one device with two names. A Class A GFCI trips at 4 to 6 mA to protect people. The shore power GFPE is set at 30 mA and the feeder GFPE at 100 mA, both protecting equipment and wiring. An answer that puts a personnel GFCI where the section wants 100 mA feeder GFPE — or the reverse — is wrong both ways. Shore power receptacle on an ordinary breaker — no 30 mA GFPE. Feeder to the dock with no GFPE, or GFPE set above 100 mA. Residential GFCI breaker substituted for the specified GFPE device. Convenience receptacles on the dock with no Class A GFCI protection. Trip settings never recorded at startup, so the AHJ cannot verify them. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 555.35: GFCI now reaches non-shore-power dock outlets on circuits no higher than 150 volts to ground and 60 amps (100 amps three-phase), plus boat hoists at every dock. Leakage testers must be listed from 2026. Non-shore-power outlets, lights and equipment included, need GFCI when the circuit is no higher than 150 volts to ground and 60 amps (100 amps three-phase). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Temporary installations — jobsite power
x: Article 590 covers power and lighting installed for a limited time: • Construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair and demolition work. • Holiday and decorative installations, and similar short-term uses. • Emergencies, experiments and testing. Chapters 1 through 4 still apply except where this article specifically changes them. The article relaxes a few wiring methods for the temporary case, but the safety core stays fully in force: overcurrent protection, grounding, and GFCI protection for people. Time is part of the rule — under 590.3, construction power lasts for the duration of the work, and holiday and decorative installations are limited to 90 days. • Every 125-volt, single-phase, 15-, 20- and 30-ampere receptacle outlet that is not part of the permanent wiring needs GFCI protection for personnel (590.6(A)(1)). • On a construction site, receptacles may not share a branch circuit with temporary lighting, and cords and cables used as feeders or branch circuits may not lie on the floor or ground (590.4). Temporary power is the most abused wiring on any site: cords run over by lifts, panels rained on, spider boxes moved daily by every trade. The hazard is not lower because the installation is temporary — the exposure is higher. That is why the article trades method flexibility for an unrelaxed core of GFCI protection, grounding and overcurrent protection. Sharma's standard temp pole on a Marion Oaks rough-in: meter and a Siemens load center on the pole, two 20-ampere GFCI-protected receptacles for the crew's tools, and a ground rod driven its full 8 ft with the GEC clamped above grade where it can be inspected. The temp service paperwork carries a removal date; when the permanent service is energized and accepted, the pole comes out instead of lingering for the next trade to trip over. S-01 does not set temp panel sizes, but Sharma temp work still uses listed gear and Siemens breakers in our own panels per S-02. Temp is not a license for mixed-brand breaker swapping (S-03). The trap answer is “GFCI is not required — it is only temporary power.” 590.6(A)(1) requires GFCI protection for personnel on the 125-volt 15-, 20- and 30-ampere receptacle outlets used for the work, temporary or not. The second trap: holiday lighting on a 90-day limit treated as a permanent installation. Temp panel receptacles with no GFCI protection — “it is only temporary.” Cords and cables lying on the ground across walkways and doorways. Temporary service still feeding the site months after the permanent service was accepted. Exposed lamps without guards and open splices without enclosures in the temp runs. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Time constraints on temporary installations
x: 590.3 is the clock on every temporary installation. Temporary wiring is permitted only for the period the work actually lasts — and each kind of use gets its own limit: • During the period of construction (590.3(A)): construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair, and demolition power stays for that work. There is no day count — the limit is the job itself. • 90 days (590.3(B)): holiday decorative lighting and similar decorative uses get a hard cap of 90 days, and then the temporary power comes out. • Emergencies and tests (590.3(C)): emergencies, tests, experiments, and developmental work may use temporary wiring for the duration the need actually lasts. • Removal (590.3(D)): whatever the use, temporary wiring must be removed immediately upon completion of the purpose it was installed for. Temporary wiring that quietly becomes permanent is a violation, not a value add. Article 590 trades method flexibility for time. Cords, temp panels, and relaxed methods survive a supervised construction site because everyone knows they are coming out. Left in place, they take permanent-service abuse with temporary-grade protection — cords get driven over, panels weather, and nobody owns the removal. The time limits are what keep the trade fair: the installation is only as safe as the promise that it ends. Sharma's standard temp pole on a Marion Oaks rough-in goes in with a removal date written on the temp service paperwork. The permanent service is energized and accepted, and the pole comes out that same week instead of lingering for the next trade to trip over. The mirror case is retail holiday lighting: a storefront display wired in early November hits its 90 days at the end of January, and the calendar — not the tenant's memory — says when it is removed. The trap is applying the 90-day cap to construction power. The 90 days in 590.3(B) belongs to holiday decorative lighting and similar uses only. Construction power under 590.3(A) lasts for the duration of the work — but the reverse trap is worse: 'the job is done, but the temp pole can stay until the next phase.' 590.3(D) requires removal immediately when the purpose ends. Holiday decorative lighting still energized in March, long past 90 days. Temp service left in place after the permanent service was energized and accepted. Temporary wiring feeding an occupied building as a stand-in for permanent wiring. Temp installation with no removal date on the paperwork and no owner for taking it out. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: General requirements for temporary wiring
x: This is the working section of the article. A temporary service is installed to the service rules of Article 230, feeders and branch circuits keep the overcurrent protection of Article 240 (590.4(B) and (C)), and hard or extra-hard usage cords and cables do much of the distribution work. • Receptacles on a branch circuit may not share it with temporary lighting on a construction site (590.4(D)). • Receptacles in wet locations need weatherproof protection with a plug inserted — an in-use cover, not a flip lid. • Every temporary circuit needs a way to disconnect all its ungrounded conductors. • Lamps for general illumination need protection from accidental contact or breakage — a suitable fixture or lampholder with a guard (590.4(F)). • Splices need a box, conduit body, or other enclosure with a cover (590.4(G)). The construction-site exceptions cover splices in cord and cable assemblies and in permanent wiring used temporarily — not open-air twisted joints. • Cables and cords used as feeders or branch circuits may not lie on the ground or floor — support them, protect them where they cross doorways and pinch points, or use the extension cord and protection routes the section actually allows. Temporary wiring gets dragged, driven over, rained on, and reworked daily by every trade on the site. The guards, covers, enclosures, and support rules in this section are what stand between that abuse and a broken lamp, an open splice, or a cord cut in a doorway — the three ways temp power starts fires and shocks workers. Walk a temp installation weekly: guards on lamps, covers on splice boxes, cords up off the ground and out of doorways, and disconnects working. Most temp-power citations are housekeeping items from this one section. On a multi-story build-out, give the weekly walk a route: spider boxes fed with cords supported overhead instead of lying in the walk path, string lights with every guard in place, in-use covers on the receptacles at the wet deck, and the temp panel disconnects exercised so they still open every ungrounded conductor. The trap is the word "temporary" itself: it does not relax the rest of the Code. Article 590 modifies specific rules — services still follow Article 230 and overcurrent protection still follows Article 240. The second trap is the shared circuit: on a construction site, receptacles may not share a branch circuit with temporary lighting, even though the same layout would be legal in finished work. Temporary string light with a missing or broken lamp guard (590.4(F)). Open splice in a cord run — no box, conduit body, or enclosure with a cover (590.4(G)). Feeder cord lying on the floor across a doorway with no protection. Receptacles sharing a branch circuit with temporary lighting on a construction site (590.4(D)). Wet-location receptacle with a flip cover instead of weatherproof protection with the plug inserted. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 590.4(F): Eliminated some existing text concerning various socket styles at Section 590.4(F), and the words "metal guarded sockets" and "metal guard" were added. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: GFCI protection and the assured grounding program
x: Temporary-power receptacles need GFCI protection for personnel — or, outside the GFCI list, a written assured equipment grounding conductor program. All receptacles used for temporary power are of the grounding type. • The GFCI list, 590.6(A): (A)(1) all 125-volt, single-phase, 15-, 20-, and 30-ampere receptacle outlets that are not part of the permanent wiring and are in use by personnel; (A)(2) receptacles of any other rating — including the building's permanent receptacles — used for temporary power during construction, remodeling, maintenance, repair, or demolition: GFCI protection, or a listed cord set or device with listed GFCI protection; (A)(3) 125-volt and 125/250-volt, single-phase, 15-, 20-, and 30-ampere receptacle outlets on a portable generator rated 15 kW or less, with listed GFCI protection. • The program alternative, 590.6(B): for receptacles outside that list, the choice is GFCI protection or the assured program — written procedures; tests before first use, when there is evidence of damage, and before equipment returns to service after repairs; intervals not exceeding 3 months; records available to the AHJ. Two of the familiar details are OSHA rules, not NEC rules — both from OSHA 29 CFR 1926.404(b)(1)(iii): the 6-month test interval, allowed only for cord sets and receptacles fixed in place and not exposed to damage, and the color coding or tagging of tested cords. Each test verifies the grounding conductor's continuity and correct termination. An undocumented program is treated as no program. Construction power is the roughest service in the trade: cords dragged across wet slabs, cut, spliced, and run over, feeding tools held by people standing on grade. A ground fault there does not announce itself — the tool keeps running while its frame sits at line voltage. GFCI protection, or a tested and documented grounding program, is what stands between that fault and the worker holding the tool. On a Sharma remodel in Orlando, the spider box off the temp panel feeds the saws and chargers; every receptacle on it is GFCI-protected and tested device by device at setup (S-07: the house panel's pattern does not cover a jobsite distribution box), and the test log stays with the temp panel. The larger receptacles outside the (A) list run under the assured grounding program: cords tested before first use and every 3 months or less, tagged, records in the job trailer before the inspector asks, not after. S-07 caution: a DFN breaker feeding a receptacle can be the GFCI method on a house's permanent wiring used temporarily, but a spider box or temp panel on site needs its own GFCI protection verified device by device — do not assume the upstream house pattern covers a jobsite distribution box. The trap is stretching the test interval to 6 months for every cord on site, or treating the program as a paperwork-free alternative. Under the NEC the interval is 3 months; the 6-month allowance is OSHA's, only for cord sets and receptacles fixed in place and not exposed to damage. No written program and no records means no program at all. Spider box receptacles with no GFCI protection, on the assumption that the upstream panel covers the jobsite distribution box — protection is verified device by device (S-07). An assured equipment grounding conductor program claimed on site with no written procedures and no test records — an undocumented program is treated as no program. Cord set returned to service after a repair with no retest, and no test records for intervals past 3 months. Non-grounding-type receptacles installed for temporary power. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Overcurrent devices in temporary installations — new in 2020
x: This section was added in the 2020 edition, and it speaks to the reused breakers and fuses that end up in temp panels. • Where reused (590.8(A)): an overcurrent device that has been used before may go into a temporary installation only after it is examined, to confirm it has been properly installed, has been properly maintained, and shows no evidence of impending failure — arcing, overheating, loose or bound parts, visible damage, or deterioration. • Current-limiting service devices (590.8(B)): the overcurrent devices for a temporary service fed from a solidly grounded wye system of more than 150 volts to ground, but not over 1000 volts phase-to-phase, must be of the current-limiting type. A 277/480 volt temp service is the common case. The 2020 text sets no fault-current threshold for this rule. • The section closes the old habit of treating the temp panel as a junk drawer for retired breakers: a device with an unknown history does not get a second life protecting temporary wiring. A breaker that has already cleared faults, sat in a damp gang box, or been swapped from panel to panel may not open when it should. Temporary wiring is handled, moved, and reworked more than any other wiring on the job, so it leans hardest on its overcurrent devices. The current-limiting rule for the bigger wye services also keeps fault energy down where a temp service ties into a stiff utility source. Retire damaged or unknown-history breakers instead of cycling them into temp panels. When a temp service is large, confirm the current-limiting requirement with Mike Holt at takeoff, not at energization. On a 277/480 volt temp service for a commercial build-out, spec current-limiting breakers or fuses in the temp panel from the start: that service is over 150 volts to ground, so 590.8(B) applies before the first circuit is pulled. On the 120/208 volt spider boxes, the foreman examines every reused breaker at setup — heat discoloration, a loose handle, or a cracked case sends it to the dumpster, not back into the box. S-03 reinforces this: breakers go only in panels they are listed for, temp panels included. The trap is importing the 2023 threshold into a 2020 answer. Under the 2020 text, a 277/480 volt temporary service needs current-limiting overcurrent devices because it is a solidly grounded wye system over 150 volts to ground — the 2020 rule has no 10,000-ampere trigger. "Only when the available fault current exceeds 10,000 amps" is the 2023 revision; it is wrong on a 2020 exam and wrong on a 2020 permit. Reused breaker installed with no examination — heat-damaged or cracked case visible in the temp panel (590.8(A)). 277/480 volt temporary service protected by standard, non-current-limiting overcurrent devices (590.8(B)). Reused breaker installed in a temp panel it is not listed for — the S-03 violation that shows up with recycled devices. Oversized reused breaker protecting smaller temporary conductors — feeder and branch protection still follows 240.4. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 590.8: Temporary services on 3-phase wye systems over 150 volts to ground now need current-limiting overcurrent devices only when available fault current exceeds 10,000 amps. Current-limiting service overcurrent devices are now needed only when the available fault current goes above 10,000 amps. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 600 — Electric Signs and Outline Lighting
x: This article covers signs, outline lighting, and skeleton tubing — the lighted advertising and identification equipment on commercial buildings. Its field core is simple: a proper sign branch circuit and a real disconnect at the sign. The numbers that size a sign job: • Sign branch circuit — 20A minimum, serving signs and outline lighting only (600.5) • Pedestrian entrances — at least one outlet in an accessible location at each entrance to each tenant space of a commercial building or occupancy accessible to pedestrians, for sign or outline-lighting use, supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that supplies no other load (600.5(A)); service hallways and corridors are not considered accessible to pedestrians • Load calculations — each required sign branch circuit is figured at not less than 1,200 VA in feeder and service calculations (220.14(F)) • Neon and skeleton tubing — the high-voltage secondary wiring follows its own part of this article (600.31 and 600.32), and the tubing and its power supplies are listed equipment, not field-fabricated parts • Circuit ratings — 600.5(B): circuits supplying signs with incandescent and fluorescent sources are rated 20A maximum; neon transformer or power-supply circuits are rated 30A maximum • Disconnect — each sign needs a disconnect per 600.6 A sign is serviced by sign techs, not electricians, often years after the install, on a ladder, on a building face. The dedicated circuit keeps sign faults and sign work off the building's other loads, and the disconnect at the sign gives the tech a real way to kill the letters before opening them. The entrance outlet exists so the sign circuit is planned at rough-in, not borrowed later. If a bid has signage, price the circuit and the disconnect, not just the sign. On a strip-center tenant build-out, that means the dedicated 20A sign circuit back to the panel, the outlet at the tenant entrance, and the disconnect at the sign itself per 600.6 — and 1,200 VA carried in the service calculation for the required circuit, whether the letters' nameplate adds up to that or not. The trap is figuring the sign circuit at the connected load of the letters — a few hundred volt-amperes of LED — and moving on. For feeder and service calculations, 220.14(F) floors each required sign branch circuit at 1,200 VA. Undersize the calculation and the service is wrong before the sign is even hung. Sign fed from a general lighting circuit shared with other loads. No disconnecting means at the sign (600.6). Sign circuit figured at connected load instead of the 1,200 VA minimum in the service calculation. Required outlet missing at a tenant entrance accessible to pedestrians. Neon secondary parts field-fabricated instead of listed tubing and power supplies. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Sign branch circuits — 20A, signs only
x: 600.5 puts a dedicated circuit behind every storefront sign, in two parts: • 600.5(A) requires at least one receptacle outlet in an accessible location at EACH ENTRANCE of each commercial building or occupancy that is accessible to pedestrians, supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that serves no other load. That outlet is there for the sign and outline lighting at that entrance. • The sign circuit itself is the same family of rule: a sign or outline lighting system is supplied by a branch circuit rated at least 20A that serves no other loads, other than signs and outline lighting tied to the same work. • Service hallways and corridors are not considered accessible to pedestrians, and delivery doors are not pedestrian entrances — the entrance-outlet rule does not reach them. • In feeder and service load calculations, each required sign branch circuit is figured at not less than 1,200 VA. The sign is the one load every storefront has to run, service, and relamp — often by a sign contractor who is not the tenant's electrician. A dedicated 20A circuit means the sign never shares with whatever gets plugged in beside it, and the entrance outlet means the sign crew is not running cords through a doorway or tapping a circuit that was never meant for them. Don't hang storefront lighting or receptacles on the sign circuit. On a strip-center storefront in Kissimmee with two pedestrian entrances, the layout is: one receptacle outlet at each entrance, and the sign on its own 20A home run back to the new Siemens panel, breaker labeled SIGN, with nothing else on it — not the display lighting, not the window receptacles. The service calculation carries that circuit at 1,200 VA. Sharma's S-01 already sets a 20A minimum on commercial branch circuits, so the code and company practice land in the same place here. S-01 already sets a 20A minimum on commercial branch circuits — the code and company practice land in the same place here. The trap is tapping the sign circuit for the storefront display lighting because the sign circuit is right there and 'only half loaded.' Under the 2020 rule the 20A circuit serves signs and outline lighting only. Feeding the sign's own control gear — a time clock or photocell — off that circuit is a 2023 change, not the 2020 rule. Storefront or display lighting tapped off the sign circuit. No receptacle outlet at a pedestrian entrance of a commercial occupancy. Sign circuit rated under 20A, or shared with another tenant's loads. Sign circuit figured below 1,200 VA in the service load calculation. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 600.5: The sign circuit can now also feed equipment that controls the sign, and the delivery-door and service-corridor exemption became a formal exception. The dedicated sign circuit can now also carry loads that control the sign, such as a time clock or photocell (Exception No. 2). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Sign disconnecting means
x: Every circuit that feeds a sign, an outline lighting system, or skeleton tubing gets a real disconnect — not just a breaker back at the panel. • The control is an externally operable switch or circuit breaker that opens all ungrounded conductors at the same time. • Location: at the point where the circuit enters the sign enclosure, the sign body, or the pole the sign is mounted on. • The 2020 rules in 600.6(A) also cover the within-sight, lockable, and remote-location marking situations: a disconnect that is not within sight of the sign must be capable of being locked in the open position, and a disconnect in a remote location must be marked at the sign, so service people and first responders can find and kill it. Sign work happens on ladders, on rooftops, and inside metal cabinets full of ballasts, drivers, and high-voltage neon secondaries. The person servicing the sign has to know the circuit is dead — and stay sure of it while both hands are in the cabinet. A disconnect at the point of entry, opening every ungrounded conductor, is the one control that does that; the lockable and marking rules keep it true when the disconnect has to live somewhere else. Pylon sign at a Winter Garden shopping center: the sign circuit comes out of the tenant panel on a dedicated 20 A Siemens breaker (the sign circuit family in 600.5), runs up the pole, and lands first on an externally operable disconnect mounted at the point where the circuit enters the sign structure — one switch opening all ungrounded conductors. The sign tech kills it, locks it, and opens the cabinet with nobody able to re-energize from the panel. On a monument sign whose disconnect ends up remote, inside the building, the sign itself gets a placard telling the tech where that disconnect lives. The trap answer is 'the breaker in the panel is the disconnect.' A panel breaker is overcurrent protection and a control, but 600.6 puts the disconnecting means at the point where the circuit enters the sign enclosure, body, or pole — and if it is not within sight, it must be lockable in the open position and marked. Naming the panel breaker leaves the sign tech with no local, lockable kill point. No disconnect at the sign — when the inspector asked, the crew pointed at the panel breaker. Disconnect opens only one ungrounded conductor; the second hot stays live inside the cabinet. Disconnect mounted remotely with no marking at the sign telling anyone where it is. Disconnect not within sight of the sign and not capable of being locked in the open position. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Retrofit kits (new in 2020)
x: Converting an existing sign to new lighting technology is a listed-kit job, not a lamp swap. • A general-use or sign-specific retrofit kit must be listed and labeled, and it must include installation instructions for field conversion of the host sign. • The kit is installed per those instructions. • Wiring methods follow Chapter 3, with the Class 2 path in 600.12(C), 600.24 and 600.33. • Parts that are not replaced are inspected, and damaged parts are repaired or replaced. • Workmanship follows 110.12. • The retrofitted sign is marked per 600.4(B) — including the alert label where tubular LED lamps run on the existing sign sockets, so nobody later installs fluorescent lamps. The 600.2 retrofit definitions — host sign, subassembly, and general-use and sign-specific kits — ride with this section. A lamp swap leaves the old sign's ballasts, sockets and wiring in service with lamps they were never listed for. Heat, mismatched drivers and tired lampholders are how sign fires start. The listed kit, its instructions and the marking tie the converted sign to a tested combination — and the alert label stops the next technician from screwing fluorescent tubes into a sign that has been rewired for LED. A shopping plaza on Orange Blossom Trail is converting its cabinet signs to LED. Before quoting, the estimator confirms the kit is listed for that host sign and plans the 600.4(B) label as part of the job — an inspector can fail an unlisted conversion even if it lights. On the first sign the crew finds two heat-damaged lampholders; because the kit job includes inspecting the parts that stay, those sockets are replaced before the LED tubes go in, not after a callback. The trap is treating the job as a lamp swap: pull the fluorescent tubes, drop in LED tubes, done. If the kit is not listed for the host sign, or the sign is not marked per 600.4(B), the conversion fails even though it lights — and where tubular LEDs run on the old sockets without the alert label, the next lamp change can put fluorescent tubes back into a rewired sign. Sign converted with an unlisted retrofit kit — 600.35 requires a listed, labeled kit with installation instructions. Retrofitted sign not marked per 600.4(B); no alert label where tubular LED lamps use the existing sign sockets. Heat-damaged lampholder left in service during a retrofit — parts not replaced must be inspected, and damaged parts repaired or replaced. Kit installed contrary to its instructions, with the old ballast left connected where the kit requires it removed. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 600.35: Section 600.35 had redundant requirements removed, which are already covered in Chapters 1-4 of NEC. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 604 — Manufactured Wiring Systems
x: Manufactured wiring systems are factory-built wiring assemblies — plug-together branch-circuit and feeder components — used heavily in office fit-outs. The system is field-installed, but the assemblies cannot be inspected at the site without destroying them, so the listing does the inspecting: components must be listed and used as one system, never mixed between manufacturers (604.1, 604.6). • Permitted in accessible, dry locations, and in ducts, plenums, and other air-handling spaces where listed for it and installed per 300.22 (604.4) • Cables are listed Type AC or Type MC, or listed flexible metal conduit, with 600-volt copper conductors from 8 AWG to 12 AWG and a full-size copper equipment grounding conductor (604.6(A)) • One exception: a luminaire tap not over 6 ft long, feeding a single luminaire, may drop to conductors as small as 18 AWG (604.6(A) Exception) • Support follows the Chapter 3 article for the cable or conduit type used (604.6(E)) Where Sharma meets it: relocatable wiring for office partitions, pre-wired workstation feeds, and raised-access-floor whips on tenant fit-outs. The connectors are keyed to the system — a whip that will not mate is the system telling you the parts came from different manufacturers, and forcing the connection voids the listing. Home runs land in the panel like any other branch circuit; the manufactured part is only the distribution between the connection point and the outlets, and every run stays accessible so it can be inspected and reconfigured without disturbing the building wiring. A factory assembly arrives with its splices and terminations already made, and nobody on site can open it up and check them without destroying it. The listing, the keyed connectors, and the one-manufacturer rule stand in for that missing inspection: they keep a 277-volt lighting whip from being plugged into a 120-volt system and keep untested field splices out of a ceiling plenum. Sharma hits these on tenant work: an Orlando office fit-out with 40 workstations fed from raised-floor whips on two 20 A branch circuits. Keep one manufacturer's system end to end and follow its instructions — the home runs are field-wired to the panel, and everything past the connection point is the listed system. Get the furniture vendor's power plan into the job file before rough-in: it shows where each feed lands, and finding out at trim that the whips are another maker's costs a day, not an hour. The trap answer treats a manufactured wiring system like ordinary cable: mixing one maker's whips with another maker's distribution boxes because the plugs almost fit, or assuming any AC or MC cable qualifies. The system is listed as a system — the cables are listed Type AC or MC with 600-volt, 8 to 12 AWG copper conductors, and parts are not interchangeable between manufacturers. Whips from two manufacturers mixed in one run — the system is listed as a system, not as loose parts. Manufactured wiring run in a plenum without the listing for air-handling spaces (604.4, 300.22). Home run connected with a cord and plug through a wall instead of landing at the system's fixed connection point. Cable left unsupported — support follows the Chapter 3 article for the cable type used (604.6(E)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 605 — Office Furnishings
