x: Article 605 covers the electrical equipment, lighting accessories, and wiring systems used with office furnishings — cubicle panels, partitions, workstations, desks, shelving, and storage units that interconnect mechanically and electrically to form one system (605.2). A lone motorized desk on its own cord is not a system, and is not covered. • Powered furnishings connect to the building wiring at the fixed connection point the system is listed for — never by a cord pushed through a wall or ceiling. • Partitions interconnect only with the manufacturer's listed connectors, or a flexible assembly identified for the use, in the combinations and circuit counts the listing allows. Where flexible cord makes an interconnection, it must be extra-hard usage, 12 AWG or larger, with an insulated equipment grounding conductor, not over 2 ft long, joining mechanically contiguous partitions (605.5). • Fixed partitions — secured to building surfaces — are permanently connected by Chapter 3 wiring methods; freestanding partitions may be hard-wired the same way (605.7, 605.8). • A freestanding group may instead be fed by a single cord and plug when every 605.9 condition is met — see the checklist table. • Lighting accessories must be listed for use with the partitions and supported; they carry no receptacles, and a cord-connected light uses hard-usage cord not over 9 ft (605.6). • Wired partitions are not permitted to extend from floor to ceiling unless the AHJ specifically permits it. Cubicle systems put receptacles and lighting inside fabric-covered furniture that office staff rearrange with hand tools. The listing, the listed connectors, and the hard caps on cords and receptacle counts keep a furniture layout from becoming unlisted field wiring hidden inside a partition — and keep an overloaded furniture circuit from cooking unseen. Office fit-out in Lake Mary: Sharma's scope is the building side. Two dedicated 20 A circuits on Siemens breakers feed receptacles set within 12 in. of where the furniture plan lands the powered partitions — roughed in before the furniture truck arrives, not after. The furniture vendor's shop drawings are an electrical document on this job: they show where each building feed lands and how many circuits the system is listed for, and they belong in the job file before rough-in. Coordinate furniture power early; the furniture system is listed equipment, not field-built wiring. The trap is treating the furniture feed as a convenience problem: "plug the cubicles into the nearest receptacle on a shared circuit." A cord-connected group needs its own dedicated circuit, a receptacle within 12 in. of the partition, one cord not over 2 ft — and never more than 13 receptacles in the group. Second trap: running a multiwire circuit inside a cord-connected group. Not permitted at all. Furniture fed by a cord pushed through a wall or ceiling to a receptacle in the next room. Partitions interconnected with unlisted jumpers, or more circuits combined than the listing allows. Cord-connected group on a shared circuit, with the supply receptacle several feet from the partition. More than 13 receptacles in one cord-connected group, or a multiwire circuit inside it. Feed landed by guesswork — the furniture shop drawings were never obtained before rough-in. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 610 — Cranes and Hoists
x: Article 610 covers the wiring, disconnects and controls for cranes, monorail hoists, hoists and all runways (610.1). Rare in Sharma's current work — recognize it, and price from the article when a warehouse job includes one. • Runway disconnect (610.31): the contact conductors along the runway get their own disconnect between them and the power supply — readily accessible and operable from the ground or floor level, lockable in the open position (110.25), opening all ungrounded conductors at once, and within view of the runway contact conductors. • Crane disconnect (610.32): every crane and monorail hoist carries a second disconnect in the leads from the runway conductors, also lockable open. Its rating is a 610 rule, not a 430 rule: at least 50 percent of the combined short-time ampere rating of the motors, and at least 75 percent of the sum for any single motion (610.33). • Sizing follows the article's duty-based approach (610.14(E)), not a straight Article 430 feeder calculation: largest motion at 100 percent of nameplate, next largest at 50 percent, and a Table 610.14(E) demand factor when several cranes share one conductor system. • Contact conductors are located or guarded so nobody touches energized parts by accident (610.21(A)). Festoon and pendant wiring is supported so strain never lands on the terminations — a traveling crane beats on its wiring every cycle. A crane runway can stay energized along a whole building, out of reach, while people work under moving loads. The mechanic on the bridge and the rigger below both need the conductors dead when the job says dead. The two lockable disconnects — runway and crane — make a real lockout possible, and guarded contact conductors keep hands and tools off live parts the rest of the time. On a warehouse bid, find the crane's disconnect and runway-conductor scope in the drawings before pricing. Worked case: a bridge crane with a 30 A hoist motor and a 12 A bridge motor — the 610.14(E) conductor load is 30 A plus half of 12 A, 36 A, not an Article 430 build-up. If the crane package is by others, say so in the bid notes — otherwise the runway disconnect and the lockout point land on Sharma by default. The trap is sizing the crane feeder like an Article 430 motor feeder — biggest motor at 125 percent plus the rest at full rating. Article 610 runs on duty: largest motion at 100 percent, next at 50 percent, demand factor for shared runways (610.14(E)). The 430 answer oversizes the run and misses the question. No disconnecting means for the runway conductors, or one that cannot be locked in the open position (610.31). Runway disconnect mounted where it cannot be operated from the ground or floor level (610.31). Crane or monorail hoist with no disconnect in the leads from the runway conductors (610.32). Contact conductors where a person can touch them inadvertently — not located or guarded (610.21(A)). Festoon cable supported by its own conductors, strain on the terminations. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 620 — Elevators, Dumbwaiters, Escalators, Moving Walks, Platform Lifts, and Stairway Chairlifts
x: Article 620 covers the electrical installation for elevators, dumbwaiters, escalators, moving walks, platform lifts, and stairway chairlifts. Sharma's scope is the electrical side; the machine itself belongs to the elevator contractor under ASME A17.1. • Each driving machine gets its own disconnecting means — an enclosed, externally operable fused switch or circuit breaker — and it must be lockable in the open position only, never lockable closed (620.51). • The disconnect kills the driving machine only. Car lighting, receptacle, and ventilation circuits (620.22, 620.23, 620.24) are arranged to stay energized, so service work in the car is not done in the dark. • GFCI protection: every 125-volt, single-phase, 15- and 20-ampere receptacle in pits, hoistways, on cars, and in wellways and machinery spaces is GFCI type, and machine-room receptacles carry GFCI protection too (620.6). • Where several machines share one feeder, the disconnect overcurrent devices are selectively coordinated with the supply-side devices, selected and documented by a licensed professional engineer or other qualified person (620.62, 620.65). A mechanic working in a hoistway with a machine that can still move, or in a car gone dark because the disconnect killed the lights too, is how people get hurt on elevator work. These rules split machine power from the service circuits: the machine can be locked out dead while the car stays lit, and the receptacles a mechanic plugs into are GFCI protected. On a Central Florida medical-office job with two hydraulic elevators, Sharma's piece is the two machine-room disconnects, the car light and receptacle circuits tapped ahead of them, the pit GFCI receptacles, and the machine-room circuits — the elevator contractor sets the machines and traveling cables. Confirm that split in the bid, not on site: where one feeder serves both machines, the coordination selection and its documentation are a line item too, not a free extra. One disconnect per machine, lockable open only, and the car circuits stay live when it is off. The trap is treating the elevator disconnect like an ordinary motor disconnect and feeding the car lights through it. It feels tidy and it is wrong twice: the disconnect must not kill the 620.22, 620.23, and 620.24 car circuits, and it must be lockable in the open position only. A disconnect that can be locked closed fails even if everything else on the job is right. Car lighting fed through the machine disconnect — disconnect off, car dark (620.51, 620.22). Disconnect lockable in the closed position — 620.51 permits lockable open only. Plain receptacle in the pit — 125V pit receptacles must be GFCI type (620.6). Two machines on one feeder with no selective-coordination documentation (620.62). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 620.36: Received substantiation specifies which cable types may be installed in elevator raceway or traveling cable. Shielded pair cables, coaxial cables, and communication cables complying with 800.179 are now specifically permitted in Section 620.36. 620.51(A) Type. Ex. No. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: GFCI protection in elevator spaces
x: 620.6 puts GFCI protection where elevator work puts people in contact with water, grounded metal and machinery: • All 125V, single-phase, 15A and 20A receptacles installed in pits, in hoistways, on elevator and dumbwaiter cars, in escalator and moving-walk wellways, and in the runways and machinery spaces of platform lifts and stairway chairlifts must be of the GFCI type — the protection is at the receptacle, not just a GFCI breaker upstream. • Receptacles in machine rooms, control rooms, machinery spaces and control spaces must also have GFCI protection for personnel. • A permanently installed sump pump in the pit must be permanently wired or supplied by a single GFCI-protected receptacle — the blanket sump-pump exemption as printed in the 2017 edition is gone in 2020. The pit is the worst receptacle location in the building: standing water, a sump, grounded rails and car metal on every side, and a technician working on a ladder or kneeling in the damp. A tool or trouble light that faults there puts current through the worker to the rails. GFCI protection at the outlet trips in milliseconds, before that fault becomes a fatality. Small medical office in Orlando, two-stop elevator: Sharma's scope is the pit and machine-room receptacles. The crew installs GFCI receptacles — not a breaker alone — at the pit and hoistway locations, and the pit sump pump goes on a single GFCI-protected receptacle instead of being treated as exempt. One caution stays in the estimate notes: the 2020 Handbook notes the hard-wired sump-pump wording sits awkwardly with 422.5(A)(6), so that detail is worth an AHJ conversation on a real job before rough-in. The trap is protecting the pit receptacle with a GFCI breaker in the panel and calling it done. For pits, hoistways, cars and wellways, 620.6 requires receptacles of the GFCI type — the device is at the outlet. The second trap is 2017 habit: the blanket sump-pump exemption is gone in 2020, so an unprotected pit sump pump fails. Pit receptacle is a standard receptacle fed from a GFCI breaker — 620.6 requires the GFCI type at the receptacle in pits and hoistways. Pit sump pump plugged into an unprotected receptacle with the old exemption claimed — the 2017 blanket exemption is gone in 2020. Machine room receptacles installed with no GFCI protection for personnel. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Car lighting, receptacle, ventilation, heating and air-conditioning branch circuits
x: This section puts the car loads on their own dedicated circuits, apart from the driving-machine supply. • 620.22(A): a separate branch circuit supplies the car lights, receptacle(s), auxiliary lighting power source, and ventilation on each car. The required car lighting must not be connected to the load side of a GFCI — a tripped service receptacle must not black out the car. • 620.22(B): car heating and air-conditioning units are supplied by their own separate branch circuit. The overcurrent device protecting each circuit is located in the machine room or control space for that car, and neither circuit is opened by the driving-machine disconnect (620.51), so the car stays lit and ventilated while the machine is locked out for service. The mechanic servicing the driving machine locks out the machine disconnect — and is often standing in the car or the hoistway when he does it. If that disconnect also killed the car lights and ventilation, he would be working in a dark, unventilated shaft. The same thinking keeps the car lighting off the load side of a GFCI: one tripped receptacle must not strand passengers in a black car between floors. Small commercial job — a two-stop elevator in a Florida medical office. Sharma runs two dedicated 20 A circuits to each car from the machine-room panel: the first for the car lights, the car receptacle, and ventilation; the second for the car heating and air-conditioning unit alone. Both breakers live in the machine room, where the inspector looks for them. The car receptacle is a GFCI type (620.6), wired so its load terminals never feed the car lights — a receptacle trip leaves the car lit. The common wrong answer is one circuit for everything in the car — lights, receptacle, ventilation and the AC on a single 20 A run, because it is all 'car load.' 620.22(B) wants the heating and air-conditioning on their own separate branch circuit. Second trap: feeding the car lights through the load side of the car's GFCI receptacle — convenient, and exactly what 620.22(A) forbids. Car lights, receptacle and ventilation combined with the car heating and air-conditioning on one branch circuit (620.22(B)). Required car lighting fed from the load side of a GFCI, so a receptacle trip blacks out the car (620.22(A)). Car circuit breakers located in the car or at the service instead of in the machine room or control space for that car. Car circuits opened by the driving-machine disconnect (620.51) — the car goes dark when the machine is locked out. Non-GFCI receptacle installed on the car, in the pit, or in the machine room (620.6). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Disconnecting means — one per unit, lockable open only
x: Each elevator, dumbwaiter, escalator, moving walk, platform lift, or stairway chairlift gets its own disconnecting means: an enclosed, externally operable fused motor-circuit switch or circuit breaker that disconnects the driving machine. • One disconnect per unit — two machines never share one. • The disconnect must be lockable in the open position only. It is not permitted to be lockable in the closed position. • It must not disconnect the car lighting, receptacle, and ventilation circuits covered by 620.22, 620.23, and 620.24. Those stay energized so service work in the car is not done in the dark. The lock tells the story. A mechanic working on a machine locks the disconnect open so nobody can re-energize it mid-job — and the code forbids a lock in the closed position so the switch can never be locked ON against the mechanic. At the same time, killing the machine must not strand a second worker in a dark, unventilated car, which is why the car circuits live outside this disconnect. Two elevators in a Winter Park medical office: each machine room disconnect is its own enclosed switch, labeled for its unit — 'ELEVATOR 1', 'ELEVATOR 2' — and each locks open with the mechanic's padlock. The car light and ventilation breaker sits in its own enclosure beside them and stays on while a machine is locked out, so the tech in the car keeps light and air. One disconnect per unit, labeled, and never let it kill the car light circuit — a serviceman in a dark car is exactly what the rule prevents. The trap is the fire pump habit: a 695 disconnect is lockable in the CLOSED position so nobody can casually shut the pump off. Article 620 wants the exact opposite — lockable open only, never lockable closed. Picking 'lockable in the closed position' on a 620.51 question imports the wrong article's rule. One disconnect feeding two driving machines. Disconnect that can be locked in the closed position. Machine disconnect also kills the car lighting and ventilation circuits. Disconnect not identified for its unit in a multi-car machine room. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Selective coordination
x: Where one feeder supplies more than one elevator driving machine, the overcurrent device in each machine's disconnecting means must be selectively coordinated with any other supply-side overcurrent device. Coordinated means a fault at one machine opens only that machine's device — the feeder device and the other machines' devices hold, so one fault does not strand every car on the feeder. • The rule is triggered by the arrangement: two or more driving machine disconnecting means supplied by a single feeder. • The selection must be made by a licensed professional engineer, or by another qualified person engaged primarily in the design, installation, or maintenance of electrical systems. • The selection — including the device settings, a documentation point the 2020 edition added — must be documented and made available to those authorized to design, install, inspect, maintain, and operate the system. • Enclosures containing selectively coordinated devices are marked per 620.65. A car stalled between floors is an inconvenience. Every car in the bank dark and dead because one motor faulted is an entrapment problem: passengers stuck in all of them, and no working car to move people or bring up tools. Coordination keeps a single fault local, so the healthy machines keep running while the faulted one is repaired. Two-car bank in a Winter Park medical office. One feeder from the switchboard supplies both machine disconnects, so 620.62 applies. Sharma's scope is the feeder and the two disconnects — Siemens gear, as always on new work — but the coordination is an engineering deliverable, not a field decision. Get the documented study, with the device settings, into the job file before trim-out, and confirm the enclosures carry the 620.65 marking. An inspector who asks for the study and hears "the elevator vendor is sending it" writes it up. The trap answer: "Selective coordination is only an Article 700 emergency-system rule." Wrong — 620.62 requires it on an ordinary elevator feeder that supplies more than one driving machine, in a building with no emergency system at all. The second trap is treating coordination as a field adjustment: the installer does not dial it in. A licensed PE or other qualified person selects it, and the settings are documented. Two machine disconnects on one feeder and no coordination study on file. Devices selected but settings never documented — nothing available for the inspector or the maintenance contractor. Enclosure containing coordinated devices not marked per 620.65. Feeder breaker trips on a single-car fault and strands both cars — the devices were never coordinated. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 625 — Electric Vehicle Power Transfer System
x: The 2020 edition renamed this article from 'Charging System' to 'Power Transfer System' because the equipment now moves power both ways — charging, power export, and bidirectional flow are all inside the article's scope. The field core for Sharma: • One dedicated branch circuit for each EV outlet (625.40) — no sharing with other loads. • EV charging is a continuous load, so overcurrent protection and conductors are sized at 125 percent (625.41, 625.42). • A lockable disconnect where the equipment is rated over 60 A or over 150 V to ground (625.43). • GFCI protection for personnel on every receptacle installed for EV charging (625.54) — the EVSE's own internal protection does not take its place. • The output cable to the vehicle is limited to 25 ft of overall usable length unless the listed equipment includes a cable management system (625.17(B)(3)); power-supply cords on cord-and-plug EVSE have their own length limits. A longer cord draped across a garage floor or a parking space is a trip hazard and a listing problem at the same time — plan the charger location so 25 ft reaches the charge port of the vehicles the space serves. A charger pulls its full rating for hours at a time — a steady load, more like a range that never cycles off. Shared circuits, 100 percent sizing and cords stretched across walk paths turn that draw into heat and trip hazards. The article answers with a dedicated circuit per outlet, 125 percent sizing, GFCI protection and a hard limit on cable length. A Winter Park garage gets a 48 A hardwired EVSE. Continuous load, so the branch circuit is 48 × 1.25 = 60 A — one dedicated circuit for that one outlet (625.40) out of a new Siemens panel, and the wall unit is placed so its 25 ft output cable reaches the charge ports on both parking spots without crossing the walk-door path. Garage EV points follow Sharma's garage rules (S-07, S-01) only where they don't conflict with Article 625 — the article wins where they differ. Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020. The trap is treating a bidirectional EVSE as outside the article because 'it exports instead of charging.' The 2020 rename to Power Transfer System was deliberate — export and bidirectional equipment sit inside Article 625. Answering 'charging rules do not apply' is the wrong answer. EV outlet sharing a branch circuit with other loads — 625.40 requires an individual branch circuit for each EV outlet. Charger circuit sized at 100 percent of nameplate; EV charging is a continuous load at 125 percent (625.41, 625.42). Receptacle installed for EV charging with no GFCI protection for personnel (625.54). Output cable longer than 25 ft with no listed cable management system (625.17(B)(3)). Equipment over 60 A or 150 V to ground with no lockable disconnect (625.43). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 625.6: Clarified which electric vehicle equipment involved in electric vehicle power transfer systems should be listed in Section 625.6. • 625.49: Created a new Section 625.49 stating that electric vehicle power export equipment (EVPE) and bidirectional electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) are permitted to be a part of interconnected power systems operating in an island mode condition. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Electric vehicle branch circuit — one outlet, one circuit
x: In NEC 2020 the rule is flat: each outlet installed for the purpose of charging an electric vehicle must be supplied by an individual branch circuit, and that circuit must have no other outlets. • It applies to every EV charging outlet, whatever its size — there is no small-charger carve-out in the 2020 text. • A 240 V wall connector, a 14-50 receptacle installed for charging, and a 120 V outlet installed for Level 1 charging each get their own circuit. • Sharing happens upstream, not here: listed load management under 625.42 can cap what several chargers draw from a service or feeder, but each outlet still lands on its own branch circuit. A charger is a continuous load that can pull its full rating for hours. Two chargers doubled onto one circuit means conductors and a breaker sized for one car carrying two — nuisance trips at best, cooked insulation at worst. One outlet per circuit also means one fault or one bad charger never takes out the other car. Two-car garage in Winter Park: the owners run two 48 A wall connectors. Under Florida's 2020 rules that is two circuits — a 60 A individual branch circuit to each charger (48 A × 125% per 625.41), two home runs, two breakers, nothing else on either one. The chargers talk to each other and share the service through load management (625.42), which is legal because the sharing happens upstream of the branch circuits, not by doubling up an outlet. Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020. The exam trap is importing the 2023 text early: 'outlets rated 16 A or less at 120 V can share, and managed chargers can share a circuit.' Both statements belong to NEC 2023, which Florida applies only to permits filed on or after Dec 31, 2026. On a 2020 exam — and on a 2020 permit — every EV outlet gets an individual branch circuit with no other outlets, full stop. Two EV chargers landed on one branch circuit, with load management offered as the reason. EV receptacle added to an existing garage receptacle circuit. Branch circuit for a charger also feeding a workbench or freezer outlet. 2023 sharing exception applied on a permit filed under NEC 2020. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 625.40: Only EV charging outlets rated over 16 amps or 120 volts now need an individual branch circuit, and a new exception allows several chargers on one circuit when the load is managed. An individual branch circuit is now required only for outlets serving EV supply equipment (EVSE) rated more than 16 amps or more than 120 volts. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Overcurrent protection — 125% of maximum load
x: EV charging is a continuous load — a charger can pull its full rating for three hours or more on an overnight charge. So the overcurrent device protecting a feeder or branch circuit that supplies EV charging is sized at not less than 125% of the equipment's maximum load, and the conductors are sized to the same figure (625.42). • 32 A charger → 125% is 40 A → a 40 A breaker. • 40 A charger → 125% is 50 A → a 50 A breaker. • 48 A charger → 125% is 60 A → a 60 A breaker. Size from the charger's maximum setting, not from the car plugged in today and not from a lower setting picked in an app. Where access to the adjustment is restricted, or a listed load management system caps the load, 625.42 lets the service and feeder be figured at the capped load — but each EV outlet still gets its own branch circuit (625.40). A breaker and its conductors sized at exactly 100% of a load that runs all night sit at their thermal edge for hours at a time. Breakers trip on heat, terminations loosen and cook over repeated long cycles, and insulation ages fast when it runs hot. The 125% factor is the Code's continuous-load margin: it keeps the device, the lugs and the wire in their comfortable range for the whole charge, every night, for years. Two-car garage in Orlando on a 200 A Siemens panel. One side is a plug-in charger set to 40 A on a 240 V receptacle: 40 × 1.25 = 50, so it lands on a 50 A two-pole GFCI breaker — 625.54 requires GFCI protection for the charging receptacle — with 8 AWG copper, good for 50 A at 75 °C. The other side is a hardwired unit set to 48 A: 48 × 1.25 = 60, a 60 A breaker, and the wire steps up to 6 AWG copper because 8 AWG stops at 50 A. The panel schedule is written from the chargers' maximum settings, not from the two cars that happen to live there now. The trap is sizing from the setting on the screen: 'the charger is set to 32 A, so a 40 A breaker is plenty' — until the owner raises it to 48 A in the app and the 40 A breaker cooks every night. Unless the adjustment is restricted the way 625.42 requires, the maximum load is the equipment's maximum setting. The other trap is a 48 A charger on a 50 A breaker because a 50 A receptacle was handy: 50 is less than 60, and the math fails before the receptacle question even starts. 48 A charger protected by a 50 A breaker — 125% of the maximum load is 60 A (625.41). Charger circuit sized from the car's current charge setting instead of the equipment's maximum setting. Two EV outlets sharing one branch circuit — each EV outlet gets its own circuit (625.40). 60 A breaker landed on 8 AWG copper — conductor ampacity (50 A at 75 °C) is below the 125% load figure. EV charging receptacle with no GFCI protection (625.54). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Rating — charging is a continuous load; load management
x: Two ideas live in this section: • EV charging is a continuous load. That single fact drives the 125% sizing of branch-circuit conductors and overcurrent devices in 625.41. • Load management changes the math upstream. Where a listed automatic load management system is used, the maximum equipment load on a service or feeder is the maximum load the system permits — the managed cap, not the sum of every charger's nameplate. Equipment with adjustable settings is figured at its setting only where the adjustment means meets the section's conditions. What load management never does: it does not merge branch circuits. Each outlet keeps its own circuit under 625.40, sized at 125% of that charger's maximum load. Services in Florida homes were not built for two cars charging all night on top of air conditioning. Without the continuous-load rule, breakers and conductors would cook at full rating for hours. Load management is the release valve: a listed system watches the service and throttles the chargers, so the house can charge both cars without a service upgrade — while the cap, not wishful thinking, becomes the number the service is sized on. Orlando house, 200 A service, two 48 A chargers. Unmanaged, the pair is 96 A of nameplate — 120 A once the 125% continuous factor lands — on top of the house load. With a listed load management system capped at 80 A combined, the service and feeder are figured at 80 A for the EV load. Each charger still gets its own 60 A branch circuit (48 A × 125%), because 625.40 and 625.41 do not bend. The chargers slow down when the AC and range run together, and speed back up overnight. The classic wrong answer: 'the load manager caps the pair at 80 A, so run one 80 A circuit and split it between both chargers.' Load management caps the service and feeder figure only. The branch circuits stay individual and stay sized at 125% of each charger's maximum. The second trap is figuring an adjustable charger at the low setting a homeowner picked in an app — the setting counts only when the adjustment means meets the section's conditions. Service calculation uses the sum of charger nameplates even though a listed load management system caps the load — or uses a cap from an unlisted add-on. Adjustable charger figured at a low app setting with no restricted adjustment means. EV load figured as noncontinuous; branch-circuit breaker trips on long overnight charges. One branch circuit split between two chargers, justified by the load manager. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 625.42: The two ways to size services and feeders below the nameplate, load management and restricted adjustable settings, now sit in 625.42(A) and (B) and tie to the energy management rules in 750.30. Every EV charger counts as a continuous load, so size its circuit conductors and overcurrent device at 125 percent of the rating. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Disconnecting means — over 60A or 150V to ground
x: EV charging equipment rated more than 60 A, or more than 150 V to ground, needs its own disconnecting means under this section: • The disconnect must be readily accessible — reachable quickly, without climbing over or moving anything. • It must be capable of being locked in the open position, and the locking provision stays in place whether the lock is on it or not, as 110.25 requires. • Equipment rated at or under both thresholds — 60 A or less and 150 V or less to ground — does not need the separate disconnect under 625.43. The rating that counts is the equipment's rating, not the size of the breaker feeding it. A 48 A charger on a 60 A circuit is still 48 A equipment. Big chargers move enough energy to hurt someone fast, and their electronics can leave parts energized after the vehicle is unplugged. A lockable disconnect within reach lets a technician, a firefighter, or the building owner kill the equipment for certain and keep it dead while hands are inside it. The lock is what turns “somebody switched it off” into “it stays off until I say so.” Fleet depot in Lakeland: two DC fast chargers rated 100 A each. Both are over the 60 A threshold, so each gets a lockable disconnect on the wall beside it, readily accessible from the drive aisle — planned at rough-in, while the wall is open and the gear layout can still move, not discovered at the final. Across the lot, the employee chargers are 48 A wall units on 60 A circuits: the equipment rating is under 60 A, so 625.43 does not force a separate disconnect for them. Same article, two answers — the nameplate decides. The trap is rating the circuit instead of the equipment: a 48 A charger on a 60 A breaker does not trip this rule, and a charger rated exactly 60 A does not either — the section starts at MORE THAN 60 A. The second trap is a disconnect that can only be locked with a removable hasp kept in the truck: 110.25 wants the locking provision to remain in place with the lock removed. 100 A fast charger with no disconnect at the equipment — the panel breaker two rooms away offered as the disconnect. Disconnect fitted with a locking hasp that lives in the gang box; nothing left to lock to once it walks off (110.25). Disconnect mounted behind the charger's bollards, where nobody can stand in front of it and reach the handle. Lockable disconnect installed, but on the far side of a locked fence the service technician cannot open. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 625.43: When the disconnect for larger EV equipment (over 60 amps, or more than 150 volts to ground) is remote, the equipment now needs a plaque telling where it is. New: if the disconnect sits away from the EVSE or wireless power transfer equipment (WPTE), a plaque on that equipment must show its location. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Equipment connections — how the charger plugs in
x: 625.44 sorts electric vehicle equipment by how it connects to the premises wiring, and each style carries its own connection rule. • Portable equipment connects cord-and-plug through a receptacle. • Stationary equipment may also be cord-and-plug connected where the section permits it. • Fastened-in-place equipment has its own provisions, including direct wiring. Where a receptacle is the connection, it must be a listed receptacle of the rating and configuration the equipment requires — the charger nameplate, not habit, picks the receptacle. The dwelling case crews see most is a 240-volt receptacle feeding a plug-in charger: the receptacle rating, the branch-circuit rating, and the charger's continuous draw all have to agree, which is why this section is read together with 625.41 and 625.42. A charger draws its full rating for hours. A receptacle chosen by habit — the dryer-style outlet that happens to be in the garage — can be the wrong configuration, the wrong rating, or fed by a circuit never sized for a continuous load. Matching the receptacle, the circuit and the nameplate keeps the connection from becoming the hot spot in the system. Plug-in charger on a 50 A receptacle: the circuit is sized for the continuous load at 125 percent (a 40 A charger on a 50 A circuit), the receptacle matches the circuit, and the equipment is the listed unit the homeowner bought — not a dryer receptacle borrowed for the garage. If the charger is hard-wired instead, 625.44 steps aside and the disconnect rules of 625.43 decide. The trap is the 60 A receptacle. NEC 2023 added 60-ampere receptacles to the permitted list for portable EVSE at 625.44(A) — but a 2020 permit, and a 2020 exam, work from the 2020 list, which does not include it. Answering from the 2023 list is the wrong answer here. Dryer receptacle pressed into service for a plug-in EVSE — wrong configuration for the equipment. Receptacle rating that does not match the branch circuit or the charger nameplate. Receptacle for an EV connection that is not a listed receptacle. Fastened-in-place EVSE cord-and-plug connected where 625.44 calls for its direct-wiring provisions. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 625.44(A): Received substantiation that led to the addition of 60-ampere receptacles to the list of permitted receptacle amperages for portable electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) in Section 625.44(A). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Connector storage — 18 in. indoors, 24 in. outdoors
x: Unless the equipment is listed and marked for a different arrangement, the coupling means — the vehicle connector — must be stored or located at a height of: • Not less than 18 in. above the floor for indoor locations. • Not less than 24 in. above grade for outdoor locations. It also has to be positioned so it can couple directly to the vehicle: stored where the cord actually reaches the charge port, not coiled on a hook across the garage. The heights are minimums, and they are measured to where the connector sits in its holster or storage position. A connector stored down at floor level lives in the worst spot in the building: garage floor water, driveway runoff, tire paths and dropped tools. Water and grit in the connector contacts corrode them, and a damaged connector can damage the vehicle's inlet too. The minimum heights keep the coupling means out of standing water and out from under tires. Florida makes this one easy to get wrong. A wall charger inside a garage gets its holster mounted so the connector docks at 18 in. or more above the slab — above the water line when the floor is hosed out or a storm blows rain under the door. The same charger on an outside wall or a carport post is an outdoor location: 24 in. minimum above grade, because an afternoon storm can pond water against that wall in minutes. Measure to where the connector actually sits docked, not to the top of the holster bracket. The trap is carrying the indoor number outside: 18 in. is the indoor floor measurement. Outdoors the minimum is 24 in., measured from grade — not from the driveway's high spot or the top of a paver. The second trap is measuring to the holster's mounting screws instead of to the stored connector itself; the rule is about where the coupling means sits. Connector holster mounted 12 in. above an exterior driveway — the outdoor minimum is 24 in. above grade (625.50). Connector left lying on the garage floor instead of docked in its storage holster. Indoor holster height of 18 in. used as the pattern for the outdoor unit on the same job. Connector stored where the cord cannot couple directly to the vehicle from its storage position. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Ventilation — only where the listing requires it
x: Indoor EV charging needs mechanical ventilation only where the listing says so: • Equipment listed as requiring ventilation for indoor use: mechanical ventilation is required. • Equipment listed for indoor charging without ventilation: none is required — most modern residential EVSE is listed this way. • Where ventilation is required, it is a permanent system: supply air and exhaust, vented directly to the outdoors, arranged for the vehicles being charged. The listing and the installation instructions are the rule here — equipment is installed per its listing (110.3(B)), and 625.52 keys the ventilation question to that listing. Some charging equipment and battery chemistries can give off gases while charging, and in a closed garage those gases must not be allowed to build up. Equipment listed for indoor use without ventilation has that hazard engineered out, so the Code does not make every garage charger carry ductwork it does not need — the ventilation follows the listing, not a blanket rule. Garage install in a Florida home: a 48 A wall-mounted EVSE on a 60 A circuit (625.41) — the nameplate and instructions say listed for indoor use, no ventilation required. The crew prices no ductwork, and notes the listing line on the work order so the inspector sees the basis at rough-in. Across town, a fleet shop buys chargers whose listing requires ventilation for indoor use: that job carries a permanent supply-and-exhaust system vented straight outdoors, priced before the chargers are mounted. The trap is the blanket answer — every indoor EV charger needs mechanical ventilation. 625.52 requires ventilation only where the equipment is listed as requiring it for indoor use. The reverse trap also fails jobs: skipping ventilation where the listing does require it, or offering a portable fan where a permanent supply-and-exhaust system vented outdoors is required. Ventilation required by the EVSE listing, but no system installed. Exhaust dumped into the attic instead of vented directly to the outdoors. Portable fan offered as the ventilation system — the system must be permanent. EVSE installed indoors that is not listed for indoor use at all. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: GFCI protection for personnel — every EV receptacle
x: All receptacles installed for the connection of electric vehicle charging must be provided with GFCI protection for personnel: • The requirement is in addition to the dwelling garage rules in 210.8 — it stands on its own. • A 240 V charging receptacle is not exempt. • Indoor locations are not exempt. • The charger receptacle is the outlet being protected. The EVSE's own internal personnel protection system does not substitute for the required GFCI protection. If a receptacle exists to plug in a charger, 625.54 protects it — the voltage and the room do not matter. A charge cord lives a hard life: driven over, kinked, rained on, and plugged in with wet hands on a concrete slab. A ground fault through a damaged cord or a wet connector puts current through the person holding it, and a 50 A breaker will never notice a few milliamperes going the wrong way. GFCI protection watches for current leaking where it should not go and opens the circuit fast — that is the difference between a scare and a fatality. Spec home in Ocala: the garage gets a 240 V, 50 A receptacle for the buyer's charger, fed from the Siemens panel on a 2-pole GFCI breaker — 50 A because the 40 A charger is a continuous load under 625.41. The receptacle itself is a standard heavy-duty 14-50; the protection lives in the breaker, and the crew labels the receptacle “EV charging — GFCI protected” so the inspector and the homeowner both see it. Per the Sharma note on this page, the 240 V circuit is not an S-07 dual-function point — S-07 is a 120 V device rule — so nobody specs a dual-function breaker here; the listed 2-pole GFCI breaker is the protection method for this job. Sharma note: S-07's dual-function point is a 120V device. A 240V EV circuit is not an S-07 point — meet 625.54 with the listed protection method specified for the job (Mike/Sanjay decide the device per job), and never describe a 240V charger circuit as a DFN point. Two traps. First: “the EVSE already has personnel protection built in, so the receptacle needs nothing.” 625.54 protects the receptacle, and the charger's internal system does not substitute for it. Second: “GFCI is only for 120 V receptacles.” This section covers every receptacle installed for EV charging, 240 V included, indoors or out. 14-50 EV receptacle on a standard 2-pole breaker — no GFCI protection anywhere on the circuit. Crew pointed at the EVSE's internal protection when the inspector asked where the GFCI protection was. Indoor charging receptacle left unprotected because the garage “stays dry.” 240 V receptacle written up on the work order as exempt from GFCI. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wet location — weatherproof enclosure
x: 625.56 is one sentence long: receptacles installed outdoors or in wet locations for EV charging must be enclosed so the enclosure is weatherproof with the attachment plug cap inserted or removed. In plain terms, weatherproof while in use — the same duty other outdoor receptacles carry under 406.9(B)(1). • A standard flip cover is weatherproof only with nothing plugged in. It fails this rule the moment a charge cord is connected. • The cover that passes is an in-use ('bubble') cover: a deep hood that closes over the plug and cord for the whole charge. • The receptacle still owes GFCI protection for personnel under 625.54. The cover and the GFCI are separate duties — one does not excuse the other. An outdoor EV receptacle stays plugged in for hours, usually unattended and often overnight, through Florida rain. A cover that only works with nothing plugged in protects the receptacle exactly when it is not being used. Water tracking into a live receptacle corrodes the contacts, builds leakage paths and can energize the enclosure — the in-use cover keeps the weather out for the entire charge. Florida spec home with the charger receptacle on the driveway wall: a 240 V, 50 A receptacle on GFCI protection (625.54) with a bubble cover over it, so the EVSE plug stays dry through an afternoon thunderstorm in the middle of a charge. Sharma standard: put the in-use cover on the rough-in material list for every outdoor charger receptacle — standard flip covers don't meet in-use duty, and swapping a cover after final is a callback, not a change order. The trap is 'weatherproof means a flip cover.' A flip cover is weatherproof with the plug removed; 625.56 requires weatherproof with the plug inserted OR removed. The other wrong answer is that the EVSE's own internal protection covers the receptacle — it does not substitute for the 625.54 GFCI, and it does nothing for the 625.56 enclosure duty. Flip cover on an outdoor EV receptacle — not weatherproof while the charger is plugged in. In-use cover too shallow for the plug, left propped open so the hood cannot close. Outdoor charging receptacle with no GFCI protection for personnel (625.54). Receptacle enclosure open to driven rain at the conduit entry — the cover is right, the box is not weatherproof. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 626 — Electrified Truck Parking Spaces
x: Article 626 covers electrified truck parking spaces: the pedestals, receptacles, and disconnects that let a parked truck run cab heat, air conditioning, and appliances — and a refrigerated trailer keep its load cold — without idling the engine. The article covers the equipment external to the truck. The numbers that drive a bid: • 626.11(A) — every space is figured at not less than 11 kVA in feeder and service load calculations, before the climate-zone demand factors of 626.11(B). The 11 kVA is built from the receptacles each space must have: two 20 A, 120 V receptacles plus one 30 A, 208 V circuit. • 626.24(B) — each space's connection means provides at least three receptacles, on at least two different branch circuits, and the receptacles get GFCI protection (626.24(D)). • 626.22 — supply equipment on a pedestal or raised pad mounts at least 2 ft above grade, or above the high-water mark where flooding reaches, and a remote disconnecting means that can be locked in the open position kills the supply to one or more spaces. • 626.10 — each stand is supplied from a 208Y/120 V or 480Y/277 V system. Where Article 626 conflicts with another article, 626.3 says Article 626 applies. A diesel idling all night burns fuel, makes noise, and wears the engine — shore power is the clean answer, but it puts a serious continuous load in a parking lot full of fuel, water, and road salt. Pedestals get hit, cords get driven over, and drivers plug in during rainstorms. The receptacle, GFCI, mounting-height, and lockable-disconnect rules are written for equipment that lives outdoors and gets abused. Distribution warehouse in Polk County adds six electrified spaces for overnight tractors. The load math starts at 6 × 11 kVA = 66 kVA before the 626.11(B) climate-zone demand factors — a real feeder, not a site-lighting tap — so the pedestals get their own panel and a disconnect that locks open for the row. Each pedestal mounts at least 2 ft above grade (the lot ponds in summer storms), carries the 626.24(B) receptacle set with GFCI protection, and is priced from the pedestal schedule: spaces counted, receptacle types confirmed, disconnect per the layout. Treat each pedestal like a small service with its own grounding, exactly as the old note on this page said — now with the article's numbers filled in. The trap is sizing a space like a 20 A convenience receptacle. 626.11(A) fixes the floor at 11 kVA per space before demand factors, and the branch-circuit loads are continuous. Second trap: applying another article over 626 where the two conflict — 626.3 gives the tie to Article 626 on its own turf. Feeder sized from the receptacle count at face value — no 11 kVA per space in the load calculation. Pedestal receptacles with no GFCI protection (626.24(D)). Supply equipment mounted at grade on a lot that floods; 626.22 wants it at least 2 ft up. No lockable remote disconnecting means for the row of spaces. All three receptacles for a space landed on a single branch circuit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 630 — Electric Welders
x: Article 630 gives electric welders their own conductor and overcurrent rules, because a welder welds in bursts and rests between welds. The whole article runs on one nameplate number: the duty cycle. • Duty cycle is the share of time the machine can weld at rated output — 60 percent means about 6 minutes welding out of every 10 at that output. • Supply conductors: ampacity not less than the I1eff value on the rating plate. If the plate gives no I1eff, multiply the rated primary current by the Table 630.11(A) factor for that duty cycle (630.11(A)). • Motor-generator arc welders use their own column of Table 630.11(A). Resistance welders follow Part III instead (630.31). • A group of welders on one feeder: 100 percent of the two largest, plus 85 percent of the third largest, plus 70 percent of the fourth, plus 60 percent of all the rest (630.11(B)). • Overcurrent protection is generous on purpose: not more than 200 percent of the rated primary current, and not more than 200 percent of the conductor ampacity (630.12). • Shop work: get the duty cycle off the nameplate before sizing anything. Never guess it. Conductor heating follows the current squared times the time it flows. A machine that rests between welds never heats its supply conductors the way a continuous load of the same nameplate current would. Sizing to full nameplate current wastes copper; sizing by guesswork cooks insulation. The duty-cycle table splits the difference with physics, and the 200 percent breaker ceiling exists so striking an arc does not nuisance-trip — the welder's own thermal protection guards the machine. Worked example: a welder with a 50 A rated primary current at a 60 percent duty cycle takes the 630.11(A) multiplier of 0.78 for a nonmotor-generator arc welder (motor-generator welders use a different column), so its supply conductors need an ampacity of at least 50 × 0.78 = 39 A. Read the duty cycle off the nameplate every time, not guessed. On a fabrication-shop job off OBT adding a welder bay, that one calculation sets the whole circuit: conductors at 39 A minimum ampacity, and a breaker that may run well above the conductor size, up to the 630.12 ceiling of 200 percent of 50 A — 100 A. Show the duty-cycle math on the panel schedule so the inspector sees Article 630, not a mistake. The trap is protecting the welder circuit like an ordinary load: a breaker matched to the 39 A conductor ampacity, or conductors sized at the full 50 A nameplate. 630.12 keys the breaker ceiling to the rated primary current — up to 200 percent — not to the derated conductor size, and 630.11 keys the conductors to the duty cycle, not the nameplate. Welder circuit sized off the machine's output current (the 225 A on the front of a stick welder) instead of its rated primary current. Breaker above 200 percent of the rated primary current — past the 630.12 ceiling. Duty cycle guessed or taken from the sales sheet instead of the rating plate, leaving conductors undersized for the machine's actual cycle. Welder tapped onto a general shop circuit with lighting and receptacles, with no 630.11 calculation behind it. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 630.8: Created a new Section 630.8 requiring ground-fault circuit-interrupter (GFCI) protection for personnel involved with electric welder applications. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 640 — Audio Signal Processing, Amplification, and Reproduction Equipment
x: Article 640 covers the power and wiring rules for audio signal processing, amplification and reproduction equipment — the professional and commercial sound systems in studios, performance venues, houses of worship and distributed-audio fit-outs. • Line-voltage power to the equipment — the rack circuits — follows the general rules of Chapters 1 through 4 as Article 640 modifies them. • The audio side — speaker wiring and signal cabling — follows Article 640's own wiring rules, and it is not interchangeable with line-voltage wiring. • Most of the article lands on the specialty AV contractor. Sharma touches it when a commercial fit-out includes distributed audio and somebody has to feed the rack. A sound system puts two very different kinds of wiring in the same rack and the same ceiling: 120 V power that can start a fire, and speaker cable carrying signals that pick up every bit of noise nearby. Run them like one system and you get hum in the speakers, line voltage where nobody expects it, and faults on cable that was never built for it. The article keeps the two sides separated and gives each its own rules. A restaurant fit-out with distributed audio shows the split. Sharma's bid carries the rack power — two 20 A branch circuits to the AV rack location, the circuit size we install as a commercial minimum — and the AV contractor owns the speaker wiring, pulled and terminated under Article 640. Settle who owns what before rough-in: line-voltage power and low-voltage audio cable follow different rules and different trades' habits, and that split belongs in the bid, not in a change order at trim. The trap is treating speaker cable like any other low-voltage wire that can ride along with power: 'it's only speaker wire — run it in the rack power conduit.' Article 640 gives the audio side its own wiring rules, and mixing the two sides in one raceway is exactly what the article is written to prevent. The scope trap runs the other way too: assuming the whole sound system is the AV contractor's problem when nobody has scoped the line-voltage rack power. Speaker cable run in the same raceway as the 120 V rack power circuits. Rack power never scoped — no circuits in the bid, and a change order written at trim. Audio wiring installed with no separation from line-voltage wiring above the ceiling. Sound system energized with the power side and the audio side roughed in as one system. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 645 — Information Technology Equipment
x: Article 645 gives special wiring allowances to IT equipment rooms that meet the article's conditions — including wiring under raised floors and the room disconnecting means. The allowances apply only when every condition in 645.4 is met; otherwise Chapters 1–4 govern as usual. The room-level items Sharma would actually wire: • A disconnecting means for the IT equipment — and for the dedicated HVAC serving the room — with remote disconnect controls at approved locations, readily accessible in case of fire to authorized personnel and emergency responders (645.10(A)) • The HVAC disconnect must also cause required fire/smoke dampers to close • Underfloor branch circuits run only in the wiring methods 645.5 permits • 645.10 also allows the remote disconnect controls to cover designated zones within the room, and there is an exception for Critical Operations Data Systems The disconnect button at the door is the visible part of this article on a data-room job, and its location is settled at rough-in, not at trim. A data room concentrates a building's most expensive energized equipment in one locked space. In a fire, responders need to kill the equipment, its dedicated HVAC, and close the dampers from an approved spot outside the smoke — without hunting for panels. The underfloor allowances are the trade: the room earns relaxed wiring methods only because it is dedicated, separated, and protected as a system. Before using any 645 allowance — underfloor wiring, the room disconnect arrangement — verify the room meets every condition in 645.4: dedicated IT room, the required disconnecting means, separation, and fire protection as the article lists them. On a small commercial server-room rough-in, walk that list with the plans before a single underfloor circuit goes in. If one condition fails — the HVAC is shared with the office, say — wire the room under Chapters 1 through 4 like any other space, and price it that way. The trap answer is “the room has a raised floor and racks, so Article 645 applies.” A raised floor buys nothing by itself: the allowances switch on only when every 645.4 condition is met. Miss one condition and the underfloor wiring and the room disconnect arrangement were never permitted — the room is a Chapters 1–4 room. Underfloor branch circuits in a room that doesn't meet 645.4 — shared HVAC or not a dedicated IT room. Remote disconnect controls at a location that is not approved, or not readily accessible in a fire. HVAC disconnect that does not close the required fire/smoke dampers. Underfloor wiring methods outside the ones 645.5 permits. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 646 — Modular Data Centers
x: Article 646 covers modular data centers: factory-built, prefabricated units rated 600 volts or less — an outer enclosure housing racks or cabinets of information technology equipment plus the support equipment, power distribution and cooling, that runs them. The article was added in the 2014 cycle; it is not new in 2020. • A listed module is treated as listed equipment: it complies with the specific sections the article points to, and its internal wiring is the manufacturer's listing — the listing route commonly runs through UL's Subject 2755 outline for modular data centers. A module that is not listed must comply with Article 646 in full. • 646.5: a nameplate on each enclosure gives the full-load current and the short-circuit current rating. Supply conductors are sized at not less than 125 percent of the nameplate full-load current. • 646.9: flexible cords and cables listed for extra-hard usage may interconnect separate module enclosures — but may never connect a module to an external power source such as the building service. • 646.18: space about electrical equipment inside the module complies with 110.26. • 646.19: for equipment over 6 ft wide or deep, there is an entrance to and egress from the working space at each end, each at least 24 in. wide and 6½ ft high, with listed panic hardware or listed fire exit hardware. A single entrance is permitted only where 646.19(A) or (B) is met. A modular data center packs a room's worth of energized distribution into a steel box with room for one person to work. If a fault or fire starts at the far end, the only safe direction is out — which is why the article fixes the working space and the exits at the factory instead of leaving them to whoever sets the box on the pad. Treat the module as listed equipment: Sharma's scope is the supply feeder, the disconnect, and the grounding connection landed on the module's marked terminals. Never field-modify the module's internal wiring to make a site condition fit — that is the manufacturer's listing you would be voiding. Worked example: a module lands on a pad behind a Winter Park warehouse with a nameplate full-load current of 160 A. The supply conductors are sized at 125 percent — 200 A minimum — before any other adjustment, and the feeder lands only on the marked supply terminals. The nameplate stays visible after the unit is set; if the pad layout parks it against a wall, that is a punch item, not a detail. The trap is answering 646.19 with 110.26(C)(2): that trigger is 1200 A. Article 646's trigger is size — equipment over 6 ft wide or deep needs an entrance at each end whatever its ampere rating. Supply conductors sized at 100 percent of the nameplate full-load current instead of 125 percent (646.5). Flexible cord used to connect a module to the building service instead of only interconnecting enclosures (646.9). Nameplate blocked or facing a wall after the module is set, so its ratings cannot be read. Field-modified internal wiring inside a listed module, voiding the listing. Equipment over 6 ft wide with a single entrance and neither 646.19(A) nor (B) met. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 646.19: The revision of Section 646.19 specifies the requirements for egress doors located in modular data centers. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 647 — Sensitive Electronic Equipment
x: Article 647 covers a special power system for sensitive electronic equipment: a 120 V, single-phase system whose transformer secondary is center-tapped, with the center tap grounded, so each ungrounded leg sits at 60 V to ground while the voltage between the legs stays 120 V. • The two legs are equal and opposite to ground — that balance is what cancels the ground noise that hums through audio and video work. • The system has its own receptacle and grounding rules; receptacles are identified for this system so ordinary equipment is not plugged into it by mistake. • It is rare, and it is always an engineered installation — nobody wires one from habit. Production audio and video gear picks up noise through its ground connections, and on a normal circuit that noise lands in the recording. With both legs balanced at 60 V to ground, noise coupled equally onto the two legs cancels instead of adding. The same balance is the hazard if it is improvised: a receptacle that looks normal but carries 60 V on both slots confuses the next person who meters it or plugs into it — which is why the system uses identified receptacles and an engineered design. If a studio or production client asks for 'clean power,' do not improvise a balanced 60/60 system in the field — it is an engineered installation with its own identified receptacles and grounding arrangement. Route the request to Mike for a design before anyone quotes it. And if you ever meter one that is already installed: each slot reads about 60 V to ground, and the two slots read 120 V to each other. On a normal circuit that reading means a lost neutral; on a 647 system it is exactly right. The trap answers are 'a 60 V system' and 'wire it like a normal 120 V circuit.' It is a 120 V system — 120 V leg to leg — and neither leg is a grounded neutral you can treat like one. The field trap is worse: building a 'balanced' feed out of a standard transformer hookup because the client asked for clean power. Article 647 work is engineered, or it is not done. Standard receptacle installed on a balanced-power circuit — 647 receptacles are identified for the system. Balanced 60/60 feed improvised in the field from a standard transformer connection, with no engineered design. One leg of a 647 system bonded and treated as a normal neutral, destroying the balance the system exists for. Sensitive-equipment system installed without the grounding arrangement its design requires. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 650 — Pipe Organs
x: Article 650 covers the electrical circuits and parts of electrically operated pipe organs that control the sounding apparatus and the keyboards — the action system. Electronic organs are a different animal: 650.3 sends them to Article 640. • 650.4: the action runs on dc from a transformer-type rectifier, and the dc potential must not exceed 30 volts. • 650.5: the rectifier is bonded to the equipment grounding conductor under Article 250 — the case is grounded, the low-voltage output is the working circuit. • 650.6(A): conductor minimums are tiny and specific — 28 AWG for electronic signal circuits, 26 AWG for electromagnetic valve supply and the like, and the main common-return conductor in the electromagnetic supply not less than 14 AWG. • 650.6(B)–(D): conductors carry thermoplastic or thermosetting insulation, are cabled together outside the organ proper, and each cable gets an outer covering — flame-spread resistant where the cable is not in metal raceway. • 650.7: cables are fastened in place, may attach directly to the organ structure, and must not lie in contact with other conductors. • 650.8: circuits are arranged so the 26 AWG and 28 AWG conductors are protected by an overcurrent device rated not more than 6 amperes. An organ action system is hundreds of hair-thin conductors bundled through a wooden chamber full of dust, bellows, and century-old timber. A short on an unfused 28 AWG conductor cannot trip a normal breaker — it just glows. The 30-volt cap, the 6-ampere fuse cap, and the cabling rules keep a fault in that bundle from becoming a church fire. On a church job with an organ, coordinate two separate scopes: the blower is an ordinary motor circuit under Article 430, and the low-voltage action wiring is the organ builder's listed system. Sharma's rough-in is the line-voltage side — a 20 A branch circuit to the blower disconnect and a 20 A circuit feeding the rectifier location the builder picks. Get the builder's power requirements before rough-in — organs are usually discovered in the attic conversation, not on the electrical drawings. The trap is treating the whole organ as one low-voltage system. The action circuits are capped at 30 volts dc by 650.4 — but the blower that feeds the wind is a line-voltage motor, wired and protected under Article 430 like any other motor. Legacy generator or replacement supply putting more than 30 volts dc on the action circuits (650.4). 26 AWG and 28 AWG action conductors protected at 20 amperes instead of not more than 6 amperes (650.8). Action cables run in contact with 120-volt conductors inside the organ chamber (650.7). Cotton- or enamel-insulated legacy wire reused instead of thermoplastic or thermosetting insulation (650.6(B)). Rectifier case left unbonded from the equipment grounding conductor (650.5). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 660 — X-Ray Equipment
x: Article 660 covers X-ray equipment — medical, dental, and industrial — and its field core is how the equipment is rated, disconnected, and fed. • Two ratings run the article (660.2): the momentary rating is based on an operating interval of 5 seconds or less; the long-time rating on an interval of 5 minutes or longer. • Disconnect (660.5): a disconnecting means in the supply circuit, rated at not less than 50 percent of the input required for the momentary rating or 100 percent of the input required for the long-time rating, whichever is greater — and operable from a location readily accessible from the X-ray control. • Branch circuits (660.6(A)): conductor ampacity and overcurrent protection at not less than 50 percent of the momentary rating or 100 percent of the long-time rating, whichever is greater. • Feeders (660.6(B)): a feeder supplying two or more X-ray branch circuits is figured at 100 percent of the momentary demand of the two largest units, plus 20 percent of the momentary ratings of the rest. • Connection (660.4): fixed and stationary equipment is wired with a Chapter 3 method; equipment on a branch circuit of 30 A or less may be cord-and-plug connected. • Healthcare work coordinates with Article 517, which carries parallel X-ray rules for health care facilities. An X-ray tube draws its load in violent bursts — full power for a fraction of a second, then nothing. Sized like an ordinary load, the circuit is copper nobody needs; sized off the wrong rating, the breaker trips mid-exposure or conductors run hot during long fluoroscopy work. The two-rating system matches the wire to how the machine actually draws, and the disconnect by the control lets the operator kill the equipment from where it is run. Dental fit-out in Winter Park: the manufacturer's sheet for the panoramic unit gives a momentary rating of 100 A and a long-time rating of 20 A. The branch-circuit math is 50 percent of 100 A = 50 A against 100 percent of 20 A = 20 A — the bigger number governs, so the unit gets a 50 A branch circuit and a disconnect rated at least 50 A, mounted where the operator stands at the control. Sized off the 100 A headline alone, the circuit would be double what the Code asks; off the long-time rating alone, it would fail 660.6(A). The trap is sizing from the nameplate's biggest number — or from the small one. A unit marked 100 A momentary does not need a 100 A branch circuit: 660.6(A) asks for 50 percent of the momentary rating or 100 percent of the long-time rating, whichever is greater. Picking 100 percent of momentary oversizes; picking long-time alone undersizes. Run both numbers and take the greater. Disconnect for the X-ray unit placed at the panel, out of reach of the operator's position at the control. Branch circuit sized from the long-time rating only — 50 percent of the momentary rating was the greater number. Feeder supplying two X-ray branch circuits sized with the branch-circuit 50 percent rule instead of 660.6(B). Cord-and-plug connection used as the disconnect for equipment fed above 30 A. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 665 — Induction and Dielectric Heating Equipment
x: Article 665 covers the construction and installation of induction heating, induction melting, induction welding and dielectric heating equipment and accessories for industrial and scientific applications (665.1). Medical and dental applications, appliances, and line-frequency pipeline and vessel heating sit outside it — pipeline heating lives in Article 427. • Wiring from the source of power to the equipment follows Chapters 1 through 4 unless this article amends it (665.3). • The equipment stays out of hazardous (classified) locations unless it and its wiring are approved for that location (665.4). • The output circuit — everything external to the converting device — may be isolated from ground, and its current to ground is limited so that no 50 V or more to ground appears on any accessible part (665.5). • Multiple control points are interlocked so the applicator can be energized from only one point at a time, with a way to de-energize at every point; foot switches get a shield against accidental closing (665.7). • Supply conductor ampacity is built from the nameplate ratings of the largest group of equipment that can operate at the same time, plus the standby currents of the remaining equipment (665.10). This equipment makes heat with high-frequency energy, and the output side does not behave like a branch circuit: RF voltage can appear on frames and nearby metal, capacitors hold a charge after shutdown, and an applicator energized from a second control point can start while a worker's hands are in it. The interlock, guarding and bonding rules exist because the hazard is invisible energy, not a sparking fault you can see coming. Industrial only for Sharma: if a bid shows induction or dielectric heating, price only the supply disconnect and feeder shown on the engineered drawings. The disconnect belongs within sight of the equipment and capable of being locked in the open position (665.12). The equipment's shielding, guarding and interlocks are the manufacturer's listing — not field work, and not value-engineering targets. If the drawings don't show the supply, that is an RFI, not an allowance. The trap is treating the output circuit like ordinary wiring that has to be grounded — 665.5 permits it isolated from ground, and grounding it 'to be safe' can defeat the design. The second trap is sizing the feeder by adding every nameplate on the floor: 665.10 counts the largest group that can run at once at full rating and the rest at standby current. Applicator can be energized from two control stations at once — control points not interlocked. Foot switch with no shield over the contact button. Feeder sized from Chapter 3 habits instead of the 665.10 nameplate method. Equipment frames not bonded — RF voltage standing on exposed metal (665.26). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 668 — Electrolytic Cells
x: Article 668 covers electrolytic cells — the cell lines that make chlorine, caustic, aluminum and similar products by passing heavy DC current through a process. The recognition points: • A cell line and its DC process power supply, inside the cell line working zone, are treated as one functional unit — a single line can run over 400,000 A DC at over 1000 V DC. • Inside the zone, ordinary grounding logic is reversed on purpose. The DC process power supply conductors are not required to be grounded (668.11). • Where that supply runs over 50 V between conductors, its metal enclosures are grounded through protective relaying or by a copper bonding conductor not smaller than 2/0 AWG (668.11). • AC systems and exposed conductive surfaces inside the zone are not required to be grounded (668.30); the workers and their tools are insulated from ground instead. • Any part of a crane or hoist that contacts an energized cell or its attachments must be insulated from ground (668.32). • Each DC power supply to a cell line must be capable of being disconnected; a removable link in the busbar can be that disconnecting means (668.13). • Outside the working zone, none of this applies — the rest of the NEC governs in full (668.3). Cell line crews have to touch energized cell surfaces to run the process — the work cannot be done with everything dead and grounded. If the line, the tools and the crane were grounded the ordinary way, the worker would become the bridge between live parts and ground. So the article insulates the worker and the workplace from ground, and keeps the DC system floating, instead of insulating the conductor. Recognition only. If a scope ever shows a rectifier room, a cell line, or busbar runs feeding process tanks at a Florida chemical or plating plant, that is Article 668 territory — heavy industrial, and not Sharma work. Flag it to Sanjay and Mike the day it appears in a scope. If Sharma ever services ordinary building equipment in such a plant, that work sits outside the working zone and follows the normal rules — but nobody from a residential crew improvises inside the zone.
