The trap is the ordinary-practice answer: ground the DC conductors, ground the crane, ground the tools, and apply 110.26 working-space logic inside the zone. Inside the cell line working zone that is exactly backwards — 668.11 does not require the process conductors to be grounded, 668.32 requires crane parts contacting cells to be insulated from ground, and 668.3 keeps the ordinary articles for work outside the zone. Cell line treated as an ordinary grounded system — process conductors grounded against the 668.11 design. Crane hook block contacting energized cells with no insulation from ground (668.32). Portable tools in the zone fed from an ordinary grounded receptacle circuit instead of an isolated, ungrounded supply (668.20). DC power supply with no means of being disconnected from its cell line (668.13). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 669 — Electroplating
x: Article 669 covers the electrical components and accessory equipment that supply power and controls for electroplating — and anodizing, electropolishing and electrostripping ride under the same rules; the Code calls all of it electroplating (669.1). This is industrial work: a rectifier feeds plating tanks at low voltage and very high current, often over bare busbar instead of ordinary branch-circuit wiring. • Equipment must be identified for electroplating service (669.3). • Branch-circuit conductors supplying the equipment need an ampacity of at least 125% of the total connected load (669.5). • Busbars follow 366.23: bare copper busbar is capped at 1000 A per square inch of cross-section (669.5). • At 60 V DC or less, insulated conductors may run without insulated supports if protected from physical damage, and bare copper or aluminum may run supported on insulators (669.6(A)). • Over 60 V DC, insulated conductors need insulated supports, and bare conductors on insulators must be guarded against accidental contact up to the point of termination (669.6(B)). • More than one power supply means a disconnecting means on the DC side of each supply (669.8(A)). A plating line is a burn and fire hazard wearing a low-voltage disguise. The volts sound harmless, but hundreds of amps through one loose busbar joint makes heat fast, and a DC arc does not self-extinguish at a zero crossing the way AC does. The 125% conductor rule, the busbar density cap and the guarding rules above 60 V exist because the failure mode is a glowing joint or an accidental touch in a wet, conductive chemical shop — not a tripped breaker. Recognition only for Sharma. On an industrial bid for a plating shop, the rectifier nameplate and the plant engineer's busbar design drive everything. Say the connected load is 400 A of DC plating load: the branch circuit is sized at 500 A minimum (125%), and the bare copper busbar needs at least half a square inch of cross-section at the 1000 A per square inch cap — before voltage drop even enters the talk. Do not price plating-line conductors from Chapter 3 ampacity habits: the job needs the plant engineer's design before it needs an electrician. The trap is sizing the supply like an ordinary Chapter 3 branch circuit — conductor ampacity equal to the load, or busbar picked by eye. 669.5 demands 125% of the total connected load, and busbar is capped by current density under 366.23, not by a Table 310.16 lookup. The other wrong answer is 'it is only 48 volts, so it is harmless' — at plating currents, low voltage is exactly where the burn hazard lives. Busbar joint discolored and hot — the run was pushed past the 1000 A per square inch density cap. Branch circuit sized at 100% of the rectifier load — the 125% factor of 669.5 never applied. Bare busbar over 60 V DC run where a worker can brush against it — no guarding to the termination. Two rectifiers feeding one line, one disconnect — no DC-side disconnect for the second supply. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 670 — Industrial Machinery
x: Article 670 covers industrial machinery — machines with combined motor and control loads fed by one supply circuit. The machine's nameplate does the math: 670.3(A) requires the nameplate to supply the full-load current, the short-circuit current rating, and the largest-motor data, and 670.4(A) sets the supply-conductor ampacity: • Not less than 125% of the full-load current of all resistance heating loads, plus • 125% of the full-load current of the highest-rated motor, plus • The full-load currents of all other motors and apparatus that can run at the same time, based on duty cycle Use the supply-conductor ampacity the machine's nameplate or documentation states per 670.4(A) — not a 430 calculation run on the machine's internal motors. A machine is not a motor. Inside one cabinet, heaters, the main drive, and auxiliaries cycle together in combinations the installer cannot see from outside. Sizing the supply from the nameplate formula keeps the feeder matched to the worst combination the manufacturer designed for — undersize it and the supply runs hot on a normal production cycle; open the machine and guess under 430 and the numbers are fiction. Worked example: a machine whose nameplate gives a supply-circuit rating of 46 A is fed with conductors of at least that ampacity — use the supply-conductor ampacity the machine's nameplate/documentation states per 670.4(A) — not by opening the machine and adding its internal motors under 430. Photograph the nameplate for the takeoff; it is the calculation. Run the formula on a packaging machine in Kissimmee: resistance heat 16 A × 125% = 20 A, largest motor 24 A × 125% = 30 A, two auxiliaries at 6 A each = 12 A — the supply needs at least 62 A of ampacity before the breaker is even discussed. The trap is opening the machine and adding up its motors under Article 430. Article 670 forbids the detour: the nameplate and the 670.4(A) formula — 125% of the heat, 125% of the largest motor, 100% of everything else that can run together — set the supply ampacity. Supply sized from a 430 motor calculation instead of the machine nameplate (670.4(A)). Conductors smaller than the supply-conductor ampacity the nameplate states. Nameplate data never recorded for the takeoff — the SCCR and largest-motor data never reached the job file. Machine SCCR lower than the available fault current at its supply point. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 670.1: Revised Section 670.1 to now include overvoltage protection for supply conductors for industrial machinery. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 675 — Electrically Driven or Controlled Irrigation Machines
x: Article 675 covers electrically driven or controlled irrigation machines that are not portable by hand — center pivots, linear-move machines, and similar farm equipment. It does not cover the pumps that bring water to the machine. The parts a Sharma crew actually touches: • 675.8 — the machine needs a main disconnecting means with overcurrent protection, at the point where power connects to the machine, or in view of the machine and not more than 50 ft away, readily accessible and capable of being locked in the open position. • 675.11 — collector rings at the pivot carry power and control across the rotating joint. The rings are sized for the loads they carry, and the grounding ring is sized to the same rating as the power rings. • 675.12 — all electrical equipment and enclosures on the machine are grounded, with the grounding path run to every motor and control on the spans. • The irrigation cable interconnecting enclosures on the machine is an armored cable built for wet, flexing service, supported at least every 4 ft. A center pivot is hundreds of feet of steel pipe and motors standing in a wet field, and it can start moving on a timer or a remote command while someone is working on a span. Workers have been hurt by pivots that started on their own, and by machine frames made live by a fault with no ground path back. The lockable disconnect and the full grounding are what make the machine safe to touch. Service call on a center pivot outside Ocala: before anyone touches the collector rings or the span wiring, the crew opens the machine disconnect at the pivot point, locks it, and tags it — the farm's controls can start a pivot remotely, so “the panel said off” is not enough. Then the checks: the disconnect sits in view of the machine and inside the 50 ft limit, the grounding conductor runs unbroken out the spans, and the grounding ring at the pivot is intact. The usual Florida finds are lightning damage at the pivot and a ground conductor cut at a span box. The trap answer puts the main disconnect “anywhere on the farm panel.” 675.8(B) is specific: at the point of connection, or visible from the machine and not more than 50 ft away — with overcurrent protection included, and it must lock open. Second trap: the article does not cover the well pump that feeds the pivot; the pump is ordinary motor work under Article 430. Main disconnect 200 ft away at the barn panel, not in view of the machine (675.8(B)). Disconnect with no overcurrent protection and no way to lock it in the open position. Grounding conductor cut at a span junction box, leaving the far spans floating. Collector-ring enclosure open to the weather, with the grounding ring undersized. Ordinary cord substituted for armored irrigation cable along the span. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 680 — Swimming Pools, Fountains, and Similar Installations
x: Article 680 covers swimming pools, fountains, and similar installations, organized by installation type. The first job on any pool job is knowing which part you are in: • Part I — general rules that ride with every part • Part II — permanently installed pools • Part III — storable pools • Part IV — spas and hot tubs • Part V — fountains • Part VII — hydromassage bathtubs • Part VIII — pool lifts Two systems run through all of it and must never be confused. Grounding is the fault path back to the source. Equipotential bonding under 680.26 ties everything a swimmer can touch — the water, the deck, the pump — to one potential, and it never has to run back to a panelboard or a grounding electrode. Distances are measured the way a cord would travel: the required receptacle for a permanently installed pool sits not less than 6 ft and not more than 20 ft from the inside wall, and not more than 6 ft 6 in. above the deck or grade (680.22(A)). A junction box for an underwater light sits at least 4 ft from the inside wall and at least 4 in. above the deck, or 8 in. above the maximum water level, whichever is higher (680.24(A)). Florida is pool country — this is the highest-value article in the chapter for Sharma. Water, bare skin, and bare feet make the body a good conductor, and a swimmer cannot let go of a fault. A few volts between the water and the deck can paralyze a swimmer's muscles and drown them — electric shock drowning often leaves no mark. Bonding holds everything the swimmer can touch at one potential, GFCI protection cuts the fault off, and the distance rules keep receptacles and cords out of the splash zone. Classify the install before pricing: a storable pool, an outdoor spa, and a permanently installed pool carry three different rule sets out of the same article. On a new Orlando backyard pool, Sharma's rough-in starts with the tape: the required receptacle lands in the 6–20 ft band from the inside wall, the deck box sits 4 ft out, 8 in. above the maximum water level, and the bonding grid ties shell steel, deck, and pump pad together before the pour. Miss the classification or the bonding and the fix is a saw cut, not a change order. Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020. The trap is treating bonding as grounding. Running the grid back to the panel, or offering an EGC as a substitute for the 680.26 grid, both miss the rule: bonding ties everything the swimmer can touch to one potential, it is not required to extend to a panelboard, a service disconnect, or an electrode — and it never replaces the EGC in the branch circuit. Receptacle for the pool equipment 4 ft from the inside wall — 6 ft minimum, and GFCI protection required (680.22(A)). Bonding grid not tied to the pump motor, or the deck steel left out of the equipotential grid (680.26). Deck box for the underwater light 2 ft from the inside wall and set below the water-level elevation — 4 ft out and 8 in. above maximum water level (680.24(A)). Storable-pool rules applied to a permanently installed pool — wrong part of the article, wrong rule set. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 680.10: Pool heat pumps and chillers finally have their own rule: listed, and wired by the nameplate. The 48-amp element split and 125 percent sizing now belong to resistance heaters only. Electric heat pumps and chillers that heat or cool pool water must be listed and installed to their nameplate ratings (680.10(B)). • 680.14: Wiring in corrosive pool areas now has to be suitable for the location. LFNC joins the accepted list, aluminum conduit and tubing are out, and other equipment gets its own rule. Aluminum conduit and aluminum tubing aren't allowed in a corrosive pool environment (680.14(A)). • 680.5: Pool ground-fault protection now depends on voltage to ground: Class A GFCI up to 150 volts to ground, and special purpose GFCI (SPGFCI) above 150 volts, up to 480 volts phase to phase. On circuits above 150 volts to ground, through 480 volts phase to phase, the device must be a special purpose GFCI (SPGFCI), 20 mA max. • 680.54: New 680.54(C) brings pool-style equipotential bonding to splash pads and settles where to measure from: the walking area and collection basin are the shell, and their outer edge is the inside wall. Splash pads now need equipotential bonding the way pools do, including the bonded perimeter surface around them (680.54(C)). • Article 680: Article 680 underwent a major reorganization to improve usability and compliance with the NEC Style Manual. • 680.12: Text at Section 680.12 has been revised and subdivided to require equipment rooms, vaults, or pits with equipment to have drainage or be suitable for submersion in first-level subdivision A. New first-level subdivision B requires a 125-volt, 15-or 20-ampere receptacle and requires any receptacle in the space rated 150 volts or less to be ground-fault circuit-interrupter (GFCI) protected. • 680.32: Received substantiation to revise the title and text of Section 680.32 to indicate that both ground-fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) and special-purpose ground-fault circuit interrupter (SPGFCI) requirements are covered in this section and add a reference back to 680.5(B) and (C). • 680.44: Revised Section 680.44 to indicate that both GFCI and SPGFCI requirements are addressed for spa and hot tub installations. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Overhead conductor clearances
x: In the 2020 edition the overhead rules live at 680.9(A) with Table 680.9(A) — older sources that cite 680.8 are working from a previous edition. • The clearance in any direction from the water level, the edge of a diving structure, or the base of a diving platform is 22.5 ft for the conductors the table covers. • Measured from maximum water level, the clearance to an observation stand, tower, or diving platform is 14.5 ft. • All clearances are measured from maximum water level, not from the deck. • Read Table 680.9(A) by its rows: the figures apply to the conductor types and voltages the table lists, measured as the table directs — they are not a blanket clearance for every wire over water. • Overhead communications conductors and cables have their own rule at 680.9(B): a horizontal clearance of at least 10 ft from the pool and its associated structures. Around a pool, people dive, stand on towers, and carry long metal poles upright — vacuum poles, skimmers, even sailboat masts on a marina job. A wire that looks high enough from the deck can sit inside the arc of a diver or the reach of a pole. Measuring from maximum water level, in every direction, keeps the conductor outside the space a person and a long object can occupy. Survey the overhead lines before the pool layout is final — moving a pool shell is cheaper than relocating a service drop, and 22.5 ft in ANY direction includes diagonals. On a Lakeland backyard pool the utility drop crossed the deep-end corner: measured from maximum water level along the diagonal over the diving board it came in under 22.5 ft, so the pool shifted on the lot and the board moved to the shallow end before the shell was set. The trap is measuring 22.5 ft straight up from the water and calling it done. The table clearance runs in any direction — a conductor well above the water can still fail on the diagonal from the edge of a diving board. The second trap is the citation: 680.8 is a previous edition; the 2020 overhead rules are at 680.9. Overhead conductor inside 22.5 ft of the water or a diving structure, measured in any direction (Table 680.9(A)). Clearance measured from the deck instead of from maximum water level. Observation stand, tower or diving platform inside 14.5 ft of an overhead conductor. Communications cable over the pool or within 10 ft horizontally (680.9(B)). Permit set citing 680.8 — previous-edition numbering; the 2020 rules are at 680.9. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 680.9(A): In Section 680.9(A), clarifies that open overhead wiring in raceways is not subject to the clearance requirements in Table 680.9(A) and Figure 680.9(A). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Underground wiring
x: Underground wiring is not permitted under a pool, or within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall of the pool, unless it is necessary to supply pool equipment permitted by this article. That one sentence decides most pool-deck trenching before it starts. • Wiring that does run in the 5 ft zone uses the article's methods: rigid metal conduit, intermediate metal conduit, rigid polyvinyl chloride conduit, reinforced thermosetting resin conduit, or Type MC cable, suitable for the conditions at that location. • Minimum cover for those runs comes from Table 300.5 — in general locations, 6 in. for rigid and intermediate metal conduit and 18 in. for rigid PVC and RTRC. • Equipment grounding for anything in the zone follows the pool rules of this article, not the general rules alone. • When in doubt, route around the 5 ft band. A longer trench outside the band is almost always cheaper than a failed inspection inside it. Water, bare feet, and a faulted buried conductor are a bad mix: a damaged cable under a deck can put voltage into the water and the wet concrete around it, and a swimmer has no way to let go or step away. Keeping foreign wiring out of the band — and the wiring that must cross it inside a tough raceway, buried deep — keeps pool faults on pool equipment, where the bonding and GFCI rules can manage them. On a Winter Park pool job, the equipment pad sits 4 ft from the water's edge, so the pump and heater feeds cross the band: they run in rigid PVC at 18 in. of cover, the minimum Table 300.5 asks of PVC in a general location. The site-lighting conduit for the back fence tells the other half of the story — it does not serve the pool, so it stays outside the 5 ft band even though cutting the corner would save 30 ft of trench. Keep site lighting and landscape conduits out of the band unless they serve the pool itself. The trap is "any conduit, buried deep, is fine in the band." Depth is only half the rule — the method list in 680.11 is closed, and under the pool itself the answer is simpler: nothing runs there except what the pool equipment needs. Direct-buried UF cable crossing the 5 ft band to feed landscape lighting. Conduit run under the pool shell as a shortcut to the equipment pad. Rigid PVC in the band buried with only a few inches of cover instead of the Table 300.5 minimum. Site-lighting or irrigation wiring threaded through the band when a route outside it existed. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 680.11: Underground runs within 5 ft of a pool's inside wall now count as suitable only when the wiring method is installed as a complete system, from one outlet, junction or splice point to the next. The underground methods for the zone within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall now count only when installed as complete systems (680.11(A)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Motor wiring and equipment grounding conductor
x: Pool motor circuits carry an equipment grounding conductor with two pool differences from ordinary motor work: • The EGC is insulated copper — not a bare conductor in the raceway, and not aluminum. • It is sized from Table 250.122 by the overcurrent device ahead of the circuit — but never smaller than 12 AWG, even where the table would allow smaller. The one place the floor bites: a 15 A circuit, where Table 250.122 pairs the breaker with a 14 AWG copper EGC. On a pool motor circuit that 14 AWG stays in the truck — the EGC is 12 AWG. At 20 A the table and the floor agree on 12 AWG; at 30 A and above the table takes over (10 AWG at 30, 40 and 60 A). The equipment pad is wet, outdoors, and tied into the pool's equipotential bonding. A bare ground wire in a damp raceway corrodes quietly for years, and the first anyone knows is when a fault has no path back and the breaker never trips — with swimmers in the water. The insulated copper conductor, held to a 12 AWG floor, keeps the fault path intact so the overcurrent device opens fast. Florida pool pad, new build: the pump motor is fed from a 20 A GFCI breaker (680.21(C)) in the Siemens panel. The crew pulls two circuit conductors and a green insulated 12 AWG copper EGC in the raceway to the motor — the table size for 20 A and the 680.21(A) floor are the same number here. On the same pad, a 15 A circuit for a small auxiliary pump still gets a 12 AWG insulated EGC, not the 14 AWG the table alone would allow. The trap is sizing the pool EGC straight off Table 250.122 and stopping there: 14 AWG for a 15 A circuit is the table's answer for ordinary work, and it is the wrong answer at a pool. 680.21(A) sets a floor of 12 AWG and requires the conductor to be insulated copper — a bare ground pulled in the conduit fails even at the right size. Bare equipment grounding conductor in the pool motor raceway — 680.21(A) requires it insulated. 14 AWG EGC on a 15 A pool motor circuit — below the 12 AWG floor. Aluminum EGC on a pool motor circuit — the section requires copper. EGC sized by the conductor size instead of by the overcurrent device ahead of it (Table 250.122). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: GFCI protection for pool motors — re-checked
x: GFCI protection is required for outlets supplying pool motors on branch circuits rated 150 volts or less to ground and 60 amperes or less, single-phase or three-phase. • The protection covers the outlet — by receptacle or by direct connection. A hardwired pump is inside the rule, not outside it. • The scope is all pool motors inside those ratings, not just cord-and-plug pumps. This page was re-checked against 2020-based sources before the chapter was written, and the v1 lookup (L-088) states the scope the same way. • The motor circuit still needs its insulated copper equipment grounding conductor under 680.21(A), sized from Table 250.122 and never smaller than 12 AWG. The protection device is planned at design and chosen for the job — see the Sharma note below. A pool motor works within reach of the water, bonded into a system swimmers touch. A ground fault in a pump winding can put voltage on the equipment pad and into the water instead of tripping anything. GFCI protection watches for that leakage current and opens the circuit in milliseconds, before the fault becomes a shock in the pool. A hardwired 240V pool pump needs GFCI protection just as much as a plug-in one — plan the protection device at design, not at the final walk. On a Florida pool-equipment job, a 240-volt, 20-ampere pump circuit gets its GFCI protection arranged at the panel, the insulated copper equipment grounding conductor is 12 AWG minimum, and the protection is tested with the pump running before the final. Finding out at the final walk that the circuit is unprotected means a return trip and a failed inspection. Sharma note: like 625.54, a 240V pool circuit is not an S-07 120V DFN point. Meet 680.21(C) with the listed method specified for the job; device choice is Mike/Sanjay's per job. The trap answer is that only cord-and-plug pool pumps need GFCI protection — the word 'outlet' fools people into picturing a receptacle. 680.21(C) covers outlets supplying pool motors by receptacle or by direct connection, so the hardwired 240-volt pump is covered. The second trap is stretching the scope: above 150 volts to ground or above 60 amperes, this subsection ends — check which rule applies instead of stretching this one. Hardwired 240V pump on a standard breaker — no GFCI protection on the outlet (680.21(C)). Protection arranged for a receptacle that is not there — the direct-connected outlet left unprotected. Pool motor equipment grounding conductor smaller than 12 AWG, or bare in the raceway (680.21(A)). Replacement pump motor left running on the old unprotected circuit (680.21(D)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 680.21: Repairing a pool pump motor now triggers ground-fault protection, just like replacing one. The device matches the circuit: a GFCI, or a special purpose GFCI (SPGFCI) above 150 volts to ground. Repair now counts: a pump motor covered by 680.21(C) that's repaired, not only one that's replaced, needs ground-fault protection on its circuit (680.21(D)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Replacement pump motors
x: 680.21(D) is a service rule: where a pool pump motor is replaced, the replacement work must provide the GFCI protection 680.21(C) requires for that outlet. A service call that swaps a motor on an old unprotected circuit does not get to leave it unprotected. • The duty rides with the replacement, not with the age of the pool — an existing unprotected circuit is not grandfathered once the motor is changed. • The (C) scope it points back to: outlets supplying pool motors on branch circuits rated 150 V or less to ground and 60 A or less, single-phase or three-phase, by receptacle or by direct connection. Pump motors live wet, tied into the same circulation system the swimmers touch. A motor swapped onto an unprotected circuit keeps the old shock hazard alive under a new motor's invoice. Tying the GFCI upgrade to the replacement closes the grandfather gap: at the one moment a qualified person is already standing at the equipment, the protection goes in. Service crews: a motor swap triggers the GFCI upgrade — quote it with the replacement, not as a surprise. A typical Florida call is a 240 V, 20 A hard-wired pump on a plain breaker: the replacement price carries the GFCI protection up front, and the tech verifies protection at the outlet before the new motor is left running — not after the callback. The trap is 'we only changed the motor — we never touched the circuit.' 680.21(D) makes the replacement itself the trigger, so the job fails if the outlet is left without the 680.21(C) GFCI protection, even though the wiring predates the rule. And read the edition note before quoting future work: under the 2023 change, a repair triggers the same duty. Motor replaced and the circuit left on a plain breaker — no GFCI protection at the outlet. Quote written for the motor only; the GFCI upgrade sprung on the customer after the swap. Replacement motor cord-connected to a receptacle that is not the protected outlet 680.21(C) requires. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 680.21(D): The revisions at 680.21(D) expand the requirement to provide ground-fault circuit-interrupter (GFCI) protection for replaced pool pump motors and also include those that are repaired, but not replaced. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Receptacles — the 2020 lettering
x: 680.22(A) is where receptacles at a permanently installed pool live in the 2020 book. The lettering below was re-checked against 2020 before writing — older sources print different letters for the same rules, so cite the 2020 letters. • (A)(1) The required receptacle — not less than 6 ft and not more than 20 ft from the inside wall of the pool, and not more than 6 ft 6 in. above the floor, platform, or grade serving the pool • (A)(2) Receptacles serving pool circulation and sanitation equipment — not less than 6 ft away, grounding type, GFCI protected • (A)(3) All other receptacles — not less than 6 ft from the inside wall • (A)(4) GFCI protection — for all 125V, single-phase, 15A and 20A receptacles located within 20 ft of the inside wall • (A)(5) A pool equipment room — at least one 125V, 15A or 20A receptacle, and GFCI protection for receptacles in the room • (A)(6) How distances are measured — the shortest path a supply cord would follow, without passing through a floor, wall, ceiling, doorway, window, or other effective barrier The band is a compromise written around a wet body. Inside 6 ft, a cord-connected appliance can reach the water with someone in it. Past 20 ft, the required receptacle is too far away to be the one people actually use, so cords get stretched across the deck instead. GFCI protection covers the whole 20 ft zone because that is where wet hands and bare feet meet receptacles. Lay out the required receptacle in the 6–20 ft band at rough-in, before the deck and the screen enclosure fix every measurement. On a lanai pool, set the required receptacle on the house wall inside the band and under the 6 ft 6 in. height cap, and put the sanitation equipment receptacle at least 6 ft out with GFCI protection. Remember the tape follows the cord path: a receptacle that measures 8 ft in a straight line through the screen wall can measure much longer once the cord has to run around through the screen door — long enough to push it out of the band. Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020. The trap is measuring with a straight-line tape through the screen enclosure, or quoting the letters from an older edition's study guide. 680.22(A)(6) measures the shortest path the cord would actually follow, with no pass-through at walls, doors or windows — and the 2020 lettering is what the inspector is holding. Required receptacle 4 ft from the inside wall — inside the 6 ft minimum. Required receptacle 24 ft out — past the 20 ft end of the band, so it doesn't count. Receptacles inside 20 ft with no GFCI protection. Distances taped straight-line through the screen wall instead of along the cord path. Pool equipment room with no receptacle, or receptacles in the room without GFCI. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Lighting and fans over and near the pool
x: 680.22(B) sets the heights for luminaires, lighting outlets and ceiling-suspended fans over a pool and in the band around it. Every height is measured from maximum water level — not from the deck. • New work (B)(1): a new luminaire, lighting outlet or fan above the pool, or within 5 ft horizontally of the inside wall, must be at least 12 ft above maximum water level. • Existing work (B)(3): an existing luminaire or fan in that same zone may stay where it is if it is at least 5 ft above the water, rigidly attached, and GFCI protected. • The 5 to 10 ft band (B)(4): luminaires in the band from 5 to 10 ft horizontally need GFCI protection, unless they are at least 5 ft above the water and rigidly attached. • Low voltage (B)(6): listed low-voltage luminaires have their own path through 680.23(A)(2). A swimmer standing in the water is wet, barefoot and holding onto whatever is overhead. A fixture inside arm's reach puts line voltage one wet hand away from a person whose body is a good path to the water. Height is the protection: 12 ft puts new fixtures beyond reach and beyond the splash zone of a fixture that falls, and the GFCI and rigid-mount conditions are what let an older, lower fixture stay in service safely. A lanai job in Winter Haven: the homeowner wants a new ceiling fan centered over the shallow end, under a roof that sits 10 ft 6 in above the water. That is new work inside the zone, so (B)(1) wants 12 ft — the fan cannot go there. It moves out past the 5 ft line, or the plan changes. The existing wall lantern beside the pool, 6 ft above the water and rigidly mounted, stays — once its circuit gets GFCI protection per (B)(3). Measure both from maximum water level; the deck tape lies to you by the depth of the pool wall. The trap answer: '5 ft is the minimum height over a pool.' Five feet is the floor for existing fixtures that are rigidly attached and GFCI protected. A new fixture over the water or within 5 ft of the inside wall needs 12 ft above maximum water level. The second trap is measuring from the deck — every height on this page starts at maximum water level. New luminaire over the pool at 10 ft above the water — new work needs 12 ft (B)(1). Heights measured from the deck instead of maximum water level. Existing fixture kept at 5 ft with no GFCI protection, or hanging from a chain instead of rigidly attached. Luminaire in the 5 to 10 ft band, under 5 ft above the water, with no GFCI protection (B)(4). Ceiling fan installed over the water inside the 5 ft zone at lanai roof height. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Switching devices — 5 ft from the water
x: Switching devices — the switches that control pool-area equipment and lighting — must be located at least 5 ft horizontally from the inside wall of the pool, spa, or hot tub, unless they are separated from the water by a permanent barrier, such as a solid wall or fence, that keeps a person in the water from reaching the switch. • The measurement follows the same thinking as the receptacle rules in 680.22(A): distance is about what a wet hand can reach, not about where the device looks convenient on the plan. • Switches that are part of a listed assembly, or that the article specifically permits closer in, are exceptions to read on the equipment itself — not a general permission. A person in the water is bonded to the water and surrounded by grounded, wet surfaces — about the best ground path a fault could ask for. A switch within reach invites that swimmer to run the pump or the lights with a wet hand, and any fault in the equipment then has a path through the swimmer's body. Five feet of distance — or a permanent barrier that does the same job — breaks the reach. Florida pool with a screen enclosure: at rough-in, Sharma puts the pool light switch and the pump control on the house wall or the equipment pad, outside the 5 ft line — on this job the light switch landed 7 ft from the inside wall. The classic correction is the switch roughed in on the pool-side face of a screen-enclosure post, about 3 ft from the water, where a swimmer can touch it without leaving the pool. Moving it after the tile and deck are in costs ten times what the rough-in layout did. The trap is measuring from the wrong line. The 5 ft runs from the inside wall of the pool — not the deck edge, not the coping, not the outside face of the pool wall. Measured from the deck edge, a switch can look legal on the plan and still land within a wet reach of the water. Pool light switch roughed in on the pool-side face of a screen-enclosure post, inside the 5 ft line from the inside wall. Pump and light controls at the equipment pad within reach of the water, with no permanent barrier between the switch and the pool. Switching device measured from the deck edge and landing less than 5 ft from the inside wall of the pool. Pool lighting timer inside the 5 ft zone on the pool wall, reachable by a person standing in the water. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Underwater luminaires
x: Underwater luminaires must be listed for the purpose and installed by niche type — wet-niche, dry-niche, or no-niche — with transformers and power supplies for low-voltage units listed for pool use under 680.23(A)(2). • Units operating above the low-voltage contact limit get GFCI protection. • Wall-mounted units sit with the top of the lens at least 18 in. below the normal water level, unless the luminaire is listed and marked for use at a lesser depth. The 'low-voltage contact limit' this section leans on is a defined term (680.2): not more than 15 V AC sinusoidal (RMS), 21.2 V peak for nonsinusoidal AC, or 30 V for continuous DC, with its own limits for interrupted DC. A listed low-voltage luminaire system at or under that limit is the path that avoids GFCI protection for the luminaire circuit; anything operating above the limit is GFCI protected. When a pool-light quote says 'low voltage,' confirm which side of that definition the system sits on before the protection is priced. The fixture lives in the water swimmers touch, fed through the pool wall. If the luminaire, its niche and its supply are not one listed system, a fault can put the water itself at voltage. The 18 in depth keeps the lens submerged, cooled and out of easy reach, and the contact-limit line decides where GFCI protection has to stand behind the system. The light, its niche, its transformer, and its junction box are one system — check all four against the listing. On an Orlando pool, the wall light mounts with the top of its lens 18 in. below normal water level and the transformer is listed for pool use; the system operates at or below the 680.2 contact limit, so the luminaire circuit takes the path the listing allows — confirmed from the luminaire's paperwork, not from the words 'low voltage' on the quote. The trap is hearing 'low voltage' and skipping GFCI without checking the definition. The contact limit is hard numbers in 680.2 — 15 V RMS sinusoidal, 21.2 V peak nonsinusoidal, 30 V continuous DC. A system above the limit is not low voltage for this section, whatever the quote called it, and it needs GFCI protection. Wall luminaire with the top of the lens less than 18 in. below normal water level, and not listed and marked for the lesser depth. Luminaire operating above the low-voltage contact limit with no GFCI protection. Transformer or power supply for a low-voltage luminaire not listed for pool use (680.23(A)(2)). Luminaire not listed for underwater use, or set in the wrong niche type. 'Low voltage' taken on faith — the system was never checked against the 680.2 contact limit (15 V RMS / 21.2 V peak / 30 V DC). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 680.23(B)(2)(a): Substantiation was received that rigid metal conduit extending directly to wet niche luminaires in forming shells of pools must be as listed red brass or listed stainless steel. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Junction boxes for underwater luminaires
x: A junction box tied to a conduit that runs directly to the forming shell of an underwater luminaire has to be a real pool box, in the right place: • Listed, labeled, and identified as a swimming pool junction box. • Located not less than 4 ft from the inside wall of the pool, unless separated by a solid fence, wall, or other permanent barrier. • Set at an elevation of not less than 4 in. above the ground or pool deck, or not less than 8 in. above maximum water level — whichever gives the greater elevation. • A flush deck box is permitted only for systems at or below the low-voltage contact limit — 15 V AC sinusoidal (RMS), 21.2 V peak for nonsinusoidal AC, or 30 V continuous DC, per the 680.2 definition — and it still sits at least 4 ft out. This box holds splices for a light that sits underwater, a few feet from people swimming. Height above the waterline keeps splash, surge, and deck wash-down out of the splices. Distance from the wall keeps the box out of the wettest zone at the pool edge and leaves room to service the conduit run. A generic box at deck level puts line-voltage splices where water stands. Pool at a Marion Oaks house: the finished deck will sit about 2 in. above the normal waterline. Four inches above that deck is only 6 in. above the water, so the 8 in. above maximum water level governs — set the box on its riser at that height, a full 4 ft back from the inside wall, and check both numbers with a tape and a level at rough-in, before the deck pour. "Close enough" fails on both numbers. The trap answer reads only one height: "4 in. above the deck" and stops. The rule takes whichever elevation is greater — 4 in. above ground or deck, or 8 in. above maximum water level. On a low deck, the water number controls. The second trap: a flush deck box is fine anywhere. It is permitted only at or below the low-voltage contact limit, and still 4 ft from the wall. Generic junction box installed instead of one listed and identified as a swimming pool junction box. Box set 2 ft from the inside pool wall with no permanent barrier. Box 4 in. above the deck but less than 8 in. above maximum water level on a low deck. Flush deck box installed on a 120 V luminaire system above the low-voltage contact limit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Feeders supplying pool equipment panelboards
x: Where a feeder supplies a panelboard that serves pool, spa, or fountain equipment, 680.25 holds the feeder to a stricter standard than an ordinary feeder: • The feeder is installed in one of the raceway wiring methods the section lists — not run as a cable assembly. • It carries a copper equipment grounding conductor, sized from Table 250.122 with a minimum size set by the section, so the fault path is a wire conductor pulled with the feeder. • The point is the same as in 680.21(A) for motors: around water, the fault path is a real wire conductor, not the raceway alone. This page is not yet verified: the full wiring-method list, the minimum grounding-conductor size, and whether the 2020 text still requires that conductor to be insulated are held off this page until they are checked against the printed 2020 text — see the Check in print box. A pool panelboard feeds pumps, lights and heaters that sit in or beside the water, often at the end of a long outdoor run. If that feeder's fault path is weak — a raceway joint corroded open, a ground that was never pulled — a fault at the equipment pad can sit energized indefinitely with swimmers a few feet away. 680.25 makes the feeder itself part of the protection: a raceway for physical protection, and a real copper grounding conductor sized from Table 250.122. Feeding a pool subpanel from the house panel on a Marion County new build: the run goes in raceway the whole way, with a copper equipment grounding conductor pulled with the feeder and sized from Table 250.122. Before the pull, the foreman checks the printed 680.25 for the section's minimum size and its exact grounding-conductor wording — this page has not been verified against the 2020 text — and a feeder roughed in cable with no pulled ground is the correction waiting to happen. The trap is treating the pool panel feeder like any other subpanel feeder: cable assembly, raceway optional, ground sized by habit. 680.25 is a stricter feeder rule — a raceway method from the section's list, a copper equipment grounding conductor, and Table 250.122 sizing. The second trap is quoting the minimum grounding-conductor size from memory: on this page, that number waits for the printed book. Pool panelboard feeder run in cable with no raceway — a 680.25 feeder uses one of the wiring methods the section lists. No equipment grounding conductor pulled with the pool feeder — the raceway alone relied on as the fault path. Feeder equipment grounding conductor sized by guess instead of from Table 250.122. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Equipotential bonding — the idea
x: Bonding is not grounding, and 680.26 is where the difference lives. • What bonding does: it ties everything a swimmer can touch — the water, the deck, ladders, handrails, the pump — into one equipotential mass, so every touchable part sits at the same potential. • Why it works: current through a person is driven by the voltage difference between two points the body bridges. Kill the difference and there is nothing to drive current, whatever the absolute voltage is. • Where it stops: the bonding system is not required to extend back to a panelboard, a service disconnecting means, or a grounding electrode. • What it never does: bonding never substitutes for the equipment grounding conductor in the branch circuit. The pool gets both systems, for two different hazards. Pool water and wet concrete pick up small voltage gradients from the earth, the utility neutral and nearby faults — a volt or two is common, and a swimmer's wet body is an excellent conductor. A person bridging two points at different potentials becomes the path. Equipotential bonding removes the gradient at the pool itself, so the water, the deck and the ladder are all one voltage and there is no path through the swimmer. Two systems, two purposes, and the crew that can say it passes pool inspections: the green equipment grounding conductor in the pump conduit carries fault current back to the panel so the breaker trips; the bare 8 AWG bonding grid around the shell kills voltage differences so nobody becomes a conductor. On a new pool in Ocala both run in the same trench — the green wire in the conduit to the pump, the bare 8 AWG ring around the shell tied to the steel, the ladder cups and the pump lug. Land either one in place of the other and the inspection fails. The trap: 'bonding is just grounding by another name — run the grid back to the grounding electrode and you are done.' No. 680.26 does not require the bonding system to extend to a panelboard, a service disconnect or an electrode, and bonding never replaces the equipment grounding conductor. Grounding clears faults; bonding kills differences. The exam wants both, doing different jobs. No equipotential bonding grid installed — pool equipment 'grounded' with the green EGC only. Metal ladder and handrail not bonded into the grid. Bonding conductor connected to the pump but never tied to the pool reinforcing steel. Bonding jumper landed on the grounding electrode and stopped — deck, water and equipment never tied together. EGC omitted because 'the equipment is bonded' — bonding never substitutes for the EGC. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Equipotential bonding — what gets bonded, and how
x: The parts in 680.26(B)(1) through (B)(7) are bonded together with a solid copper conductor not smaller than 8 AWG, connected with a listed pressure connector, a terminal bar, or another listed means per 250.8(A): • (B)(1) Conductive pool shells — the structural reinforcing steel, or the copper conductor grid that serves as the alternate where a conductive shell's steel is encapsulated in a nonconductive compound or is not available. A nonconductive shell (vinyl, fiberglass) is not a conductive shell at all and needs no shell bonding grid • (B)(2) Perimeter surfaces — covered on the next page • (B)(3) Metallic components • (B)(4) Underwater lighting forming shells and mounting brackets • (B)(5) Metal fittings larger than 4 in. that penetrate the shell • (B)(6) Electrical equipment — with the (B)(6)(a) rule for double-insulated pump motors: the double-insulated motor itself is NOT bonded; instead an 8 AWG solid copper bonding conductor is provided at the grid so a future replacement motor that is not double-insulated can be bonded • (B)(7) Fixed metal parts within 5 ft horizontally of the inside walls (with the vertical-separation exception at 12 ft) The grid is not there to clear faults — the equipment grounding conductor does that. It is there so everything a swimmer can touch at once sits at the same potential: shell steel, water, fittings, the pump, the fence. A voltage difference that would never trip a breaker can still drive current through a wet body between two “safe” pieces of metal. One grid, one potential. Walk the (B) list physically at rough-in — shell, steel, fittings, equipment, nearby metal — before anything is buried or shot. On a gunite pool, that means the shell steel and the perimeter steel before the pour, the light niches and every fitting over 4 in. as they are set, and the equipment pad before it is piped in. The double-insulated pump gets no bond wire on the motor — but the 8 AWG solid stub goes in at the grid anyway, coiled and labeled, because the replacement motor in ten years may not be double-insulated. The trap answer bonds the double-insulated pump motor itself — or skips the stub entirely because “this motor doesn't need one.” 680.26(B)(6)(a) is the opposite of both: the motor is NOT bonded, and the 8 AWG solid copper conductor is still provided at the grid, waiting for the future replacement motor that is not double-insulated. Bonding run in stranded conductor instead of the required 8 AWG solid copper. Double-insulated pump motor bonded to the grid — or no 8 AWG stub left for its replacement. Metal fitting over 4 in. penetrating the shell left off the grid. Metal fence within 5 ft of the inside wall never bonded. Bonding connections made with unlisted clamps instead of a 250.8 means. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Perimeter surfaces — the ring
x: The bonded perimeter surface reaches 3 ft beyond the inside walls of the pool — the deck a wet swimmer stands on has to sit at the same potential as the water. • The ring method: one or more bare, solid copper conductors, not smaller than 8 AWG. • Placement: laid 18 to 24 in. out from the inside walls of the pool, and 4 to 6 in. below the subgrade. • Connections: attached to the pool's reinforcing steel or copper grid at a minimum of four uniformly spaced points. Get the ring in before the deck — after pavers or a pour, neither the distance nor the depth can be checked or fixed. The swimmer steps out of the water onto the deck with wet feet, one hand still on a ladder or the water itself. If the deck surface sits at a different potential from the water, that step bridges the difference. Bonding the perimeter surface out to 3 ft puts the whole step-off zone at water potential, so there is no gradient under the swimmer's feet. A new pool in Ocala, 16 by 32 ft: the ring goes in at rough — one bare 8 AWG solid copper conductor, taped off at 21 in. out from the inside walls and 5 in. below the subgrade, clamped to the shell steel at four points spread evenly around the pool. The inspector measures both numbers before the pavers arrive, because after the deck is down neither can be verified or repaired without demolition. That sequencing — ring first, deck second — is the whole job on this page. Two traps. First: 'the ring can sit anywhere under the deck.' It has a window — 18 to 24 in. out, 4 to 6 in. below subgrade, four tie points minimum. Second: measuring the depth from finished grade. That is the 2023 change, in the edition box; the 2020 rule on this page measures 4 to 6 in. below the subgrade. Permits through Dec 30, 2026 stay on 2020. Ring buried outside the window — 30 in. out from the wall or 10 in. deep; the rule is 18–24 in. and 4–6 in. below subgrade. Ring tied to the reinforcing steel at one point only — four uniformly spaced connections minimum. Deck poured before the ring was inspected — depth and distance can no longer be verified. Stranded or insulated conductor used for the ring — it must be bare solid copper, 8 AWG minimum. Perimeter bonding stops at the coping — the bonded surface must reach 3 ft beyond the inside walls. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 680.26: Perimeter bonding depth is now measured from finished grade: no deeper than 6 in under paving, 4 to 6 in under bare ground. An interim amendment later rewrote the perimeter rules again. As printed in 2023, a copper ring or grid goes in or under paving, no more than 6 in below finished grade (680.26(B)(2)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Pool water bonding — 9 square inches
x: 680.26 builds one equipotential bonding system around a pool, and (C) covers the hardest part of it: the pool water itself must be bonded. • Where a bonded part — a ladder rail, a light niche, a metal fitting — is already in direct contact with the water, that contact does the job. No extra fitting is required. • Where nothing bonded touches the water, an approved corrosion-resistant conductive surface of at least 9 sq in. must be in contact with it — the familiar listed water-bonding fitting in the skimmer or in the pump line. • The fitting is not a stand-alone part: it ties back into the equipotential bonding system with the 680.26 bonding conductor, solid copper not smaller than 8 AWG. • The math is simple: a 3 in. by 3 in. plate is exactly 9 sq in. Anything smaller does not comply. A swimmer is immersed in the water, holding the ladder, standing on the deck. If the water sits at a different voltage than the metal around it, the swimmer's body becomes the path between the two. Bonding the parts in 680.26(B) is not enough by itself — on an all-plastic pool, every listed part can be bonded and the water can still float at its own potential, because nothing bonded ever touches it. Paragraph (C) closes that last gap. All-plastic pools with vinyl liners and no metal in the water are the trap — check for the 9 sq in. contact on every job. On a vinyl-liner pool in Ocala, the shell is plastic, the ladder is plastic, and the light is a plastic niche: nothing bonded touches the water. The fix is the listed water-bond fitting in the skimmer, its plate giving the full 9 sq in. of contact, tied back to the bonding grid with 8 AWG solid copper. Check it at the bonding inspection, while the fitting can still be reached — after the deck is poured and the pool is filled, nobody wants to drain it to prove a plate size. The trap is answering that the pump motor's equipment grounding conductor bonds the water. It does not. 680.26(C) wants a bonded, corrosion-resistant conductive surface of at least 9 sq in. actually in contact with the water — or a bonded part that already touches it. All-plastic or vinyl-liner pool with no water-bond fitting — nothing bonded touches the water. Water-bond plate with less than 9 sq in. of contact area in the water. Fitting set in the skimmer but never tied into the equipotential bonding system. Contact surface painted, scaled, or corroded — no longer conductive contact with the water. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Storable pools — Parts I and III only
x: A storable pool — and a storable spa or hot tub — is governed by Parts I and III of Article 680, and 680.26 equipotential bonding does not apply to it. • The pump and equipment rules of Part III substitute for the Part II regime. • Classification is the whole game: the same backyard water is a different code job depending on whether the pool is storable or permanently installed. • 'Storable' is a defined term, not a synonym for above-ground: under 680.2, a storable pool is one built to be stored away, with a maximum water depth of 42 in. and walls of nonmetallic molded polymeric construction or inflatable fabric. • A permanently installed above-ground pool does not meet that definition — it is Part II work, bonding included. The two regimes protect people differently. A permanent pool sits in place for years with hard-wired equipment around wet bathers, so Part II wraps it in equipotential bonding and the full pump rules. A storable pool is seasonal equipment that is set up, used and put away. Bond a storable pool like a gunite pool and the work is wasted; wire a permanent pool like a storable one and swimmers lose the bonding protection the Code requires. A homeowner in Kissimmee has an inflatable-wall pool with 42 in. of water that comes down every fall — storable: Parts I and III, no 680.26 bonding grid. The house next door has a steel-wall above-ground pool that stays up year-round on a slab — permanently installed: Part II work, bonding included. Same street, same water, two different code jobs. Confirm which one it is before the quote, not at the inspection. The trap answer is 'above-ground means storable.' It does not. The 680.2 definition controls: built to be stored away, 42 in. maximum water depth, nonmetallic molded polymeric or inflatable fabric walls. A steel-wall pool that stays up is permanently installed even though it sits above ground — and it gets Part II, bonding included. Permanently installed above-ground pool wired under Part III — no 680.26 equipotential bonding installed. Pool permitted as storable with a water depth over the 42 in. limit in the 680.2 definition. Metal-wall pool classified as storable — the definition requires nonmetallic molded polymeric or inflatable fabric walls. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Spas and hot tubs — Parts I and IV (outdoor adds Part II)
x: Article 680 sorts its water by what the installation is, and spas and hot tubs land in Part IV. • Part I (general rules) rides with every spa and hot tub. • Part IV is the part written for spas and hot tubs. • An outdoor spa or hot tub also picks up the Part II rules that Part IV points to through 680.42 — receptacle distances, GFCI protection, and equipotential bonding arrive through that door. • An indoor spa follows Parts I and IV; the 680.42 door to Part II is written for outdoor installations. • A self-contained factory spa package still lands on an installation that must meet the article. The listing covers the tub as built; it does not waive the field wiring rules. A spa puts a bather's whole body in warm, moving water, in direct contact with jets, lights, and metal fittings. Wet skin and full contact drop body resistance, so a small fault that would only tingle on dry skin can drive dangerous current through a person in the tub. The layered parts exist so the protection written for pools follows the same water when it shows up in a smaller vessel outdoors. Outdoor spa on a lanai in Orlando: the tub arrives as one factory box, but the job is still a Part II checklist — receptacle distances and GFCI protection checked before trim, the equipotential bonding run in solid copper, 8 AWG minimum, and the pump circuit's equipment grounding conductor insulated copper, never smaller than 12 AWG. An indoor spa in a sunroom the following week gets Parts I and IV only: the same care with the circuit and its protection, but the 680.42 door to Part II stays closed. The trap is treating the factory package as a finished installation: 'It is listed and self-contained, so we just set it and plug it in.' The listing covers the equipment as manufactured. It does not cover the branch circuit, the receptacle location, GFCI protection, or bonding in the field — outdoors, those arrive through 680.42's reference into Part II, and skipping them is the fail. Outdoor spa wired as a plain appliance circuit — no bonding conductor run to the tub's bonding lug. Receptacle inside the Part II distance limits because 'the tub is only a spa, not a pool.' GFCI protection omitted on the spa circuit — the factory listing was treated as covering the field wiring. Pump equipment grounding conductor run bare, or in 14 AWG; 680.21(A) wants insulated copper, 12 AWG minimum. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Spa emergency shutoff — 5 ft, in sight, labeled
x: Spas and hot tubs anywhere other than one-family dwellings must have an emergency shutoff for the recirculation and jet system. • Readily accessible — a bystander can get to it without climbing, moving obstacles, or opening a locked gate. • Adjacent to and within sight of the tub — the person using it can see the water it protects. • At least 5 ft away from the tub — close enough to reach fast, far enough that a person in the water cannot touch it. • Clearly labeled as the emergency shutoff. Entrapment and medical emergencies in a spa are measured in seconds: hair or a limb caught on a suction fitting, a bather in distress with the jets driving the water. The shutoff has to be findable by a stranger — a hotel guest, a lifeguard, a parent — without instructions. The 5 ft floor keeps the person in trouble from being the only one who can reach it, and the label removes the guessing about which switch on the wall it is. Amenity-center spa at a Kissimmee condo project: the recirculation and jet pumps get an emergency shutoff on the wall facing the tub, 8 ft from the inside wall — past the 5 ft minimum — in plain sight of anyone standing at the water, with a label that reads EMERGENCY SHUTOFF. The inspector paced the distance and read the label from the deck. The same tub model installed at a single-family home the next month needs no 680.41 shutoff at all — the section does not reach one-family dwellings — so the crew's first question on any spa job is which occupancy they are in. Two traps share this section. The first: mounting the shutoff within arm's reach of the water 'so it is handy' — inside 5 ft it fails, because a person in the tub must not be able to reach it. The second: skipping the shutoff at a hotel or condo spa because the backyard version did not need one — the one-family dwelling carve-out does not travel to amenity work. Emergency shutoff mounted 3 ft from the tub's inside wall — inside the 5 ft minimum. Shutoff present but unlabeled, one of four identical switches on the amenity wall. Hotel spa with no emergency shutoff at all — the crew applied the one-family dwelling carve-out to an amenity installation. Shutoff behind the locked equipment gate: not readily accessible, and not within sight of the tub. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 680.41: Spas and hot tubs get an equipment setback in new 680.41(B): gear above the low-voltage contact limit needs 5 ft of horizontal distance from the inside wall unless a permanent barrier stands between. Anything above the low-voltage contact limit stays 5 ft or more, measured horizontally, from the inside wall of the spa or hot tub (680.41(B)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Outdoor spas and hot tubs — Part II rides along (680.42)
x: An outdoor spa or hot tub is not Part IV alone: 680.42 sends the installation back through Parts I and II as well. The Part II items that arrive with it are the ones crews most often miss on a packaged backyard unit: • Receptacle distances and GFCI protection per 680.22(A) — the receptacle layout and protection are figured the same way as at a pool • Equipotential bonding per 680.26 for the tub's equipment and the metal within reach of it • The Part I maintenance disconnecting means: readily accessible, within sight of the equipment it serves, and set back from the inside walls unless separated by a permanent barrier A listed self-contained unit still lands on a field installation. Its listing covers the tub; the pad wiring, the bonding, the disconnect, and the receptacles around it are installed work under this article. A spa puts bathers in a small body of water with pumps, heaters and lights within reach — the same shock hazards as a pool, concentrated. The factory listing can only cover the tub as it left the plant; it cannot cover the pad, the soil, the fence and the receptacles around it. That is why the article pulls the field installation back under the pool rules instead of letting the crate decide. Price an outdoor spa like a small pool. On a backyard lanai job, the takeoff carries the circuit, the GFCI protection, the bonding, the disconnect, and the receptacle layout as their own line items — the same five lines a pool would get. The tub arriving in one crate changes none of them, and the crew that roughs it in as “just an appliance outlet” is the crew that comes back for the failed inspection. The trap answer is that a listed, self-contained spa is factory-built, so Part II never shows up and the pad is wired like an appliance outlet. It is wrong: 680.42 sends the installation back through Parts I and II. The listing covers the tub — the installation around it is field work under this article. Outdoor spa wired as Part IV only — no equipotential bonding at the tub equipment. Receptacles placed without checking the 680.22(A) distances and GFCI protection. Maintenance disconnect not readily accessible, or not within sight of the spa equipment. Packaged unit set on the pad with no field disconnect — the listing treated as covering the whole installation. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Indoor spas and hot tubs
x: An indoor spa or hot tub is wired under Parts I and II of Article 680, as modified by 680.43, and any Chapter 3 wiring method may be used. • Receptacles [680.43(A)]: at least one 125V, 15A or 20A receptacle on a general-purpose branch circuit must sit not less than 6 ft and not more than 10 ft from the inside wall. • Every receptacle must be at least 6 ft from the inside walls, measured horizontally. • 125-volt receptacles rated 30A or less within 10 ft of the inside walls must be GFCI protected — and so must any receptacle that supplies spa or hot tub equipment. • Luminaires and ceiling fans within 5 ft horizontally of an inside wall must be at least 12 ft above the spa or hot tub, or be GFCI protected [680.43(B)]. • Switches must be at least 5 ft from the inside walls, measured horizontally [680.43(C)]. Indoors, no permanent-barrier exception applies to that switch distance. • Bonding [680.43(D)]: metal parts within 5 ft of the inside walls that are not separated from the spa or hot tub by a permanent barrier are tied together — the barrier language in this section belongs to bonding, not to switches. • Every distance in this section is measured by the shortest path a cord would follow without piercing a floor, wall, ceiling, or other permanent barrier. An indoor spa room puts water, wet floors and bare skin in one small space. The 6 ft receptacle band keeps plugs and cords out of reach of a person in the water, and GFCI protection trips on the small leakage currents that wet skin makes dangerous. The 12 ft or GFCI rule for lights and fans keeps a fixture over the water from putting line voltage into the spa. Winter Park remodel, indoor spa off the lanai: the required general-purpose receptacle lands 7 ft from the inside wall — inside the 6–10 ft band — on a 20A circuit with GFCI protection from a Siemens breaker. The ceiling fan over the spa sits 8 ft above the water, so it gets GFCI protection instead of being raised to 12 ft. Measure both distances by the cord path around partitions, not a straight line through them — and do not let a partition talk you into a switch inside 5 ft; indoors, the barrier counts for bonding, not for switches. The trap is importing the barrier idea into the switch rule. Indoors under 680.43, the barrier language belongs only to bonding in (D); a switch still needs its full 5 ft from the inside wall. The second trap is measuring straight through a partition instead of by the cord path. Required receptacle missing, or landed 12 ft from the inside wall — outside the 6–10 ft band. Receptacle 4 ft from the inside wall, inside the 6 ft minimum. 125V receptacle within 10 ft of the inside walls with no GFCI protection. Ceiling fan 8 ft above the spa and not GFCI protected — it needs 12 ft of height or GFCI. Switch 3 ft from the inside wall, with the crew claiming the partition is a barrier — there is no barrier exception for switches indoors. Metal parts within 5 ft of the inside walls not bonded together (680.43(D)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Spas and hot tubs — GFCI protection (680.44)
x: 680.44 is the protection rule for spas and hot tubs: the outlet supplying a spa or hot tub must have GFCI protection. • Read it with the pages around it. The outdoor installations live at 680.42 and the indoor installations at 680.43. • The protection point, the wiring method and the bonding all have to land together on the same tub — passing the GFCI check alone does not finish the job. • This page states the NEC 2020 rule Florida enforces. Any 2023 change is confirmed against the printed 2023 text before it is taught here. A spa concentrates the pool problem into a small tub: a bather sits immersed, surrounded by pumps and a heater, with wet skin that offers very little resistance. A fault in that equipment puts current into water the bather cannot step out of quickly. GFCI protection on the outlet is the personnel protection standing between that fault and the bather. On a spa or hot tub hookup, confirm the GFCI protection point before the tub is filled — breaker, receptacle or disconnect device — and test it at final with the tub's own equipment running. Pick the point at rough-in, not at trim: on a backyard spa in Ocala the protection lands at the disconnect the crew installs for the tub, it gets labeled, and the final test runs the pump and heater together so a trip on day one is found by us, not by the homeowner. The trap: 'the GFCI is in, so the spa passes.' 680.44 is one page of three. The wiring method and the bonding come from 680.42 outdoors or 680.43 indoors, and all of it has to land on the same tub. A protected outlet feeding an indoor tub wired to outdoor rules — or the reverse — is still a failed job. Outlet supplying the spa has no GFCI protection — the one thing 680.44 requires. GFCI device bypassed or replaced with a standard device after nuisance trips. Tub filled and placed in service before the protection point was confirmed and tested. Protection point never identified — no breaker, receptacle or disconnect device on the job actually provides the GFCI protection. Protection tested with the tub empty and off — never proven under the tub's own running equipment. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Fountains — Parts I and V
x: Fountains are governed by Part I (general) and Part V of Article 680. The parts are the first decision on the job: • Decorative fountain nobody enters: Parts I and V. • Interactive fountain, splash feature, or any fountain people can enter: the Part II rules the section references come in as well — treat the water like a pool. • The equipment is pool-grade listed equipment: submersible pumps, luminaires, and their supplies. Landscape-lighting stock is not fountain equipment. • Submersible equipment runs on GFCI protection (680.51(A)) — if it lives under fountain water on line voltage, it is GFCI protected. Water, electricity and bare feet are the pool problem in a smaller basin. A fountain looks harmless because it is shallow and decorative, but a fault in a submersible pump or luminaire puts voltage in water people touch — and on an interactive feature, children stand in it. Pool-grade listed equipment and GFCI protection are what keep a fault from becoming a shock. An HOA entry fountain in Florida is drawn as a dry-deck ornament, but the site plan shows steps into the basin and the sales brochure calls it a splash feature. That answer changes the wiring: the crew prices it as an enterable fountain, with the referenced Part II rules on top of Parts I and V, a listed submersible pump on GFCI protection, and listed fountain luminaires — not the landscape-lighting package the GC first suggested. Ask about entry before pricing, every time. The trap answer is that fountains live in Part II with the pools, or that a fountain is just landscape lighting that gets wet. 680.50 puts fountains in Parts I and V; Part II enters only through the reference, when people can get in the water. And the equipment is listed pool-grade equipment — a landscape transformer and a garden luminaire are not a fountain system. Landscape-lighting equipment installed as fountain luminaires — not listed fountain equipment. Submersible pump with no GFCI protection (680.51(A)). Interactive fountain wired as a dry-deck ornament — the referenced Part II rules were never applied. Line-voltage equipment in the water that is not listed for fountain use. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 680.50: Fountains now get the same 5 ft equipment rule as pools: anything above the low-voltage contact limit stays 5 ft from the inside wall unless a permanent barrier separates it. Gear running above the low-voltage contact limit needs at least 5 ft of separation from the fountain's inside wall (680.50(B)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Fountains — GFCI for submersible equipment
x: Under 680.51(A), GFCI protection is required for fountain luminaires, submersible pumps, and other submersible equipment. • The one path out: equipment that is part of a listed low-voltage system supplied through the 680.23(A)(2) path. • If it lives under fountain water and runs on line voltage, it is GFCI protected — no exceptions by habit. • Fountains are Part V work. A decorative fountain nobody enters runs under Parts I and V; an interactive fountain people can enter pulls in the pool-type rules the article points to as well (680.50). Fountain equipment lives submerged, in a basin people lean over, reach into, and — on interactive features — wade in. A fault in a submersible pump or luminaire puts voltage into the water itself, and the water spreads it to everyone touching it. GFCI protection is the device that sees that leakage and shuts the circuit off before the basin becomes the hazard. At rough-in, land every line-voltage fountain pump and luminaire on its GFCI device, and test the protection at startup with water in the basin. A fountain circuit that trips only when wet is a find-it-now problem — do not leave it as a callback or, worse, defeat the device to keep the water feature running. On a Florida decorative fountain at a community entrance, that test happens with the basin full and the pumps running, because a dry test misses the fault that only shows up submerged. The trap is treating fountain gear like landscape lighting — line-voltage submersible equipment on an ordinary circuit because 'it is only a fountain.' 680.51(A) requires GFCI protection for the luminaires, submersible pumps, and other submersible equipment. The trap in the other direction: the listed low-voltage path through 680.23(A)(2) is a real exception, but only for equipment that is actually part of that listed low-voltage system — not for line-voltage gear with a transformer somewhere upstream. Submersible fountain pump on a standard breaker — no GFCI protection (680.51(A)). GFCI device defeated or jumpered out after trips, instead of finding the wet fault. Landscape-lighting luminaires installed as fountain luminaires — not fountain-grade listed equipment (680.50). Line-voltage equipment claimed under the low-voltage exception without the listed 680.23(A)(2) system. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Hydromassage bathtubs — Part VII only
x: A hydromassage bathtub — the jetted tub in a bathroom — is governed by Part VII of Article 680 alone.
