It does not pick up the pool and spa parts. • The unit goes on an individual branch circuit, with GFCI protection that is readily accessible. • Receptacles rated 125 V, 30 A or less within 6 ft of the tub need GFCI protection. • The other electrical equipment in the room stays under Chapters 1 through 4 — that is 680.72. • The equipment must remain accessible without damaging the building finish (680.73). The access panel is a code item, not a courtesy. The bather sits immersed in water that a pump under the tub is pushing through jets. If that pump or its wiring faults, the water and the wet bather are the path. GFCI protection on a dedicated circuit is the personnel protection, and the access rule exists because a pump nobody can reach is a pump nobody inspects, services or disconnects when it starts to fail. Master-bath remodel in Clermont: the jetted tub's pump lands on its own branch circuit, and because the only receptacle location near the tub is behind the skirt — not readily accessible — the GFCI protection goes in the panel as a GFCI breaker, where anyone can reach and test it. The bidet-seat receptacle 4 ft from the tub rim gets GFCI protection too, under the 6 ft rule. Before tile, the access panel is framed to open fully: pump, junction and disconnect all reachable without cutting the finish, per 680.73. The trap answer treats the jetted tub like a small spa and reaches for the pool and spa parts — bonding grids, Part II distances, the works. A hydromassage bathtub lives in Part VII alone: individual branch circuit, readily accessible GFCI, GFCI on receptacles within 6 ft, and real access to the equipment. The other trap is hiding the GFCI behind the tub, where it can never be reached or tested. Tub pump on a shared bathroom circuit — 680.71 requires an individual branch circuit. GFCI receptacle installed behind the tub skirt where it cannot be reached or tested — protection must be readily accessible. Access panel tiled over or screwed shut — equipment not accessible without damaging the finish (680.73). Standard receptacle 4 ft from the tub with no GFCI protection. Pool/spa bonding grid roughed in for a jetted tub — wrong part of the article; Part VII governs. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Pool lifts — Part VIII
x: Part VIII of Article 680 covers electrically operated pool lifts — the accessibility lifts at commercial and amenity pools (the lift is defined in 680.2). Only Part I and Part VIII apply to the lift itself; the rest of Article 680 does not ride along. • The lift must be listed, labeled and identified for swimming pool and spa use. • A lift connected to premises wiring and operating above the low-voltage contact limit gets GFCI protection for personnel. • The lift is bonded into the pool's equipotential bonding system — metal fittings attached to the pool structure under 680.26(B)(5) and fixed metal parts under 680.26(B)(7), with solid copper not smaller than 8 AWG. • The listing exceptions are narrow: lifts running on a removable battery that is charged away from the pool, and small solar lifts, sit outside the listing rule. Read the exception before assuming one covers your lift. The lift carries a person with limited mobility into the water on a metal machine connected to premises power. If a fault energizes the frame, that user cannot jump clear. Listing proves the machine was built for wet service, GFCI protection cuts a ground fault in milliseconds, and bonding holds the lift, the water and the deck at one potential so no voltage difference can drive current through the swimmer. Amenity-pool ADA work at a Florida apartment community: the lift is electrical scope — include its circuit and bonding in the pool price, not as an afterthought allowance. On the rough-in that means a GFCI-protected circuit to the lift location and an 8 AWG solid copper bonding jumper tying the lift into the equipotential grid with the ladders and handrails. If the specified lift is a removable-battery model charged in the pump room, confirm the exception actually fits before deleting the circuit from the bid. The trap is treating the lift like pool furniture the GC sets in place — 'not electrical.' Part VIII makes it listed electrical equipment with GFCI and bonding duties. The reverse trap is bonding the lift back to the panelboard: equipotential bonding ties the lift to the pool's bonding system, and bonding jumpers in the pool area are not required to run back to a remote panel, service or electrode. Lift set and powered with no bonding jumper to the pool's equipotential grid. Lift circuit on a plain breaker — no GFCI protection for personnel. Unlisted residential-grade lift installed at a commercial amenity pool. Bonding jumper landed only on the branch-circuit equipment ground and never tied into the pool bonding system. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 682 — Natural and Artificially Made Bodies of Water
x: Article 682 covers electrical installations in and around natural and artificially made bodies of water that are not pools or fountains — lakes, ponds, and similar bodies of water. • In scope: floating structures, equipment near the water's edge, and docks that fall outside Article 555's scope. • Out of scope: pools, spas, and fountains — those stay in Article 680. • The 2020 shoreline location rule puts service equipment 5 ft back from the water, with live parts 12 in above the datum plane — the reference level the article measures heights from. • The shock-hazard logic follows Article 680's thinking: GFCI protection, grounding and bonding discipline, and heights above the water figured before anything is set. Florida lakefront work lands here. Open water has no walls, no floor, and no safe edge — a person in a lake touches the water, the dock, and the boat at the same time, and a fault anywhere in that system has all of them to travel through. The article exists because the pool rules stop at the pool wall, but the shock hazard does not. On lakefront work, treat every receptacle and piece of equipment near the waterline as shock-hazard work: GFCI protection, bonding of the metal parts, and heights above the water figured before anything is set. On a Florida lake house, that means the shoreline equipment is laid out 5 ft back with live parts 12 in above the datum plane before the trench is dug — not adjusted after the pad is poured. Where a dock is involved, Article 555 may govern instead of or alongside this article — ask Mike which one controls before rough-in. The trap is reaching for Article 680 because there is water. A lake is not a pool: 682 covers natural and artificially made bodies of water, and its shoreline rules are measured from the datum plane, not from the deck or the seawall cap. The second trap is assuming a dock is always 682 work — a marina or boatyard dock can be Article 555 work instead, and the two articles do not ask for the same installation. Shoreline service equipment set at the water's edge — inside the 5 ft setback (682.11). Live parts mounted below 12 in above the datum plane at the shoreline (682.11). Metal enclosures and equipment frames near the water with no equipment grounding conductor run with the circuit (682.31). Dock wired under 682 without checking whether Article 555 controls the job. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 682.11: Distribution equipment on land, feeder equipment included, now falls under the shoreline location rule that once covered only service equipment: 5 ft back, live parts 12 in above the datum plane. The location rules now cover distribution equipment on land, feeder equipment included, not just the service equipment. • 682.12: Floating structures can now have splices between the waterline and the datum plane if they're submersion-rated, and replacement connections in that zone must be listed and identified for submersion. Floating structures: splices can now sit below the datum plane, as long as they stay above the waterline. • 682.31: Near natural and man-made bodies of water, every metal enclosure, equipment frame and receptacle grounding terminal ties to an equipment grounding conductor run with the circuit conductors. Metal boxes, cabinets and enclosures, metal frames of utilization equipment, and receptacle grounding terminals all connect to the equipment grounding conductor (EGC). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 685 — Integrated Electrical Systems
x: Article 685 covers integrated electrical systems — unitized segments of an industrial wiring system where an orderly shutdown is necessary to ensure safe operation. It is not a size or voltage class. A system only qualifies when all three conditions in 685.1 are met at the same time: • An orderly shutdown is required to minimize personnel hazard and equipment damage — killing power suddenly is itself the danger. • Conditions of maintenance and supervision ensure that qualified persons service the system, and the names of those qualified persons are kept in a permanent record at the office in charge of the installation. • Effective safeguards acceptable to the authority having jurisdiction are established and maintained. Where a system qualifies, the article relaxes a few normal rules so a fault alarm can be answered with a planned shutdown instead of a trip: • 685.10: overcurrent devices critical to the system may be accessible rather than readily accessible, mounted at heights that keep unqualified personnel from operating them. • 685.12: two-wire dc circuits are permitted to be ungrounded. • 685.14: control circuits of 150 volts or less from separately derived systems are permitted to be ungrounded where operational continuity is required. Table 685.3 in 685.3 points to the sections in other articles — 430.44 for motors is one — that carry their own orderly-shutdown provisions. In a chemical plant, a steel mill, or over a scrap yard, sudden power loss is not the safe state — it is the accident. A lifting electromagnet drops its load, a reaction runs away, molten metal freezes in the wrong place. Article 685 trades the normal accessibility and grounding rules for supervision: alarms announce a fault, and trained people shut the process down in sequence before anyone gets hurt. Recognition only. Sharma's work is houses and small commercial, so this article shows up for us as a reading skill, not an installation method: where a facility's drawings show an integrated electrical system, its orderly-shutdown documentation is part of the electrical record — keep it with the panel directories in the job file, and do not rewire interconnections between systems without the engineer of record. If a service call ever takes a crew into a plant that runs under 685, the first question is who the named qualified persons are; if nobody can produce that record, the system is not being run the way the article requires. The exam trap is "any large industrial service." Article 685 is not about size — a big plant that fails any one of the three 685.1 conditions is wired under the normal rules, readily accessible overcurrent devices and grounded systems included. Qualified persons' names missing from the permanent record at the office in charge of the installation (685.1). Safeguards for the integrated system not established, not maintained, or never accepted by the AHJ (685.1). Critical overcurrent devices moved down to readily accessible height during a later alteration, defeating the security 685.10 allows. Interconnections between systems rewired in the field with no engineer of record and no update to the shutdown documentation. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 690 — Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Systems
x: Article 690 covers PV systems from the module terminals to the point of connection with the premises wiring: • Circuit current is figured under 690.8, and conductors and overcurrent devices are sized under 690.8 and 690.9. • Maximum voltage is set by 690.7, calculated from module open-circuit voltage corrected for the coldest expected temperature; on one- and two-family dwellings the maximum system voltage is 600 V. • Ground-fault protection is at 690.41(B) and arc-fault protection at 690.11. The old 690.5 ground-fault number was deleted in the 2020 edition. • Rapid shutdown on buildings is 690.12. The array boundary is 1 ft from the array in all directions. Outside the boundary, controlled conductors are limited to not more than 30 V within 30 seconds of initiation; inside it, not more than 80 V within 30 seconds, or a listed PV hazard control system. • Disconnecting means are at 690.13 and 690.15. • Marking is 690.56: plaques and directories that tell the next electrician — and the fire department — what the system is and where it shuts off. The rapid-shutdown label sits on or within 3 ft of the service disconnecting means. • Interconnection to the premises system runs through Article 705: the 120% bus rule lives at 705.12(B)(3)(2) in Chapter 7 and is deliberately not repeated here. A PV array makes its own power whenever the sun is up — there is no switch on a module. The article exists so a second power source on the building can be shut down, marked, and kept from backfeeding people who believe the building is dead: firefighters working the roof, and the next electrician at the panel. The voltage limits inside the array boundary protect the person cutting a vent hole over live conductors. Sharma's solar-adjacent work is mostly service, additions, and builder rough-ins that a solar contractor finishes. On a new Marion County home, Sharma's part is the service: Siemens meter-main, the rapid-shutdown initiation point at the service equipment, and the 690.56 label on or within 3 ft of the disconnect — so the solar contractor's array lands on a service that already shuts down and reads correctly. The disconnect, marking, and rapid-shutdown pages are the ones that decide whose inspection fails. Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. The NEC 2023 changes in this article apply in Florida to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.); earlier permits stay on NEC 2020. Two traps live on this page. First: "the 120% bus rule is part of Article 690." It is not — interconnection runs through Article 705, and the rule sits at 705.12(B)(3)(2). Second: quoting the old 690.5 for PV ground-fault protection. That number was deleted in the 2020 edition; ground-fault protection is now at 690.41(B). Rapid-shutdown label missing, or more than 3 ft from the service disconnecting means. Conductors inside the array boundary still above 80 V thirty seconds after initiation. Backfed breaker landed with no plaque or directory identifying the second source. Array wiring treated as dead because the inverter is off — the dc side is live in sunlight. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 690.4: New 690.4(G) covers PV that floats on ponds, lakes and reservoirs: the equipment must be identified for floating use, and the wiring method has to handle the array's movement. Floating PV, whether the gear rides on the water itself or mounts to something that floats, must be identified for that use (690.4(G)). • Article 690: The use of the term "PV output circuit" has been removed throughout • 690.1: Added new simplified illustrations to Section 690.1 identifying typical PV system dc components and conductors using new or revised definitions. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Ground-fault protection (690.41(B) in 2020; the old 690.5 was deleted)
x: PV systems must be provided with ground-fault protection that meets 690.41(B). The protection has three jobs: • Detect a ground fault in the DC circuits. • Interrupt the faulted circuit. • Indicate that the fault happened. The equipment must be listed for PV ground-fault protection. In 2020 this protection lives at 690.41(B) — the old 690.5 address was deleted, so a spec or plan note that still cites 690.5 is citing a dead number. This is the DC-side companion to 690.11's arc-fault protection: a ground fault is current leaking out of the circuit to ground, while a series arc is a break arcing inside the circuit. They are different failures, and one device does not cover both. A PV array is current-limited: a ground fault on a roof may never draw enough current to open an overcurrent device, so it can sit there heating for weeks. Wet mornings make it worse — dew gives the fault a path it does not have at noon. Detection, interruption, and a visible indication are what turn a silent roof-fire risk into a service call. Service call on a rooftop system in Winter Garden: the inverter shows a ground-fault indication and has shut down. That indication is 690.41(B) doing its third job, so the crew treats it as a find-the-fault call, not a reset-and-leave call. They work the DC circuits string by string until the faulted string shows itself — chafed insulation where a conductor leaves the array is the usual Florida find, with sun and roof heat doing the damage. The fault gets repaired and the insulation verified; only then does the system go back in service. Resetting without finding it just schedules the fire for later. The trap answer cites 690.5 — deleted in 2020; ground-fault protection moved to 690.41(B). Second trap: swapping in arc-fault protection. 690.11 answers series arcs in DC circuits operating at 80 V dc or more; it does not detect a ground fault, and ground-fault protection does not interrupt a series arc. Each section is owed on its own. Plan set and spec still cite 690.5 for ground-fault protection — a section deleted in 2020. Inverter ground-fault indication reset at the service call with no fault found or repaired. PV system with no means of indicating a ground fault — a fault would sit silent on the roof. Arc-fault device offered as the system's ground-fault protection. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Maximum voltage — correct Voc for cold
x: A PV string's voltage is not its nameplate total. Module open-circuit voltage (Voc) rises as temperature falls, so maximum system voltage is calculated from the sum of the series modules' rated open-circuit voltages, corrected to the lowest expected ambient temperature at the site. • Correct with a method 690.7(A) allows: the manufacturer's temperature coefficient of Voc from the module listing instructions, or the correction factors of Table 690.7(A) for crystalline and multicrystalline silicon modules. • The corrected voltage must not exceed the rated voltage of the connected equipment — inverter input, disconnects and conductors. • Maximum PV system voltage for one- and two-family dwellings is limited to 600V. • The factor is taken from the site's lowest expected temperature — the design low, such as the ASHRAE extreme annual mean minimum named in the Informational Note — not from the weather on install day. • Florida's lowest expected ambient temperatures usually fall in the 1.02–1.12 rows of the table. • 690.7(A)(3): systems with inverter generating capacity of 100 kW or more may use a documented, stamped engineering method — that is PE design work; flag it for Sanjay. A PV array makes its highest voltage on a cold, bright morning — a condition a summer install never shows. Gear rated 600V that sees 657V on a frosty sunrise can fail or arc months after the inspection passed, and the failure gets blamed on the equipment instead of the math. Correcting Voc to the site's design low makes the string voltage honest before the inverter and disconnects are bought. Orlando rooftop on a one-family dwelling: 12 modules at 49.8 V rated Voc total 597.6 V — under the 600V dwelling cap on paper. The site's design low is 4°C, so Table 690.7(A) gives a 1.10 factor: 597.6 x 1.10 = 657.4 V, over the cap and over a 600V inverter input. Dropping one module still fails — 11 modules correct to 602.6 V. At 10 modules the corrected voltage is 547.8 V and the string is legal. Size the string on the coldest bright morning of the year, not on the day of the install — over-voltage on a frosty sunrise is the failure this section exists to prevent. The trap is adding up nameplate Voc and stopping: 597.6 V looks safely under the 600V dwelling cap until the 1.10 cold correction makes it 657.4 V. The second wrong pick is using install-day temperature — the factor comes from the site's lowest expected temperature, and even in Florida that is a 1.02–1.12 multiplier, never 1.00. String sized on nameplate Voc with no temperature correction shown in the submittal. Corrected Voc over the inverter's maximum input voltage rating. Dwelling system over 600V after the cold correction. Table 690.7(A) factors used for a module the table does not cover — the table is for crystalline and multicrystalline silicon modules. Correction factor taken from install-day weather instead of the site's design low. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Circuit current and conductor sizing
x: PV current is figured on the article's own multipliers, not on load estimates. • 690.8(A): the maximum current for a PV source circuit is the sum of the parallel module short-circuit currents multiplied by 125%. • 690.8(B): conductors are then sized at the larger of two numbers — 125% of the (A) current before any temperature correction or adjustment factors, or 100% of the (A) current after those factors are applied. Both checks must be run. Either one can govern, depending on the rooftop temperature and the conduit fill. A PV array in full sun delivers its current for hours without cycling — it behaves as a continuous load on a hot roof, the worst combination a conductor ever sees. The first multiplier covers the array making more current than its summed nameplates suggest; the two-check sizing then covers the conductor carrying less than its table value once rooftop heat and conduit fill are counted. Skip either side and the wire becomes the fuse. Worked example, Florida rooftop. Two parallel strings of modules with an Isc of 10.4 A each: the maximum current under 690.8(A) is (10.4 + 10.4) × 1.25 = 26 A. Check 1: 26 × 1.25 = 32.5 A before factors — 10 AWG copper at 75 °C (35 A, Table 310.16) passes. Check 2: on this roof the temperature correction and adjustment factors multiply out to 0.70, so the conductor needs 26 ÷ 0.70 = 37.1 A of table ampacity to still deliver 26 A after derating — 10 AWG falls short, and 8 AWG (50 A) governs. Do the two-step check on paper; hot Florida rooftops make the after-correction figure govern more often than installers expect. The trap is stopping after the first check — '32.5 A, and 10 AWG is 35 A, done.' On a hot roof, the after-factors check can demand more than the before-factors number, and it governs. The mirror-image error is sizing from the modules' operating current (Imp) instead of the parallel short-circuit sum: 690.8 starts from Isc, every time. PV source-circuit conductors sized from module operating current (Imp) instead of the parallel Isc sum multiplied by 125%. Worksheet shows the Isc sum carried straight to Table 310.16 — the 690.8(A) maximum current was never figured. Only the before-factors check run: rooftop temperature correction and adjustment factors never applied, so the conductors fail the 690.8(B) after-factors check. Ampacity read from the 90 °C column for equipment whose terminations are rated 75 °C (110.14(C)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Overcurrent protection
x: Where overcurrent protection is required for a PV circuit, the device rating is not less than 125% of the maximum current figured under 690.8(A) — the sum of the parallel module short-circuit currents multiplied by 125%. • No overcurrent device is required at all where two conditions both hold: the conductors are sized for the full available current, and no external source can backfeed current beyond their ampacity. • Parallel strings are the usual external source. One string cannot overdrive its own conductors; two or more strings can drive current backward into a faulted third string. • String fusing questions are answered by applying those two conditions, not by habit — 'we always fuse' and 'we never fuse' are both wrong answers. A PV module is current-limited — a shorted string does not make big fault current by itself. The danger is the rest of the array: parallel strings, and any interconnected source, will drive current backward into a faulted string's conductors, past what those conductors can carry, for as long as the sun shines. The fuse is there to open that backfeed path before the conductor becomes the fuse. Three or more parallel strings is where the backfeed condition usually starts to bite — check it before deciding fuses are 'never needed' or 'always needed.' On a Florida rooftop with three strings of modules at 9.8 amperes short-circuit current each: one string's maximum current is 9.8 × 125% = 12.25 amperes. If that string faults, the other two strings can backfeed about 24.5 amperes into it — beyond what conductors sized for one string can carry — so the strings get fuses, each rated not less than 125% of the 690.8(A) current. The trap is answering string-fuse questions from habit. 'PV never needs fuses because modules are current-limited' forgets the backfeed from the parallel strings. 'Every string always gets a fuse' ignores the two-condition case where no device is required at all. The exam wants the conditions applied: conductors sized for the full available current, and no external source able to backfeed beyond their ampacity. Three parallel strings combined with no string fuses and conductors sized for one string — backfeed path unprotected (690.9). Overcurrent device rated below 125% of the maximum current figured under 690.8(A). Fuses omitted because 'modules are current-limited,' where parallel strings can backfeed the faulted string. A fuse installed by habit on a circuit that meets both no-device conditions, then blamed for nuisance openings — the conditions were never checked either way. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 690.9(D): Revised language in Section 690.9(D), providing a pointer to 705.30(F), where specific requirements applicable to interconnected systems are addressed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Arc-fault circuit protection (DC)
x: PV systems with DC circuits operating at 80 V dc or greater between any two conductors must be protected by a listed PV arc-fault circuit interrupter, or by other listed system components providing equivalent protection. • The protection must detect and interrupt arcing faults caused by a failure in the intended continuity of a conductor, connection, module, or other component in the PV DC circuits. • Exception: systems not installed on or in buildings, where the DC circuits are in metallic raceways or metal-clad cables, in enclosed metallic cable trays, or underground. A DC arc does not pass through zero 120 times a second the way AC does, so once a failing connector starts arcing it tends to keep arcing — a small, very hot plasma sitting on a roof or in a junction box. The current is normal load current, so no breaker or fuse sees a fault. The AFCI watches the circuit's signature, recognizes the arc, and shuts the string down before the connection point burns through. Rooftop retrofit in Orlando: the string voltage is far over the 80 V trigger, so the inverter's listed PV AFCI is not an option — it is the protection, and it stays enabled. The crew's part is connector discipline: matched, fully seated connectors, because a loose series connection is the classic arc source. Across town, a ground-mounted array at a warehouse keeps its DC runs underground and in metallic raceway and is not on or in a building — that is the shape of the exception. Two traps. First, reaching for 210.12: that is AC branch-circuit AFCI for dwelling rooms and has nothing to do with PV DC circuits. Second, claiming the exception for a rooftop array because the conductors are in EMT — the exception starts with 'not installed on or in buildings,' and a rooftop array fails that test before the raceway question is even asked. PV system on a home with DC circuits over 80 V and no listed arc-fault protection, or the inverter's AFCI function disabled. Exception claimed for a rooftop array because conductors are in metallic raceway — the array is on a building. Mismatched or incompletely seated PV connectors left as a series-arc source. AC dwelling AFCI breaker offered as the 690.11 protection for a DC string. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Rapid shutdown of PV systems on buildings
x: Rapid shutdown controls PV conductors on and in buildings, so firefighters can work around a live array. The sun keeps the modules energized; this section caps what the conductors may carry once shutdown is initiated. • The array boundary is 1 ft from the array in all directions. • Outside the boundary — and for conductors more than 3 ft from the point of entry into the building — controlled conductors must be limited to not more than 30 V within 30 seconds of initiation. • Inside the boundary, use one of the section's paths: a listed PV hazard control system (PVHCS, UL 3741); or conductors limited to not more than 80 V within 30 seconds; or an array with no exposed wiring methods or conductive parts, installed not less than 8 ft from exposed grounded conductive parts. The initiation device is covered at 690.12(C), and the labels at 690.56. A fire crew venting a roof or cutting an opening works blind, in smoke, around conductors that stay live as long as light hits the modules — there is no switch at the sun. Without rapid shutdown, a saw through a PV conductor can put full array voltage on the crew. Dropping the conductors outside the array to 30 V within 30 seconds, and capping or listing the hazard inside the boundary, makes the roof a place firefighters can work. On a Florida rooftop residential job, Sharma's standard path is module-level shutdown electronics, initiated at the PV disconnect beside the Siemens meter-main on the exterior wall — the 690.12(C) device a firefighter can find without entering the house. The reflective red RAPID SHUTDOWN label goes on or within 3 ft of that device, in capital letters at least 3/8 in. high (690.56). Thirty seconds after initiation, a meter on the conductors leaving the boundary must read 30 V or less. That check is what the inspector and the fire crew are really buying. The trap is applying the 30 V limit everywhere. Inside the array boundary, the 2020 limit is 80 V within 30 seconds — or a listed PVHCS, or the no-exposed-parts path. The other wrong answer is placing the boundary at the edge of the modules: it sits 1 ft out, in all directions. No rapid shutdown label at the service disconnect or initiation device, or the label sits more than 3 ft away from it (690.56). Label letters under 3/8 in. high, or not white capitals on a red reflective background (690.56(C)(2)). Initiation device for a one- or two-family dwelling located inside the building instead of at a readily accessible outdoor location (690.12(C)). Conductors outside the array boundary still over 30 V thirty seconds after initiation — module electronics not paired or not commissioned. The 2023 carport exception applied on a job permitted under NEC 2020, leaving detached-structure PV with no rapid shutdown. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 690.12: Carports, parking shades and other open detached structures can now carry PV without rapid shutdown. The third inside-array option is gone, and the building label moved into 690.12(D). New Exception No. 2: PV on nonenclosed detached structures, such as carports, parking shade structures and solar trellises, skips rapid shutdown. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Rapid shutdown initiation device
x: The initiation device is the switch that starts rapid shutdown (690.12). It has to pass three checks: • Readily accessible — reachable fast, without a ladder, a locked gate, or a trip through the building. • It clearly indicates whether it is in the off position (shutdown initiated) or the on position. • It may be the service disconnect, the PV system disconnect, or another listed switch — no special device is required. For one- and two-family dwellings, the initiation device must be located at a readily accessible location outside the building — the fire crew does not enter the house to shut the array down. What initiation buys, per 690.12: outside the array boundary, controlled conductors are limited to not more than 30 V within 30 seconds; inside the boundary, not more than 80 V within 30 seconds, unless a listed PV hazard control system is used. Sunlight keeps a PV array energized even with the utility service off, and firefighters work on and around those roofs. Rapid shutdown only protects them if the first firefighter on scene can find and throw the initiation device in seconds, from outside, and tell at a glance whether shutdown is on. A device hidden in a garage or an unlabeled switch fails the whole purpose of 690.12. On dwelling jobs, walk out front and find the initiation point the way a firefighter would — if you can't, neither can they. Sharma's standard layout puts the PV disconnect beside the Siemens meter-main on the exterior wall and makes that disconnect the initiation device: one throw, ON and OFF positions marked, and the reflective red RAPID SHUTDOWN label on or within 3 ft of it, with letters at least 3/8 in. high (690.56(C)). After initiation, the conductors leaving the array boundary must be down to 30 V or less within 30 seconds — that is the number the fire crew is counting on. The trap is naming the inverter's built-in switch, or a disconnect inside the garage, as the initiation device on a dwelling. Both fail the rule: for one- and two-family dwellings the device must be at a readily accessible location outside the building, and it must show its position clearly. Initiation device inside the garage or the house on a one- or two-family dwelling. Switch with no clear ON/OFF indication of the shutdown state. No reflective rapid-shutdown label at the device, or label letters under 3/8 in. high. Device behind a locked gate, a fence, or landscaping — not readily accessible. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: PV system disconnecting means
x: Means shall be provided to disconnect the PV system from all wiring systems — the utility power system, any energy storage system, and the utilization equipment and its premises wiring. The disconnecting means has to pass three checks: • Be installed at a readily accessible location (690.13(A)) — reachable quickly, without a ladder, a locked room, or a trip through the building. • Plainly indicate whether it is in the open (off) or closed (on) position (690.13(B)). • Be permanently marked "PV SYSTEM DISCONNECT" (690.13(B)) — a real marking that survives the weather, not tape or marker. Where all the terminals of the disconnect can still be energized with the switch open — the array side stays live in sunlight — a warning sign goes on or next to the disconnect. Where the PV disconnect is not at the service equipment, the directory and plaque rules of 690.56 point back to where it is, so every source at the building can be found from the service. A PV array makes power whenever light hits it, so opening the utility breaker does not make the solar side safe. The disconnect is the one place a firefighter, a utility crew, or the next electrician can separate the PV system from every other wiring system and know it is open. If it is hidden, unmarked, or ambiguous about its position, somebody works on conductors they believe are dead that are not. Rooftop PV on a Florida house: the inverter sits on the garage wall and the crew lands the PV system disconnect outside, beside the Siemens meter-main, where it is readily accessible from grade. It is a real switch that shows OPEN and ON, permanently marked PV SYSTEM DISCONNECT. Because it is grouped at the service, the 690.56 plaque at the same spot names it with the building's other sources. The homeowner is told plainly: the switch kills the connection, but the panels and their leads stay live in daylight. The trap is answering that the rapid shutdown switch, or the inverter's own control, satisfies 690.13. Rapid shutdown (690.12) limits conductor voltage for firefighters; it is not the PV system disconnecting means. 690.13 wants a disconnecting means that separates the PV system from all wiring systems, sits where it is readily accessible, plainly shows open or closed, and is permanently marked PV SYSTEM DISCONNECT. PV disconnect inside the attic or behind a locked gate — not readily accessible (690.13(A)). Disconnect marked with tape or a marker — the marking is not permanent (690.13(B)). Switch gives no plain indication of open versus closed position (690.13(B)). PV disconnect remote from the service, with no directory or plaque at the service equipment pointing to it (690.56). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Disconnection of PV equipment
x: 690.15 is about isolating one piece of PV equipment — an inverter, a charge controller, a dc-to-dc converter — so it can be serviced or replaced with every source cut off. The disconnecting means must open all ungrounded conductors from all sources: • The array side. The modules make power whenever there is light; opening the ac side does nothing to the dc input. • The utility side. The grid backfeeds the inverter's ac terminals until its ac disconnect is opened. • The storage side, on hybrid systems with batteries. Location (2020): the isolating device or equipment disconnect goes in the equipment, or within sight and within 10 ft of it. Where it sits farther away, it must be capable of being locked in the open position (110.25). An isolating device that is not rated to interrupt the circuit current must be marked "Do Not Disconnect Under Load." PV equipment is fed from directions that do not behave like a normal circuit. There is no switch on the sun: an inverter whose ac side is off still has live dc at its terminals in full daylight, and a hybrid inverter adds a battery that never sleeps. This section exists so the person opening the equipment can put every one of those sources behind an open, visible disconnect first. Before opening an inverter, verify both sides are dead — the array makes power whenever the sun is up. On a Florida rooftop hybrid job that is three checks, not two: open the dc disconnect at the inverter and meter the array input, open the ac disconnect and meter the output, and open the battery disconnect on the storage side. The 690.15 disconnects sit at the inverter — within sight and within 10 ft — so the tech who opened them can see them from the equipment while the cover is off. The trap is 'the PV system disconnect is off, so the inverter is safe to open.' The 690.13 system disconnect separates the system from the building and the grid; it does nothing about the array wired straight into the inverter's dc terminals. Rapid shutdown (690.12) is the other wrong answer — it limits conductor voltage for firefighters, it does not isolate equipment for service. 690.15 isolation is per piece of equipment, from every source. Inverter opened for service with only the ac disconnect off — array dc still live at the terminals. Equipment disconnect mounted out of sight and beyond 10 ft of the inverter, and not capable of being locked open. Isolating connector opened under load with no "Do Not Disconnect Under Load" marking. Disconnect that opens only one ungrounded dc conductor, leaving the other leg connected to the array. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 690.15: Rearranged 690.15 with some grammatical changes. A requirement for an equipment disconnecting means to be within 10 feet of the equipment to now be within sight was also modified. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wiring methods — PV source and output circuits
x: 690.31 is where solar wiring stops being ordinary branch-circuit wiring. • Exposed single-conductor PV source-circuit wiring is a listed PV cable type — Type PV wire, or USE-2 where the section permits it. They are built and marked for sunlight, heat and rooftop duty — not THHN pulled out of a raceway and left in the sun. • Rooftop conductors live in the hottest part of the job, so Chapter 3 temperature rules ride along: a raceway or cable close above a sunlit roof picks up a 33°C (60°F) adder under 310.15(B)(2). • Inside a building, PV dc circuits over 30 V or 8 A must run in metal raceways, in Type MC cable that complies with 250.118(10), or in metal enclosures, from the point of penetration into the building to the first readily accessible disconnecting means (690.31(D)) — so a dc fault inside a wall is contained in metal. • That rule applies inside buildings, not to runs on the building. • Conductors are identified and grouped by system (690.31(B)). Module interconnects, home runs and the inverter output each follow the part of the section written for them — read the subsection for the run in front of you. PV source circuits are live whenever the sun is up — there is no switch at the module. Ordinary insulation cooks, cracks and faults on a hot roof, and a dc arc inside a wood-framed wall does not blow itself out the way an ac arc does. Listed PV cable is built to survive the roof environment, and the metal-raceway rule keeps a dc fault inside the building contained in metal until the first disconnect. Rooftop job in Ocala, 24 modules in two strings: Type PV wire home runs clipped up off the roof surface, because a raceway or cable less than 7/8 in. above a sunlit Florida roof picks up the 33°C (60°F) temperature adder of 310.15(B)(2) before the Chapter 3 correction math starts. At the eave the dc run penetrates the roof and crosses the attic in metal raceway — it is well over 30 V, so 690.31(D) keeps it in metal from the penetration to the first readily accessible disconnect at the inverter. System voltage stays under the 600 V cap for one- and two-family dwellings (690.7). The trap is swapping the two halves of the section. Inside a building, dc over 30 V or 8 A belongs in metal from the penetration to the first readily accessible disconnect (690.31(D)); on the roof, exposed single conductors must be listed PV cable, not THHN run in the open. The companion wrong answer: the 690.31(D) metal rule covers runs on the building. It does not — it applies inside buildings. THHN run exposed across the roof as PV source-circuit wiring instead of listed Type PV wire or USE-2. Dc home run crossing the attic in PVC or open cable instead of a metal raceway, Type MC cable per 250.118(10), or a metal enclosure (690.31(D)). PV wire lying flat on the roof surface, unsecured, instead of clipped up off the surface the way the listing expects. PV dc conductors and conductors of another system mixed in one enclosure, unidentified and ungrouped (690.31(B)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 690.31(B): Section 690.31(B) was revised and a new list item (1), Conductors of Different Systems, was added while the previous text in that location was moved to list item (2), Identification. The text revisions provide conditions where PV dc circuits and inverter output circuits can now be installed in the same junction box, pull box or wireway provided they are identified, grouped, and separated in accordance with 690.31 (B)(2) and (B)(3). • 690.31(B)(1): Exception revised to permit the dc and ac conductors of a PV system to be located within the same enclosure where all the conductors are insulated for the highest voltage present and grouped appropriately. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding electrode system — PV ties into the building system
x: A PV array does not get its own separate grounding world. 690.47 ties the array's equipment grounding, and any dc grounding electrode conductor, into the building's grounding electrode system, so the array, the service, and everything else bonded in the building sit at the same potential. • 690.47(A): the array equipment grounding conductors connect to the building's grounding electrode system. That connection is the rule, not an option. • 690.47(B): one or more additional electrodes at the array are permitted as auxiliary electrodes under 250.54. A ground rod driven by the racking is the usual one. • An auxiliary electrode may connect directly to the array frame or structure, and it does not have to be bonded to the building GES, because the bonding path back to the service is the array's equipment grounding conductor (Article 250, Part VII). • The earth is never the fault-current path, and it never replaces that EGC connection. A rod in the dirt by the array, with no EGC path back, is a decoration, not a grounding electrode system — and it is not compliant. A fault on a roof array has to clear at the service, not soak into the dirt. Earth is a poor conductor, so a rod by itself can leave racking and module frames sitting at a dangerous voltage while the breaker never trips. Tying the array into the building's one electrode system keeps every bonded metal part at the same potential, and the equipment grounding conductor gives the fault a low-resistance path back to the source, so the breaker can trip. Roof array on a Marion County house: the racking and module frames bond to the array equipment grounding conductor, which runs with the PV output circuit to the inverter and the service, landing on the same grounding electrode system as the house — concrete-encased electrode and rods at the meter-main. The design also drives a rod beside the ground-mount rack in the yard: permitted as an auxiliary electrode under 690.47(B) and 250.54 and clamped to the racking, but the inspection still turns on the EGC path back to the service ground, not on the rod. The trap answer is that the rod at the array must be bonded to the building grounding electrode system — or that the array needs its own 25-ohm electrode system. Neither is the rule. 690.47(B) and 250.54 permit the auxiliary electrode connected to the array frame with no bond to the building GES, because the equipment grounding conductor is the required path back (690.47(A)). The reverse trap also appears: a rod alone is never a substitute for that connection. Ground rod driven at the array and clamped to the racking, with no equipment grounding conductor run back to the building grounding electrode system. Array EGC landed on an isolated rod at the inverter instead of the building grounding electrode system (690.47(A)). Racking bond missing, or made with a clamp not listed for the purpose; bonding jumper cut where the home run enters the building. Auxiliary electrode treated as the array's only ground — no bond between the array equipment grounding and the service grounding electrode system. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Marking — plaques, directories, and the rapid shutdown label
x: PV systems carry permanent plaques and directories so every source at a building can be found from the service equipment: • A stand-alone system follows the directory rule of 710.10 • A system interconnected with another source follows 705.10 • A permanent label on or within 3 ft of the service disconnecting means states that the system is equipped with rapid shutdown and carries the 690.56(C) diagram showing the switch locations • A reflective label on or within 3 ft of the rapid shutdown initiation device reads RAPID SHUTDOWN SWITCH FOR SOLAR PV SYSTEM — capital letters at least 3/8 in. high, white on red (690.56(C)(2)) Marking is not paperwork; it is the part of the system the fire department uses. A PV array is a power source that stays live in daylight even with the service open. Firefighters on a roof and linemen at the service have to find every source and shut the array down fast: the directory tells them the sources exist, and the red rapid-shutdown label tells them where the switch is. A missing label means crews treat the whole roof as energized. Orlando rooftop retrofit: the Siemens service panel gets the directory plaque naming the PV source, the rapid-shutdown label with the roof diagram goes on the meter-main — within 3 ft of the service disconnect — and the reflective RAPID SHUTDOWN SWITCH label goes at the initiation device by the front door. Carry the red RSD labels in the truck stock — a missing 3/8 in. label fails finals, and the re-inspection trip costs more than the roll of labels. The trap is letter size and placement from memory: 1/4 in. letters, or the label stuck anywhere on the building. The initiation-device label needs capitals at least 3/8 in. high, white on red, reflective, on or within 3 ft of the device — and the service label lives on or within 3 ft of the service disconnecting means. No directory at the service equipment naming the PV source (705.10). Rapid shutdown label missing, or mounted across the yard from the service disconnect — 3 ft is the limit. Initiation-device label with 1/4 in. letters — 3/8 in. minimum, white on red, reflective (690.56(C)(2)). Hand-written marker label instead of a permanent plaque — the marking has to be permanent. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 690.56: The building rapid shutdown label moved out of 690.56(C) into 690.12(D). What stays in 690.56 is power source identification by plaque or directory. The building rapid shutdown label, with its simple roof diagram, moved from 690.56(C) to 690.12(D). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 691 — Large-Scale Photovoltaic (PV) Electric Supply Stations
x: Article 691 covers large-scale photovoltaic (PV) electric supply stations — utility-scale PV plants, not building systems. • The line is capacity: stations with an aggregate capacity of 5 MW and up are 691 work. • Everything below that line — rooftop arrays, commercial building PV, ground-mounts serving a building — stays under Article 690. • A 691 station is an engineered installation, with its own access, fencing, and documentation rules, and access limited to qualified persons. • The article was added in the 2017 edition; it is not new in 2020. Sharma does not build these. The skill this page teaches is recognition: know the article exists, so a plant job is never priced from residential 690 habits. A 5 MW plant is a power station, not a big rooftop. Its fault energy, its switching, its access control, and its documentation are engineered the way a utility facility is engineered, and the consequences of treating it like a large residential array land on whoever priced it that way. Article 691 exists so the threshold is unmistakable: cross 5 MW and the job changes articles, changes design method, and changes who may work on it. Recognition only: a plant of 5 MW and up is an engineered, fenced, access-controlled installation with its own documentation rules. If a developer asks Sharma to 'hook up' a solar field outside Ocala, the first move is the capacity math on the plant's one-line: at 5 MW and up, this is a 691 station, and the conversation starts with the plant's engineered drawings — never with residential 690 habits, never with a rooftop takeoff, and never with a price built from 690 material lists. The trap is treating the threshold as a size detail: 'a big array is still Article 690.' At 5 MW aggregate capacity the job leaves 690. Article 691 takes over, and its engineered-design, fencing, access, and documentation rules come with it. Plant priced and permitted from a residential 690 takeoff — no engineered design package behind it. Fencing and controlled access treated as site extras instead of part of the station's installation rules. Documentation and directories missing at turnover on a plant that requires them. Unqualified crew working inside the fence — 691 stations are qualified-persons territory. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 692 — Fuel Cell Systems
x: Article 692 covers fuel cell power systems — a chemical generator that makes electricity while fuel reaches it. A system may be stand-alone or interactive with other sources, with or without battery storage (692.1). • Listing (692.6): the fuel cell system is evaluated and listed for its intended application before it is installed. • Output sizing (692.8(B)): feeder conductors from the fuel cell to the premises wiring are sized at not less than the greater of the nameplate rated circuit current or the rating of the fuel cell's own overcurrent device. • Disconnects (692.13, 692.14): a means disconnects all current-carrying conductors of the source from every other conductor in the building; it follows 225.31 and 225.33 through 225.40, and need not be suitable as service equipment. • Identification (692.4(B)): a permanent plaque or directory at each service location lists the fuel cell with every other power source on site. • Marking: the power source is marked at its disconnecting means (692.50), the manual fuel shut-off valve's location is marked at the building's primary disconnect (692.51), and a stored-energy warning goes at the service disconnect where the system stores energy (692.52). • Interactive systems also meet Article 705, and the transfer equipment keeps the fuel cell isolated from the utility network (692.61). A fuel cell is a generator with no off switch on the machine: while fuel flows, the stack makes power, and stored-energy systems keep terminals live after that. Crews and firefighters trained on 'open the breaker and it is dead' get hurt by quiet backfeed. The disconnect, plaque, and fuel-valve marking rules exist so anyone can find every source on the site, isolate it, and stop the fuel that keeps it alive. A 10 kW fuel cell on a small commercial job in Orlando: the nameplate rated current is 42 A and the unit's overcurrent device is 50 A, so 692.8(B) sizes the output feeder at the greater number — conductors with at least 50 A ampacity, not the 42 A the nameplate headline suggests. The disconnect beside the unit opens all current-carrying conductors, the service equipment gets a plaque listing the utility service and the fuel cell side by side, and the manual fuel shut-off valve's location is marked at the building's primary disconnect, so a fire crew can find it without a site walk. The trap is sizing the output feeder from the nameplate current alone. 692.8(B) takes the greater of the nameplate rated circuit current and the rating of the fuel cell's overcurrent device — when the unit's device is the bigger number, it governs. And 'disconnect open' is not 'dead': with fuel still flowing, the stack is still a source — which is why the fuel shut-off marking is part of the same job. Output feeder sized to the nameplate current where the fuel cell's overcurrent device was rated higher — 692.8(B) takes the greater. No plaque or directory at the service equipment identifying the fuel cell as a second power source. Disconnect opens the ungrounded conductors only; a current-carrying conductor of the source stays connected. Manual fuel shut-off valve location not marked at the building's primary disconnecting means. Unlisted fuel cell system set in place — 692.6 requires evaluation and listing for the application before installation. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 694 — Wind Electric Systems
x: Article 694 covers small wind electric systems: the turbine, its tower, and the generators, alternators, inverters, and controllers that turn wind into premises power, interconnected with the utility or standing alone, with or without battery storage. The article's size line is per turbine — each individual wind turbine must be rated 100 kW or less. Utility-scale machines live under utility rules, not this article. • The turbine itself is part of the electrical system (694.2 counts the tower, nacelle, and turbine output circuit as system parts), and 694.7 requires the wind electric system to be listed. • 694.10: on one- and two-family dwellings, the wind turbine output circuit is limited to 600 volts maximum. • 694.12: system currents are treated as continuous — conductors are sized at not less than 125 percent of the maximum circuit current. • 694.15: turbine output circuits, inverter output circuits, and storage conductors get overcurrent protection under Article 240, sized on the same 125 percent basis. • 694.20: a disconnecting means for the system must be readily accessible and open all ungrounded conductors. • An interactive system interconnects under 694.60 and 694.62, which send you to Article 705, using inverters listed and identified as interactive. You cannot switch off the wind. A turbine keeps generating as long as the rotor turns, and an unloaded turbine in a gust can overspeed and tear itself apart — so the article builds safety out of listing, continuous-duty sizing, and a real disconnect, instead of pretending the source can be shut down like a utility feed. Recognition only: a small wind system's disconnects, grounding, and tower work follow the turbine manufacturer's listing and this article. Sharma's likely piece is the supply-side connection — confirm the turbine's own disconnect and tower grounding are in the turbine installer's scope before pricing ours. If a quote ever does land, the sizing habit to bring is the 125 percent rule: a turbine whose maximum output current is 40 A needs conductors sized for at least 50 A before any temperature or fill adjustment. The trap is sizing wind circuits like ordinary loads. Wind output is continuous by rule — 694.12 sizes conductors at 125 percent of the maximum circuit current, not the nameplate's fair-weather rating, and the disconnect still has to open every ungrounded conductor. Turbine output conductors sized at 100 percent of maximum circuit current instead of 125 percent (694.12). AC-only breaker protecting a dc turbine output circuit — the device must be rated for the circuit it protects (694.15). No readily accessible disconnecting means, or one that leaves an ungrounded conductor closed (694.20). Grid used as the only overspeed protection — an interconnected grid is not an adequate alternate diversion load (694.7). Unlisted turbine system installed as a field-assembled kit (694.7). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 695 — Fire Pumps
x: Article 695 exists for one reason: the fire pump must run, even at the cost of the equipment itself. Everything in it runs backward from ordinary motor practice: • Sources are chosen for reliability above all (695.3). • Overcurrent devices are sized to carry locked-rotor current indefinitely rather than to trip (695.4). • Disconnects are arranged so the pump cannot be casually shut off. Recognition level is the right depth for Sharma: this is engineered, AHJ-scrutinized work, and the pages here cover what to recognize and what never to improvise. The article does not apply to sprinkler-system pumps at one- and two-family dwellings, and pressure-maintenance (jockey) pumps sit outside its scope as pumps — though their current counts in the 695.3 source sizing. In a fire, the pump is the water supply for the sprinklers and standpipes. A pump that trips on overload, or that a well-meaning employee switched off last month and forgot, leaves the building defenseless while it burns. Article 695 trades motor protection for run time: burn up the pump if necessary, but keep water moving until the fire is out. If a bid touches a fire pump, the electrical design comes from the engineer of record and NFPA 20 — Sharma prices the installation of a designed system, never a redesign in the field. On a mid-rise condo job in Orlando, Sharma's scope in the pump room is recognition and installation: dedicated source, listed controller, disconnecting means as drawn. Anything in that room that looks like an ordinary motor circuit is a question for the engineer, not a field fix. The trap is wiring the fire pump like an Article 430 motor, with overloads sized to trip and save the motor. Under 695.4 the overcurrent device is sized to carry locked-rotor current indefinitely — the pump is expendable, the water supply is not. The second trap is leaving the jockey pump out of the source math: it sits outside the article's scope as a pump, but its current still counts in the 695.3 source sizing. Fire pump overcurrent device sized to trip on locked-rotor current — 695.4 requires it to carry locked-rotor current indefinitely. Jockey pump current left out of the 695.3 source sizing. Fire pump disconnecting means arranged so the pump can be casually shut off and left off. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 695.1: Article 695 now plainly excludes fire suppression water pumps in one- and two-family homes, so a house sprinkler pump isn't treated as a fire pump. New item (4) in 695.1(B) takes fire suppression water pumps in one- and two-family homes out of Article 695. • 695.15: Diesel-driven fire pumps no longer need a surge-protective device at the controller. Electric fire pumps still do. New exception: a diesel-driven fire pump doesn't need a surge-protective device (SPD) at its controller. • 695.6: Every fitting on the controller-to-motor wiring for a fire pump now needs a wet-location listing. The wiring methods and motor connection rules carried over. New 695.6(D)(2): every fitting on the controller-to-motor run has to be listed for wet locations. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Power sources — reliable, and sized for locked rotor
x: The fire pump supply must come from a reliable source, and the source is sized for the worst event the pump can produce — a stalled pump drawing locked-rotor current. • The source must carry the locked-rotor current of the fire pump motor(s), plus the locked-rotor current of the pressure-maintenance (jockey) pump motors, plus 100% of the accessory equipment load. Locked rotor, not full load, is the design event. • Permitted arrangements include a separate utility service, arranged remote from the normal service so one event cannot take both. • A tap ahead of the normal service disconnecting means is permitted — but not within the enclosure of that disconnect. • An on-site standby generator is permitted, protected against fire damage. • Where transfer equipment is used, it sits in the fire pump room (695.3(F)). • Phase converters are not permitted as the supply (695.3(I)). The pump exists for the worst day in the building's life. If a fire, a fault, or one opened disconnect can kill the normal power and the pump together, the sprinkler system is a decoration. And a seized pump draws locked-rotor current: a source or device that lets go at that current stops the pump at the exact moment the building needs it most. Warehouse job east of Orlando: a 75 hp electric fire pump at 460 V. The motor nameplate shows 96 A full load, but locked rotor works out to roughly 590 A. Add the jockey pump at about 40 A locked rotor and 12 A of accessory load at 100%, and the source has to carry roughly 640 A indefinitely — which is why the fire pump tap lands ahead of the main, and why nobody "right-sizes" that protection down to running current. Recognize the tap-ahead-of-the-main arrangement when you see it on existing work: it is deliberate, not a violation. The trap is sizing the fire pump source the way you size any other motor circuit — from full-load current, with protection that trips on overload. Here the design event is locked rotor: pump locked-rotor plus jockey locked-rotor plus all of the accessory load, carried indefinitely (the protection rule itself is 695.4). An answer built on 96 A running current for a 75 hp pump misses the event the article is written around. Fire pump fed through the normal service disconnect — one opened main kills the pump. Source or overcurrent device sized from full-load current; lets go on locked rotor. Phase converter used as the fire pump supply (695.3(I)). Transfer switch installed in the electrical room instead of the fire pump room (695.3(F)). Fire pump tap made inside the service disconnect enclosure. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Continuity of power — protection that refuses to trip
x: Continuity rules invert ordinary practice. For a fire pump, the design goal is not a circuit that trips — it is a pump that keeps running: • A single disconnecting means is permitted where it is listed for fire pump service together with the controller (or transfer switch) it feeds • Its overcurrent device is selected to carry, indefinitely, the sum of the locked-rotor currents of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motors, plus the full accessory load — and it must be listed for fire pump use • The disconnect must be lockable in the closed position — the opposite of the elevator rule • It is identified as a fire pump disconnect with permanently marked letters not less than 1 in. high • No ground-fault protection of equipment is applied to the fire pump circuit Anything that can shut the pump down on a fault that is not a short circuit is designed out. The supply behind it is sized the same way — for locked-rotor current, not full load (695.3). A fire pump that trips on overload during a fire is worse than a pump that burns up running — the building is already on fire, and the pump is the last tool left. Locked-rotor sizing, no GFPE, and a disconnect locked ON all serve one decision made in advance: the pump runs until it cannot, and nothing in the protection scheme is allowed to second-guess that during the event. Field recognition: a fire pump disconnect that looks 'oversized' and is locked ON is correct. Never 'fix' one to ordinary motor sizing. On a Lakeland warehouse job, the fire pump disconnect carries a padlock through the closed-position hasp and 1 in. letters reading FIRE PUMP DISCONNECT. If a service call finds one tripping, the answer is to find the fault — not to add GFPE or downsize the device. The trap answers come from ordinary motor practice: size the device at 125% of full load, add GFPE 'for safety,' or pick a disconnect that locks open. Fire pump rules reverse all three — carry locked-rotor current indefinitely, no ground-fault protection of equipment, and lockable in the closed position. Fire pump disconnect lockable only in the open position — it must lock in the closed position. GFPE breaker feeding the fire pump controller — ground-fault protection of equipment is not applied to this circuit. Disconnect marked with a label maker in 1/2 in. letters — permanent marking, 1 in. minimum. Overcurrent device sized to full-load current and tripping on locked rotor — it must carry locked-rotor current indefinitely. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Transformers — dedicated and oversized
x: Transformers that sit between the system supply and the fire pump controller follow this section, not ordinary transformer practice. • Sizing (695.5(B)): not less than 125% of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motor loads, plus 100% of the fire-pump accessory equipment the transformer supplies. • Dedicated, with one door (695.5(C)): only a feeder-source transformer covered by 695.5(C) may also supply loads not directly associated with the fire pump system. • Protection (695.5(B)): primary overcurrent protection is sized to carry indefinitely the sum of the locked-rotor currents of the fire pump and pressure-maintenance motors, plus the full-load current of the accessory equipment — and no secondary OCPD is permitted. The transformer protection is not allowed to become the weak link that stops the pump. In a fire, the pump motor may stall or start against a locked rotor and sit there drawing locked-rotor current. Ordinary protection would trip to save the transformer — and the building loses its water. This section inverts the priority: the transformer is oversized, and its primary device is chosen to carry the locked-rotor sum indefinitely, so electricity is never the reason the pump stops. Warehouse job, 480 V three-phase. Nameplates: fire pump motor 96 A, jockey (pressure-maintenance) motor 11 A, accessory equipment 8 A. Transformer sizing: (96 + 11) × 125% = 134 A, plus 8 A at 100% = 142 A — about 118 kVA, so a 150 kVA unit. The controller submittal lists locked-rotor currents of 578 A and 66 A: the primary device must carry 578 + 66 + 8 = 652 A indefinitely, and there is no secondary breaker to 'correct.' If existing work shows building loads tapped off a fire pump transformer, report it — do not add Sharma loads to it, and do not re-size its protection to ordinary 450.3 sizing. The exam trap is Table 450.3 thinking: size the primary at 125% and add a secondary main for good measure. Both moves fail here — the primary must carry the locked-rotor sum indefinitely, and a secondary OCPD is not permitted at all. The second trap is tapping the 'spare capacity' for a lighting panel: only a 695.5(C) feeder-source transformer may carry other loads. Secondary overcurrent device installed on a fire pump transformer — 695.5(B) does not permit one. Primary protection sized per 450.3, too small to carry the locked-rotor sum of the pump and jockey motors indefinitely. Lighting or HVAC panel tapped from a dedicated fire pump transformer that is not a 695.5(C) feeder-source transformer. Transformer sized at 100% of the motor full-load currents, with the 125% factor of 695.5(B) never applied. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Voltage drop — 15% starting, 5% running
x: Article 695 has one of the few mandatory voltage-drop rules in the NEC — most voltage-drop text elsewhere is only a recommendation. This one is a calculation rule with two limits, and both are checked at the fire pump controller: • (A) Starting: the voltage at the controller's line terminals must not drop more than 15% below normal (controller-rated) voltage while the motor is starting. • (B) Running: the voltage at the controller's load terminals must not drop more than 5% below the motor's voltage rating while the motor runs at 115% of its full-load current. Conductors run under 695.6(B) have to satisfy both tests on top of their ampacity floor. Passing the ampacity table is not enough — on a long pump run, the starting test is usually the one that sizes the wire. A fire pump that cannot start is a sprinkler system with no water behind it. Locked-rotor inrush drags the voltage down hard; if the dip is too deep the motor stalls or the controller drops out, and the pump never comes up to pressure while the building burns. The running limit protects the motor itself: a motor held at low voltage under load overheats and can fail mid-fire. Warehouse job outside Ocala: the fire pump room sits about 350 ft from the service, so the feeder is long. The controller is rated 480 V, so the starting floor is 85% — 408 V at the controller's line terminals during the start. The motor is rated 460 V, so running at 115% of full-load current the load terminals must hold at least 95% — 437 V. The crew sizes the run for ampacity first, then runs the starting check; on this length the starting check wins and the conductors go up a size. Nobody on the job 'fixes' a failed check by swapping in a bigger breaker — the fix is copper. The trap is reaching for the familiar numbers from 210.19 and 215.2 — 3% on a branch circuit, 5% total. Those are informational-note recommendations for ordinary work, not the fire pump rule, and they measure the wrong event. On a 695.7 question the pair is 15% starting and 5% running, checked at the controller, with the running check made at 115% of full-load current — not at nameplate full load. Feeder sized from the ampacity table only; no starting voltage-drop calculation for a long pump run. Running drop checked at nameplate full-load current instead of 115% of full-load current. Voltage drop measured (or calculated) at the service instead of at the controller terminals. Conductors meet the 695.6(B) ampacity floor but the starting dip pulls the controller below 85% of its rating. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 695.7: Fire pump voltage drop was rebuilt around the fire pump installation standard's limits: 15 percent starting, 5 percent running, with two starting carve-outs that need a proven generator start. Starting (695.7(A)): the controller's line terminals must hold at least 85 percent of the controller's rated voltage. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Emergency systems — the life-safety tier
x: Article 700 covers backup power that the law classes as emergency: power for getting people out and keeping them alive, such as egress lighting, exit signs, fire alarm and similar life-safety loads. A governmental agency having jurisdiction decides that a system is emergency; the owner does not get to choose the label. Emergency power has to be there fast — available within 10 seconds of the normal supply failing (700.12) — the wiring is kept completely apart from normal wiring, and the system is tested and documented. If life safety does not depend on it, you are probably in Article 701 or 702 instead. When a building is full of people and the normal power dies, the emergency system is what lights the way out and keeps the alarm talking. If it starts late, shares a raceway that a fault takes out, or was never tested, the failure shows up at the worst possible moment. Article 700 is strict because the loads are not conveniences — they are the evacuation itself. A single-story daycare in Ocala: the fire marshal requires the egress lighting, exit signs and fire alarm to stay up on generator power, so those loads are Article 700 work before anyone picks gear. Sharma's scope: a Siemens emergency panel fed through listed transfer equipment, the generator carrying the emergency load within 10 seconds, emergency raceways marked as emergency at intervals of 25 ft or less, and no normal-power conductors in the same raceways. The same generator also backs the kitchen refrigerator — that part is Article 702, wired separately, and it never lands on the emergency panel. The trap answer is that the owner, the GC, or the size of the generator decides a system is 'emergency.' It does not. A governmental agency having jurisdiction applies the Article 700 label; a big generator feeding a homeowner's refrigerator is still Article 702. Second trap: landing an optional load on the emergency panel 'because there was space' — emergency branch circuits carry emergency loads only. Emergency and normal conductors sharing a raceway outside the transfer equipment — emergency wiring stays independent (700.10). Emergency raceways, boxes and enclosures not marked as emergency, or the marking intervals skipped. Optional loads — receptacles, comfort HVAC — landed on the emergency panel because there was space. No written test record: the emergency system was never proven under load, and nothing is documented. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 700.11: New 700.11 sets wiring rules for emergency lighting run on Class 2 power: mark it, keep it apart from other Class 2 cabling, and protect it from damage. Emergency Class 2 wiring now needs physical protection: raceway, cable tray, Type MC or Type AC cable (700.11(D)). • 700.24: Only luminaires that go into emergency mode because an outside control signal tells them to must be emergency listed. A standard fixture fed through a listed emergency control device doesn't. A luminaire that responds to an outside control input and goes to emergency mode when normal power fails must be listed for emergency use. • 700.27: New 700.27: a device that feeds Class 2 emergency lighting with both power and control, like a PoE switch, has to carry an emergency lighting control device listing. A device sending Class 2 power and control signals together to emergency lighting must be listed for that job, as an emergency lighting control device.
