FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Tests and maintenance — emergency systems
x: An emergency system is not finished when it is wired. 700.3 builds testing and maintenance into the installation itself: • (A) Acceptance testing: the AHJ conducts or witnesses a test of the complete system when the installation is finished, and periodically afterward. • (B) Periodic testing: the system is tested periodically on a schedule the AHJ approves, so it stays in proper operating condition. • (C) Battery systems: where battery systems or unit equipment are involved, periodic maintenance is required. • (D) Written record: a written record of the tests and maintenance has to be kept. • (E) Testing under load: means has to be provided to test the system under its maximum anticipated load. The manufacturer instructions and industry standards fill in the details of how the equipment is maintained, but the NEC rule the inspector enforces is simple: test it, maintain it, and prove it on paper. Emergency gear sits idle for months and is expected to work perfectly in the first seconds of the worst day. Batteries sulfate, fuel goes stale, transfer switches stick, and a system that is never tested under load fails silently: nobody finds out until the lights are already out and people are on the stairs. Scheduled testing with a written record is what turns a dormant installation into a proven system. At turnover on a Lake Nona outpatient clinic, Sharma left the owner a test binder, not just keys: the results of the AHJ-witnessed acceptance test, the periodic test schedule the AHJ approved, and the battery maintenance log with the first entries filled in. When the inspector asked how the system would be proven a year later, the answer was the binder — dates, loads, and signatures — not a promise that somebody would get around to it. The trap answer is that testing is a one-time event the contractor performs alone at startup and reports afterward. 700.3(A) puts the AHJ in the acceptance test, conducting it or witnessing it, and (B) keeps the testing going on a schedule the AHJ approves. A system with no periodic testing and no written record is not a finished emergency system, however neatly it was wired. No written record of tests and maintenance available at the acceptance inspection. Acceptance test never conducted or witnessed by the AHJ — the contractor 'tested it last week' on his own. Generator exercises with no load transfer and no log; the first real transfer happens during a storm outage and fails. Battery system never maintained — dead starting batteries found at the periodic test. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 700.3: Commissioning of the emergency system now has to be done or witnessed by the AHJ, and the hookup point for a temporary generator must be outdoors and fully labeled. The AHJ (authority having jurisdiction) has to commission the whole emergency system, or witness it, at startup and periodically after that (700.3(A)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Capacity and rating — emergency systems
x: Emergency equipment has to be suitable for the fault current available where it connects — gear that cannot safely carry or interrupt the fault it may see does not belong on a life-safety system. The system also has to have enough capacity for its emergency load, figured under Article 220 or by another method the AHJ approves. • Capacity means every emergency load that operates at the same time, carried together. • There is no user-selects-the-load shortcut here, the way there is for a manual optional standby system. On an emergency system the loads are fixed by the life-safety design, not picked at the switch. • Selective coordination of the emergency overcurrent devices is a separate requirement, covered at 700.32. When the normal source fails, the emergency system is the only thing between the occupants and a dark stairwell. Gear that fails under fault current, or a source that sags because the load outgrew the calculation, turns a power outage into an evacuation problem. The capacity and rating rules make the system prove on paper, before the emergency, that it can carry every life-safety load at once and survive the worst fault at its terminals. Take a two-story professional building in Winter Garden where the AHJ classes the egress system as emergency. The emergency loads are egress lighting at 6.4 kVA, exit signs at 0.5 kVA and the fire alarm system at 0.9 kVA — 7.8 kVA that all runs together, with nothing the user can shed. Run the Article 220 calculation before anyone promises a generator size, and check the fault-current rating on the transfer gear against the service: the marked rating has to cover the fault current available where the gear connects. If the quoted generator cannot carry the 7.8 kVA, that conversation happens at the quote, not at the first outage. The trap is sizing the emergency source the way a manual optional standby system is sized — letting the user pick which loads run and adding up only those. Article 700 has no load-picking option: capacity covers every emergency load that operates together. The second trap is checking only capacity and forgetting the rating half of the section; the equipment also has to be suitable for the available fault current. Transfer equipment installed with a short-circuit rating below the available fault current at the service. Generator sized from a load list the owner picked, with emergency loads left off the calculation. No Article 220 calculation, and no AHJ-approved method, on file for the emergency load. Emergency transfer gear found feeding non-emergency loads added after the original installation. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 700.4: Emergency capacity now has to cover transients and rapid load swings, and new rules spell out when an emergency source can run in parallel with the normal source or other emergency sources. Size the emergency system for all loads that run together, including rapid load swings and transients like motor starting (700.4(A)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Transfer equipment — emergency systems
x: 700.5 sets the bar for transfer equipment on an emergency system — the gear that moves life-safety loads from the normal source to the emergency source. • It must be automatic, listed and marked for emergency use, and approved by the AHJ. • It must be built and installed so the emergency source and the other sources cannot be connected together by accident. • An automatic transfer switch must be electrically operated and mechanically held — it stays on the source it is on; it does not drift or drop out. • Reconditioned transfer switches are not allowed on an emergency system. • The gear may feed only emergency loads. Standby and optional loads ride on their own equipment. • Meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted for emergency use — a device that is fine on a 702 dwelling job does not cross over to a 700 job. • Documentation, 700.5(E): the transfer equipment short-circuit rating is field marked on the outside of the gear. The documentation rule of 700.5(E) carries no dwelling exception — unlike 702.5(C) — so the rating is marked in dwellings too. Emergency loads are the ones that get people out of a dark, smoke-filled building. A transfer switch that can parallel the generator with the utility backfeeds a line the utility crew believes is dead. Gear that is merely big enough, but not identified for emergency use, has not been evaluated for this duty — and a switch that fails on the one transfer that matters leaves the egress lights dark. Small medical office in Kissimmee, 200 A service: the supplier quotes a meter-mounted transfer device because it is fast to install. It is rejected before rough-in — meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted for emergency use, full stop. The job gets a Siemens 200 A automatic transfer switch listed and marked for emergency use (S-02), and before the inspector arrives the crew confirms the short-circuit rating is field marked on the outside of the enclosure, where 700.5(E) wants it — the plans show 22 kA of available fault current, and the marked rating has to cover it. S-02 applies to gear Sharma furnishes: new transfer equipment is Siemens. Listing and emergency marking still govern — brand never replaces either one. The trap answer is that any listed transfer switch can serve an emergency system if its ampere rating is large enough. Rating is not the test — the switch must be listed and marked for emergency use. The second trap swaps the dwelling rules: 702.5(C) carries a dwelling documentation exception; 700.5(E) does not. Transfer switch listed for standby use installed on emergency loads — no emergency-use marking. Meter-mounted transfer switch serving a 700 emergency system. Reconditioned automatic transfer switch installed on an emergency job. Transfer equipment short-circuit rating not field marked on the outside of the gear (700.5(E)). Standby or optional loads landed on the emergency transfer equipment. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 700.5: When a single feeder carries the emergency loads, redundant transfer equipment or a bypass-isolation transfer switch is now required, so maintenance on the transfer gear doesn't kill emergency power. One feeder supplying the emergency loads now means redundant transfer equipment or a bypass-isolation transfer switch is required (700.5(D)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Signs — emergency sources
x: A sign at the service equipment tells responders and electricians what kind of on-site emergency source the building has and where it is. Nobody should have to hunt through a building during an outage to learn that a second source exists. The sign sits at the service equipment and states two things: • The type of on-site emergency source • Where that source is located It has to be permanent and legible, and it is a different sign from the panel directory — the directory says which loads are emergency; this sign says a second source exists and where to find it. Where the source has its own disconnecting means away from the service, the sign at the service is what lets a responder find and kill both sources. An emergency source is a second way for the building to be live. A firefighter or an electrician who kills the service and stops there can still meet an energized panel fed from a generator out back. The sign at the service equipment is the one place everyone looks first, so that is where the code puts the warning: a second source exists, this is what it is, and this is where you go to shut it down. Small medical office in Kissimmee: the emergency generator sits on a pad behind the building, about 60 ft from the service, with its own disconnect at the unit. Letter the sign before final inspection — type of source and where it is: GENERATOR, REAR PAD. Then stand at the service and check that a stranger could walk straight to the source from the words on it, and check the wording against the actual disconnect location before you call the job done. A sign that says 'generator' but not where the generator is has not finished this section's job. The trap answer puts the source information on the panel directory inside the emergency panel. Wrong sign, wrong place: 700.7 wants the sign at the service equipment, where a responder goes to kill power, and it states the type and location of the source. The directory only helps someone who has already found the panel. No sign at the service equipment on a building with an on-site emergency generator. Sign says 'GENERATOR' with no location — the responder still has to hunt for it. Paper label taped to the panel, faded and peeling. The sign must be permanent and legible. Sign names the source type, but the generator was moved during the job and the sign was never updated. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Surge protection — emergency systems
x: Every emergency system switchboard and panelboard has to have a listed surge protective device. This is a flat requirement of the article, not an upsell and not something to value-engineer out. The device has to be listed, and it is installed in or on the switchboard or panelboard it protects, connected the way its listing and the manufacturer's instructions direct. • Short, straight leads matter: a surge device works through its connection, and a long coiled lead-in adds impedance exactly where the surge arrives. • A failed or end-of-life SPD that nobody notices leaves the panel unprotected while looking complete — which is why the device's status indication belongs on the 700.3 test-and-maintenance rounds. Florida lightning and utility switching throw surges onto service conductors every storm season. The emergency panel feeds the loads that protect life — egress lighting, exit signs, fire alarm — and those loads are electronic. One surge through an unprotected emergency board can kill the system on the day it is needed, and a silently dead SPD gives the same result behind a normal-looking panel. The rule puts a listed clamp on every board and a status check on the maintenance rounds. Small medical office in Lakeland: the emergency switchboard and one downstream emergency panelboard each get a listed SPD on the material list — two boards, two devices, no exception for the smaller panel. Each SPD mounts on the board it protects, with its leads kept as short and straight as the enclosure allows, and its status indicator goes on the 700.3 test log. The normal-power panels on the same job are a different conversation — 700.8 speaks only to the emergency system. The trap is protecting the emergency switchboard and calling it done, because the surge 'hits the first board anyway.' Section 700.8 names switchboards and panelboards — every downstream emergency panelboard needs its own listed SPD. The other wrong answer is the unlisted device off the truck: the section's word is listed, and an unlisted SPD is a write-up, not protection. Emergency panelboard with no SPD — only the switchboard was protected. Unlisted surge device installed on an emergency panelboard. SPD leads run long and coiled in the gutter, adding impedance ahead of the device. SPD status indicator failed and never caught — no 700.3 test or maintenance record. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wiring — emergency systems stay identified and apart
x: Emergency wiring is identified as emergency all the way through: • Boxes, enclosures, transfer switches, generators and panels are permanently marked as emergency. • Emergency raceways and cables are marked as emergency at intervals not exceeding 25 ft (700.10(A)(2)) — the interval is concrete, not a judgment call. • Emergency conductors stay out of enclosures, raceways and cables that carry nonemergency wiring, with only narrow exceptions such as inside transfer equipment. • Emergency receptacles are identified by a distinctive color or marking. And 700.10(D) adds fire protection for emergency feeders in the larger installations it covers: assembly occupancies of 1000 or more persons, buildings over 75 ft high, and educational occupancies with more than 300 occupants. There the feeder is protected by a listed electrical circuit protective system, mineral-insulated cable, concrete encasement, or an approved sprinkler-protected space, as the subsection conditions state. In a fire, the emergency system is the last wiring still expected to work — it runs the egress lights and the alarm while everything else is failing. Marking keeps the next electrician from killing it by accident during a remodel, and separation plus fire protection keep a fault or a fire in the normal wiring from taking the emergency wiring down with it. Mark it as you install it, not at trim-out from memory. On a Florida church assembly job, the emergency raceway down a 100 ft corridor gets its EMERGENCY marks as the pipe goes up — at intervals of 25 ft or less, that is a mark at least every fourth stick, with no measuring arguments later. If a normal circuit and an emergency circuit want the same raceway, stop — that is the exact mix this section exists to prevent. The trap answer marks the raceway 'where visible' or 'at each end.' 700.10(A)(2) sets the interval: not exceeding 25 ft. The second trap shares one raceway between emergency and normal conductors 'because they are taped apart inside' — separation is the rule, and tape is not an exception. Emergency raceway marked at the ends only — nothing for 60 ft of corridor (the limit is 25 ft). Emergency and normal conductors sharing one raceway 'to save pipe.' Emergency receptacle a plain white device with no distinctive color or marking. Emergency feeder in a 1000-seat assembly occupancy with no 700.10(D) fire protection. Transfer switch and generator not permanently marked as emergency equipment. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Sources of power — available in 10 seconds
x: When the normal supply fails, emergency power has to be available within 10 seconds. The article lists the permitted kinds of sources, from storage batteries and generator sets to a separate service and unit equipment, and it sets conditions for each one. Engine-driven sources carry on-site fuel rules, battery sources carry a minimum run-time duty at close to full voltage, and the equipment has to be located and designed so one fire, flood or act of vandalism is less likely to kill both supplies at once. Two numbers carry most of the field weight: • A storage battery used as the emergency source has to carry the emergency load for at least 1-1/2 hours without its voltage dropping below 87-1/2 percent of nominal — a battery that fades at 40 minutes is not a 700 source, whatever its amp-hour label says. • An internal-combustion prime mover requires an on-premises fuel supply sufficient for not less than 2 hours of full-demand operation. The fuel plan is part of the source itself: it has to be there when the generator is, sized for the run the design requires, not improvised after the outage starts. Emergency loads are the loads people need to get out of a dark building: egress lighting, exit signs, the fire alarm. Ten seconds is about how long a crowd stays calm in the dark. The battery and fuel duties exist because a source that starts and then dies at 40 minutes strands everyone mid-event. The source is not just the machine — it is the machine plus everything it needs to keep running. The 10-second clock is the design test. Ask how the source starts, how fast load lands on it, and where its fuel or charge comes from before you argue about brands. Worked check on the battery duty: a battery string nameplated at 24 V nominal must still be holding at least 21 V (87.5 percent of 24) at the end of a 90-minute full-load run. If the acceptance test did not run the clock and read the voltage, the duty is unproven. Run the same discipline on fuel: sight the on-site supply before final and confirm it covers 2 hours at full demand, not just the weekly test. The trap answer sizes the battery by its amp-hour label: '200 Ah is plenty.' 700.12 never asks what the label says. It asks what the battery still delivers at the end of 90 minutes: the full emergency load, with voltage at or above 87-1/2 percent of nominal. A battery that fades at 40 minutes fails, whatever the label claims. Battery acceptance test ran 15 minutes and stopped. The duty is 1-1/2 hours at full load with voltage held at 87-1/2 percent of nominal or better. Generator installed with a near-empty tank and no on-premises fuel supply for 2 hours of full-demand operation. Normal and emergency sources arranged so one fire or flood takes out both supplies at once. Transfer scheme that lands the emergency load well past 10 seconds after the normal supply fails. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 700.12: The emergency-source microgrid rule now covers any microgrid, not just dc microgrids, and spells out how designated emergency sources must stay protected when other sources fail. Sources set aside for emergency use can now join a microgrid of any type, ac or dc (700.12(G)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Loads on emergency branch circuits
x: Emergency branch circuits feed emergency loads only. A circuit that exists to keep egress lighting and exit signs alive does not pick up convenience loads because there was spare capacity on paper. • Emergency loads are the life-safety loads classed as emergency by the governmental agency having jurisdiction: egress lighting, exit signs, fire alarm and similar loads. • General receptacles, office and task lighting, comfort equipment and break-room appliances are not emergency loads, even when the generator is big enough to carry them. • The limit is about what the load is, not about how much room is left on the circuit or in the panel. Emergency wiring is identified as emergency as it runs through the building (700.10(A)), so a load that does not belong shows up on the panel schedule before it shows up in the field. The emergency source is sized, fueled and tested for one known list of life-safety loads. Every convenience load added to an emergency circuit steals capacity and run time from that list. The theft shows up at the worst moment: during a real outage, with the building occupied, the source overloads or runs short while people are still on the stairs. Small medical office in Ocala: a Siemens emergency panel beside the normal panel, with six 20 A branch circuits carrying exit signs, egress lighting over the corridor and stairs, and the fire alarm. During the fit-out, a receptacle for the break-room coffee maker got landed on a spare emergency breaker because it was close. Walk the emergency panel schedule load by load. Anything that is not an emergency load comes off, even if the generator is big enough. The coffee-maker circuit moved to the normal panel before final. The trap answer is: the generator has capacity to spare, so one more receptacle circuit on the emergency panel is fine. 700.15 does not ration emergency circuits by capacity. It rations them by load type. If the load is not an emergency load, it does not go on an emergency branch circuit, however big the source is. Convenience receptacle circuit landed on the emergency panel during a fit-out. Normal corridor lighting mixed onto an emergency branch circuit, so the emergency circuit feeds a non-emergency load. Emergency panel schedule lists loads that were never installed, and installed loads that are not listed. Spare emergency breaker used for a later tenant load without re-checking the emergency load list. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Emergency illumination — no single failure leaves a space dark
x: 700.16 covers emergency illumination: the means-of-egress lighting, the illuminated exit signs, and every other luminaire specified as necessary to get people out. One rule drives the whole section — design for a single failure: • The failure of any single illumination source must not leave a space that requires emergency illumination in total darkness. One dead lamp, one dead ballast, one dead driver — the space stays lit. • In practice that means two sources covering the same egress space, interleaved so either one alone keeps the path visible. • Control devices on the emergency system must be listed for use in emergency systems. • Where discharge lighting such as HID is the sole source of normal illumination, the emergency system must operate until normal illumination is restored, because those lamps are slow to restrike. • Emergency illumination is also required in the area of an indoor service or feeder disconnecting means. People leave a building in the dark, in smoke, in a hurry. If one failed lamp turns an exit corridor black, the crowd slows, trips and piles up at the door. The single-failure rule buys light that survives its own weakest part, and the disconnect-area rule means the electrician working the gear in an outage is not doing it blind. Trim-out on a dental office in Ocala. The exit corridor gets five LED luminaires on the emergency system, fed alternately from two sources, so fixtures 1, 3 and 5 answer to one and 2 and 4 to the other. At the acceptance test we kill one source and walk the corridor: dimmer over the dead fixture, lit end to end. The electrical room gets its own emergency luminaire over the service disconnect, and the waiting room's exit signs ride the same system. The trap answer is 'every fixture is on an emergency circuit, so the space is covered.' 700.16 does not count circuits or fixtures — it counts sources. A short exit passageway lit by one luminaire on an emergency circuit still goes totally dark when that one lamp or driver dies, and that is exactly what the section forbids. One emergency luminaire alone in an exit passageway — a single dead lamp or driver leaves the space in total darkness. Corridor emergency fixtures all fed from one source, so one failure blacks out the egress path. No emergency illumination in the area of the indoor service disconnecting means. Emergency loads switched through a control device not listed for use in emergency systems. HID high-bays are the only normal lighting and the emergency system drops out before the lamps can restrike. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Branch-circuit emergency lighting transfer switch (700.25)
x: 700.25 covers one device: the branch-circuit emergency lighting transfer switch. Where emergency lighting is served from a branch circuit, a listed transfer switch at the branch-circuit level is the device that moves that lighting load from the normal branch circuit to an emergency branch circuit when normal power fails, so the egress lighting does not depend on an upstream decision. • The transfer happens out on the lighting circuit, not back at the service or at the main transfer switch. • The loads it may transfer are emergency lighting loads on branch circuits rated not more than 20 A. • The device is listed as transfer equipment. An automatic load control relay (700.26) is a different device: it can force emergency lights on, but it is not permitted to transfer a load between two sources. It is a narrow, listed-device rule — the switch, its listing and its wiring follow the printed section and the design documents. Egress lighting has to come on when normal power dies — including when only the local lighting circuit fails. If the main transfer switch is the only path, one tripped branch breaker can leave a stairwell in the dark while the generator runs outside. Putting a listed transfer device out on the branch circuit moves the decision to the circuit that actually failed. Emergency-system design is engineered work. If a plan shows branch-circuit transfer switches for the egress lighting in a small Orlando office corridor, land them exactly as the drawings and the device listing say: normal feed in, emergency feed in, load out to the corridor lights. Flag any field change to the designer — do not re-feed egress lighting on your own call, and do not substitute a load control relay for a transfer switch. They are different devices with different listings, and only one of them may move a load between sources. The trap answer treats the automatic load control relay as a small transfer switch. It is not. The ALCR (700.26) bypasses the local controls to force lights on from the emergency circuit; only the listed branch-circuit emergency lighting transfer switch (700.25) may move the load from the normal branch circuit to the emergency branch circuit. Automatic load control relay installed where the load had to transfer between the normal and emergency sources — an ALCR is not transfer equipment (700.26). Branch-circuit transfer switch moving emergency lighting on a branch circuit rated over 20 A. Transfer device with no listing used as a branch-circuit emergency lighting transfer switch; the switch must be listed transfer equipment (UL 1008). Egress lighting re-fed from a different circuit in the field than the drawings show, with no word to the designer. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Selective coordination — emergency systems
x: Every overcurrent device in an emergency system has to selectively coordinate with all supply-side overcurrent protective devices. Selective coordination means that for any fault the system can deliver, only the device closest to the fault opens: the branch device clears a branch fault while the feeder and service devices stay closed. • The coordination has to hold across the full range of overcurrents available at each point, not just at one fault level. • A licensed professional engineer or another qualified person selects the devices and performs the coordination design. • The coordination documentation has to be available to the people who design, install, inspect, maintain, and operate the system. That is why a breaker swap or a settings change on an emergency system is an engineering event, not a parts swap. An emergency system exists for the worst ten minutes of a building's life: a fire, a blackout, people feeling their way down the stairs. If a fault on one egress-lighting branch trips the emergency main instead of its own branch device, the whole building goes dark at the exact moment the system was installed to prevent. Selective coordination keeps a local fault local, so exit signs, fire alarm, and the rest of the egress lighting stay alive while the faulted branch is isolated. On a small medical office in Winter Park with a generator feeding a Siemens emergency distribution panel, the coordination study called out specific breaker frames and trip settings at the main, the feeder, and each branch. When the specified branch breaker was back-ordered, the crew did not substitute a same-ampere breaker from stock: a different trip curve can erase the coordination the study proved. The substitute waited for the engineer's written approval, and the study, device list, and settings went into the job record, where the owner and the AHJ can ask for them. The trap answer is that devices coordinate because their ampere ratings step down in size — a big main feeding a smaller feeder feeding a small branch breaker. Rating steps alone prove nothing. 700.32 requires the devices to be selected so that only the device protecting the faulted circuit opens, across the full range of overcurrents, and a qualified person has to design it and document it. No coordination study or device documentation on site at final inspection — 700.32 makes the documentation part of the installation. Breaker swapped for a same-ampere unit with a different trip curve during construction, with no engineering review. A branch fault on one egress circuit trips the emergency feeder device and darkens the whole floor during the acceptance test. Trip settings changed in the field to stop nuisance tripping, with the study never updated. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 700.32: Selective coordination on emergency systems now has to be rechecked after any overcurrent device replacement and after any change to the system. New 700.32(B): replace an emergency overcurrent device and coordination has to be reevaluated. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Legally required standby systems — the middle tier
x: Article 701 covers standby power that a law, code or AHJ requires, but that is not classed as emergency. These systems back up loads that aid firefighting and rescue, control health hazards, or keep ventilation, smoke removal, sewage, communications and similar loads running so an emergency does not get worse. They sit below Article 700 in priority: a 700 load always outranks a 701 load on a shared source. If nobody with authority required the system, it is not 701 — it is optional standby under 702. • Speed: the power has to be available within 60 seconds of losing normal power — slower than 700's 10 seconds, but automatic, not “someone will start it eventually” (701.12). • Capacity: the system carries its legally required loads; it may also carry 700 or 702 loads only with the capacity for them, or with automatic selective load pickup and shedding doing the sorting (701.4). • Transfer equipment follows the 700 discipline: automatic, listed, approved, and marked for its short-circuit duty; reconditioned and meter-mounted transfer gear stay out (701.5). • Wiring is the relaxed part: 701 wiring may share raceways and boxes with general wiring — the strict separation rule belongs to 700 (701.10). The middle tier exists because some loads are too important to leave to chance but are not egress life-safety loads: a sewage lift station that overflows into a Florida waterway, smoke-removal fans, a health-hazard process. If those loads wait for a portable generator and a long cord, the emergency they were meant to contain gets worse while everyone watches. The law required the backup, so the code makes it automatic, sized and tested — not a promise in a drawer. Picture a Marion County clubhouse where the county requires the sewage lift station and the smoke-control fans to stay up on an outage. That paperwork makes it 701, not 702: the generator and automatic transfer gear get sized for those loads, the power has to be on within 60 seconds, and — unlike a 700 job — the 701 feeders may share raceways with the general wiring on the way to the pumps. The egress lighting in the same building stays Article 700 and keeps its own separated wiring; one building can hold both tiers, and mixing their rules is the classic fail. The trap answer treats “legally required” as the formal name for emergency power and wires it all like 700 — or the reverse, treating it as a 702 convenience job. Both are wrong. 701 is its own tier: 60 seconds, not 10; wiring may share raceways, where 700.10 demands separation; and the classification comes from the requiring paperwork, not from how important the load feels. 701 loads wired and labeled as emergency (700) — or the reverse — because nobody read the requiring paperwork. Generator sized for the 701 loads, then 702 convenience loads added with no capacity check and no load shedding. Source that needs five minutes of cranking and warm-up to accept load, installed on a 60-second tier. 700 and 701 wiring methods swapped: 700 circuits sharing raceways with general wiring, so the 700.10 separation is lost. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 701.4(C): Made modifications to the title of Section 701.4(C), which now simply addresses load management requirements • 701.4(D): Added language that now identifies the two different types of parallel operation, normal and alternate sources, of legally required systems in new Section 701.4(D). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Transfer equipment — legally required standby
x: Transfer equipment for a legally required standby system is held to a tighter standard than the same hardware on an optional standby job: • It has to be automatic, listed and marked for legally required standby use, and approved by the AHJ. • It has to keep the standby source from ever being interconnected with the normal source by accident — in any operation of the equipment, not just the normal switching sequence. • Automatic transfer switches are electrically operated and mechanically held, so the contacts stay put if control power drops. • Reconditioned transfer switches are not permitted. • Meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted on a 701 system either — that device belongs to 702 only. • The transfer equipment short-circuit rating is field marked on the outside of the gear, where it can be read without opening the enclosure. A legally required standby system carries loads the law says must not stay dark — egress lighting, a fire alarm, a sewage lift station. If the transfer switch can parallel the generator with the utility, or a worn reconditioned switch fails halfway through a transfer, the protected load is the one that dies. Listing, marking and AHJ approval make the switch prove, before the outage, that it was built for this duty. Same discipline as Article 700: check the marking before the gear is ordered, not after it is hung. A charter school in Kissimmee adds a 60 kW standby generator for its legally required loads — egress lighting, fire alarm and the lift station. The switch is a new Siemens automatic transfer switch (S-02), ordered listed and marked for legally required standby use, with its short-circuit rating field marked on the enclosure. A cheaper reconditioned switch, and a meter-mounted switch quoted from a 702 house job, are both rejected at the desk. The 701 system also works to a 60-second availability clock (701.12), so the transfer has to be automatic — nobody is walking to the gear room to throw a handle. S-02 applies to gear Sharma furnishes: new transfer equipment is Siemens, subject to its listing and marking for this use. The trap is treating 701 like 702: reaching for a meter-mounted transfer switch, or a reconditioned automatic switch at a better price. Both are permitted thinking on an optional standby job and both are prohibited here. The second trap is the holding method — the switch must be electrically operated and mechanically held, not electrically held, so a loss of control power cannot drop the contacts mid-event. Transfer switch not listed or marked for legally required standby use. Meter-mounted transfer switch installed on a 701 system — not permitted in Article 701. Reconditioned automatic transfer switch installed on a legally required standby system. Transfer equipment short-circuit rating not field marked on the outside of the gear. Transfer equipment installed without AHJ approval. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wiring — legally required standby may share raceways
x: Unlike emergency wiring, legally required standby wiring is allowed to run in the same raceways, boxes and cabinets as general wiring. The strict separation duty belongs to Article 700: emergency conductors stay out of raceways, boxes and cables that carry nonemergency wiring, with only narrow exceptions, such as inside transfer equipment (700.10). Article 701 carries no such rule. • Importing the 700 separation duty into a 701 job wastes raceways, boxes and labor the Code never asked for. • Forgetting the separation on a 700 job is a violation. • The wiring method follows the classification, so settle which article the system is under before the first raceway goes in. The classification ladder matches the risk. Losing egress lighting in a fire can kill people in minutes, so emergency wiring is protected from faults in ordinary wiring. Legally required standby loads — smoke control, sewage, ventilation — keep an emergency from getting worse, and the Code accepts the shared-raceway risk for them. The law already weighed it; that is why sharing is legal here. Community clubhouse in Marion County, with a sewage lift station and smoke-control fans on a legally required standby system. The standby feeder and the general feeders share the same raceway run out to the pump house. That is legal under 701.10, and it saved a second run. The same building's emergency lighting is Article 700 work, and those conductors stayed in their own raceway, start to finish. Know which article the job is under before you decide how to run the raceways. The wiring method follows the classification, not habit. The trap answer is that all standby wiring must be kept separate from general wiring, just like emergency wiring. That is the Article 700 rule. Under 701.10, legally required standby wiring may occupy the same raceways, boxes and cabinets as general wiring. The reverse answer fails too: sharing on a 700 job because 701 allows it. Emergency conductors found in the same raceway as general wiring — the 701 permission was applied to a 700 system. Standby and general circuits mixed into the emergency raceway, contaminating the emergency run. System reclassed as emergency by the AHJ at plan review; the shared-raceway installation had to be re-run separately. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 701.10: Added a new first-level subdivision (B) and new figure informational notes concerning wiring requirements for legally required standby systems to Section 701.10 FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Sources of power — available in 60 seconds
x: Legally required standby power has to be available within 60 seconds of the normal supply failing — slower than the 10 seconds of Article 700, far faster than a portable generator someone drags out of a garage. The section lists the permitted source types and their conditions, including on-site fuel for engine-driven sources and battery duty where batteries are the source. One source may also carry optional loads only where capacity is truly there, or where automatic pickup and shedding protect the legally required loads first. The battery duty mirrors the emergency tier: a storage battery source has to supply and maintain the legally required load for at least 1-1/2 hours without the voltage falling below 87-1/2 percent of nominal. This section asks two different questions of a battery system — the 60-second availability clock, and the 90-minute endurance duty — and a system can pass one and fail the other. Legally required loads are the ones a law, a code or the AHJ says may not go dark — the building's legal duty to the people inside it. A source that starts late leaves them unprotected in the gap; a battery that fades at 40 minutes fails them in a long outage. Both clocks exist because both failures happen. Annual test at a small medical office in Ocala, with a standby set and a battery string carrying the 701 loads. We time the transfer on a pulled meter: power is available in 42 seconds, inside the 60-second clock. Then the battery gets its turn — it has to hold the legally required load for the full 90 minutes without sagging under 87-1/2 percent of nominal voltage. The optional waiting-room circuits ride the same source only because the shedding relay drops them first. The trap answer gives 701 the 700 clock: 10 seconds. Article 701 allows 60 seconds. The reverse trap catches just as many: a battery that answers instantly but fades at 45 minutes has passed the availability clock and failed the 1-1/2 hour duty. The section grades both. Standby power not available within 60 seconds of the normal supply failing — slow start or slow transfer. Battery source cannot carry the legally required load for 1-1/2 hours, or its voltage sags below 87-1/2 percent of nominal under load. Optional loads connected so they can starve the legally required loads — no capacity, and no automatic pickup and shedding to protect the 701 loads first. Engine-driven source without its required on-site fuel supply. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 701.12(C): Added an informational note at Section 701.12(C) to reference classification information for emergency power supply systems (EPSS) used with legally required standby systems. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Selective coordination — legally required standby
x: Legally required standby overcurrent devices have to selectively coordinate with all supply-side overcurrent protective devices, so a fault on one standby branch opens the device at the fault instead of tripping devices upstream and darkening healthy standby loads with it. • The coordination is selected by a licensed professional engineer or another qualified person engaged primarily in the design, installation, or maintenance of electrical systems. • The selection has to be documented and made available to the people authorized to design, install, inspect, maintain, and operate the system. • Coordination is not required between two devices in series where no loads are connected in parallel with the downstream device. It is the Article 700 duty at 700.32 carried one tier down. Legally required standby loads — egress lighting, smoke control, sewage lift, fire alarm power — exist because a code or the AHJ said the building needs them when the normal source fails. If one branch fault trips the feeder, every one of those loads goes dark together, in exactly the emergency the system was installed for. Coordination keeps the outage at the fault. Same discipline as the emergency tier: this is a study, not a field adjustment. On a Florida school standby job, the coordination selection for the 200 A standby feeder and its 20 A branch devices is made before the gear is released, and the documented selection goes into the job record where the inspector and the owner's maintenance people can reach it. A breaker swapped in the field for a different frame or trip curve is a change to the study, not a parts swap. The trap answer is 'selective coordination is an Article 700 emergency rule only.' 701.32 imposes the same duty on legally required standby systems. The second trap claims the exception backwards: the series exception only helps where no loads are connected in parallel with the downstream device — a normal feeder-and-branch run with loads on it gets no exception. No coordination documentation on the job when the inspector asks for it. Branch breaker swapped for a different trip curve without updating the coordination selection. Coordination claimed by rule of thumb — no licensed PE or qualified person made the selection. Feeder device trips on a branch fault and takes every standby load down with it. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Optional standby systems — home and business generators
x: Article 702 covers standby systems nobody required: the homeowner who wants the fridge, the well pump and a few lights through a Florida outage, or the business protecting product and comfort. Life safety does not depend on these systems, and that single fact is what keeps them out of Articles 700 and 701. The article still regulates them hard where it counts: • Capacity: the system has to carry the loads connected to it, with load management where the design uses it (702.4) • Transfer equipment: listed equipment that can never tie the generator to the utility by accident (702.5) • Signs: a sign at the service equipment says a standby source is on the premises (702.7) • Wiring, and the outdoor generator set rules, fill out the article Portable generators that are never connected to the premises wiring are outside this article. The moment one is connected through an inlet and transfer equipment, 702 is in play. Optional does not mean casual. A standby system connects a second source to a building that utility crews and firefighters expect to go dead when the service opens. A backfeed through a bad transfer setup can put full voltage on a line a crew believes is dead. The capacity, transfer and sign rules are what keep a comfort system from becoming the most dangerous wiring on the property. Most Sharma generator work lives here. Start every quote by sorting the loads into what runs automatically, what the owner will switch by hand, and what never runs on the generator. On a Marion Oaks house with a well, the must-run list reads: fridge 200 VA, well pump 1,800 VA, lights 900 VA, microwave 1,500 VA, TV and network gear 300 VA — 4,700 VA in all. A 6,500 W portable set on an inlet, through Siemens transfer equipment (S-02), carries that list with headroom. The range at 12,000 VA and the dryer at 5,600 VA stay off the generator list entirely. S-02: transfer equipment Sharma furnishes is Siemens. S-09 only enters if the standby work changes the meter/panel layout. Florida hurricane season is why this article earns its keep here — but no Florida amendment relaxes the transfer or sizing rules in this chapter. The AHJ and the printed NEC 2020 govern. The trap is 'standby is standby' — filing every generator under 702. If a governmental agency requires the system, or life safety depends on it, it is not optional: it lands in Article 700 or 701, with their separation, testing and 10-second rules. Article 702 is only for the systems nobody required. Generator backfed into the panel through a dryer receptacle and a double-male cord — no transfer equipment at all. Inlet and transfer equipment installed, but the transfer equipment is not listed, or can tie the generator to the utility (702.5). No sign at the service equipment showing that a standby source is on the premises (702.7). Standby system connected to more load than it can carry (702.4). Transfer switch amp rating matches the service, but its short-circuit rating sits below the available fault current (702.4(A)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Available fault current — optional standby equipment
x: Optional standby equipment has to be suitable for the maximum available short-circuit current at its terminals. That is a different rating from the amp rating. A transfer switch can match the load exactly — 200 A switch on a 200 A service — and still be the wrong switch, because its short-circuit current rating sits below what the service can deliver into a fault. • Get the available fault current before ordering: from the utility, or from the field marking on the service equipment. Other than in dwelling units, service equipment is marked with the maximum available fault current and the date it was figured (110.24). • Compare that number with the short-circuit current rating marked on the transfer equipment, not with its amp rating. • The same duty runs through the rest of the circuit: interrupting ratings (110.9) and the short-circuit current ratings of the components (110.10) must suit the fault current at their terminals. A bolted fault at the switch does not draw load current. It draws everything the utility transformer can push until an overcurrent device clears, and the switch has to survive those cycles without welding its contacts shut or coming apart. A switch that fails closed can also tie the generator to the utility, the one connection transfer equipment exists to prevent. Strip-center tenant in Marion County: 200 A service, standby generator for the coolers and lights. The marking on the service gear read 22,000 A available fault current. The first transfer switch in the quote was a 200 A switch with a 10,000 A short-circuit rating: right amps, wrong fault duty, and it went back. The switch that stayed is rated 22,000 A. Pull the available fault current from the service gear or the utility information and match the transfer equipment rating to it before ordering, not at rough-in. The trap answer matches amps to amps: a 200 A switch on a 200 A service must be the right switch. Amps say what the switch can carry all day. The short-circuit rating says what it can survive for the cycles a fault lasts. 702.4(A) grades the second number. Transfer switch short-circuit rating below the available fault current marked on the service equipment. Switch selected by amp rating only; the fault duty was never checked against the utility figure. Available fault current taken from the generator nameplate only, ignoring the utility side at the line terminals. Fault-current calculation not documented, or not available to the inspector. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: System capacity — the sizing fork in Article 702
x: 702.4(B) is the fork that decides how big an optional standby source has to be, and the fork is the transfer equipment. • Manual transfer, 702.4(B)(1): the user stands at the switch and chooses the load. The source only has to supply the loads intended to be operated at one time — the user is the load management. • Automatic transfer, 702.4(B)(2): nobody is standing there choosing, so the source is sized to the calculated load, figured under Article 220 or by another approved method. It must then either carry the full load the transfer equipment connects, or be paired with automatic load management that limits what gets connected. There is no third branch. "Automatic transfer, partial load, no load management" is the combination this section exists to forbid. Which side of the fork a job is on gets decided on paper, before anything is sized or quoted. A generator sized by optimism fails at the worst moment: the automatic switch transfers the whole house at 2 a.m. in a storm, the air conditioner and the well pump start together, and the undersized source stalls or trips — leaving the house dark and the food warm. The fork forces the sizing question to be answered by who chooses the load, not by what source happens to be on the truck. Two Marion County houses, same week. The first takes a portable 9 kW generator on a manual interlock: the owner's intended loads — refrigerator, well pump, a few lights and the TV — total about 7.5 kW at one time, so the source fits 702.4(B)(1). The second house wants a whole-home automatic switch: the Article 220 calculation comes to 24 kW, so the standby source is a 24 kW unit — or a smaller unit only if listed automatic load management is part of the design. Same street, two different sizes, and the transfer equipment is the whole reason. Exam writers love the middle answer: an automatic transfer switch with a generator sized to "the essential loads only" and no load management. That is not a legal configuration under 702.4(B)(2). With automatic transfer, the exits are the full calculated load or automatic load management — the homeowner's promise to behave is neither. Automatic transfer switch installed with a source sized below the calculated load and no load management. Load management claimed on the permit, but no listed management equipment on the job. Manual-transfer sizing used to justify the source on an automatic system. No Article 220 calculation or approved demand record in the job file for an automatic system. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Manual transfer — the user selects the load
x: Where manual transfer equipment is used, the optional standby system has to be able to supply all the equipment intended to be operated at one time, and the user is permitted to select which loads are connected. That selection is what sets the practical size of the source: a homeowner who will run the fridge, a few lights and the well pump — and leave the range and dryer off — does not need a generator sized for the whole house. • This is the manual-transfer fork of 702.4(B). Its twin, 702.4(B)(2), covers automatic transfer, where nobody stands there choosing: the source either carries the full calculated load or a load-management system does the choosing. A portable source is small, and a house is big. Without a written selection, every outage becomes an argument at the panel — someone adds the range, then the dryer, and the little unit drowns or the breaker does. The intended-load list turns the owner's choice into the design: the source is sized to a promise, and the promise is written down before the storm, not negotiated during it. Lake County house, manual transfer switch, owner's list agreed at the kitchen table: refrigerator 200 VA, well pump 1,800 VA, lights 900 VA, microwave 1,500 VA, TV and network gear 300 VA — 4,700 VA of intended load, all of it allowed to run at once. A 6,500 W portable covers the list with room to spare. The range at 12,000 VA and the dryer at 5,600 VA are not on the list, so they are not counted and not promised. The list goes in the job record, where the owner and the next tech both read the same deal. The trap answer sizes the source from the service calculation or the whole-house load — that is the automatic-transfer thinking of 702.4(B)(2). Under (B)(1) the user selects the loads, so the source must carry the intended list all at once — no more, but also no less: a unit that cannot run the whole list together fails this section. Source sized below the intended-load list — the listed loads cannot all run at once. No written load list in the job record; the owner's selections live in a phone call nobody can check. Range or dryer promised to the owner “if there's room” — loads off the list got sold as standby loads. Manual-transfer job priced and sized from the whole-house calculation — the (B)(2) method on a (B)(1) job. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Automatic transfer — full load, or load management
x: Where automatic transfer equipment is used, 702.4(B)(2) sizes the standby source to the calculated load — figured under Article 220, or by another approved method. For an existing installation, recorded maximum demand is one of the approved routes the code recognizes through 220.87: real metered history instead of a fresh calculation. The system then has to satisfy one of two duties: • Full-load duty: the source carries the entire load the automatic equipment transfers. Nothing is shed and nothing is managed — the source is simply big enough. • Load-management duty: an automatic system manages the connected load, and the source only has to carry the maximum load that management system will actually connect. Loads above that ceiling are shed or locked out by the equipment, not by the owner's good intentions. Pick the duty on paper. The source size, the equipment list and the permit all have to tell the same story. Automatic transfer happens with nobody home to make good choices — the switch moves the whole load the moment the utility drops. If the source cannot carry what the switch connects, the generator overloads and drops everything it was bought to save. Load management is the honest alternative: the equipment, not optimism, decides what runs. Existing house in Ocala going whole-home automatic. The Article 220 calculation says 24 kW, and twelve months of utility demand history — the 220.87 route — backs up sizing from real use instead of the paper worst case. The design claims the load-management duty: a listed management system sheds the second air conditioner and the range, capping the connected load at 16 kW, and a 20 kW Siemens standby source carries it with margin. The management equipment is on the truck and on the permit — a load-management claim with no listed equipment on the job is just a smaller generator and a hope. The trap is using the demand route or the management duty on the wrong job. Recorded maximum demand under 220.87 is a route for existing installations, not new work with no history. And the management duty is not the owner promising to turn things off — if the shedding is not automatic, the source must carry the full transferred load. Automatic system sized to "essential loads" with no load management equipment installed. Load management settings raised after inspection, leaving the source undersized for the connected load. Recorded-demand sizing used on a new installation with no demand history. Source smaller than the maximum load the management system can connect. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Transfer equipment — required, listed, and built to keep sources apart
x: Transfer equipment is required to connect an optional standby source to the premises wiring, and in the 2020 code it has to be listed — a tightening over earlier editions that catches unlisted interlock hardware. • What counts: a listed transfer switch, or a listed interlock arrangement that mechanically keeps the normal source and the standby source from ever being connected at the same time. • One narrow exception: a temporary portable generator connection without transfer equipment, only where maintenance and supervision ensure qualified persons service it and the normal supply is physically isolated by a lockable disconnect or by disconnecting the normal conductors. The four duties that follow it in the section — meter-mounted transfer switches, documentation, inadvertent interconnection, and parallel operation — get their own pages next, in the section's own order. The transfer point is where a generator can kill someone it never meets. If generator power reaches the utility lines, a line worker on a pole blocks away can touch a conductor the utility has grounded and declared dead. Listed transfer equipment is tested to make that connection impossible; an unlisted kit is a promise nobody verified. Marion Oaks house, 200 A Siemens panel, homeowner wants storm backup from a 12 kW portable generator. Sharma's answer is a listed Siemens interlock kit made for that panel and a 50 A inlet: the sliding plate lets the main and the generator breaker be on one at a time, never both. The homeowner's online 'universal' kit, tested only on someone else's panel, stays in its box — no listing, no install. S-02: transfer equipment Sharma furnishes is Siemens, and it still has to carry the listing this section requires. The trap answer is that an interlock kit 'tested to fit' your panel is good enough. Tested is not listed. 702.5 requires transfer equipment to be listed in the 2020 code, and the narrow no-transfer-equipment exception is for temporary portable connections under qualified supervision — not a permanent house hookup. Unlisted interlock kit installed on the panel — no listing mark for the panel it is mounted in. Generator backfed through a dryer receptacle with a male-to-male cord. Transfer equipment wired so the utility and generator can be on together. Permanent portable-generator hookup with no transfer equipment, claimed under the temporary-connection exception. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Meter-mounted transfer switches
x: A transfer switch that mounts in the meter socket — between the utility meter and its enclosure — is allowed for optional standby systems, but only as a listed meter-mounted transfer switch. • Manual operation is the default: a meter-mounted switch is manual unless it is rated in accordance with the automatic-transfer sizing duty of 702.4(B)(2). • The meter socket is not a loophole around generator sizing: automatic transfer still has to meet the same capacity rules as any other automatic switch, sized to the calculated load or paired with automatic load management. • The contrast to remember: Articles 700 and 701 do not permit meter-mounted transfer switches at all. This device exists only in the optional standby world of Article 702. The meter socket is the one point where utility equipment, the service, and the premises wiring all meet, and it was never designed as a switch enclosure. A listed meter-mounted transfer switch is built and tested for that spot: interrupting service current and keeping the generator from ever backfeeding the utility. An unlisted gadget in the socket risks the life of a lineman working a line he was told was dead. For a standby generator at a single-family home in Oviedo, the listed meter-mounted transfer switch kept the job simple: no separate transfer switch on the wall, and manual transfer — the homeowner starts the generator and transfers by hand. Because the switch was manual, the automatic sizing duty of 702.4(B)(2) never came into play. The utility still had to approve the work in its meter socket before the seal was cut, and that approval was separate from the county electrical inspection. The trap answer is 'permitted anywhere a transfer switch is permitted.' Meter-mounted transfer switches are an Article 702-only device: Articles 700 and 701 forbid them outright. The second trap is calling every meter-mounted switch automatic. It is manual unless it carries the rating 702.4(B)(2) demands for automatic operation. Unlisted meter-socket transfer device installed — 702.5(B) requires a listed meter-mounted transfer switch. Meter-mounted switch used on an Article 700 emergency system, where meter-mounted transfer switches are not permitted. Automatic meter-mounted switch installed without the rating the automatic-transfer duty of 702.4(B)(2) requires. Meter seal cut and socket work done without utility approval. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Documentation — short-circuit rating marked on the gear
x: On jobs other than dwelling units, the short-circuit current rating of the transfer equipment has to be field marked on the outside of the equipment. Not inside the door, and not left in the submittal package: on the outside, where the next person to work on the gear sees it. • The marking states the rating the equipment was installed for, so it is read off the equipment data after the 702.4(A) fault-current match is made. • The person maintaining or replacing that gear years later should not need the original submittal to learn what fault duty it was built for. • Dwelling units are the exception in this paragraph. The marking duty here is for other-than-dwelling work. Fault duty is invisible. Two identical-looking switches can carry different short-circuit ratings, and a service upgrade can raise the available fault current years after the switch went in. The outside marking is the one place the installed rating survives lost paperwork, staff changes and repainted enclosures, and it is what an inspector checks against the service marking. It also settles the question at final inspection in seconds: the rating is on the gear, in the open, or the job is not finished. Same strip-center tenant as the fault-current check: once the switch rated 22,000 A was in, the rating went on the outside of the enclosure — short-circuit current rating: 22,000 A — as a durable field marking, and a photo of the finished marking went into the job record. Carry a marker and the rating from the equipment data to every non-dwelling transfer install, and photograph the finished marking for the job record. The trap answer is that the factory nameplate already lists a rating, so nothing has to be added in the field. On other-than-dwelling 702 jobs, 702.5(C) wants the short-circuit current rating field marked on the outside of the equipment, whatever the nameplate inside the door says. No field marking of the short-circuit rating on the outside of non-dwelling transfer equipment. Rating marked inside the enclosure door instead of on the outside. Marking shows the switch amp rating (200 A) instead of its short-circuit current rating. Paper label used for the marking outdoors; illegible within a season. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Inadvertent interconnection — the heart of 702.5
x: 702.5(D) is the paragraph the whole transfer-equipment section hangs on: • Transfer equipment has to be suitable for the use, listed, and designed and installed so that all sources of supply can never be inadvertently interconnected — in any operation of the equipment. • "Any operation" includes the sloppy one nobody planned: a switch left mid-travel, a homeowner flipping breakers in the dark, an interlock installed wrong. • This is the rule that kills backfeeding: a generator pushing power out through the service can energize a utility line that a line crew believes is dead. • The listing requirement in this paragraph is the 2020 change — the unlisted interlock hardware that got by under older editions runs into it now. Backfeed kills line workers. When a generator feeds a house panel without real transfer equipment, its power runs backward through the service and the utility transformer and comes out on the primary side at thousands of volts — on a line the crew has opened and believes is dead. The listed-equipment and never-interconnect rules exist so that no switch position, mistake or half-finished install can ever put the two sources together. A homeowner in Ocala wants a portable-generator inlet for hurricane season on a 200 A Siemens service. Sharma's answer is listed transfer equipment — a listed transfer switch, or listed interlock hardware made for that panel — never a double-ended cord, and never a breaker held off by a zip tie and a label. After the install, the crew tests the finished job through every switch position, not just the normal one: normal, generator, and everything in between, confirming the utility and generator breakers can never be closed together. If the panel cannot take listed hardware, it gets a transfer switch beside it; the inlet alone is not a system. The trap answer is "the two breakers are never on together because we labeled them." Labels and instructions are not transfer equipment. 702.5(D) demands equipment designed and installed so interconnection cannot happen in any operation — a mechanical impossibility built into listed hardware, not a promise written on the panel directory. The second trap is reading the rule as covering only the normal switching sequence; it covers every operation, including the wrong one. Generator inlet wired to a panel with no listed transfer equipment — a backfeed path to the utility. Unlisted breaker interlock hardware installed; 702.5(D) requires listed transfer equipment. Transfer equipment able to parallel the generator with the service in an intermediate switch position. Double-ended (suicide) cord provided as the generator connection method. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Parallel installation — Article 705 takes over
x: Transfer equipment and electric power production systems installed to operate in parallel with the normal source also have to comply with Article 705. • A standby source that only ever replaces the utility is a 702 job: transfer equipment, and no interconnection. • The moment a source is meant to operate alongside the utility, the interconnection rules of Article 705 join the transfer rules. • On a parallel job the two articles are not either/or: 702 governs the transfer, 705 governs the handshake with the live source. A source connected to a live utility system can backfeed conductors, fight the utility's protection, and keep a 'dead' service energized. Article 705 exists for exactly that handshake — where the source may connect, how much current the connection and the busbar may carry, and how the equipment is marked so the next person knows a second source exists. A parallel source wired to transfer rules alone skips every one of those protections. Ask one question on every generator quote: will this source ever run in parallel with the utility? A homeowner in Lake Mary wants a standby set that only takes over in an outage — that is a 702 job, priced and wired as transfer equipment. A small commercial customer who wants the generator to parallel the utility for peak shaving gets a different answer: the same transfer gear, plus an Article 705 interconnection — connection point, busbar and conductor checks, and marking that tells the next electrician a second source exists. Price and wire it as both, or do not sell it as parallel. The trap is treating 702 and 705 as alternatives and picking one. On a parallel installation both apply: 702.5(E) sends you to Article 705 on top of the transfer rules. The reverse trap also fails — a standby source that never operates in parallel does not pick up Article 705 just because a generator is present. Generator installed for parallel operation with no Article 705 interconnection review — no connection-point or busbar check. Parallel-capable source wired as a plain 702 transfer installation. Equipment containing a parallel source left unmarked, so the next electrician has no warning of the second source. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Signs — standby sources, and the power inlet sign
x: Signs close the loop that transfer equipment starts. • At service equipment, a sign identifies the type and location of each on-site optional standby source. • For a house, the sign sits at the 230.85 emergency disconnect and points to the permanently installed standby source disconnect, or to the means to shut down the prime mover. • Where a power inlet is used for a portable generator, a sign at the inlet states which kind of generator system may be connected there: a separately derived (bonded neutral) system only, or a nonseparately derived (floating neutral) system only. Two signs, two different jobs — and the inlet sign cannot be lettered until somebody has checked how the generator's neutral is actually bonded. Standby power makes a building dangerous to anyone who thinks it is dead. A firefighter or the next electrician kills the service and still has a generator holding the panel up. The service sign tells them a second source exists and where to kill it. The inlet sign prevents the quieter mistake: the wrong neutral arrangement at a portable connection, which puts neutral current on grounding paths and defeats ground-fault protection. Marion Oaks house with a portable-generator inlet box on the garage wall. The service sign goes at the outdoor 230.85 emergency disconnect and reads where the standby source disconnect is. Before the inlet sign is lettered, the generator on site is checked: its neutral is bonded at the frame, so the inlet is lettered for a separately derived system only. Had the generator been a floating-neutral model, the same inlet would carry the opposite sign — same box, different words, decided by the machine, not the wall. The common wrong answer letters the inlet sign from the transfer equipment, or copies the sign from the last job. The inlet sign states a property of the generator system — separately derived only, or nonseparately derived only. Letter it for the wrong neutral and the sign itself becomes the hazard, because the next generator that plugs in gets trusted on the strength of it. No sign at the service equipment identifying the standby source and its location. House standby sign placed at the generator instead of at the 230.85 emergency disconnect. Power inlet with no sign stating which generator system may connect. Inlet sign lettered for a floating neutral while the generator's neutral is bonded — the sign lies. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 702.7: Every building except a one- or two-family dwelling now needs the standby source sign at its service, not just commercial and industrial sites. Homes still get theirs at the outdoor emergency disconnect. Every building except a one- or two-family dwelling, apartments included, now gets the sign at the service equipment. In 2020, only commercial and industrial did. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Wiring — optional standby wiring may share raceways
x: Optional standby wiring is allowed to occupy the same raceways, cables, boxes and cabinets as other wiring. That permission is the opposite of the Article 700 rule, where emergency conductors stay independent of nonemergency wiring. • The permission covers the whole run: raceways, cables, boxes and cabinets. • It is one more reason the classification question comes first: the same physical run can be legal under 702 and a violation under 700. • The permission is not a shortcut around the identification, transfer equipment and sign rules elsewhere in this article. It answers only the raceway question. • Sharing the raceway does not merge the systems. The standby circuits still have to be findable later, which is why they stay identified in the panel directory. Optional standby protects property and comfort: the fridge, the well pump and a few lights through a Florida outage. Nobody's escape route depends on it, so the Code does not buy it the expensive protection of separate raceways. The danger Article 702 does police is different — a generator tied to the utility by accident — and that is handled by the transfer equipment rules, not by separation. New slab home in Ocala with a permanently installed standby generator on a 200 A Siemens service. The generator feeder shares the underground run and the panel gutter with the normal circuits.
