That is permitted under 702.10, and it kept the job to one trench. Use the permission, but keep the standby circuits identified in the panel directory so the next electrician knows what the generator feeds: refrigerator, well pump and kitchen lights, marked as standby circuits in the directory. The trap answer is that standby wiring always needs its own raceway, separate from general wiring. That is the emergency rule from Article 700. Under 702.10, optional standby wiring may share raceways, cables, boxes and cabinets with other wiring. The trap cuts both ways: the 702 permission never licenses sharing on a 700 system. Optional standby conductors run inside the emergency raceway on a mixed 700/702 job. Panel directory does not identify which circuits the standby source feeds. Standby system reclassed as emergency by the AHJ; the shared-raceway work had to be separated and re-run. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Outdoor portable generators
x: 702.11 covers the portable generator that lives in the garage and rolls out to the driveway when the power fails. The disconnect relief is exact: • Under 702.11(B), a portable generator rated 15 kW or less, connected through a flanged inlet or other cord-and-plug connection, does not need an additional disconnecting means where its ungrounded conductors serve or pass through a building. • Under 702.11(A), permanently installed generators and portable generators over 15 kW need a readily accessible disconnect per 445.18, within sight of the building. The connection to the house is still through listed transfer equipment and a proper power inlet (702.12(C) covers inlets 100 A and up); a cord through a window to a dryer receptacle is backfeeding, not a connection method. The neutral question decides the transfer equipment: whether the portable set's neutral is bonded to its frame determines whether the transfer switch must switch the neutral, and the generator's documentation — not habit — answers it. Portable generators hurt people two ways: carbon monoxide when a set runs in a garage or too close to openings, and backfeed when a cord puts generator power onto utility lines a lineworker is repairing. These rules keep the set outdoors, make the connection a listed inlet and transfer equipment instead of a suicide cord, and make sure the bigger sets have a real disconnect that someone can reach and see from the building. Hurricane setup on a slab home in Ocala: a 12 kW portable set, a 50 A power inlet on the outside wall, and a listed interlock kit on the Siemens panel inside. At 15 kW or less on a flanged inlet, 702.11(B) asks for no additional disconnect for the generator conductors. Roll the set out clear of windows and doors while it runs — the exhaust is the fast killer, not the outage. Before you choose the transfer equipment, check the set's manual for whether its neutral is bonded to the frame; that answer picks the switch. Label the inlet for the size of set it accepts. The trap: 'Every generator connection needs a disconnecting means at the building.' Not for the small portable — 15 kW or less through a flanged inlet gets the 702.11(B) relief. The reverse trap fails just as many: claiming the same relief for a 22 kW portable. Over 15 kW, the readily accessible disconnect per 445.18, within sight of the building, is required. Generator cord run through a window to a dryer receptacle — backfeeding, with no transfer equipment. 22 kW portable set connected with no readily accessible disconnect within sight of the building. Transfer switch that does not switch the neutral paired with a bonded-neutral generator — the neutral bonding was never checked. Power inlet installed with no label for the size or type of generator system it accepts. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Outdoor generator sets — when a building disconnect is not required
x: 702.12 is about not duplicating a disconnect that already does the job. • For permanently installed generators and portable generators over 15 kW used outdoors, if the generator has a readily accessible disconnect within sight of the building it supplies, no extra disconnect is required at the building — provided that generator disconnect is in accordance with 445.18, and where the generator supply conductors terminate at a disconnecting means in or on the building, that disconnect meets 225.36. • For a portable generator of 15 kW or less connected through a flanged inlet or another cord-and-plug connection, no disconnecting means is required at the building for the ungrounded conductors serving or passing through it. Within sight has a code meaning: visible and not more than 50 ft away. Neither rule removes the transfer-equipment duty in 702.5. A second disconnect nobody needs adds cost and one more thing to maintain, but the relief only works if the generator's own disconnect is genuinely there — reachable in a hurry and close enough to see from the building. The conditions are the safety case: accessible, within sight, and built to the generator and outdoor-feeder rules. Whole-house standby set on a pad outside a Marion Oaks home: the generator's own disconnect is readily accessible and 22 ft from the house, in plain view of it, so no second disconnect goes on the building. The crew still checks the two conditions before relying on that — disconnect per 445.18, and the building disconnect where the supply conductors land meets 225.36. On the next job, a 12 kW portable on a flanged inlet needs no building disconnect for its ungrounded conductors at all. The trap answer is 'outdoor generators never need a building disconnect.' The relief is conditional: over 15 kW it needs the generator disconnect readily accessible and within sight — visible and not more than 50 ft — and per 445.18. The second trap is thinking 702.12 relief waives transfer equipment; 702.5 still applies in full. No disconnect at the building, and the generator's own disconnect is around the corner — not within sight. Generator disconnect locked inside a fenced enclosure, claimed as readily accessible. Building disconnect where generator conductors terminate not rated in accordance with 225.36. Portable generator over 15 kW on a cord connection with no disconnecting means at the building and none within sight at the generator. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Power inlets 100 A and up — listed, with an interlocked disconnect
x: Where a portable generator connects through an inlet rated 100 amps or more, the 2020 code adds two requirements on the inlet equipment. • The equipment must be listed for the intended use. • It must be provided with an interlocked disconnecting means, so the inlet arrangement cannot leave the building connected the wrong way. Two exceptions soften it: the inlet device itself may serve as the disconnecting means where it is rated for that duty, and supervised industrial installations with a permanent generator space within line of sight follow their own conditions. Below 100 amps this paragraph does not apply — the 702.12(A) and (B) rules on the previous page govern instead. At 100 amps and up, a portable hookup moves serious energy through a connection someone makes by hand, often in the dark after a storm. The interlock makes the wrong connection physically impossible instead of merely against the rules, and the listing proves the inlet gear was tested for generator duty. Small commercial dock in Leesburg takes storm power from a portable generator through a 100 A inlet. Before any conductor lands, the crew reads the inlet's listing and works the interlocked disconnect through its positions: inlet live only in the generator position, building isolated from the utility in that same move. If either the listing or the interlock is missing at 100 A, the job stops at the dock — it is a stop-and-call, not a field fix. The trap is applying this paragraph to every inlet. The listing-plus-interlock duty starts at 100 A; below that, 702.12(A) and (B) govern. The other trap runs the opposite way: calling any inlet a disconnect. The inlet device may serve as the disconnecting means only where it is rated for that duty. Inlet rated 100 A or more with no interlocked disconnecting means. Unlisted inlet equipment on a 100 A portable generator hookup. Inlet device used as the disconnecting means without a rating for that duty. Inlet arrangement that lets the generator parallel the utility service. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Interconnected electric power production sources
x: Article 705 governs sources that operate in parallel with another source — most often a solar inverter, storage system or generator tied to a live utility service. It answers three practical questions: where may the source connect, how much current may the connection and the busbar carry, and how does everyone after you know the extra source exists. • Connections land on the supply side under 705.11 or the load side under 705.12, and a power control system under 705.13 can change the math. • On the load side, the busbar rules in 705.12(B)(3) cap the backfeed: with the sources at opposite ends of the bus, 125 percent of the source output plus the rating of the device protecting the busbar must not exceed 120 percent of the busbar rating. Article 690 in Chapter 6 governs the solar array itself; this article governs its handshake with the premises wiring. A panel busbar was built and tested for current entering at one point. A second source feeding the same bus can push a section of that bus past its rating without any single breaker seeing an overload — the bar overheats quietly inside a closed panel. Article 705 exists to keep the combined math honest, and to make sure the next person who opens the panel knows a second source is there. An Orlando homeowner adds a 7.6 kW solar inverter to a 200 A Siemens panel with a 200 A main. The load-side math: 120 percent of the 200 A busbar is 240 A; minus the 200 A main leaves 40 A of room, and the inverter's 32 A output at 125 percent is exactly 40 A — it fits, with the backfed breaker at the opposite end of the bus and its do-not-relocate label. The same house with a 10 kW inverter needs 52.5 A of room at 125 percent (42 A output), which this panel does not have: the choice becomes a supply-side connection under 705.11 or a power control system under 705.13, decided on paper before anyone drills. The trap answer is that the 120 percent rule lets you add 120 percent of the busbar rating in solar. It does not. The rule caps a sum: 125 percent of the source output current plus the rating of the device protecting the busbar, at 120 percent of the busbar — and only with the two sources at opposite ends of the bus. Put the backfed breaker next to the main and the plain 100 percent method in 705.12(B)(3)(1) governs instead. Backfed breaker landed next to the main while the paperwork claims the 120 percent opposite-end method. No do-not-relocate warning label on a backfed breaker installed under the 120 percent rule. Second source in the panel with no marking that the equipment contains more than one source. Busbar math done with the inverter's breaker size instead of 125 percent of its output current. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 705.50: The language describing the operational modes of a Microgrid in Section 705.50 was rewritten to clearly state that a microgrid can operate in parallel with other systems or in island mode. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Identification of power sources — the directory
x: Where sources are interconnected, 705.10 makes somebody write down where the power can come from: • A permanent plaque or directory is installed at the service equipment, or at another approved, readily visible location. • It shows the location of the disconnect for every parallel power source — every source that can feed the building alongside the service. • It carries the caution that multiple sources of power are present. • Any diagram on the plaque has to be oriented the way the building actually sits — the garage on the plaque is the garage on the ground. This is the page a firefighter or a utility worker reads at 2 a.m. It has to be right, not approximate. A building with solar, a battery or a generator can stay energized after the service disconnect opens. A firefighter pulling a meter, or a lineman who has opened the cutout, can meet a live bus fed from the roof. The directory exists so the first person at the service can find and open every source disconnect before touching anything. A Winter Park house gets a roof array and a battery in the garage on a 200 A Siemens service. Before the plaque is engraved, the Sharma lead walks the property with the plan in hand: service disconnect at the meter, PV disconnect beside the inverter in the garage, battery disconnect on the garage wall by the door. The plaque at the service lists all three, with a site diagram drawn the way the lot actually sits — house front to the street, garage on the left. The inverter moved two studs during the install, so the plaque shows where it is, not where the plan put it. The trap is the paper directory card inside the panel door, or a plaque that shows the disconnects where the plan drew them. 705.10 wants a permanent plaque or directory at the service equipment — or another approved, readily visible location — and any diagram oriented to the real building. A pencil sketch taped inside the door is neither permanent nor verified against the building as built. No plaque or directory at the service equipment on a building with PV and a battery. Directory lists the PV disconnect at its planned location; the inverter was moved during installation. Plaque diagram rotated — it shows the garage on the wrong side of the house. Directory missing the caution that multiple sources of power are present. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Supply-side source connections
x: A source may connect on the supply side of the service disconnect, at the points the service rules allow, under its own set of conditions for conductor sizing, overcurrent protection and grounding. A supply-side connection steps around the panelboard busbar limits entirely, which is why it is the escape route when the 120 percent math in 705.12 will not close. It trades that freedom for service-level work: the connection is ahead of the main, so its protection and its disconnecting means have to be planned like service equipment. Two consequences follow in the field: • There is no busbar sum to pass — but the conductors from the tap to the source disconnect are sized and protected as the section requires, and the disconnect is located, grouped and marked the way service disconnects are. • The utility is part of the job: the tap is made on their side of the main, so coordination and a meter pull are scheduled, not improvised. Everything ahead of the main breaker is unforgiving: no panelboard breaker stands between a fault at the tap and the utility transformer. A casual tap — undersized conductors, a disconnect nobody can find, no marking — leaves a permanently energized hazard that the next electrician meets by surprise. That is why the section trades the busbar limits for service-level discipline. An Ocala house with a 200 A panel gets a 9.6 kW PV array — 40 A of inverter output. The load-side math will not close: the panel is full, and there is no legal landing spot for the backfed breaker. Sharma prices the supply-side route instead: a tap between the meter and the main, a 50 A fused disconnect — 125 percent of the 40 A continuous output — mounted with the service equipment and marked as a PV service disconnect, conductors sized for the source, and a scheduled meter pull with the utility. Priced as service work with utility coordination, not as 'one more breaker.' The trap is calling the supply-side tap 'the easy way around the code.' It steps around the 705.12 busbar sums only — the conductor sizing, overcurrent protection and grounding conditions in 705.11 still apply in full, and the work is service work. Second trap: on a 2023 permit the tap conductors are service conductors under Articles 230 and 250. Do not back-read that into a 2020 job, and do not use 2020 habits on a 2023 one. Tap conductors not sized or protected for the source — ahead of the main, nothing downstream protects them. PV disconnect not grouped or marked with the service disconnects — nobody can find the second source. Meter pulled and the tap made without utility coordination. Tap landed on equipment not listed for a supply-side connection — load-side habits on a service job. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 705.11: Conductors from a supply-side tie-in to a power source's disconnect are now service conductors, so the Article 230 and 250 service rules govern them. The 2020 inside-building length limits dropped out. Conductors from the tie-in to the power source's disconnect are service conductors now, and that disconnect is a service disconnect located like one (230.70(A)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Load-side source connections — the shape of the rule
x: A source output may connect on the load side of the other source's service disconnect, at any distribution equipment on the premises. That freedom is what 705.12 spends its sub-rules controlling. Where the equipment is fed by two sources at once and feeds branch circuits or feeders, work the list in order: • A dedicated breaker or fusible disconnect for each source, 705.12(A). Two inverters never share one device, and a source never lands on a breaker that also feeds a load. • Conductor and busbar ampacity, 705.12(B). For a busbar, one of the (B)(3) methods must pass: the 100 percent method (125 percent of source output plus the rating of the device protecting the busbar must not exceed the busbar rating — the breaker may sit anywhere), the 120 percent rule (the same sum may reach 120 percent of the busbar, with the sources at opposite ends), the sum-of-breakers method, or the center-fed method. • Marking of equipment that contains more than one source, so the next person knows it can be live from two directions. • Breakers suitable for backfeed, and fastening where a backfed breaker could work loose — a plug-in breaker feeding the bus needs a hold-down. Where a power control system is installed under 705.13, the controller setting stands in for the source output current in these calculations. A busbar fed from both ends can carry the sum of two sources in its middle while each end looks fine. The 705.12 methods are thermal bookkeeping: they keep the bus from becoming the fuse. The marking and hold-down rules protect the next person — a backfed breaker that pops loose, or a panel nobody warned about, is how a "dead" bus stays live. Rooftop solar on a Marion Oaks house, 200 A Siemens panel with a 200 A main. The inverter's maximum continuous output is 32 A. Under the 120 percent rule the sum may reach 240 A — 120 percent of the 200 A bus — so 125 percent of the inverter output, 40 A, lands exactly at the cap: 200 + 40 = 240. The solar breaker goes at the opposite end of the bus from the main, gets its hold-down kit, and the panel gets its multi-source warning label. Under the 100 percent method this same inverter would not fit at all — position is what buys the room. The classic trap puts the solar breaker anywhere it fits and still claims the 120 percent rule. Position is part of the method: 120 percent buys its extra room only with the sources at opposite ends of the bus. A breaker that may sit anywhere means the 100 percent method — and there the sum may not exceed the busbar rating itself. Two inverters landed on one shared breaker — no dedicated device per source (705.12(A)). 120 percent method claimed with the source breaker beside the main instead of at the opposite end. Backfed plug-in breaker with no hold-down fastener. Panel fed by utility and solar with no multi-source warning marking. Source output over the busbar method's cap — the sum exceeds 120 percent of the bus. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Dedicated overcurrent and disconnect — each source gets its own
x: Each source interconnection is made at its own dedicated circuit breaker or fusible disconnecting means. Two inverters do not share one breaker because the math happened to fit, and a source does not land on a breaker that also feeds a load. • One source system, one dedicated device — every time. • The dedicated device is both the overcurrent protection point for the interconnection and the place that source is disconnected. • A breaker that feeds loads is never an interconnection point, and a source breaker never doubles as a load breaker. A shared breaker hides what is feeding the bus. Open the wrong device and a source is still backfeeding the panel while someone works in it; trip one shared device and two sources drop together, or a source ends up protected at a rating that has nothing to do with its own output. A dedicated device per source makes each source visible, protected at its own rating, and disconnectable on its own. A small commercial rooftop in Clermont gets two string inverters: one with a 32 A maximum output current, one with 16 A. On the takeoff that is two dedicated breakers in the panel — a 40 A for the first inverter and a 20 A for the second, each sized from its own inverter's continuous output, and neither breaker feeds anything else. When a panel schedule shows one 60 A breaker with both inverters landed on it because the total 'fit,' send it back: 705.12(A) counts sources, not sums. The trap answer lands two inverters on one breaker sized for their combined output, because the total ampacity works. 705.12(A) is not an ampacity rule — it is a one-device-per-source rule. The second trap lands a source on a breaker that also feeds a load; a dedicated device serves its source and nothing else. Two inverters landed on a single breaker sized for their combined output. Solar or battery source landed on a breaker that also feeds branch loads. Two sources connected through one shared fusible disconnect. Dedicated source breaker found feeding a receptacle after a panel change. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The 100 percent busbar method — breaker anywhere
x: The plainest load-side method: 125 percent of the source output current, plus the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the busbar, must not exceed the busbar ampacity itself. Meet that sum and the source breaker may sit anywhere on the bus. Fail it and you do not argue with the arithmetic — you move to one of the other methods in 705.12(B)(3), derate something, or go to the supply side. Worked on the example from the lookup entries: a 225 A bus protected by a 200 A main leaves 25 A of room in the sum. At 125 percent, that room is a 20 A source output. One amp more of output and this method is done, even though the panel still has empty spaces. A busbar fed by two sources can carry the utility current and the source current at the same time, and the bus sees the sum. Breakers trip on their own current, not on the total flowing through the bus under them, so an unchecked sum overheats the bus in silence. The 100 percent method is the conservative answer: if the worst-case sum can never beat the bus rating, breaker position stops mattering. Run this method first because it is the one with no position condition. On a Winter Garden house: 225 A bus, 200 A main. The sum leaves 225 − 200 = 25 A, so the largest source this method takes is a 20 A inverter output — 125 percent of 20 A is 25 A, and 200 + 25 = 225, exactly the bus. The customer wants a 32 A inverter instead: 125 percent is 40 A and the sum is 240 A, which fails here. That is not a dead end. The 120 percent method on the next page allows 120 percent of 225 A, or 270 A, so the same 240 A sum passes there — with the source breaker at the opposite end of the bus and its warning label in place. The trap is feeding the sum the wrong current: candidates plug in the inverter's breaker size, or its nameplate output without the 125 percent. The method takes 125 percent of the source output current, every time. Second trap: comparing the sum to 120 percent of the bus on this method. The 100 percent method compares the sum to the busbar ampacity itself — 120 percent belongs to the methods that control breaker position. Source breaker landed in an empty space with no busbar sum ever run — 'it fit' is not a method. Sum figured with the inverter output at 100 percent instead of 125 percent. The 120 percent allowance used on the 100 percent method — position rules skipped and the sum still over the bus rating. Main breaker swapped for a larger one after the solar was approved, breaking a sum nobody rechecked. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The 120 percent rule — sources at opposite ends
x: 705.12(B)(3)(2) is one of the load-side methods for connecting a power source to a panelboard: the two sources sit at opposite ends of a busbar that also carries loads. • The sum is the same as the plain method — 125 percent of the power source output current, plus the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the busbar. • Here the sum may reach 120 percent of the busbar ampacity, because the sources feed from opposite ends. • The busbar must still be sized for the connected loads under Article 220. • Position is part of the method, so a permanent warning label goes on the distribution equipment next to the backfed breaker: it is a power source output connection and must not be relocated. • On the common 200 A bus with a 200 A main, the cap is 240 A, so the method allows a 40 A backfed breaker — 125 percent of a 32 A inverter output. Two sources feeding one busbar can push more current into the bus than either one alone, and a busbar overheats quietly inside a closed panel. Feeding from opposite ends spreads that current along the bus instead of stacking it at one point — the only reason the code lets the sum run to 120 percent under this method. Rooftop solar on a new house in Marion Oaks: a 200 A Siemens panel, 200 A main at the top, and an inverter with a 32 A continuous output. At 125 percent the inverter needs a 40 A breaker; 200 plus 40 is 240 A, exactly 120 percent of the bus, so the breaker lands in the bottom space, opposite the main, and the do-not-relocate label goes on before the inspection. Mid-bus, the same gear fails the 100 percent method. S-03 matters here on existing work: in an existing Square D panel, the backfed breaker is a Square D breaker listed for that panel — the 120 percent math never licenses a mixed-brand breaker. The trap is running the sum with the breaker size instead of 125 percent of output current. A 40 A inverter output is not a 40 A entry in the sum — it is 50 A, and 200 plus 50 blows through the 240 A cap. The second trap is treating the backfed breaker's spot as a free space: move it off the end and the 120 percent method is gone. Backfed breaker relocated away from the end of the bus — the 120 percent method no longer applies and nobody rechecked the math. No permanent warning label at the backfed breaker marking it as a power source output connection that must not be relocated. Sum figured with the inverter breaker rating instead of 125 percent of the inverter output current, pushing the total past 120 percent of the busbar. Sources landed at the same end of the busbar while the 120 percent allowance was used. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The sum-of-breakers method
x: 705.12(B)(3)(3) is a third load-side method for connecting a power source to a panelboard, and it works by counting breakers instead of trusting the main: • Add up the ampere ratings of all load and supply breakers on the board, excluding the device protecting the busbar — that device is the only one left out of the sum. • The total must not exceed the ampacity of the busbar. • Equipment using this method carries permanent warning labels at the distribution equipment identifying that all sources are present. It fits panels where the breaker population, not the main breaker rating, is the honest limit on the bus. A busbar does not care which breaker fed it — it carries the sum of everything connected to it. A panel can respect its main breaker rating and still be overfed once a supply breaker is added on top of a full row of load breakers. The sum-of-breakers method caps the total iron on the bus, and the warning labels tell the next electrician that more than one source can feed the panel. A 200 A Siemens panel in a Clermont home gets a solar supply breaker, and the crew counts what is actually in the panel, including the source breaker: load breakers totaling 170 A plus the new 40 A supply breaker is 210 A — over the 200 A busbar, so this method fails as built. The honest fixes are removing breakers that are genuinely spare, downsizing the supply breaker, or using a different 705.12(B)(3) method — worked out before the inspection, with the sum written in the job record. A panel that passes today can fail this method after one added circuit, so the count gets done again at every addition. The trap is adding the main breaker into the sum — or leaving the supply breaker out of it. The method excludes only the device protecting the busbar, and it counts every other overcurrent device, load and supply together, against the busbar ampacity. The second trap is treating the count as a one-time event: the method is re-tested every time a breaker is added to the panel. Sum of breaker ratings exceeds the busbar ampacity on a panel connected under 705.12(B)(3)(3). No permanent warning label at the distribution equipment identifying that all sources are present. Supply breaker left out of the installer's breaker sum. Breaker added after the solar inspection with no recount — the panel is now over the bus rating. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The center-fed busbar method — one end only
x: Some dwelling panelboards are center-fed: the main breaker or main lugs sit in the middle of the busbar instead of at one end, a construction common on combination meter-and-panel equipment in some regions. • This method permits a source connection at either end of that busbar — but never at both ends. • The math is the familiar 120 percent check applied to the connection: the sum of 125 percent of the power source output circuit current and the rating of the overcurrent device protecting the busbar must not exceed 120 percent of the busbar rating. Because a center-fed bus can concentrate load on one half of the busbar, the option is limited to dwellings. A center-fed busbar is really two half-buses fed from the middle. Land sources at both ends and each half can be fed from two directions at once — the middle of the bus ends up carrying current the busbar was never checked for, and it overheats quietly inside a closed panel. One source, one end, one math check keeps every part of the bus within its rating. Identify the panel construction before reaching for the 120 percent rule: if the main sits in the middle, this paragraph is the method, not (3)(2). Florida new-build with a center-fed Siemens 200 A combination meter-panel: the inverter's continuous output is 32 A, so the source breaker is 40 A — 125 percent of the output — landed at the bottom end of the bus. The check: 200 A main plus 40 A equals 240 A, exactly 120 percent of the 200 A busbar, so it passes with nothing to spare. The top end stays source-free, and the job file records which end was used. The trap is reaching for the opposite-end method of (3)(2) — or worse, landing a source at each end because each one passes the 120 percent check by itself. A center-fed panel is not a (3)(2) panel: (3)(4) allows one end only, and the two ends are never used together. Source breakers landed at both ends of a center-fed busbar. Opposite-end method (3)(2) applied to a center-fed panel. Math run on the inverter nameplate current without the 125 percent factor. Center-fed method used on a commercial panelboard — it is a dwelling-only method. No record of which end of the bus carries the source connection. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Power control systems — a listed controller can limit the current
x: New in the 2020 code, this section recognizes a power control system: listed equipment that monitors and limits how much current a source puts onto conductors and busbars. Where one is installed, its controller setting is treated as the source output current for the 705.11 and 705.12 calculations, so a system set to a lower limit can fit a panel the raw inverter rating could not. The 2020 rules around the controller: • Monitoring, 705.13(A): the controller must monitor all current within the system. A busbar or conductor it does not monitor is sized under 705.12 the ordinary way. • Settings, 705.13(B): the PCS currents plus the other monitored source currents may not exceed the ampacity of any busbar or conductor they supply. • Overcurrent protection, 705.13(C): the system must provide it, by devices or by its own listing. • Access, 705.13(E): settings are restricted to qualified personnel — sealed covers, bolted or locked doors, or a password (240.6(C)). A busbar cannot tell the difference between current that was calculated and current that actually shows up. If a controller setting is raised after inspection, or a conductor the controller cannot see gets loaded anyway, the panel quietly runs past its rating on every sunny afternoon. The monitoring and access rules exist so the limit on paper is the limit in fact. A Kissimmee house has a 200 A Siemens panel with a 200 A main and a 200 A bus. The PV inverter's nameplate output is 40 A, so the ordinary 705.12 sums fail: 125 percent of 40 A is 50 A, and 200 + 50 = 250 A beats even the 120 percent method's 240 A cap. The design instead uses a listed power control system set to 32 A. The setting stands in for the source output current: 125 percent of 32 A is 40 A, and 200 + 40 = 240 A — exactly the 120 percent cap, with the source breaker at the opposite end of the bus. The 32 A setting is recorded on the plans, marked at the panel, and locked behind the controller password. The trap is treating the controller like a homeowner thermostat — a setting anyone can turn up later. Raise the setting and every calculation that relied on it is void; the busbar math fails silently. Access to PCS settings is restricted to qualified personnel (705.13(E)). Second trap: assuming the controller protects conductors it does not monitor. Unmonitored conductors are sized under 705.12, full stop. Controller setting raised in the app after inspection — the 705.12 calculations on file no longer match the installation. Unlisted controller relied on to limit busbar current — a power control system has to be listed equipment. Conductors landed on a busbar section the controller does not monitor, sized as if it did. No record of the controller setting on the plans or at the panel — the method cannot be proven later. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 705.13: Most of the requirements that were located in Section 705.13 have been deleted by CMP-4. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Disconnecting means for sources
x: Every interconnected power source — PV inverter, battery system, generator tying in under this article — needs its own disconnecting means that meets this section. In 2020 the source disconnect rules were gathered into this one place. • The disconnect has to separate the source from the conductors of the other systems, opening all the ungrounded conductors at the same time. • It has to be readily accessible and operable from outside without exposing the operator to live parts. • It has to plainly show whether it is open or closed — no guessing from the handle position alone. • Its ratings have to suit the load it carries and the fault current available where it lands. • Where both sides of the disconnect can stay energized, the equipment carries a warning — a source can feed a panel from the far end. • Under the 2020 rule, an enclosure cover on a disconnect that unqualified people can reach has to be locked or need a tool to open where opening it would expose live parts. A second source turns “I opened the breaker” into a lie. A panel fed by the utility and a battery or PV inverter can stay live from the far end after the normal disconnect is open, and the person who finds out is usually holding a meter lead or a pair of cutters. This section exists so every source has one known, visible, rated way to separate it — and so nobody has to trust that a silent panel is a dead panel. On a Palm Coast house with rooftop PV and a battery inverter landing in the same Siemens panel, land each source on its own disconnect where the 705.10 directory at the service says it is, so the next person can find both without opening the house. Check the open-position condition before you call it done: open the disconnect and meter both sides. The line side from the panel can still be live, and the source side can wake up when the sun hits the array — terminals that stay live get the warning label the equipment rules call for. The trap answer: one main disconnect ahead of the panel separates everything, so the sources behind it need nothing of their own. Wrong — 705.20 wants a disconnecting means for the source itself, separating that source from the other systems' conductors. A shared switch that leaves the inverter tied to a live bus has not separated anything. Two sources landed in one panel behind a single shared disconnect — each source needs its own separating means. Disconnect handle shows nothing: no plain OPEN or CLOSED indication an inspector can read at arm's length. PV or battery disconnect where the line side stays live, with no both-sides-energized warning. Enclosure cover on a publicly reachable disconnect that flips open by hand and exposes live parts (2020 rule). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 705.20: The requirement for enclosure covers in Section 705.20 requiring a tool to open or be locked has been deleted. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Overcurrent protection — interconnected sources
x: Conductors and equipment on an interconnected system get overcurrent protection under 705.30, working with the circuit-current sizing in 705.28 and with Article 240. • Protection from all sources (705.30(A)). A conductor fed from both ends can be overcurrented from either direction, so protection is planned for the source output the same way it is planned for a utility feed. • Device ratings follow the calculated source currents. The source output current is the nameplate current (705.28), and conductors and overcurrent devices are sized at not less than 125% of that maximum current — the continuous-output factor is built in. • Equipment containing overcurrent devices supplied from more than one power source is marked to indicate that all sources are present (705.30(C)). • A circuit breaker not marked line and load is suitable for backfeed; one marked line and load is not (705.30(D)). Two sources can push current into the same conductor from opposite ends. Protection planned only around the utility feed leaves the conductor exposed to the inverter or generator feeding it backwards, and fault current does not care which end it came from. The marking and backfeed rules exist because the second source is invisible until somebody opens the wrong device. On a small commercial rooftop in Orlando, the interactive inverter's nameplate continuous output is 32 A. Sharma sizes the output conductors and the backfed breaker at 125% — 32 × 1.25 = 40 A — using a Siemens 40 A breaker that is not marked line and load. The panelboard is marked for multiple sources, because that panel is now fed from two directions and the next person who opens it needs to know. Sizing the inverter's output breaker at exactly its 32 A nameplate current, because 'the inverter limits its own output anyway.' The inverter does limit its current, but 705.28 still requires conductors and protection at not less than 125% of the maximum source current. Skipping the factor is the classic wrong answer — and so is landing a line/load-marked breaker where it will be backfed. Backfed breaker marked line/load landed in a panel — not suitable for reverse current (705.30(D)). Inverter output breaker sized at nameplate current with no 125% factor (705.28). Panelboard fed by the utility and a PV system with no marking that multiple sources are present (705.30(C)). Source output conductors protected at the utility end only, with nothing protecting them from the source end (705.30(A)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 705.30(F): New language has been added at Section 705.30(F) to address transformer requirements for interconnected systems. The revised language now correlates with the transformer installation rules of Articles 240, 450, and the transformer product safety standard. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Loss of primary source — the source must stop and stay off
x: When the primary source — normally the utility — is lost, an interconnected power production source has to stop feeding it, and stay off: • The source must be automatically disconnected from all ungrounded conductors of the primary source, and it must not reconnect until the primary source is restored. • The duty bites even if only one line or one phase of the utility supply opens. • It exists so a solar array or a cogeneration source can never backfeed lines that utility crews are treating as dead. • The listed utility-interactive inverter is the exception path: it may keep producing ac power for local loads as long as no power reaches the service conductors, which in effect turns the premises into their own island. • A source serving an emergency or legally required standby system through transfer equipment is not shut down by this section — those systems are supposed to run during the outage. After a storm, line crews ground and work conductors they have every reason to believe are dead. A rooftop array quietly backfeeding the service turns a 'dead' line live from the wrong end. This section is the anti-islanding duty that keeps a customer's source from becoming the crew's hazard. Hurricane outage in Ocala, full sun, and the homeowner's rooftop array is silent. That is this section working, not a failed inverter — the array disconnected itself when the grid dropped, and it stays off until the utility is restored. The fix we quote is equipment listed to island legally, with transfer equipment, so the house can run as its own island next storm. Defeating the anti-islanding control is never the answer. The trap answer is that the source only has to disconnect when the whole service drops. One open phase is enough — the duty bites on a single lost line. The other wrong pick is 'reconnect as soon as the inverter sees voltage on one leg': the section says not until the primary source is restored. Interconnected source still tied to the service conductors during an outage — no automatic disconnect on loss of the primary source. Source reconnects before the primary source is restored. Anti-islanding protection defeated or jumpered so the array runs grid-parallel during outages. Only one ungrounded conductor opened on loss of source, leaving the source connected to the other line. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Energy storage systems — batteries under the code
x: Article 706 covers energy storage systems over 1 kWh that can feed a premises wiring system, on their own or alongside other sources. • Only qualified persons install and maintain these systems. • Each system is listed, and its nameplate carries the ratings the installer and the inspector both work from. The two hazards that shape the article are stored energy that is still live when everything looks off, and fault current a battery bank can deliver without any utility behind it. Dwellings get extra attention: the disconnect a first responder can reach, and a dc voltage limit inside the home — 100 volts between conductors or to ground, with up to 600 volts allowed where live parts are not accessible during routine maintenance (706.20(B)). A battery does not go dead when you open a switch — the energy is still in the cabinet, and a shorted bank can deliver enormous fault current with no utility behind it. That is why the article insists on listed systems, qualified hands, a nameplate everyone works from, and a disconnect a firefighter can find in the dark. Garage wall of a Marion Oaks house: a listed ESS cabinet, nameplate rated over 1 kWh, goes in with its disconnect where a first responder walking up the driveway can reach it. Before landing a single conductor, the crew meters the battery terminals — the inverter display says off, and the meter is the only opinion that counts. The bank's dc voltage stays under the 100 V dwelling limit with its live parts as installed. Florida note: hurricane-driven battery work is arriving in houses that were never designed for it. The ESS rules in this article, plus the fire-code siting the AHJ enforces, both apply — ask the AHJ about location limits before the batteries are set. The trap is quoting 600 V as the dwelling limit. Inside a home the limit is 100 V dc between conductors or to ground; 600 V is allowed only where live parts are not accessible during routine maintenance. The second trap is trusting the inverter's 'off' state — stored energy is live until a meter proves otherwise. Energy storage system installed with no listing — unlisted battery cabinet tied into the panel. No readily accessible ESS disconnect a first responder can reach at a dwelling. Dwelling ESS running over 100 V dc with live parts accessible during routine maintenance. Nameplate missing or unreadable — ratings the install was based on cannot be checked. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Commissioning and maintenance — energy storage
x: Away from one- and two-family dwellings, an energy storage system is commissioned when it is installed. Every system — dwellings included — is kept maintained in proper and safe operating condition, following the manufacturer instructions and industry standards. • Commissioning proves the installed system works as a system: connections, controls and protective functions checked and documented at installation. • Maintenance is not optional, and it is not guesswork: the manufacturer's instructions set the tasks. • Storage is not fit-and-forget equipment: connections, ventilation, controls and firmware all age. A battery system stores enough energy to hurt someone on a day when every switch looks off. Connections loosen and heat, ventilation gets blocked by stored material, firmware and protective settings drift — and none of it announces itself until the system is asked to perform, or fails hot. Commissioning catches the installation errors on day one; maintenance catches the aging before it becomes a fire or a dead system. Sharma wires a listed battery system — over 1 kWh, so Article 706 applies — at a small warehouse in Orlando. Because it is not a one- or two-family dwelling, the system is commissioned at installation: operation verified, settings and protective functions checked, and the commissioning record written up. Hand over the commissioning record and the maintenance instructions with the job. If the owner cannot say who maintains the system, that conversation happens at sale, not at the first fault. The trap is treating commissioning as a rule for every installation. In the 2020 text the commissioning duty stops at one- and two-family dwellings — but the maintenance duty does not: a dwelling system still has to be maintained in proper and safe operating condition. The second trap: 'commissioned' does not mean 'turned on once.' It means tested, verified and documented. Battery system in a commercial space turned over with no commissioning performed or documented. No commissioning record or maintenance instructions handed to the owner at turnover. Storage system found with its ventilation blocked and connections never re-checked — no maintenance since installation. Protective settings and firmware never verified after installation. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 706.7: Revised the existing text, adding commissioning requirements for energy storage systems in a new subdivision (A). The existing requirements for maintenance of these systems were moved into the new (B). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Disconnecting means — energy storage systems
x: 706.15 requires a disconnecting means that separates the energy storage system from everything else — the other power sources, the utilization equipment and the premises wiring. • Listed equipment with an integral disconnect can serve as that disconnecting means. • The disconnect is readily accessible and sits at the system or within sight of it. Within sight means visible and not more than 50 ft away. • It plainly indicates whether it is open or closed, and it is permanently marked as the energy storage system disconnect. • The marking package also carries the system's nominal ac voltage, its maximum dc voltage and the available fault current, where the section requires them, plus an arc-flash warning label. Where that label rests on an arc-flash hazard analysis, it shows the date the analysis was performed. • For a dwelling, the disconnect or its remote control is at a readily accessible location outside the building, where responders can reach it. Marking items (2), (3) and (4) of the list are waived for systems in one- and two-family dwellings. A battery does not go dead when the service drops. Kill the main and the storage system is still holding energy, still able to feed the house and to bite anyone who opens the wrong box. The disconnect, the outside location and the marking package exist so a firefighter at 2 a.m. — or the next electrician — can find the one switch that truly isolates the system, and read its voltages before touching anything. Marion Oaks house: a garage-wall battery and inverter beside a new 200 A Siemens service. We set the ESS disconnect outside, next to the meter — a separate, marked device, not the 230.85 emergency disconnect — where it stands 12 ft from the battery and in plain sight of it. Its label marks it as the energy storage system disconnect and carries 240 V nominal ac, plus the maximum dc voltage and available fault current copied off the equipment nameplates. Then the walk-away test from the old page: stand at the street and ask whether a responder who has never seen this house could find and open it in the dark. If not, the install is not finished. The trap is answering from the 2023 book: a field-serviceable battery set apart from its ESS electronics needing its own within-sight disconnect under 706.15(E). That rule is real — for permits from Dec 31, 2026. On a 2020 permit it is not in the book. The second trap runs the other way: the dwelling waiver covers marking items (2), (3) and (4) — it never waives the disconnect itself. ESS disconnect inside the garage on a dwelling, with no disconnect or remote control at a readily accessible location outside the building. Disconnect not marked as the energy storage system disconnect, or the nominal ac voltage, maximum dc voltage and available fault current markings missing. Arc-flash warning label based on a hazard analysis but carrying no date for the analysis. Disconnect that does not plainly show whether it is open or closed. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 706.15: A field-serviceable battery installed apart from its energy storage system (ESS) electronics now gets a dedicated disconnect within sight, string breaks above 240 volts and a hazard label. A field-serviceable battery located away from its ESS electronics now needs a readily accessible disconnect, within sight of the battery, opening every ungrounded conductor (706.15(E)). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Circuit sizing and overcurrent protection — storage circuits
x: Storage circuit currents come from the nameplate ratings (706.30(A)), and the rest of the sizing follows from them: • For an ESS circuit, use the nameplate-rated current. For an inverter, use its continuous output current on the ac side, and its continuous input current at the lowest input voltage on the dc side. • Conductors must have an ampacity at least the greater of the nameplate current or the rating of the overcurrent device protecting them (706.30(B)). • The overcurrent protection that follows in 706.31 must be rated not less than 125% of the 706.30 current, unless the assembly, overcurrent devices included, is listed for operation at 100% of its rating (706.31(B)). • On the dc side, devices must be listed for dc use, with the appropriate voltage, current and interrupting ratings (706.31(C)). Battery circuits punish borrowed ac-only habits: a device that cannot interrupt dc fault current is not protection, whatever its amp number says. A battery bank is a fault-current machine sitting inside the building: very high available fault current at its terminals, and dc has no zero crossing to help a device put out an arc. A breaker chosen by amp number alone can weld shut on dc fault current, leaving the circuit defended on paper only — inches from the largest energy source on the job. On a solar-plus-storage house in Winter Garden, the ESS inverter's nameplate continuous output is 40 A, so the ac breaker is 50 A — 40 × 1.25 — and the conductors are sized to that breaker, not to the 40 A nameplate. On the dc side, read the dc rating on every fuse and breaker in the battery circuit out loud during the rough-in inspection of your own work. If it does not say dc, it comes out. Two wrong answers live here. First: the battery breaker at exactly the 40 A nameplate current, because the inverter limits its output — 706.31(B) wants not less than 125% unless the assembly is listed for 100% operation. Second: an ac-rated breaker on the dc side because the amp number matched. On a battery circuit, the amp number is the least important thing on the device. AC-rated breaker installed on the battery dc circuit — not listed for dc use (706.31(C)). Overcurrent device sized at nameplate current with no 125% factor, and the assembly is not listed for 100% operation (706.31(B)). Conductors sized to the nameplate current but smaller than the rating of the overcurrent device protecting them (706.30(B)). DC fuse with an interrupting rating below the battery bank's available fault current. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Critical operations power systems (COPS)
x: Article 708 covers power systems for facilities an AHJ or governmental authority has designated as critical operations areas — places like certain 911 and emergency operations centers, critical infrastructure and national-security functions, where losing power is a public-safety event, not an inconvenience. The article layers extra reliability, testing, documentation and risk-assessment duties on top of the standby ideas in Articles 700 to 702. • The designation comes from the authority — never from the owner, the engineer, or the size of the generator. • A documented risk assessment (708.4) comes first, and it drives the design, the physical security, and the source choices. • The alternate source has to carry the designated area at full load for at least 72 hours (708.22(C)). Sharma's residential and light-commercial work will rarely be designated COPS, and the practical skill is recognizing the designation on the rare job that carries it. A 911 center or emergency operations center that goes dark in a hurricane cannot simply close for the day — calls stop routing and responders stop moving. Article 708 exists so the facilities a community leans on hardest are designed against a written list of hazards instead of hope. The risk assessment comes first because the right generator, fuel supply, and protection all depend on what can actually go wrong at that site. A county emergency operations center in Central Florida asks Sharma to bid a generator replacement, and the front-end documents call the building a designated critical operations area. That one phrase changes the job. Before pricing, confirm the designation in writing and ask for the facility's risk assessment — it sets the physical security, the protection, and the 72-hour full-load run the alternate source has to prove. Price the documented testing and maintenance program as part of the work, not as a favor afterward. And if the designation is not in the documents, say so in the bid: a big generator alone does not make a job a 708 job. The trap answer is that any building with a large generator and a transfer switch is a COPS installation. It is not. Article 708 applies only where an AHJ or governmental authority has designated the facility or an area in it as critical operations. A warehouse with a big standby set is still an Article 702 job unless somebody with that authority designated it. COPS job built and turned over with no documented risk assessment in the closeout package (708.4). Alternate source that cannot show 72 hours of full-load capacity for the designated area (708.22(C)). COPS equipment in a room any building occupant can wander into — no restricted access or physical security per the assessment (708.5). No documented testing and maintenance records for the AHJ to review. Standby system labeled COPS on the drawings with no designation from the authority anywhere in the documents. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 708.24: Added new requirements for the separation of Class 2 circuits designated as emergency or nonemergency circuits in Section 700.11(C). FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Stand-Alone systems — power with no utility to lean on
x: Article 710 covers systems that operate in island mode — not connected to a power production and distribution network. The off-grid house, the remote pump, the microgrid that runs alone: if there is no utility behind the source, this article owns the job. • The supply may be smaller than a normal Article 220 calculated load — but never smaller than the floor 710.15 sets: the combined sources must at least carry the largest single piece of utilization equipment. • Sources combine freely here: solar, storage and a generator can all feed the same stand-alone system. • The sources still have to be identified: 710.10 requires a permanent plaque or directory naming each source and its disconnect. The same equipment often also appears under Articles 702, 705 and 706 when it works alongside a utility, so the first job on any of these systems is deciding which mode it is actually in. A utility-fed system borrows the grid's capacity and the grid's fault current. An island system has neither. If the combined sources cannot carry the biggest load the building will ever switch on, the system fails on an ordinary day, not in an emergency — and with no utility to fall back on, a dark off-grid house or a dead well pump is the whole story. The mode decision matters because the wrong article sizes the system by the wrong rule. Grove pump house outside Ocala with no utility service available and none coming. Solar array, a battery inverter and a small generator feed one panel — no utility feed exists, so the job is Article 710 from the first sketch, not 702. The load list starts with the well pump, the largest single load on the place. Combined source capacity has to clear that pump load under 710.15, and the 710.10 plaque at the disconnect names all three sources so the next person can shut the system down. The trap answer is Article 702, picked because the system has a generator. A generator alone does not make it optional standby. Article 702 needs a utility service for the generator to stand by for. With no utility connection at all, the system is stand-alone and Article 710 governs — and 710 sizes the supply by its own floor, not by the standby rules. Stand-alone system permitted and wired as a 702 standby job, with no 710.10 plaque anywhere. No plaque or directory identifying the power sources at the disconnecting means. Plaque lists the solar array but not the generator, so one source stays live after shutdown. Sources listed one at a time on the permit, with no combined-capacity figure for the AHJ to check. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Identification of power sources — stand-alone systems
x: New in the 2020 code, 710.10 requires the power sources of a stand-alone system to be identified by a permanent plaque or directory. It is the same instinct as the 705.10 directory for interconnected sources: anyone working on or responding to the building can find every source and its disconnect. • The plaque or directory is installed at the disconnecting means location, or another approved, readily visible location. • It denotes the location of each power source disconnecting means serving the building. • Where more than one source supplies the building, the marking carries the multiple-sources caution, the same as 705.10. • A diagram on the plaque must be oriented the way the building actually sits. On a system with solar, batteries and a generator scattered around a property, the identification is the difference between a safe shutdown and a scavenger hunt. A stand-alone system has no utility to call and no single service main to pull. Open the wrong disconnect and the building is still live from the battery inverter in the garage. The plaque is how a firefighter, a responder, or the next electrician finds every source before anyone touches the wiring. On an off-grid house outside Ocala, the plaque at the house disconnect lists all three sources: the PV inverter disconnect and the battery disconnect on the garage west wall, and the generator disconnect in the detached shed. List every source on the identification, including the small generator that 'only feeds the barn.' If it can energize the wiring, it belongs on the list. Walk the property and verify each location before the plaque is made — a directory that points to where a disconnect was planned, instead of where it is, fails its only job. The system is off-grid, so there is no service equipment, no utility — and, the trap answer says, no directory. Wrong. Section 710.10 was added in 2020 precisely for stand-alone systems, and it asks for the same thing 705.10 asks of interconnected systems. The second trap is citing 705.10 on a stand-alone job: the requirement is real, but on a 710 system it lives in 710.10. No plaque at all on an off-grid house — the inspector has to hunt for the battery and generator disconnects. Plaque lists the PV and the battery but leaves off the generator in the detached shed. Directory diagram drawn rotated from how the building actually sits, so the responder is sent to the wrong wall. Hand-lettered paper label taped inside the panel instead of a permanent plaque (110.21(B)). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: General rules — sizing a stand-alone supply
x: Premises wiring fed by a stand-alone system still has to meet the code the way a feeder- or service-fed installation does, with the modifications on this page. • The supply may be smaller than the Article 220 calculated load. Article 710 does not make an island system pretend the utility is behind it. • The floor: the combined capacity of all the stand-alone sources must at least equal the load of the largest single piece of utilization equipment connected. • General lighting load does not count as that single load — the floor is set by real equipment, not by the lighting calc. • The 2020 code expressly permits these systems to supply three-phase, three-wire or four-wire loads. The largest single load is the one demand the system cannot dodge: sooner or later that pump, compressor or range runs by itself, and the sources either carry it or the inverter trips and the building goes dark. Sizing to an average or a diversified number works only while the grid absorbs the peaks — an island has nothing to absorb peaks with. The floor keeps a small system honest without forcing it to be a utility. Off-grid house in Marion County. The Article 220 worksheet says 12,000 VA, but nobody has to build a 12,000 VA island. The load list is built around the well pump at 3,000 VA — the largest single piece of utilization equipment. A 4,500 VA inverter plus a 3,000 VA generator gives 7,500 VA of combined capacity, comfortably over the pump and well under the 220 number. The lighting load, 1,500 VA, never enters the floor test. What does get checked with the inverter maker is the pump's starting surge, because carrying the running load and starting it are two different days. The wrong answer treats the general lighting load as the largest single load and sizes the sources to it — 1,500 VA on the diagram's house. Section 710.15 takes lighting out of that test by name. The floor is the largest single piece of utilization equipment, the well pump at 3,000 VA, and a system sized to the lights fails the section's own test the first time the pump starts. Combined source capacity below the largest single connected load — the system cannot carry its own well pump. General lighting load used as the 'largest single load' in the sizing calculation. Stand-alone premises wiring not held to the same code as a feeder-fed installation. Sources listed one at a time on the permit, with no combined-capacity figure for the AHJ to check. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Direct-current microgrids
x: Article 712, confirmed in the printed 2020 table of contents, covers dc microgrids: systems that distribute dc power from dc sources to dc loads, with converters tying them to ac systems where needed. It is a young article for a young technology, and Sharma's Florida work has not hit one yet. It earns its place in this book so the reader recognizes the article number and does not mistake a dc microgrid for an Article 710 stand-alone system or a 705 interconnection, which it can sit alongside. • A dc microgrid is one or more interconnected dc sources, dc-dc converters and dc loads on a common dc bus; ac loads are fed through dc-ac inverters, and the grid ties to the ac system through an ac-dc converter or a bidirectional inverter. • Dc loads are the point: LED lighting, communications gear, computers and servers, variable-speed drives and HVAC equipment can all run straight off the bus. • 712.10 wants a directory: a plaque or directory at each service equipment location naming every dc source, and directories at the interconnectable source locations as well. Dc sources do not behave like a utility feed. A battery or PV array on a dc bus can keep that bus energized from several directions at once, and dc arcs do not self-extinguish the way ac arcs do at the zero crossing. An electrician who walks up expecting Article 705 or 710 rules — or plain ac habits — can open the wrong thing in the wrong order. The article exists so the system is recognized, directed and labeled as its own animal. If a plan set shows a dc bus feeding loads, find this article before you assume the familiar ac rules answer everything. On the first one Sharma lands — most likely a commercial job with LED lighting and a battery-backed server room — the field habit to build early is the directory: at the service equipment, a plaque naming the service and every dc source on the bus, the same discipline 705.10 and 690.56(B) already drill into us on the ac side. No directory, no way for the next crew to know the bus has three parents. The trap: calling it a stand-alone system under Article 710 because it can run without the utility, or wiring it under 705 because sources interconnect. A system built around a common dc bus with dc sources and dc loads is a dc microgrid — Article 712 owns it, whichever articles it sits alongside. Dc bus treated like an ac panel: no directory at the service equipment naming the dc sources (712.10). System permitted and wired as a 710 stand-alone job when the drawings show a common dc bus — wrong article, wrong rules. Ac loads tapped straight off the dc bus instead of through a dc-ac inverter. Second dc source added to the bus with the directory never updated. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Directory — dc microgrid sources
x: 712.10 is Article 712's directory rule, the dc counterpart of 705.10 and 710.10: • A permanent plaque or directory denoting all electric power sources on or in the premises. • Installed at each service equipment location, and at the locations of power production sources capable of being interconnected. • Subsection (B) covers the directory for a building supplied by a dc microgrid. Anyone working the building should be able to find every source and its disconnect from the directory. Other articles send dc microgrid work here for its plaques and directories: battery systems under 480.7(G)(1), PV under 690.56(B), fuel cells under 692.4(B)(2) and wind systems under 694.54(B). A dc microgrid hides its sources in plain sight: a battery rack in a closet, a PV combiner on the roof, a fuel cell by the pad. Open the service and the dc bus can still be live from three directions at once. The directory is how the next electrician — or a firefighter at 2 a.m. — learns that the building has more than one way to be energized, and where each disconnect is. Sharma has not installed a dc microgrid; this page is the signpost for the day one appears on a plan set. When it does — say a small Orlando warehouse with rooftop PV and a battery rack feeding a dc bus for LED lighting — the directory work is roughed and priced like 705.10 work: a permanent directory at the service equipment naming every source, directories at each source that can interconnect, and the disconnect location for each one shown. The field habit transfers directly: directory at the service, every source named, disconnect locations shown. The trap answer puts the directory only at the service equipment. 712.10 also wants directories at the locations of the power production sources capable of being interconnected. The other wrong turn is citing 705.10 or 710.10: those are the ac counterparts. The dc microgrid directory rule is 712.10, and subsection (B) is the part written for a building supplied by a dc microgrid. Dc microgrid energized with no directory at the service equipment location. Directory names the PV array but leaves the battery system off the plaque. Paper directory taped inside the panel door instead of a permanent plaque or directory. Directory at the service only — nothing at the locations of the sources that can interconnect. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Circuits and equipment operating at less than 50 volts
x: Article 720 is the small general article for circuits and equipment running under 50 volts, ac or dc, that are not claimed by a more specific article (720.1, 720.2). Most low-voltage work Sharma does is claimed: thermostats and controls by Article 725, fire alarm by 760, communications by Chapter 8. Article 720 is what remains — and what remains still has teeth: • Conductors not smaller than 12 AWG copper or equivalent; on an appliance branch circuit supplying more than one appliance or appliance receptacle, not smaller than 10 AWG (720.4). • Standard lampholders rated not less than 660 W (720.5), and receptacles rated not less than 15 A (720.6). • Receptacles of not less than 20 A in kitchens, laundries, and other locations where portable appliances are likely to be used (720.7). • Storage batteries follow the Article 480 rules named in 720.9, and the work is installed in a neat and workmanlike manner, cables supported so normal building use will not damage them (720.11). Fifty volts sits below the shock hazard that drives most of the Code, but not below the fire hazard. A low-voltage circuit on a stiff supply can push enough current to cook undersized conductors for hours. The minimum wire sizes and real receptacle ratings exist because low voltage tempts everyone to wire it like it cannot hurt anything. Name the owning article for every low-voltage run on the plan. On a shop remodel in Apopka, the crew found a legacy 32 V appliance circuit feeding three receptacles in a detached workshop. No specific article claims it, so Article 720 does: the run is rewired in 10 AWG copper — an appliance branch circuit with more than one receptacle — the receptacles are rated 15 A minimum, and 20 A receptacles go in at the bench where portable tools plug in. 'Low voltage' is a description, not a wiring method. Treating every circuit under 50 volts as an Article 720 circuit. Most are claimed first: 720.2 takes the circuits of Articles 725, 760, 411 and Chapter 8 out of 720 entirely. The second trap is wiring a genuine 720 circuit in bell wire because 'it is only low voltage.' The floor is 12 AWG copper, and 10 AWG where an appliance branch circuit feeds more than one outlet. Article 720 circuit wired in 18 AWG bell wire — the minimum is 12 AWG copper (720.4). Appliance branch circuit feeding several receptacles wired in 12 AWG where 720.4 requires 10 AWG. 15 A receptacle installed at a laundry location where portable appliances are used — 720.7 requires 20 A receptacles there. Low-voltage cable draped unsupported across a ceiling where normal building use can damage it (720.11). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 720: Article 720 was deleted in the 2023 NEC — the Code panel found the equipment it covered had not been manufactured for decades and no known systems remain in service. Low-voltage work is governed by the specific articles that claim each circuit instead. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 722 — not in the 2020 code (a 2023 number)
x: There is no Article 722 in NEC 2020. The number was first used in the 2023 edition, where a new Article 722 gathers the cable rules for power-limited circuits that the 2020 book spreads across three articles: • Class 2 and Class 3 cable types, listing and substitution rules live in Article 725. • Power-limited fire alarm cable rules live in Article 760. • Optical fiber cable rules live in Article 770. Florida work under the Florida Building Code 8th Edition — permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 — is NEC 2020, so a 2023 study book, app or exam sheet that sends you to 722 is pointing at a page this code does not have. Edition mix-ups are not academic. A crew that follows a 2023 citation on a 2020 permit can pull cable to rules the inspector cannot accept, and a document written to the wrong edition in one place is usually wrong in others too. This page exists so the citation gets caught at the truck, not at the inspection. A Lakeland warehouse package lands with a supplier submittal citing 722 for the Class 2 cable listing. Translate it back before anyone orders: a Class 2 or Class 3 cable question goes to 725, a fire alarm cable question goes to 760, and a fiber question goes to 770. Then flag the citation to the lead, because the rest of that submittal may be written to the 2023 edition too — and every other citation in it gets checked before the material is released.
