Firestopping closes the hole back up so the assembly keeps the rating its label promises. Every poke through a rated assembly gets firestopped — putty, collars, or a listed system matched to the cable type and the assembly. On a Florida retail buildout, a bundle of two dozen Cat 6 and four coax through a 1-hour corridor wall gets a listed firestop system sized for that bundle, not a smear of caulk. Do not leave an oversized hole stuffed with scrap insulation and call it done. In Florida commercial work this is one of the most common communications corrections on a final inspection. The trap: “Firestopping is a Chapter 3 power rule, so communications cables are exempt.” Wrong — 800.26 restates the duty inside Chapter 8 precisely because Chapter 8 stands alone. Second trap: a hole packed tight with insulation is not firestopped; only an approved method restores the rating. Coax bundle through a rated corridor wall with the annular space left open. Penetration stuffed with scrap insulation or foam instead of a listed firestop system. Firestop system that does not match the cable type or the assembly it protects. Sleeve through a rated floor sealed on one side only. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Never run a cable hotter than its rating
x: No wire or cable may be used in a way that makes its operating temperature exceed the temperature rating of the wire or cable. It is a one-sentence general rule — the Chapter 8 counterpart of the temperature limits the rest of the Code puts on conductors. The heat it guards against can come from anywhere: • The space itself — a hot attic, a boiler room, or a sun-baked exterior run. • The cable's own load — communications cables that deliver power to devices warm up from the inside. • The bundle — the middle of a fat bundle of powered cables warms up most, because its heat has nowhere to go. The cable types in 800.179 are built around temperature: suitable for at least 60°C, with any higher rating marked on the cable. This section is the installation rule that says the rating has to be respected in the field, not just on the reel. Heat ages insulation. A jacket run past its rating turns brittle and cracks, and a bundle cooking from the inside can degrade for years above a ceiling before anyone sees it. The first symptom is usually intermittent data faults on the hottest runs; the end of the story is a cable plant that has to be replaced. Florida attic in July: the air at the roof deck is already hot before any current flows, and a PoE switch feeding cameras and access points puts real load on every pair in the bundle. Split the home runs into two smaller bundles instead of one fat one, keep them low in the attic and out of the insulation where the layout allows, and never strap a powered bundle against a flue or a recessed luminaire housing. If a design truly needs one big powered bundle, that is a design conversation — not a field shortcut. The trap answer is that temperature only matters for power conductors, or that a cable marked 60°C may be installed anywhere because 'it is rated.' 800.27 is about operating temperature in the actual installation: a hot space, the cable's own load, and bundle heating stack up, and together they can push a cable past its rating even when every circuit is inside its own limits. One fat bundle of powered Ethernet cable pulled through the hottest part of a Florida attic. Communications cable buried in blown insulation so the heat it makes cannot escape. Powered bundle strapped tight against a flue, steam line, or recessed luminaire housing. Long powered runs cinched into one solid bundle with no air between cables. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Overhead wires and cables coming into a building
x: Overhead communications wires and cables that enter a building have clearance and separation rules where they cross roofs and where they run near the power service. • A communications drop keeps a vertical clearance of at least 8 ft above roofs it passes over, with limited exceptions. • Where a power service drop of 750 volts or less runs above and parallel to a communications or coax drop, the two keep at least 12 in of separation through the span and at the building attachment. • That separation rule holds provided the power conductors are insulated and at least 40 in of clearance is kept between the two services at the pole. Two drops age at different rates. A communications drop that sags onto a power drop puts line voltage on the phone and coax network, and on every piece of equipment and every hand that touches it inside. The roof clearance keeps the drop out of reach of roofers, ladders, and antennas — the people and things that move around up there — and the separation keeps a failed support from becoming a cross-contact. Before you set a ladder, look up: check the comm drop's height over the roof and its distance from the power drop at the wall and back at the pole. Measure, do not eyeball — 8 ft over the roof, 12 in at the wall, 40 in at the pole. Never use the power service mast to support a communications drop. If the existing drop sags into the power drop, that is a provider call, not something to fix by pulling it tighter yourself. The trap answer is “12 in of separation everywhere covers it.” The 12 in is only half the rule: it runs through the span and at the attachment, and it only holds while the power conductors are insulated and the pole keeps 40 in between the two services. Second trap: 8 ft is the clearance over a roof the drop passes over — not over the ground, and not a suggestion when the roof is 'barely' under the span. Communications drop crossing a roof with less than 8 ft of vertical clearance. Comm and power drops touching or nearly touching at the building attachment. Communications drop supported from the power service mast. Separation fine at the wall but gone at the pole, where the two services share hardware. Sagged existing drop left in contact with the power drop after a service change. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Underground cables where power is also present
x: Underground communications wires and cables that share a manhole, handhole, or similar enclosure with electric light, power, Class 1, or non-power-limited fire alarm conductors must be kept apart from those conductors by a suitable barrier. The point is simple: a space where a worker may reach in and grab a cable cannot mix exposed power conductors with communications cable as if they were the same system. The barrier has to be permanent and suitable, not a scrap of cardboard or a cable draped to the far side. A handhole is dark, wet and crowded, and a worker reaching in cannot tell a communications cable from a power conductor by feel. If a jacket is nicked or a power conductor faults, the 'harmless' cable in the same space can carry line voltage to the next person who grabs it — possibly a telephone tech who never expected voltage at all. The barrier keeps two systems that share a hole from ever sharing a touch. Sharma rarely opens manholes, but the same thinking applies at underground entrances and pull points on light-commercial work. On a Clermont strip plaza, the crew opened a handhole to pull a camera feed and found the existing comm cable lying across the lot-lighting conductors with no barrier at all. Do not just close the lid — report it and get the separation corrected before the new cable goes in. The trap answer is that draping the communications cable to the far side of the manhole is separation. Wrong. 800.47 wants a suitable barrier — a permanent, physical separation built into the enclosure — not distance by habit that disappears the first time someone re-dresses the cables. Communications cable lying against exposed power conductors in a handhole, with no barrier. A scrap of cardboard or plywood offered as the barrier — neither suitable nor permanent. Barrier removed during another trade's work in the enclosure and never replaced. Lid closed on a known mixed enclosure without reporting it to anyone. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding a metal conduit that carries the entrance cable
x: When the communications entrance wire or cable arrives inside a metal conduit, the conduit stops being just a sleeve. Section 800.49 requires that metal conduit to be connected, by a bonding conductor or a grounding electrode conductor, to a grounding electrode — or to the building grounding electrode system where one exists — using the connection points given in 800.100(B). First choice on that list is the intersystem bonding termination; after that come the building's grounding electrode system and the other accessible points the section names, and in a building with no grounding means at all, an electrode installed for the purpose. A floating metal entrance conduit can sit at a very different potential from the building during a surge, which is exactly what the bond prevents. The entrance conduit is a long piece of metal that starts outside the building, where lightning and utility surges arrive, and ends inside next to grounded equipment. Left floating, it can charge to a different voltage than everything around it and flash across to the nearest grounded metal — or to a person touching it. Bonding ties it to the same earth reference, so the whole entrance rises and falls together. On a Winter Garden house, the provider's entrance cable comes down the wall in a 3/4 in EMT sleeve to the demarc box. Before the provider's appointment, we set a bonding clamp on the EMT and ran the bond about 8 ft to the intersystem bonding termination at the Siemens meter-main — a listed 800.100(B) point, not the water pipe that happened to be closer. Plastic conduit would not need the bond, but it also would not extend the point of entrance the way a grounded metal raceway can, so the metal sleeve plus its bond is the better entrance. The trap is landing the conduit bond on the nearest water pipe because metal is metal. Section 800.49 sends you to the connection points in 800.100(B) — the intersystem bonding termination first, then the building grounding system points the section lists. A random pipe may not be bonded to anything. Second trap: skipping the bond because the cable inside is fiber. The rule is about the metal conduit, not the signal inside it. Metal entrance conduit left floating — no bonding conductor or clamp installed (800.49). Conduit bond landed on a nearby water pipe or a receptacle ground instead of an 800.100(B) connection point. Bonding conductor smaller than 14 AWG, or run long and looping — 800.100(A) sets the floor and wants the run short; at a dwelling it may not exceed 20 ft. Building with no grounding system bonded to a short scrap rod — 800.100(B) describes the purpose electrode as at least 5 ft long and 1/2 in in diameter. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Keeping communications cable away from lightning protection
x: Where it is practicable, communications wires and cables on a building — coax included — are kept at least 6 ft away from lightning protection system conductors. • The 6 ft is measured between the communications cable path and the nearest lightning conductor, down leads included. • Where 6 ft genuinely cannot be had, the separation is not guessed: it is calculated from the sideflash equation in NFPA 780, the lightning protection standard. A down conductor carries an enormous surge for a few microseconds. A communications cable run alongside it can pick up enough of that energy by induction to destroy equipment or start a fire inside. A lightning strike does not have to hit a cable to wreck what is on it. The surge racing down a down lead throws a fast, huge magnetic pulse, and any long cable running parallel and close couples to it like the secondary of a transformer. The induced surge rides the coax or data cable straight into modems, panels and TVs. Six feet of air breaks that coupling down to a level the equipment can survive. Florida is lightning country, so this one is not theoretical here. On any building with air terminals and down leads — churches, schools, larger custom homes — route the data and coax entrances to a different wall or corner whenever you can. On a church job the down lead came down the east wall, so we put the coax and Cat 6 entrance on the south wall and held 9 ft between the two paths at the closest point. If the only entrance is beside a down lead, raise it with the lead before the rough-in, not at final. Florida has more lightning than any other state; AHJs and insurers here take separation from lightning protection conductors seriously. Confirm the local position where a building has an existing lightning protection system. The trap answer is that bonding fixes it: "the comm system is bonded to the lightning protection system, so the cable can run with the down lead." Bonding ties the grounding electrodes together; it does nothing about induction along a parallel run. The 6 ft separation is still required where practicable. Coax entrance run about 2 ft from a lightning down lead where the adjacent wall was open. Communications cable strapped to the lightning down conductor for support. Separation under 6 ft with no sideflash calculation and nothing documented. Down lead relocated beside the existing communications entrance, and the cable never moved. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bonding and grounding at the entrance — the heart of Chapter 8
x: This is the section the whole chapter hangs on. It covers how communications cables and primary protectors get bonded and grounded: the metallic parts that arrive from outside — cable sheaths, protector grounds, coax shields handled under their own articles — must be tied to the building's grounding system at the entrance. The bonding or grounding conductor has its own rules, broken out on the next three pages: • Material and size: copper or another corrosion-resistant conductive material, not smaller than 14 AWG, with capacity at least equal to the sheath or conductor it serves — and never required to be larger than 6 AWG (800.100(A)). • Length: run as short as practicable; in a one- or two-family dwelling it may not exceed 20 ft (800.100(A)). • Where it lands: first choice is the intersystem bonding termination; without one, the grounding electrode system or another accessible point 800.100(B) names. • A separate communications electrode is allowed past the length limit only when it is bonded to the power grounding system with a conductor not smaller than 6 AWG (800.100(D)). Done right, a surge arriving on a phone line or coax shield is carried to the same earth reference as the power service, so the two systems rise and fall together instead of sparking across to each other. Two systems with two separate earths is the failure this section prevents. Lightning or a fault can raise one ground thousands of volts above the other for a fraction of a second, and that difference appears across the television, the modem, and the person touching both. One bonded system means one reference: everything rises and falls together, and the surge leaves by the path built for it. Pick the protector and grounding-block location to keep this conductor as short and straight as you can. Land it at the intersystem bonding termination when one is there — that device exists precisely for this job (see 250.94, item L-060). Photograph the finished bond; it is the first thing a communications inspector looks for. S-09 puts the meter outside with the panel directly behind it inside, where the house allows. That same service spot is where the intersystem bonding termination belongs, so plan the communications bond to land at the service, not at a random rod driven by the cable installer. The trap answer is “drive a separate rod for the cable system and keep it away from the power ground — cleaner that way.” Backwards. A separate communications electrode must be bonded to the power grounding electrode system with 6 AWG or larger (800.100(D)); two unbonded earths are the hazard, not the cure. Second trap: sizing the bond off the service size. The floor is 14 AWG, and it never has to be larger than 6 AWG. Protector or grounding block bonded to a separate rod with no bond back to the power grounding system. Bonding conductor smaller than 14 AWG. Bonding conductor run long and wandering in a dwelling — over the 20 ft limit. Bond landed on a random water pipe or lug instead of the intersystem bonding termination or a point 800.100(B) names. Metal raceway carrying the bonding conductor left unbonded at one end. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The bonding conductor itself — material, size, and length
x: The conductor that bonds the protector or cable sheath has to be copper or another corrosion-resistant conductive material, solid or stranded, and listed for the purpose, with the insulation choices the section allows. • Not smaller than 14 AWG • Its ampacity at least that of the metallic sheath or protected conductor it serves — but it never has to be larger than 6 AWG • Run as short as practicable, and in a one- or two-family dwelling not over 20 ft • Where it runs in a metal raceway, that raceway is bonded at both ends • Run in as straight a line as practicable, and protected from physical damage This conductor is the path a lightning surge or a power-contact fault takes off the cable sheath and the protector. A thin, long, or wandering conductor has impedance exactly when the surge needs a low-impedance path, so the surge looks for another route — through equipment, or through a person. Short, straight, and adequately sized keeps the surge on the conductor and off everything else. That is why this section cares about the conductor itself — its material, its size, and its length — and not only about where it lands. On a Winter Garden slab home, the coax and phone protectors land on the garage wall and the intersystem bonding termination sits beside the Siemens meter-main, 11 ft away. A 14 AWG copper bonding conductor run straight along the wall lands at 11 ft — inside the 20 ft dwelling limit with room to spare. At a second house the only legal landing point measured 24 ft from the protector, so the protector moved to the other side of the meter instead of stretching the conductor past the limit. Measure the run before you mount the protector, not after. The trap is reading 6 AWG as the minimum size. Six AWG is the ceiling — the conductor never has to be larger than 6 AWG, however big the sheath. The floor is 14 AWG, and between the two the conductor's ampacity must at least match the metallic sheath or protected conductor it serves. Bonding conductor run 24 ft across a dwelling garage to reach the panel — over the 20 ft dwelling limit. Protector bonded with 18 AWG bell wire stripped out of thermostat cable — smaller than 14 AWG. Bonding conductor in EMT with the raceway bonded at one end only. Conductor draped in loops around the water heater instead of run short and straight, and left unprotected where it can be struck. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Where the bonding conductor is allowed to land
x: This part lists, in order, the places the entrance bonding or grounding conductor may terminate. • First choice is the intersystem bonding termination, if the building has one. • Without one, it lands on the building's grounding electrode system or one of the accessible grounding points the section names, such as the grounding electrode conductor or the service equipment enclosure, following the exact list in the printed section. • In a building with no grounding means at all, it lands on an electrode installed for the purpose — a rod at least 5 ft long and 1/2 in in diameter is the minimum the section describes for that case. Every communications entrance has to end up at the same electrical reference as the power system. If the cable plant bonds to one point and the power system to another, lightning or a fault puts the difference between those points across the equipment — and across anyone touching both. The ordered list exists so the installer takes the best available landing instead of inventing one. New townhouse in Winter Garden: the Siemens meter-main has an intersystem bonding termination, so the cable and phone bonds land there — first choice, done. On an older Orlando ranch with no IBT, land on the grounding electrode conductor at the service, the nearest accessible point on the list. Use the first landing point on the list that the building actually has, and use the nearest accessible one. Do not land the bond on a random receptacle ground, a plumbing vent, or a rod you cannot prove is bonded to the power system. Item L-060 (250.94) explains the termination device itself. The trap is driving a fresh rod wherever the cable enters and calling it grounded. A rod installed for the purpose is the last landing on the list, for a building with no grounding means at all — and at minimum 5 ft long and 1/2 in in diameter. If the building has a grounding electrode system, the bond belongs on the list, not on a new rod of your own. Bond landed on a receptacle ground or a water pipe stub instead of a point on the 800.100(B) list. New rod driven at the cable entrance while the building's grounding electrode system sits unused. Purpose-installed rod shorter than 5 ft or under 1/2 in diameter. Bond landed on a rod with no proof it is bonded to the power grounding electrode system. IBT present at the meter-main but the bond run past it to a farther point. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bonding a separate communications electrode back to the power system
x: Sometimes the bonding conductor for a communications entrance cannot stay inside its length limit — in a dwelling, 800.100(A) caps that run at 20 ft. When it cannot, a separate ground rod may be driven for the communications system at the entrance. Section 800.100(D) then adds the condition that makes that separate electrode safe: • The separate electrode is never allowed to stand alone • It must be bonded to the building's power grounding electrode system • The bonding conductor is no smaller than 6 AWG Two unbonded earth connections at one house are worse than one, because a surge can put thousands of volts between them — right across the equipment inside the house. Earth is not at one uniform voltage during a lightning strike or a utility surge. Two separate rods can sit at very different potentials for the instant that matters, and the difference shows up between the coax shield and the power ground inside a TV or a modem. The 6 AWG bond forces both systems to rise and fall together, so that difference never appears across the equipment. Orlando two-story: the meter-main is on the west wall and the cable and phone demarc is on the east wall, about 34 ft of bonding-conductor route away — past the 20 ft dwelling limit. We drive a rod at the demarc, land the protector bond on it, and then run a 6 AWG copper bond from that rod back to the power grounding electrode system at the meter-main. The same 6 AWG bonding rule shows up again for antennas in 810.21(J) and for CATV in 820.100(D) — learn it once, use it three times. The trap answer is 'the separate rod is the communications ground, so the job is done.' A separate electrode standing by itself is exactly what 800.100(D) forbids: the rod is permitted only with the 6 AWG bond back to the power system. The second trap is the size: 14 AWG is the floor for the protector bonding conductor in 800.100(A), but the electrode-to-system bond in (D) is 6 AWG minimum. Rod driven at the cable entrance and left unbonded — no conductor back to the power grounding electrode system. Bond between the communications rod and the power system smaller than 6 AWG. Protector bonded to the separate rod only, with that rod treated as the building's ground. Bonding conductor routed past the 20 ft dwelling limit with no separate electrode installed — neither path of 800.100 followed. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding the primary protector at a mobile home
x: A mobile home gets its own version of the 800.100 protector-grounding recipe, because the power service usually is not on the home itself. Under 550.32(A) the service equipment or disconnecting means sits nearby — in sight from the home and not more than 30 ft from its exterior wall. • Where that equipment is in place, the primary protector is grounded and bonded into that grounding arrangement, as 800.100 describes. • Where there is no mobile home service equipment or grounded disconnect in sight and within 30 ft, 800.106(A) sends the grounding to the electrode options in 800.100(B)(3) — the same list used at a building with no intersystem bonding termination and no grounding means. • Either way, 800.106(B) adds a step an ordinary house does not need: bond the protector's grounding terminal to the mobile home's metal frame, or to the grounding terminal the home provides, with copper not smaller than 12 AWG. This section is also why the 6 AWG bond-back rule in 800.100(D) carries a mobile-home exception — at a mobile home, 800.106 replaces it. A mobile home sits on piers, and its metal frame is the biggest thing the occupants touch. If the telephone protector grounds to one electrode and the frame sits at another potential, a surge puts that difference across the phone, the appliances and the people between them. The 12 AWG frame bond forces the protector ground and the frame to rise and fall together. Manufactured home in a Florida park: find the pedestal first. It stands 18 ft from the home's exterior wall, in plain sight, so the protector grounds into the pedestal's grounding system — and the crew still adds the 12 AWG copper bond from the protector's grounding terminal to the home's frame rail. On the next call the pedestal is 45 ft away: that job is on the 800.100(B)(3) electrode list, and the frame bond is still required. A rod by itself never replaces it. The trap is "the protector has its own ground rod, so it is grounded." A lone rod does not tie the telephone ground to the frame the occupants touch, and it does not satisfy 800.106. The frame bond — copper, 12 AWG minimum — is required in every case, whichever grounding route the protector takes. No bond between the protector grounding terminal and the mobile home frame — the write-up on almost every manufactured-home call. Frame bond smaller than 12 AWG, or run in aluminum — 800.106(B) calls for copper. Protector grounded to a lone rod beside the home while a grounded pedestal sits 20 ft away in plain sight. Protector grounded into the pedestal system when the disconnect is 45 ft from the wall — wrong case; the 800.100(B)(3) electrode list applies. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Raceways and cable routing assemblies for communications
x: Communications wires and cables may be run in communications raceways and cable routing assemblies, as long as both are listed and chosen for the space they serve — plenum, riser, or general-purpose — under the application tables in 800.154. The raceway levels track the cable levels in 800.179 and the listing rules in 800.182, and a point from 800.182 is worth memorizing here: a rated raceway does not upgrade the cable inside it, so a plenum raceway in an air-handling space still has to contain plenum-rated CMP cable. Chapter 9 conduit-fill rules do not govern ordinary communications cables in these raceways. The section keeps one exception: medium-power network-powered broadband cables. In other words, a listed low-voltage raceway is its own wiring method here; do not borrow a Chapter 3 conduit rule and assume it decides the question. The raceway levels exist because of fire and smoke, not electricity. A pathway that runs through an air-handling ceiling or a vertical shaft is a ready-made route for smoke to travel between spaces, so the pathway and the cable in it are both rated for the space. The fill exception exists for the opposite reason: a medium-power broadband cable carries real power alongside the signal, so it is treated more like a power cable than a whisper of data. On a light-commercial job in Kissimmee — a small medical office — the data runs cross an air-handling ceiling, so the spec is plenum-level raceway with CMP cable inside; the run down the shaft to the first floor is riser level with CMR. We kept the manufacturer's fill guidance for the cable routing assembly even though Chapter 9 fill percentages are not the governing rule — the listing still expects the cable supported and not crushed. And one boundary to respect: if the job is really Class 2 or Class 3 control wiring, you are in Article 725 (Chapter 7), not here. Two traps meet on this page. First: the raceway is plenum-rated, so the CM cable inside it is fine in the plenum. No — 800.182 is explicit that the raceway does not upgrade the cable; each is matched to the space on its own. Second: applying Chapter 9 conduit-fill percentages to a listed communications raceway. Chapter 9 fill does not govern ordinary communications cables here — the only exception the section keeps is medium-power network-powered broadband cable. General-purpose raceway installed in an air-handling ceiling where plenum level is required (800.110, 800.182). CM cable pulled through a plenum raceway in a plenum space — the raceway's rating does not upgrade the cable (800.182). Unlisted channel or hardware-store PVC used as a raceway for communications cable — 800.110 requires listed raceways and cable routing assemblies. Cable routing assembly stuffed past the manufacturer's fill guidance and left unsupported between floors. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Installing cables inside the building — ducts, plenums, and risers
x: This long section is the inside-the-building installation rulebook for communications cable. • Cables in ducts made for environmental air follow the duct rules the section references. • Cables in other air-handling spaces (plenums) must be the plenum types allowed there — CMP. • Vertical runs that pass through one or more floors — risers — need riser-rated cable (CMR), or one of the protected alternatives the section lists, such as cable in a metal raceway or a fireproof shaft with firestops at each floor. • One- and two-family dwellings get their own, more relaxed list, which is why house work and commercial work part company here. • Cables installed inside must be listed, and a voltage rating is not to be marked on a communications cable, because that marking invites someone to treat it as power wire. In a fire, cable jackets are fuel and smoke spreaders. A plenum is part of the air system, so a burning ordinary cable pumps smoke into every room the air handler serves. A riser shaft is a chimney between floors. Matching the cable's fire rating to the space keeps the cable from becoming the path the fire and smoke take through the building. Before rough-in, ask one question per run: is this space moving air, or does this run pass a floor? A yes to the first means CMP; a yes to the second means CMR or a listed protected path. On a two-story Winter Park office, the Cat 6A home runs cross a return-air ceiling plenum and then drop down a shaft to the first-floor rack — one cable has to satisfy both spaces, so CMP goes in everywhere on that job. At a house, CM or CMX from the dwelling list is normally the right shelf to shop from. The trap is shopping by category instead of by fire rating: a Cat 6 cable is not automatically legal in a plenum or a riser. The letters CMP, CMR, CMG, CM and CMX rate fire behavior, not speed. A second trap: a voltage rating printed on the jacket — the section forbids marking one on communications cable, because it invites someone to treat the cable as power wire. CM cable run above a return-air ceiling plenum in a strip-mall tenant space. Riser run between floors in CM instead of CMR, with no raceway or shaft protection. Unlisted cable pulled from a bulk spool with no listing mark on the jacket. CMX carried out of the dwelling list into a commercial riser shaft. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Separation from power — the section in one view
x: Communications cables must be kept apart from electric light, power, Class 1, and non-power-limited fire alarm conductors. This page is the whole section in one view; the next two pages take the halves one at a time. • Sharing: comm cable may not sit in the same raceway, box, or enclosure with power conductors unless a separation setup covered on the next page genuinely applies (800.133(A)(1)). • Open runs: where comm cable runs alongside power wiring in the open, keep at least 2 in between them (800.133(A)(2)). • Support: never use the outside of a raceway as a support for communications cable (800.133(B)). Power conductors are the energy source in the wall. A comm cable lashed against them picks up induced voltage on a good day. On a bad day — a fault, a surge, a nail through both cables — full line voltage lands on phone and data jacks all over the house, on equipment and people never built for it. Separation is what keeps the low-voltage system low-voltage. Keep low-voltage cable out of power boxes and power raceways unless a listed barrier setup on the next page genuinely applies. Do not strap, tape, or tie a data or coax run to the outside of a conduit for support. The classic Florida spec-house fail is the shared stud bay: Cat 6 zip-tied to a branch-circuit home run down the same stud. Split them — their own holes, 2 in apart in the open. When an inspector says 'separation,' this section is what they mean, and the distance is 2 in, confirmed against the 2020 text, not the larger figures in some exam-prep sheets. The trap answer is 12 in — or 'they can never be in the same building.' In the open, the number is 2 in. The reverse trap catches just as many: because 2 in works in the open, apprentices assume a shared box is fine with a little space inside it. It is not. Sharing a raceway or box is the (A)(1) half of the rule, with its own barrier conditions. Cat 6 or coax in the same box or raceway as power conductors, with no listed barrier. Data run zip-tied to a branch-circuit home run down a stud bay — no 2 in on the open run. Coax strapped to the outside of an EMT run and supported by it. Comm cable draped across the top of a panel or a power raceway in the attic. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Sharing a raceway, box, or enclosure with power
x: Communications conductors are not permitted in the same raceway, box, or enclosure as electric light, power, Class 1, or non-power-limited fire alarm conductors as a general rule. The exceptions are narrow: • Sharing is allowed where the two systems are separated by a permanent barrier or a listed divider. • Power conductors may be brought into a communications enclosure only to feed the communications equipment itself, routed inside the enclosure to keep at least 1/4 in (6 mm) of separation from the communications wiring (800.133(A)(1), Exception No. 2). A shared box with a listed divider is a designed product, not two cables stuffed into one handy box. Communications cable insulation is not rated to sit against power conductors, and a fault on the power side can put line voltage on a cable that runs to every room and out to the street plant. Mixing the systems in one raceway or box also puts a line-voltage surprise in front of the next technician who opens the box expecting low-voltage work. The barrier and the divider are what make the exception safe. Structured-wiring panel in a Lake Nona home: the panel needs a receptacle inside it to power the switch and modem. That power feed may enter the communications enclosure because it feeds the communications equipment itself — and inside, we route it dressed away from the Cat 6 bundle, keeping at least 1/4 in (6 mm) of separation. Default answer on site: separate boxes, separate raceways. If a plan shows a divided box, verify the divider is the listed one made for that box before rough-in, not after the drywall is up. The trap is reading the 1/4 in (6 mm) figure as a general mixing allowance: "keep a quarter inch apart and you can share the box." Wrong. The 1/4 in separation belongs to Exception No. 2, inside a communications enclosure, for power feeding that equipment only. A junction box shared without a permanent barrier or listed divider fails the general rule. Cat 6 and a 120 V branch circuit pulled in the same conduit "because the run was short." Power and communications cables landed in one handy box with no barrier or listed divider. Divider snapped in from a different box line: not the listed divider made for that box. Power feed inside the structured-wiring panel dressed tight against the Cat 6 bundle, no 1/4 in separation. Non-power-limited fire alarm conductors sharing a raceway with communications cables. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The 2-inch separation in open runs
x: Where communications conductors run near power or Class 1 conductors outside a shared enclosure, they must be separated by at least 2 in. That 2 in can be provided by space alone, or by one of the constructions the section recognizes: • Power conductors in a raceway, or in a metal-sheathed, armored, nonmetallic-sheathed, or UF cable assembly — the sheath or raceway already provides the separation • The communications cable in its own raceway What the rule will not accept is communications cable laid directly against open power wiring with nothing between them. Communications cable is built for signals, not for line voltage. Run tight against power wiring, it picks up induced voltage and hum, and a fault — or a nail through both cables — can put 120 V on a phone line, a network jack, or the technician holding it. Two inches of space, or a sheath or raceway doing the same job, keeps the two systems out of each other's failures. Sharma practice is stricter than the code here: in a stud bay, drill separate holes and keep the 2 in, and in an attic do not lay Cat 6 across a bundle of Romex and call the joist a separator. The Code itself is satisfied where the power conductors are in a raceway or a sheathed cable assembly (the NM sheath counts) — the house habit keeps the 2 in anyway. If a crossing is unavoidable, cross at right angles rather than running parallel in contact, and keep the parallel distance honest everywhere else. The trap is demanding 2 in of empty air everywhere. Where the power conductors are in a raceway or a sheathed cable assembly — NM counts — or the communications cable is in its own raceway, the bare 2 in is not demanded, because the construction already provides the separation. The opposite trap also fails: inside a shared box, the rule is (A)(1)'s barrier or divider, not this 2 in. And a joist between the two cables is not a construction the section recognizes — the separation is measured between the cables themselves. Cat 6 zip-tied along a bundle of Romex for a 30 ft attic run. Coax stapled directly against open power conductors in a stud bay. Parallel run holding 2 in at the bored holes but pinched into contact where both cables pass the same fire block. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Where each cable type may be used — the application tables
x: The tables in this section are the permission slip for cable types: they match listed communications cables against the places each type may be installed — plenums, risers, general use, dwellings. A higher-rated cable may substitute for a lower one down the ladder; a lower-rated cable may never substitute upward. • CMP — plenum spaces, and anywhere a lower type may run • CMR — risers and general use; not plenums • CMG and CM — general use and dwellings; not plenums or risers (one shared rung — either may stand in for the other) • CMX — limited use in dwellings, and in raceways and short exposed runs within the conditions the table sets The ladder order and the substitutions are the same ones stated on the cable-types page (800.179). The ladder exists because fire behaves differently in each space. A plenum moves air — and smoke — to every room it serves. A riser shaft is a chimney between floors. A cable rated for a harsher space can serve a milder one, but the reverse puts a cable that burns and smokes too freely into the space where that does the most harm. Downward substitution is safe; upward substitution hands smoke a distribution system. The tables in this section are where the ladder becomes the rule for each space: they say, space by space, which types may run there. When a supplier substitutes cable, check the jacket legend against the space, not against the purchase order. On a Lake Nona medical office rough-in, the delivered Cat 6A was CM where the ceiling was a return-air plenum; the CMP on the order was the right cable and the CM went back, because CMP can go almost anywhere communications cable can go and CM cannot go in that ceiling. CMX cannot leave its dwelling lane at all. The trap is substituting upward to finish the job: CM in a plenum or CMX in a riser 'because it was on the truck.' Substitution runs one way only — down the ladder. The mirror trap is wasting CMP money everywhere out of habit; the table lets each space take its own type, and dwellings have the widest list. CMX installed in a commercial riser shaft because it was left over from a house job. CM cable above a return-air plenum ceiling, substituted by the supplier without a jacket-legend check. CMR pulled into a plenum as 'one step down' from CMP — the substitution ran upward. Installed cable with an illegible jacket legend, its type claimed from the purchase order instead. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The cable types themselves — CMP, CMR, CMG, CM, CMX
x: This section defines the listed communications cable types by how they behave in fire. Type CMP is the plenum type, tested for low flame spread and smoke in air-handling spaces. Type CMR is the riser type, for vertical runs between floors, and Types CMG and CM are general-purpose types for ordinary horizontal runs. Type CMX is the limited-use type, restricted in size and use, and at home mainly in one- and two-family dwellings. Conductors in these cables are copper, other than in coaxial constructions handled under Article 820. The letters say nothing about speed or category — a CMP Cat 5e and a CM Cat 6 are rated by fire behavior, not performance. Substitutions run downhill only (800.154): • CMP may stand in for any type below it. • CMR may stand in for CMG, CM or CMX. • CMG may stand in for CM or CMX, and CM may stand in for CMX. • Nothing substitutes upward — CMX never replaces CM, and CM never goes in a riser or a plenum. In a fire, cable is a fuse that runs through the whole building. The wrong jacket carries flame from floor to floor through a riser, and cable burning in an air-handling space puts smoke straight into the breathing air of every room the system serves. The type ladder exists so the cable in each space has been tested for exactly the way fire and smoke behave in that space. Read the jacket before you pull: the type letters decide where the cable may go, and the category marking decides what it can carry. Do not let a cheap roll of CMX talk you into a commercial riser. Keep one shelf rule in your head: plenum space, CMP; between floors, CMR; same floor, CM or CMG; house, CM or CMX within its limits. The trap answer is “Cat 6 outperforms Cat 5e, so a CM Cat 6 may go in the plenum where CMP Cat 5e was specified.” Category is performance; the type letters are fire behavior. A CM cable in a plenum fails no matter what it can carry. Second trap: reading CMX as a general commercial type. It is limited-use, and at home mainly in one- and two-family dwellings. CM or CMG cable installed in a riser shaft between floors. CMR cable run exposed in an air-handling (plenum) ceiling. CMX cable used for a general commercial run. Jacket print unreadable or unmarked cable installed as if it were listed. Coaxial-style construction assumed to follow the twisted-pair type letters. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 800.179: Moved hybrid power and communications cable general requirements to Article 800 with the other communication cable types. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding hardware has to be listed
x: Where bonding or grounding is required, the devices used to connect a shield, sheath, or other non-current-carrying metallic member of a cable to a bonding conductor or a grounding electrode conductor must be listed — or be part of listed equipment. • 800.100 specifies the conductor itself — its material, its size, its length, and where it may land. This section governs the clamp or fitting that joins the cable's metal to that conductor. • A primary protector or network interface device with its own grounding terminal satisfies the rule through its listing. • A random piece of hardware does not. If the fitting is not listed for grounding and bonding, it does not count, however solid it looks. The clamp is the weak link in every entrance bond. An unlisted fitting corrodes, works loose, or bites through the shield it was supposed to protect, and the bond silently opens — the conductor still hangs there looking grounded while surge energy has no path out. Listed hardware is tested to clamp the cable it is made for, stay tight, and carry the current the bond exists to carry. Use the grounding terminal built into the protector or interface device, or a listed grounding clamp made for bonding a cable shield or sheath. At a house entrance that is the listed clamp on the grounding block, landed with the 14 AWG bond from 800.100. A hose clamp, a sheet-metal screw driven through the sheath, or an unmarked clamp off the hardware shelf is not a listed grounding device — and the fitting at the entrance is exactly where a sharp inspector looks first. The trap is answering with conductor rules. '14 AWG copper, 20 ft max' is 800.100 — the conductor. This section is about the device that makes the connection. A perfect conductor landed with an unlisted hose clamp still fails 800.180. Shield bonded with a hose clamp or an unmarked hardware-store clamp. Sheet-metal screw driven through the cable sheath as the 'ground connection.' Bond conductor landed under a random screw on the protector instead of its grounding terminal. Bond wire held against the shield with a plastic zip tie — no listed device at all. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Communications raceways and cable routing assemblies — the listing rules
x: This section is the listing home for the two support systems Article 800 builds communications installations with: • Communications raceways — the enclosed nonmetallic channels defined in Article 100, close cousins of ENT. • Cable routing assemblies — the single or multiple channels that support high densities of cable. The raceway rules follow the same three fire levels as the cables themselves — plenum, riser, and general-purpose — and the section carries two marking tables, Table 800.182(a) for cable routing assemblies and Table 800.182(b) for communications raceways, so the level is printed on the product. One point installers miss: a rated raceway does not upgrade the cable inside it. A plenum communications raceway in an air-handling space under 300.22(C) still has to contain plenum-rated CMP cable. The raceway and the cable are each matched to the space on their own. In a fire, the pathway is part of the fuel and part of the smoke path. Plenum spaces move air toward people's lungs, and vertical shafts carry fire from floor to floor. Matching the raceway's fire level to the space keeps the support system from spreading flame and smoke — and the cable inside needs its own matching rating, because the raceway is not a fireproof box. Office fit-out in Orlando with a return-air ceiling plenum. The print on the raceway has to read plenum level before it is hung, and the cable pulled into it is CMP — both, not one of two. The run down the shaft gets riser-level raceway and CMR cable; the ordinary office runs get general-purpose. Nonmetallic communications raceways go in under the ENT rules this section points to — bends, supports, and joints per 362.24 through 362.56 — and cable routing assemblies support their cable at the intervals the listing allows. The trap: 'The raceway is plenum rated, so the CM cable inside it is fine in the plenum.' Wrong. The raceway does not upgrade the cable. Each is matched to the space on its own, so a plenum space needs plenum-level raceway and CMP cable together. General-purpose raceway hung in a return-air plenum ceiling. CM cable pulled into a plenum-rated raceway in an air-handling space and passed off as a plenum installation. Riser shaft run made in general-purpose raceway. Raceway fire level never checked — the print on the product ignored at rough-in. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 805 — Communications circuits
x: Article 805 is where the old pre-2020 Article 800 went to live. It covers the traditional communications circuits — the telephone-style circuits that run from the service provider's demarcation point to the customer's communications equipment — and the specific rules for those circuits that Article 800 does not already state generally. Its working topics: • Which circuits need a primary protector, and where it goes (805.90) • How the metallic sheath of an entering cable is grounded or interrupted at the entrance (805.93) • The one communications outlet every new dwelling unit owes (805.156) If Article 800 is the chapter's foundation, Article 805 is the phone-and-data entrance built on it. A communications circuit is a wire that starts miles away, on poles and in plant the building owner does not control, and ends at a phone or a modem inside. Lightning and accidental contact with power conductors ride that wire indoors. Article 805 is the entrance discipline that stops the energy at the door: a protector to shunt it, a sheath grounded or interrupted so it cannot carry a surge deep into the building, and a bond that ties it all to the same earth as the power service. Most of Sharma's houses touch this article lightly: a demarc, a protector, a bond, and one outlet. On a new house in Sanford the whole 805 job is the demarc box on the garage wall, the provider's primary protector bonded under 800.100 with a run of about 6 ft to the intersystem bonding termination, the entering cable's sheath bonded at that same point, and one communications outlet roughed in and cabled back to the demarc. The failures are just as light — no protector where one is required, a sheath left floating, no outlet roughed in. Catch them at rough-in, when they are still cheap. Florida enforces NEC 2020 through the Florida Building Code 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; the FBC 9th Edition (2026) adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026. NEC 2023 applies in Florida only to permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026 (FBC 9th Ed.), so until then a 2023 study book may show different Chapter 8 numbering or wording. The trap is citing 800.156 for the dwelling-unit outlet. That was the pre-2020 address; the 2020 reorganization moved the rule to 805.156, and older checklists and study guides still carry the old number. Second trap: treating Article 800 as the whole story for a phone circuit. Article 800 states the general rules; the circuit-specific duties — protectors, sheath, the outlet — live in 805. Exposed communications circuit entering the building with no listed primary protector (805.90). Metallic sheath of the entering cable left floating — neither grounded per 800.100 nor interrupted by an insulating joint (805.93). New dwelling unit finished with no communications outlet cabled back to the demarcation point (805.156). Unshielded entrance wiring on the outside of the building run closer than 4 in to open power wiring (805.50(B)). NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 805.170: Moved communication equipment listing requirements to Article 800 leaving two subdivisions (A) and (B) for primary and secondary protectors. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Scope of communications circuits
x: This short section fixes what Article 805 covers: communications circuits and the equipment on them. A communications circuit, as the chapter defines it, is the path that extends service from the communications utility or service provider up to and including the customer's own communications equipment. • Phone and provider data circuits and their entrance equipment: Article 805, with the general rules of Article 800. • Inside wiring that is really power-limited control or signaling work: Article 725 in Chapter 7 instead. The same physical cable can fall under different articles depending on what system it serves, so the system, not the jacket color, decides. Each article carries its own separation, listing, and cable rules. Wire a control circuit under the communications rules — or a phone entrance under the control rules — and the installation can be legal-looking and still wrong: wrong cable type, wrong separation from power, wrong protection at the entrance. The scope line is what keeps the two worlds sorted. When a low-voltage scope is handed to you, ask what system each run serves before you pick an article. Phone and provider data entrance: 805 and 800. Door access, HVAC controls, and most security signaling: usually 725. On a Florida small-commercial fit-out, the same spool of Cat 6 can feed a provider phone jack in the morning (805) and a thermostat after lunch (725) — the paperwork, separation, and inspection standard change with the system, not the spool. Guessing the article is how separation and listing rules get crossed. The trap: “Cat 6 is communications cable, so every Cat 6 run is Article 805.” Wrong — the same cable serving HVAC controls or door access is power-limited circuit work under Article 725. The system the run serves decides the article; the jacket decides nothing. Provider phone entrance wired and inspected as Article 725 control work. HVAC control runs held to communications-cable rules — or the reverse — because nobody asked what the run serves. Low-voltage scope priced and roughed in with one article assumed for every run. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Circuits that require primary protectors — and the 4-inch rule outside
x: 805.50 works with 805.90: it identifies the communications circuits that require primary protectors and sets the conditions on the wiring that feeds them. • Part (A): the drop and entrance conductors used to extend circuits to a building must be listed for the purpose. • Part (B): specified unshielded communications wires and cables installed on the outside of a building must be separated at least 4 in from open electric light or power wiring that is not in a raceway or a cable assembly — subject to the alternatives and exceptions the section allows. • Part (C): circuits entering the building ahead of the primary protector must be protected by a bushing or a metal raceway, unless an exception applies — entry through masonry, or a listed fuseless-protector arrangement, for example. The outside run is the exposed run. A communications drop sitting against open power wiring picks up fault voltage and surge energy before the protector ever sees it, and conductors that enter ahead of the protector unprotected carry that energy straight past the device meant to stop it. The 4 in of air and the protected entry keep the primary protector as the first thing a surge meets. Rear wall of a small office in Ocala: the telephone drop comes down the wall about 2 in from open power wiring carried on insulators. That fails part (B) — rework the drop so the separation is 4 in or more, or use one of the alternatives the section allows. Do not reach for the indoor number here: the 2 in separation of 800.133(A)(2) is an inside rule, and the two numbers are not interchangeable. At the entrance, the circuit comes in ahead of the primary protector through a metal raceway — not through a plain hole drilled in the wood framing. The trap answer carries the indoor number outside: 2 in, from 800.133(A)(2). On the outside of the building, 805.50(B) requires 4 in from open light or power wiring that is not in a raceway or cable assembly. The reverse trap also appears — demanding 4 in between cables sharing an indoor box, where 800.133(A) governs. Unshielded communications cable strapped down an outside wall 1 to 2 in from open power wiring. Circuits entering ahead of the primary protector through a bare hole in wood framing — no bushing, no metal raceway. Drop and entrance conductors extended to the building that are not listed for the purpose. The indoor 2 in separation cited to justify an outside run that requires 4 in. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Primary protectors — where they are required and where they go
x: A listed primary protector is required on each communications circuit that is exposed to lightning, or exposed to accidental contact with power conductors operating at over 300 volts to ground. The protector is an arrester connected between each line conductor and ground, mounted the way its listing directs, with its terminals marked for line and ground. • It sits in, on, or immediately next to the building it serves, as close as practicable to the point where the circuit enters. • It never goes in a hazardous (classified) location, or near easily ignitible material. • The section recognizes fused and fuseless designs; a fuseless protector is permitted only where the conditions the section lists are met. • Secondary protectors may be added inside, in series between the primary protector and the equipment it serves. An outside drop is a long conductor hanging in the weather. It collects lightning energy and, if a support fails, it can land on a power conductor. Without an arrester at the entrance, that energy rides the pair straight to the phone system, the network gear, and anyone touching it. The protector gives the surge a short, deliberate path to ground at the door instead of through the building. Aerial phone and coax drops come into a Winter Garden house on the same wall as the Siemens meter-main. Mount the listed primary protector in its enclosure right at the entrance, beside the service, and bond it under 800.100 with the shortest honest run to the intersystem bonding termination — short protector ground, short trouble. If a circuit arrives exposed with no protector, that is a stop-and-call item for the provider or the lead, not a detail to wave through at trim. The trap answer is “the protector can go anywhere inside, as long as it is ahead of the equipment.” Location is part of the rule: in, on, or immediately next to the building, as close as practicable to the entrance, and never in a classified location. Second trap: picking a fuseless protector because it is cheaper. Fuseless is permitted only under the conditions 805.90 lists, not as a free choice. Exposed aerial circuit landed on the block with no primary protector at all. Protector mounted deep inside the building, far from the point of entrance. Protector installed in a classified location or next to stored paint and solvents. Fuseless protector used where none of the conditions in 805.90 for fuseless designs are met. Protector terminals landed backwards — line and ground markings ignored. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding or interrupting the cable sheath at the entrance
x: The non-current-carrying metallic sheath members of a communications cable entering a building must be dealt with at the entrance: either grounded following 800.100, or interrupted by an insulating joint or an equivalent device, as near as practicable to the point where the cable enters. A floating metallic sheath is a long antenna that delivers surge energy deep into the building. Grounding it at the entrance, or breaking its continuity there with an insulating joint, keeps that energy outside the living space. Section 805.93 gives exactly those two choices — there is no third option of leaving the sheath floating. The sheath is bonded to the outside plant, so it arrives at the wall carrying whatever the outside world put on it — lightning energy, fault voltage, induced surges. If that metal runs unbroken and ungrounded into the building, the energy goes looking for a path through equipment and people indoors. Dealing with the sheath at the entrance keeps the energy at the wall, where it belongs. At the demarc of an Orlando duplex rewire, the entering communications cable's shield disappears into the wall unbonded and there is no insulating joint — flag it before anything gets closed up. The fix at the entrance: bond the sheath per 800.100 with a 14 AWG minimum conductor to the intersystem bonding termination, or fit an insulating joint at the entry point. This is the communications twin of the coax rule in 820.93 — same entrance, same idea. The sheath can be grounded anywhere convenient inside the building — say, at the far-end equipment rack. Wrong. 805.93 puts the treatment as near as practicable to the point of entry. Ground it deep inside and the surge energy still travels the full length of the building to get there. Entering cable sheath left floating — no bond and no insulating joint at the entrance. Sheath bonded deep inside the building instead of at the point of entry. Insulating joint installed mid-run, leaving the entrance section of sheath unbroken and ungrounded. Bonding conductor landed on an unlisted point instead of following 800.100. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: One communications outlet in every new dwelling
x: For new construction, every dwelling unit gets at least one communications outlet. Three conditions ride on it: • The outlet is installed inside the dwelling, in a readily accessible area • It is cabled back to the service provider demarcation point • It is roughed in whether or not a provider has been chosen yet This is the rule that used to live at 800.156 before the 2020 reorganization moved it to 805.156, which is why older checklists and study guides still cite the old number. One outlet is the floor, not a design. Sharma's builders routinely want data and coax in several rooms, but the Code's own minimum is this single, cabled, accessible outlet. A dwelling with no cabled communications outlet is a house the phone and internet installers have to retrofit later — surface wiring, drilled floors, or a wireless-only service the owner never chose. The rule treats one outlet as basic infrastructure that has to be roughed in while the walls are open, because adding it after the drywall costs far more and usually looks it. New slab home in Kissimmee: the demarc lands on the garage wall where the provider drops arrive. From there we run one Cat 6 home run — about 55 ft — to a communications outlet on the living room wall, on an open stretch the owner can reach without moving furniture. The builder's plan adds coax and data to the bedrooms and the office, and we rough those in too, but if the plan had shown nothing, the one living room outlet is what the inspector is looking for. Rough it in even when the buyer has not picked a provider — a cabled outlet at the demarc is the requirement, not a live dial tone. And when an old Sharma checklist says 800.156, translate it: in the 2020 book it is 805.156. The trap is the old number and the wrong count. An answer citing 800.156 is citing the pre-2020 book — in the 2020 edition the rule is 805.156. The other wrong answer is 'one outlet per room': the Code minimum is one outlet per dwelling unit. Extra outlets are a builder spec, not a Code count. No communications outlet roughed in at all on a new dwelling — the crew treated low-voltage as the provider's problem. Outlet installed behind a fixed appliance or inside a sealed cabinet, where it is not readily accessible. Outlet plate on the wall but the cable never run back to the demarcation point. The only outlet placed in the garage — the rule wants it inside the dwelling unit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 810 — Radio and television equipment
x: Article 810 covers antenna systems: • Receiving antennas for radio and television, and satellite dishes • Their masts and lead-in conductors • Amateur and citizen-band transmitting and receiving stations Uniquely in this chapter, Article 810 is not covered by the general rules of Article 800 — it stands alone, and its own grounding section, 810.21, is the complete recipe for bonding an antenna system: the mast, the discharge unit and the run to ground are all answered inside the article. Its concerns are the ones Florida weather writes large: lightning, wind-blown lead-ins, and keeping antenna wiring clear of power conductors. An antenna is usually the tallest metal on the house, wired straight into the most sensitive electronics in it. A strike on or near the mast — or a lead-in blown across a power conductor in a storm — puts that energy on the coax and into the building. Article 810's grounding recipe gives the energy a deliberate path to earth that does not run through the television, the receiver, or the person touching them. A dish or antenna job is a grounding job with a picture at the end of it. Price and plan the mast bond, the discharge unit, and the run to a legal grounding point before anyone climbs: the bonding conductor is 10 AWG copper minimum under 810.21(H), and if a separate rod gets driven for the antenna, it bonds back to the power grounding system with 6 AWG under 810.21(J) — it never stands alone. If a mast stands within 5 ft of a swimming pool, it also has to bond to the pool's equipotential grid — see the pool rules in Chapter 6. Florida's lightning exposure makes 810.21 the most safety-critical page in this article here. Local amendments and insurer requirements on existing lightning protection systems vary; confirm with the AHJ on larger homes. The trap is reaching for Article 800 on an antenna job. Article 810 stands alone: the bonding sizes and the whole grounding recipe are in 810.21, not in 800.100. The second trap is treating the antenna's own ground rod as the finished job — a separate electrode still needs its 6 AWG bond back to the power system. Mast never bonded — the dish was mounted and aimed, and left with no grounding conductor at all. Bonding conductor smaller than 10 AWG copper landed on the mast or discharge unit. Separate rod driven for the antenna and left unbonded to the power grounding system. Lead-in entering the building with no listed discharge unit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding the mast and its supporting structure
x: Outdoor antenna masts, and the metal structures that support antennas, must be grounded following 810.21. • The mast bonding or grounding conductor is sized by 810.21 — not smaller than 10 AWG copper (810.21(H)). • There is one narrow escape: an antenna and its supporting mast or structure that sit inside a zone of protection — the area sheltered by a lightning protection system, described with a 150 ft radius rolling sphere in the lightning standard — are not required to be grounded under this section. Outside that protected zone, which means nearly every ordinary house dish and mast Sharma will meet, the mast gets its 810.21 bond, full stop. A mast is usually the highest metal on the house, holding a conductor that runs straight inside to the TV or receiver. Lightning does not have to hit it directly — a nearby strike can drive surge energy down the lead-in. The 810.21 bond gives that energy a controlled path to earth at the mast instead of through the equipment and the house wiring. Do not let “the dish is small” talk you out of the mast bond. Look for a nearby lightning protection system before claiming the zone-of-protection exception — on a normal subdivision house in Florida there is none, so ground the mast. Keep the bond run straight and protected, per 810.21, and land it on the building grounding system where 810.21 points. The trap: “The house sits next to a tall building with lightning rods, so the dish is in a zone of protection.” Wrong — the zone belongs to a lightning protection system and is measured with the 150 ft rolling sphere; a tall neighbor is not an LPS, and without one there is no zone and no exception. Dish mast with no bond at all — “it is only a small dish.” Zone-of-protection exception claimed with no lightning protection system on or near the building. Mast bond conductor smaller than 10 AWG copper. Bond run left loose and unprotected where it can be damaged. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Clearances for antenna lead-in conductors
x: Lead-in conductors from an outdoor antenna have clearance rules in three directions: • On the building: keep the lead-in from swinging closer than 2 ft to conductors of circuits of 250 volts or less, and at least 10 ft from conductors of circuits over 250 volts. • From lightning protection: at least 6 ft from lightning protection conductors. • Underground and indoors: underground lead-ins keep at least 12 in from power conductors, and indoor antenna and lead-in conductors keep at least 2 in from light and power conductors. The conductors themselves are sized from the table in 810.16 by material and length — a lead-in under 35 ft can be as small as 19 AWG copper, while runs over 150 ft step up to 12 AWG copper, with copper-clad steel and bronze sizes listed alongside. A lead-in is a long wire on a mast, swinging in the wind, wired straight into the house. If it swings into a power conductor — or a power conductor falls across it — line voltage rides the antenna wire indoors to the equipment and to whoever touches it. The clearances are written to the swung position, not the calm-day position, and the 6 ft from lightning conductors keeps a strike's sideflash from jumping onto the antenna system. Route the lead-in like it will move in wind, because in a Florida storm it will: the clearance is to the swung position, not the calm-day position. On a house with a roof mast, check the swing against the 120/240 service drop before the mast height is final — that drop is a circuit of 250 volts or less, so the number is 2 ft. Keep the indoor tail 2 in off power wiring, the same number as 800.133(A)(2). Long spans need the bigger wire from the 810.16 table, not whatever is on the truck. The trap is swapping the two building numbers: 2 ft is for circuits of 250 volts or less; 10 ft is for circuits over 250 volts. The size trap runs with it — a 160 ft lead-in is not a 19 AWG job. Over 150 ft, copper steps up to 12 AWG (Table 810.16). Lead-in passing within a foot of the service drop in its swung position. Antenna wire run down the same mast leg as the lightning down conductor, well under 6 ft away. Underground lead-in buried against the power lateral with no 12 in separation. 19 AWG lead-in stretched across a 160 ft span to a barn antenna. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Antenna discharge units
x: Each lead-in conductor from an outdoor antenna gets its own listed antenna discharge unit, or an equivalent means the section allows. The unit's job is to drain static charges off the antenna system before they reach the equipment inside. Placement has three parts: • As near as practicable to the point where the lead-in enters the building — inside or outside the wall • Not near combustible material • Not in a hazardous (classified) location A discharge unit with nowhere to drain is decoration: the unit itself must be bonded or grounded following 810.21, which is what gives the drained charge somewhere to go. An antenna and its lead-in are a collector: wind-driven rain and dust build static charge on them, and a nearby lightning strike induces a surge on the wire. Without a discharge unit at the entrance, that energy rides the lead-in straight to the tuner, the TV, and whatever else shares the rack — and can arc inside the wall on the way. The unit bleeds the charge to ground at the door instead of letting it hunt for a path indoors. A Lake Mary house has two lead-ins: a roof antenna for local channels and the dish. That means two discharge units, mounted on the outside wall right where the lead-ins enter, each bonded with 10 AWG copper down to the intersystem bonding termination — about a 9 ft run, straight. The dish lead-in came with a factory grounding block; we checked its listing before counting it as the discharge unit instead of assuming the block was listed for that duty. One unit per lead-in, at the entrance, bonded per 810.21 — that is the whole checklist. The trap answer is one discharge unit for the whole antenna system, mounted wherever the lead-ins happen to end up — a distribution block in the attic, say. Section 810.20 wants a listed unit for each lead-in conductor, placed as near as practicable to the point of entrance. Second trap: assuming the factory grounding block on a satellite lead-in automatically qualifies. It serves only if it is listed for the discharge-unit role. Lead-in conductor entering the building with no antenna discharge unit at all (810.20). One discharge unit shared by two lead-in conductors — the section requires one for each lead-in. Discharge unit mounted deep inside the attic run instead of as near as practicable to the point of entrance. Discharge unit installed next to stored combustibles, or its ground landed on a convenient pipe instead of bonded per 810.21. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The antenna bonding and grounding recipe, (A) through (K)
x: 810.21 is the complete recipe for the conductors that bond an antenna mast and its discharge unit to ground — subsections (A) through (K). • Material: copper, aluminum, copper-clad steel, bronze, or a similar corrosion-resistant conductive material.
