Copper-clad aluminum is not on the 810.21(A) list. • The conductor may be solid or stranded, and it does not have to be insulated. • Securely fastened in place, and protected where it is exposed to physical damage. • Run in as straight a line as practicable, inside or outside the building. • Landing: the intersystem bonding termination first, where one exists. Otherwise the nearest accessible point on the building grounding electrode system, or the other points the section lists. • A building with no grounding means gets an electrode described in 250.52. • Aluminum and copper-clad aluminum must not touch masonry or earth directly, and outdoors must not come within 18 in of the earth. Conductor size and the bonding of separate electrodes get their own pages — 810.21(H) and 810.21(J) — because they are the two numbers inspectors actually measure. A mast and a lead-in are lightning collectors on the roof. The bonding conductor is the one planned path that carries a strike or a static charge to earth without side-flashing into the attic or the panel. Bends, corrosion and loose fastenings all raise the impedance of that path at exactly the moment it has to work, which is why the section reads like a recipe instead of a suggestion. Gable-end mast on a Florida ranch home, dish and over-the-air antenna on the same mount. The crew runs 10 AWG copper — the 810.21(H) minimum — straight down the gable wall from the mast clamp, through a protective sleeve where the run passes the side walkway, and lands it on the intersystem bonding termination beside the meter. Total run 22 ft, no sharp bends, no attic tour. The termination was installed for exactly this conductor. The trap answer is copper-clad aluminum, picked because copper-clad steel is on the list and the two sound alike. They are not alike to the Code: copper-clad steel is a permitted 810.21(A) material; copper-clad aluminum is not named and is not permitted for this conductor. Bonding conductor run with sharp bends and a loop through the attic instead of a straight line. Copper-clad aluminum used for the mast bond — not a permitted 810.21(A) material. Aluminum bonding conductor buried, touching masonry, or run within 18 in of the earth outdoors. Conductor hanging loose down the wall, not securely fastened, with no protection where the mower and trimmer reach it. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Antenna bonding conductor size — 10 AWG copper
x: Section 810.21(H) sets the floor for the conductor that bonds an antenna mast or an antenna discharge unit to ground. It cannot be smaller than: • 10 AWG copper • 17 AWG copper-clad steel or bronze • 8 AWG aluminum The 17 AWG size looks impossibly thin until you know what it is: the messenger-style wire molded into the jacket of much satellite coax, copper-clad steel or bronze, which is why a factory dish lead-in can carry its own bond. Ten AWG copper is noticeably heavier than the 14 AWG floor for a communications protector bond in 800.100(A). That is deliberate — antennas sit up in the lightning, and the Code sizes their bond accordingly. The conductor itself follows the rest of 810.21: approved materials, securely fastened, protected from damage, and run as straight as practicable. A mast and a dish collect static charge and sit where lightning energy arrives first. The bond is the path that carries that energy to earth. A conductor that is too small can be damaged by the very surge it is supposed to drain, and a thin corroded wire can part without anyone noticing — leaving the discharge unit draining into air while the next surge looks for a path through the receiver and the house wiring instead. On a Sharma house in Ocala, the dish and an over-the-air antenna share one mast. The bond is 10 AWG bare copper, run straight down the wall about 22 ft to the intersystem bonding termination at the Siemens meter-main. The dish lead-in arrived with the molded 17 AWG messenger, and it checked out as copper-clad steel, continuous to the grounding block — legal, but the 10 AWG run is still the one we pulled for the mast itself. If a helper reaches for the 14 AWG spool from the phone-protector work, stop him: that spool is for 800.100(A) bonds, not antennas. The trap answer is 14 AWG, because 14 AWG is the Chapter 8 bonding floor everyone remembers. That floor belongs to 800.100(A), for protector and sheath bonds. Section 810.21(H) sets its own, heavier floor for antennas: 10 AWG copper. The second trap runs the other way — rejecting a 17 AWG messenger as too small to be legal. It is legal, but only as copper-clad steel or bronze, never as plain copper or copper-clad aluminum. Antenna mast bonded with 14 AWG copper — the 800.100(A) protector floor used where 810.21(H) requires 10 AWG copper. 17 AWG messenger accepted without checking the material — plain copper or copper-clad aluminum at 17 AWG does not meet 810.21(H). Bonding conductor run with sharp bends and a long attic detour instead of as straight a line as practicable (810.21). Separate ground rod driven at the dish and left unbonded to the power grounding electrode system — 810.21(J) requires a bond of at least 6 AWG copper. Aluminum bonding conductor run in contact with the earth — 810.21 bars aluminum from earth and masonry contact and keeps it 18 in above the earth outdoors. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Bonding a separate antenna electrode — 6 AWG again
x: If a separate ground rod or other electrode is installed to serve the radio and television equipment, it cannot stand alone. It must be bonded to the building's power grounding electrode system with a conductor no smaller than 6 AWG copper or the equivalent. This is the same anti-islanding rule as 800.100(D): one building, one earth reference, no matter how many systems drive their own rods. A separate electrode is permitted; a separate, unbonded electrode is a hazard wearing a ground rod's clothes. Two electrodes that are not tied together do not sit at the same voltage. In a surge or a nearby lightning strike, thousands of volts can appear between them (800.100(D)) — and the equipment connected to both systems, or a person touching it, becomes the path that equalizes them. The 6 AWG bond keeps every rod at one reference so the difference never builds. Driven a dish rod because the service was far away? The job ends when the 6 AWG bond ties it back to the power grounding system, not when the rod disappears below grade. Budget that conductor run when the dish location is chosen — on a wide Florida lot it is often the longest wire in the whole antenna job, and finding an unbonded rod on a service call means the original job was never finished. The trap: “A second rod makes the ground better, so bonding it back is optional — two grounds are better than one.” Wrong. An unbonded second rod is worse than none: it creates a second earth reference that can sit thousands of volts away from the first in a surge. 810.21(J) allows the rod only with the 6 AWG bond. Separate dish rod driven and left unbonded to the power grounding system. Bond run made with a conductor smaller than 6 AWG copper. Rod “grounded” to a hose bibb or an isolated pipe instead of the grounding electrode system. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Amateur and citizen-band transmitting stations
x: Transmitting antennas for amateur (ham) and citizen-band stations get the receiving-station rules plus their own. • Each outdoor antenna lead-in conductor needs an antenna discharge unit or another suitable means of draining static (810.57). • The bonding and grounding conductors then follow 810.58: the protective bonding or grounding conductor must be at least as large as the lead-in and never smaller than 10 AWG copper, bronze, or copper-clad steel. • The operating bonding or grounding conductor cannot be smaller than 14 AWG copper or its equivalent. These stations also still owe the mast grounding of 810.15 and the installation rules of Part III of this article. A transmitting antenna is a tall conductor in the sky, and it transmits: it couples real energy into whatever it touches. Wind builds static charge on the wire, and a nearby lightning strike can raise the lead-in to a dangerous voltage. The discharge unit bleeds that charge to ground before it reaches the radio, and the two bonding conductors keep the station's metal at one potential, so a fault or surge does not use the operator as the path. Custom home in Ocala with a ham shack roughed into the garage. The owner runs a coax lead-in from a mast-mounted antenna to the shack. At the entrance we set a listed antenna discharge unit where the lead-in enters, run the protective bonding conductor in 10 AWG copper — never smaller than the lead-in — straight to the intersystem bonding termination at the Siemens meter-main, and run the operating bond in 14 AWG copper to the station ground bus. The mast itself is bonded under 810.15. One reference, one system: nothing in the shack floats at its own potential. The trap is sizing the protective bond like a receiving dish: 14 AWG is the communications floor elsewhere in the chapter, so it feels right. Wrong here. For a transmitting station the protective bonding or grounding conductor must be at least as large as the lead-in and never smaller than 10 AWG. The 14 AWG minimum belongs to the operating conductor. Lead-in brought into the shack with no antenna discharge unit and no other static drain at the entrance. Protective bonding conductor run in 14 AWG: transmitting stations need at least as large as the lead-in and never smaller than 10 AWG. Operating bonding conductor smaller than 14 AWG copper equivalent. Station ground tied to its own rod with no bond back to the building grounding electrode system. Mast left unbonded: 810.15 mast grounding still applies to transmitting stations. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 820 — Community antenna television and radio distribution (coax)
x: Article 820 covers coaxial cable systems that distribute television and radio signals — cable TV, and closed-circuit television of the same construction. The defining part of the system is the coax itself: a center conductor inside a metallic outer shield, and that shield is where this article's safety rules concentrate. • The shield of a coax arriving from outside must be grounded at the entrance; the bonding and grounding conductor follows the recipe in 820.100. • The cable types are listed in this article, and the general rules of Article 800 — separation, installation, fire — layer on top unless 820 changes them. • No primary protector is required at a coax entrance, unlike a telephone circuit. If one is installed, it must be listed and applied at the entrance. The coax shield is a long metal path from the provider's plant straight into the house. Left ungrounded, it can carry lightning energy and fault voltage from outside plant to the television — and to anyone who touches the connector. Grounding the shield at the entrance gives that energy a path to earth before it gets inside, and it holds the shield at the same potential as the power system's ground, so the two systems never sit at different voltages. For Sharma this is the cable company's drop, the grounding block on the side of the house, and the coax distribution inside. On a Marion Oaks spec house the block lands beside the Siemens meter-main: bond it there with 14 AWG copper, short and straight, to the intersystem bonding termination (820.100). Our scope is usually the bond at the block and clean, separated inside runs — the provider owns their drop up to the demarc, but the bond at our service is everybody's inspection item. Keep inside coax 2 in off power wiring in open runs (820.133). The trap is treating coax like a telephone entrance and calling the job — or the exam answer — failed for a missing primary protector. Article 820 does not require one. The shield ground at the entrance is the requirement. A protector is optional, and if one is installed it must be listed. Coax shield never grounded at the entrance — no grounding block, or a block with no bond run from it. Bond from the grounding block landed on a random pipe or a driven rod of its own instead of the grounding electrode system. Inside coax strapped tight against power runs — no 2 in separation in open runs (820.133). Abandoned coax left in a ceiling, accessible part not removed (800.25). No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding the coax shield at the point of entrance
x: The outer conductive shield of a coaxial cable run to a building must be grounded as close as practicable to the point where the cable enters the building, following the conductor rules at 820.100. • The connection can be made where the cable terminates outside the building, or just inside it. A grounded metal raceway can effectively extend the point of entrance — but 'as close as practicable' is the standard either way. • The bond conductor is copper or another corrosion-resistant material, not smaller than 14 AWG, with capacity at least equal to the coax's outer shield — and never required to be larger than 6 AWG. • At a one- or two-family dwelling the conductor runs as short as practicable and not more than 20 ft. Where that length cannot be met, a separate electrode may be installed and bonded back to the power grounding electrode system with 6 AWG or larger. A coax shield left floating at a house is the single most common Chapter 8 defect in residential work. The shield is the first part of the cable a surge meets. Lightning on the drop, a utility fault, or accidental contact with a power line puts voltage on that shield, and the shield runs straight indoors to the television and the modem. A short, solid bond at the entrance gives the energy a path into the grounding electrode system before it travels through the building. A floating shield does the opposite — it carries the surge inside and finds its own way out, usually through the equipment. Coax rough-in on a Marion County spec house. The drop lands on the same wall as the Siemens meter-main, so set the grounding block within a few feet of the entrance hole and run the bond — 14 AWG copper is enough here — straight to the intersystem bonding termination. No coils, no scenic route. Land it before trim-out, then look at it again at trim: a block screwed to the wall with an empty ground lug is the classic write-up on this page. If the entrance is on the opposite wall from the service, measure the run before you pull it — over 20 ft at a one- or two-family dwelling means the separate-electrode route, bonded back with 6 AWG. The trap answer bonds the shield wherever it is convenient inside the house, or to the nearest water pipe. 820.93 fixes the location — as close as practicable to the point of entrance — and the conductor follows the 820.100 recipe. The second trap sizes the bond out of Table 250.66 like a service grounding electrode conductor. It never has to be larger than 6 AWG. Grounding block mounted at the entrance with the ground lug empty — the bond was never landed. Coax shield bonded to a water pipe or panel deep inside the house instead of at the point of entrance. Bond conductor run far past 20 ft at a one-family dwelling with no separate electrode installed. Bond conductor smaller than 14 AWG, or spliced along the run. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Coax bonding and grounding conductors
x: This section sends the coax shield's bonding and grounding conductor back to the same recipe as 800.100: • Material: copper or another corrosion-resistant material. • Size: no smaller than 14 AWG, with capacity at least equal to the coax's outer shield — but never required to exceed 6 AWG. • Length at a house: in a one- or two-family dwelling, as short as practicable and no more than 20 ft. If that length cannot be met, a separate electrode may be installed and then bonded back to the power grounding electrode system with at least 6 AWG (820.100(D)). • Systems that never leave the building: for coax isolated from outside plant, an exception allows the shield to be bonded through an equipment grounding conductor of a listed type instead. The shield is bonded for the same reason every entrance metal is bonded: outside plant brings lightning and fault energy to the side of the house, and the bond gives it a short, direct path to the grounding electrode system instead of a trip through the television. The 20 ft limit keeps that path short at a house — a long, thin bond is an inductor at lightning frequencies and barely bonds at all. Same numbers as the phone protector, because the Code means them to rhyme: 14 AWG floor, 6 AWG ceiling, 20 ft at a house, 6 AWG bond for a separate rod. On a spec house, set the grounding block where the bond runs straight down to the intersystem bonding termination beside the meter-main — a 6 ft run, not a 25 ft tour of the garage. If the cable system is purely internal — a camera system that never exits — read the exception before driving anything. Otherwise, bond at the entrance like every other system in this chapter. Two traps. First, sizing the bond to match the shield with no cap and pulling 2 AWG 'to be safe' — the section never requires larger than 6 AWG. Second, applying the 20 ft limit to every building: the cap is written for one- and two-family dwellings. Elsewhere the rule is as short as practicable. Bond run in 18 AWG bell wire, or in a strand peeled off the coax itself. Grounding block bonded with a long, wandering run at a house instead of a short, straight path. Separate rod driven at the dish with no 6 AWG bond back to the power grounding electrode system. Shield bonded to a random water-pipe stub instead of the grounding electrode system. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Installing coaxial cable inside the building
x: Listed coaxial cable inside a building follows the installation framework of Article 800 as this section applies it. Two rules drive the work: • The cable type must match the space — plenum, riser, or general use — from this article's cable list: CATVP for plenums, CATVR for risers, CATV for general use, and CATVX for limited use in dwellings and raceways. • Unlisted outside-plant coax may come into a building only a limited distance — 50 ft from the point of entrance — before listed cable is required, under 820.48. Past that point, the run must be listed coax of a type permitted for the space it passes through. An outside-plant jacket is built for sun and water, not for fire. Run it deep into a building and it becomes fuel and smoke load in exactly the spaces people breathe from, and a path for flame to travel. The 50 ft limit caps how much of that unlisted jacket gets inside, and the type-for-space rules keep a fire on one floor from riding the coax to the next. Measure the entrance path on long custom homes: if the distribution panel sits more than 50 ft of cable run from where the drop enters, the whole run needs listed cable, not the provider's outdoor spool. In commercial ceilings and shafts, treat coax exactly like communications cable for fire rating — plenum type (CATVP) in plenums, CATVR riser cable between floors. The trap is measuring the 50 ft from the distribution panel, or as the crow flies. It is 50 ft of cable run from the point of entrance. The second trap is "listed is listed": a listed general-use CATV run through a plenum ceiling or up a riser shaft still fails — the type has to match the space. Unlisted outside-plant coax run about 80 ft from the entrance to the distribution panel. General-use CATV coax run above a return-air plenum ceiling. General-use coax run floor to floor in a riser shaft instead of CATVR. Listed coax of the wrong type for the space, substituted because it was on the truck. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Separation for coaxial cable
x: Coaxial cable obeys the same separation discipline as the rest of the chapter. Article 800's 800.133 states the general rule; this section carries it into the coax world, so a helper who learns one has learned both. • Coax may not share a raceway or box with electric light and power conductors. • Coax may not be supported from a raceway that contains power conductors. • Coax keeps at least 2 in from light and power conductors — unless those conductors are in a raceway or in a sheathed cable assembly such as nonmetallic-sheathed, armored, or UF cable. Separation keeps a power fault from putting line voltage on a coax shield that a customer touches at the TV, and it keeps power-conductor heat and noise off the signal. It also keeps the two systems honest at inspection: a shared raceway hides which system a conductor belongs to, and coax strapped to a power raceway inherits every problem that raceway has. Run coax in its own holes, on its own supports, 2 in off the power runs — the same muscle memory as Cat 6. The classic fail is a coax home-run bundle zip-tied along an EMT or draped over a Romex bundle in the attic. Separate supports cost minutes; a failed inspection costs a return trip. The trap runs both ways. "Coax can never come within 2 in of Romex" is wrong — nonmetallic-sheathed cable is a sheathed cable assembly, so the 2 in open-conductor separation is not what governs there. And "coax in the same conduit is fine if both are insulated" is always wrong: sharing a raceway with power conductors is prohibited outright. Coax home-run bundle zip-tied along an EMT run and supported from it. Coax pulled into the same raceway as branch-circuit conductors. Coax draped over open power conductors, touching, in the attic. Coax and power conductors sharing one junction box. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Where each coaxial cable type may be used — Table 820.154
x: Article 820 sorts coaxial cable into four listed types, and the ladder runs in one direction. CATVP, the plenum type, sits at the top; CATVR, the riser type, below it; then CATV, the general-purpose type; and CATVX, the limited-use type, at the bottom. Table 820.154 carries the substitution hierarchy: a higher type may be used in place of a lower one — plenum for riser, riser for general — and a lower type may never be substituted upward. Which type a given space demands is set by the article's installation and listing rules — not by the jacket color, and not by what the supplier shipped. Cable jackets burn, and they burn differently in different spaces. In a plenum, smoke from one burning jacket is pumped through the whole building by the air handler. In a riser shaft, a burning cable is a fuse that carries fire floor to floor. The ladder matches each cable's fire and smoke listing to the space, so a cable never becomes the path that spreads a fire. Coax home runs through a return-air plenum in a light-commercial ceiling in Winter Park: CATVP, or a listed raceway — the CATV reel from the truck does not become legal because the ceiling is almost never opened. Before the pull, read the jacket legend on every reel and stage the plenum reels separately from the general-purpose stock. The supplier shipped CATV and the run crosses a return-air plenum, but the ceiling is sealed and 'nobody will ever see it.' Wrong answer. The space sets the type: a plenum takes CATVP (or a raceway), and substitution only runs downhill — CATV can never substitute upward into a plenum or a riser. Type CATV pulled through a return-air plenum without a raceway. Type CATVX installed in a commercial riser shaft. Type CATV run vertically through more than one floor where riser cable is required. Coax with no legible type marking installed and claimed as plenum-rated. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Coaxial cable types — CATVP, CATVR, CATV, CATVX
x: 820.179 lists the coaxial cable types and their markings. CATVP is the plenum type, CATVR the riser type, CATV the general-purpose type, and CATVX the limited-use type, restricted to dwellings and raceway. The substitution rule follows the chapter's pattern: a higher-listed type may be substituted for a lower one — plenum for riser, riser for general — and a lower type may never be substituted upward. The cable's voltage rating is not marked on the cable, so nobody mistakes coax for a power conductor. Read the print legend on the jacket; coax that carries no type marking carries no permission. The type letters are a fire listing, not a brand. A plenum jacket is tested for flame spread and smoke in moving air; a riser jacket is tested to keep fire from riding the cable floor to floor. If the marking is not on the jacket, there is no tested listing behind the cable — and no way for the next person, or the inspector, to know what the cable is allowed to do. CATVX is the trap type: fine in the dwelling work it is listed for, a violation pulled into a commercial riser. On a Winter Park strip-center rewire, the reel marked CATVX stays on the truck — the riser pulls get CATVR. Check the legend before the pull, not at the inspection. The jacket is black and heavy and stamped with the manufacturer's name and 'RG-6,' so it must be riser-rated. Wrong. Trade size and brand are not a listing. Only the type letters in the print legend — CATVP, CATVR, CATV or CATVX — say what the cable is listed for, and unmarked coax has no permission at all. CATVX pulled into a commercial riser or plenum. Coax installed with no type letters in the jacket legend. General-purpose CATV run in a plenum space without a raceway. Riser run made with CATV because the jacket 'looked heavier.' No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 830 — Network-powered broadband systems
x: Article 830 covers broadband systems where the network itself sends the power: the provider's network powers the network interface unit at the customer's building, over the same plant that carries the signal. Because power arrives from off the premises on a communications cable, this article is stricter at the entrance than plain CATV: • Its circuits get primary protection. • Its shields, protectors, and interface-unit enclosures all get grounded. The general rules of Article 800 still layer underneath, and 830 borrows the 800.100 grounding recipe for its conductors. Sharma meets 830 as the powered cable-broadband entrance on commercial and multi-dwelling work more than on single houses. A plain communications cable brings signal; a network-powered broadband cable brings energy from a plant the building does not control, and it keeps bringing it during a building outage. Without primary protection and grounding at the entrance, a surge or fault on the provider's plant has a straight path into the customer's wiring and equipment. Article 830 exists to put the same entrance discipline on powered broadband that the older articles put on telephone and CATV. Mid-rise condo in downtown Orlando: the cable provider's powered entrance lands in the telecom room, network interface units on the wall, powered from the street plant. Our scope stops at the demarc: we verify the primary protector is in place and the NIU enclosures and shields are grounded on the 800.100 recipe the article borrows. Recognize the powered entrance by the network interface unit and the provider's powering arrangement, not by the shape of the cable. Keep hands off the provider's powered plant beyond the demarc — that side is theirs. The trap is treating the powered broadband entrance like plain CATV under Article 820 because the cable looks the same. Wrong article. Where the network powers the interface unit, Article 830 governs: primary protection is required and the grounding follows the 800.100 recipe, not the CATV pages. Powered broadband entrance installed with no primary protector: treated as plain CATV. NIU enclosure and cable shield left ungrounded at the entrance. Provider's powered plant reworked on the network side of the demarc. Entrance grounded on a made-up recipe instead of the 800.100 pattern the article borrows. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Primary protectors on network-powered broadband circuits
x: Because a network-powered broadband circuit brings both signal and network power in from outside plant, each of its conductors gets primary protection at the entrance, in the pattern of the protector rules used across this chapter (805.90): • A listed primary protector — an arrester connected between each line conductor and ground. • Mounted in, on, or immediately next to the building, as close as practicable to the point of entrance. • Ahead of the network interface unit and the inside distribution. The protector deals with the same two threats as at a telephone entrance: lightning energy riding in on the outside plant, and accidental contact between that plant and power conductors out on the poles. Outside plant is exposed plant. A lightning strike blocks away, or a fallen power conductor touching the drop, can put surge energy on a circuit that runs straight to equipment inside — and broadband circuits carry network power as well as signal. The protector gives that energy a path to ground at the door instead of through the building. If a powered broadband entrance has no protector, treat it like a phone entrance with no protector: a provider-side correction to raise before the installation is signed off. On a Florida home or small office where the cable provider lands a network-powered drop, check the entrance before trim-out: protector present, ahead of the interface unit, and grounded — the shield, the protector, and the interface enclosure all land on the one building grounding reference (830.93). Sharma's part is usually the bond and the space: leave the protector accessible and its grounding path short and straight. The trap: “Broadband is data, not power, so it needs no protector.” Wrong twice — the circuit is network-powered, and 830.90 puts a primary protector on each conductor at the entrance. Second trap: mounting the protector after the interface unit; protection belongs at the point of entrance, ahead of it. Network-powered broadband entrance with no primary protector installed. Protector mounted after the network interface unit instead of ahead of it. Protector present but its ground not tied to the building grounding system. Protector buried behind finishes where it cannot be reached or inspected. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding shields, protectors, and the interface unit
x: Three things at a network-powered broadband entrance must be grounded: the metallic shield of the broadband cable, the primary protector, and the metallic enclosure of the network interface unit. Section 830.93 sends all three to the grounding conductor rules of 800.100 — the same rules that ground the other Chapter 8 systems. Everything metallic that the outside plant touches at the entrance ends up on the one building grounding reference: shield, protector ground, and enclosure alike. Bond only the shield and the job is two-thirds done; the enclosure is not optional. The grounding conductor itself follows 800.100 for size, routing and where it may land. A broadband drop is a metal path from the outside plant straight into the building. Lightning and utility surges ride that path, and the protector can only dump energy it can reach ground with. Any metallic part left floating at the entrance — the enclosure is the one most often skipped — can sit at a dangerous voltage next to grounded equipment, waiting for a hand to bridge the gap. New townhome rough-in, Kissimmee: the provider's coax lands on the primary protector at the garage demarc and the interface unit mounts beside it. Bond all three — shield, protector, enclosure — with 14 AWG minimum copper, run short and straight to the intersystem bonding termination, per 800.100. Photograph the entrance assembly at rough-in; broadband entrances get buried behind provider equipment fast, and the photo is your proof at final. The shield is bonded and the protector is grounded, so the metal interface enclosure can float — it is 'just a box.' Wrong. 830.93 names the enclosure as the third item that must be grounded. A floating enclosure next to bonded metal is exactly the touch-voltage setup the rule exists to prevent. Interface unit enclosure never bonded — shield and protector grounded, enclosure floating. Bonding conductor smaller than 14 AWG, or run long and coiled instead of short and straight. Protector ground landed on a random pipe clamp instead of a point 800.100 permits. Entrance buried behind provider equipment with no bond visible at final inspection. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Broadband bonding and grounding conductors
x: The bonding and grounding conductors for a network-powered broadband entrance follow the same dimensional rules as the rest of the chapter: • Not smaller than 14 AWG, and not required to exceed 6 AWG. • Run as short as practicable. • Not more than 20 ft long in a one- or two-family dwelling. The section carries the same escape hatch as 800.100 and 820.100: where the length cannot be met, a separate electrode is permitted, and the exception structure requires that electrode to be bonded back to the power grounding electrode system with a conductor of at least 6 AWG. By this point in the chapter the pattern should be familiar, because the Code intends it to be one pattern repeated. The bonding conductor is the path that drags a surge or a fault on the broadband plant down to the building's one grounding reference. A long, thin conductor has impedance that defeats it: the surge arrives faster than the path can carry it away, and the difference shows up as voltage between the cable plant and everything else in the house. Short, adequately sized, and bonded back is what keeps the potentials together. Cable broadband entrance on a two-family in Kissimmee: the provider's network interface unit lands on the garage wall, 12 ft of conductor run from the service. We run 14 AWG copper from the NIU ground lug straight to the intersystem bonding termination at the meter-main — inside the 20 ft dwelling limit, no upsizing needed. On a bigger commercial entrance where the run cannot stay short, the answer is not a longer skinny wire: it is a separate electrode at the entrance, bonded back to the power grounding electrode system with 6 AWG. The trap is treating 6 AWG as the required size: "bonding conductors are 6 AWG." Wrong direction. 14 AWG is the minimum and the conductor is never required to exceed 6 AWG; 6 AWG is the size of the bond-back when a separate electrode is used because the length limit cannot be met. Bonding conductor run 30 ft across a dwelling attic: the dwelling limit is 20 ft. Separate ground rod driven at the broadband entrance and never bonded back to the power grounding electrode system. Bond-back from the separate electrode run in 14 AWG: it must be at least 6 AWG. Conductor smaller than 14 AWG, or coiled and slack instead of short and straight. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Separation for network-powered broadband cable
x: Broadband cable under Article 830 keeps the same separation discipline as the rest of Chapter 8. • In a raceway, box, or enclosure, it does not run with electric light and power conductors except where 830.133's own conditions are met — a permanent barrier or listed divider between the two systems is the classic way those conditions are satisfied. • In open runs, it keeps the chapter's familiar 2 in separation from power conductors. • The 2 in is not required where one side or the other is in a raceway or a sheathed cable assembly, or where a continuous, firmly fixed nonconductor separates the two. The network power on a broadband circuit makes the separation worth more, not less: this is the one communications-style cable whose network side arrives carrying power from outside the building. Every other communications cable in the chapter is a guest in the building; a network-powered broadband cable arrives already energized from the network side. A cross-contact, a crushed jacket or a fault in a shared box can put that outside power — or building power — onto inside wiring and equipment that nobody expects to be live. Separation is the cheap, permanent insurance that the two systems never meet. Broadband entrance and inside runs: own holes, own supports, 2 in off the power runs — the same muscle memory as 800.133 and 820.133, because the Code intends one pattern for the whole chapter. On a Kissimmee rental rehab, the broadband drop crossed the garage ceiling 2 in clear of the open power runs; at the one place it had to cross the EMT feeder, the raceway itself satisfied the rule, so the crossing needed no extra spacing. The trap answer is that broadband is 'just cable TV,' so it can share a box or raceway with power like any low-voltage cable. Wrong. It does not share a raceway, box or enclosure with power conductors except under 830.133's own conditions — and because the network side arrives carrying power, the separation matters more here, not less. Broadband cable pulled into the same EMT as the feeder 'for one short run.' Open broadband run stapled tight against an open power run — no 2 in separation. Broadband and power conductors landed in the same box with no barrier and no condition met. Separation lost where another trade re-dressed the runs and nobody restored it. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Article 840 — Premises-powered broadband systems
x: Article 840 covers broadband systems where the power is supplied at the premises instead of by the network. The classic case is fiber arriving at an optical network terminal — an ONT — that plugs into a local receptacle. • The fiber itself carries no metallic path and no power, so there is no outside metallic shield arriving on glass. • The protection focus shifts to any metallic members that do enter, and to the terminal equipment at the premises. • The fiber cable itself follows the optical fiber rules of Article 770 in Chapter 7. • Grounding questions go to the Chapter 8 pattern: the protector rules at 805.90 and the entrance bonding and grounding rules at 800.100, as the specific sections direct. It is the shortest article in the chapter, and for Sharma it is mostly a fiber-to-the-home entrance on new custom work. One census note, so nobody hunts for pages that do not exist: in NEC 2020 this chapter ends here. Chapter 8 has exactly six articles — 800, 805, 810, 820, 830 and 840 — and the article numbers 850 through 890 are not assigned in the 2020 edition. If a study aid or a newer book lists communications articles above 840, it is describing a different edition, and its section numbers will not match this one. Network-powered systems push the protection problem out to the provider's plant. Premises-powered broadband brings live terminal equipment onto the customer's side of the entrance, fed from the building's own receptacles, while the drop can still carry metallic members in with it. Article 840 exists so that combination — local power, glass fiber, stray metal — gets its own entrance rules instead of borrowed ones. Fiber-to-the-home on a new custom build: the provider mounts the ONT in the structured-wiring enclosure, and Sharma's scope is the premises side — a receptacle at the enclosure so the ONT plugs in where it lives, and a bond on the drop's metallic strength member at the entrance, run per 840.93. The glass itself gets no bond. Getting the receptacle location onto the rough-in plan is the whole game; after drywall it is a change order. The trap is hunting Chapter 8 for the fiber rules — or for an Article 850. In NEC 2020 there is no Article 850, and the fiber-optic cable rules are not in this chapter at all: they are Article 770 in Chapter 7. Answers that cite a communications article above 840 are quoting a different edition. Metallic strength member or locate wire on the fiber drop left unbonded at the entrance. ONT powered by an extension cord because no receptacle was roughed in at the enclosure. Hybrid cable treated as pure fiber — its metallic member cut back and left floating inside the enclosure. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounding at a premises-powered broadband entrance
x: Premises-powered broadband arrives at the building on a cable that may carry metallic members — a metallic shield, a strength member, or a similar conductive part. Where those members require grounding, 840.93 grounds them following the chapter's entrance-grounding pattern, as close as practicable to the point of entrance. • The rule is about the metal in the cable, not the glass. All-dielectric fiber has nothing conductive to ground. • The grounding conductor is the chapter's standard 800.100 recipe: copper or another corrosion-resistant conductive material. • Not smaller than 14 AWG, and never required to be larger than 6 AWG. • Run it as short as practicable — at a one- or two-family dwelling, not over 20 ft. • If that length cannot be met, use a separate electrode and bond it back to the power grounding electrode system with 6 AWG, the 800.100(D) route. Same numbers as the telephone and coax entrances, applied here to the metallic members that actually exist. A metallic shield or strength member is a wire into the building from the pole or the pedestal. Lightning and utility surges ride it inside and look for a path to earth through whatever the cable touches — the terminal, the enclosure, a person. Grounding the member at the entrance gives that energy its path outside, before it reaches the equipment. Fiber itself carries light, not surges; the metal that travels with it is the hazard. New custom home, fiber-to-the-home: the provider's drop arrives at the ONT enclosure on the garage wall, and this drop carries a metallic strength member. Sharma's crew bonds that member at the entrance with 14 AWG copper, run 8 ft straight down to the intersystem bonding termination beside the Siemens meter-main — well inside the 20 ft dwelling limit. The next month, a second house gets an all-dielectric drop: no bond, and the job record says "all-dielectric drop, no metallic member," so nobody hunts for a missing bond later. The trap is reaching for Table 250.66 and sizing this conductor like a service grounding electrode conductor. It is not sized from the service. The 800.100 recipe controls: 14 AWG minimum, and 6 AWG is the largest size ever required, no matter how big the service is. Metallic strength member on the entrance cable left unbonded because "it is a fiber job." Bond landed deep inside the building instead of as close as practicable to the point of entrance. Grounding conductor run 26 ft across the attic at a one-family dwelling — over the 20 ft limit, with no separate electrode and no 6 AWG bond back. Grounding conductor smaller than 14 AWG — 18 AWG thermostat-style wire used for the bond. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Powering circuits — one cable carries the signal and the power
x: Section 840.160 is titled 'Powering Circuits,' and it answers a narrow question: may a communications cable carry power as well as signal? Yes — with conditions: • The cable is a listed communications cable (805.179), and the equipment it feeds is listed communications equipment (805.170) • The power source is listed for the purpose (840.170(G)) • What the cable carries is power for communications equipment — this is not permission to put branch-circuit power on a communications cable Where communications cables are substituted for Class 2 and Class 3 cables under 725.154(A), the installation must also comply with 725.144, the rules that keep power-and-data bundles from overheating. One exception: listed 4-pair cables where the rated current does not exceed 0.3 amperes in any conductor, 24 AWG or larger, do not have to comply with 725.144. The typical case is a 4-pair data cable carrying Ethernet and PoE-type power to a camera, a phone or an access point. Power on signal pairs is heat in a bundle. One cable carrying a fraction of an amp is nothing; dozens of powered cables tied tightly together can cook their own insulation, because the middle of the bundle cannot shed heat. The listing conditions and the 725.144 hook exist to keep the power inside what the cable system was tested to carry — and to keep 'powering' from becoming a back door for unlisted energy on a signal cable. Small Orlando office fit-out: a listed PoE switch in the rack feeds 14 ceiling cameras and access points over Cat 6. Each run is a listed 4-pair cable, the current per conductor sits well under the 0.3-ampere exception line, and the power source is the switch's own listed supply — the installation sits inside 840.160 without needing the 725.144 bundle calculation. The answer changes when the design grows: a fat bundle of powered runs, or communications cable substituted for Class 2 wiring, sends you to 725.144 and its table before you tie the bundle up. The trap is reading 840.160 as a general permission to mix power and communications. It is not a separation exception, and it does not let a 120-volt branch circuit share a cable or a box with broadband drops. The permission runs the other way: listed communications cables may carry circuits that power communications equipment, from a listed source, inside the stated limits. Unlisted cable used to carry powering circuits to communications equipment. Powering circuits fed from a power source that is not listed for the purpose. A large bundle of powered communications cables tied up with no 725.144 check, where the cables substitute for Class 2 or Class 3 cables. 840.160 cited to land a 120 V branch circuit in the same enclosure as broadband drops — the section covers power for communications equipment on listed communications cables, not branch circuits. NEC 2023 CHANGE: • 840.160: Changed the reference from Section 725.154(A) to Section 722.135 as cable substitution, and installation requirements are now in Article 722. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Chapter 9 — the table room
x: Chapter 9 is not a set of wiring rules for one kind of job. It is the data the rest of the book points back to: • Table 1 — the percentage of a raceway conductors may occupy • Table 2 — minimum radius of conduit bends • Table 4 — raceway inside diameters and usable areas • Table 5 and Table 5A — insulated and compact conductor dimensions and areas • Table 8 — conductor properties and DC resistance, the voltage-drop input • Table 9 — AC resistance and reactance, for finer voltage-drop work • Tables 11(A) and 11(B) — how much power a Class 2 or Class 3 source may deliver Behind the tables sit the informative annexes — Annex B on ampacity calculation under engineering supervision, Annex C's same-size fill tables, Annex D's worked load-calculation examples, Annex I's recommended torque values. Annex material explains and illustrates; it does not add mandatory requirements on its own. Every sizing answer in the trade is only as good as the table it came from. Chapter 9 keeps the numbers in one printed place, so a fill percentage, a raceway area and a resistance all trace to the same source instead of memory and habit. The annexes sit behind a fence for a reason: a worked example shows one way through a calculation, and treating an example as a rule is how a legal installation gets failed — or an illegal one gets built. Come here in this order: Table 1 for the allowed percentage, Table 4 for the raceway, Table 5 for insulated conductors, and Table 8 when a voltage-drop check needs resistance. One pass through a real check: three or more conductors means 40 percent from Table 1; 1/2 in EMT allows 0.122 sq in at that percentage from Table 4; the conductors on the list — two 6 AWG THHN and one 10 AWG THHN — total 0.1225 sq in from Table 5, so the run goes up to 3/4 in EMT. Do not size conduit from a memorized count you heard on another job — raceway type, insulation type, and conductor count all change the answer. Reference aid only; the AHJ and the printed NEC govern. Florida work in this book is NEC 2020 as adopted by the FBC 8th Edition (2023), for permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026; NEC 2023 applies under the FBC 9th Edition from Dec 31, 2026. The trap answer treats Annex C like a requirement table: 'Annex C says nine fit, so nine are legal.' Annex C is an informative shortcut built from Tables 1, 4 and 5 for same-size conductors only. It cannot bless a mixed-size pull, and no annex overrides the tables it was built from. Mixed-size pull sized from an Annex C count table, which only works when every conductor is the same size and type. Fill figured from the EMT row of Table 4 for a PVC Schedule 40 run — the raceway installed is smaller inside than the raceway calculated. Voltage-drop check run on a resistance remembered from another conductor size instead of the Table 8 row for the conductor in hand. Annex example cited to the inspector as if it were a Code requirement. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Table 1 — how much of a raceway you may fill
x: Table 1 sets the share of a raceway's inside cross-section that conductors may take up: • 1 conductor — 53 percent • 2 conductors — 31 percent • 3 or more conductors — 40 percent • A nipple 24 in or less between enclosures — 60 percent, covered on the nipple page The percentage is taken against the raceway's total inside area in Table 4, and the conductor areas come from Table 5. Those percentages already allow for the fact that conductors do not pack like water — two round conductors side by side waste more of the circle, which is why the two-conductor number is the lowest of the three. A raceway filled past its percentage cannot be pulled without a fight: conductors jam at the bends, insulation skins against the raceway wall, and a damaged jacket is a fault waiting for a damp day. The limits also leave the breathing room a bundled run needs. The odd dip at two conductors is geometry, not a typo — two circles side by side waste more of the pipe than one large conductor or a bundle of three or more. Count every conductor in the run, including the equipment grounding conductor, then pick the percentage for that count before you open Tables 4 and 5. The most common house and light-commercial case is three or more conductors, so 40 percent is the column you will use most — but never use it for a one- or two-conductor pull. Short stubs earn their own number: a 1/2 in EMT nipple has a 60 percent area of 0.182 sq in in Table 4, which at 0.0133 sq in for one 12 AWG THHN is 13 conductors by fill alone. The trap is reaching for 40 percent every time because it is the familiar number. Two conductors get only 31 percent — a two-wire pull figured at 40 is overfilled before it starts. The reverse trap: 53 percent is not a bonus rate for three conductors. It belongs to a single conductor only. Two-conductor pull figured at 40 percent instead of 31 — the raceway is overfilled on the approved calculation itself. Equipment ground left out of the conductor count, so a three-conductor run was figured as two — wrong percentage and the ground's own area missing. The 60 percent nipple allowance applied to a full-length run between panels. Percentage read off one raceway's Table 4 row and applied to another — an EMT answer used for a PVC run. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The 60 percent nipple allowance
x: A short raceway nipple — 24 in or less between boxes, cabinets, or similar enclosures — may be filled to 60 percent instead of the Table 1 percentages. The extra room is allowed because a short, straight stub is far easier to pull and far less likely to jam than a long run. The allowance belongs to the nipple only; the long runs on either side of it still use 53, 31, or 40 percent as their conductor count requires. Note 4 to Table 1 carries a second gift: the 310.15(C)(1) ampacity adjustment factors do not have to be applied to conductors in a nipple 24 in or shorter. The fill percentages protect the pull and the insulation: conductors jammed into an overfilled raceway skin against the wall at every bend, and a bundled run needs room to shed heat. A nipple is short and straight, with an enclosure open at both ends, so the jam risk that drives the lower percentages barely exists — that is why the Code trades up to 60 percent there, and waives the bundling adjustment there, and only there. Worked check: a 1/2 in EMT nipple has a 60 percent area of 0.182 sq in in Table 4. At 0.0133 sq in for one 12 AWG THHN, that is 0.182 / 0.0133 = 13.68, so 13 conductors by fill alone. And Note 4 to Table 1 goes further than the 60%: the 310.15(C)(1) ampacity adjustment factors do NOT have to be applied to conductors in a nipple 24 in or shorter — the Code waives that check here expressly, so do not saddle the nipple with it. The trap is carrying the 60 percent past the nipple. The allowance ends at 24 in and at the nipple's own walls: a 30 in stub, or the full run between the same two panels, is back to 53, 31, or 40 percent. The second trap runs the other way — derating a legal nipple anyway and upsizing gear that never needed it. The 60 percent nipple allowance applied to a full-length run between panels. A 30 in stub figured as a nipple — over 24 in, the Table 1 percentages govern. 310.15(C)(1) adjustment waived on the long runs because the nipple in the middle earned the waiver. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Table 2 — minimum radius of conduit bends
x: Table 2 sets the smallest radius a field bend may have, measured to the centerline of the conduit — not to the inside face of the bend. It has two columns, and the bending method picks the column, not a section number: • One-shot or full-shoe bender: the first column. The shoe is made for the conduit type and size, so a bend on the right shoe lands on this column by construction. • All other bends: the second column. A PVC heat bend falls here, however smooth it looks. The table is a floor, not a target. A factory sweep or a segmented bend laid out well above these numbers is fine. The printed table runs to 6 in; the sizes Sharma bends most are below. A bend that is too tight kinks or flattens the raceway, and a flattened bend drags on every conductor pulled through it — insulation scrapes, conductors jam, and the inside diameter the fill math assumed is no longer there. The radius floor keeps the bend gentle enough that the wire survives the pull and the conduit keeps its shape. A bender's shoe sets the radius for you: use the shoe made for the conduit type and size and the bend lands on the first column by construction. Heat-bent PVC is where crews get caught — form the sweep to at least the 'other bends' number, because a tight heat bend that kinks or flattens also fails the 'do not damage, do not effectively reduce the inside diameter' half of the bending sections. Worked check: a 2 in PVC stub-up sweep formed at a 10 in centerline radius fails Table 2 by 2 in even if it looks smooth. Re-form it at 12 in or better before the concrete truck is called. A 2 in PVC heat bend formed at 9½ in matches Table 2, right? Wrong column. 9½ in is the one-shot / full-shoe number for 2 in; a heat bend is an 'other bend' and needs 12 in. The method picks the column before the size picks the number. Heat-bent PVC stub-up sweep formed at a 10 in centerline radius on 2 in conduit — Table 2 needs 12 in for other bends. Bend kinked or flattened so the inside diameter is effectively reduced, even where the radius itself is legal. Radius checked to the outside of the bend instead of the centerline, so a tight bend passes on paper only. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Table 4 — raceway inside dimensions and usable area
x: Table 4 gives, for each raceway type and trade size, the inside diameter, the total inside area, and the usable area at each Table 1 percentage. It is the denominator of every fill check: conductor areas from Table 5 are added up, then compared against the usable area this table allows. • Trade size is a name, not a measurement: 1/2 in EMT is actually 0.622 in inside and 0.304 sq in total, with 0.122 sq in usable at 40 percent. • Raceway type matters as much as trade size: 1/2 in PVC Schedule 40 is a little smaller inside (0.285 sq in total, 0.114 at 40 percent), so an EMT answer does not carry over to PVC. • PVC Schedule 80, the thick-wall PVC used where conduit is subject to physical damage, runs smaller inside than Schedule 40 at every size. Flexible metal conduit (FMC) is its own row too — close to EMT at the small sizes, but never the same row. A fill that passes in Schedule 40 or EMT can fail in Schedule 80, so when the raceway changes, rerun the division with the new row. Every fill check is a division, and Table 4 is the bottom half of it. Use the wrong raceway's row and the answer is wrong with confidence — the crew pulls a fill that passed on paper and jams in the pipe, or an inspector reruns the math with the right row and the run fails after it is in the ground. Read the row for the exact raceway you are installing, then take the column that matches your conductor count from Table 1. Flag carried from v1: the 1/2 in EMT total area is carried as 0.304 sq in; one secondary source showed 0.305, but the 40 percent value of 0.122 sq in agrees across sources. Do not change 0.304 without re-checking the printed table. Half-inch conduit, so the hole is 1/2 in across and about 0.196 sq in? Wrong twice. Trade size is a name: Table 4 puts 1/2 in EMT at 0.622 in inside and 0.304 sq in total — and the number a fill check actually uses at 40 percent is 0.122 sq in, not the total. Fill check run on the EMT row for a Schedule 80 run — passes on paper, overfilled in the pipe. Trade size used as the inside diameter (1/2 in taken as a 0.500 in hole) instead of the Table 4 row. Fill never rerun when the spec changed the raceway from Schedule 40 to Schedule 80. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Table 5 — how much room an insulated conductor takes
x: Table 5 gives the approximate diameter and area of insulated conductors and fixture wires, by size and insulation type. Fill is figured on the insulated conductor you are actually pulling, insulation included — not on the bare metal. • Read three things together: the AWG size, the insulation type, and that type's column. A different insulation type in the same AWG can have a different area, so the insulation column is part of the answer. • The table below carries the THHN / THWN / THWN-2 column — the insulation Sharma pulls most. • Bare conductors are not sized from this table; a bare grounding conductor's area is figured from its own dimensions in Table 8. Fill limits exist because a stuffed raceway damages insulation on the pull and traps heat in service. Table 5 is where the honest size of each conductor comes from — the whole insulated circle, not the metal inside it. Understate the area and the conduit that fits on paper jams halfway through the pull. On a Sharma rough-in, the fill check for a 1/2 in EMT stub full of 12 AWG THHN home runs goes like this: each conductor takes 0.0133 sq in from Table 5. Nine conductors total 0.1197 sq in — inside the 0.122 sq in that Table 4 allows at 40 percent in 1/2 in EMT. A tenth conductor makes 0.1330 sq in, which is over, so the run moves up to 3/4 in EMT before anyone pulls. And confirm the insulation type on the reel first: if the job switches from THHN to a thicker insulation type, redo the math with that type's Table 5 area instead of assuming the count still fits. The trap: figuring fill from the bare conductor, or from the area of a different insulation type in the same AWG. Table 5's answer is the insulated area in the column for the insulation actually on the wire. Read the size off a bare-wire table and every count comes out too small. Fill figured from bare-conductor dimensions — the recount with Table 5 insulated areas puts the raceway over its Table 4 allowance. Conductors jammed and insulation scored on the pull: raceway filled past the Table 1 percentage. Fill calculation run with the THHN column for a thicker insulation type actually installed — areas understated, raceway over the limit. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Table 5A — compact conductor dimensions and areas
x: Table 5A is Table 5's sibling for compact-stranded conductors. In a compact conductor the strands are compressed during manufacture, so the finished conductor is rounder and smaller across than a standard concentric-stranded conductor of the same AWG — a stranding common in larger aluminum feeder conductors. • Fill is figured on the conductor actually in the raceway: compact conductors take their diameter and area from Table 5A, standard conductors from Table 5. • Figuring a compact conductor from Table 5 overstates its area, so a fill can fail on paper that would pass in the raceway. • Figuring a standard conductor from Table 5A understates it, and that direction is the violation. The conductor's marking and its manufacturer tell you which stranding you hold. Fill limits exist so conductors can be pulled without damage and can shed heat inside the raceway, and both protections depend on the real cross-section in the pipe. Read a compact conductor out of the standard table and you waste raceway and money on a phantom size. Read a standard conductor out of the compact table and the raceway is overfilled in fact while the paperwork says it passes — skinned insulation and a jammed pull are how that shows up. A 4/0 aluminum compact feeder: open Table 5A, not Table 5, before you tell the foreman the conduit size. The difference between the two tables is regularly the difference between the conduit on the truck and the next size up. Confirm the stranding before the math: "compact" is in the conductor's print legend and in the submittal. For scale, a standard-stranded 4/0 THHN reads 0.3237 sq in in Table 5 — if the reel does not say compact, the standard table is the one the fill has to carry. The trap is treating Table 5A as a discount table anyone can claim. It is not a smaller number for the same wire — it belongs only to conductors actually manufactured as compact strand. A standard-stranded conductor figured from Table 5A is an understated fill and a violation, however good the math looks. Compact feeder figured from Table 5 — the calculation fails a fill the raceway would actually pass, and the raceway got upsized for nothing. Standard-stranded conductors figured from Table 5A to make a tight fill pass on paper. Fill calculation with no stranding identified — the submittal says compact, but the reel that arrived is standard strand. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: The conduit-fill method, step by step
x: Every fill problem is the same four steps: • Step 1 — List every conductor in the raceway, including equipment grounds, with its size and insulation type. • Step 2 — Take each conductor's area from Table 5 (the Table 8 area for a bare conductor) and add them. • Step 3 — Pick the Table 1 percentage from the conductor count: 53 for one conductor, 31 for two, 40 for three or more, and 60 for a nipple 24 in or less. • Step 4 — Open Table 4 for your raceway type and take the first trade size whose usable area at that percentage is equal to or larger than your conductor total. If the total is even slightly over, go up a trade size; close does not count. Conductors need room. In an overfilled raceway the pull jams, insulation scrapes and stretches, and a conductor can be damaged before it ever carries a load. The percentages sit well under the raceway's full area because round conductors do not pack like water — the air between them is part of the math, and two conductors side by side waste the most space, which is why two get the lowest share, 31 percent. Four steps, done in order, make the answer come from the tables instead of from how the pull feels. Worked example, Sharma commercial: three 20 A branch circuits share one EMT — six 12 AWG THHN plus one 12 AWG THHN equipment ground. Seven conductors at 0.0133 sq in each total 0.0931 sq in. Seven conductors take the 40 percent column, and 1/2 in EMT allows 0.122 sq in at 40 percent, so it fits. If the lead picks CCA, one AWG larger under S-10, the same run is seven 10 AWG at 0.0211 — 0.1477 sq in, over 0.122 — and the raceway goes to 3/4 in EMT at 0.213. Say the steps out loud on a mixed pull before you order material. Most failed fills come from a skipped step — a ground left out of the list, an EMT row used for a PVC run, or the 40 percent column used for a two-conductor pull that only gets 31 percent. S-01 and S-10 apply only when an example uses Sharma's sizing: commercial branch circuits are 20A minimum on 12 AWG copper, and CCA, when the lead picks it, goes one AWG size larger. That is Sharma practice, not a Chapter 9 requirement — the fill method is identical either way, you just take the larger conductor's Table 5 area. The trap is the two-conductor percentage. Three or more conductors get 40 percent, so 40 feels like the default — but two conductors get only 31 percent, the lowest number in Table 1. The second trap on this page: leaving the equipment ground off the list because 'it carries no current.' Fill does not care what a conductor carries. If it is in the raceway, its area is in the total. Equipment ground left off the fill list; the pull jams mid-run and insulation comes back scraped. EMT row of Table 4 used for a PVC run — same trade size name, smaller inside area. 40 percent column used for a two-conductor pull that Table 1 limits to 31 percent. Conductor total a hair over the Table 4 allowance and the crew pulled it anyway — close does not count. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Same-size fill — divide, then round down
x: When every conductor is the same size and type, the count is one division: the raceway's usable area divided by one conductor's area. • Worked example: how many 12 AWG THHN fit in 1/2 in EMT? The 40 percent area is 0.122 sq in and one 12 AWG THHN is 0.0133 sq in, so 0.122 / 0.0133 = 9.17 — the answer is 9, because a tenth of a conductor does not exist. • One exception, from the Chapter 9 notes: when all conductors are the same size and the division leaves a decimal of 0.8 or more, the count may be rounded up to the next whole conductor — 8 AWG THHN in 3/4 in EMT is 0.213 / 0.0366 = 5.82, so 6 are permitted by that note. The round-down rule is the raceway's safety margin doing its quiet work: 9.17 is a paper number, and the 0.17 that 'almost fits' is exactly the conductor that would have been skinned on the pull or cooked in the bundle. The 0.8 exception is narrow on purpose — it trusts the geometry only when every conductor is identical, so the packing the table assumed is the packing you actually get. Default to rounding down. Use the 0.8 round-up only when every conductor in the raceway is truly the same size and type, and be ready to show the inspector the division. Mixed sizes never get the round-up — add their areas instead. Two traps share this page. First: rounding 9.17 up to 10 because 'it is close' — the round-up exists only at a decimal of 0.8 or more. Second: using the 0.8 round-up on a mixed-size pull. Mixed sizes never divide and never round up; their areas are added, conductor by conductor. 9.17 rounded up to 10 conductors — the round-up starts at a 0.8 decimal, not at 'close enough.' The 0.8 round-up used on a mixed-size pull figured by division instead of by adding areas. Ground left out of the same-size count, so the division was run for one conductor too few. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Mixed-size fill — add the areas
x: Mixed sizes cannot be divided; each conductor contributes its own Table 5 area and the total is compared with the Table 4 area for the raceway, at the Table 1 percentage for the count. • Worked example one: two 6 AWG THHN plus one 10 AWG THHN total 2 x 0.0507 + 0.0211 = 0.1225 sq in — just over the 0.122 sq in that 1/2 in EMT allows at 40 percent, so the run goes to 3/4 in EMT at 0.213. • Worked example two: three 1/0 THHN plus a 6 AWG THHN ground total 3 x 0.1855 + 0.0507 = 0.6072 sq in; 1-1/4 in EMT allows 0.598 and is too small, so 1-1/2 in EMT at 0.814 is the answer. There is no rounding a mixed total down to fit. Over is over, even by 0.0005 sq in. A mixed pull is where the same-size shortcuts break. One large conductor eats area that a division method assumes is shared evenly, and a total that lands a hair over the limit does not pull like one that lands a hair under — it jams at the bend and skins insulation. Adding the areas one conductor at a time is slower, and it is the only arithmetic that matches what is physically in the pipe. Write each conductor's area on the takeoff, not just the sum. When a run fails by a hair — like the 0.1225 example, over by five ten-thousandths — the written list is how you prove the next trade size was required and not a guess. It is also how the next electrician, adding a circuit to that raceway next year, knows exactly how much room is left: in the 3/4 in EMT from example one, 0.213 - 0.1225 = 0.0905 sq in of the 40 percent allowance is still open. The trap answer rounds: '0.1225 is basically 0.122 — it fits.' Fill has no 'basically.' The only round-up in Chapter 9 belongs to same-size division that leaves a remainder of 0.8 or more, and it never applies to a mixed-size total. 0.1225 sq in of conductor in a 0.122 sq in allowance is an overfilled raceway. Mixed-size pull figured by dividing the raceway area by the largest conductor's area — the smaller conductors' real areas never entered the calculation. Conductor total rounded down to the raceway allowance on the fill schedule — 0.1225 shown as 0.122. Ground left off the mixed list; the total passes without it and fails with it. Annex C count used for a mixed-size pull. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Grounds count, and bare conductors use Table 8
r: Tables 5 and 8, grounds and bare conductors
x: An equipment grounding conductor takes up room in the raceway like any other conductor, so it counts in fill — a note to Table 1 says so directly, and says to use the conductor's actual dimensions. • Insulated ground: take its area from Table 5, in the column for its insulation type. A 12 AWG THHN ground is 0.0133 sq in, the same as any 12 AWG THHN. • Bare ground: there is no insulation to measure, so Table 5 has no row for it. Take its diameter from Table 8 and use the area of that circle — a bare 12 AWG is 0.081 in across, about 0.0051 sq in. • One ground, counted once: a shared equipment ground serving several circuits in one raceway still gets its one line on the list. Leaving the ground out is the most common reason a fill calculation passes on paper and jams in the field. Fill is physical, not electrical. The ground carries no load current, but the pull does not care — every conductor in the pipe adds friction on the bends and one more chance to skin insulation. A calculation that leaves the ground out approves a raceway the wire cannot actually get through, and the crew finds out halfway through the pull, with the insulation paying for it. On every fill list, write the ground as its own line with its own area before you add. A Florida home run in 1/2 in EMT: three 12 AWG THHN circuit conductors at 0.0133 sq in each total 0.0399 sq in. With an insulated 12 AWG THHN ground the list totals 0.0532 sq in; with a bare 12 AWG ground it totals 0.0450 sq in. Both fit the 0.122 sq in that 1/2 in EMT allows at 40 percent — but on a tight pull the ground's line is the difference between passing and going up a trade size. Say on the list whether the ground is bare or insulated, and take its area from the right table. The trap answer: 'The ground does not count — it carries no current.' That mixes up two different checks. Current-carrying status matters for the ampacity adjustment in 310.15(C)(1); fill is about space, and the ground takes space. Count it, at its real area: Table 5 if it is insulated, Table 8 if it is bare. Fill calculation on the permit set omits the equipment grounding conductor — the raceway is over its Table 1 percentage once the ground is counted. Bare ground figured at the insulated Table 5 area, or an insulated ground figured as bare — wrong table for the conductor as installed. Pull jammed mid-run and insulation damaged on a raceway that only passed because the ground was left off the list. Fill schedule shows no ground line at all for a raceway that contains one. No NEC 2023 change found for this page in the public 2023 change sources reviewed. FBC 9th Ed. adopts NEC 2023 for permits applied for on or after Dec 31, 2026; permits applied for through Dec 30, 2026 stay on the NEC 2020 rule above.

t: Annex B — ampacity calculation under engineering supervision
x: Informative Annex B is the Code's application information for calculating conductor ampacity under engineering supervision — the formula route that accounts for load diversity, conductor arrangement, duct banks and ambient conditions instead of reading a single table cell. Its own tables give ampacities for specific free-air and underground electrical duct arrangements that Table 310.16 does not cover. Two limits define it: • It is informative, not mandatory. No annex number is a requirement an inspector can cite the way a Chapter 3 section can be cited. • It is engineering work. The calculation has to be performed and documented for the actual installation by a qualified person — never estimated in the field. Field sizing stays on the adopted tables: Table 310.16, with the correction and adjustment factors of 310.15. An Annex B number belongs to the design that produced it, with that design's duct spacing, soil conditions and loading assumptions attached. Table 310.16 is built on standard assumptions about conductor count, ambient and arrangement. A real duct bank or an unusual grouping does not always match those assumptions, and one table cell cannot know your soil or your spacing. The formula route exists so an engineer can model the installation that is actually being built. The supervision requirement is the guardrail: an ampacity nobody calculated is just a smaller conductor with a story attached, and an undersized conductor runs hot for the life of the building.
